Pliny, in the same: the flesh of the starfish, applied, is effective against the strikes of the sea-dragon.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the starfish is a fish in the western sea, whose shape is like a star: this one, when it has eaten some creature, is soon found in its belly hard, like twice-baked bread. The sturgeon is a large fish dwelling in river waters that are great and broad. It cannot live long in ponds unless it has passage to the fresh waters of rivers. It takes in little or no food into its body. Indeed, sufficient nourishment for it is the very calm of clear air. Wherefore it also has a small belly, and is almost solid where the belly would be, as in the rest of its body. It has intestines, though small in proportion to its size. Its liver, however, is quite large and so sweet that it can scarcely be eaten without the stomach's disgust. Whence its gall, which is adjacent to the liver, is customarily rubbed on it, so that the excess of sweetness in the liver may be tempered by the excess of bitterness in the gall. It lacks a mouth, and that part is whole, which in other animals usually occupies the mouth, and it has only a small opening beneath its throat, closed, which it opens when it wishes, to the calm of the air. It fattens more quickly with the south wind, but when the north wind blows, it sinks into the depths. The same, placed in milk for a long time, lives as it does in water.

div.head: DE TEUCHA ET TITHIMALLO ET TORPEDINE

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'teucha' is a river or pond fish, known to all: nourished in mud, like the eel, whence it is also of its color, namely muddy or black. Both fish are of sweet taste, but of poor digestion.

Isidore: the 'tithymalus' [spurge-fish] took its name from a flower. For 'thymum' is the name of a flower. For although it is of pleasant appearance and agreeable taste, yet, like a flower, it has a fragrance and breathes odors from its body. The torpedo [electric ray] is so named because it makes the body grow numb [torpescere], if anyone touches it while it is alive. Pliny relates that the torpedo of the Indian sea, even touched from a distance by a spear or a rod, numbs even the strongest arms, and even the swiftest feet for running are made to stiffen. For its power is so great that it affects the limbs even by the mere current from its body.

Pliny: the torpedo, like the angel-shark, is of the kind of fish that have cartilage instead of a spine. All such are fleshy and feed lying on their backs. They report that the torpedo hides in a hollowed-out shallow of the sea through the winter, and gives birth around the equinox. It has eighty young; it bears very soft eggs within itself, transferring them to another place of the womb and hatching them there. In the same way, too, all that we call cartilaginous, like the skate, the stingray, the angel-shark, and the like. So it happens that alone among fish they both bear living young and conceive eggs. The torpedo knows its own power, and, itself not numbed, hides submerged in mud. It seizes fish that, swimming carelessly, have gone numb: no tenderness is preferred to its liver.

Pliny, in the same: the torpedo, taken as food, softens the bowels, and, applied, heals the spleen; applied, it also prevents prolapse of the intestine. Finally, if a torpedo is caught while the sun is in Libra and kept for three days in the open air, it makes childbirth easy. Afterward, as often as it is applied, the genitals are stimulated by smearing on the gall of a living torpedo. Likewise the brain of this creature, smeared on when the moon is six days from the light, heals the female genital organs.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'trebius' [remora] is a black fish, only a foot long, yet five fingers thick. Pliny records that it has this power, that a part of it, kept in salt, when applied draws out gold that has fallen into the deepest wells and makes it float: this fish changes to a white color in winter and turns black in summer. Alone among all fish it nests from seaweed and lays its eggs in the nest. The 'trebius' is in the ocean, and pierces ships with its hard beak.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the trout is indeed varied on the outside, like the perch, but red inside. This fish, as is reported, as long as it is of lesser age and body, is nourished only in fresh waters and is called the trout. But when it has grown and, descending as far as the borders of the sea, has drunk of its saltiness, it becomes a salmon - which, however, is by no means asserted to be true by everyone. Both fish, however, are delicious and tasty.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the trout is a fish dwelling in fresh rivers that run down from the mountains with great force. It has scales like the salmon and very similar flesh, but much more suited for eating, and this only in summer, from the month of July until November; in winter, however, it has white flesh like other fish and of lesser flavor. It has saffron and blood-red spots on its back.

div.head: DE VENTH ET VIPERA ET UMBRA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'venth' is a fish commonly so called; in Latin, however, 'aristosus' [bony], since its flesh is armed with countless fish-bones, so that it can be eaten only with difficulty and not without distaste: whence it is food for the poor, as the cheapest of all edible fish. It dwells frequently in fresh waters, yet in those made brackish by the flow of the sea. It is caught thus: nets are stretched lengthwise or crosswise across the water, and before the nets, above the water, an instrument like a bow, so that it floats on the waves; on its upper part, moreover, a small bell is hung, whose sound the fish, hearing, come to in a shoal, foolishly following the tinkling of the bell. And by this evidence it is clear that they have the sense of hearing: falling, then, into the nets, they are caught in great numbers. The sea-viper is a small fish, a little more than a cubit long. On its head, above its eyes, it bears one small, sharp, and deadly horn. For with this, whatever it wounds it infects with venom: fishermen, being wary of this, cut off the fish's head once caught; but the rest of its body serves for human use.
Isidore: the 'umbra' [shade-fish] is named from its heat [an apparent scribal confusion for 'color'], since it has the color of shadow.

div.head: DE URANOSCOPO ET URTICA ET VULPE

cit.quote: Pliny, book 32: the 'uranoscopus' [sky-gazer] is named from the eye it has on its head, from which it gazes both below and above. It is called by another name, the 'gallio.' Its bile heals scars and consumes excess flesh of the eyes, as Menander says in his comedies.

Pliny, book 9, in the same: the sea anemone [urtica] wanders by night and changes by night. It has a fleshy front, and feeds on flesh. Its power is a biting itch, the same as the land nettle's. It contracts itself, then, stiffening as much as possible, and, as a small fish swims past, spreads its front, embracing what it means to devour. At other times it is like something withering, and, letting itself be tossed by the wave like seaweed, seizes fish that have contracted, and, by rubbing against the rock, invades their sense of itching. And at night it likewise searches for scallops and sea urchins. But when it senses a hand approaching it, it changes color and contracts. Touched, it produces a burning sting; and if there is even a little space, it hides itself. Its roots are said to serve as its mouth, and its excrement is expelled through a thin passage above. I judge, then, that sense is present in these creatures, which have neither the nature of animals nor of shrubs, but a third nature made of both - I mean the sea anemones and the sponges.

Aristotle: the kind of animal called 'akalabia,' believed to be the sea anemone, is a creature that stings by itself when touched. They do not have a shell, but their care is like that of flesh. And this kind has sense and seizes whatever comes near with its hands, and attaches itself to stones with its feet, like the many-footed animal. And its body perhaps swells when it attaches itself to something. It has, moreover, an opening in the middle of its body and hunts whatever small fish pass through it, and eats wheat-grains and the scallop, that is the 'plais.' Nor is any surplus found in its body at all, and in this it resembles trees.
Pliny: sea foxes, in danger of being caught, swallow not only the hook, but also, further, up to the weak part of the line, which they easily gnaw through.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: these things have been said of fish that have the pure nature and appearance of a fish.

Pliny, in the same place: but in the sea, so broadly open, soft, and fertile in growth, nature, taking causes of generation from on high and always giving birth, produces many monstrous things, tangled and coiled in themselves now one way, now another, now by a gust, now by a wave, into seeds and beginnings, so that the common belief becomes true, that whatever is born in any part of nature is found in the sea, besides many things found nowhere else. Not only likenesses of animals but of things, as one may understand by observing: a grape, a sword, saws. So that we should be less amazed that the heads of horses project from such small shells. There are, moreover, very many and very great animals in the Indian sea, among which whales of four acres, sawfish of two hundred cubits. Indeed lobsters there reach four cubits. Eels too in the river Ganges reach thirty feet. The people called the Cedrosii dwell along the river Arabis; the prefect of Alexander the Great's fleets reported that in their houses they make doorways from the jawbones of sea beasts, and roof their dwellings with bones, among which many of forty cubits' length were found. Beasts resembling cattle also come out onto land there, and, having fed on the roots of shrubs, return. The largest animal in the Indian sea, however, is the sawfish and the whale. The belief in Nereids is not false, their bodies bristling with scales in the manner of a woman, even where they have a human form. For one of these was observed on the shore, whose sad wailing, as it died, the inhabitants heard even from far off. And a legate of Gaul wrote to the deified Augustus that several dead Nereids appeared on the shore. I have authorities of distinguished equestrian rank that a sea-man was seen by them in the ocean off Cadiz, climbing aboard ships at night, entirely resembling a man in his whole body, and that immediately the parts he sat on grew heavy, and, if he remained longer, even sank. Under the emperor Tiberius, the ebbing ocean left more than three hundred beasts of wonderful variety and size stranded on the shore facing the islands of the province of Lyonnaise; and no fewer on the shore of the Santones. Among the rest were sea elephants and rams distinguished only by their white, horn-like protrusions, and many Nereids. Tauranius reported that on the shores of Cadiz a beast was washed up, whose tail, between its two fins at the end, measured sixteen cubits. Its teeth were one hundred twenty, the largest three-quarters of a foot, the smallest half a foot. The bones of the beast to which Andromeda was said to have been exposed were brought to Rome from the town of Joppa in Judea and shown, among his other marvels, by Marcus Scaurus during his aedileship: sixty feet long, with a rib-height exceeding that of Indian elephants, and a spine a foot and a half thick.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: [a] sea creature, and every kind of fish that walks, consequently breathes.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'ahune' is a sea monster, more gluttonous than all sea beasts: it lives by prey, and whatever it eats turns into the bulk of its body: whence, since it lacks a stomach, its belly, when it eats much, is stretched and swollen beyond measure, and when it can be stretched no further, it ejects fish through its mouth, and this easily, since, lacking a neck as other fish do, its mouth is adjacent to its belly. This animal, moreover, is so bulky that when it fears danger, it draws in its skin and flesh and folds the extremities of its body within itself, like a hedgehog, hiding them so that they do not appear. Yet it does not always do this without harm to itself. For it fears death so much that, when it senses danger and cannot free itself or escape the beast lying in wait for it, it in no way draws its head outside, which it hides within its own body, but, when afflicted by hunger, devours its own flesh, choosing rather to be partly consumed than to become prey and be wholly consumed by beasts.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'barchora' is a sea creature, having the strongest mouth-opening of all creatures. For if it takes a stone into its mouth, it breaks it: this creature sometimes comes out to the shores and grazes on grasses, and, when it must, returns to the water and submerges itself there, lest the skin of its back be dried out by the sun, and it be unable to bend itself as needed. It also eats small fish, and by these it is caught. For fishermen throw small live fish, sewn on a line, into the sea, which, unable to escape but floating together, lie open to the bites of the aforesaid creature. But the creature itself, while it labors to swallow one after another, is meanwhile caught, occupied.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'caab' is a sea creature having feet small in proportion to its body, which is indeed large. Its feet, moreover, are like those of a cow; one of these is long, cartilaginous, lacking bone, which it uses in place of a hand for everything. For with it it digs out what it wants, and takes food through it and brings it to its mouth. And when it swims in water, it breathes in it. But by breathing it draws water into its body through its breath, and when it is filled with this, returning to the air, it expels it, and thus breathes. The sea-dog is a sea beast, terrible and hostile to every living thing that its blows strike; it has very strong gills, shaped like nails. These hunt shoals of fish through the sea, in the manner of dogs hunting wild beasts on land, except that they cannot bark, but have a horrible blast of breath in place of barking. Pursuing, then, the shoals of fish, they drive them into narrow places, and thus rage cruelly upon those thus confined. Fishermen, however, marking the places where the fish, hiding, lay hid from flight, catch them enclosed with nets. These beasts, however, can with difficulty be finished off, and only with many tridents.
Isidore: the sea-dog is so named from its resemblance in habits to the land dog, namely because it bites.

Avicenna: they said the gall of the sea-dog is a poison, of which, if anyone eats even the quantity of a lentil, it kills after a week. But its treatment is that cooked cow butter be drunk with Roman gentian and cinnamon, and again hare's rennet.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'celethi,' according to Aristotle, is a sea creature that, contrary to the habit of others, generates eggs in its own womb. These, warmed there for the due time, produce worms from them. And once they have given birth to these, with incredible speed they become perfect animals, similar to their parents. It has a large heart, and yet is very timid. It sleeps deeply, so that it can be caught by hand.

Aristotle: the 'celethi' is among the flesh-eating animals. The 'celethi,' moreover, has eggs, one complete inside, which it also bears outside. The rest of the fish, however, lay incomplete eggs outside, except the sea frog. These eggs, after their smallness, grow quickly, like worms, which are generated from a very small animal, then grow by themselves. The 'celethi' does not have fins, but has something like roots growing in the earth. It breeds often, namely every six months. It comes out from the depth of the sea and breeds near land, which it does for the sake of color and to remove fear from its young.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'ceruleum' is a monster in the river Ganges, having, like a crab, arms seven cubits in length, with which it seizes an elephant and drags it under the waves.

Pliny, book 9: in the Ganges of India, Statius Sabinus reports, not without considerable wonder, blue-black worms with two gills each, sixty cubits long, which took their name from their appearance, and that these have such strength that they seize elephants coming to drink by the trunk, gripping with their bite, and drag them into the depths.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'chilon,' unlike all other kinds, does not feed itself, but is fed and nourished only on the viscous moisture that comes out from it. Whence it happens that this creature is always hungry yet strong in body. For we see too that in women fasting can be endured for many more days than in men, because of the moist and viscous surpluses that abound more in them, that is in women. The 'chricho' has a shelled skin, smooth, black, and reddish in some parts: it has two clefts in its foot, which make three toes; its right foot is small, its left large. And so, when it walks, it carries its whole body on its left. In clear air it moves about freely; but disturbed by winds, it attaches itself to stones and rests motionless: whatever thing it clings to, it clings with a strong grip. And this is remarkable, that in clear weather it has its full power, but in stormy weather is weakened and made feeble.

Isidore: the crocodile is so named from its saffron [croceus] color. It is born in the Nile and is a four-footed creature, powerful on land and in water: generally twenty cubits in length: armed with the enormity of its teeth and claws, and of such hardness of skin that, although struck on the back even by the blows of strong stones, it does not feel it. By night it rests in the water, by day on land. It warms its eggs on land. Male and female keep watch in turns. Certain fish, having a serrated crest, kill it by cutting the tender parts of its belly. Alone among animals it is said to move its upper jaw.

Avicenna: the crocodile's bite, however, is treated like the bite of a rabid dog, with the drawing out of the venom, of which the bite itself is not free, although the crocodile itself is safe from venom or rabies.
Pliny, in the same: against the bite of a crocodile, dregs of vinegar with black cumin are effective.
Pliny, in the same: the herb pondweed [potamogeton] is opposed to crocodiles: and so those who hunt them carry it with them.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: those who hunt crocodiles, having the fat and gall of the water-dove, are said to be marvelously helped by it. And against the bites of crocodiles, it is beneficial to eat salted fish that have been kept in store.

Solinus: the crocodile, an evil four-footed creature, has no tongue: it moves its upper jaw. Its bite closes with horrible tenacity, the row of teeth pressing together like a comb. It lays eggs like a goose. It marks out the place for its nest with natural foresight. Nor does it lay its brood anywhere except where the rising waters of the Nile cannot reach. In warming its young, male and female take turns. The ichneumon and dolphins are hostile to it. On an island of the Nile dwell men of very small stature, but such boldness that they offer themselves in the crocodiles' path. For these monsters pursue those who flee, but fear those who resist. They are caught, then, and, subdued by fear, carry their victors mounted upon their backs. This island and this people, wherever they are perceived by the judgment of smell, the crocodiles flee far off. In water they see rather dimly, on land most sharply. In winter they take no food at all.

Physiologus: the crocodile, if ever it finds a man and can overcome him, eats him, and afterward weeps over him. Alone among animals it moves the upper parts of its mouth, while the lower remains motionless. From its dung a certain ointment is made, with which old and wrinkled women anoint their faces and become beautiful, until flowing sweat washes their face.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the crocodile lacks a tongue: it has a wide-open mouth and a gape reaching to its ears. By day it rests on land, so motionless that, unless you knew its habit beforehand, you would believe it dead. With eyes closed it pretends to sleep, and invites birds with its gaping mouth for the sake of food, killing and swallowing those that come down to feed on it. Some have believed that this animal, like the bear, always keeps growing. It dwells along the banks of the Nile; on an island there is a certain small but spirited race of men, hostile to these beasts: for they alone dare to swim the river in which crocodiles dwell, and leap onto their backs and ride them. So, as the beasts gape, the riders, their heads thrown back, hold a club in their right and left hand in the gaping mouth as if reining them, and drive their captives onto land, and, terrified by voice alone, force them to vomit up the bodies they have recently consumed. This creature, its heart torn out, lives on for a while afterward, which is indeed contrary to the nature of all animals, which have their life from the heart: the Saracens eat its flesh.

Aristotle: the crocodile dwells in water, yet does not take water into itself, but air, and gives birth outside. It has blood and two larger feet and a tail. And all such creatures are of cloven foot and many toes, and share the instrument of sense in the tongue, except the crocodile, whose tongue is like that of certain fish. This animal, too, does not have ears, but only openings, which are the passages of hearing. Nor do they have teats or testicles or a visible member outside, but inside, nor does it have hair, but over its whole body it has a scaly hide. It has large, sharp, and well-spaced teeth; it also has eyes similar to those of pigs, and has eyelids. In water it sees weakly, since water is thicker than air. But its sight outside the water is very sharp. Its dwelling is more by day on land and by night in water, since water is warmer by night than the air outside. It has a single belly, like other egg-laying four-footed creatures, such as the 'hardon' and the small lizard. The plover-bird enters its open mouth and cleans its teeth and feeds on their filth. The crocodile, sensing the benefit in this, does it no harm, but when it wants to remove it, moves its neck, and does not eat it. Alone among blood-having animals it lacks a tongue. For since it is a land animal, it has the place for a tongue, yet, since it is a water creature, it lacks a tongue. Its scales are like the nature of bone and stronger than many bones. It moves only its upper jaw for this reason, that its feet, being very small, are not suited to seizing and holding. And so nature provided it, in place of feet, with a mouth-opening suited to two functions. Likewise, because of its need for a lung, it has a neck and takes breath in through a windpipe.

Pliny, book 8: the crocodile generally exceeds eighteen cubits in size. It is armed with claws, and its hide is unconquerable against all blows. It lays eggs, and, moving them outside that place, always broods over them by a kind of divination, as to how high the Nile will rise that year, and to what point it will reach. Nor does any other animal grow from a smaller origin to a greater size. On its belly, indeed, it has soft and thin skin, and so dolphins, which for this very use have a knife-like fin on their back, cut open its belly. And thus they drive off this predator, which reigns as if alone in its own river, and, though unequal in strength, kill it by such cunning. A small bird, called there the plover, king of birds in Italy, invites the crocodile, sated with fish and always with its mouth full of food, given to sleep on the shore, to open wide for the sake of its own feeding; soon its teeth and the throat within gape open for the sweetness of this scratching. In which pleasure, while it lies weighed down with sleep, the ichneumon, observing it, gnaws through its belly by way of that same throat, as if another dart had been shot in.

Pliny: of the kind of crocodiles, whose life is shared between water and land, teeth from the right jaw, bound to the right arm, are said to stimulate mating. The canine tooth, too, wards off fevers. Little stones, too, taken from its belly, are reported to be powerful against the onset of feverish chills, and for this reason the Egyptians anoint their sick with its fat. The other kind, much smaller and very similar to it, lives only on land, and lives on the most fragrant flowers. Because of this they carefully seek out its intestines, filled with a pleasant fragrance, which they call 'crocodilea,' and this, mixed with leek juice and smeared on, is most useful for eye ailments and against cataracts or dimness. Smeared on with water, too, it removes freckles and all blemishes from the face. And drunk with honeyed vinegar, two obols' worth, it is effective against epileptic diseases. Applied, it also brings on menstruation. The best kind is friable, very white and light, fermenting when rubbed between the fingers. Otherwise, the eyes are anointed with its gall mixed with honey, against cataracts. It is reported that fumigating with its intestines and the rest of its body is beneficial for women suffering from womb trouble, and that they should be wrapped in fleeces infected with its vapor. The ash of the hide of either kind, smeared on with vinegar, removes all sensation from those parts that must be cut, or the smell of the burning does; the smoke of the burnt scalpel does the same. The blood of either kind gives clarity of vision, and, smeared on, corrects scars of the eyes. The body itself, head and feet removed, boiled, is eaten by sciatica sufferers. And it heals a longstanding cough, especially in children. Likewise pains of the loins. They have a fat by which, when touched, hair falls out; this protects those anointed with it from crocodiles. Its heart is effective against quartan fevers.
Dioscorides: the juice of the land crocodile, gathered and applied, makes the complexion pleasing and snow-white, especially if it is white and smooth and, put into water, quickly dissolves.
Avicenna, in the second book: crocodile dung is effective for white spots of the eye.

Isidore: dolphins have a definite name, since they follow the voices of men. Or because they gather in shoals at music: nothing in the sea is swifter than these. For often, leaping, they fly over ships. But when they play beforehand in the waves and cast themselves headlong upon the masses of the waves, they seem to signal coming storms. These are properly called 'simones' [snub-nosed].

Pliny: the swiftest of all animals, not only sea creatures, is the dolphin, faster than a bird, swifter than a dart, and unless its mouth were set well below its snout, almost on its belly, no fish could escape its speed. But nature's foresight brings delay, since they cannot seize prey except turned on their backs and reversed - a fact that especially betrays their speed. For when, driven by hunger, they have pursued a fleeing fish into the depths and held their breath too long, they shoot up like an arrow released from a bow to breathe. And they leap out with such force that they often fly clear over the sails of ships or before the wind. They hide for thirty days around the rising of the Dog Star and are concealed in an unknown manner. This is all the more remarkable, since they cannot breathe underwater. They are accustomed to break out onto land for an uncertain reason, and do not die at once upon touching earth, but much more quickly once their blowhole is blocked. Their tongue, contrary to the nature of aquatic creatures, is mobile, short, and broad, not unlike a pig's. In place of a voice they have a groan similar to a human one; their back is curved, their snout blunt, for which reason everyone recognizes the name 'simo' [snub-nosed]. They have no gills, just as whales do not, as said above.

Pliny, in the same: those that have cartilage instead of a spine are more fleshy and feed lying on their backs, like the dolphin. And this kind alone, like the cetaceans, bears living young, except the frog, for the rest lay eggs.

Aristotle: the dolphin has no gall, and lives one hundred twenty years or more. This is proven when one is caught and, its tail cut off, released. And thus, after much time, it is found again; it is pregnant for ten months and grows for ten years. Likewise the dolphin breathes, which other fish do not do, yet not underwater, but at the water's surface. Likewise it is swifter and lighter than all animals. It has no spine, but bones. Nor does it have a member projecting outside, as man and horse do, but inside. And although it has hearing, yet no instrument of hearing is entirely visible; it has teats, not above, but near the joints. Nor visible nipples, but two depressions resembling channels, with which it suckles its young. It gives birth only in summer, and swims beneath the deep with its young following it for a long time. It takes in water through a windpipe, like sea creatures, and air through a lung, like land creatures. It does not have a spine but bones for this reason, that it bears living young. Some, however, have the mouth-opening opposite, some in front, and some on the back or belly, like the dolphin and the whole kind of animal called the 'celethi'; these do not take food except when they turn over on their backs. And nature did this not for their safety, but so that they would be slowed in taking food, since this kind of animal eats much. And it has a thin, round appendage, and is not good at cutting, since it dies quickly from excessive fullness. Its testicles, and those of all great-bodied sea creatures, are inside the body, since the nature of their hide is not suited, because of its hardness, to cover them, if they were outside.

Physiologus: dolphins have their eyes on their back and their mouth on the opposite side, whence they do not catch their prey well because of the twisting of the mouth away from the eyes. Hence it is that they turn their mouths toward the sky and their back and eyes toward the ground, so as to catch their prey. When a storm is imminent, they play, appearing on the surface of the waves. They are also taught to have offered aid to shipwrecked sailors. They are also reported to weep when caught.
Pliny, book 10: dolphins sleep, so much so that they are even heard snoring.
Pliny, in the same: the dolphin has no ears, yet it is clear it hears, for it is even charmed by singing.
Pliny, book 18, in the same: dolphins foretell from which direction the wind will come, by frolicking in the sea and again by splashing water, and likewise by disturbing calm water.
Pliny: dolphins, on whose backs there is, as if for this very purpose, a knife-like fin, kill crocodiles, though unequal in strength, by cunning.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: in place of a voice they have a groan similar to a human one, and this because they have a lung and a windpipe, and their tongue is not free, nor do their lips protrude or project to shape the voice. They have no ears, but an opening in place of ears. Their sense of smell, however, has no visible trace at all, and yet they smell most keenly. They sleep on the water's surface, so that they can be heard snoring. They live up to one hundred forty years. They are charmed by music, whence it is told that when sailors at sea were preparing to kill the lyre-player Arion, he obtained from them that he might first play the lyre. At the sound of his playing, shoals of dolphins gathered, and when he threw himself into the sea, he was caught by one and carried to shore. The dolphin alone, as Aristotle says, lacks gall among fish.

Solinus: dolphins, often leaping, fly over the sails of ships, and, wherever they go, their mates roam with them. They bring forth young. The tenth month brings the birth to maturity. Contrary to the nature of aquatic creatures, they alone move their tongues. Their back fins are spined. When they are subject to anger, they bristle; when their spirit has calmed, they are covered by certain sheaths. They are said not to breathe in the water, and to draw the breath of life only in the air above. They have a definite name, and, hearing it, come when called, for they are properly named 'simones'; they catch the voices of men more quickly when the north wind blows. When, on the contrary, the south wind blows, their hearing is obstructed. They are charmed by music: they delight in the songs of flutes, and wherever there is a concert, they come in shoals. There is, moreover, a kind of dolphin in the Nile, whose backs have serrated crests. These deliberately lure crocodiles to swim, and, submerging, with fraudulent cunning, swim beneath their bellies and cut the tender parts and kill them.

div.head: DE AMORE DELPHINORUM AD PROLEM ET AD INVICEM

cit.quote: Aristotle: the dolphin loves its young greatly, and so feeds them for a long time. Alone among fish it produces a complete animal and has teats and suckles its young.

Pliny: dolphins mate in spring, and give birth in the tenth month, only in the summer season; they sometimes nurse two young at their teats. And they even carry their offspring, weak in infancy, and accompany even the grown ones for a long time, with great love toward their offspring. They mature quickly, and are believed to reach their full size in ten years; they also live to thirty years, a fact known by an experiment on the tail.
Solinus: dolphins nourish their young at their teats: they take the tender ones into their throat, and accompany the weak ones for some time.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: dolphins give birth only in the summer season, never in winter. The males devour the young of the females giving birth, but the mothers hide themselves with their offspring. For they love them most tenderly and lead them behind them for a long time, and these follow their mothers underwater. But when they reach the strength of maturity, even the mothers then pursue them, unless they are strong. Their young, as Aristotle says, grow quickly and continue growing up to ten years, but, once ten months are complete, they mate and become pregnant. Young dolphins are always together like herds and have two large dolphins as guardians, so that if one of them dies, the others carry it on their shoulders and guard it, lest it be eaten by other fish, until it is cast onto the shore by a storm at sea. For they love one another in a wonderful way. Whence, on Pliny's testimony, it is told that when a dolphin was caught by the king of Caria, an immense multitude of the rest gathered at the port where the dolphin was held bound, and, as these mourned and seemed to beg for pity, the king ordered it released. A multitude of other fish follows dolphins, which fishermen, knowing this, exploit, hunting fish where the dolphins have passed. If anyone eats dolphin flesh and falls into the sea, if he is found by dolphins, he is at once devoured by them. But if he has not eaten it, they lift him on their snouts, drag him to land, and defend him from other fish.
Aristotle: finally, once a dolphin has died, the other dolphins rush together, and, surrounding it, carry it into the depths and bury it, lest it be eaten by fish.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the dolphin is called man's brother, since it resembles human habits in a certain way. Hence many examples are read in various authors.

Pliny: the dolphin is not only a friend to man, but is also charmed by the art of music, by the song of a concert, and especially by the sound of the water-organ. The dolphin does not fear man at all, as a stranger, but comes to meet ships, playfully sporting, even competing, and outstrips them even under full sail. In the Narbonensian province, in the territory of Nemausus, there is a lagoon called Latera, where men fish for mullet in partnership with dolphins: an immense number of mullet, at a fixed time, bursts out from the narrow mouth of the lagoon into the sea, watching for the ebbing of the tide, for which reason nets cannot be set out that would withstand the mass and weight in any way, even without the skill lying in wait for the right moment. By the same reasoning they head straight for the deep, which they can achieve in the nearby channel, and hasten to escape the one spot suited for spreading nets; and as soon as fishermen notice this by some sign, a crowd gathers, aware of the timing and even more eager for this pleasure. For the people from the shore shout for the 'Simo,' whose call the dolphins heed, the north wind carrying the voice further, but the south wind bringing it back more slowly against itself. And then, unexpectedly, they fly to their aid. A battle line quickly appears and is at once arranged in the place where the fight is joined; they block off from the deep and drive the frightened fish into the shallows. Then the fishermen surround them with nets and lift them with forks. Yet the speed of the mullet leaps over these nonetheless. But the dolphins catch them and, content for the present with having killed, put off eating until after the victory; the work of battle grows hot, and, enclosing in the nets those pressing hard against them, they rejoice; and lest this very thing spur the enemy's flight, they gradually slip away among the boats and nets and swimming men, so that their exit does not appear.

Solinus: under the deified emperor Augustus, in Campania, a boy first enticed a dolphin with pieces of bread, and the habit grew so strong that it even trusted itself to be fed by his hand. Soon, as the boy's boldness persisted, it carried him across the reaches of Lake Lucrinus. Whence it happened that it bore the boy, riding it, from the shore of Baiae all the way to Puteoli. This went on for very many years, until, through constant spectacle, it ceased to be a marvel. But when the boy died, before the public's eyes, the dolphin perished from grief and longing. On the African shore too, a dolphin was fed by the people of Hippo and offered itself to be handled, and often carried those placed on it; even Flavianus, proconsul of Africa, touched it and anointed it with perfumes. Stupefied by the novelty of the scent, it was cast up for a while as if lifeless, and for many months stayed away from its accustomed company. Near the city of Ialysus in Babylonia, a dolphin fell in love with a boy, and when, after their accustomed play, it followed him too impatiently as he withdrew, it was found stranded, stuck in the sand. Alexander the Great, interpreting that love as a sign of divine favor, appointed the boy to the priesthood of Neptune. Near the same city, when a more turbulent wave drowned another boy similarly riding on it through the sea, the dolphin carried it back to land and, as if confessing its own guilt, punished its own penitence with death, and never wished to return to the depths again.

Pliny: dolphin's ash, applied with water, heals lichen-sores and leprosy. Further, the treatment should follow the ulceration through to scarring. Some, however, place a dolphin in an earthen vessel until its fat flows like oil, or cook it, and anoint with this. A dolphin's liver, tasted before the onset, removes the recurrence of fevers. Dolphin fat, melted and drunk with wine, heals dropsy sufferers. Dolphin tooth-ash with honey greatly benefits the gums and teething, and likewise if the gums are touched with the tooth itself. The same, bound on, removes sudden terrors.
Isidore: the sea-dragon has spines on its gills, pointing toward its tail. When it strikes with these, wherever it strikes, it pours out venom, whence it also got its name.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the sea-dragon is a monster horrible in cruelty, extended in length like the land dragon; it lacks wings, has a twisting tail, a head small in proportion to its body's size, but a horrible gape of the mouth, scales and hard skin. It has fins, however, in place of wings, which it uses in swimming, crossing great stretches of the sea in a single thrust, and this more by the strength of its power than by the oarage of its fins. Its bite is deadly to all, even to fish. For it brings death. The ash of its bones, however, heals toothache.
Pliny: the sea-dragon, once caught and put onto sand, digs a cave for itself with its snout with marvelous speed.
Pliny: wormwood is opposed to the sea-dragon.
Pliny: starfish, applied, are effective against the strikes of the sea-dragon. Salted fish with vinegar are also applied against it.
Pliny: the sea-dragon's own venom, from the spine with which it strikes, applied, is beneficial against it.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the bite of the sea-dragon and of similar large serpents of great body is treated only insofar as it is a wound, not insofar as there is venom to be treated. The bite of the sea-dragon, as they said, is anointed with sulfur and vinegar. Crocodile fat, applied as a plaster, and lead ground and rubbed on it, benefit it.
Avicenna: the sea-dragon, as Galen says, is split open and placed on its own bite, and helps. The juice of wormwood also benefits its bite. White lead too, rubbed on, benefits its sting.

div.head: DE EQUO MARINO ET EQUONILO ET EQUO FLUMINIS

cit.quote: Isidore: sea-horses are so named because in their front part they are horses, but their hindquarters dissolve into a fish.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sea-horse is a most powerful monster; it can do nothing outside the water, as Aristotle says, but as soon as it lacks the nature of the waters, it will also lack life. It lives on the flesh of other fish. In battle it is cruel, but fears man and dreads to make war against him. The 'equonilus' [Nile-horse], as Michael says, is a huge and most ferocious monster, dwelling in the Nile. It has legs, feet, and claws like the crocodile, but much larger. It is most eager for human deaths: for when a ship comes upon it in harbor, fixing one foot on land, and seizing the front of the ship with the other, it very easily splits it apart, or sometimes tips and sinks it. Whence, in the places it inhabits, a vast number of men are lost to it, but this evil is very rarely found. It cannot be caught by any instruments except an iron net made of chains, made for this purpose by the people of Damascus. Once caught, too, it is killed only with iron mallets; its hide is said to have the thickness of one cubit, and to be of such hardness that it cannot be pierced by any javelin or armor. The river-horse [hippopotamus], as Aristotle says, is a monster in the East, of marvelous form, with a lofty face. It has a mane like a horse, cloven feet with soles like a cow's, a tail like a pig's. Its hide is very thick; its innards are like a horse's; its size, however, like a donkey's; it neighs like a horse, and is said to dwell equally on land and in water.

div.head: DE FELCO ET FOCA ET GALATA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'felcus,' also called the sea-calf [seal], has a hairy skin, marked with white and black spots. On land, in the manner of cattle, it gives birth, and never raises more than twins. It also suckles its young at the teat, and does not lead them into the sea before the twelfth day; its cry is like a low bellow. No animal is weighed down by heavier sleep: whence they say that its right fins, which it uses in the sea, have a sleep-inducing power, if placed beneath anyone's head. They are killed with difficulty, however, unless the head is crushed. Of this animal, too, this marvel is reported, that once it is dead and skinned, the hair on the hide, wherever it may be, by a certain natural instinct, behaves according to how the sea behaves. For if the sea, disturbed, rises into waves, the hair too rises up erect in the same way. But if the sea has become calm, the hair lies flat: and thus the state of the sea is detected in a senseless, dead thing.
Isidore: they say seals are sea-oxen, as it were 'boacae.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the seal is a sea-ox, an animal, that is, most powerful in its kind, spirited and irascible, not only toward other living things, but even toward its own kind. For it always fights with its mate, until it kills her. Once killed, however, it casts her from the place and brings in another, and does not cease bringing in females this way, until it happens to die a natural death, or is overcome and killed by its own mate. Nor does it easily change its place, but always remains there where nature established it; its jealous offspring live by preying on its ruin.

Dioscorides, on the seal: the rennet of the sea-seal has a power similar to castoreum. It benefits epileptics. It is also effective, drunk, for women's hysterical fits, that is, suffocations of the womb. It is tested thus, whether the rennet is from a seal: if lamb's rennet, dissolved in water, is left for one hour and does not dissolve itself, and afterward that same water is poured over seal's rennet - for if, once taken, it dissolves, it is not genuine. For genuine rennet, once water is taken, does not dissolve itself.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'galata,' contrary to the habit of all animals, when it senses its young living in its womb, draws them out. And if it finds any of them mature enough for life, it leaves them outside. But if not, it puts them back into the womb, so that they may be further warmed.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the lobster [karabos] lives on dung and mud, and is fouled by its food; because of this the creature is heavy: it has a broad tail. And so, when it fights, it turns itself lightly. For monstrous creatures of this kind fight most fiercely among themselves, like rams, and opposing sides fortify themselves with a multitude of allies: whence they have often been seen walking like herds and dividing up wars among themselves. Wars occur among animals for four reasons, namely because of natural pride, because of food, because of mating, because of offspring: just as the hen fights with the crow because of her brood, and the goose with the magpie.

Aristotle: the lobster, like the crab, has no blood; it is hard outside and soft inside, and that hardness is not nutritious - indeed it withstands fire. It takes fish, like the crab, in the depth of the sea with its two lips, and divides them into two parts and brings them to its mouth. Likewise the lobster and all that have a soft shell swim head-first. The lobster, of the hard-fleshed fish, moves with its tail in a swift motion, just as by the motion of its fins. There is, moreover, a certain kind from which the lobster is generated, which is of good flesh before it lays eggs, but of poor flesh afterward. This kind sheds its covering in spring, like a snake. Thus the crab and the lobster shed their old age, as do those of soft shell. The soft-shelled sea creature mates with the lobster and becomes pregnant, and the same happens to soft-bodied creatures. The lobster and its like in kind, that is a soft-shelled animal, lay eggs by mating. Likewise is the generation of soft-bodied creatures, like the cuttlefish and its like. And male lobsters alone guard the eggs. The soft-bodied creature, however, lays outside, and the male ejects semen over the females, as male fish do over the eggs.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the lobster, according to Aristotle, is a fish that, when it is afraid, moves backward, but when it is not afraid, moves forward naturally. The 'chylon' is a sea creature that, contrary to the common order of nature, has its liver on the left and its spleen on the right. For in all land animals, great and small, it is the opposite.

Aristotle: the 'kolki' is a sea creature having sharp teeth and even placing one over another. For thus its kind differs from the kinds of fish, since certain fish have sharp teeth, but among them there is no animal having two rows of teeth.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'kolki' is itself the 'felcus,' of which mention was made a little above, and the same as the sea-calf, of which more will be said below.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'kolki' dwells on land as in the sea: it has a cartilaginous body, like the cuttlefish. And its bones are less robust than they should be: whence it happens that, from weakness of its legs, it can sometimes scarcely walk and support itself on its feet. Its walking, then, comes more from the vigor of its spirit and the lightness of its body than from strength. It has very sharp teeth, a small tail like a stag's, kidneys like a cow's. Its belly lacks blood, since the two veins that branch over the kidneys do not reach as far as the belly in these creatures. The other members of its body, however, have blood, which never freezes: this animal has four feet, and each foot has five flexible toes; and the shape of its foot is like a fish's tail. It cannot breathe in water, but sleeps on land near the sea, and there gives birth to two or three young. Twelve days after the birth, the young follow their mother to the sea, and this many times a day, so as to grow accustomed to sea water. This animal has teats, from which the young suckle. Its voice is like a bull's, especially when it is being killed; it can, however, be killed only with difficulty, and only with mallets.

div.head: DE LEVIATHAN ET LUDOLACHRA ET LOLIGINE

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: leviathan is a serpentine fish, of which more will indeed be said below in the treatise on serpents. The 'ludolachra' is a creature marvelous in nature and form, having two wings on its face, two on its back, with which it strives with marvelous speed, wherever its will drives it. The squid is a monster in which nature seems to have played. For, scaly-skinned, it searches the depths of the sea with shoals of fish. But when it grows weary of the waters, it lifts itself up with feathered wings, which nature gave it for this purpose, and rises into the sky with the birds. But since it cannot withstand the blast of the winds, after a little while, when shaken by the winds, it is forced to return to the waters and sinks back into the depths.

Pliny: the squid is a soft, bloodless fish, like the cuttlefish, with eight small feet. It has a head, like the cuttlefish, between its belly and feet. The cuttlefish and squid have two feet among these that are the longest and roughest, with which they bring food to their mouths and steady themselves in the waves as if with anchors. The squid also flies, lifting itself out of the water. The cuttlefish indeed lays on land among reeds, and squid, kept in the deep, produce these eggs. Likewise squid, like cuttlefish, mate by joining their tongues, arranging their arms together and swimming in opposite directions, and give birth through the mouth too. Squid on the shore of Carteia are of marvelous size, but in our sea five cubits, and have neither bones nor spines.
Pliny, in the same: a flying squid is a sign of a storm.
Isidore: they report that in the ocean off Mauretania such a multitude of squid fly up out of the water that they can even sink ships.

Physiologus: the squid is sometimes caught at five cubits. It has its head between its feet and belly. Its life beyond two years is rare. A certain kind of these is very fierce, and, about to fight, steadies itself, fortifying itself in troops.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: sea-monks are so called because they have a head in the manner of a recently shaved monk, a crown shaved bare and white above, and a ring in the manner of hair over the places of the ears; its face, however, is not entirely like a man's, since it has a nose similar to a fish's and a mouth continuous with the nose. Otherwise, in its lower parts, it has the form of a fish. This monster gladly lures men walking along the sea-shores and plays before them on the water. And if it sees the wondering man draw near, it too draws near, and, if given the chance, seizes the man and hurls him into the deep, and is thus sated on his flesh. The 'monoceros' is a sea monster having on its forehead a very great horn, with which it can pierce and destroy ships in its way and destroy a multitude of men. But in this the creator's mercy has provided for mankind, since, as this creature was created slow, ships, once they see it, can flee.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: Nereids are sea beasts, bristling with shaggy hair over their whole body. And they have some form shaped like a man. When one of them, imitating the condition of mortals, must die, its groan and lament are heard from afar.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: more was said of these above, fully, in the chapter on sea monsters, and also of killer whales, in the chapter on whales.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the killer whale is a sea monster, as Pliny says, whose form cannot be expressed by any representation, except that it is a mass of immense flesh: it pursues whales with heavy hatred, breaking into the secret parts of the females with savage teeth and tearing them with its bite. But those, immobile for turning, sluggish for fighting back, burdened by their own weight and weak of fin, know only one aid, to flee into the deep sea and defend themselves throughout the whole ocean. The killer whales, on the contrary, persistent in malice, strive to meet those fleeing and to slaughter the unwary in narrow straits, drive them into shallows, dash them against rocks.

div.head: DE PERNA ET PISTRO ET PLATANISTA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'perna' is a great creature, born, in the manner of oysters, among shells of sky-blue color, and among them is clothed with a most noble fleece, tawny and deeply reddish; whence precious garments are made for the adornment and ornament of men and women, and veils too for women's heads. The 'pistrix' is in that part of the ocean facing Gaul, a beast of such height that, raising itself above the waves, it presents the likeness of a huge column, taller than the sails of ships, and, belching forth a kind of flood, terrifies those sailing by. The 'platanista' is a beast born in the river Ganges of India, having the snout of a dolphin, a tail sixteen cubits long. Companion to these are beasts called 'statios,' with two gills each. These are said to have such strength that they attack elephants coming to drink with their bites and tear away their trunks.

Aristotle: the octopus, or many-footed creature, has the benefit of the scaliness of its feet: for by this it wraps around whatever comes near it. This is the only bloodless animal that has a brain, unless it has another member suited to serve as a brain, like the many-footed animal and its like. The belly members in the cuttlefish and the octopus are similar in shape and touch. The octopus has semen in its upper part, and the discharge of semen happens to it from fear, just as it also happens to it, from fear, that it changes color. Whatever it eats, it gathers in the caverns where it dwells. And once it has eaten everything suitable for it, it then casts out the remaining shells and even the shells of crabs. Its color changes to match the color of the stones near it, which happens to it when it is afraid. Octopuses, for the most part, do not live beyond two years, since when a certain moisture flows out of them, they die naturally. And the same happens to females after giving birth, that they become stupefied and so die. The flesh of the males, however, hardens and becomes gelatinous. The octopus has four large middle feet and eight in total. It has a small body, and what nature diminished in the body, it increased in the feet: it has appendages by which it anchors and by which it moves, like a ship, and by the same it grasps whatever is at a distance from it. The member, moreover, that it has for support is narrow, because of the smallness of the body, and is not visible to sight. It is, moreover, naturally cold because of the length of its body. The octopus overcomes and eats the crayfish [carbo].
Solinus: octopuses in the sea, like chameleons on land, take on the smoothness of skin of whatever thing they approach, though by their own nature they are rough.

Pliny: there are many kinds of octopuses; the land-dwelling ones are larger than the pelagic. All use their gills as feet and hands. The tail, however, is cloven and pointed, for mating. The octopus has, moreover, a siphon on its back, by which it passes water, and this it directs now to the right, now to the left; it swims obliquely, head-first, which is very hard, being inflated by the breath of the living creature. Otherwise, through its arms, spread out like suckers, once these have drawn in, wherever they have clung, they hold themselves upside down, so that they cannot be torn away, at the depths where they have taken hold. And larger ones have less tenacity. Alone among soft-bodied creatures they go out onto dry land, but only rough ground, for they hate smoothness. They feed on the flesh of shellfish, whose shells they crush in the grip of their legs. And so their resting place is detected by the shells lying scattered before it. Octopuses hide away for two months at a time. They do not live beyond two years: they perish always from wasting, the females always more quickly, and mostly after giving birth. The octopus changes color to match its surroundings, especially in fear; it is a false belief that it gnaws its own arms. For this happens to it from congers. But they grow back for them, as tails do for lizards: they are covered with soft skin, like morays too. They have no fins, but their feet take their place. A kind of octopus called 'onigena,' named from the heavy odor of its head, is for this reason especially hunted by morays. Of bloodless fish, as said above, the first kind is that called soft-bodied, like the octopus and the squid and the cuttlefish; these have their head between their feet and on their belly, and all have eight small feet.
Pliny: [on] the octopus. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]
Pliny, in the same: the weasel, once disturbed, springs back at once from its smell.

Isidore: the octopus, that is the many-footed creature, has very many coils, and is clever; seeking a hook, it embraces it with its arms, not with a bite, and does not let go before it has gnawed all around the bait.

Ambrose: the octopus, having found a rock on a shallow shore, attaches itself to it, and, its back covered with a cloudy color like the rock's, catches, without any suspicion of trickery, most fish that, swimming, take no precaution and think it a stone, enclosing them in the nets of its stealthy craft and intercepting them in a certain fold of its own flesh. For it has many coils with which it entangles whatever falls upon the rocks of its deceit.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the octopus is a fish having such power in its arms that it sometimes seizes a sailor standing carelessly on a ship by force and drags him into the sea, and is sated on his flesh. For it gladly feeds on flesh. Lying on its back, it clings to rocks and cannot be torn away: if a foul-smelling thing is brought near it, it springs back at once from its smell. These are most frequent in the sea near Venice.
Aristotle: the octopus, as said, overcomes the lobster and eats it. Whence, if both are caught together in one net, the lobster is found dead because of its company.

Pliny: the octopus, though otherwise held a stupid animal, in that it swims up to a man's hand, is in a certain way skilled in domestic matters. For indeed it carries everything into its home. Then, its flesh consumed, it discards the shells, and hunts the small fish that swim up to them. Finally, the lobster fears the octopus so much that if it sees one nearby, it dies outright. But congers tear apart the octopus. Great is the cunning of octopuses, animals otherwise the dullest. Trebius Niger reported that octopuses are most eager for shellfish. These, once touched, close up, cutting off the octopus's arms, yet of their own accord take bait from their predator, since shellfish lack sight and every sense but that of food and danger. Octopuses, then, lie in wait for them open, having placed a small stone outside the shell so it cannot be ejected by the shellfish's throbbing, and, thus secure, grow fat and draw out the flesh. But the shellfish contract themselves, though in vain, wedged apart - so great is the octopus's cunning: besides, he denies that any animal is more savage for destroying a man in water, for it wrestles by embracing and sucks with its suckers and, by numerous suction, drags him down. It launches an attack on shipwrecked or diving men, but if it is turned over, its strength grows faint, for they stretch themselves out when turned on their backs.

Pliny, in the same: octopuses mate joined by one tentacle to the female's nostrils, with the head turned toward the ground, and give birth in winter, but lay in spring; the females sometimes brood the eggs, sometimes close the cave with a lattice-work weave of their arms. Octopuses, as said, always perish by wasting, and the females more quickly, mostly right after birth, so that they do not live beyond two years.

Aristotle: the octopus places its head on the ground and stretches its feet with the female's feet, so that the openings of their veins are joined, and thus complete their mating, and they do this in winter, but lay or give birth in spring. The male's head is longer than the female's; it nests for two months and lays only one small egg, similar to a nut's fruit, and from that egg countless fish arise without number. And once the female has laid, she sits over the eggs. And so she is of poor flesh at that time, since she is not fed nor satisfied. Yet all fish are of good flesh at the beginning of pregnancy, even the octopus. It lays its eggs, however, in some shelled or deep thing, and those eggs also hang from the top of the nest, and are as many as the vessel, larger than the female's head, can fill from those impregnated by them. They crack open after fifty days, and from them comes forth a small many-footed creature, which walks like a spider, and the shape of its members does not appear, but its whole form appears. Because of their weakness and smallness, however, such creatures quickly perish. It happens to females, as said, that after giving birth they become stupefied and do not feel the waves nor easily take hold of things with their feet. And their flesh becomes gelatinous, and they hunt nothing, and so they die. The flesh of the males, however, hardens and becomes gelatinous. And so this animal does not live two years; the proof of this is that when small octopuses are born in spring and autumn, hardly any of the large ones are found, whereas shortly before many of them were found. And it is said that when they lay eggs, they swim, and males and females are so weakened that they are eaten by small fish and are easily caught in caverns, which, however, does not happen to them before breeding. This does not happen to young and small ones; rather, they are stronger than the large ones.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: octopuses mate with heads turned to the ground, and produce eggs of such abundant fecundity that they cannot be contained even by the shell of a slain man's skull, and, sitting and brooding over them with arms as if in a lattice, they make a shelter.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the octopus, or many-footed creature, is deceived and caught by the smoke of stag's horn or dry storax, since it loves this scent, and for this reason enters hunters' vessels. With this, too, roasted and placed on a hook, hunters catch many fish. If the octopus and the lobster are caught together in a net, the lobster is found dead.

Pliny: indeed all sea creatures marvelously seek out the smell of octopuses, for which reason fishermen smear their traps with them. Lucullus relates that at Carteia, in the fish-tanks, a certain octopus was accustomed to come out into their open pools from the sea and there raid the fish and salted provisions. The guards, however, thinking that other thieves were taking the fish, made great hedges there. But the octopus climbed over by way of one large tree, and could only be detected by the keenness of dogs; at last the indignant guards, at night, surrounded the returning octopus, and, roused, were terrified by the novelty - for it was indeed unheard of before, how, with a dire odor and terrible blast of breath, and even how, whipping the dogs with its outermost tentacles and gills like clubs, it fought with them. It could scarcely, then, be finished off with many tridents. They showed Lucullus its head, capacious as a large jar, able to hold fifteen amphorae, and its beard, scarcely embraceable with both arms, knotty like clubs and thirty feet long. Its suckers, or little cups, resembled basins, and its teeth matched its size. Its remains, preserved, were said to weigh seven hundred pounds.
Pliny, in the same: they think that a pounded and applied octopus stops bleeding.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: Scylla is a monster dwelling in that sea called the Italian, which separates it from Sicily. It is hostile to sailors and to all men, and delights in their blood and flesh. It has a head and feet shaped like a maiden's, like the sirens, and a gaping mouth-opening and horrible teeth, a beastly belly, and a dolphin's tail. It is of marvelous strength, and is not easily overcome in water, but on land is nearly powerless. It also has a somewhat musical voice, and the beast itself is marvelously delighted by song.
Isidore: [the sawfish has] a serrated crest, and, swimming beneath, cuts open a ship.

Physiologus: the sawfish is a sea beast having huge fins; when it sees a ship sailing on the sea, it raises its fins and strives to sail alongside the ship. But when it has run thirty or forty stadia, sustaining the effort, it grows weak, and, lowering its fins, draws them in to itself. Then the waves of the sea carry it, now exhausted, back to its original place in the depths.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the sawfish has a serrated crest, and, swimming beneath ships unseen, cuts them open at the bottom, so that, water entering, it drowns the men by deceitful cunning and is sated on their flesh. There is also another sea beast of the same name, huge and having very broad fins, with which it strives to sail against ships.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the skink is a beast most common around the Nile, similar to a crocodile, but of much smaller and narrower form: it foresees storms, and, having blocked the caverns from the direction the wind will blow, opens its openings on the other side; this creature too has a rather hairy tail for a covering, and cups of wine tainted with its flesh kill by poison.

Avicenna: the skink is the 'guaril' of the Nile, caught in Egypt. And some have believed it is born of a crocodile. But better than this is that part of it near the kidneys; it sometimes increases mating so much that it cannot be calmed except by sipping the broth of lettuce and lentils.

Dioscorides: the skink is a creature found in India, four-footed and similar to a lizard, but longer and more full-bellied; this, salted, is used for venereal purposes if its flesh is drunk in a cup of wine, for if more is taken, it harms the sinews.

Physiologus: sirens are deadly creatures, having up to the navel the form of a human, but the remaining part, down to the feet, has the form of a bird and a fish. They sing a certain musical and sweet-sounding melody, so that they draw to themselves the hearing of men sailing far off, and, soothing their ears and senses with the excessive sweetness of the prolonged melody, turn them to sleep. Then at last, when they see them overcome by the heaviest sleep, unaware and deceived through their own folly, they attack them and tear apart their flesh.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: sirens are deadly creatures, which from the head to the navel have the form of a woman of no small size, with a horrible face, and the hair of their heads very long and filthy. They appear, moreover, with their offspring, which they carry in their arms, for they suckle their young at the breasts, which they have large on their chest. Sailors, when they see these, are greatly afraid, and throw them an empty flask, and the siren plays with the flask until the ships pass by: the rest of their body they have like an eagle, and their feet have claws suited for tearing. Further, at the end of their body they have the scaly tails of fish, with which, as with oars, they swim in the depths. They also have a certain musical and most sweet melody in their voice, by which sailors, delighted and drawn in, are dissolved into sleep, and, overcome, are torn apart by the sirens' claws. But some sailors, using wise counsel, firmly stop up their ears and thus pass by unharmed, so as not to be lured into sleep by the sirens' deadly song. These beasts, indeed, dwell on certain islands of the deep whirlpool, and sometimes in the waves. And what has been said of the flask, those who said they had seen the sirens attested. Isidore, however, described these sirens as not truly beasts, but certain prostitutes, who led those passing by to ruin. But philosophers and some of the holy commentators hold the contrary, saying that they are true sea monsters. There are also sirens that are serpents dwelling in parts of Arabia, stronger than a horse in running, some of which, having wings, can fly; the venom of these is so effective at harming, in their bite, that death follows before the pain does.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'testeus' [shelled one] is a sea monster, so called because it has a shelled skin. It is born in the Arabian sea, and sometimes falls ill, from the fact that the internal heat in its body, because of the thickness and hardness of its skin, cannot find an outlet for breathing. When it falls ill, however, it seeks fresh waters and drinks from them for some time, and by their change its skin becomes finer and sweats through narrow pores, and it recovers. Once healed, then, it returns to salt waters and returns to its original state. That there is fresh water in the sea can be proven thus: let a wax vessel be taken and closed on every side, and, empty, cast into the sea for the space of a day and a night; afterward it will be found full of fresh water. This creature is largest in the Red Sea.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: sea turtles mate in the manner of cattle, and, having come out onto land, lay up to a hundred eggs, similar to goose eggs, which some say are warmed by them only by looking at them with their eyes.

Isidore: the turtle, moreover, is so named because it is covered by the covering of its shell in the manner of a vaulted chamber. There are four kinds of these, of which one is dealt with here, the sea turtle. Another is the mud turtle, of which mention will be made below in the treatise on worms. Indeed, there too fuller mention will be made of all the kinds of turtles.
Solinus: the peoples of Thrace delight in catching sea turtles, whose size is so great that their shell makes a house, and does not too tightly hold a numerous household.

Pliny: the Indian sea sends forth turtles of such size that the shell of a single one covers a livable hut, and between the islands, especially of the Red Sea, men sail in these as boats. They are caught, moreover, in many ways, especially when, carried up to the surface of the open sea, they float along in calm weather with their whole back exposed; and the pleasure of breathing freely so deceives them, forgetful of themselves, that, their shell dried by the heat of the sun, they cannot dive, and float unwillingly, ready prey for opportunistic hunters. Turtles breathe and sleep. They report, moreover, that those that have gone out to feed at night and been greedily sated grow weary, and, once they have returned in the morning, fall asleep at the water's surface. This is betrayed by the sound of their snoring, and they are easily caught, one by one, by three men. For by two, indeed, it is turned onto its back. The third throws a noose on it, and thus it is dragged to land by several men. In the Phoenician sea they are caught without any difficulty, and come of their own accord at a fixed time of year into the river Eleutherus, in a great multitude poured forth: some think that the eggs of these too are warmed merely by looking at them with their eyes, and that the females flee mating until the male places a straw against her averted mouth. The troglodyte turtles have horned shells, like a lyre with broad, mobile horns attached, by whose oarage they help themselves in swimming. There are also land turtles in the deserts of Africa, living on dewy moisture. Turtles are covered with a shell; in mating they come from above, and their eggs mature on dry land. Turtles have no teeth, but sharp edges of the beak, the upper part closing on the lower in the manner of a box's lid. In the sea they live on shellfish, with such hardness of mouth that they crush stones. Having come out onto land, they lay in the grass, eggs similar to bird's eggs, up to a hundred in number, and these, buried outside the water and covered with earth, they brood at night, and bring forth their young over the span of a year.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: the sea turtle has no tongue and no teeth, but crushes everything with the edge of its beak, and although it has a very large lung under its protected shell, it nevertheless has it without blood. Among egg-laying creatures, the turtle alone has kidneys, and also has all the other organs. Likewise, in creatures that lay eggs, the hiss is abrupt in the turtle, but long in serpents.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the tuna is a sea monster, having a tail two cubits in breadth. It breeds only in the sea, but comes out onto land to feed. The tuna, moreover, according to Isidore, has a Greek name. This one, according to Pliny, pursues ships out of curiosity to see the sails driven by the wind, and is affected by such astonishment that even when a trident is thrown into it, it is not moved by terror: in winter it hides in whirlpools, and grows so fat that its life span is at most three years.

Pliny: [on] the multitude of tunas. We find that a tuna of exceptional size weighed fifteen talents, and that the length of its tail was two cubits and a palm. The males have no fin beneath the belly. They enter the Black Sea from the great sea in springtime, in shoals, and breed nowhere else. The offspring is called 'cordyla,' and this accompanies the mothers as they return to the sea in autumn; from the mud, or slime, they begin to be called 'palamides,' and once a year has passed, tunas have dull eyes and, terrified at the sight of a certain rock of marvelous whiteness gleaming from the shallow to the surface, head in a headlong rush against the promontory of Byzantium. At Byzantium, indeed, the catch is great. They wait, however, for the blast of the north wind, so as to go out from the Black Sea with a following current, and are caught only when entering the Black Sea at Byzantium. In winter they do not wander, wherever caught, but hibernate there until the equinox. They grow so fat, however, that they burst open. The catching of tunas runs from the rising of the Pleiades to the setting of Arcturus. For the rest of the winter season they hide in the deepest whirlpools, unless roused at some time or by the full moon. They enter on the right side of the bank, and leave on the left. This is thought to happen because they see better with the right eye, both eyes being naturally dull; their longest life is two years.
Pliny, in the same: tunas sleep near banks or rocks.

Solinus: the tuna is most abundant in the Black Sea, nor does it breed elsewhere. For nowhere do they grow faster, namely because of the fresher waters; they enter in springtime on the right side, and leave on the left.
Dioscorides: salted tuna, if eaten in quantity, eases the bites of the viper. Applied as a poultice, it heals dog bites.

Pliny: Attalus used fresh tuna fat for ulcers of the mouth. Tuna blood and gall and liver, whether fresh or preserved, serve as a depilatory. The liver, too, ground and mixed with cedar-resin, kept in a lead box. And, as a depilatory, it corrects eyelashes, unwanted hairs removed, dripped into the places where they were plucked.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the sea tortoise is a huge monster, shaped like the land tortoise, but exceeding its size immensely. For its length is eight cubits, its breadth four. It has a shield with which it is protected against darts. Like a common shield in shape, triangular, but much larger, being of five cubits. It also has large legs, large claws, and toes on its foot larger than those of lions. It is also marvelously strong and bold, in that it does not fear to attack three men. Its strength is thwarted, however, if its back is turned to the ground. For it rises with difficulty once turned onto its back, because of the breadth of the shield, by which so great a beast is enclosed from behind.
Aristotle: the tortoise, after it has eaten a viper, eats wild marjoram, lest it die.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the sea-cow is a great and powerful monster, quick to anger at injuries; it does not lay eggs, but bears living young, one usually, or two at most, and loves its young tenderly, leading it with it wherever it goes. This creature lives thirty years, which has been proven by cutting off their tails.
Isidore: the sea-calf [seal] is so named from its resemblance to the land calf.

Aristotle: the seal has a hard and fleshy body, and so is killed with difficulty, except by a wound to the jaw; its voice is like a bull's. It has four feet, but no external ears, since the governance of its life and its dwelling are in water. For if it had ears set over passages, they would take in much moisture and hinder motion and swimming in water. They generate a complete animal, and its birth occurs at any season, like man's, and especially at the time when goats give birth.

Pliny: the seal is clothed with hair. It gives birth on land, in the manner of cattle. It never has more than twins, and does not lead its young into the sea before the twelfth day, gradually accustoming them to it from then on. They are killed with difficulty, unless the head is crushed. They have a sound like lowing, whence they also get the name 'vitulus' [calf]. Yet, trained, they greet people with their voice and, called by name, respond. No animal is weighed down by heavier sleep: with the fins they use in the sea, they also crawl on land in place of feet. Their skins, too, once removed from the body, are reported to retain a sense of the sea, and always to bristle when the tide recedes.
