Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: camels have four stomachs. The first receives raw food. The second, somewhat digested. The third, more digested. The fourth, completely digested.
Ambrose: since the camel is tall, so that it may feed on the smallest plants, it has been given a neck long enough to reach the ground for the purpose of grazing.

Basil of Caesarea: the camel has a tenacious memory of wrongs; finally, if it has been struck, having long concealed its resentment, when it finds the opportune time, it at once repays the injury done to it. Hear this, then, you irascible men, to which beast you are shown to be similar.

Aristotle: camels are like horned animals, since their bellies are like those of horned creatures. And since their food is thorny, their tongue was necessarily fleshy because of the hardness of the palate. Nature, then, uses the palate as an earthy substitute for teeth. And so the camel ruminates, like horned animals, since it has stomachs like theirs. The formation of its teeth, however, is like that of a horned animal. Proper to the camel is the hump of its back, and it sometimes has two. The camel has no distinct gall bladder, but small veins in which the gall is. Under its foot is much fleshy padding, and in its cleft a hide similar to that on the feet of geese: and so, when it has much traveling to do, shoes are made for it. When it walks, it first moves its right foot; it lives thirty years and more, and some even live a hundred years; rabies too befalls these, as it does certain other animals. They urinate backward, like lions. For camels have their members set toward the rear, and tails like donkeys'. On each foot there is a knee, above which the foot bends. On each foot there is a hoof-pad similar to a cow's foot-pad, since it is small in proportion to the body. Camels endure thirst for four days and afterward drink much; nature gave this animal a body's size like a beast of burden, as it did the elephant too. An animal, moreover, whose food is of woody and thorny matter, has many stomachs, and the camel is of this kind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the camel is an ugly, humped animal, having a long neck, bent legs, a slow gait, and, as it walks, never wears down its feet: it is an unclean animal according to the law, since although it has a hoof, it does not divide it. When they must be loaded, they are struck lightly on the knees and at once bend down with necks lowered for the load; they avoid hard water, and drink muddy water, and this for the sake of nourishment, for every element, the more it is mixed with others, the more it nourishes, and conversely: angry camels shriek horribly. Rabies and gout also befall these, from which they die most easily. They do not shed their hooves, but are burdened with most vehement pain when they travel hard and laborious roads. For this reason they have, on their feet, shoes of strong hide. They swallow barley quickly and store it, so as to chew it again all night by rumination. This devotion is said to be present in camels, that if in a herd or stable one, held back by illness, does not eat, the others, sympathizing, abstain as well. Those called 'straight' camels have only one hump on the back. There is also another kind of these, called dromedaries, vigorous in marvelous speed and having two humps on the back.

Solinus: female camels are prepared for war, and it is thought they become stronger if kept from mating by castration. Camels are castrated by the men who use them for battle, since then they do not grow fat. Certain peoples, dwelling in the highest places, have three thousand camels that run faster than a horse, and this happens to them only because of the length of their stride.

Pliny: camels, as said, are had, differing, by Bactria and Arabia. All in these lands, however, serve as beasts of burden on their backs and for cavalry in battles; their speed is like a horse's, but each has its own measure or strength. Nor do they go beyond their accustomed distance, nor take on more than their established load.

Vegetius, on Military Matters: among the ancients, certain nations brought camels into battle formation. But this kind of animal, tolerable indeed on sand, is so suited to it that they are said to direct their paths without error even through confused, wind-blown dust. Otherwise, apart from the novelty, if it seems to be used this way, it is ineffective in war.

Aristotle: male camels have their members set toward the rear: whence they mate facing away from each other. Their members, moreover, are sinewy and hard: whence bowstrings are made from them. At mating time they seek solitude or secluded places.

Aristotle, in the same: the camel is very ill-tempered at mating time. And if any animal or man approaches it at this time, it harms them. It mates, however, after three years; at the time of lust it is solitary with the female, fierce and wild, and mates by mounting throughout the whole day. But although it is otherwise lustful, it is chaste toward its mother, whence in a certain city they used to cover the female camel's head, so that her young might mount her. The young, its mother's head covered, mounted her, and, once the covering was removed, recognizing its mother, broke off the shameful act it had begun, dismounted, and, biting the very man who had contrived this, killed him. The female camel is pregnant for a year; after birth too she rests from mating for a year, and produces only one offspring, like the elephant, the horse, and every solid-hoofed animal.
Solinus (Pliny, book 10): camels are driven wild by desire for procreation, so much so that they rage when they seek mating.

From the book On the Nature of Things, of an uncertain author (Pliny, book 10): the camel mates from behind, like other animals whose genitals are set backward. They seek solitude or secluded places; at this time no interruption is granted without danger. For them mating lasts the whole day, as for those alone that have a solid hoof; they produce single offspring. Females have four teats, like cows. They carry for twelve months and give birth in spring, and again a year after giving birth are ready.

Avicenna: camel's flesh provokes urine. Fat, which is in the camel's hump, fumigated, benefits hemorrhoids. Camel's brain, dried and drunk with vinegar, benefits epilepsy. Its blood is effective for the same. Dried and fried, it too, checks bleeding; drunk with wine, it also benefits the harm of an Armenian arrow-wound. Drunk after the purging of the menses, it aids conception and benefits suffocation of the womb.

Avicenna, the same: milk of pregnant female camels is fine and very watery, and does not cause obstructions like other milks, because of the scarcity of its cheese-content and the dissolving of its wateriness. In it there is saltiness, since camels love sour things, and this makes better milk. It is said, moreover, to be of vehement slowness in the stomach and upper belly. From it, unlike other milks, filth is rarely feared. It benefits asthma and rapid breathing, but greatly harms dropsy, and benefits spleen and liver ailments. It stirs the appetite for food and causes cough, provokes the menses, soothes the bowels, and benefits hemorrhoids. Camel's urine benefits dropsy; it also benefits strong odor of the nostrils and opens obstructions of the filter [kidneys] with vehement power; a washing made from it benefits dandruff. Camel's dung cleanses and destroys warts, stops bleeding from the nostrils. And when drunk with medicines it benefits epilepsy. Likewise it dissolves pimples and ulcers, and scrofula too, powerfully. It also calms pains of the joints and their abscesses.
Pliny, book 24: its dried tail loosens the bowels.
Dioscorides: white camel dung, ground with honey and applied, represses swellings and thoroughly cleans delicate wounds.
Haly Abbas, on the camel: rubbed blood benefits dysentery and chronic looseness, and drinking of poison; camel's milk benefits corruption of the constitution and increases mating.

Isidore: some have said the goat [capra] is named from browsing on shrubs [carpendis virgultis], others because it seeks out rough places [captet aspera]. Some derive it from the crackling of its legs, whence the wild goats are called 'creae.'

Aristotle, in the same: the goat is a ruminant animal, which, however, has teeth in both jaws. Goats at pasture move quickly from their places, which sheep do not do, and take only the tops of plants. When they move about after midday they will drink more water, and when they have eaten salt before giving birth, they will have much discharge from their udders. In Germany goats' ears are the size of one palm and of a marvelously large gall bladder in proportion. Goats are naturally swift, and so shepherds do not set a leader for them. The goat does not see well by day, but its sight sharpens at night. It sometimes has eyes of different colors: when shot with an arrow, it seeks and eats stag's pennyroyal, so that the arrow may be drawn out. If someone catches a goat, the others suddenly rise up and watch this with a dull expression. The goat, moreover, is prey for the vulture.

Pliny: goats are reported to see no less by night than by day. And so, if goat's liver is eaten, it is said to restore evening sight to those called night-blind. They say that goats do not look at one another in pastures when the declining sun sets toward evening, but lie turned away from each other; but at other hours face each other and know each other better. From the chin of all of them hangs a tuft, which they call the 'aruncus,' by which, if someone seizes and pulls one from the flock, the rest stand watching, stupefied. Their bite is deadly to a tree. By licking, too, they make the olive sterile, and for this reason they were sacrificed to Minerva; Mucianus reported having himself witnessed this cunning of the animal, that is of the goat: on a very narrow bridge two met each other coming from opposite directions, and since, because of the bridge's narrowness, they could not turn aside, nor go back because of its length, on that blind narrow path, with a rushing torrent threateningly flowing beneath, one lay down and the other walked over her. Goats in Sicily, like sheep, are clothed with shearable fleece. In Ethiopia goats live up to eleven years, in the rest of the world mostly eight. A goat relieves suffused eyes with the blood of a rush-prick, the he-goat with that of a bramble.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: goats' eyes shine at night and cast light. Sharp, thick hairs grow on he-goats, but finer ones on the females. Likewise male goats have more teeth than females. Nor do goats have teeth except the front ones; they have paired ones. And they have two teats on the thighs, and nowhere else, as sheep do too.
Pliny, in the same: the herb oleander is poison to goats.
Pliny: black hellebore, however, purges goats when eaten.
Pliny, in the same: the woodpecker and the goat, if they eat the leaves of oleander in water or drink the water, are said to die.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the goat is a bearded animal with long, sharp horns; it feeds in valleys and on mountains, and on the branches of trees it can reach with its mouth, but its bite, as said, is deadly to a tree. Goats that lick honey die; they live on poisonous plants.
Constantine the African, in the same place: if goats drink from or eat tamarisk vessels, they will have no spleen.

Serapion (John): I saw, says Galen, goats licking tamarisk leaves, and I found them without a spleen; and I also saw some licking serpents that had shed their skin, and, afterward turning white, aging less.

Pliny: goats bear even four at a time, but quite rarely; they carry for five months like sheep, grow fat from poison, and become sterile from fatness. A mutilated one is useful in either sex; the first mating of the day does not conceive, the following one is more effective; then they conceive in November, so as to give birth in March, when the shrubs are budding. Sometimes yearlings, always two-year-olds, but at three years old give birth to useless offspring. When pregnant, they are fatter, as are sheep too. Males are approved of when they are as snub-nosed as possible, with long ears and broken-looking shoulders, and as shaggy as possible. A mark of good breeding in females is a pair of dewlaps hanging from the neck on their bodies. Not all have horns, but those that do have, in these, indications of their age through the growth of the rings. In many, the abundance of milk is greater. Archelaus is the authority that they breathe through their ears, not their nostrils, and never lack fever. Perhaps for this reason their spirit is more ardent than sheep's, and their mating is reported to be hotter.

Aristotle: a he-goat mates at one year, but generates something weak: in Ethiopia the goat properly lives thirteen years, mates its whole life, and bears twins, and if the food is suitable, the he-goat will be vigorous. The goat, like the sheep, if impregnated, comes against the force [of the wind]. One facing north bears a male, one facing south bears a female: since it is not usual for milk to be present in animals before impregnation, in certain regions the goat's impregnation is not waited for, but her udder is rubbed with urine, and at first indeed blood, then something like pus, comes, but afterward good milk, no worse than the milk of impregnated ones. There is, moreover, a bird that sucks the udders of goats, and the milk is annihilated and dries up.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the goat abounds in milk, and her milk is most pleasant, but once curdled it is spoiled, for cheese made from it is of almost no use. The goat sometimes bears twins, but quite rarely; she carries for five months, like the sheep, and more usefully conceives in November, so as to give birth in March. They give birth up to eight years of age, and miscarry from harmful cold.

Palladius: a three-year-old goat can be raised best, but a female kid of large body should be chosen, with thick legs, a short neck and full throat, folded and heavy ears, a small head, a shiny, thick, and long coat, and large udders. Nor should many goats, like sheep, be shut in one enclosure, which should also be free of mud and dung. That the more tender males breed is not to be overlooked. But females should not be kept as breeding stock beyond eight years, since this kind becomes sterile through weakness and age.

div.head: DE CARNIBUS CAPRINIS IN MEDICINIS EX EARUM CORPORIBUS

cit.quote: Isaac Judaeus: since oxen have thick flesh, disobedient to digestion, and heat is weak in creatures living quietly, their flesh is necessarily not digested by them, except when they are suckling. For then it obeys digestion, because of the tenderness of their flesh and the smallness of their age. He-goats, too, generate worse blood than female goats.
Aristotle: the goat has poor flesh because of the scarcity of its fat. And so the Greeks call goats similar to barren vines.

Avicenna: goat's flesh is dry and of more difficult digestion than sheep's, and is not very good, but its moisture is perhaps very bad. Further, he-goat's flesh is absolutely bad and causes quartan fevers to occur.
Pliny: goat's flesh, toasted on a pyre, is given to epileptics as a remedy for their illness.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: kid's flesh, however, which is good even as food, will be discussed below, where kids are treated.

Aesculapius: goat's brain with honey heals carbuncles of the belly. Its tallow helps every bite and wound. Its fat, mixed with roses, removes pustules that worsen at night; the same, dripped into the ears, heals deafness. Its cheese, applied, represses all stings and pains. Its burnt hairs calm all fluxes. Its hooves, toasted and ground with liquid pitch and applied, cure baldness: its milk, drunk, frees the windpipe, kills worms, and heals itching and bites. Its blood does the same, and, drunk, neutralizes poison; its urine, drunk, heals dropsy sufferers. Its dung is effective for every pain, internal and external.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: burnt goat's horn, if held before the nostrils in spring at shedding-time, causes them to fall out at once.

Avicenna: burnt and whitened goat's horn cleans the teeth thoroughly, tightens the gums, and eases the pain of swollen gums. When it is applied with vinegar from the ash of goat's hoof, it greatly benefits baldness. Shavings of goatskin, placed on a bleeding wound, check it. It is also said that fresh, white goatskin, applied over a viper's bite, draws out the venom. Goat's fat is more astringent than all fats. It benefits gnawing pain of the intestines and their ulcers, and is stronger in treating ulcers of the intestines than pig's fat, because of the speed of its congealing. Pig's fat, however, calms the gnawing pain more vehemently. Likewise goat's fat benefits [poisoning by] blister-beetles. Goats' liver, and especially he-goats', reveals whether one is epileptic, and when an epileptic eats it, he has an attack. Water of goat's liver benefits ringworm, eaten and applied to the affected area, and leaning over its vapor. Goat's blood, drunk with honey, benefits dysentery. Likewise, dried and fried, it checks bleeding.

Pliny: they say serpents are driven off by burning goat's horn or hair, and that the ash, drunk and applied with a carving knife, is effective against their bites. The same ash also checks sweating. Goat's blood, boiled with marrow, is taken against toxic poisons. The same is also given to dysentery sufferers this way, and helps dropsy sufferers. Goat's liver is beneficial against the moth that flies to lights; roasted, it also helps celiacs. Its hide, boiled with its hair, or the juice drunk, heals the spleen. Goat's gall with Cimolian chalk and vinegar corrects baldness. The same gall, too, is taken with honey against cataracts; with the ash of its hooves and pitch, falling hair is checked. Against the strikes of serpents, those who wish for a more effective cure at once bind on the cut-open belly of a slain goat with the dung found inside. The marrow of he-goats and goats is also praiseworthy.

Dioscorides, on goat: its fat is more astringent than others because of its pasture, whence it is mixed into enemas for dysentery sufferers. The broth of its gall also helps consumptives. It also helps those who have drunk blister-beetles. Goat's gall is applied to fistulas with leek juice, and is also applied to medicines for wounds, healing them without swelling. It is also mixed into theriac antidotes; joined with honey, it relieves pain of the testicles and genitals. Mixed with soda, it suits leprosy sufferers and those with dandruff on the head.

div.head: DE CETERIS MEDICINALIBUS EX CAPRA PROCEDENTIBUS

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: goat's milk, as is read, is the most temperate after human milk, which is also clear from what follows.

Avicenna: goat's milk is temperate, that is, in fineness and thickness. And so it harms the internal organs less than others, since most of what it feeds on is astringent. It benefits catarrh and checks it and improves its sharpness; it also benefits ulcers of the palate and cough, wasting, and coughing blood, and ulcers of the bladder; it is also useful for hectic fever and dropsy and hardness of the spleen. Urine of domestic and mountain goats benefits nervous ailments, and especially spasm and stretching. The same, alone or with myrrh, calms ear pain; the urine, especially of mountain goats, is also effective for edema. Goat dung has a drawing power from this, for it draws out wasp venom. Dry goat dung with wool checks flux of the womb. From it too, by rectification through decoction in dark wine, a plaster is made for a viper's bite that causes thirst. It also powerfully dissolves scrofula. Likewise it is administered in every flux of blood; burnt, however, it becomes finer and is not hot, and this suits baldness. Likewise the dung is effective for chafing, and with vinegar for burns from fire, with wax and rose oil. The same with pig fat suits gout, applied, and sciatica too. It is also effective for hardness of the joints and their abscesses, especially mixed with vinegar.

Pliny: [remedies made from] a draft of goat's milk with Aminean grapes or urine or vinegar. Likewise its cheese with oregano applied, or tallow with wax, and moreover many remedies are shown from this animal, which indeed I marvel at, since it is said never to lack fever, and the power is even greater in the wild kind of the same.

Pliny, in the same: goat's milk is most suited to the stomach: since they feed more on foliage than on grass, the spleen is healed by it; a drink of it with salt and honey loosens the bowels; the richest butter is made from sheep and goats. Goat broth is effective against blister-beetle poisoning, and milk likewise; with this milk too, they say, nits are removed, and with dung and honey baldness is filled in. Fresh goat cheese is effective for those who have drunk mistletoe-glue; dry, with vinegar and honey, it purges ulcers: goat tallow with lime cures scrofula, or goat dung well boiled with vinegar; this dung, applied with wine, is also praised against the bite of a rabid dog. They report that consumption and cough are healed by goat's tallow in porridge; it is especially praised for broken ribs. Goat dung with old wine opens, draws out, and thoroughly heals. Likewise goat dung applied is effective for eye discharges, and the marrow against eye pains. The same too, boiled in vinegar with honey, is thought most useful for pains of the sinews.

Dioscorides, on goat: its urine, drunk, breaks and expels stones. The same, boiled in a vessel and applied with wool as a pessary, cures hysterical pains. It also removes eye wounds. Goat dung is sharp and diaphoretic in power.

Avicenna: ladanum, as already said elsewhere, is a moisture hanging on the hairs and beards of grazing goats. It is a very fine, morning kind of thick, viscous moisture, dissolving, drawing, warming, opening the mouths of the veins, and the rest that has been said above.

Pliny, book 8: roe deer take on very many similar forms. For there are roe deer, there are chamois, there are ibexes, there are also wild goats called by some 'orges alone,' clothed with fur turned the opposite way and toward the head. There are also fallow deer and pygargs and 'strepsicerotes' and many other different kinds. But the Alps send the former, overseas regions the latter. Roe deer or ibexes are of marvelous swiftness, although their heads are burdened with vast horns like sword-sheaths; onto these they balance themselves, as if whirled by some engine, especially on rocks, and, wishing to leap from one mountain to another, they spring back nimbly wherever they please.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: [on] branching [horns] in roe deer. Nature gave horns to roe deer, but made them small and not shed. This animal's blood does not thicken. Nature gave to red roe deer horns curved back onto the spine.

Isidore: they call wild roe deer 'creae,' which the Greeks, because they see most sharply, properly called 'dorcades.' For they dwell on high mountains, and although they are far off, they nevertheless see all who approach. The same are also called 'caprae' and 'ibices,' as if 'avices' [little birds], since, in the manner of birds, they hold and inhabit steep and lofty places: so much so that they are scarcely visible to human sight from their heights, whence the southern region also calls 'ibices' the birds that dwell along the streams of the Nile. These animals, then, as we have said, dwell on the highest rocks, so that if ever they sense the hostility of wild beasts or men, they throw themselves down from the highest peaks of the crags and land unharmed on their own horns.
Ambrose: the goat or roe deer, harmed by scent alone, avoids it; wounded, it seeks out dittany and expels the arrows from the wound; the leopard is healed by drinking its blood.
Aristotle: goats struck by arrows seek stag's pennyroyal, so as to draw them out of the body. The goat, moreover, is prey for the vulture.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the wild goat, also called the 'capreola' or chamois, is a fierce beast toward its own kind. Toward other beasts, however, it is timid and very gentle. This one, on the island of Crete, when wounded, seeks pennyroyal, which, once eaten, causes the arrow to leap from the body: it can scarcely be caught, however, since it is most swift, and when pressed by dogs, flees to the highest mountains. There is very great discord among the males because of the females, and this at mating time.

Dioscorides: dung of wild goats, drunk with wine, heals jaundice; drunk with spikenard leaf, it commands the menses. It checks other fluxes of blood, applied with vinegar; burnt and ground with vinegar or oxymel, it heals baldness. Mixed with fat, it heals gout.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: more will also be said of the roe deer below, under the name of the ibex, where the ibex is treated.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the he-goat is of two kinds, domestic and wild, of which authors speak confusedly, as of the goat and the roe deer, because of the similarity of kind and the shared name.

Aristotle: he-goats' feet are cloven in two, and at the ends of these parts are hoof-shoes in place of claws. The he-goat dreams, as man does. A he-goat mates at one year, but the offspring it first produces is better and stouter than those born later, which is not the case with other animals. He-goats too fattened much do not mate much, except rarely; for this reason shepherds make them lean before mating. He-goats have a particular voice by which they call to one another, since at mating time they separate and fight. The he-goat has many stomachs, like cows and sheep, and has poor flesh because of the scarcity of its fat. In Germany certain he-goats' tails are pulled down to the ground; in a certain region, too, he-goats are shorn, as sheep are elsewhere.
Pliny: the he-goat relieves suffused eyes of blood by pricking with a bramble, the goat with a rush.

Palladius, on the he-goat, in the same place: a he-goat to be admitted for mating should be chosen that has, as it seems, two small warts hanging under its jaws, of large body, thick legs, a short and full neck, folded and heavy ears, a small head, a shiny, thick, and long coat, suited to covering the females, and, before a year old, is not yet fit; it does not last beyond six years. A female kid similar in body should also be chosen, but with large udders.

From the book On the Nature of Things, of an uncertain author: [on] the he-goat having both natures, as happens among men. The wild he-goat is a most cunning animal, loves high mountains, and watches men walking from a distance, whether they be hunters or travelers.
Avicenna: he-goat's gall benefits blindness, especially of the mountain kind.
Isidore: the stag [cervus] is named 'apo ton keraton,' that is, from horns: for the Greeks call horns 'cerata.'

Pliny: stags are charmed by the shepherd's pipe and by song; they flee at the sound of dogs barking; the stag is astonished at everything. And so it more easily offers itself to archers. Old age is shown in these by their teeth, for an old one has few or none, nor at the base of the horns either; otherwise, they project in front of the forehead in old ones, as in younger ones.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: the eagle does battle with stags, and, settling on their antlers, shakes off a great deal of gathered dust into their eyes, beating their faces with its wings, until it drives them over cliffs. No single enemy is fiercer to them than this: their females cannot bear force, and for this reason enter into conception. Stags pass in turn to other females and return to the earlier ones.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: nowhere else has nature played with greater wantonness in the weapons of animals than in scattering the stag's horns into branches. These alone have solid horns, shed every year. Nor do stags have upper front teeth. Those who think these are consumed into the horns are easily refuted by the nature of hinds, which have no upper teeth, as the males do, and yet have no horns either: in other animals, horns are attached to the bone, but in stags alone they grow from the skin: stags have little worms in the head, beneath the hollow of the tongue and around the joint where the head joins the shoulder, twenty in number, it is reported. Stags' ears are cleft and, as it were, divided; stags have four kidneys; the stag's breath burns serpents, and its blood does not thicken.
Gloss: stags, when their eyes are about to grow dim, eat serpents, and, having drunk from a spring, recover their sight and cast off what is excessive.

Aristotle: the stag is a timid animal, having horns and a cloven hoof. Its teeth incline downward; it has four teeth on one side of the mouth and four on the other, with which it grinds, and also has two other large teeth, which are larger in the male and smaller in the female. The male's voice is thicker and deeper than the female's. The male cries out much at mating time, and the female when afraid. The stag, then, like other great-hearted animals, is timid, and fears the voice of foxes. It delights, however, in whistling and song, and so follows one who whistles and sings, and another kills it - whence, when its ears are erect, it notices the ambush of one following, but once it has lowered them, it does not notice. Likewise stags fight, and the defeated obeys the victor with forced obedience; but when a stag is pregnant, it hides because of hunters. A stag's intestines are very foul-smelling, whence they are not eaten by dogs unless very hungry. A stag's blood does not coagulate strongly, but gently, like milk in which no rennet is mixed. Alone among animals it sheds its horns, whose casting off happens once a year, once the stag is two years old, and then others grow. If it is castrated before the growth of the horns, they do not grow at all, and if after, they never grow again, nor do they shed the ones they have; they shed their horns for relief, since they are hard, solid, and heavy. No wild animal is seen to chew the cud except the stag; this one has no gall attached to the liver. It has two cloven feet, and, at the tips of the hooves, shoe-like coverings, as goats and sheep have. The bear fights with stags, and stags too fight one another, striking each other forcefully with their horns, and the defeated one obeys the victor.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the stag is an animal of marvelous swiftness, having its forehead roughened with branching horns. Their formation happens thus: once it is two years old, up to six years it adds branches according to its age. After that they cannot become more numerous, but only larger. This animal alone sheds its horns, and glories in this beyond measure. It has one worm in its head, which almost constantly torments it. But every animal, and man himself, has a worm beneath the tongue.

Pliny, book 8: stags have a fight with the serpent; they hunt out its caverns and draw it out, though it resists, by the breath of their nostrils. And so a singular scent for driving off serpents is burnt stag's horn. Against bites, however, the chief remedy is the rennet from a fawn cut from its mother's womb.
Isidore: stags, enemies of serpents, draw them out of their caverns by the breath of their nostrils, and, having overcome the venom's ruin, are restored by feeding on them.
Ambrose: the serpent, then, flees the stag, and venom is food for the stag.

Physiologus: when the stag recognizes that there is a serpent, it fills its mouth with water and pours it into the burrow, then, with a certain breath of its mouth, draws the serpent out and, trampling it with its feet, kills it. There are, moreover, two kinds of stags: one which, when it has found a serpent in the cave where it hides, sends in its breath, so that it comes out, and, striking the neck of the one emerging, kills it this way and devours it. Afterward, however, because of the swelling, it runs to the purest waters and vomits out the venom, but amid this swelling changes its hair and casts off its horns. There is another kind, which, if it finds a serpent, kills it, and after the victory heads to the mountain, where it may find pasture.

Pliny, book 18: no one is ignorant that stags are hostile to serpents, dragging them out and chewing them. Nor indeed do they oppose them only by breathing, but also limb by limb. For if their horn is burnt, serpents are said to be driven off by the smoke and to gather at the top of the throat from the burnt bones. Their skins, removed, provide safe sleep from that fear. A stag's blood too is effective against serpents. Serpents flee entirely even from those having a stag's tooth, or anointed with its marrow, tallow, or by its touch. Its rennet, drunk with vinegar, renders one safe from a serpent's strike. And if one has been handled with it, a serpent will not strike that day.
Aristotle: the stag is a wise animal, of which it is also thought that it is more discerning among four-footed animals, since it gives birth near a road, where animals do not go, close to men.

Pliny: stags too have their own malice, although they are the most peaceable of animals; pressed by the force of dogs, they flee of their own accord to man, and in giving birth are less wary of paths worn by human footsteps than of those that are secluded and convenient for wild beasts. They swim across seas in herds, swimming in a line, resting their heads on the haunches of those in front, and taking turns returning to the back - this is especially noted by those crossing from Cilicia to Cyprus. Nor do they see the land, but swim by its scent; these have a fight with the serpent, as said above. Also envying their own good, they say the right horn cannot be found, as if endowed with some medicinal power. And this is all the more remarkable, since although they shed both every year, even in enclosed parks, they are thought to bury this one. Females too purge themselves before giving birth with an herb called 'syle,' and so give birth more easily. This animal does not feel fever - indeed, it is a remedy for this very fear.

Ambrose: the stag, when it does not yet have horns, nevertheless practices with its forehead beforehand, and imitates weapons it has not yet experienced. The stag, when it is sick, eats olive-tree twigs and is healed.

Isidore: stags, as said, enemies of serpents, when they sense they are burdened with illness, draw them out of their caverns by the breath of their nostrils, and, having overcome the venom's ruin, are restored by feeding on them. They discovered the herb dittany for us. For, having fed on it, they shake out arrows they have taken. They marvel, moreover, at the whistling of pipes; with ears raised, they hear sharply, but lowered, nothing at all: but when they swim across vast rivers or seas, they place their heads on the haunches of those in front, and, taking turns following one another, feel no burden of weight.

Solinus: by the barking of dogs, they set their course with the wind, so that their scent departs with them. If they swim across seas, they do not seek the shore by sight, but by smell. They place the weak ones last, and support the heads of the weary on their haunches in turns.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: stags change their horns in the waters, since they do not want the right horn, useful for medicines, to be found by man; but when it has devoured a serpent, driven by the seething of the venom, it hurries to a spring of water: for it loves to be near the purest fresh water.

Aristotle: the male stag, when it grows fat, hides, so that it is not hunted because of its fatness. The hind too, with her young, goes to hidden places, like clefts in rocks, which have only one entrance. The hunting of stags happens in this manner: two men go together to hunt, of whom one whistles and sings, and the stag follows the song, since it delights in it, and then the other pierces it with a hunting spear. And indeed if the stag's ears are raised, it will hear keenly and will at once recognize the one who wishes to strike it, but if they are lowered, it will not recognize him.

Pliny: male stags, freed from the desire of lust, eagerly seek pasture; but once they sense they have grown too fat, they seek hiding places, confessing the burdensome weight. At other times, however, they always rest in flight, and even standing they look back, and when pursuit draws near, again they seek the refuge of flight; they flee, however, when they hear the barking of dogs, always with a following wind, so as to keep track of them by scent. They are charmed, however, by the shepherd's pipe and by song; otherwise this is a simple animal, astonished at every marvel, so much so that, with a horse or a young cow approaching closer, it does not notice the hunter nearby, or, if it does notice, marvels at the bow and arrows themselves. Further, stags showed us the herb dittany, powerful for drawing out arrows, once struck by a dart and, feeding on that herb, expelling it. Pressed too by the force of dogs, they flee of their own accord to man.
Gloss: stags, pursued by dogs through thickets, with their horns laid back on their backs, escape unharmed.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: hunters say that if a stag, pursued by dogs, enters and drinks water, it is refreshed from its weariness and restored for running.

Gloss: stags, at the time of love, leave their homeland, and then one supports itself with its head placed on another's haunches, walking in order, and, once the first is tired, the last one takes its place.

Pliny, in the same place: the hind, in giving birth, is less wary, as said, of paths worn by human footsteps than of those that are secluded and convenient for wild beasts. Their conception occurs after the constellation of Arcturus; they carry for eight months, and give birth sometimes to twins; from conception she separates herself, but the males left behind rage in the frenzy of lust and dig pits. Then their muzzles blacken, until some rains wash them. But now, freed from the desire of lust, they eagerly seek pasture. Hinds, as said, purge themselves before giving birth with an herb called 'syle,' and thus have an easier womb.
Pliny, book 28, in the same: they report, too, that hinds, when they sense themselves pregnant, swallow a small stone found in their droppings, which, bound on, guards the pregnancy.

Aristotle: the stag, as said, the male, cries out much at mating time. The hind cannot endure mating because of the hardness of the male's member, but receives it while fleeing. The hind, about to give birth, first eats dragon-wort; but when she gives birth, she at once eats the afterbirth of her young before it falls to the ground, and her afterbirth is poison. She gives birth near a road, since animals do not go to that place because of men. After birth, however, she leads her young to hidden places having one entrance. Whence they can fight with other animals.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: male stags, at the set time of love, rage with the frenzy of lust. The females, however, conceive before the constellation of Arcturus, that is, as August ends and September begins. They separate themselves at the time of conception. The hind gives birth on a trodden path, and runs with her young following the wind, lest, if she ran facing the wind, the wind, carrying her scent, should announce her path to those pursuing her, so that she would die. Further, according to Solinus, stags carefully hide their tender young, and, hidden among the depths of foliage or grasses, chastise them with a blow of the foot to keep them hidden. And once they have matured strength for flight, they teach them by the exercise of running, and accustom them to leap over steep places.

Pliny: the stag sometimes becomes so weak from intestinal pain that it bursts internally. It does not feel the diseases of fevers, as said, and indeed is a remedy for this very fear. Stags too, struck by the 'phalangium,' which is a kind of spider, or by something similar, heal themselves by eating crabs.

Isidore: stags, when they sense they are burdened with illness, draw serpents out of their caverns by the breath of their nostrils, and, having overcome the venom's ruin, are restored by feeding on them. Fed also on the herb dittany, they shake out arrows they have taken.
Ambrose: stags too, as said, when they are sick, eat olive-tree twigs and are healed.

Solinus: stags add branches according to their age. Likewise their growth continues until six years old. Finally, they can become no more numerous, but thicker, which indeed never grow in castrated ones, nor do they shed - it is clear these never have fever. Their teeth, however, show their old age in them, when either few or none are found. To ascertain their longevity, Alexander the Great fastened many collars on stags, which, caught after a hundred years, still showed no sign of old age.

Gloss: the stag, weighed down by age, its hair and horns growing excessive, draws in a serpent through its nostrils, and, having drawn it in, seethes with venom, whence it desires most ardently to drink from a spring, and, having drunk, sheds its hair and horns.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the old stag, as Aristotle says, has no teeth, or has few. Hunters, however, as a most certain proof, have reported that when a stag comes to a burdened old age, a bone of the head beneath the eye being pierced through, wasps naturally form and take shape inside from the excess moisture, or, as others hold, from the marrow, and come forth flying out. And then they say it cannot live longer, unless it is renewed according to what was said above. Sometimes, too, they say wasps come forth formed in the same way from the stag's nostrils.

div.head: DE CARNIBUS CERVINIS ET ADIPE ET SANGUINE

cit.quote: Isaac Judaeus: stag's flesh is harder to digest than beef and melancholic, but nevertheless varies according to constitutions and ages, as we said of the ox. For sucklings are more suitable than the rest, young ones harder, and decrepit ones the worst. But young ones, if castrated, are better, since they are tempered by heat and dryness.
Avicenna: stags' flesh, with its thickness, is of quick descent and causes quartan fevers to occur.
Avicenna, the same: stag's flesh benefits spasm, and its fat likewise, which fat, that is, is of vehement warming power. And a liniment made from it drives away venomous things.
Aristotle: stag's liver, however, is very bad, since its body is of a very poor constitution.

Solinus: it is clear that stags never have fever, for which reason remedies made from their marrow and hoof calm the fevers of languishing men. We read that very many, accustomed to taste stag's flesh in the morning, lived long without fevers, which indeed will only be of benefit if they were killed with a single wound.
Pliny: [on] stag's flesh. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]
Pliny, in the same: ulcers are healed by applying stag's marrow; its blood checks the bowels.
Dioscorides: stag's blood, applied, checks spider-bites and bad wounds.
Haly Abbas: [on] stag. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Aristotle: the stag alone has horns solid to the root and hard, and alone sheds them each year, that is, once they are complete. For it casts them off from necessity and because of their weight, and this benefits the speed of its body, for the great branching of the horns harms it more than it helps. It casts them off, however, where it is difficult to find them. Whence the proverb: go where the stag sheds his horns. Especially, however, the stag's right horn - for the left is sometimes found - it hides, whence it is thought that there is some great benefit in it. Once the horns are shed, it does not appear, since it lacks weapons. And so, fearing wolves, it hides, but at night goes out to pasture, and when the horns grow back, it stands in the sun, as if ripening and drying them, and once they have grown, it tests them by rubbing them against trees, and then goes out safely, since it has weapons. Once a stag was caught on whose horns ivy had grown, that is, from rubbing against trees, according to Pliny, and this happened since the horns were then soft, having hollow depths within themselves. The stag alone, as said, has hard, not hollow horns, for those of other animals are hollow. Its horns increase up to six years, and from then its age is known. It is known to be old, however, since it has no teeth. Some, however, have teeth, but few.

Pliny, book 8: among stags, the males have horns, and alone among animals lose them every year at a set time in spring. And, once shed, they hide as if disarmed. They also bear signs of age in these, adding branches each year, up to six years old. From that time similar ones grow back, and age cannot be discerned, but old age is shown by the teeth. Horns do not fall off in castrated ones, nor do they grow: as long as they lack these, they go out to pasture by night. They burst forth, however, as new knobs regrow, at first similar to dry skin. As they grow, they harden in the heat of the sun.
Pliny: stags, as said above, have a fight with serpents. And so a singular scent for driving off serpents is burnt stag's horn.

Pliny: the smoke of burnt stag's horn detects epileptic or falling sickness. The ash of the same horn, applied with vinegar or rose oil, calms headache. The same ash strengthens loose teeth, rubbed on or used as a mouthwash, and eases their pain. The powder of the raw horn is also effective for the same. Likewise the aforesaid ash heals rheumatism and cures the coughing up of blood. It heals celiacs and dysentery sufferers, taken three fingers' worth in a drink of water. It also expels kinds of intestinal worms, drunk. It benefits jaundice, taken in wine. Ulcers, too, are healed by it, or by stag's marrow, as said, applied.

Solinus: of stag's horns, the right is more effective for healing. But if you wish to drive off serpents, burn either one. And what is burnt, moreover, by its very smoke reveals and detects whether one has the falling sickness.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: [on] the right horn: the stag, begrudging man this, hides the right horn so it cannot be found. The book On the Nature of Things also says the same. Aristotle, however, says it hides the left horn, as if there were some benefit in it.

Avicenna, in the second canon: stag's horn, burnt until it whitens, thoroughly cleans the teeth and tightens the gums, and eases the pain of swollen gums. Likewise burnt and whitened stag's and goat's horn, like washed salt, prevents matter from reaching the eye. Burnt, washed stag's horn benefits coughing blood and dysentery. Likewise it makes the side deswell and does not harm the stomach, and benefits jaundice.

Aesculapius: stag's horn dries all humors and is put into eye-salves. Burnt, it strengthens teeth rubbed with it. Powdered and drunk with wine, it cures epileptics and checks flux of the bowels and kills intestinal worms; if it is burnt in a house, serpents flee that smell.
Physiologus: stags' tears, gathered, and bones found in their hearts, are suited for a drink for those suffering from heart palpitations.

Platearius, on the stag: in the stag's heart is found a certain bone on the left side, in which there is a certain hollow, to which the spleen has an outlet and sends its surplus, which there, by its own inherent dryness, is changed into a bony substance. That is from the blood of the heart, somewhat reddish, and has the power of purifying melancholic vapor. It is given against cardiac ailments and fainting and against hemorrhoids.
Aesculapius: besides, if anyone wraps himself in stag skin, he does not fear serpents; stag's marrow also calms pains.

Haly Abbas: stag's rennet is beneficial against drinking hemlock and eating mushrooms. Stag's urine helps pain of the spleen. It benefits bloating of the stomach and intestines. Dripped into the ears, it heals their ulcers, and dripped into the nostrils of one deprived of smell, it clearly benefits him, and even, if the head is washed with it, removes dandruff. Stag's testicles, dried and taken in wine, help the bite of small venomous reptiles. The tip of a stag's tail, however, if drunk, kills.

Avicenna: in the stag's tail there is venom, and to one who drinks it there follows vehement distress and fainting and death. But its treatment is that he vomit it up with butter and dill, then hazelnuts and pistachios and prepared [an uncertain compound] be given together in a drink.

Pliny, book 28: stag's lung, dried somewhat in smoke with the throat, then ground with honey, heals cough. Stag's rennet with vinegar checks bleeding, but the rennet of a fawn cut from its mother's womb is preferred above the chief remedies.
Isidore: rabbits are a kind of wild animal, so called as if 'caniculi' [little dogs], since they are caught by the tracking of dogs or driven out of their burrows.

Pliny, book 8: there are kinds of hares that the Spanish call rabbits. Varro is the authority that a town in Spain was undermined by rabbit burrows. Rabbits are of countless fecundity, and bring famine to the Balearic Islands by devastating the crops; and it is certain that the Balearic people sought military help from the deified Augustus against their increase. Their young, cut from the belly or taken from the teats, their innards not yet cleaned, are held most pleasing as food; they are called 'laurices.' There is great favor, too, on land, for their hunting. They cast ferrets into the burrows, which are full of holes in the ground, whence the animal's name too, and thus catch them as they are driven out above. Archelaus is the authority that however many hollows for excrement there are in the hare's body, so many years old it is. A varying number is indeed found, however. He also says both sexes are present in each individual. But that they conceive without a male, as mares do too, and that kindly nature, in this regard, has produced harmless and edible creatures that are fecund.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the rabbit is a beast smaller than the hare, close to it in color and shape. This creature, digging burrow-dwellings in the earth, feeds on vineyards and crops by night. In the morning, however, entering its burrow, it levels the entrance with earth-dust from within, lest men coming upon it by day discover its dwelling. Wherever rabbits dwell, they multiply excessively, since they breed many times a year, and when some of them sense any misfortune there, they flee elsewhere. Without delay the rest of their companions, disdaining the wrong done, abandon the place with them. These mate with their hindquarters turned away from each other, since their genital member is set backward.
Isaac Judaeus: the rabbit has a dissolving power, properly strengthens the stomach, loosens the bowels, provokes urine, and is also more useful for those prepared for elephantiasis.

Isidore: the fallow deer [damula] is so named because it flees from the hand [de manu effugiat], a timid and unwarlike animal. Whence Martial: the boar is feared for its tusk, horns defend the stag - unwarlike fallow deer, what are we but prey?
Gloss, on Proverbs: the fallow deer is a clean animal, swift, sharp-sighted, whence it is written: deliver yourself like a fallow deer from the hand, and so on.

Pliny, in the same place: fallow deer are rarely tamed, since they can scarcely be called truly tame even then. For many creatures are neither gentle nor wild nor of a nature midway between the two, as among winged creatures the swallow, the bee in the field, in the sea the dolphin.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: nature gave fallow deer horns turned forward, upright, but twisted in a circuit of ridges and sharpened into a smooth tip, so as to resemble lyres.

Avicenna, in the second canon: fallow deer's flesh is applied like a plaster on pains of the joints. The same, mixed with wine, is drunk for epilepsy or headache. Likewise, dried and taken with wine in a drink, it benefits against poisons.
Haly Abbas, on serpents: the dried, ground, and drunk member of the fallow deer benefits the bite of serpents. The stag's member does the same.

Isidore: the dromedary is a kind of camel, of smaller stature indeed, but swifter, whence it also has its name. For 'dromos' in Greek means running and speed. For it is accustomed to cover a hundred miles or more in a single day. This animal, like the ox and sheep and camel, chews the cud.
Isidore: the kid [hedus] is named from eating [edendo]. For young ones are the fattest and of the most pleasant taste. Hence it is also called 'edulium' [food].
Palladius, in the same place: for raising kids, besides an abundance of milk, ivy or mastic tips should often be provided.
Pliny: kids should be castrated as the moon wanes, as calves too.

Pliny, in the same: a hot drink of fresh kid's blood with sharp vinegar helps coughing up blood. Its lung wards off drunkenness and checks incontinence of urine. Some also fumigate with the fresh flesh of kids along with the hair, and by that same smoke drive off serpents. They also use the fresh skin for wounds. In women's flux they think it useful to fumigate with their hair, and in flux of blood to drink kid's rennet. Kid's rennet benefits against mistletoe-glue and against the chameleon-lizard, both the white and the bull-colored kind. The same, with vinegar, checks bleeding. Goat's blood, indeed, as said above, is taken boiled with marrow against toxic poisons. Kid's blood, however, against other things. The ash of a kid's thigh is said to marvelously heal ruptured intestines. Kids, the further they are from birth, the worse they become; but with piglets it is the opposite. For the drier the offspring is, the closer to birth the better it is, but the moister it is, the worse. Kids or he-goat young, while suckling, obey digestion, because of the tenderness of their flesh and the smallness of their age. The opposite is true of goat's flesh, as said above.

Avicenna: the flesh of old goats is of thick nourishment and vehement heating power and difficult digestion. The flesh of young ones, however, is better, like the kid's, for this is of finer nourishment and more receptive to digestion.

Avicenna, the same: kid's flesh has fewer surplus humors than the ram's. And also, of every animal of dry constitution, the flesh of the young is better than that of the old, like kid's flesh. Kid's rennet heals from all venomous bites. And fresh kid's blood, taken before it curdles and drunk warm with vinegar for three days, is effective, as some have testified, also for preserving the breast, so that it remains firm. The kidneys of a suckling kid are more praiseworthy than other kidneys.
Haly Abbas: young kid's rennet is beneficial against drinking hemlock and for one who has eaten mushrooms.

Isidore: horses [equi] are so named because, when they were yoked to four-horse chariots, they were matched [equabantur] and, equal in form and similar in speed, were paired together. The steed [caballus], however, was earlier named from the hollow [cavo], since, walking, its hoof-print hollows out the ground, which other animals do not do. Hence too 'sonipes' [sounding-foot], since it sounds with its feet.

Pliny, book 8: the Scythians prefer to use mares rather than stallions in war, since they pass urine without hindering their running. Males live sometimes fifty years, females a shorter span. Females reach the end of their growth at five years, males with one year added.
Pliny, book 10, in the same: animals having continuous teeth drink by sucking, like horses and oxen.
Pliny, book 28, in the same: wolves' teeth bound onto horses are said to grant tireless running.

Aristotle: the horse has eyes of different color, one from the other. Nor is variation of eye color found except in men and horses. It is also contrary to the nature of all animals that, as a horse grows old, its teeth whiten. Likewise the horse lacks gall. In the heart of the horse and the cow there are bones. The ibis is a bird that hates the horse and, imitating its voice, stuns it and forces it to flee, and sometimes kills it. The horse loves to drink muddy water, as the cow loves clear water.
Gloss: Egypt, perhaps, abounds in horses for this reason, since the Nile is muddy.

Aristotle, on the horse: finally, if the water is clear, the horse usually muddies it with its foot. It also greatly loves to swim in water. It has gall attached to the liver, like the stag and the mule. Horses' voices vary according to age. For at first they are weak. But the male's voice is deeper; in old age the voices become firmer and greater. And when they begin to mate, the voice of both will be greater, the female's, however, clearer. Likewise animals having equal teeth, which do not make a saw of them, suck water, like the horse and the bull. Animals having hooves, too, like the horse and mule and donkey, have a single womb: an animal lacking cloven feet and having few offspring has a distinction of teats near the armpit, like the mare and the female camel. The milk of the mare and the female donkey is not suited to be the matter of cheese. Nature ordered the tails of horses to be long with hairs, and manes on the neck, and gave horses speed as a benefit. The horse dreams too, as man does, and the bull and he-goat and dog: it fights, and sheds teeth in time, but not all at once.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: only the horse and the stag and the cow have cartilaginous bones in the heart, and this because of their size, so that the heart may be supported by its own bones.
Aesculapius, in the book On the Limbs: if the 'zosach,' that is the horse, treads where there is the track of the 'dorim,' that is the bear, numbness befalls its foot.

Vegetius, on Military Matters: bristles from horses' tails and manes are said to be useful for ballistae, although bows or ballistae and other equipment, unless strung with sinew cords, are said to be of no use.

Solinus: it has been shown by very many proofs that judgment is present in horses. For Alexander's horse Bucephalus, though gently ridden by others when equipped with an ordinary saddle, once given the royal harness, deigned to carry no one but his master. There are many proofs of him in battles, by which he raised up Alexander in the most brutal contests by his aid. Julius Caesar's horse received no one but Caesar on its back, whose front feet are reported to have had the appearance of a human footprint. When the king of the Scythians was slain in single combat, and the victorious adversary wished to despoil him, he was torn apart by the king's horse with kicks and bites. A horse's affection, too, is proven by tears. Finally, when King Nicomedes was killed, his horse ended its life by starvation. They also know the enemies of their own side, so much so that in battles they attack enemies with their bite. But these traits are found in the most outstanding kind of horses. For those bred beneath nobility have shown no such proofs. That pleasure is present in these, the spectacles of the circus have shown. For some horses are provoked to the race by the songs of pipes, some by dancing, some by variety of colors, and not a few even by lit torches.

Isidore: some horses sense enemies in war, so much so that they attack adversaries with their bite. Some too recognize their own masters, forgetting their tameness unless they are overcome. Some receive no one but their master on their back. When their masters are killed or dying, many shed tears. For the horse alone, it is said, weeps for man and feels the affection of grief, whence in centaurs the nature of horses and men is mixed together. They are also accustomed, from horses' either sadness or eagerness, to gather the future outcome of those about to fight.

Alexander Neckam: it is most certain that noble horses love their masters affectionately, which was evident in the horse of a certain 'rodatus,' which, after Charlemagne died, became a monk at Meaux, and, after a long time, when pagans were attacking, mounted the horse he had left there, and the horse gladly, although already aged, received him and carried him willingly until he triumphed over his enemies. And this was one of those horses that would admit no rider but its own master.

Pliny, book 8, on horses: an understanding of kinship is present in horses, and in a herd it more willingly accompanies a sister of the previous year than its mother. We find that a horse, once the covering was removed from its eyes and it recognized that it had mated with its mother, threw itself off a cliff and died. And for the same reason we likewise find that a mare tore apart a charioteer in the territory of Reate. The horse, then, is a most faithful animal toward men, like the dog too. It senses coming battle beforehand and mourns a lost master, and has such teachability that the entire cavalry of the Sybarite army was found accustomed to move in a certain dance to the sound of a concert.

Aristotle: the horse and mare love mating more than other animals, except man. The mare, too, rages with the desire of mating, and, smelling one another mouth to mouth, they provoke desire in each other. The male does not mount his own mother. Whence a horse sometimes, as said above, recognizing its mother substituted for another, suddenly fled and threw itself off a cliff. A horse mates at two or three years, but generates something weak. It is strong, however, from four years up to twenty, and is strong as long as it breeds. It mates its whole life. And it lives up to thirty or thirty-five years. A mare, however, up to forty. A stallion mates with a mare even while she is pregnant. No female accepts mating after impregnation, except a woman and a mare. The stallion fills the female's womb not on fixed days, but sometimes in one, or two, or three, or more. And the mating of young horses occurs before the determined time, if they have had good food. The mating of horses is not harmful, as the mating of bulls is. The birth of mares is better than that of all other four-footed creatures. And menstruation appears especially in mares and cows.

Pliny, in the same place: for breeding, indeed, few animals have less fertility than horses. In this kind, the pregnant one gives birth standing: beyond the others, she loves her offspring; if the mother is lost within the herd, the other mothers raise the young. Mating occurs at the spring equinox; in this kind they carry for eleven months, and give birth in the twelfth. It is established that in Lusitania, around the town of Olisipo and the river Tagus, mares turned to face the blowing west wind conceive a living breath, and this becomes offspring, and thus is born the swiftest of creatures, but does not exceed three years of life.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: horses produce single offspring, as do camels and elephants. They prescribe that mares' manes be shorn, so that they submit to donkeys' mating, humbled, for, with flowing manes, they are said to be proud of their glory. Alone among animals, mares run, after mating, facing north or south, depending on whether they have conceived a male or a female. They change color at once, to a redder coat or whatever is fuller. Horses and dogs and pigs are said to seek a morning neigh; more attentive females, however, are said to coax after midday. Likewise they think it useful for mares to be admitted for mating after one or three days from foaling, and force them though unwilling.

Solinus: mares' lust is extinguished by shearing their manes. In their offspring is born a love-charm, which the newly born bear on their foreheads, of tawny color, resembling the size of a dried fig, called 'hippomanes.' And if this is noticed at once, the mother by no means offers her udder to the foal to be nursed. The keener and more promising a foal is, the more deeply it plunges its nostrils in drinking. The male, as said, is never brought to war among the Scythians, since the females can relieve their bladders even in flight. In the neighboring lands of the town of Olisipo, mares are wanton with marvelous fecundity. For, the west wind blowing, they conceive, and, thirsting for males, are wedded by the breath of the breezes. Mares, then, bring forth offspring even of the winds, but these never live beyond three years.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: a mare is understood to be sterile if she does not begin to breed at first mating. If pregnant, however, she sometimes miscarries, if a wax candle is extinguished before her nostrils.

Palladius, book 4: breeding stallions, fattened or fed beforehand in the month of March, should be admitted to well-bred mares, and, once the females are filled, gathered back to the stables again. Nor, however, should we grant an equal number of mates to all, but, the strength of each stallion having been assessed, few or many unions should be assigned. This practice will make the stallions last to a considerable age. To a young horse of steady strength and form we should assign no more than twelve or fifteen, according to the quality of its strength. The same things must be considered especially in mares, that they be of long and large belly and body, but this should be observed among well-bred herds. The rest, released among the pastures with the males all year, may be filled indiscriminately. It is the nature of mares to complete their birth in the space of twelve months. This must be observed with breeding stallions: that they be kept some distance apart, because of the harm of jealous rage against one another. But for these herds the fattest pastures should be chosen in winter; cold and shaded areas should be provided in summer, and not areas born too soft, so that the firmness of the hooves feels nothing from roughness. If a mare refuses to submit to the male, crushed squill applied to her genitals will stir her lust. Then, once pregnant, they should not be pressed, nor should they endure hunger and cold, nor be crowded together in narrow spaces.

Pliny: [on] the kind of horses. They carry the offspring eleven months, and give birth in the twelfth. Mating occurs at the spring equinox, and is common at two years old for either sex, but the birth is stronger from three years old. The male breeds up to thirty-three years, since indeed after twenty years they are sent from the circus to breeding.
Zeno, in the book On Animals: a pregnant mare, when she smells what is in the fat around a cow's kidneys, her offspring emerges.

div.head: DE PULLIS EQUORUM NUTRIENDIS ATQUE DOMANDIS

cit.quote: Pliny: the mother, moreover, beyond other animals, loves her horse-offspring, which they say cannot touch the ground with its mouth for the three days nearest its birth.

Aristotle: the kind of horse naturally loves its own kind, so much so that, when a mare dies, another sometimes takes up the raising of her orphaned foal. Sometimes indeed a barren mare takes it up, but since she has no milk, the foal is endangered. A horse's foal touches its head with the back part of its foot, but a horse cannot.

Palladius, in the same place: we should submit mares, including those nursing males, in alternate years, so that the foals are pure and infuse the strength of abundant milk. The rest should be filled indiscriminately. The age of a stallion beginning service should be the start of his fifth year. A female will properly conceive even at two years old, since after ten years what is born from her will be slow. Newborn foals of mares should not be touched by hand, since constant touch harms them. As far as reason allows, they should be protected from cold. In foals, according to the merit of their age, those things should be considered that show a sign of good nature, which I have prescribed to be observed in the mothers or fathers. Cheerfulness, liveliness, and agility will also give proof. Foals should be tamed in March, unless they have passed the age of two years. Large, long, dark, muscular, and alert bodies should be considered, paired, small testicles, and the rest that has been said concerning the fathers. Their temperament, that they be either easily roused from the greatest calm, or, once roused to haste, not held back with difficulty: such is the reckoning of age - at two years and six months, the middle upper teeth fall; at four years, the canine teeth change; below the sixth year, the upper molars fall; in the sixth year, those it first changed are matched; in the seventh year, all its teeth are complete. From here signs of age are hidden, but in more advanced ones the temples begin to hollow, the eyebrows to whiten, the teeth generally to protrude.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: horses are bred in almost every part of the world, but those especially outstanding are in Scythia and Cappadocia; these delight in the sound of the trumpet and glory in encounters. Their lust is extinguished by shearing their manes. For it is their pride in these that drives them to mate. In horses especially, and in every kind of beast of burden, the ears show the mind's state - drooping in the weary, wavering in the fearful, limp in the sick, raised in the raging. Among the colors of horses, black is best, and chestnut or grey; white too is generally good. The rest are judged inferior.

Isidore: four things, as the ancients say, are sought in horses: form, beauty, merit, and color. Form: that the body be strong and solid in vigor, of fitting height, with a long side, very large and round haunches, a broadly open chest, the whole body knotted with density of muscles, and a dry foot, firm too with a hollow hoof. Beauty: that the head be small and dry, the skin close-adhering to the bones, short and alert ears, large eyes, open nostrils, an erect neck, thick mane and tail, solidity of hooves, fixed roundness. Merit: that it be bold in spirit, lively of foot, with trembling limbs, which is a sign of strength, and one that is easily roused from the greatest calm, or, once roused to haste, is not held back with difficulty. The horse's alertness is understood in the ears, its vigor in the trembling limbs. This is the color especially to be sought: bay, golden, rose-colored, myrtle, grey, dappled, hoary, white, spotted, black. In following order, however, varied, distinguished from black and bay. For the rest, a varied color, and ash-grey the worst. The ancients called bay 'vadium,' since among other animals it goes ['vadit'] more strongly. This is also the 'spadix,' which they call date-colored, and 'spadix' is named from the color of the palm-frond, which the Sicilians call 'spadica.' Grey is, as it were, having painted eyes, suffused with a certain color. Hoary is that of white and black color. Spotted is so named because of the white circles it has amid the darker patches; myrtle-colored, however, is a deep purple.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the horse, as Solomon says, is prepared for the day of battle, whose nobility and boldness the Lord describes to Job, speaking thus: will you give strength to the horse, or clothe his neck with thunder? The glory of his nostrils is terror; he digs the earth with his hoof. He exults boldly, goes forth to meet armed men, scorns fear and does not retreat before the sword, seething and fuming, he swallows the ground, and does not think it strange when the trumpet sounds. They are also said to smell battle from afar, the exhortation of the leaders and the howling of the army. Such horses, as said, are especially found in Scythia and Cappadocia; other proofs in battle were mentioned above in the chapter on the intelligence and affection of horses, and likewise on the choosing of the best. Aristotle says, moreover, that when a horse hears the neigh of the one it fights against, it recognizes it.

Solinus: in wars, horses know the enemies of their own side, so much so that in battles they attack enemies with their bite. The Scythians never bring males to war, since females can relieve their bladders even in flight.

Vegetius, in the first book on Military Matters: the training of horses to leap was rigorously demanded not only of recruits but also of paid soldiers. And such was the usual care given to this matter, that they learned to leap onto them not only from the right but also from the left side, and from bare stone, for they did this by constant practice, so that, namely, those who trained themselves so diligently in peace might mount without delay in the confusion of battle.

Vegetius, in the same book: armored horses, because of the protective gear and arms they bear, are indeed safe from wounds, but because of the hindrance and weight of the armor, they are easily captured, since they are frequently more exposed against scattered infantry than against cavalry in combat. Better, however, are those placed before the legions or mixed with the legionaries, when fighting occurs hand to hand at close quarters, since they often break through the enemy's battle line.

Isidore: horses have much vivacity. For they exult in the fields, smell battle, are roused to fight by the sound of the trumpet, and, fired by the voice, are urged to run. They grieve when defeated and exult when victorious, and so on, as said above. The lifespan of Persian, Epirote, and Sicilian horses, then, is up to fifty years. Shorter, however, for Spanish, Numidian, and Gallic horses.
Solinus: the lifespan is longer for males; we read of a horse that lived seventy years.

Aristotle: the horse alone among animals turns grey in old age, except man. For greyness is a certain measure of weakness of moisture in the brain and scarcity of digestion, and yet appears in horses because of the thinness of the bones of the head. The horse is strong, as said, from four years up to twenty, and is strong as long as it breeds; it lives up to thirty or thirty-five years. A mare, however, up to forty. It is contrary to the nature of all animals, however, that when a horse grows old, its teeth whiten.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the horse has forty teeth, of which it loses the first ones from birth at thirty months, two on each side, and in the following year as many more next to them. Some, however, say that in our part of the world, as Pliny says, from the fifth year beginning it loses two, which regrow in the sixth year. In the seventh year, however, it has all its teeth regrown and unchangeable. Further, in old age they whiten, as said.
Pliny, book 8: a horse is reported to have lived seventy-five years; this animal, however, is subject to almost the same diseases as man.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: from the flesh of horses, wasps and hornets are born.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: they report that mares touched by menstrual blood, while pregnant, suffer miscarriage, indeed even at the mere sight of it from a distance, however far off. Horse's gall alone, among things forbidden, is condemned as a poison, and so it is not lawful for the flamens of sacred rites to touch a horse, although at Rome it is sacrificed in public rites.
Pliny, in the same: frogs boiled in water thin out the mange of horses, until they can be smeared on it, and they say that, once healed this way, it does not return.

Aristotle: horses that graze suffer from a foot-ailment like gout, and they cast their old hooves and grow new ones in their place. Likewise, when they are pastured indoors, this happens to them too. And a sign of this is that the hind limbs draw together from the tightening. Likewise a horse sometimes stops eating, and it benefits it to be bled a little. Likewise a contraction of the humors occurs in horses, a sign of which is that all the veins stand out, as do the head and neck, and it is a burden to them to walk. A gathering of venom occurs in them. There also occurs in them another ailment of the mouth, called 'formi,' a sign of which is that the palate sags and the breath grows hot; this ailment has no remedy unless it heals of itself. Rabies occurs in horses, a sign of which is that their ears then turn back toward the neck. There is also a bladder ailment, a sign of which is that they cannot urinate, and drag their hindquarters and hooves. A pregnant mare, if she smells a candle just extinguished, will miscarry.

div.head: DE DIVERSIS EQUORUM GENERIBUS ET EQUIFERO ET EQUICERVO

cit.quote: Isidore: there are three kinds of horses. One noble, suited for battles and honors; another common and herd-like, suited for carrying loads or riding. The ancients called these 'veredi,' as if 'carrying carriages' [vehentes redas], that is, drawing them. A third arises from the mixing of different kinds, which is also called 'bigenerum' [of two kinds], since it is born from different parents, like the mule.

Pliny: from a female donkey and a mare, indeed, a mule is produced in the thirteenth month, otherwise an animal outstanding in strength for labor. For such offspring, they choose mares neither younger than four years nor older than ten, and they say each kind is kept from the other, except in the infancy of the offspring, which they approach once nursed with milk. For this reason they bring stolen foals in darkness to the udders of mares or the young donkeys to the udders of female donkeys. And so it has been observed that what is born from two different kinds becomes of a third kind, and resembles neither parent, and that these very creatures, so born, do not breed - true of every kind of animal - and so mules do not give birth. Theophrastus, however, reports that in Cappadocia they do give birth, and that this animal there is of its own separate kind.

Isidore: the appearance of centaurs gave the name to that species, that is, men mixed with horses, whom some say were horsemen of the Thessalians. But because, dashing about in war, they seemed like a single body of horses and men, they asserted centaurs were invented from this. So they tell certain fabulous portents of men, which do not exist, but are invented from the circumstances of things.
Isidore, the same: we call those horses 'wild' [equiferi], moreover, that are driven from the wild kind, and so cannot pass to civic dignity.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'equicervus' [horse-stag] is an eastern animal of the size of a stag, but having hooves on its feet and hair on its neck, like a horse, descending along the shoulders. The male has horns; the female lacks them.
Aristotle: the 'equicervus' is found in a region of Greece, according to some, around the Phasis. It has hair under the neck domestically, resembling a beard, and horns similar to those of a fawn.
Dioscorides: the blood of breeding stallions is mixed into caustic remedies. Mare's milk softens the bowels and disturbs a man. Horse dung, both raw and burnt, checks flowing blood.
Haly Abbas: [on] horse, of horses, woman. [Fragmentary heading list in the source.]
