If a cow is separated from the herd, it is lost, since it is eaten by wild beasts. The wild cow has horns curving toward each other, and for this reason nature gave it another benefit, namely the casting of dung to a distance, so that the hunter is held off by it. In the region of Greece around the Phasis, wild cows abound. They are black, very strong, having feet cloven into two hooves, long hair, and drooping faces. Cow's milk, among other things, is very thick; it has more milk, moreover, like the sheep, than the offspring needs. And so it is fitting for cheese to be made from it. In the region called Ephesus in Greek there are small cows, from which milk is drawn in abundance. There are, moreover, certain bloating foods that multiply milk, like beans, which suit cows and goats. At mating, the cow follows the bull and mounts him. And the bull's own mounting of her is heavy, so that she must bend. The time fitting for mating and birth is after two years. And the cow's time of pregnancy is nine months, and birth occurs in the tenth. And when cows breed often, they think it signifies much rain to come in winter. The cow lives, for the most part, fifteen years. Cows and female donkeys menstruate and discharge much, because of the size of their bodies.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: Pliny denies that pregnant cows carry except in the right side of the womb, and when they bear twins, menstruation appears both in cows and mares, especially in warm regions, where humors and surpluses abound more in animals. But the menstrual matter is sometimes expelled through the bladder in the urine. Cow's urine is very sharp. A cow grazing in a meadow at thunder time flees from the face of the lightning, the bull remaining and not afraid.
Rhazes: beef is thick and nourishes much, generates foul and thick blood, and is unsuited except to those who take much exercise: those subject to melancholic illnesses should abstain from it.

Avicenna, in the second canon: beef is of very abundant nourishment, thick, melancholic, generating melancholic illnesses. Better than it is the flesh of calves. Beef generates vitiligo, cancer, scabies, bad impetigo, leprosy, elephantiasis, and varicose veins, and quartan fevers. Likewise beef and other such flesh cause mental derangement through dryness, and thicken the spleen. Sour broth of beef is good for choleric looseness, for it checks it. Melon rinds dissolve beef, namely when it is cooked with them. The better season to eat it, however, is spring and the beginning of summer.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: beef is dry and generates turbid and thick blood, yet nourishes much, but is digested slowly, unless taken with wine and garlic. Cow's milk is very thick and does not easily freeze from cold, but its wateriness separates from it, and the thick residue is formed. By fire, however, it thickens. In the region of Ambedor cows are of such large body that the milker must stand on his feet; these provide an abundance of milk beyond measure, and dogs too in that region are large, and all animals except donkeys.
Avicenna: cow's milk has the most butter, and is thicker and richer than sheep's.

Isaac Judaeus: cow's [milk] is less watery than others and sharp, and more nourishing. It suits the stomach, strengthens the members, cools the heat of the liver and stomach. It is also good for other things, once its buttery quality is removed. For, given to drink, it eases the gnawing pain of hot humors, strengthens and tempers natural heat, increases flesh, removes choleric diarrhea and choleric tenesmus, and aids ulcers of the intestines and bladder and womb. It should be given thus, and it will be best when as much cold water as there is milk is added, and it is cooked so long until all the water is gone. And the more often you do this, the better it will be for these purposes.

Avicenna, in the second canon: cow's gall is stronger than the other galls of four-footed animals. It is put in plasters for wounds that are erysipelas and of vehement pain. Cow's shins, that is the burnt bones of the legs, check bleeding and looseness of the bowels. Cow dung is among those things given for the lung and consumption and the like. From it a plaster is made for sciatica. Likewise, applied with vinegar over hot boils, it calms them. It also suits abscesses that are behind the ears. Necks of cowhide, applied with vinegar, benefit impetigo and scabies that can be scraped off when not of vehement depth. Likewise applied with honey and vinegar over wounds, and burnt and washed, they are effective for curing nits.
Belbetus: cow's blood, if poured over a wound, checks bleeding.
Aristotle: cow's horns, if heated, bend in every direction, as said, and if anointed with oil and pitch, are effective against foot pain and against harm from snow.
Pliny: cow's liver, too, heals celiacs and dysentery sufferers.
Isidore: the wether [vervex, castrated ram] is male, or named because it has worms in its head, which, roused by an itch, cause them to butt one another, and, fighting, strike with great force.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the wether, or ram, has horns curled in the manner of a circle, with which it strives to defend the flock. From natural fierceness it strikes the ground with its right foot, when it is angry or stunned or afraid, and this especially at mating time: for half the year it lies on one side, and for half on the other. Its flesh is hotter and less moist than that of ewes, and harder to digest. The lamb, naturally abhorring the wolf, though it has never seen one, flees at once, whereas it would neither flee nor fear a horse or another animal it saw. Its flesh does not easily submit to excretion, yet descends easily from the stomach, but is dissolved from the members with great difficulty. For it generates a viscous humor. A yearling lamb, however, is more praiseworthy because of the temperateness of moisture and dryness. Everything in the sheep is useful, namely wool, hide, flesh, milk.

Dioscorides: wether-fat has a power similar to pig's. It usefully cures hysterical or anal ailments, and helps burns. Wether's gall, applied on wool and placed on the navel, loosens infants' bowels. Wether dung, applied as a poultice with vinegar, corrects black blemishes: it removes growing corns from the body. Applied, it cures erysipelas. Mixed with wax and oil, it heals burns.

Isidore: the calf [vitulus] and heifer [vitula] are named from greenness [viriditas], that is from a green age, like 'virgo' [maiden]. The heifer, then, is young and has not yet calved. For one that has calved is a young cow [iuvenca] or a cow. The young bull [iuvencus], however, is so named because it begins to help [iuvare] the uses of men in cultivating the land, or because among the Jews only a young bull, never a full-grown bull, was ever sacrificed to God. For age, too, is considered in sacrificial victims.

Palladius, book 5, on calves: calves are usually born in the month of April; their mothers should be aided by abundance of fodder, so that they can suffice for the burden of labor and milk. To the calves themselves, however, roasted and ground millet mixed with milk should be given, in the manner of spelt-porridge.

Aristotle: they say the gestation of calves is ten months, and if born before this time, it will not live, since its hooves will not be complete. If a calf is castrated, it can live twenty years and more, if only its body happens to be so. The calf alone, among every kind of animal, has a deeper voice than that of older oxen. For all other creatures have a sharper voice in youth, thicker in old age. When male calves reach a certain age, they go alone and graze without females until the time of mating. But when the time of mating approaches, they no longer graze alone, but with the cows. They begin to mate after two years, but then their offspring are few, weak, and small.

Pliny: to this alone, among all animals whose tail is rather long, is it not, as with the rest, of full measure as soon as born, for it grows until it reaches the ground. Wherefore the testing of sacrificial victims rests on the calf's tail, that it should reach the joints of the hocks.

Palladius: calves, however, as the Carthaginian [Mago] says, should be castrated in May, at a tender age, so that, with a split rod, the testicles are compressed, and, gradually crushed, are dissolved. But he prescribes this be done as the moon wanes, in spring or autumn. Others, with the calf tied to a frame, grasp with two narrow tin rods, as if with forceps, those very sinews, which the Greeks call 'cremasters.' Having gripped these, they cut the stretched testicles with iron and cut them out with force, so that something of the heads of these sinews is left clinging. This procedure both prevents excessive bleeding and does not entirely unman the young bulls by removing their manly vigor. Nor should it be overlooked, as many do, that they force them to mate immediately after castration. For it is certain, indeed, that offspring is generated by them, but that they themselves perish from the flow of blood; the wounds of castrated animals, however, should be smeared with ash of vine-cuttings and silver dross. The castrated animal should be kept from drink and fed sparse food. And for the following three days it should be given tender treetops and soft shrubs and green herbs, sweeter foliage, fattening or riverine. With liquid pitch too, mixed with ash and a little oil, the wounds should be carefully anointed after three days. But a better kind of castration, subsequent practice has found. For, the young bull tied and thrown down, the testicles are enclosed in tightened skin, and there, with a wooden rod pressing, they are cut off with heated axes or hatchets. Or, what is better, with an iron tool shaped for this purpose, so that it holds the likeness of a sword. For thus the edge of the falling iron is pressed around the rod itself with each blow, and so it removes the delay of pain by the benefit of speed, and, the veins and skins burnt and constricted against bleeding, the scar, formed in a way together with the wound itself, protects the wound.
Aristotle: calves should be castrated after one year. Otherwise they will be small. Castrated ones, however, live longer.
Pliny, book 18: further, young bulls should be castrated as the moon wanes.

Pliny: they apply calf's flesh to a human bite and do not remove it before the fifth day. All marrows, indeed, soften, fill out, dry, and warm. Among the rest, however, calf's marrow is praiseworthy. Calf's tallow too, ground with salt, is praised as most useful for ulcers of the head. But also for ulcers and cracks of the mouth, calf's or ox's tallow with donkey's fat or basil juice heals. Besides, swelling of the testicles is checked by calf's tallow, with soda added, or even with the same animal's dung boiled with vinegar. For bloating that occurs in the area of the rear, too, calf's tallow with rue is effective. Likewise, against poisons that kill through ulceration, calf's tallow helps, and against aconite and hemlock. Warmed calf's gall thins dark scars. Calf's gall too effectively heals oozing ulcers of the head. With this, warmed with vinegar, nits too are removed. Calf's spleen, boiled and ground with honey in wine and applied, heals oozing ulcers. Calf's dung too, boiled in wine, benefits ailments of the intestines. Fumigating those stung by a scorpion with the same dung is useful for them. The dung of a calf that has not yet tasted grass benefits gout sufferers. And dropsy sufferers are helped by applying the dung of a male calf. Fresh calf's dung is also applied to erysipelas. Ash of the same dung, applied with vinegar, checks bleeding. Ash of the same dung, too, boiled with lily bulbs with a little honey added, calms the pains of varicose veins, and all inflammations and suppurations threatening to develop. It also benefits gout and joint diseases, especially from male calves.

Isidore: [the term 'beast' applies] to lions, leopards, tigers, wolves and foxes, dogs and apes and the rest that are fierce with mouth or claws, except serpents. Beasts [bestiae], moreover, are so named from the force [vis] with which they rage. Wild creatures [ferae], however, are so called because they are carried [ferantur] by their own natural desire, exercising freedom. For they wander freely here and there, and are carried wherever their spirit leads them.
Aristotle: the fighting of beasts occurs only because of food, or because of territory, or because of a female.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: wars occur among animals for four reasons, namely because of natural pride, because of food, because of offspring, namely to defend it.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: some beasts injure by their bite even without rabies, since they have venom in their teeth, like the cat and the crocodile and the like. Some, too, fall into rabies, like the dog; it is also said that the fox becomes rabid, and the weasel likewise. Many too, according to some, have become rabid and bitten their masters, and have contracted the madness that arises from the other forms of rabies. The leopard, however, and the lion, these predators and those similar to them, are not, like dogs, safe for men. Rather, their teeth and claws are not empty, but are venomous. Wherefore their bites must be treated, and the wound of their claws, first with drawing out, then with healing over; but in drawing them out a small remedy suffices. The sweat of beasts is venomous, and from drinking it the face turns green and develops abscesses, and a foul-smelling sweat runs from the body, as from the armpits. Its treatment is vomiting with warm water and theriac made with sealed earth.
Haly Abbas: [on] beasts: it is a remedy for arthritic conditions. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: there are, moreover, certain animals that seem to hold a middle place between beasts and herd animals, or to belong to both kinds in common. For, for example, it is agreed that the boar is especially fierce with its tusks, which nevertheless, following Isidore, we have counted among herd animals, since it is suited for men to eat. Pliny too calls the wild donkey a wild beast, and so does Jerome, though the book of Deuteronomy counts the wild donkey among the clean animals fit for eating. Many such animals, moreover, are found. Whence Pliny, as said above, says fallow deer are rarely tamed, and yet cannot properly be called wild beasts. For many creatures are neither gentle nor wild, but of a nature midway between the two, like the boar in the field, the dolphin in the sea. Having spoken, then, of herd animals according to the order of the letters of the alphabet, we intend, God helping, to proceed next concerning beasts according to the same order.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: [on] stags, men, an animal. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Helinand of Froidmont: the elk is an animal in the Hercynian forest, quite similar to goats in form, with varied hide, but somewhat exceeding them in size. They lack horns, and their legs are without joints and have no knuckles. They do not lie down for the sake of rest, nor, if by some misfortune they have fallen, can they raise or lift themselves up. For them, trees serve as resting places; they lean against these, and thus, reclining slightly, take their rest. When hunters have noticed, from their tracks, the place where they are accustomed to take refuge, they undermine the roots of the trees there, or cut them, only so much that the topmost appearance or the stump of the standing trees is left. When, by habit, they lean there, they burden the weakened trees with their weight, and fall together with them. The elk is to be compared to a mule, its upper lip so pendulous that it cannot graze unless walking backward. The island of Gangania, off the region of Germany, sends forth an animal like the elk, whose hocks, like the elephant's, cannot bend. And so it does not lie down when it must sleep, but a tree alone supports the drowsy creature, one that threatens to fall nearly to the point of collapse, so that the wild creature causes its ruin while leaning on its accustomed support - thus it is caught. Otherwise it is difficult to capture, since it is endowed with a stubborn agility of the hocks and an ungraspable speed of flight.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: this beast seems to be the same as the 'maclin,' of which, indeed, more will be said below.

Physiologus: the 'anabulla' is a beast of Ethiopia, having a neck like a horse's, feet and legs like an ox's, a head like a camel's; it has white spots, of a very ruddy color, marking each limb; and since the animal is sprinkled with such beauty, its hide, most striking to see, is sold dearly for the delight of the eyes. The 'aptalon' is an animal similar to a roe deer, exceedingly foul-smelling, which a man cannot approach. And it has two very sharp horns, like two sickles, curved back: this animal, when thirsty, comes to the Euphrates to drink, and once it has drunk, it approaches a certain thicket of vines planted with small and slender branches, so that there, as if playing, it may rub itself among those withes. From this it happens that it gets entangled among them, so that it cannot pull itself free. And then it lets out a great cry, which, when the hunter hears it, he rushes upon it and kills it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'aptalon' is a most fierce animal, so much so that the hunter cannot approach it; it has, however, long horns having the shape of a saw, such that it can even cut down large and tall trees and bring them to the ground. And when thirsty, it comes to the river Euphrates and drinks. There is, moreover, a shrub called 'herecin' in Greek, having thin and long branches, in which, playing, it entangles its horns with its branches, and thus, crying out for a long time, it is heard and killed by the hunter.
Aristotle: the 'aucatinor' is an animal the size of a hunting-hound puppy; its intelligence is greater when it is small than when it is grown.

Solinus: the 'bonasus' is an animal born in the regions of Phrygia; it has a bull's head, and thereafter its whole body, but a mane like a horse's alone. Its horns, however, curve back upon themselves in such manifold coils that if one runs into them, one is not wounded, but whatever defense its forehead denies that monster, its belly supplies. For when it turns to flight, it discharges dung from its excited belly, spreading it over a length of three acres. The heat of this scorches whatever it touches. Thus, by this noxious discharge, it drives off its pursuers.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: perhaps this animal is the same as the wild cow, of which mention was made above according to Aristotle, which has horns curving toward each other. For wild oxen or buffaloes are also called by another name, bisons, as said above.

Aristotle: the 'bonasus' is an animal on Mount Messapus in Paeonia, similar to a bull, but in it too there is a mane descending to both sides of the shoulder-blades; its hairs are softer than a horse's and shorter; its manes are all continuous and reach as far as the eyes. And those of its hairs that are lower resemble wool. But the hairs that are over its forehead meet, until they are separated by a parting. Its color is red, and it may incline toward black. Its voice resembles a bull's voice, nor does it have upper teeth, just as the bull does not. It has two hoof-coverings and a tail short in proportion to its body, and digs the earth. It has a hide that endures many blows; its flesh is sweet, and so it is hunted. And when it is struck, it flees and rests. But when weakened, it fights, and ejects dung over a distance of four paces. When, however, the time of its giving birth approaches, many of that kind gather, and beforehand pile up dung around it, and set it up like a wall. This is, moreover, an animal of much dung.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: Cacus is a monster in Arcadia, entirely bristled like a pig. And, as the philosopher Adelinus writes, it belches flames from its breath by its breathing, that is a fiery breath, especially when moved by anger. It dwells in caves above the Tiber and suddenly attacks herds of bulls and cows, seizing three or four by the tails and, by the force of its strength, dragging them secretly into its cave, walking backward, so that it cannot easily be tracked. Nor is it hostile to animals alone, but lies in wait most dangerously for the horned owl too, although it greatly fears man himself. If one asks how flame can be vomited from an animal's mouth, so effective that it burns whatever it touches nearby, and yet the animal's own body is not consumed by such flame, the answer can be given that, while the breath is still within the animal's innards, spread widely through its various members, it is merely warm, and does not everywhere overflow into flames. But once belched out and continued and multiplied against some object, it receives a body and the power of burning, just as we see the light of the sun multiply its rays through the middle of a beryl gem, and, at the very point of a sharpened tip, the rays receive the power of fire upon the matter beneath them, and fire is made violent. Similar to this animal were those of which it is read in the book of Wisdom, that they breathed fires from their mouth.

Isidore: the chameleon does not have one color, but is sprinkled with varied hues, like the leopard. This little creature's body varies with the most ready change to match the colors it sees, whereas the bodily substance of other animals is not so readily changeable.
Radulphus of Flaix, on Leviticus: the chameleon pretends to be gentle when ill, although otherwise it is an untamed animal.
Gloss: the chameleon is an animal born to mock, deceitful, rapacious, gluttonous, and so unclean according to the law.
Ambrose: the chameleon is said to feign different appearances, with varied color.

Aristotle: the chameleon is a very fearful animal, on account of which it changes into many colors. The cause of its fear, indeed, is the scarcity of its blood and heat. Whence it is also very lean, and is called the 'lion of the earth.' Its face is like that of an animal composed of a pig and an ape. It has claws similar to the hooked claws of birds. The alteration of its color occurs when its hide is inflated. It dwells in caverns, like the small lizard.

Solinus: throughout all of Asia the chameleon is very common, a four-footed animal, with the face of a lizard, except that its legs are straight and longer, joined to its belly; a long tail, likewise twisted into a spiral. Its claws are hooked, with a fine curvature. Its gait, however, is sluggish, and much the same as a tortoise's motion. Its body is rough of skin, such as we find in crocodiles. Its eyes are sunken and received inward in a hollow recess, which it never covers by blinking. It directs its sight not with round pupils, but with the gaze of a rigid, fixed orb. Its gape is perpetual and without the use of that function. Indeed, since it takes no food nor is nourished by drink nor lives on any nourishment other than the air it draws in. Its color is varied and changeable in an instant, so that it becomes the same color as whatever thing it joins itself to. There are two colors it cannot mimic: red and white; the rest it easily imitates. Its body is almost without flesh. Its vital organs lack a spleen, and only a very little blood is found, and only in its tiny heart: it hides in winter, comes forth in spring. It is vulnerable to the crow, by whom, when it is killed, it kills its victor once it is itself devoured. For if the bird eats even a little of it, it dies at once. But the raven has a remedy for healing, nature extending a helping hand. For when it senses itself afflicted, it takes a laurel leaf and recovers its health.
Solinus, on chameleons: on land, then, octopuses become similar to whatever thing they approach. For the smoothness of their skin mimics what is near them.

Pliny: although Judea produces the chameleon more frequently, its shape and size are those of a lizard, except that its legs are straight and taller. Its sides are joined to its belly, as in fish, and likewise its spine. Its snout projects, so that, on a small scale, it is not unlike a pig's. Its very long tail tapers to thinness, and coils itself in viper-like spirals. Its claws are hooked, its movement rather slow, like a tortoise's. Its body is rough, like a crocodile's. Its eyes are in a hollow recess, of slight separation, very large and the same color as its body. It never covers them, nor by moving the pupil, but by turning the whole eye it looks about. It itself stands tall, its mouth always agape. Alone among animals it is nourished neither by food nor drink, but by air alone. Around wild fig trees it is fierce but otherwise harmless; and more remarkable still in the nature of its color. For it changes this repeatedly, in its eyes and tail and whole body. And it always renders whatever it touches nearby, except red and white; upon death it turns pale. There is flesh on its head and jaws and at the joint of the tail, exceedingly little, and nowhere else on its whole body. Blood is only in its heart and around its eyes. Its organs are without a spleen; in the winter months it hides, like the lizard.
Pliny, in the same: they report that the chameleon's eyes turn all the way around. Its lung, moreover, is proportionally the largest, and there is nothing else inside it.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: the chameleon is similar in size to the crocodile, differing only in the fault of its spine and its curvature and the breadth of its tail. No animal is thought more timid, and so it is of a changeable, varicolored nature. Its power is greatest against the hawk kind. For it is said to pull down one flying above it toward itself, and to offer itself willingly to be torn apart by other animals.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: the chameleon too is reported to have many things useful for medicine in itself. Its head and throat, if burnt with oak wood, are said by Democritus to cause a gathering of rains and thunder. Likewise its liver, burnt on roof tiles. The rest, pertaining to sorceries, which he relates, we shall omit as false. Its right eye, if torn out while it is living, removes white spots of the eye with goat's milk; its tongue too, bound on, prevents the dangers of childbirth. Its tongue, if removed while living, is said to be powerful for the outcomes of judgments. Its heart is beneficial against quartan fevers, bound on with black wool of the first shearing. Its right front foot, bound onto the left arm in hyena skin, is said to benefit against robbery and nocturnal terrors. Likewise its right teat against fears and terrors. But also its left foot, roasted in an oven with the herb of the same name, an ointment added, made into little cakes from it, is said, if we believe it, to make a man invisible. Its right jaw too, like its foot, is effective against fears and terrors. Its gall is believed to correct cataracts and suffusions, especially with a three-day anointing; it is also believed that, dripped onto the spleen, it puts serpents to sleep.

Isidore: the giraffe [camelopardus] is so named because, although it is spotted with white marks like a leopard, and has a neck like a horse's and feet like an ox's, it is nevertheless similar to a camel in its head. Ethiopia produces it.

Pliny, book 8: a certain resemblance to camels is transferred into two animals. The Ethiopians, indeed, call a beast the 'nabun,' having a neck like a horse's, feet and legs like an ox's, a head like a camel's, with white spots marking a ruddy color, whence it is also called the 'camelopardalis.' This was first seen at the circus games of the dictator Caesar at Rome. From then on it has been seen from time to time, more remarkable for its appearance than for its ferocity. Wherefore it has also acquired almost the name of a sheep.

Isidore: the dog [canis] seems to have its name from Greek, for in Greek it is called 'cynos,' although some think it was named from the resonance of its bark. Their nature is such that they cannot exist apart from men. In dogs there are two qualities: strength and speed.

Aristotle: the dog is an irascible animal, and one that fawns on men, hairy over its whole body, like the pig and the bear; it has teeth above and below and a single belly, and after the belly, intestine. It has many offspring and many teats, and many clefts in its feet, like the pig too. It has five toes on its front feet and four on its hind feet, like the lion and wolf. It also has dry dung, like the wolf, and a long spleen, like man and the pig; besides, sleep and waking, growth and decay, life and death, and other accidents arising from the senses, are present in dogs, as in horses and men: dogs shed no teeth except the front ones, and this only in one way; both male and female shed them after four months. And so some say they do not shed teeth at all, others that they change all of them. The dog flees, however, with lowered ears. The dog has a belly, that is a stomach, similar to a man's stomach, although it is larger than a man's. The dog does not shed any tooth until a similar one grows in its place. Nor are young dogs distinguished from older ones except by their teeth, since the teeth of the young are white and sharp, but those of the old are black and blunt.

Alexander Neckam: the dog is an unclean animal, returning to its vomit, irascible, horrible in barking. It tears at a strange dog and gnaws bones. When it has these, it shuns the company of another dog. It alone, however, knows its own name.

Physiologus: the dog is said not to be able to live without man; but when it has swum across a river holding meat or something like that in its mouth and sees the shadow of a dog, it opens its mouth, and, while hoping to have the other, loses the very thing it holds. The same, applied to the intestines of men or bound to the wounds of a wounded man, heals them. Its tongue, too, heals ulcers. Its voice, as age advances, becomes deeper and thicker than at first.

Pythagoras, in the book of the Romans: if a man carries with him wood by which a man's bone was burnt, dogs will not bark nor rise up against him. Moreover, if you place in someone's wine a stone that a rabid dog has bitten, whoever drinks it will become irascible and quarrelsome.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: male dogs do not easily harm female dogs. It is a shameful habit of dogs that they foully befoul the most beautiful and green places. In urinating, moreover, they raise a leg and smell their own urine. For some of these are sometimes of a pleasant smell, and this animal is much affected by pleasant smell, especially in the urine of dogs of this kind, and for this reason they also smell each other's hindquarters in turn. Many have said that a dog, if outside human habitation, is driven by a kind of frenzy. A dog's tongue is medicinal, and by licking its own or another's wounds it heals them. If it cannot reach its own wound with its tongue, it licks its foot and, having smoothed it with the medicine of its saliva, applies it to the wound, confident of the remedy that the nature of its tongue has instilled in it.

Pliny: dogs have many teats over the whole belly, in a double row. There is no marrow in dogs' legs as there is in beasts of burden. Teeth change in the lion and the dog, but only those called canine ones. Their fierce attack is calmed by a man crouching on the ground.

Pliny, book 29, on suckling puppies: the ancients considered dogs so pure for food that they even used them in place of sacrificial victims to appease the gods. Further, just as geese earned honor by defending the Capitol while the dogs stayed silent, so dogs hang as an annual punishment, fixed on a fork of elder wood on an alder tree: whoever passes his own urine into a dog's urine feels numbness of the loins.
Avicenna, in the second canon: cheese-whey fattens dogs greatly and nourishes them well.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the dog, then, as is read, is born blind, is affected by the moon, and is very strong in smell. It has sharp teeth and a very wide-cleft mouth; it bites and licks, does not chew the cud, but gnaws. It returns to its vomit; before it lies down it circles its bed; it suffers from 'boulimos,' that is a most ravenous hunger.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the dog is a beast teachable for every game; it loves its master and guards his dwelling by keeping watch, and by night betrays wrongdoers with its barking. There is also a certain kind of dog that recognizes thieves by smell and distinguishes them from other men with implacable hatred.

Isidore: nothing, moreover, is more sagacious than dogs. For they have more sense than other animals. For they alone recognize their own names, they recognize their masters and love them, and defend their dwellings. They throw themselves to death for their masters, alone and voluntarily, and run with them after prey. They do not abandon even their master's body when dead.

Ambrose: the dog is a sagacious animal, which, when it has found the track of a wolf or hare, gathers certain proofs directed toward following it along the path, comes to a fork in the path, and silently investigates the beginnings of each individual path, so as to recognize by scent in which direction it turned. It is also naturally implanted in this animal to keep the memory of shared food and to return gratitude, and to extend anxious vigilance for the safety of its masters.
Solinus: dogs alone recognize their own names, remember their routes. Egyptian dogs never lap from the Nile except while running, wary of the ambushes of crocodiles.

Pliny: dogs alone know their own master and recognize a stranger if he suddenly comes. They remember routes, however long. They alone recognize a familiar voice, nor is any creature's memory greater, except man's. In hunting there is great skill and sagacity in them; the dog searches out and follows almost every track. Dragging by a leash the tracker accompanying it to the wild beast, and even leaping across water, it catches the wind and scent; and it stretches its snout toward the lairs.

Pliny, book 25, in the same: dogs [eat] a certain herb, by which they relieve loss of appetite, and chew it in our sight, but in such a way that it is never understood which one it is, since it is already seen eaten. It is also said to heal itself with a certain herb when struck by a serpent, but, with a man watching, does not pluck it, out of its own cunning. This animal also seems to have shown vomiting to man.
Aristotle: for when a dog is sick, it eats the root of some herb in order to vomit.

Physiologus: the dog excels other dumb creatures in three things: in discerning, in loving, in serving. For they discern their master from strangers, nor do they hate those they pursue, but are zealous for the one they love, and, from the consciousness of anxious love, keep watch. Its custom is to play with its shepherd, to know the flock, to pursue wild beasts lying in wait. To this alone, by nature, is it implanted to be willingly driven to what it is prepared for, and, by a certain formula of obedience, to be held in suspense by the expectation of trained fear alone, until, by a nod or a sign, it is sent to carry out its task.

div.head: DE AFFECTU CANUM AD DOMINOS SUOS

cit.quote: Solinus: dogs love all their masters equally, as is clear from examples. For in Epirus, a dog's barking betrayed its master's attacker, recognized in an assembly. When Jason of Lycia was killed, his dog, refusing food, died of starvation. King Lysimachus's dog threw itself into the flames when its master's pyre was lit, and was consumed by the fire along with him. Two hundred dogs brought back the king of the Garamantes from exile, fighting against those who resisted. The Colophonians and Castabalans, leading dogs into war, drew up their front lines with them. When, under the consuls Appius Junius and Publius Silius, a master was condemned, his dog, when it could not be driven away, accompanied him into prison, and, when he was soon struck down, followed him with howling. And when, out of pity for this, the chance of food was offered to it, it carried the food to the mouth of the deceased; finally, when the corpse was thrown into the Tiber, it swam alongside and tried to support it.

Pliny: [on] horses and dogs. A dog is also reported to have fought against robbers on his master's behalf, and, worn out with wounds, not to have left the body, driving off birds and wild beasts. Of another, too, in Epirus, we have an account: it recognized, in an assembly, its master's attacker, and, by tearing and barking, drove him to be forced to confess his crime.

Ambrose: no one can be so faithful in keeping a benefit as a dog, and mindful of gratitude. Since indeed it knows how to leap upon robbers on its master's behalf and to prevent nocturnal approaches by strangers, dogs are prepared to die for their masters and to die together with their masters. Often, too, dogs have provided evident proofs to convict the guilty of a murder committed. For at Antioch, in a more remote part of the world, they say a man was killed who had a dog attached to him. For a certain soldier, out of desire for plunder, had killed him and departed to other regions; but as the corpse lay unburied, a frequent crowd of onlookers stood by, and the dog, with a tearful expression, mourned the misfortunes of its master. But the one who had brought about the death, with human cunning, so as to gain the presumed trust of innocence, approached that circle of the watching crowd as if grieving. Then the dog, its lament of grief set aside for a moment, took up the boldness of vengeance, and, having seized him, held him, and, as if murmuring some pitiable epilogue, moved everyone to tears and brought proof to the trial, since it held only him, out of the many, and did not let go.
Physiologus: there are, moreover, several kinds of dogs. For some track down wild forest creatures for catching, some birds, some herd flocks, some guard houses.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: there are three kinds of dogs. Of these the noblest are the greyhounds, otherwise hunting hounds, whose form is more elegant and swifter for running and better suited to hunting; these are strong in the chest, do not know how to bark, and, unless led out for the chase, keep themselves within the house. Others are suited for hunting, with long, hanging ears; these pursue the beast by scent and persistent barking and drive it to exhaustion, until they bring it down into the hands of the hunters or the greyhounds. And once they begin to pursue the one ordered by the hunters, they do not abandon it, even if they find many others. The third kind is that given generally to all for guarding. And these, although coarser than the rest, are nevertheless more suited to men's service. Among these, moreover, some are large, some medium, some small. There are also very tiny lapdogs, which noble ladies carry in their laps. All of these defend houses by barking and are hostile to strangers. When they lie before tables, they arrange themselves so that with one eye they watch their masters' generous hand, and with the other so that they can see the door of the house.

Aristotle: it is proper to greyhounds that they can leap better with exertion than at rest. The greyhound mates at eight months, and male greyhounds live about ten years, and female greyhounds twelve. The greater part of other dogs, however, fourteen. In greyhounds, females are more suited to training than males. Greyhounds have a large nose and good smell. In Egypt dogs are very small, since their food is scarce there. Likewise dogs that follow sheep vary in size.
Pliny, book 10: Laconian, that is greyhound, dogs live ten years, females twelve. The other kinds, however, fifteen years, sometimes twenty.
Pliny: [on] dogs. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Solinus: dogs born among the Albanians are preferred to wild beasts, they break bulls, overpower lions, and hold fast whatever is set against them. For these reasons they have deserved to be recorded in the annals. We read that, when Alexander sought India, two dogs were sent to him by the king of Albania, of which one so despised the pigs and bears offered to it that, offended by the base prey, it lay down for a long time like a lazy creature, resembling a coward, and Alexander, through ignorance, ordered it killed as if useless. The other, however, at the urging of those who had accompanied the gift, killed a lion that was released against it. And soon, when it saw an elephant, exulting remarkably, it first wore out the beast by cunning. Then, to the greatest horror of the onlookers, it brought it down to the ground. Dogs of this kind grow to a very large form, with terrifying barks, resounding as if with a roar. These traits are proper to Albanian dogs; the rest are common to all, for they all love their masters equally, and the other things said above.

Physiologus: dogs, as said, male ones do not easily harm female dogs, and this happens in many kinds of beasts. In every kind of animal, moreover, males live longer than females, except in greyhounds, in which the opposite occurs.

Aristotle: greyhounds indeed live about ten years, female greyhounds twelve. In the kind of greyhounds, indeed, females live longer than males, because of the labor of the males themselves. In others, however, males live longer than females. Likewise, among greyhounds, females are easier to train. Female dogs, when they reach mating age, have signs, as a woman does, since their teats swell, and cartilage is found in their chest, but this is difficult to recognize except by one experienced: this does not happen to males, but for the most part they raise a leg in urinating, and this only after six or eight months, and generally once they stiffen. All females, however, sit when they urinate; some females, nevertheless, have sometimes been seen to raise a leg in urinating. In female dogs milk is found five days before giving birth, and in some for seven, and their milk after giving birth is suitable. The female greyhound has milk for thirty days after mating, and at first it is thick, afterward it becomes finer. And dog's milk is thicker than all milk, except that of pigs and hares.

Aristotle: the dog is of many offspring and many teats. The dog, like the pig, mates at eight months, but generates something weak then. It mates almost its whole lifetime, and lives up to fourteen years; it is pregnant for forty days, or seventy, or ninety. It bears five or six puppies, and can bear twelve. Female greyhounds, however, bear eight. And males and females always engage in mating, as long as they live. And it happens to greyhounds that they can leap better with exertion than at rest. Deformity occurs in animals having many clefts of the feet, more than in others, because of the abundance of their offspring, and since they bear incomplete offspring, as the dog does, since it bears them for the most part blind. From the tiger, as is said, Indian dogs are generated, and they do not come from the first mating, but the third, and it is said that the one from the first litter will be wild. It also happens to some that dogs mate with wolves and produce greyhounds. Likewise animals whose nature is close to one another, like dogs and foxes and wolves, mate together, whence they think that the dogs of India are born from a dog and a wolf.

Pliny, book 8: they also think Indian dogs are conceived from tigers, and for this reason, at mating time, they tie females in the forests, and think that the first and second litter are born too fierce. Only with the third do they raise them. The Gauls think the same of wolves, whose flocks each have their own leader chosen from the dogs, and accompany him in the hunt and obey him, for they too exercise mastery among themselves.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: female greyhounds, or Laconian dogs, breed at eight months on each side, over sixty days, and carry mostly for three months. Other dogs, however, endure mating even at six months old. All conceive from a single mating, and those that have conceived before the proper time keep their puppies blind longer; litters of twelve are the most numerous, others have five or six, sometimes even single ones, but this they consider a portent, just as all males or all females being born; the first-born, however, are usually males, in the rest they alternate. They are also mated from six months after giving birth; female greyhounds bear eight, and eagerness for labor is proper to that kind. The other kinds of dogs live fifteen years, sometimes twenty. Nor do they breed their whole life, but generally stop from the twelfth year.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: dogs begin to breed in the eighth month and stop in the twelfth year. In the midst of mating they become stuck together on both sides from excessive ardor of lust. They carry, however, for sixty days; it is thought a portent if a dog produces a single puppy.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: all dogs are born blind and remain blind for twelve days. Some, however, for three months.

Pliny, book 8: some report that if only one is born, it sees on the ninth day; if twins, on the tenth. And the same is added for each additional one, and there are as many days of delay before seeing; the best of the litter is the one that begins to see last, or the one the mother carries first into the den: dogs, then, bear blind puppies, and the more abundantly they are nourished with milk, the more delayed their sight, but never beyond the twenty-first day, nor before the seventh.

Pliny: female dogs, as said, that have conceived before the proper time keep their offspring blind longer. And all puppies are thought to raise a leg in urinating around the same number of days, at about six months. This, however, is a sign of completed strength, namely in males; females do this same thing sitting.

Physiologus: a newborn dog sometimes sees before the sixth day, sometimes not usually before the ninth. Sometimes even not before the sixteenth, and this is all because the viscous moisture, with the diminished heat that is in the eyelids, from the weak natural heat that belongs to the first age, cannot be consumed. But it can be consumed by heat that grows stronger with greater age. Young dogs have sharp, white teeth, but old ones black and blunt.

Isidore: 'catuli,' moreover, is the diminutive properly used for the young of dogs. Loosely, however, the young of any beasts are called 'catuli': dogs born from wolves and dogs, when they happen to mate together, are called 'lycisci.' The Indians, as said, are accustomed to tie female dogs in the forests at night, letting them be mounted by tigers, from which mating dogs are born of such fierceness and strength that they can throw down lions in their grip.

Aristotle: finally, any four-footed animal having many clefts in its feet, like the dog and the lion and the wolf and the fox, generates blind offspring, and their eyes separate on both sides and see. The female greyhound is impregnated for about sixty days, which is a sixth part of the year, and then her offspring remain blind for twelve days. And likewise the male mounts her again after giving birth in the sixth month, or perhaps before. And some are impregnated for seventy days, which is a fifth part of the year, and their offspring are blind up to fourteen days. Some, however, for three months, which is a fourth part of the year, and their offspring will be blind for seventeen days.
Aesculapius: a dog's puppy, killed before the ninth day, cleaned, cooked, and eaten, cures pain of the intestines forever.

Pliny, book 30, on a suckling puppy: the chest organs, or internal organs of a man, when aching, are healed if a suckling puppy is pressed to the aching parts, and the disease is said to pass into it. It also benefits epileptic diseases, a suckling puppy taken with myrrh and wine, its head and feet cut off.

Platearius, in the book On Simple Medicine: against phrenzy, a puppy is effective, cut open along the back like a pig, its innards removed, and applied to the head so that the heart, liver, and lung remain in it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the kinds of dogs, as said above, live fifteen years. Sometimes even twenty. Nor do they breed their whole life, but begin in the first year and stop around the twelfth. Further, in every kind of animal, males, as said, live longer than females, except in the kind of greyhounds, in which the male can live ten years, the female twelve, and this because of labor, and in this kind males and females always engage in mating as long as they live.

Aristotle: young dogs are not distinguished from old ones except by their teeth, since the teeth of the young are white and sharp, but the teeth of the old are black and blunt. Dogs menstruate for five days, and during this time the openings of their wombs develop abscesses, and they do not desire mating; after giving birth, then, they discharge much thick, phlegmatic moisture, and because of this their bodies grow lean. Besides, illnesses befall dogs: greyness, canine quinsy, and gout. Quinsy kills dogs, and few of them escape gout. Deformity too, as said, befalls dogs and animals of this kind having many clefts in the feet, because of the abundance of their offspring, and since they bear incomplete offspring, for the dog too bears offspring for the most part blind. When dogs are sick, moreover, they eat the roots of some herb in order to vomit.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: among the illnesses of dogs, moreover, there is also the lunatic disease and rabies, of which mention will be made afterward.
Pliny, book 36: the smell from silver mines is hostile to all animals, but especially to dogs.
Pliny, book 34, on dogs: the breath of lead furnaces too is felt to be harmful and pestilent, but most quickly [to dogs].
Avicenna, in the fourth canon: hellebore too kills dogs, and musk likewise.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: dogs' voice is called barking, as foxes' is yelping, oxen's lowing, horses' neighing.
Pliny, book 25: they say that those who have the herb 'peristereon' are not barked at by dogs.

Pliny: [on] not being barked at by dogs: the magicians report that those who have a hyena's tongue in their shoe under the foot [are also not barked at]. [The citation continues in the following entry.]
[Pliny:] dogs having [something canine] flee and do not bark. Likewise a dog's tongue placed in a shoe under the big toe, or a live weasel's tail cut off, and dogs do not bark at one who has this.
Pythagoras, in the book of the Romans: if a man carries with him wood by which a man's bone was burnt, dogs will neither bark nor rise up against him.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: a small, moderate green frog, called the 'calamites,' of which it is usually said that if it is thrown into a dog's mouth, it renders it mute, whence from its effect it is called 'mute.' Whence in Ecclesiasticus it is said: gifts and presents blind the eyes of judges, and, like something mute in a dog's mouth, turn aside their reproofs. A frog of this kind is frequently found on hazel trees, and there constantly utters the cries of the 'caradrion'; but also 'tortellidae,' thrown into dogs' mouths with sour wine-must, hinder their barking. The cause of this is clear enough, namely the viscous moisture of the sour must.

div.head: DE MORSU EORUM AC REMEDIIS CONTRA EUM

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the second canon: if a non-rabid dog bites someone, the spot should at once be sprinkled with vinegar and rubbed often by hand. Then soda with vinegar should be placed on it, and removed every three days: or it can be treated with onion and salt and rue and beans and bitter almonds, with honey, or with plantain.

Pliny: a dog's bite is healed with the leaves of any cultivated melon with wine. Wild onions too, applied with vinegar, or dry with honey and wine, so that they are removed after the third day, heal the same. Garlic too is applied to dogs' bites and wounds with honey. Besides, many are accustomed to apply the root of wild fennel in its juice or with honey against dog bites.
Pliny, book 22, in the same: nettle, with salt added, heals bites. Mushrooms too are applied to them with water.

Pliny, book 22, in the same: vinegar is medicinal for dog bites. Dregs of vinegar too, with a cheese-rind, benefit against these. Likewise the tender shoots of fig branches are applied to the skin. Milk too, curdled in cheese on a wild fig twig, heals a dog's bite. Besides, the softest leaves of the wild fig heal fresh dog bites with wine. Almonds too, with honey. Walnuts too, with onion and honey and salt, cure dog and human bites.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: the wounds of some are aggravated by the entry of those who have ever been injured by a dog's tooth or by serpents. A man's hair, however, with vinegar, heals dog bites. One's own urine, too, is especially beneficial, poured at once over a dog's bite.
Pliny, book 29, in the same: a stone, too, thrown at by a dog, has become proverbial for discord.
Pliny: [on] the dog. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Aesculapius: dog's blood, drunk, frees those with tremors. Its burnt, ground, and powdered head, or its sinewy flesh and figs, heal a dog's bite if drunk. Powder of its teeth cures toothache and gums. Its heart, drunk, keeps dogs from barking. Its gall with honey cures the eyes. Its milk, drunk, prevents hair and locks from growing; given with honey or wine, it quickly expels a dead fetus. A tooth touched by it comes out easily, and it thins scars of the eyes. Its fat heals gout and ear pain.

Avicenna, on the dog: dog's blood prevents the regrowth of plucked hairs, as Galen wrote. Dog's urine, too, is administered on warts. A dog's testicle is like a fox's testicle; it dissolves phlegmatic abscesses, cleans ulcers, and prevents an ant-like sore from spreading, and opens fistulas and fills in deceptive, corrosive ulcers with new flesh. It also benefits the kidneys, and when a man takes the larger of the two, the male becomes stronger. A woman, however, if she takes the weaker one, becomes more feminine. It is also said that the moist one increases mating. The dry one, however, checks it, and each of the two destroys the effect of the other. Dog dung, from a dog fed on bones, benefits old ulcers with honey. Likewise it is placed on the palate with a finger for quinsy. It also benefits looseness and ulcers of the intestines, given as an enema or drunk boiled in milk with iron or stones.

Dioscorides, on the dog: dog-related [remedies made with] soda or a prepared medicine remove leprosy and itching. Dog dung, gathered in the dog-days and dried, drunk, checks the bowels with wine. White dung of the same heals the arched [rainbow-shaped, i.e. arcing] disease.

Pliny: nothing is thought more effective against toxic poisons than dog's blood. Apollonius used to cure suffusions of the eyes, and likewise white spots, with dog's gall and honey. Dripping of dog's milk calms pain and heaviness of the ears. Nits are removed from hair with dog's fat.
Pliny: dog hide, wrapped around any finger, calms discharges. Dog gall, applied with a feather, benefits gout; fresh dog urine, applied, heals warts of every kind. And the ash of its dung with wax.
Ambrose: a sick wild dog is cured by drinking its own blood.

Physiologus: a dog, sometimes after eating from a corpse of the dead, goes mad, and then dreads water, whence the disease of a man wounded by a rabid dog is called 'lymphatic': besides, the dog, like certain other beasts, thins its tongue by licking, and if its saliva touches the blood of the tongue, it drives it into rabies.

Isaac Judaeus: the dog, as said, is naturally cold and dry, and black bile dominates it, whence, from its abundance, once altered and putrefied and dominating the whole body, thus corrupted, it necessarily makes them rabid, especially in autumn and spring.
Pliny, book 2: who does not know that at the rising of the Dog Star the vapors of the sun are kindled, and there is no doubt that dogs are especially driven into rabies during that whole span.

Pliny, book 8, in the same: the rabies of dogs, when Sirius burns, is pestilential for men and their bite is deadly, causing an aversion to water in those bitten. Wherefore it is countered for thirty days, especially by mixing chicken dung into dogs' food, or, if the disease has already begun, with hellebore. Columella is the authority that if, on the fortieth day after a dog is born, its tail is bitten off and its topmost joint removed, with the following sinew taken out, the tail does not grow further, nor do dogs become rabid.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: there is also a little worm on dogs' tongues, called 'lytta' by the Greeks, which, if removed from puppies, keeps them from becoming rabid and from losing their appetite. So great, indeed, is the power of this evil that even the urine of a rabid dog, trodden upon, especially harms those with an ulcer. The remedy is horse dung sprinkled with vinegar, warmed, and applied on a fig. There is, again, a moisture of saliva beneath a rabid dog's tongue, which, given in a drink, prevents those bitten from becoming 'lymphatic,' otherwise called hydrophobic. The flesh of those that have been rabid is also salted for the same remedies, to be given as food.

Pliny: the ash of the burnt heads of dogs showing rabies, without the flesh, with cyprus oil, heals toothache, dripped into the ear on the side that aches: for pains of the side too, the ash of a rabid dog's skull, sprinkled in a drink, is applied by itself.

Avicenna, in the same place: the blood of a rabid dog, moreover, is suited to its own bite and to the poison of an Armenian arrow-wound: the liver of a rabid dog is given in a drink for its bite and benefits, and also prevents the aversion to water.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon, the same: canine rabies occurs, which is a conversion of the constitution to malignant, venomous melancholy, and this conversion happens to it either from the air or from food and drink. From the air, indeed, since vehement heat scorches its humors. Whence it becomes rabid in autumn; or vehement cold congeals its blood, making it inclined to blackness, and thence it becomes rabid in spring. From food and drink, however, since it licks the blood of the slain and eats from carcasses, and drinks from putrid waters. For this reason it becomes filled with putrid melancholy, and its constitution is altered, just as happens to leprosy sufferers.

Isaac Judaeus, in the Viaticum: a rabid dog can be recognized by these signs, since other dogs flee it, and, a fugitive and wandering alone, it staggers as if drunk, with its mouth open, its tongue hanging. Excessive saliva always runs from its mouth. Its eyes are turned inward and reddened, its ears turned back: its tail is between its legs, its eyes wide open, and when it strikes against a stone or some other object, gnashing its teeth, it grinds and shrieks, and, resisting whatever it sees, barks even at its own shadow. When dogs see it, they flee it, and, fearing it, bark at it from a distance.

Avicenna, in the same place: the dog, as said, sometimes becomes rabid, since from putrid food or drink it becomes filled with melancholy, and its constitution is altered, as happens to leprosy sufferers. And sometimes its body develops abscesses, and its color turns ashen. It also suffers hunger and neither eats nor drinks. But when it meets water, it fears it and shrinks from it and trembles, and its bristling of the fur multiplies, and this is on the skin of its face; indeed it sometimes dies from this very fear. Great dimness of the eyes also befalls it, and it is always solitary, sluggish, not recognizing its master. Its eyes have a vehement and horrible look, and it puts out its tongue, and foamy saliva runs from its mouth. Its nose runs too, its head already lowered and its ears softened, wherefore it moves them both. And now its back is already bent and inclined to the side. Whence it now seems twisted both upward and to the side. And if its tail is fixed still, it walks fearfully, drooping, as if drunk, sad, distressed, headlong in its gait, and when some shape appears to it, like that of a wall or a tree or an animal, it runs against it, attacking it; nor is its attack accompanied by barking at what it attacks, according to the custom of dogs, but it is silent and squalid. And when it barks, you will see dogs flee from its path. But if it comes upon one of them, it suddenly fawns on it and becomes obedient in its presence and tries to flee from it.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the bite of a rabid dog is called 'lymphatic,' and is recognized thus: a plaster made from well-pounded walnut, placed over the wound for a day and a night, should afterward be given to a hungry cock or hen; if it drinks after eating, it is not the disease of a rabid dog; but if it dies, though not immediately, sound advice is that the wound be kept open and nothing be applied over the scars. It is remarkable, however, that one bitten by a rabid dog sometimes licks and barks at puppies.

Avicenna, in the same place: when a rabid dog bites a man, at first indeed nothing appears but a painful wound, like other wounds, but after some days corrupted thoughts and dreams and other signs appear in him, of which mention will be made below. Among the remarkable features, moreover, is that he is quick to bite a man, and if he bites him, after his own agitation, that same thing happens to the other, namely the same rabies. And sometimes indeed such a dog's bite kills within a week, if severe, up to within six months. The moderate span, however, is forty days.
Aristotle: [those] bitten by a rabid dog go mad, except man.
Pliny, book 8: the rabies of dogs, as said above, is pestilential to man, and its bite too is deadly.
Pythagoras, on the dog, in the same place: if anyone places in someone's wine a stone that a rabid dog has bitten, whoever drinks it will become irascible and quarrelsome.

Avicenna, in the same place: the rabid dog, as said, when it bites a man, at first indeed only a simply painful wound appears. After some days, corrupted thoughts and dreams appear in him, and a disposition as if of anger, and murmuring, and confusion of reason, and answering without being asked, and you see spasms in his extremities, contracting them toward himself. He has hiccups and thirst and dryness of the mouth, and flees from crowding and loves the kindling of light. Sometimes he shrinks from light, and his limbs redden, especially his face, and his voice grows hoarse, and he weeps in fear of water, and as often as water is brought near him, he imagines a dog and fears it because of that. Sometimes, however, he is not terrified, but is nauseated by it, and sometimes loves to roll on the ground. Rufus said this happens to him because his constitution already favors dryness. And so he shrinks from its opposite. Besides, an involuntary emission of semen befalls him without desire, and sometimes he is brought to cold sweat and fainting and death. Sometimes, however, he dies before these conditions, from thirst, and sometimes he desires water, then cries out against it when he encounters it, and sometimes, sipping it, is choked by it and dies. Likewise sometimes he barks like a dog and is as if hoarse; sometimes, however, his voice is cut off and he becomes like an apoplectic; sometimes he urinates a fatty substance in which there are marvelous fleshy things, like small dogs; sometimes he urinates black, and sometimes his urine is retained and he cannot urinate. Among the remarkable conditions of this disease, moreover, is that he is quick to bite a man, and sometimes makes him rabid, sometimes kills him, as was said before.

Avicenna, in the same, the same: a royal walnut, or another, should be taken and placed over the wound of the bite, and left for one hour, then thrown to a hen; if she refuses it, it is clear that the dog that bit was rabid, and if she eats it and dies, then the dog is indeed rabid again. In the same way, too, you can test this if you smear a scrap of cloth with what runs from that wound and throw it to dogs, for if they refuse it, it is clear the bite was that of a rabid dog.

Isaac Judaeus: a certain sign of this bite is that a morsel of bread smeared, as said, be thrown to dogs; for such creatures have terrible dreams. Upon waking from sleep they are fearful, they grow angry without cause, are dazed and constantly looking about, unable to bear being looked at by anyone. Those who fall into this affliction fear water and bark like dogs and grow hoarse, fearing when they look into water, or even fall trembling, and, unless medicine comes to their aid, they die.

div.head: DE REMEDIIS CONTRA EUM IN USU MEDICINE

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the second canon: a rabid dog's bite is benefited by human urine poured over it. Onion-water is also beneficial if applied over it, or made into a plaster from it with rue and salt; a plaster too is made from walnut and onion over the same bite. Likewise burnt herd-animal dung is applied over it, especially prepared with vinegar. Blood of a rabid dog too, according to Dioscorides, is effective for its own bite. Ground and powdered wheat, too, is a help for it. Likewise the liver of a rabid dog is given for its bite and benefits, and prevents aversion to water. Almonds too benefit it, and cucumber leaves, and likewise fennel root ground and applied. Unripe figs too, or its fresh leaves. Swallowing honey too helps in treating a rabid dog's bite. A plaster is made from horehound with salt for its bite; oyster flesh too benefits its bite. Likewise gentian with wine, or burnt ram's flesh likewise with wine, or human hair applied as a plaster with vinegar. Besides these, warmed honey swallowed with rose oil.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon, the same: do not allow the wound of a man bitten by a rabid dog to close up to forty days, but keep it open and lanced, and occupy yourself first in drawing outward, since when it draws humors inward, it draws the poison with them. Onions and garlic, however, resist poisons and cut them off and repel them from the body.

Pliny: wild cabbage, called 'erratica,' is applied to a rabid dog's bite, better with 'laser' and sharp vinegar. The plant called 'hipposelinum,' drunk and applied, heals the same bite, or rue juice too is drunk with wine, and the leaves, ground or chewed, are applied with honey or salt or with vinegar and pitch boiled together. Likewise fig leaves with vinegar quench the same bite.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: wounds made by a rabid dog's bite are cut around to the living flesh, and calf's flesh is applied, and its broth, boiled with the flesh, is given to drink, or the flesh itself pounded with lime. They affirm that with a he-goat's liver applied, no fear at all is felt; they also praise goat dung applied with wine, and the boiled and drunk decoction of a cuckoo and a swallow.

Pliny: [one] is protected from fear of water after a rabid dog's bite by the ash of a dog's head applied to the wound; the same too is beneficial in a drink, and some have given it to be eaten for this reason. There is also a moisture of saliva under a rabid dog's tongue, which, if given in a drink, prevents becoming 'lymphatic.' Likewise help comes from a cock's brain, but it benefits only when eaten in the same year. A cock's comb too, crushed, is effectively applied, and goose fat with honey; it is also effective applied with vinegar. Burnt cock and chick dung, and swallow's dung too, the membrane a serpent has shed in spring, ground with a male crab. Besides, unwashed wool, pressed on rabid dog bites, is applied and removed after the seventh day. Likewise, most usefully against the lymphatic disease, the liver of the one that bit while rabid is given raw, if it can be chewed, or, if not, cooked, or the broth of its cooked flesh.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: salted fish kept for eating are also applied against rabid dog bites. Likewise those terrified of drinking after such a bite have their faces anointed with the fat of a sea calf.
Pliny, book 34, in the same: rabid dog bites are healed by cauterizing with iron, and those terrified of drinking, as the disease worsens, are freed at once once the wound is cauterized.
Pliny, book 8, the same: for the bite of a rabid dog a remedy recently discovered is the root of the wild rose, called 'cynorhoda' [dog-rose].
Haly Abbas: [the flesh] of a rabid dog, if roasted and eaten, clearly benefits a dog's bite.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the beaver is an animal like a Pontic dog, that is, long and slender. It has very sharp teeth, a delicate and noble pelt, which is more precious the blacker it is. It has colors in its fur like the badger's, but the fur is fine and beautiful. It cannot stay long unless it keeps its tail in the water, which indeed resembles a fish's tail, both in taste and appearance. Whence it is also eaten by Christians during a fast. For part of its tail is edible; part is forbidden for use, and the rest of it is flesh; the tail itself is a cubit long, having much fat. Its hind feet, however, are like a goose's, though larger, and clawed, but its front feet like a dog's. For nature prepared this for it so that with its hind feet, like a bird, it might swim in water, and with its front feet walk on land like a four-footed creature.

Isidore: beavers [castores] are named from castrating [castrando]; for their testicles are suited to medicines, on account of which, when they sense a hunter, they castrate themselves and cut off their own genitals with their bite. Of which Cicero, in the speech for Scaurus, says: they redeem themselves by the part of the body for which they are especially sought.
Juvenal, on the eunuch: he who makes himself a beaver, wishing to escape the loss of his testicles. These same creatures are also called 'fibri,' which are also called Pontic dogs.

Solinus, on the otter: the beaver is an animal most powerful in its bite, so much so that, when it has attacked a man, it does not release the grip of its teeth before it perceives that the broken bones have crunched.

Pliny: the beaver is an animal of horrible bite. For it fells trees near rivers as if with iron, and, once it has gripped a part of a man, does not release its bite before the broken bones have crunched. Its tail is like fish, its other appearance like the otter's; both are aquatic, and in both the fur is softer than down.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: the beaver, an aquatic and terrestrial animal, of this kind the stronger reduces the weaker to servitude, and cuts off, by biting, its testicles and its scrotum, so that, lighter, it may turn to flight.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: beavers, as the Experimenter says, live in a herd and go together to the woods, and, cutting off wood with their teeth, carry it back to their dens in a marvelous manner. For they throw one of the beavers onto its back, feet raised, onto the ground, as a vehicle, and skillfully arrange the cut wood between its legs, and thus, dragging it by the tail, lead it to their own dwellings. But they do not do such an injury to those raised among them, but only to those that have come to them from other regions, for these they reduce to servitude under strict guard. There is, however, another opinion, that they do this to those that, worn out by old age and labor, have blunted teeth and cannot cut wood. Hunters recognize such creatures, reduced to servitude, by the loss of hair on their backs, and, moved by pity, let them go unharmed. They put the cut wood to a double use. For they eat the bark and make quite skillful dwellings from the wood. The beaver feeds on the bitter leaves and bark of trees as its greatest delicacy, whence its whole flesh, though good, is nonetheless suffused with a bitter smell. About to eat the bark, it sits raised on its hind feet, and, holding the wood with its front feet, strips the bark only from the part it held between its feet, eating it; but what is beyond its feet, it discards and disregards. It builds its home over the water, making various chambers in it, so that it can rise and descend as the water rises or falls. When the beaver cuts down a tree, having dealt a blow with its teeth, it runs off away from the tree, to avoid its fall, and does this for as long, or as often, as needed, until, struck by repeated blows, it falls.

Physiologus: when the hunter pursues the beaver, it throws its severed testicles before his face, and the hunter, having what he desired from it, pursues it no further. But if another hunter should follow it, it rears up and shows that it does not have its genitals, and thus escapes. This animal, moreover, is exceedingly gentle.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the hunting of this animal happens in this way. A dog trained for this is thrown into the water, and, reaching the entrance to its dwelling, enters, and the beaver does not yield to its bites until that skillfully made dwelling is broken open by the hunters. As for what is said, that a beaver already castrated rears up and shows the hunter that its testicles have already been cut off, very many say this is false, in the case of the beavers found among us, since the beaver's testicles do not project externally, but lie inside the belly, like small kidneys. It excretes, moreover, like a goose. It also vomits gall, as Pliny says, useful for many medicines. Besides, as for what is said, that it castrates itself when it senses hunters pursuing it, and cuts off its own testicles in order to escape, Platearius denies this, especially since men hunt it more for its pelt than for its testicles, even though the animal itself is not of such great discernment. Its gall, as said, is useful for many things. Its rennet too calms the falling sickness.

Platearius: the beaver's cut-off testicles, hung in a shaded place, are dried, so as to be kept for medicinal use, and are called 'castoreum.' Good castoreum, that is unadulterated, has a moderately sharp taste, is glutinous, and has a very unpleasant smell, tangled sinews adhering to little membranes. It can be kept effective for six years, but the fresher it is, the better. In medicines it is used with the outer membrane discarded; it has the power of dissolving, drawing, and especially strengthening sinewy parts. Against epilepsy and other cold afflictions of the head, castoreum is given with rue juice in a drink, or wine of its decoction. Against paralysis of the tongue, its powder is placed under the tongue until it dissolves and is consumed by itself. Against paralysis of the whole body, wine of its decoction with rue and sage is given. Against lethargy, sneezing is provoked with castoreum; it rouses and strengthens the brain.

Dioscorides, on the beaver: castoreum is the testicles of the animal called the beaver, which sustains a life sometimes aquatic, sometimes terrestrial. The best is Pontic, which is waxy inside and enclosed by natural membranes: some, however, adulterating the testicles, insert into bladders a drop of ammoniacum sprinkled with beaver's blood. Those should be chosen, then, that are anointed [glossy], clinging together from a single root, full, sticky, brittle, separating readily from their own little pouches. For they should be cleansed, and the inner part mixed into medicines. Castoreum, moreover, warms and dries and thins; it is most useful, then, for those who suffer spasm or tremor of the sinews from fullness. But for those to whom this happens from emptiness or dryness, the opposite is true. It also corrects faults of the lung, and the moist and cold humor of the brain, with pennyroyal. Drunk with wine, it removes bloating, heals gripes, and does not allow poisoned drinks to harm. It is a singular remedy for the lethargic. It heals tremor and contractions and all afflictions of the sinews when soothingly applied and anointed, for its power is warming and restorative; mixed with emollient plasters and pain-relieving ointments, it helps paralytics, sciatica sufferers, and the like.

Avicenna: castoreum has a fine outer skin, which breaks at any touch. It is, moreover, finer and stronger than everything that warms and dries. It dissolves bloating, and, applied, warms the body; it benefits pernicious ulcers and the sinews, and tremor and moist spasm and numbness and paralysis. It also benefits forgetfulness and lethargy with vinegar and rose oil, and cold deafness and windiness in the ear, dissolved in nard oil. Drawing in through the nostrils by its fumigation benefits abscesses of the lung and its ailments. It is drunk with vinegar for hiccups, but causes thirst. It removes stabbing pain of the belly, drunk with vinegar; it dissolves windiness, provokes the menses, draws out the afterbirth and the fetus. It benefits the bite of small venomous creatures, and what of it inclines toward blackness is poison, so that it sometimes kills within a single day.

Pliny: Sestius says the beaver's testicles are small, drawn together, and adhering to the spine, and cannot be removed without the animal's death. They are adulterated, however, with kidneys of this kind that are large, whereas true testicles are found rather small: these, drunk by themselves in water, are useful for frenzied sufferers; they also rouse the lethargic by the fumigation of their scent, and, with pennyroyal, expel the afterbirth and bring on the menses. They also heal vertigo, tremors, spasms, ailments of the sinews, sciatica, mouth ailments, paralysis. All when anointed, or ground to the thickness of honey with nettle seed and rose vinegar. Thus, too, they are effective taken against epilepsy. Drunk, however, against bloating, colic, poisons. Indeed against scorpions they are drunk with wine. Against 'phalangia' and spiders with honeyed wine, so that they are brought up by vomiting or, with rue, retained. Against 'chalcidae' [venomous lizards] with myrrh-oil, against horned vipers and 'prestera' serpents with panacea-herb or rue in wine. Against blind serpents with wine. And privately against mistletoe-glue it helps with vinegar. Against aconite with milk or water. Against white hellebore with honeyed water and soda; they also heal the teeth, ground with oil, and poured into the ear on the side that aches. They give clarity of vision, anointed with Attic honey. They also check hiccups with vinegar.

Pliny, in the same: castoreum benefits ulcers of the head with sulphurwort and rose oil. Also clarity of the eyes with honey; it is also most useful for the ears with poppy juice, and softens stiffness of the neck, with pepper mixed in honeyed wine, boiled with frogs in oil and salt so that the juice may be sipped; in three cups of honeyed vinegar it is given to epileptics while fasting. Castoreum also helps those with tremors, if they are anointed with oil.
