The same, drunk with honeyed wine, benefits women's purgations, but if a pregnant woman takes too much, it will cause miscarriage; it is also effective for many other things in medicine.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: for the rest concerning the beaver and castoreum, see below, where the 'fiber' is treated.

Pliny, book 8: the 'catoblepa' is called a modest and sluggish wild beast near the source of the Nigris, which is, among the western Ethiopians, thought by most to be the source of the Nile. This beast, sluggish in its other limbs too, bears its head, which is very heavy, with difficulty, and this is always cast down toward the ground; otherwise it is the destruction of the human race, for all who see its eyes die at once - the same power the basilisk serpent has too.
Solinus: near the river Tigris is born the 'catoblepa,' a modest and sluggish beast, of a pestilential gaze.

Isidore: the cat [catus] comes from Greek, meaning 'clever.' It is called 'musio' [mouse-catcher], since it is a threat to mice. Common folk call it 'catus' from catching ['captura']. Others say it is because it 'captat,' that is sees keenly. For it sees so sharply that it overcomes the darkness of night with the gleam of its eyes.

Avicenna: from a cat's bite there sometimes follows vehement pain and greenish discoloration of the body, and its treatment is the common treatment. It is helped, however, by a plaster of onion or wild catmint.
Rhazes: wild cats flee from the smoke of rue and bitter almonds.
Haly Abbas: [remedies made from] cats [that] are also dry; they heal pains of hemorrhoids, warm the kidneys, benefit pains of the back.
Aesculapius: dung of a male or female cat with mustard and vinegar cures baldness.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the same is also called 'musio' or 'murilegus' [mouse-catcher], of which fuller mention will also be made below.
Pliny: Ethiopia sends the 'cephi.' Their hind feet are like human feet and legs; their front feet are like hands. Rome saw this animal afterward only at the games of Pompey.
Solinus: in the time of the dictator Caesar, monsters were seen at Rome, called 'cephi'; their hind legs and feet mimic human limbs, their front feet, human hands.

Physiologus: the 'leucrocota' is a creature that outstrips all beasts; its body resembles a donkey's, its haunches a stag's, its chest and legs a lion's; its mouth gapes wide to the ears, and it imitates the human voice.
Pliny: Ethiopia produces, among other monsters, the 'crocuta,' as if conceived from a dog and a wolf, breaking everything with its teeth and, once swallowed, digesting it at once in its belly.

Pliny, in the same: by mating with a hyena, the Ethiopian lioness bears the 'crocuta,' which imitates the voices of men and herd animals. It has a continuous ridge of teeth on both sides of its mouth, with no gums, a single unbroken tooth, which, so that it not be dulled by opposing contact, is enclosed like something kept in a case.
Solinus: the 'crocuta' never moves the pupils of its eyes, but fixes its gaze without blinking; in its mouth there is no gum, its tooth is flat and continuous.
Radulphus of Flaix: the 'cherogryllus' is a spiny animal, similar to the hedgehog.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is read that it is larger than the hedgehog, yet spiny, whence it is clear that some have wrongly said this is the rabbit. Elsewhere too it is read that the 'cherogryllus' is itself the hedgehog or 'erinacius,' that is an animal having the form of a small pig, but spiny, of which fuller mention will be made below. Whence in Psalm 103, where it is read in our translation, 'the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs.' Another translation has 'for cherogrylli.' The Gloss on the Proverbs of Solomon [says likewise]. In Proverbs too, where according to our translation it is read: 'the little hare, a weak people, which places its dwelling in the rock.' Others have 'cherogryllus' for 'little hare.' And it is an animal no smaller than the hedgehog, similar to a mouse and a bear, of which there is a great abundance in Palestine, in pits and in the caverns of rocks. Hence in the Psalter, where we say, 'the rock is a refuge for hedgehogs,' others put 'for hares,' others 'for cherogrylli.' But some here have 'hedgehog' for 'little hare.' For Jerome interprets the Hebrew word 'saphan' as both 'cherogryllus' and 'hedgehog' and 'hare.'
Hesychius of Jerusalem: they say the 'cherogryllus' is a weak animal indeed, but rapacious and deadly.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'duran,' as Aristotle says, is a swift and most powerful animal, which, pursued by hunters, when it begins to weaken with despair of escaping, by natural cunning violently discharges its dung against the dogs pursuing it and slows them with the smell of the putrid excrement.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: perhaps, indeed, this name, that is 'duran,' is given to the beast that was called above, following the same Aristotle, the 'bonasus,' and this is, as it seems, the wild cow, of which Aristotle says it has horns inclining toward each other. And so nature gave it another benefit, namely the casting of dung to a distance, so that it may keep the hunter from approaching it closely.

Solinus: the 'yale' is an animal among the Indians, otherwise like a horse, with an elephant's tail, of black color, with a boar's jaws, bearing horns longer than a cubit's measure, suited to the service of any motion. For they are not rigid, if the need for fighting arises. It extends one of them when it fights, and folds back the other, so that if the point of the one is blunted by some blow, the edge of the other may take its place; it is compared to the hippopotamus, and, indeed, it too delights in the waters of rivers.
Pliny: the 'yale' has the size of the river-horse, movable horns, which it holds alternately in battle, varied and oblique.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'yale' is a beast whose body is, as it were, a horse's, but its jaw like a boar's, bristling with black color, equally powerful in water and on land; it has very large horns, of which, when fighting, it folds one back behind its back. And when that one, namely the one it fought with, is blunted, it directs the other for the fight.

Isidore: they think the Greeks named the elephant from the size of its body, since it presents the shape of a mountain. For 'mountain' is called 'elephon' in Greek; among the Indians, however, it is named from its cry, 'barro,' whence its voice is called 'barritus,' and its teeth 'ivory' [ebur].

Solinus: there are two kinds of these; size marks the nobler ones, the smaller they call bastards. They eat tree-trunks, swallow stones, and find palm-fruits most pleasing as food. The Moors fear Indian elephants, and, as if conscious of their own smaller size, avoid being seen by them. They are most impatient of cold. If, however, one has swallowed the chameleon worm, taking wild olive cures the affliction. Its back has a very hard hide, its belly is soft, and it is entirely without bristles.

Aristotle: some elephants drink oil, and some do not. And those that drink oil, if there is iron in their belly, it is drawn out by drinking oil. The elephant also drinks wine, and when it cannot drink, they boil medicines with oil and give it to drink. This animal is very fond of rivers and stays near rivers and submerges itself in water, so that its trunk is above the water's surface, and it breathes through it. Nor can it endure long swimming, because of the heaviness of its body. Nature indeed gave the elephant a large body as a benefit, as it did the camel too. For largeness of body wards off dangers from other animals. The elephant, then, is larger than all, since it is born as large as a dog and grows for sixty years. It lives, however, two hundred years, sometimes three hundred. Its dwelling is in deserts; it fells large trees by its strength and knocks down great walls with its tusks.

Pliny: elephants delight in rivers and wander around streams, though otherwise they cannot swim, because of the size of their bodies. They knock down palm-fruits taller than their heads and thus gather the fruit of the fallen trees. They chew with their mouth, breathe and drink and smell with what is not improperly called a hand. It is reported that the elephant, noticing a man's footprint before the man himself, trembles with fear of an ambush, stops to smell it, looks around, breathes out its anger, and does not trample it, but passes on certain judgment to the one following. That one does the same for the next, with a similar signal, down to the last; then the column wheels around and turns back, and the battle-line is directed elsewhere. Elephants always proceed in herds, least solitary of all creatures; the oldest by birth leads the column, the next in age drives it from behind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the elephant does no harm unless provoked; it kills flies settling on its back by contracting its skin into wrinkles, and this serves it in place of a tail's fur. This animal, as said, is very fond of rivers, since in India, where they are born, they always dwell along rivers. And when it wants to be cleaned, it submerges itself in the water up to its trunk, for it breathes through this.

Aristotle: the elephant is a gentle animal, quickly tamed, and more obedient and disciplined than all animals, whence it is even trained to worship the king, and in this it is better than all animals.

Pliny, on these, in the same place: great clemency, too, is reported of them, and they harm only when provoked. When surrounded by cavalry, they receive the weak or tired or wounded into the middle of the column, and, as if by command, or by reason, take turns coming to the front. Once caught, they are most quickly tamed by the juice of barley. Rabid ones are tamed by hunger and blows, with other elephants brought up to restrain the disturbed one with chains.

Ambrose, on elephants: nature seemed to have created nothing stronger than elephants, nothing so terrible, so towering, and yet these serve at the nod of men and lay aside their own nature through human training. They are taught like children, they serve like the weak, they are beaten like the timid, they are corrected like subjects. They forget that they were born wild and take on what they are commanded. And while they pass over into our ways, they lose their own impulses.

Physiologus: while the elephant, by human craft, entrusts its huge limbs to trees that have been cut through, weighed down by such a great weight, it cannot rise by its own strength, since its feet have no joints, but rises with human help, by whose craft it had lain down. And so, once the beast is restored to its own gait, it knows how to be mindful of the kindness shown to the master it recognizes as having helped it. It moves its steps at his direction alone, takes food at his will. Finally, in place of a hand, it extends its trunk to its master, gladly accepting what will benefit it, since it understands that it can live by his care. Its breath is said to heal human headache, which it breathes out when asked. When it comes to water, however, requested, it pours out a shower through the hollow of its trunk in the manner of rain. Finally, by the motion of its body it asks various people for what it may hand to its master, and considers its own food a means of compensating its keeper. But if anyone refuses to provide what is asked, it is said, by opening the outlet of its bladder, to discharge such a flood that a certain river seems to have entered his house, avenging the refusal with a foul stench. It looks with disdain on those playing buffoonishly, and gladly attends to anything honorable.

Solinus: there is, moreover, in them the good quality of mercy. For if by chance they see a man wandering in the desert, they lead him back to familiar paths, or, if they happen upon crowded herds, they make a way for themselves gentle and calm with their hand, lest they kill any animal in their path. If by chance a fight breaks out, they take no small care of the wounded.
Isidore: elephants indeed are strong in understanding and much memory; they proceed in herds, and greet men with such motion as they can.

Solinus: elephants have understanding close to human sense, are strong in memory, keep the discipline of the stars, and when the moon shines, they go in herds to rivers, and, soon sprinkled with the water's moisture, greet the rising sun with such motions as they can, then return to the woods. They wander in herds, and the oldest by birth leads the column, but the next in age drives on those following: about to cross a river, they send the smallest ahead first, lest the larger ones, entering, wear down the riverbed and make deep channels out of shallow fords. When pressed by hunting, they break off both their tusks at once, so that, the ivory forfeited, they are no longer sought - for they sense this to be the cause of their danger.

Pliny: elephants have an understanding of their native speech. And, above all, obedience, and memory of the duties they have learned. The pleasure of love and glory, indeed even a probity, prudence, and fairness rare even in man. And, as far as trainability goes, they worship the king, bend their knees, offer garlands. Indian elephants are larger than African ones, which they call bastards. At a gladiatorial show given by the emperor Germanicus, certain ones even performed unrehearsed movements in the manner of dancers. They also relate that on the coasts of Ethiopia, groups of five elephants, interlaced among themselves like a raft, with their trunks raised as sails, are carried by the waves to the better pastures of Arabia.
Pliny: the elephant, having devoured the chameleon along with the foliage of the same color, meets its poison with wild olive.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: elephants, on Cassiodorus's testimony, surpass the understanding of all four-footed creatures, whence the elephant does not hesitate to worship, at first sight, the one it understands to be the ruler of all. If a tyrant should appear to it, it remains unbending: it separates flour mixed with the finest dust excellently, so that, gathering the flour for food, it takes in none of the dust: but those that are injured are said to keep the offense and, after a long time, to render vengeance for the wrong.

Solinus: there is constant discord between elephants and dragons. Finally, ambushes are prepared by this cunning: serpents hide near the paths by which elephants wander in their accustomed tracks, and thus, passing over the leaders, attack those at the rear, so that those who have gone ahead cannot come to their aid, and first bind the feet with coils, so as to hinder, with the legs snared, the ability to walk. For elephants, unless forestalled by this delaying coil, press themselves against trees or rocks, so as to crush the entangled serpents with their toppling weight. The chief reason for the fight, however, is that elephants, they say, have cold blood, and for this reason are most eagerly sought by dragons scorched with heat, wherefore they never attack them except when heavy with drinking, so that, their veins more fully engorged, they may take greater satisfaction from those they overwhelm. Nor do they aim for anything more than the eyes, which alone they know to be vulnerable, or the interior of the ears, since only that spot cannot be defended by the trunk; and so, once they have drunk the blood, while the beasts collapse, the dragons are crushed beneath them. Thus, blood poured out on both sides soaks the earth and becomes a pigment, whatever the ground has dyed, which they call 'cinnabar.'
Pliny: [on] elephants of India, when [they fight] with dragons, so that they may coil around them with an easy loop and bind them tight in a knotted grip.

Pliny, in the same: dragons first bind the elephants' gait with their tail, and the elephants loosen the coils with their trunk. But the dragons hide their head in the elephant's nostril, and at the same time block its breath and tear the softest parts, since the elephant's blood is very cold, for which reason, scorched by heat, they are especially sought by dragons. Dragons, moreover, are so large that they can hold all the blood. For it is certain that elephants, drained of blood by them and dried out, collapse, and that the intoxicated dragons are crushed and die together with them. The rhinoceros also attacks the elephant, aiming its horn at the belly, which it knows to be softer.

div.head: QUALITER HOMINES UTUNTUR ELEPHANTIBUS IN PRELIIS

cit.quote: Isidore: the kind of elephants is suited to matters of war. For in these, the Persians and Indians, with wooden towers set upon them, fight with javelins as if from a wall.

Vegetius, on Military Matters, book 3: elephants in battle, by the size of their bodies, and, by the horror of their trumpeting and the novelty of their shape, throw men into confusion too, against which various kinds of armament for resisting them have been devised. Curio, in Lucania, cut off with a sword the hand, which they call the trunk, of one of them. And pairs of armored horses were yoked to a chariot, mounted on which men directed very long poles against the elephants. Especially the ancient light-armed skirmishers were arrayed against elephants, namely young men in light armor, agile of body, who cast missiles most effectively from horseback. Iron is fixed more broadly on the lower part, however, against them, so that in such large bodies the wounds might be greater. This too was added, that slingers with slings and slingshots, with round stones aimed, should strike down and kill those by whom the elephants were guided, together with their towers - than which nothing safer is found. Besides, as the beasts approached, as if they had broken through the line, the soldiers would give them room. And once they had come into the middle of the column, surrounded on all sides by masses of armed men, they were captured together with their handlers, unharmed, without wounds.

Solinus: elephants provide great use in matters of war. The Indians and the fierce Persian people, strong in war and in archery, hedged about with elephants as if with great towers, advance into the middle of the field, fighting from these as if from a wall, and, as if placed on a watchtower, watch the battles more than they engage in them. Elephants, indeed, rush upon the enemy with unbearable force, nor can they be repelled or slowed; like immovable mountains, they turn about in battles, and disturb everyone's confidence with the roar of their trumpeting. And not even unarmored, indeed, are they easily pierced by iron; armored with mail, however, without danger to themselves, they cut through battle lines and crush squadrons; they are also always armed with their own tusks, as if with natural spears, and, with their trunk, break whatever they entangle. And whatever they press with their foot, they kill, as if by the fall of some huge ruin.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: elephants, then, use their trunk in war too, and with it seize men opposing their side. For they are very warlike and bold, especially when the blood of grape or mulberry is shown to them in battle; with unbearable force, as said, they rush upon the enemy, so that they are slowed by no battle-line, no crowding of soldiers, no interposed shields. And when they trumpet, the sound through their mouth is horrible, since it comes with much breath. The Persians and Indians are accustomed to fight with these, carrying wooden towers with forty or fifty armed men on their backs. And so it is read that Alexander the Great, about to fight against the Indians, ordered bronze statues filled with burning coals, which the elephants, thinking them men, burned themselves extending their lips toward. And at once they began to flee, daring to touch no one further. On another occasion, by the grunting and screeching of pigs, together with the sound of trumpets, he overcame many elephants, since they were not accustomed to such sounds. Elephants fighting together take no small care of the wounded. For they receive the tired and wounded into their midst.

Avicenna: men are helped in battle by female elephants as well as males, but the females' bodies are smaller than the males', and along with this, too, of lesser boldness. The elephant, however, as said, is of such strength that it can knock down great walls with its tusks, and great trees with its forehead.

Pliny: elephants delight especially in silver trappings and seek glory; once tamed, they serve in war. And they carry towers of armed men against the enemy and crush a great part of them; yet these same creatures, wounded and terrified even by the slightest shrieking of their own kind, always retreat, no less to the destruction of their own side. The African elephant fears the Indian one, and does not dare to look at it. For the Indian one is also of greater size. Elephants spare the point of one tusk, so that it not be blunted, for battles. The use of the other, by habit, is to dig up roots and push aside soft obstacles. In Hannibal's time, one man fought against an elephant in the arena and killed it to the great grief of the Carthaginians. That the elephant's trunk can most easily be cut off was shown by the experience of Pyrrhus's battles. The greatest care in war, then, is devoted to these; and, remarkably, once overcome by shame, it flees the voice of the victor.
Physiologus: to rouse them for battle, grape-blood is shown to them. But if a pig comes before it grunting, it loses all its boldness.

Physiologus: elephants have no desire for offspring in themselves, but at the time when they wish to produce young, they go eastward all the way to the border of paradise, where they may find the mandrake, of whose fruit the female tastes first, then the male, at her urging, and then they come together and the female conceives. At the time of giving birth, however, she enters the water up to her udders, and there gives birth above the water, because of the dragon that lies in wait for her. And if she gave birth outside the water, it would devour her offspring. The male, too, does not withdraw from her while she gives birth, because of the serpent that is hostile to her, like the dragon. For the bones and skin of this animal, wherever they are burned, at once their smell drives off serpents, and no venomous creature approaches.

Solinus: they know nothing of mating before ten years for females, before five for males. They mate for two years, and only five days a year, no more, not returning to the herd's usual number until washed in flowing water; they never fight over females, for they know no adultery.

Isidore: elephants mate facing away from each other; when giving birth, however, they leave their offspring in waters and on islands, because of dragons, which are hostile to them, and, entangled by them, are killed. They carry their offspring for two years, and produce them no more than once, nor more than one at a time, but only a single one. They live, however, three hundred years. Formerly elephants were born only in Africa and India; now only India produces them.

Aristotle: the elephant mates in a wild place, especially near rivers; the female sits, the male mounts her. The female mates from the tenth year up to the fifteenth, the male, however, after five years, and this in spring. It produces a single offspring, like the horse and camel. The female is impregnated for two years, that is, carries in the womb, because of the extreme size of what is conceived. Once impregnated, too, she is not touched at all by the male, and after birth she rests for three years. She bears offspring, however, similar to a calf of two or three months. Elephants, at the time of mating, become wild and tear down houses and do many other astonishing things.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: elephants keep their offspring in deserted places, because of the dragon, which, when it finds it, kills it at once.

Pliny: elephants, out of a sense of modesty, never mate except in hiding. The females of this kind are much more timid. Aristotle, however, says they produce single offspring once every two years, no more. Whereas other animals have destructive fights among themselves over females, these have none, not because the force of love is lacking to them, nor is it strange that love is present in these creatures, in which memory is present. In India, especially around the time of mating, elephants become fierce and knock down the Indians' stables with their tusks. Wherefore they keep them from mating and separate the herds of females, which they keep in no other way than they do herds of cattle.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: Solinus says the elephant gives birth only once, but in truth it gives birth three or five times in its lifetime.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: as soon as the elephant is born, teeth appear, formed together with it at once, but the large tusks do not appear until it grows up. Its tongue is very small, and quite far inside; its nose is long and strong; it lacks gall, and does not have many toes on its front feet. Nor does it have cloven feet or hoof-coverings, but, because of the heaviness of its body, nature gave it feet strong only for bearing the body. And so it does not use its front feet in place of hands, as other animals do. Its front feet are much larger than its hind ones. Bending two feet, it sits, and, propping itself on one side, it sleeps. Around the hips it has additional joints, for it bends four joints. In animals the left foot is not of light movement, except in the elephant. The toes of its feet are not divided by a visible division, as in other animals, and it has five toes on its hind feet. The female has two teats, not on the chest, but nearby, namely under the armpit. And the elephant's teat is very small, not proportioned to the size of its body. And so they do not appear on either side. Males sometimes have two teats. The female has only two, since she bears only a single offspring. Nor are they near the hips, since it is a cloven-footed animal, but they are in the sub-armpit region, which is the proper place of teats. The elephant has a coiled, shaggy intestine. And so it is thought to have four stomachs, though it does not have another stomach. And its whole interior is similar to a pig's interior. Its liver is four times larger than an ox's liver, and the rest of its interior is similarly proportioned. Its spleen, in proportion to its body, is modest. Every animal having cloven feet has toes, except the elephant, which indeed has toes joined by a hidden joint. For they are not cloven, and so they have no claws at all. And so nature gave them very strong feet, for carrying so heavy a body. The position of the elephant's member is similar to the position of the horse's member, but it is small, not proportioned to its body. Its testicles do not appear outside, but are near the kidneys, inside. And so its leap in mating is swift. This animal's testicles, I say, like the tortoise's and the hedgehog's, are inside the body, since the skin of these animals is not suited to cover them. The elephant does not have a distinct gall bladder, but small veins, in which the gall is.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: elephants that fall cannot rise, since they have solid bones without joints. Whence too they cannot bend their legs and shins except in youth. Their legs, however, are equal in thickness, like stakes, from the bottom of the foot to the belly. Their feet, however, are round, like an apple. Since, as they walk, both by the weight of their body and the power of their strength, they press their feet very deep into the ground, so that it is dangerous for other animals, like horses and bulls, to walk behind them.

Pliny, in the same place: the elephant's back hide is very hard, its belly soft. It has no covering of bristles at all, not even on the tail, a protection given for driving off the annoyance of flies.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: the elephant has four teeth for chewing, apart from those that project; the males' are curved back, the females' straight and level. Elephants have four stomachs, but the rest resembles pigs'. Elephants' backs have impenetrable hides. Yet, among all four-footed creatures, subtlety of mind is attributed to them especially. Their testicles are hidden, adhering to the loins internally, for which reason they are most quick in mating, that is coupling.

Ambrose: the elephant has a small neck in proportion to its body. It does not bend its knees, so that so great a mass of limbs can be supported by rather rigid legs, like columns. It bends its heel slightly. The rest of its feet are rigid from top to bottom. It is propped up on either side by very large beams, so that in sleep it may lean back a little, since its foot is not marked by any joint of the limbs. But these props are made only for tame ones. For wild and untamed ones, however, danger looms: if, leaning against a tree, they rub their sides, or relax themselves in sleep, the tree, if bent and weighed by so great a body, sometimes breaks, and the elephant collapses, nor can it raise itself, but, lying there, dies, or, betrayed by its own groan, is felled, while its belly and other exterior parts are not easily pierced by any weapon. Finally, the elephant's limbs are compact, not distinct as ours are, whereby they are stronger than man's.

Physiologus: the elephant neither lowers itself onto its haunches, as we do, nor bends its knees, but only bends its heel slightly. The rest of its body, however, not at all. Its eyes are small, but move with weight. It looks with disdain on those playing buffoonishly; it gladly attends to anything honorable. The elephant's skin is furrowed with ulcerous valleys, from which the affliction of lepers, that is elephantiasis, took its name. This skin hardens to such solidity that you would think it made of bone. Finally, it is pierced by no force, and by scarcely any sharp point. And so the kings of the Persians brought it into war, since, struck by no blows, it does not yield. But the elephant's belly and what is near it are soft. Its interior is similar to a pig's interior, and, consequently, to man's interior.
Isidore: the elephant's snout is called the trunk [promuscis], since with it food is brought to the mouth, and it is similar to a serpent, defended by an ivory rampart.

Aristotle: the elephant's nose is long and strong, and it uses it in place of hands in taking food and drink and in everything it needs, and also in uprooting trees. And so the formation of this member in it was soft and flexible, so that it can hold the food it receives outside and bring it to its mouth. Likewise, because of breathing and its extension outward and its stay in water, nature placed that long appendage, capable of being coiled and doubled. And so nature deprived it of the use of feet, but it uses that appendage as other animals use their front feet. To this creature the nose is like a heel, formed of cartilage, which it uses in place of a hand. Through it it takes food and drink and returns it to its mouth, and through it too gives its master whatever he wishes. It alone among animals does this. In water too, when it swims, it breathes through it and expels water; indeed this animal's nature suits it for dwelling in deserts and near waters, so that its food is in moist places. And since it is an animal having blood, and walks with difficulty from a dry place to a moist one, for this reason it needs much breath, according to the size of its body. Finally, just as men submerging themselves in water prepare an instrument for themselves by which they breathe in water for a long time, so that air may reach them in the moisture by means of that instrument, so too nature devised, by giving elephants long appendages, which they raise above the water when they swim, to draw in air; they also use these for trumpeting. But the elephant sometimes trumpets through its mouth without the nose, and then its trumpeting is with much breath, as when a man pants heavily. But when it trumpets through the nose, then it will be like a sweet-sounding pipe.

Pliny: the elephant, around its nostrils, produces with its very mouth something like a sneeze-like sound; through its nostrils, however, something like the hoarseness of trumpets. The elephant's breath, or breathing, draws out serpents.

Ambrose: the horse and ox, indeed, were given rather long necks, since they graze on grasses. The elephant, however, since it is taller than all others, cannot bend down to graze, so has a trunk, that is a snout in the likeness of a serpent, for gathering food and for pouring in moisture for a great drink; this trunk, moreover, is hollow, so that, to quench the thirst of so great a beast, it may draw from full pools.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the elephant, then, a large and robust animal, has a snout of ten cubits, projecting like a wide intestine, of hard, cartilaginous flesh, which they call the trunk, and uses it in place of a hand, adapted to every action. Whence through it it takes food and drink and returns them to its mouth. For even wine, which it naturally drinks gladly when given to it, it sucks up with its trunk and pours into its mouth, and then, feeling delight in its palate, gratefully expresses its pleasure to the giver with a soothing sound of its mouth.

div.head: DE ETATIBUS ET MORBIS ET NOCUMENTIS ELEPHANTORUM

cit.quote: Pliny: the youth of elephants begins at sixty years, and they live mostly two hundred years, and some even three hundred. They are impatient of cold, and suffer bloating and looseness of the bowels. I find that objects stuck in their bodies fall out after drinking oil, but adhere more easily from sweat. Among animals they most hate the mouse, and feel the greatest torment in drinking from the leech or bloodsucker, when it fixes itself in the very stream or channel. The dragon, as said above, fights against the elephant and aims especially at the eyes, so that it happens that elephants are often found blind and wasted away from hunger and the decay of grief. The rhinoceros too attacks it, aiming its horn at the belly, which it knows to be softer. It is destructive for elephants to have eaten earth, unless they chew it often. The elephant, having by chance devoured the chameleon worm, meets its poison with wild olive. They have no covering of bristles at all, not even on the tail, a protection given for driving off the annoyance of flies.

Solinus, on elephants: youth is understood by the whiteness of the tusks, of which one is always in service. The other is spared, so that, dulled by constant striking, it does not lose its vigor, should there be need to fight. But when pressed by hunting, they break both tusks at once, so that, the ivory forfeited, they are no longer sought. For they sense this to be the cause of their danger; they live three hundred years, most impatient of cold. They flee especially the smell of the mouse.

Ambrose: the elephant, then, dreads bulls, fears the mouse. Nor do I marvel more that the elephant, tall as it is, fears the mouse, than that elephants are said to prolong their life three hundred years and more, since, though their limbs are compact and not distinct, if they stand long, or run rather swiftly, or walk continuously, their knees and soles are troubled.
Aesculapius, from the book On the Senses: the elephant, when it sees a ram, fears it and flees.

Aristotle: wind harms elephants, and if an elephant eats earth, it will die, unless accustomed to this, and it may perhaps swallow stones too. There also befalls them a bloating illness, because of which they cannot pass urine or dung; but when the elephant is troubled from not having slept, its shoulder-blades should be anointed with oil and water, and it will be cured. But if its shoulder-blades ache, roasted pork should be placed on its shoulders and it will be healed. Pain of the joints sometimes befalls them, and against this a drink of warm water and grasses steeped in honey helps them. For these two things check flux of the bowels. If one of them has iron in its belly, it is drawn out by drinking oil. And the elephant drinks wine, and when it cannot drink, they take medicines and boil them with oil and give it that to drink. They grow for sixty years, and then feel cold and winter and cold wind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: wind, as said, greatly harms elephants, and through it they contract illnesses. If an elephant eats earth, it dies. Some, however, are accustomed to eating it and do not die from it, since habit, which is a second nature, prevails in them. Wine, which they drink gladly - when they cannot drink it, it is a sign that they are ill, and so they must be purged with medicine.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the elephant has no joints in its shins, and as is read in the Bestiary, sleeping elephants never lie down, but, when exhausted from labor, lean against large trees and refresh themselves, and sleep propped against them. Hunters, noticing this, mark the place and the trees and cut them nearly through. When the elephants, according to their custom, unwittingly lean on these, the trees fall, and the elephants are brought down to the ground with them, and thus are caught, for when an elephant has fallen, it cannot rise. But at its trumpeting, other elephants usually come running, and, since they cannot bend down and raise their companion, they groan and trumpet together. The young elephants, however, as best they can, placing themselves under it with their trunks, sometimes raise it, and thus free it from the hunters' hands. The reason a larger elephant, once fallen, cannot rise, however, is that it has solid bones without joints. Whence it cannot bend its shins and legs; a young one, however, can.

Pliny: Africa or India catches elephants in pits, into which, when one strays, the rest at once gather, roll down soft branches, build up mounds, and try with all their strength to pull it out. For the sake of the tusks, they hurl spears at their feet.

Ambrose: elephants, as we said above, when wild, leaning against a tree, either rub their sides or relax themselves in sleep. This tree, sometimes overcome and bent by so great a body, breaks, and the elephant, collapsing, dies lying there, or, betrayed by its own groan, is felled. Some, too, for the sake of the ivory, prepare traps for them, cutting the trees somewhat through on the side against which they are accustomed to lean more frequently, so that, as they lean back, they fall more easily.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: elephants, hearing a man's footstep behind them, not having seen him first, tremble and stop still from fear of an ambush. They are caught, moreover, in this way: two virgin girls go naked into the desert where they dwell, one carrying an urn, the other a sword. As they sing with raised voice, when the elephant hears them it hastens near, and soon, by natural instinct, recognizes the innocence of virgin flesh, and, with the sweetness of love, venerates their chastity, and, licking their chest and breasts, is marvelously delighted and falls into a deep sleep. Without delay, the girl with the sword pierces its tender belly and the falling creature pours out its blood, while the other catches what flows into the urn; with this blood royal purple is dyed. There is also another way of hunting them, on the philosopher's testimony.

Aristotle: for a man rides a tame elephant, hunting for other elephants. And once he has caught them, he orders some of the tame elephants to strike some of the wild ones until they obey. And when an elephant is caught, its trainer leaps upon it. And he strikes it with an instrument resembling a small shield, and then it suddenly becomes calm, and as long as the trainer is on it, it obeys. But when the trainers dismount, some of them become tame, some do not, and so, until they grow calm, their front feet are tied. Yet, of all wild animals, the elephant is the most tame and obedient, and receives training well and understands, as already said above.

Pliny, in the same place: elephants are tamed by ravenous hunger and by blows, some elephants being warned, others brought up to restrain the disturbed ones with chains, and others especially grow fierce around mating and knock down the Indians' stables with their tusks, wherefore they keep them from mating. And they separate the herds of females, which they keep in no other way than herds of cattle. Once tamed, however, as said above, they serve in war and carry towers of armed men against the enemy, and accomplish a great part of the wars of the East.
Solinus: elephants, as said, when caught and come into the hands of men, are tamed by drinking the juice of barley.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: and so hunters, as Aristotle said above, seeking wild elephants in the desert, when they find them, order the tame ones to pursue and strike them until they obey and, exhausted, stand still. Then the hunters mount them and strike and prod them and move them to fear men, and tie their front feet until they grow tame. They grow tame and are domesticated more quickly than wild animals, however. There is also another way of taming elephants. First, once caught by a hunter, it is struck and afflicted with many blows. Another, who wishes to have it obedient to himself, approaches and rescues it from the hand of the one striking it. Noticing this, the elephant grows tame in his hands, and, recognizing him as its liberator, always obeys him and loves him.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: elephants have little flesh but much bone. This bone, called ivory, is white, smooth, shining, cold, and the older it is, the ruddier it becomes, and this consists in the tusks.

Solinus: the youth of elephants is understood, as said, by the whiteness of their tusks. Of these, one is always in service, but the elephant spares the other, so that, dulled by constant striking, it does not lose its vigor, should there be need to fight. And when pressed by hunting, they break both tusks at once, so that, the ivory forfeited, they are no longer sought; they sense, as already said before, this to be the cause of danger to them.

Pliny: elephants indeed, as said, surrounded by hunters, know that the prey being sought from them lies only in their weapons, which Juba calls horns, and when they are tired, they strike their tusks against a tree and break them, and ransom themselves with this booty; but tusks that have fallen off by some accident or old age they bury - this alone is ivory. The great size of tusks, however, is now rarely found, except from India.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the elephant, as Pliny says, has four teeth inside for chewing, apart from those that project, curved back in males, but straight or level in females. In these lies the special nobility of ivory, which is not found in the other bones of the body. If cloth is placed over this ivory and fire set on the cloth, the cloth is not burnt, but is extinguished by the natural coldness of the ivory.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: an elephant's blood, especially the male's, checks flux of rheumatism. Also, by the smoke made from an elephant's hoof and hair, any venomous animals are driven off.

Platearius: the elephant has certain solid bones, like the tusks, and these are not burnt, but are kept for various uses. Others, however, have marrow, and these, burnt, are called 'spodium,' cold in the third degree, dry in the second. It is sometimes adulterated with burnt dog bones, sometimes with burnt marble, but this is less heavy. Whence that should be chosen which is whitish, very light, and uniform. It is put into syrups for cooling. Its powder, given with plantain juice, is effective for dysentery and coughing blood. Against flux too, its powder placed in the nostrils checks bleeding. Avicenna says, however, that 'spodium' is burnt reed roots, but, as Jerome says, shavings of ivory are used for various remedies.

Pliny, book 28, on the elephant: the male's blood checks all rheumatisms, and also benefits dysentery sufferers. Ivory shavings or filings with Attic honey, they say, remove blemishes on the face. By the touch of the trunk, head pain is relieved, more effectively if it also sneezes. The right part of the trunk, bound on with red ochre, stimulates the urges of lust. The blood too benefits sciatica sufferers. The liver, however, benefits epileptic diseases.
Avicenna, in the second canon: elephant fat, when a liniment is made from it, drives off venomous things. Its dung, applied beneath, is said to prevent conception.
Haly Abbas: [an elephant's] belly, if fumigated with it, benefits one suffering fever, but if placed with wool beneath a woman, she does not conceive.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'enchires' is an animal in the East, similar to a bull, but having long hairs descending to the shoulder-blades like a horse, horns much curved back and suited for fighting, and a tail short in proportion to its body. Its hide is very hard and able to withstand blows; its flesh, too, is most sweet. When it grows weak fleeing hunters, it fights, and in fighting discharges dung over a distance of four paces out of fear, for it is an animal of much dung. Then, when the time of its giving birth approaches, many animals of the same kind gather around it, and, excreting, pile up dung like a wall around it.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'enchires' seems, moreover, to be the same beast that was called above the 'duran' or 'bonasus' according to Aristotle.

Isidore: the 'enydros' is a small beast so named because it lives in the water, and especially in the Nile. If it finds a sleeping crocodile, it first rolls itself in mud, and even enters through its mouth into its belly, and, gnawing all its innards, kills it thus; this is called 'ichneumon' in Greek, as will be said below under this name, 'ichneumon.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'enitra' is a modest animal in Germany, male and female, which, making mounds in the earth, gather food in summer, on which to live in winter. The female is naturally eager and lavish with food. The male, on the contrary, is exceedingly sparing and stingy, and so blocks the entrance, lest the female be able to reach the food. But she, naturally cunning, makes a hidden hole on the other side, through which she steals what suffices for her eagerness. And so it happens that the sparing male wastes away in leanness, while the female glows with fatness.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the hedgehog, also called the 'cherogryllus,' is an animal having the form of a small pig, but spiny everywhere except on the belly. It is enclosed on all sides by its spines against ambushes, and offers itself with difficulty to being seen or touched, but when placed in warm water, delighted by it at once, it relaxes its limbs into a flat, exposed position, and thus is seen and touched without harm. This creature, as Aristotle says, hears more dully than any animal having a shell on its head. For it is from the resonance that occurs in the shell that sound is heard. The hedgehog has five teeth, and between them a fleshy member; it uses its spines in place of weapons, as the ox uses its horns. For the nourishment of its body passes into spines because of the scarcity of heat, which does not suffice to digest food. Because of this, much surplus is generated in its body, from which, because of great coldness, hard spines are generated like stones. The hedgehog is fat and medicinal. It alone has two years during which it discharges waste. It alone, moreover, among four-footed animals that generate young, has testicles near the kidneys, like birds. For the rest have them in the front part: the male and female of this species mate standing, pressed together and joined to each other, and this because of the sharp spines that are on its back. For if they mated back to back, they would prick each other with their spines.

Pliny: [on] the hyena's and hedgehog's food. For, having rolled themselves over apples lying above, with the fruit stuck to their spines, carrying no more than one at a time in their mouth, they take them into hollow trees: these same creatures, sensing the change from north wind to south, foretell it by hiding in their den, but when they sense a hunter, drawing in their mouth and feet and their whole lower part, where they have sparse and harmless down, they roll themselves into the shape of a ball, so that nothing can be grasped except the spines. In despair, however, they release from themselves a wasting urine, harmful to their own hide and spines, aware that this is why they are caught. Wherefore the hunter's skill lies in first emptying out the urine, for then the chief value of the hide, once spoiled, is fragile, with rotting and falling spines.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the ermine is a small beast of the weasel kind, but smaller in form and different in color; in winter it whitens like snow, except at the tip of the tail. In summer, however, it whitens only on the belly, and appears dark on the back. It pursues mice, feeds on flesh. Human vanity is accustomed to use the pelts of these small beasts as the topmost trim on garments.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'falena' is an animal that, by a certain natural indignation, detests pride in man. And so, if it gets the chance to engage, it presses the fight persistently, and, victorious, strives mercilessly to tear the proud man apart. But if, on the contrary, in a man it encounters, it detects, by flight and fear, a sign of humility, it sometimes stops and lets him escape.

Solinus: the 'fiber' is very common throughout the Black Sea region; they call it the beaver; it is similar to the otter, an animal most powerful in its bite, so much so that, when it has attacked a man, it does not release the grip of its teeth before it perceives that the broken bones have crunched, as indeed already said above.
Pliny: Pontic beavers, when danger presses, cut off their own testicles, aware that it is for this remedy that they are sought.

Pliny, in the same: the beaver lives on land. 'Castorea' are called their testicles, which are said to be cut off by them when caught. Sestius, most diligent in medicine, says these are small, drawn together and adhering to the spine, and asserts they cannot be removed without the animal's death. They are adulterated, however, with kidneys of those that are large. They are effective, however, for much medicine, as already said above. Beaver's urine too resists poisons, for which reason it is added to antidotes and is best kept, as some think, in its own bladder.

Pliny, book 22, in the same: gout sufferers benefit from wearing shoes of beaver skins, especially Pontic beaver. Ash of beaver skins, burnt in boiling water, is beneficial. The same ash too, with liquid pitch, stops bleeding of the nostrils, and, softened with leek juice, draws out things embedded in the body.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the rest concerning the 'fiber' and its medicines has already been said above under the name of the beaver.
Isidore: the ferret [furo] is named from the oven [furnus], whence too the thief [fur]. For it digs dark and hidden burrows and drives out the prey it finds.

Aristotle: female ferrets are very obedient to mating, and males call out for mating at the time of lust. Nor do males mate with the female from behind, but the male is raised and the female matched by lying beneath.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the polecat is very similar to the ferret, a little larger than the weasel. Its color is between white and boxwood, and it is a spirited and exceedingly fierce animal, beyond what its strength allows nature to grant it. It is trained for this purpose, that it be put by hunters into the burrows where rabbits hide, which it boldly enters, and attacks the little creature with bites until, cornered, it drives it out, forced into the nets. Nor do they hate this animal alone, but attack whatever animal seems to breathe, however large, to the extent of their strength, not out of desire for flesh, which indeed they do not eat, but from a will to do harm, or, as some say, for the blood of the beasts, which indeed they gladly take as drink. They are said to mate lying flat. If the female has no male, when stirred by lust she swells up and dies. She is indeed fertile in birth, producing seven or eight offspring at once, and carries in the womb for forty days. And once the young are born, they are blind for thirty days, but from the time they begin to see up to forty days, they begin to hunt.

Isidore: the 'galy' is an animal of much boldness, fighting with serpents. For it gladly eats mice, and this kind of serpent lives on the flesh of mice. So it pursues serpents as if rivals for its food, and, when it has overcome and eaten them, soon eats rue, which is opposed to serpents; this animal makes the entrance of its burrows toward the north, so that it is not troubled by an unfavorable wind. The genet is a beast somewhat larger than a small fox, having a color between saffron and black. It sometimes has black spots arranged in order on its skin. It is a quite gentle beast, unless provoked by injuries. Nor does it climb to steep places, but wanders in low places and along streams of water, and there seeks food when hungry.
Aristotle: the hedgehog is a spiny animal, whose sense often shows itself against the north and south winds. For it makes holes in the ground facing opposite to the winds.
Pliny: garments are trimmed with this creature's hide.

Isidore: the hedgehog is an animal covered with spines, so named because it raises itself up when it closes itself with its spines, by which it is protected on every side against ambushes. For as soon as it senses anything, it first raises itself and, curled into a ball, gathers itself into its own weapons, and is thus defended by a spiny covering, so that it cannot even be touched. There is a certain cunning in it: when it has cut a grape from the vine, it rolls itself onto its back over it and thus brings it to its young.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: the hedgehog gathers fruit with the spines of its back. But if any of this food falls off, it discards the rest entirely and returns, so as to refill its spines as before; the wolf, however, fears and flees this creature.

Ambrose: the hedgehog, foreseeing the future, prepares for itself twin passages for breathing, so that, namely, when it has gathered that the north wind will blow, it may block the northern one. When it has recognized from the south wind that the clouds of the sky are clearing, it betakes itself to the northern passage, so as to avoid the opposing blasts.

Gregory the Great, in the Moralia: when the hedgehog is caught, its head and feet and whole body are seen as it is. But as soon as it is grasped, it gathers itself into a sphere, draws its feet inward, hides its head, and, within the captor's hands, all at once hides what had all at once been visible.

Avicenna: one hedgehog is terrestrial, having arrow-like spines. The other is marine, and is a species of shelled fish. The ashes of both are cleansing and dissolving and sharpening and drying. Hedgehog fat prevents effusions to the internal organs, and likewise its liver. Its flesh benefits scrofula and misshapen, hard lumps, and the bite of venomous worms. Likewise the hedgehog benefits a malignant constitution, and what is salted from it, with oxymel, is good for dropsy. What is burnt from the hedgehog's skin benefits baldness, mixed with pitch. Ash of its skin benefits filthy ulcers, and cleans away excess flesh. The terrestrial hedgehog is good for the stomach, soothes and provokes the bowels. What is salted from it benefits baldness; its flesh benefits leprosy because of the vehemence of its dissolving power. The same benefits wasting and long-standing fevers. It also benefits a child who wets the bed, so that continual eating of it will perhaps cause urine to come out with difficulty. The same, however, salted, benefits paralysis and spasm and all sinew ailments and elephantiasis. With oxymel too it benefits kidney pain. The skin of the sea hedgehog is put in medicines for scabies, and its flesh greatly benefits scrofula.

Haly Abbas: hedgehog flesh, if pressed with 'hausal,' that is squill vinegar, benefits sufferers of elephantiasis and those thin in body and having spasm and repletion. But it is effective for arthritics and those suffering pain in the kidneys, and dropsy sufferers. For it gathers by the power of its dissolving and thickening action. Hedgehog's gall roots out spots of ulcers that are in the eyes. It also benefits sufferers of elephantiasis if they drink it: its hide, dried and mixed with honey, benefits baldness if applied as a poultice.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: hedgehog's flesh has a drying and dissolving power, and especially strengthens the stomach, loosens the bowels, provokes urine, and is useful for those disposed to leprosy and elephantiasis.

Solinus: Africa nourishes the hyena: since its spine is rigid, its neck cannot be bent except by turning the whole body around. There are many marvels about it. First, that it follows the stalls of shepherds, and, by constant listening, learns a name it can pronounce in imitation of the human voice, so that, having lured a man by name into the night, it rages against him, and mimics human vomiting with false gasps, and thus devours the dogs it has lured, that is, those which, if hunters happen to be following its shadow, and touch it, lose their voice and cannot bark. This same hyena, in searching for buried bodies, digs up tombs. Besides, it is easier to catch the male. For a more cunning craftiness is innate in the females; there is a manifold variety in its eyes, and a change of color. In its pupils a stone is found, which they say is endowed with such power that whoever holds it under his tongue predicts the future: besides, whatever animal a hyena has circled three times cannot move, whence they have said it possesses magical knowledge. In part of Ethiopia it mates with the lioness, from which is born the monster called the 'leucocrota' or 'crocuta.'

Aristotle: the hyena is an animal the size of a wolf, on whose neck there are hairs, as on the neck of horses; it has hard or strong hairs over all its vertebrae. It deceives shepherds and dogs by gasping as if it were a dog, and thus eats the flocks. For, deceiving men and dogs themselves, it preys on them, and digs up graves when it desires to eat such flesh.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the hyena has two natures, namely male and female; it changes color when it wishes, and always dwells among the tombs of the dead; it carries a gem in its eyes, or, as some say, in its forehead.

Pliny: common folk believe that hyenas have both natures, becoming male in alternate years and female in alternate years, and giving birth without a male. Aristotle denies this. Its neck and mane are extended by the continuity of the spine, and it bends only by turning the whole body around.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: the hyena's eyes pass through a thousand colors, and its neck is rigid with straight bones.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: the magicians have held the hyena in the greatest wonder of all animals, to which they have attributed magical arts and the power to lure men to itself, their minds deranged. Panthers especially are said to be in fear of the hyena, so that they do not even attempt to resist, and one who carries something of its hide is not attacked. And, remarkable to say, if the skins of both are hung facing each other, the panther's hairs fall out. When they flee a hunter, however, they turn to the right, so as to get ahead of the man's footprints. And if this succeeds, it deranges his mind, or makes him fall from his horse. And if he turns to the left, this is a proof of his weakening and an easy catch.

Gloss: the hyena is a nocturnal beast that devours the corpses of the dead, and even digs bodies out of tombs, and feeds on every kind of filth; the people of Israel are compared to its uncleanness. Whence it is also said by the Lord through the prophet: is my inheritance to me a cave of the hyena?
Jerome, against Jovinian: hyena's gall restores clarity of the eyes; its dung heals putrid wounds.

Pliny, book 28: they also say that the skin of a hyena's head, bound on, benefits headache, but its gall, applied to the forehead, benefits watering eyes, or, to prevent watering altogether, cooked with three cups of Attic honey and applied with an ounce of saffron. Thus too dimness is dispersed and clarity is restored to suffusions of the eyes. It is better, however, with an aged remedy kept in a bronze box. By the same, too, cataracts are healed and roughness growing in the eyes. Likewise scars, and cataracts by the pus of the roasted fresh liver, joined with skimmed honey; its teeth benefit toothache by touch, or bound in order on the shoulders, benefit pains of the shoulders and arms. Its teeth too, if extracted from the left side and bound in the skin of a herd animal or a goat, benefit stomach cramps; its lungs, taken as food, benefit celiacs; ash of its stomach applied with oil [benefits] the stomach. Marrow from its spine with old oil and gall [benefits] the sinews. Its liver, tasted before the onset, [benefits] quartan fevers. Something eaten from its heart [benefits] those with tremors, sciatica, palpitations, and those whose heart flutters, so that the ash of the rest be applied with the hyena's brain; that mating be stimulated by its genital taken in honey according to their sex. Even if men hate intercourse with women, they have the first joint of its spine among remedies for epileptics. With its fat lit, they say serpents are driven off; its dried palate, warmed with Egyptian alum or turned three times in the mouth, corrects bad smells and ulcers; and those who have its tongue in a shoe under the foot are not barked at by dogs. Applied on the left side to those with brain disorders, dangerous diseases are eased, whether of men or four-footed creatures. Its forehead's hide, too, resists spells. Its liver, drunk, heals colic and stones. Its heart, taken as food or drink, helps all pains of the body. Its marrow too, for pains of the spine and weariness of the sinews of the kidneys; and many other things of this kind.

Jerome: the porcupine, most common in Ethiopia, is similar to the hedgehog, bristling on the back with spines. It frequently releases these, loosened, by voluntary shooting, so as to wound with a constant shower of quills the dogs attacking it.

Pliny: India and Africa produce porcupines, covered with spines and of the hedgehog kind, but the porcupine's quills are longer, and, when it tenses its skin, they are missile-like; in the winter months, however, it hides itself. This is the nature of many creatures, and especially of bears.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the porcupine is a beast commonly called the spiny pig; it dwells around coastal areas and sometimes in mountain caverns, namely when it has no refuge near the sea; it is equally powerful on land and in water. It is so quick to take vengeance that it very often wounds dogs or men approaching it with quills freely released from its back.
Aristotle: the spiny pig, in place of hair, has spines of its own hide, and these cover it as hair does. They are also like weapons to it, with which it wounds one seeking to catch it.
Isidore: the 'icinus' is a land animal, which common folk call the hedgehog, from which the sea 'icinus' also took its name.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: on the sea 'icinus,' also called the sea urchin, enough has already been said above in the treatise on fish. The land 'icinus,' however, is likewise called by several names, namely 'echinus' and 'ericius' and 'herinacius.' These names, moreover, are sometimes written with an aspiration, sometimes without it, and so this animal has been discussed in several places.

Dioscorides: the land hedgehog's burnt hide, mixed with liquid pitch, heals baldness. Its flesh, drunk with oxymel, is a singular remedy for kidney sufferers, for edema sufferers, and for contracted dropsy sufferers and those with scrofula and choleric conditions, and dries the flux of the internal organs. Its liver, dried in a shell in hot sun and stored, and applied as an ointment, marvelously heals all the aforesaid.

Pliny, book 8: they report that the 'inaclin' [elk] in Scandinavia, having no bend in its hocks, therefore does not lie down, but, leaning against a tree in sleep, is caught by ambush when it is cut through, being otherwise of the swiftness already mentioned; its upper lip is very large, and for this reason it walks backward while grazing, lest, reaching forward, it become entangled in it.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'inaclin,' under another name, seems to be called the 'cale,' of which mention was made above.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'lamia,' as the book of things says, is a large and most cruel animal. By night it leaves the woods and enters gardens, breaks trees and scatters their branches, and this with arms exceedingly strong, suited for every action. And when men come to stop it, it fights with them and bites them; this, moreover, is remarkable about its bite, as Aristotle relates, that a man wounded by a lamia's teeth is not healed of the bite until he hears the roaring beast's voice; perhaps these are the 'lamiae' of whom Jerome says: the lamiae have bared their breasts, and so on. For there the Gloss says that the lamia is a most ferocious beast, which nevertheless offers milk to tender young seeking it. In this it shows the Jews to be more cruel than lamiae, since little children sought bread and there was no one to break it for them. This animal is called 'ledith' in Hebrew. And certain Jews suspect it to be one of the Furies, who are called the sparing ones, since they spare no one. I have heard that lamia beasts are in the East, around those regions containing the Tower of Babel, in the plain of Shinar, and these are larger than goats, exceedingly rich in milk, and are domesticated by men so as to be led to pasture, for they are useful in abundance of milk.
Gloss: the lamia has horse's feet, but the rest resembles a goat's, of which the prophet says: there the lamia lay down and found rest for herself.

Gloss, on Lamentations: the lamia is so called as if 'lania' [tearer], since it is harder and crueler to its offspring than other beasts, for it is said to tear them apart and yet suckle them, as it is written: the lamiae have bared their breasts, and so on.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'lauzani' is an animal from whose cruelty no beast can be safe, for it wears down even the lion, formidable to all, yet it spares its own kind, but rages against the rest, preying on other beasts. And though it pursues this crime in others, it does not remember its own iniquity.
Isidore: the lion has a name adapted from Greek; 'leo' in Greek is indeed interpreted in Latin as 'king,' since it is the prince of all beasts.

Aristotle, in the same place: the lion is a bold, strong, generous, noble, magnanimous animal; the male of this kind has a mane. The lion is among the four-footed animals cloven at the extremities, and has hooked and curved claws. It urinates backward and, like a dog, raises a leg. And when it opens its mouth, an odor comes from it; it is an animal of many toes, having five toes on its front feet and four on its hind feet, like the lynx and dog and wolf. Likewise every animal having teeth above and below has a single belly, like the lion, and, after the belly, intestine. Again, every animal having blood and producing a single offspring has only one belly, like the lion and dog and man. The lioness has only two small teats, in the middle of the belly, not proportioned to the size of her body, and the reason for this is not that she has few offspring, but that she has little milk: for the food that passes into the body is that which she eats, and this only rarely, and she eats flesh. In the lion's bones there is no marrow except a little, for which reason it is imagined that they have no marrow at all. It has sharp teeth of separate arrangement, and places one over another. And all animals of this kind have a more divided mouth. The lion's whole interior, however, resembles the dog's interior. And so the lion has a mane, a saw-like row of teeth, and a terrible split of the mouth. It has very hard bones, so that, if rubbed together, fire comes out of them, as from stones. Nor is there marrow in them, except in the hip bone and in the sole [of the shoulder], that is, from the shoulder to the elbow. The bone of the lion's neck is continuous, and in it there is no jointed segmentation. The lion and the camel, when they walk, move the right foot first.

Pliny: male lions pass urine with a raised leg, of heavy smell, and no less bad breath. They drink rarely, and feed on alternate days. They go three days without food, so that, in eating, they can devour solid things, and, their belly unable to hold their greed, they draw out with their claws thrust into their throat what they have swallowed, so that, if they must flee, they are not full. The color of lions is black only in Syria. It is remarkable, however, that panthers and leopards and lions and similar creatures walk with the tips of their claws hidden in sheaths of their body, lest they be broken or blunted, and run with their little claws turned back, extending them only when attacking.

Pliny, book 2, in the same: lions shed their teeth, but only those called canine ones; lions' tongue is rough like a file, resembling a cat's, and, by licking, thins a man's skin. The lion has twisted ankle-bones. The lion alone and the camel walk foot by foot. This is such that the left foot does not pass the right, but follows it; the hair of the lion's tail is at the very bottom, as with oxen.
Aesculapius: the 'sarim,' that is the lion, when it sleeps, if a ship carries it, sinks more than usual. But once the lion wakes, its buoyancy returns.
From the book On the Nature of Things, of an uncertain author: the lion is foul-smelling, especially in the mouth; sleeping, it has open eyes. When it sleeps in a ship, the ship is endangered.
Isidore: the lion's strength is in its chest, its firmness in its head; its forehead and tail indicate its spirit.

Aristotle: the lion, then, is a strong animal, as we have said, having sharp teeth like a saw and a terrible split of the mouth, and very hard bones, almost entirely without marrow. Nor is there marrow in all bones, but only in those that are hollow, and perhaps there is no hollowness in some, as in the lion's bones. It has, then, dense and strong bones, since there is no marrow in them, except a little, and so it is imagined there is none at all. And so, if the lion's bones are rubbed together, fire will come out of them, as said.
Pliny, book 8: the bear indeed has a most feeble head, whereas the lion's, on the contrary, is strongest.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: lions' necks are rigid with straight bones; in these there is marrow in the thigh and arm bones, very slight and scant, but otherwise their bones are of such hardness that fire is struck from them as from flint.

Ambrose: nature, moreover, formed narrower necks for lions, as for bears and tigers, since they do not lower their neck and mouth to the ground for the sake of grazing, but either attack a stag or tear apart an ox or a sheep.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the lion's strength is in its chest and in its feet and in its tail. Its bones are larger than the bones of other animals, and of such hardness that from their mutual collision fire flashes, as from flint. In these, however, there is a small hollow and no marrow except very rarely. The bone of its neck, and the flesh of its neck, is cartilaginous, whence it can bend its neck backward or to the side. Some have thought this was a sign of indignation or stupidity, ignorant of the reason for the continuous bone in the neck; it is most renowned for strength, but is naturally heavy, and for this reason has difficult digestion. And when it runs vigorously, it overshoots the limits of its intended course, since in the force of its spirit it cannot restrain itself. The lion is never found fat or adorned with plumpness. Its interior resembles fittingly the dog's interior. Its bones are harder than the bones of other animals, except the dolphin's. In its front part it is of hot nature, in its rear, cold. So too the sun, when it is in Leo.

Ambrose: the lion, proud in the ferocity of its nature, as king disdains the company of other wild beasts. Nor does any beast dare to associate with it, since such terror is naturally present in its voice that even creatures which by their speed can escape its charge fail, as if struck and stunned by some force, at the sound of its roar. It even scorns yesterday's food and rejects the very leftovers of its own meal. It fears the cock, however, and especially a white one. When it is sick, however, it seeks out and devours an ape, by which it can be healed.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: at the lion's roar all animals freeze in their tracks, even those that have never seen or experienced it. And this is by nature's command, which instilled fear of the lion in them. Its anger is more frequent, for sometimes, when its fury within is immoderate, it is said to be consumed and to perish by fiery blood and the heat of its wrath. Accordingly, at the beginning of its anger it lashes the ground with its tail, and, as it grows, whips its back with a kind of incitement. The captured lion's anger is calmed by this trick: a cub is beaten before it, and it believes, by that example, that it too ought to fear the man whom it sees has power over the constraint of a dog; hence it is said in the proverb that he is well chastised who chastises himself through another. It terrifies other wild beasts not only by its roar, but also, always eager for prey, by drawing a circle with the trace of its tail over the surface of dust or snow, whose circumference the beasts enclosed within do not presume to cross.

Pliny: the lion leaps in pursuit, a method it does not use in flight. The lioness, when she fights, pregnant, on behalf of her cubs, is said to fix the gaze of her eyes on the ground, lest she be frightened by the hunting spears.

Gloss, on Amos: does the lion, it says, roar in the forest unless it has prey? The lion, when it suffers hunger, if it sees prey, gives a roar, at whose sound wild beasts stand frozen in their tracks, stunned.

Pliny, in the same place: the tail is the index of lions' spirit, as horses' ears are. For nature grants these signs to each of the noblest creatures. The lion's tail, then, is motionless when it is calm, gentle when it is being coaxed - which is rare, for its anger is more frequent, at whose onset the tail beats the ground, and, as it grows, the back is whipped as if by some incitement; its greatest power is in the chest. From every wound, whether made by claw or tooth, black blood flows; once sated, these same creatures are harmless. Its nobility is most detected in danger. Not only in this, that, scorning weapons, it long protects itself by terror alone, and, as it were, protests and is compelled, not as if forced by danger, but as if angered. That is the nobler sign of spirit, that, whatever the great force of dogs or hunters pressing upon it, resisting with contempt, it gives itself up in open fields, and where it can be seen. But the same creature, once it has penetrated thickets and woods, is carried off in the swiftest run, as if it accounted hiding a disgrace. While it pursues, as said, it leaps in a bound, a method it does not use in flight; wounded, it recognizes, by remarkable observation, the one who struck it, and, in however great a multitude, attacks him. But the one who indeed threw a weapon but did not wound it, it seizes and drags down and lays flat, but does not wound him. Otherwise they are without guile and without suspicion, nor do they look with sidelong glances, nor do they wish to be looked at in a similar way.

Isidore: the lion's nature toward man is such that it cannot grow angry unless injured. Its mercy is proven by constant examples. For it spares those who lie prostrate, and lets captives it meets return home; it kills a man only when in great hunger.

Pliny, in the same place: there are many signs of lions' clemency. They rage against men rather than women, and kill infants only in great hunger. Of all wild beasts, clemency toward suppliants belongs to the lion alone; where it rages, it spares those who lie prostrate. Libya believes that an understanding of prayers reaches it. Indeed I have heard a captive woman, once returned, relate that she had calmed the attack of many lions in the forest by speaking to them, having dared to say that she was a fugitive woman, weak, a suppliant, an unworthy prey for the glory of that most noble of all animals, ruler over the rest.

Ambrose: lions too submit to the yoke and are teachable, and these serve man and lay aside their nature through human training. They forget that they were born wild and take on what they are commanded. Finally, they are taught like children, they serve like the weak, they are beaten like the timid, they are corrected like subjects. And while they pass over into our ways, they lose their own impulses.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the lion does not easily grow angry unless injured, but when it is provoked without cause, it utterly crushes its opponent. Pliny relates that a man of Syracuse, meeting a lion in Syria, rolled about it suppliantly, stunned with fear, and, as the lion, though he kept fleeing, confronted him on every side and licked his footprints as if fawning, noticed a wound on its foot, and, drawing out a splinter, freed it from its torment. Similarly Elpis, having fled to a tree when he met a lion, saw the lion, its mouth gaping, howling before him, showing that a bone had lodged in its teeth from too greedy a bite. Seeing this, he approached and removed the obstruction from the middle of its gaping mouth. And the lion, recognizing that it had been healed by his hand, gave thanks in a manner, as if fawning. Its tail is indeed motionless when it is fawning and pleased, but this is rare, for its anger is more frequent; it is said to spare a man, or even one humbling himself before it, even when driven by the fiercest hunger, whence the noblest lions know how to spare those who submit to them.
