Isidore: those of lions that are short and maned, I have written, are unwarlike. Those long and of simple fur, however, are fierce; their forehead and tail indicate their spirit. Their strength is in the chest, their firmness in the head.

Solinus: on the land of Africa there are very many wild beasts indeed, but lions hold chief place, which, as Aristotle reports, alone among that kind called toothed, see at once when born. Their kind is divided into three types. For the shorter ones, with curly manes, are generally cowardly and unwarlike; the longer ones, with simple fur, are more fierce. But those that leopards sire remain among the common kind, lacking manes. All alike perish from excess fatness. First, because they take drink on alternate days and food on alternate days, and often, if digestion has not followed, they skip a day of their accustomed feeding. Then, too, if they have devoured more flesh than is right and are burdened, they voluntarily draw it out with their claws thrust into their mouth; and, indeed, they do the same when they must flee even while sated.

Pliny: the lion's special nobility is then present when manes clothe the shoulders and neck. For this happens, with age, to those conceived from a lion. But those that leopards have sired always lack this mark, and likewise the female. Europe has lions far superior in strength to those Africa and Syria produce. There are two kinds of lions: the compact and short-maned, with curlier manes, are more timid, but those of long and simple fur are scorners of wounds. Nobility, however, is most detected in dangers, as already said above: that they have a long life is shown by the fact that many are found lacking teeth.

Polybius, companion of Aemilianus: he relates that men are attacked by lions in their old age, since they no longer have the strength to pursue wild beasts, and then besiege the cities of Africa, for which reason he says he saw men crucified together with Scipio, so that the rest might be deterred by a fear of similar punishment from the same crime.
Physiologus: the lion loves to go to mountain peaks. And when it is sought by hunters, it senses their approach and covers its own tracks with its tail, so that hunters cannot track it by them.

Pliny, in the same place: catching lions was once a work of great difficulty, and mostly by pits; under the reign of Claudius, chance provided an almost shameful method: a Gaetulian shepherd, named Thales, threw his cloak over the charging beast's head. This spectacle was immediately transferred to the arena. It is almost incredible, moreover, how they grow numb with all their great fierceness once their head is lightly covered, so much so that they are bound without resistance, since all their power lies in their eyes - so it is less surprising that a lion was strangled by Lysimachus, shut in with it by Alexander's order.

Isidore: lions, hemmed in by hunters, look at the ground, so as not to be terrified by the sight of hunting spears. They fear the noise of wheels, but fire more. When they sleep, their eyes stay watchful. When they walk, they cover their tracks with their tail, so that the hunter does not find them.

Solinus: lions, when pressed by dogs, retreat with disdain and, sometimes stopping, disguise their fear or flight with an uncertain withdrawal. This they do even in open and exposed fields. For in wooded places they dread hiding, as if it were a witness to cowardice, and, as much as they can, they withdraw themselves by flight. And indeed, when pursuing, they approach their quarry with a leap. When fleeing, they cannot leap. Walking, however, they enclose the tips of their claws in sheaths of their bodies, lest the points be blunted by friction. And they guard this so carefully that they run only with their little claws turned back.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: lions are of such hot nature that they desire to mate at every season. Females have great lust for mating. And for this reason there is anger among the males. The female has two teats in the middle, namely of the belly, and these small in proportion to her body. And this is because she has little milk, for the food that passes into the body is that which she eats, and since she eats only rarely, and only raw and predatory flesh, which does not easily pass into the matter of her own flesh.

Solinus: lions, moreover, mate facing away from each other. Lionesses bear and raise five cubs in their first litter. Then, in the following years, they lose one from the number each year, and finally, when maternal fertility is reduced to one, they become sterile forever.

Pliny: lionesses have great lust for mating, and for this reason there is anger among the males. The lion detects, by scent, the mating of a leopard with an adulterous lioness, and rises up with all his force in punishment. And so either the lioness's guilt is washed away in a river, or she accompanies him at a greater distance. I see that the common people have believed that she gives birth only once, her womb torn by the claws in labor. Aristotle, however, reports that the lioness bears five cubs in her first litter, and becomes sterile by one fewer each year. But when the lioness fights, pregnant, on behalf of her cubs, as said, she is said to fix the gaze of her eyes on the ground, lest she be frightened by the hunting spears. It is reported that lion cubs are shapeless and have very little flesh, of the size of weasels, at the start. They can scarcely walk at six months, and do not move before two months.

Aristotle: cloven-footed animals produce offspring that are not complete, and, perhaps evidently, undistinguished, incidental, like the fox and wolf and lion. Finally, any four-footed animal having many clefts in its feet, like the lion and dog and wolf and fox, generates blind offspring, and the eyes separate afterward and see. The reason for the scarcity of the lion's offspring, however, is this, that food does not pass into semen. And when youth passes and semen diminishes, breeding will cease entirely. And so the lioness first bears six or five, then four, then three, then two, and after this one, then afterward none.
Physiologus: the lioness bears her cubs dead, and thus guards them for three days until their father comes and breathes on their faces, so that they are brought to life.

Isidore: the lion and lioness, when they have produced a cub, are reported to sleep for three days and nights. Then, at the father's growling or roaring, the place of the den, as if trembling, is said to rouse the sleeping cub.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: the lion, exceedingly anxious for itself and its cubs, sleeps with open eyes, as if watching, and, scattering earth over its tracks with its tail, covers them all the way to its den.

div.head: DE ETATIBUS ET MORBIS AC NOCUMENTIS EORUM

cit.quote: Physiologus: the offspring of lions, then, are produced dead up to the third day. For lions indeed are hottest and driest by nature, which their nobility and strength, along with boldness and irascibility, prove. Their offspring, however, have moisture from the temperament of the species, which becomes more viscous through the dryness and heat of the constitution, and especially around the brain, where dryness dominates and the vital spirit cooperates with itself. Whence, when the sinews are blocked, the spirits cannot enter nor move the faculties to their actions. So, as the parents roar around the offspring, the spirits, entering through the mouth and ears and pores of the head, grant motion to the offspring. Further, old age in lions is proven by the loss of teeth, as Solinus says. But although the lion is formidable to every beast, it is nevertheless agitated by the small sting of the scorpion, and flees it wherever it sees it, as an enemy of its life. It hunts the wild donkey and naturally approaches it, but flees fire, or one who carries it, and also flees the noise of wheels. It fears the cock and its crowing, especially a white cock. The lion develops fever from the sight of man. And it seems healthy in winter, but subject to any fever in summer. Finally, it always suffers a quartan fever, and then especially craves the flesh of the ape, so as to be healed. The same too, having drunk dog's blood, heals its own illness.
Rhazes, in the Almansor: the lion flees even because of a mouse, and also fears the wood called 'sethim.' Hellebore too, and squill, kill dogs and lions and very many beasts.
Aesculapius, in the book On the Limbs: further, if the 'zarim,' that is the lion, treads on oak bark, it will be terrified at once.

Ambrose: the lion, king of wild beasts, is agitated by the small sting of the scorpion and killed by a serpent's venom. The lion's exceptional beauty, through the maned muscles of its neck, is shaken off when a serpent's mouth is suddenly raised against its chest. And so the serpent flees the stag, but kills the lion. The lion fears the cock, especially a white one. When it is sick, however, it seeks out and devours an ape, by which it can be healed.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the lion's anger, as said above, is more frequent. And sometimes, when its fury within is immoderate, it is said to be consumed and to perish by fiery blood and the heat of its wrath.

Pliny: [it is said] that the lion bites the ground and gives tears at its death, and that so fierce an animal is more frightened by the turning circles of wheels and empty chariots, and the crests and crowing of cocks, but most of all by fire. That lions have a long life is shown by the proof that many are found lacking teeth. Polybius, companion of Aemilianus, relates that in old age they attack men, since they no longer have the strength to pursue wild beasts, and then besiege the cities of Africa, for which reason he says he saw men crucified together with Scipio, so that the rest might be deterred from the same crime by a fear of similar punishment. It suffers illness only of loss of appetite, in which it is helped by the insult of monkeys tied nearby driving it into rage. Blood then tasted is the remedy.
Isaac Judaeus: lion's flesh is hotter than others, thick, heavy, and difficult. If eaten, it generates pain and cramping in the belly.

Aesculapius: lion's flesh heals those with hallucinations, and benefits ear pain and every other ailment. If anyone sits on a lion's skin, hemorrhoids will withdraw from him. But whoever smears his body with the fat of a lion's kidneys, wolves are terrified of him.
Haly Abbas, on the lion: its fat is hotter than others and of stronger dissolving power against hard abscesses.
Dioscorides, on the lion: [effective against] four-footed beasts and serpents. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Avicenna, on the lion: its fat dissolves the hardness of abscesses.

Pliny: lion's fat with rose oil protects the skin of the face from blemishes, and preserves its whiteness, and heals frostbite, and also swellings of the joints, and the vanities of magicians promise those anointed with it easier favor with kings or peoples, especially, however, with that fat which is between the eyebrows, where none can be. The same fat too, with rose oil, benefits daily fevers, since wild beasts flee those anointed with it. Its gall, with water added, gives clarity to anointed eyes, and, with the same fat, disperses epileptic diseases with a light taste, and, provided those who take it digest it at once by running. Its heart, taken as food, heals quartan fevers.

Isidore: the leopard is born from the adultery of a lioness and a leopard-male, or a lion and a leopard-female, and produces a third kind. As Pliny also says, degenerate offspring are created from such mating, as the mule from a mare and a donkey.

Ambrose: this creature, when sick, drinks a roe deer's blood and escapes the force of its illness. It flees garlic, however. Finally, wherever someone has rubbed garlic, it leaps away at once and does not resist, since it cannot bear its smell.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the leopard is an animal generated from a lioness and a leopard-male, of reddish color, having black spots all over. The female is stronger than the male. Although the leopard is a most cruel beast, it is sometimes tamed, but never so as to forget its own cruelty. It is tamed, however, for hunting. And so, when it is led to prey in the hunt, it is released, and if it cannot catch it within four or five leaps, it stops, fiercely angered. And unless the hunter at once offers the raging beast some animal whose blood may appease it, it rushes at the hunter himself or at whoever is nearby. For it is impossible for it to be appeased except with blood. But hunters are provident in this, that they always keep lambs or other animals with them, with which they appease it when angry. Whoever wishes to resist this raging creature, however, should rub garlic between his hands, and it will at once leap away, since it cannot bear the smell of garlic. This creature, when it has eaten something poisonous, seeks human dung, and, having eaten it, is healed.

Physiologus: the leopard is an animal similar to the lion in head and arrangement of limbs, although it is not as large or as strong; it is so tamed by man that it is used, like a dog, for hunting. This one catches prey not by running, but by leaping. And if it does not catch the prey in the second or third leap, it indignantly abandons it entirely. This creature, afflicted by internal illness, drinks the blood of a wild roe deer and escapes the force of its weakness.
Aristotle: among animals, males are stronger than females, except in the bear and the leopard, in which they think the females are stronger and bolder.
Ambrose: the leopard, by the variety of its color, reveals the various movements of its spirit. Whence Jeremiah says: if the leopard can change its spots, and so on.
Avicenna, on the leopard: a leopard's gall is poison to one who drinks from it. Vomiting and its own proper theriac help him.

Avicenna, on the leopard: the leopard too, and the lion, these predators and those similar to them, are not, like dogs, safe for men and animals. Rather, their teeth and claws are not empty of venomous nature, for which reason their bites must be treated, and the wound of their claws, first with drawing out, then with healing over; but in drawing them out a small remedy suffices.
Aesculapius: the leopard, when it sees a human skull, flees.
Rhazes: the leopard is also terrified of the herb called 'leopard's herb.' And it is killed by the herb called 'leopard's-bane.'

Isidore: the 'leontophonos' is a modest beast, so named because, once caught, it is burnt, and flesh sprinkled with its ash and placed at crossroads kills lions, if they take even the smallest amount of it.
Solinus: because of this, lions hold this creature in natural hatred, and, where the opportunity is given, indeed abstain from biting it, but examine it, torn apart, with the effort of their paws.

Pliny: we have learned that the 'leontophonon' is called a small animal, born nowhere but where the lion is born. Once tasted by a lion, it has such power that, though it rules over the other four-footed creatures, it dies on the spot. And so they burn its body and sprinkle other flesh with it in the manner of meal, laying an ambush for the beast, and kill it with an ash so contrary to wild beasts. Not without reason, therefore, does the lion hate this creature, and, at the sight of it, breaks its gaze, and kills it without biting. That creature, however, in turn, sprays its urine, knowing this too to be fatal to the lion.

Solinus, and Pliny, book 8, in the same: the 'leucrocota' surpasses all wild beasts in speed. It is about the size of a donkey, with a stag's haunches, neck, tail, chest, and legs. A lion's head, cloven hooves, a mouth gaping to the ears, otherwise cut back, in the places of teeth having a continuous ridge, they say. This beast, too, is said to imitate human voices. For it mimics the sounds of speaking men's voices; it is found among the Indians.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'leucrocota' seems to be the same beast that was called above the 'crocuta.'
Solinus: Ethiopia sends the 'lychaon,' a wolf maned at the neck and varied in so many ways that they say no color is lacking to it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'lychaon' is a beast in the eastern regions, which some place among the kind of wolves, but it is longer than a wolf and has shorter and unlike legs, a maned neck too, and a manifold variety of color. It is swift in leaping and harmless to man. It lives by hunting; it changes its coat according to the seasons. For in winter it is shaggy and bristling with fur, but in summer bare.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: but by Pliny the kind is called 'thoes.' For of the 'lychaon' he says this.
Pliny: [on] the 'lychaon,' to which a maned neck is attributed. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading phrase.]
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: and of the 'thoes' mention has already been made.
From the book On the Nature of Things, of an uncertain author: [the discussion] continues on the 'lychaon.' [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny, in the same: for the 'thoes' are a kind of wolves, taller in length, unlike in the shortness of their legs, swift in leaping, living by hunting, harmless to man; they change their coat, not their color; shaggy through the winters, bare in summer.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'lyciscus' is a four-footed animal, as the Experimenter says in his book, which is born from a dog and a she-wolf. For each parent is so lustful that, though a natural hatred stands between them, which exists between dog and wolf, they nevertheless come together in mating, for the delight of lust. And thus it happens that the offspring draws to itself the color and habits of both.
Pliny: the Gauls believe their dogs are conceived from wolves, whose packs each have their own leader from among the dogs. They accompany him in the hunt, and obey him.
Isidore: 'lycisci,' as Pliny says, are dogs born from wolves and dogs, when they happen to mate together.

Isidore, book 12: the lynx is so named because it is counted among the wolf kind, a beast marked with spots on its back, like the leopard, but similar to the wolf, whence the one is called 'lycos,' the other 'lynx.' Lynxes, he says, following Pliny, do not admit more than one offspring.
Algazel: the lynx is an animal that acts according to the sense of sight. For by its sight it penetrates solid things, and if something transparent comes before it, it is quickly blinded by it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the lynx has such piercing eyes that by the fineness of its sight it even penetrates solid bodies. For it is agreed that the eye is situated in moisture, following the philosopher. There are, however, three things in water, namely watery moisture, transparency, and the clarity of light, and this last it shares with the celestial nature. And this ultimate purification from matter belongs to the nature of light. Since, then, light is the ultimate clarity in a bounded body, if the substance of water is placed at its ultimate purification, as regards transparency, in the eye, the lynx will be able to penetrate a solid and dark body. The lynx has a tongue similar to a serpent's, but larger, which it extends far in length and curls around its neck. It has large claws, produces a single offspring, and its urine hardens into a gem.

Alexander Neckam: the lynx, by the keenness of its transparent sight, is said to penetrate nine walls, so much so that if someone carries raw flesh with nine walls in between, walking beside the wall, the lynx follows the one walking; and it stands still when the one carrying the flesh stands still. Some, however, learned in the natures of things, attribute this rather to the power of smell than of sight.

Pliny, book 28: lynxes are foreign creatures, which see more clearly than all animals; they say that all lynx claws, with the hide, are most effectively burnt in Carpathia, and that, this ash drunk, the foreskins of men, and, sprinkled on women, their lusts, are checked.

Isidore: they say the lynx's urine hardens into a precious stone, called 'lygurius'; that the lynxes themselves sense this is proven by this evidence, that they cover the discharged liquid with sand, out of a certain jealousy of nature, lest such an excretion pass into human use.

Pliny: the moisture the lynx releases, where they are born, freezes or dries into gems similar to carbuncles and gleaming with a fiery color, called 'lygurium,' and for this reason it is said by very many to be generated as amber too; the lynxes know this and, out of jealousy, cover the urine with earth, whereby it hardens more quickly.
Pliny, book 28, in the same: it is reported that itching of the body is checked by a drop of lynx's urine. The same is shown to benefit pain of the nails too.

Solinus: they affirm that the lynx's urine hardens into a precious stone, called 'lygurium.' This stone has the color of amber, drawing to itself with the same breath things that approach. It eases pains of the kidneys, heals jaundice.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: the lynx has a form like a wolf's. And the stone called 'lygurius' is generated from its dripped urine over the span of seven days.
Dioscorides: the urine of the lynx, which they call 'lygurium,' becomes a stone as soon as it urinates; it removes stomach pains and checks flux of the bowels.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: concerning this stone, namely 'lygurium,' which is created from the frozen urine of the lynx, and its power or efficacy, fuller mention has been made above in the treatise on precious stones.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the locust is a four-footed animal, small, about the size of a rabbit; it has a fleshy, large, and edible head, and dwells around the region of Jerusalem. Whence John the Baptist fed on the flesh of animals of this kind. Some, however, say that around the deserts of the Jordan there is a sweet herb good for eating, called the 'locust,' and John used this kind of food, not locust animals: this animal proceeds in flocks. Whence Solomon says: the locust has no king, and so on. This indeed cannot be understood of locust worms, which are of much fear and proceed not in troops, but solitarily. Aristotle says that a certain woman raised a locust from the time it was young and small, and, once it had grown, found it impregnated by itself and without a male.

Isidore: the wolf, 'lycos' in Greek, is named from biting, since, with the frenzy of rapacity, it slaughters whatever it finds. Some say wolves were named as if 'leopos,' since power like the lion's is in their feet, whence whatever they press with their foot does not live. It is, moreover, a rapacious beast, eager for blood. Of which country folk say that a man loses his voice if a wolf sees him first. Whence, of one suddenly falling silent, it is said: the wolf is in the tale. Certainly, if it senses it has been seen first, it lays aside the boldness of its ferocity.
Isidore, book 9: the wolf, moreover, has uneven teeth, whence their bite is vehemently harmful.
Gloss: the wolf, rigid in bodily nature, cannot easily bend itself. It is carried by its own impetus and so is often deceived.

Aesculapius: if the 'zebet,' that is the wolf, treads on wild onions, its leg is weighed down; the wolf, however, flees the hedgehog. But if anyone smears his body with the fat of a lion's kidneys, or anoints it with a lion's dung, wolves are terrified of him.
Pythagoras: when domestic four-footed animals see a wolf's eye gouged out, they fear it and flee. And if any animal urinates on warm wolf's urine, it will never conceive.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the wolf is most foul-smelling and ravenous, has a horrible howl. In the evening, however, it is especially hungry. Whence it is written: its judges were wolves who left nothing until morning; it particularly fears fire, according to Aristotle. The wolf is wild at every season, like the lion and bear too: it is also strong and cunning. Whence stags, having lost their horns, hide and feed at night, since they flee wolves. And these wolves themselves sometimes flee too, with lowered ears, as dogs do. And according to Homer, the wolf, although watchful, fears fire and flees. Its member is made of bone, as the fox's and the like are too. It is an animal of many toes, for it has five toes on its front feet and four on its hind feet, like the lion and dog and lynx and wolf. Likewise a hairy animal has a short tail with few hairs, as happens with wolves. Animals too of sharp, flesh-eating teeth open their mouths wide, so as to bite more strongly. For this reason the opening of wolves' mouths is very large. Wolves' internal members are weak and easily suffer corruption in their wounds. The rest of their body, however, endures many blows. Their head, too, is strong. Males' bones are as strong as females' teeth. Wolves' teeth are strong, and their tips are hooked for cutting and grinding and also for strength: the wolf has teeth above and below and makes a saw with its teeth; it has a single belly, like man and lion and dog and bear, and, after the belly, intestine. Further, the poison aconite kills the panther and also the wolf.

Pliny: the wolf's eyes shine and cast light, like the goat's. The wolf's right canine tooth is held in great value for its uses: the wolf, lion, and hyena alone have a neck rigid with single, straight bones. In a wolf's bladder a small stone is born, called 'syrtites.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the wolf is a most rapacious and deceitful animal; some have said this is the wild dog, since its form and howling are similar to a dog's, but it lacks barking. The short-maned kind of these is bolder than the long. Its brain grows and shrinks according to the state of the moon. Although this is true in all four-footed creatures, it is more so in the wolf and in the dog; the wolf's fur, however, is worm-infested in its flesh.

Ambrose: if the wolf sees a man first, it robs him of his voice and despises him as a victor over his lost voice. But if it senses it has been seen first, it lays aside its ferocity and cannot run; it hates and flees squill leaves, which the turtledove places in its nest so that the wolf does not attack its chicks.

Gloss: the wolf also lies in wait for sheep, circles the sheepfold, testing the dog's sleep and the shepherd's laziness or absence. If it seizes one, it attacks the throat and inflicts a wound on the vital parts.
Solinus: in the wolf's tail there is a very small love-charm hair, which it discards of its own accord in preference to being caught, nor does it have power unless torn from the living creature.

Aristotle: wolves, when they come out of their dens, first eat dragon-wort and chew it with their tongue, as if to sharpen their teeth. When they flee, however, they carry their young with them. And if hunters catch them, they leap onto trees and lie there. Further, if a fleeing wolf sees many hunters closing in on it, it will walk slowly and look back. And if it must indeed flee, it will run and not leap. And its course is continuous, like a dog's course. But if, in fleeing, it finds some animal, it falls upon it.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the wolf sometimes gathers willow leaves in its mouth and hides beneath them, so as to catch goats coming to the leaves unnoticed. Likewise, when it walks among leaves, lest it be detected by the sound, it licks its feet with its tongue and thus makes them slippery and moist. It is also said that when it has seized a sheep, with the shepherd in pursuit, it does not harm it with its teeth, but makes it lie gently on its back, lest, if the sheep, moving itself, should feel that injury, it would slow the wolf's flight: wolves are said to divide their plunder among themselves in equal shares. A wolf, passing secretly through a hedge to lie in wait for sheep, if it happens to make a noise with its foot, at once bites that foot as if it were guilty. Entering the sheepfold, it kills all the sheep before eating any of them. It buries the remaining food in the ground. Sometimes, however, it is tamed and plays with men like a puppy. Yet it naturally flees hunters, nor does it forget its perpetual hatred and its former deceitfulness in eating lambs and animals of this kind. There is also a certain kind of wolf that produces human voices and thus deceives shepherds. It also deceives dogs by gasping, as if it were a dog; sometimes, indeed, dog and wolf are joined in a kind of friendly alliance, so much so that, like thieves, they enter sheepfolds together at night.

Physiologus: the wolf, as said, silences the man it sees first, since it sends the rays of its eyes into him and dries up his visible spirit. Once dried, this dries up the man's other spirits, and these in turn dry up his throat, and so the man becomes hoarse. The wolf has dim sight by day, but sees more clearly by night. If it sees you first and takes away your voice, loosen your cloak, so that you may release your speech. But if it pursues you, gradually so as to ambush you, while it is watching, place something else between you and it, and it will stop, out of fear of being ensnared. When the wolf enters a sheepfold, however, it is not content to satisfy its hunger with one sheep strangled, but strangles all it can.

Pliny: the sight of wolves is said to be harmful, and to take away, for the present, a man's voice, if they look at him first. Africa and Egypt, however, produce sluggish and small ones. A colder region produces rough and fierce ones.

Aristotle: the wolf is strong and bold and fierce, not timid. If, however, it is found eating while famished, it is most fierce, but if sated, it rests somewhat, without hunger. And sometimes, without anger, it is tamed, indeed loves to play with affection: near the sea called the Maeotic marsh, wolves come to places near fishermen, and if they are given some of the fish, they do not harm them. But if not, they tear apart the nets when they are spread out on the ground to dry. Wolves, when they grow old, often approach cities and harm men, since they can no longer hunt: the wolf harms with teeth and claws.

Pythagoras: if anyone puts on the skin of a sheep that a wolf has eaten, the itching and vehement irritation in it does not cease. But if a sheep's skin is placed with a wolf's skin, the wool is scraped off the sheep's skin. Finally, if a string of wolf-gut or intestine is stretched with strings of sheep-gut, it breaks them and takes away all their harmony from them. Wounds that arise from its bite and claws are very bad, since venom comes out from them and passes through the bindings into the sponge placed over them. The remedy against these wounds, however, is the same as against the bite of a rabid dog. If it is ever stoned, it will first watch the one throwing the stone, and if the stone has hurt it, it will focus on him to kill him. But if it has not hurt it, it will still focus on him, yet will not harm him with its claws, except a little, as if provoking him.

Gloss, on the Acts of the Apostles: wolves are fiercer nearer nightfall, roused to rabid madness by daytime hunger. Whence it is written: they will be swifter than evening wolves. Wolves are rightly understood as heretics, cunning indeed in deceit, strong in disputation, cruel in slaughter. Whence the Apostle, to the Ephesians, says: rapacious wolves will enter among you.

Aristotle: wolves indeed bear hunger for a long time, and after long fasts devour much. The wolf eats greedily without chewing, and in one day what suffices for three days. They eat only flesh; afterward they take some medicine against illnesses and vomit and are healed. A hungry wolf is bold, and when it eats, is most fierce; the wounds it inflicts are, like those of rabid dogs, and the same is their remedy. And so wolves sometimes eat men too, especially those who are solitary. And when they have eaten much flesh and swallowed it without cutting or chewing, they remain without food for two days, since they are much satisfied in one meal, and live on little water, and likewise excrete for three days. Its dung is dry, without the moisture of water, like dog dung. And with it comes strong wind from the lower part, and its urine has a smell, on account of which, like dogs, they smell trees. The opening of a wolf's mouth is very large, so that its bite is stronger, since it eats flesh. It also eats fish, as said above, indeed it is said that wolves sometimes eat earth, but they eat nothing of plants, except, as said before, for the sake of medicine. The wool of sheep that wolves have eaten - cloth from it takes on more lice.
Pliny: they say the wolf, in hunger, feeds on earth: this creature too, they say, although eating in hunger, if it looks back, forgets its food and, having moved away, seeks something else.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: insatiable are those animals whose food passes at once from the belly through a straight intestine, like the lynx-wolves.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the wolf by no means grows fat, since it devours food that it swallows without chewing, and so it does not pass into the body's nourishment. For this reason too it often happens that it falls ill, and it remains without food for two days because of the digestion of its food; it lives, however, on little water, since drink does not aid undigested food. Its dung, too, is entirely dry and passed with difficulty. Its urine has a smell, and it raises its foot, like a dog, when it urinates. And when it is sick, it eats earth and grasses as medicine, and vomits at once and is healed; the dog does the same thing when it is sick. For no flesh-eating animal eats plants with impunity, except man and the bear. Besides, the wolf, in hunger, eats earth. It also loads itself with a meal of earth, when it seeks to attack an ox or horse or a robust animal of this kind. Indeed it attacks by the nostrils, and when the animal wishes to shake it off, it is worn down by the deceptive weight and falls to the ground, overcome. Then, having eaten earth, it unburdens itself and returns to its prey: it is said, however, that the wolf does not eat man unless it has first, by some chance, eaten from the corpse of a slain man, which it perhaps found lifeless from weapons; for then, lured by the sweetness of human flesh, it does not fear to fall into danger by attacking man.
Isidore: wolves, in the whole year, mate no more than twelve days.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: wolves have bony members; they mate for twelve days a year, and only at that time proceed in a pack, and howl together, one leading and the rest joining in the cry, and are then more fearsome and dangerous. Wolf cubs, indeed, are sometimes tamed by a trainer's skill, but sometimes nature overcomes the training. Whence, abandoning their trainer, they return to their own kind.

Aristotle: the wolf mates like the dog; at mating time, when it has young, it is very fierce. Any four-footed animal, however, having many clefts in its feet, like the dog and lion and fox and wolf, produces blind offspring. Afterward, however, their eyes separate and they see. And so the fox and lion and wolf bear offspring that are not distinct, but incidental. Animals whose nature is close to one another mate together, especially if they do not differ in appearance and size, and are suited in the span of pregnancy. And all of this applies to dogs and wolves and foxes. Whence some think that the dogs of India are generated from a dog and a wolf. Dogs and wolves, moreover, and animals having cloven feet with much cleft, bear many offspring. Sometimes dogs mate with wolves and produce greyhounds. When they grow old, they go toward places near cities, so as to find prey more easily, which they can now hunt only with the greatest difficulty. For the wolf's life is very long, and in old age it loses its teeth. Whence a lame wolf was once caught whose many teeth were broken, which was a sign of old age.
Isidore: Ethiopia nourishes wolves maned at the neck, and so varied that they say no color is lacking to them.

Solinus: it is proper to Ethiopian wolves that in leaping they have such power of a bird's flight that they gain no more from running than from leaping, yet they never attack men. In winter they are furred, in summer bare; these they call 'thoes.'

Pliny: Africa and Egypt produce small wolves; a colder region produces rough and fierce ones. Among the authors, Greece, not to be scorned, reports the following: they write that the Arcadians, from the family of a certain Anthus, chosen by lot from the tribe, are led to a certain pool of that region, and, their clothing hung on an oak, swim across and go away into the desert, and are transformed into a wolf, and gather with others of the same kind for nine years. During which time, if they have abstained from human flesh, they return to that same pool, and, once they have swum across, recover their form, their original appearance, with nine years of old age added. It is remarkable how far Greek credulity proceeds. There is no lie so shameless that it lacks a witness. We ought, indeed, to confidently judge false that men are turned into wolves and restored to themselves again. There are wolves called 'lynx-wolves,' such as was seen from Gaul in the arena of Pompey the Great; this creature, they say, although eating in hunger, if it looks back, forgets its food and, having moved away, seeks something else, namely forgetful of the abundance before it. The 'thoes' are a kind of wolf, taller in length, unlike in the shortness of their legs, swift in leaping, living by hunting, harmless to man.
Pliny: lynx-wolves, however, as said above, are insatiable, whose food passes at once from the belly through a straight intestine.

Aristotle: the 'cabonecia' is a wolf maned like a lion. In Greece there is a wolf called 'manticorion,' that is manticore, having three rows of teeth above and below. Likewise, near a certain sea, a certain kind of wolf approaches fishermen, and if they are given some of the fish, they do not harm them. But if not, they watch the fishermen's nets when they are set out to dry, and, once they are absent, tear them apart. In some places, indeed, dogs mate with wolves. Of wolves, one kind is round, another long, and its hairs rough. And their kind that is short is bolder than the one that is long.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of degenerate wolf kinds too are the 'lychaon' and the lynx and the 'lyciscus' and the hyena, as said above.
Pliny: it is commonly believed that a small hair on the wolf's tail contains a love-charm venom, which the creature discards when caught, nor is it effective unless torn from the living animal.

Pliny, in the same: wolf's lard is medicinal. Its gall benefits ulcers of the head, applied equally with mustard. Wolf's liver, with warm wine, heals cough. They order the eyes rubbed with wolf's fat against watering eyes. The same fat, applied, softens the womb; its liver [eases] their pains: pains of the liver too are calmed by dried wolf's liver with honeyed wine. Wolf's testicles disperse scrofula. Having eaten wolf's flesh also benefits those about to die. Bones found in the extremities of a wolf, bound to the neck or arm, are beneficial. It is also beneficial for suffusions of the eyes to be anointed around with wolf's excrement, and their ash, with Attic honey, applied for dimness. The same, bound on, strengthens loose teeth and eases their pain. Likewise fat applied from wolves excellently softens all hardnesses of the body. A wolf's tooth, bound on, prevents infants' fears and diseases of teething. Bound on horses too, it is said to grant tireless running. They report, however, that horses burst if they follow the tracks of wolves while a rider is on them. It is also reported that wolves do not approach a field if, from one head with its feet broken and a knife thrust in, blood is gradually sprinkled around the borders of the field, and it is buried in that very spot from which it was taken, or if the plowshare with which the first furrow was drawn in the field that year is thrown into the household hearth around which the family gathers and consumed, and no wolf will harm any animal in that field as long as this is done. An aged wolf's snout is said to resist sorceries, and for this reason they fix it on the doors of farmhouses.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: a wolf's heart, if dried and kept, is said to become very aromatic. The same, burnt, ground, and drunk, helps epileptics, provided the sufferer is not afterward tainted by any excess.
Physiologus: [wolf's heart], dried and ground and taken with sweet wine, works against all distempers. And it aids the proper substance of the liver.
Aesculapius: wolf's flesh, cooked and eaten, heals those with hallucinations. Its fat and gall [work] like the dog's.

Haly Abbas: wolf's liver, carefully dried and ground and mixed with medicines for liver pain, clearly benefits. If the pelt of a wolf cub is hung on one who has been struck by a rabid dog, he will not fear water. Dung of a white wolf benefits colic.

Avicenna, in the second canon: wolf's flesh is bad. But the flesh of wolves having [particular] snouts and claws benefits the eye and strengthens it. It is also effective for hemorrhoids, but the stomach recoils from it.
The Physicus: wolf's blood, and also its dung, benefits colic affliction.
Pythagoras: [on] wolf's canine teeth. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the otter is a cunning and malicious animal, of the size of a cat, of nearly similar form, except that it is dark and black in color on the head, with a shining hide, whose fur is softer than down, and whose sheen does not easily yield to age, whence ornaments are made from its pelt for the collars of men's and women's garments. This beast dwells around pools and rivers, and there has burrows and rears its young. It lives on fish, which it hunts with remarkable frequency. Although it can live long underwater, it nevertheless draws breath from the air. Whence sometimes, in its eagerness for prey, it enters a wicker fish-trap, that is a weir-basket. And since then it can neither return through the entrance nor tear apart the trap quickly enough, unable to recover its breath in the air, it suffocates in the water. It is, indeed, so eager and greedy for food that it gathers caught fish in its den in such a heap that, from the stench of their putrefaction, it infects not only the den but even the air. Some who wished to catch this beast have found this out not without danger to themselves. It is sometimes tamed by fishermen and trained by skill so that, circling around, it drives fish into the dangers of the nets, and, by its help, they are caught. Whence it seems to provide great profit to its owners.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'mammonetus' is an animal smaller than an ape, dark on the back, white on the belly, having a furry tail and a neck as thick as its head. Whence, once caught, it is not tied by the neck, as other beasts are, since a noose cannot hold it there, but by the belly. It has, moreover, a face most closely resembling a human's, black however and hairless, from the neck up to the forehead. Nor is the nose continuous with the mouth, as in the ape, but there is a definite space between the two, as in man. Between these beasts and apes there is an implacable hatred and frequent warfare, and although they do not surpass them in strength, they are nevertheless preferred to apes in cunning and boldness in fighting. They are also said to be strong in tenacious and great memory.

Solinus: the 'manticora' is born among the beasts of India, with a triple row of teeth meeting in alternating rows. It has a human face, sea-blue eyes, blood-red color, a lion's body, a tail tipped like a scorpion's sting. Its voice is so whistling that it imitates the melodies of pipes and a trumpet's blast blended together. It craves human flesh most eagerly. It is so vigorous on its feet, so capable in leaping, that neither the most extended distances nor the widest obstacles can hold it back.

Pliny: [on] the 'manticora,' namely a beast with a triple row of teeth meeting like a comb's, a human face and ears, sea-blue eyes, blood-red color, a lion's body, a tail like a scorpion's fixing its sting, and a voice imitating the blended sound of pipes and trumpets. It is, moreover, of great speed, especially craving the human body.

Avicenna: in parts of India there is a certain wolf called 'maricorion' in Greek, that is 'manticora' in Latin. It has three rows of teeth below and above. It is, moreover, large and hairy, and its feet are like a lion's, its face and eyes and ears like a man's. Its eyes are golden and its color is ruddy, like vermilion. Its tail is like a wild scorpion's. And there is redness in it. It sheds its own hair, and speaks and neighs. Its voice is like a trumpet's voice, and it runs swiftly like a stag, and it is a wild man-eating creature.

div.head: DE MELONE ET MELOSO AC MONOCEROTE

cit.quote: Isidore: it is called 'melo' either because it is [a badger], or because it seeks honeycombs and constantly hunts honey. It is, moreover, a four-footed animal armed with claws.

Gloss: the 'melo,' or 'melotus,' is an animal also called the badger, whose very shaggy pelt is called 'melota.' Whence it is read of certain ancient saints: they went about in badger-skins. More will be said fully of this below.
Pliny: [on] dogs. [Fragmentary heading in the source, unclear relation to context.]

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'melosus' is a very large beast, which pursues savage enemies, as if created for this purpose. It has huge jaws, strong and prominent teeth too, with which it boldly wages war against its adversaries; although it is terrifying to strong men, it nevertheless marvelously dreads the innocence of children and their smallness, and flees their blows. In this the greatness of innocence is worthily demonstrated. The unicorn [monoceros] is a monster with a horse's body, a stag's head, a pig's tail, an elephant's feet, a horrible bellow, but armed with one very sharp horn in the middle of its forehead. Once caught, it can be killed, but never tamed. Indeed, as James says, it never comes alive into man's power, since, seeing itself overcome, it casts off its life in fury.
Physiologus: the unicorn is a very small animal, similar to a kid, most fierce, having one horn on its head.

Pliny: [on] the unicorn, similar in the rest of its body to a horse, in its head to a stag, in its feet to an elephant, in its tail to a boar, with a deep bellow, one black horn two cubits long projecting in the middle of its forehead; they deny it can be caught alive.
Isidore: the mouser [musio], as said above, is called the cat, since it is a threat to mice.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the mouser, or 'murilegus' [mouse-catcher], is called 'catus' in Greek, as if 'clever'; it is an unclean and venomous animal, and pursues every kind of mouse, and is also said to fight with toads. Although resisted by their venomous stings, it is nevertheless not killed. Mice it has caught, it first torments in play, and afterward, once mocked, eats them. With its carbuncle-like eyes it sees so sharply that it spies mice even in the darkest caverns as if in daylight. It has teeth in the manner of a saw. It has hairs, however, around its mouth, which, once removed, cause it to lose its boldness. It delights in caresses, loves warm places, whence, from excessive laziness, it burns its own fur; it delights in being handled by a man's hand and is most easily provoked to play. It imitates the washing of its face by licking with its front feet. It is kindled most impatiently by lust, and gladly grows wild at mating time. But when a domestic cat begins to grow wild, its ears are cut off, so that, namely, with the places of its ears open to the elements, it cannot bear the drops of night dew and rain, and is thus forced to return to the shelter of the house. Not only, however, do mousers fight most cruelly with the aforesaid animals, but also among themselves, and this more often to secure the accustomed boundaries of their hunting grounds.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the musk-deer is an eastern beast, having the size of a roe deer. In its groin an abscess grows from gathered humors. When this has matured, it strikes it and rubs it against a tree, and thus it opens and the discharge flows out, and there thickens and hardens, and a substance of this kind is called musk. Also all its flesh and dung is called musk, but that which flows from the abscess is much better. Musk, having lost its scent, recovers its power amid foul smells and latrines; it struggles against the stench and thus, as if by that struggle, revives. It is effective against fainting and weakness of the heart, and of the brain and liver and stomach.
Constantine the African: [on the] musk-deer, a roe deer-like animal, [found in] some part of India. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Constantine the African, the same: musk is a major among aromatics, hot and dry in the third degree. It strengthens failing members; sneezing induced by musk also helps against paralysis.

Avicenna: musk is a follicle of an animal like the gazelle, except that it has two white teeth turned inward, like two horns. It is hot and dry in the second degree, fine and strengthening. It benefits cold ailments and strengthens a temperate brain and heart, and heals its tremor and melancholy from anxiety. It also strengthens the eye and dries its moisture, and clears fine white spots, and is also a theriac for poisons and especially for wolfsbane.

Dioscorides: musk is hot in the second degree, dry in the third. It is also put into eye-salves and pills or eye-powders, whose power thins white spots of the eyes, dries harmful moisture. Applied, it drives off heaviness of the head and gives it strength, since it is strengthening. It gives relief to all members and increases strength in the bones. It corrects dizziness born from an abundance of moisture, invites sleep, stimulates mating, strengthens the heart and all the internal organs, applied in the manner of a poultice.

Isidore: 'onager' is interpreted as 'wild donkey,' for the Greeks call the donkey 'onos,' and 'wild' 'agrion.' The wild donkey, on the twenty-fifth day of March, brays twelve times in the night, and likewise by day, and by this the equinox is known to have occurred. By its braying, too, at each hour, the number of the hours is known from its braying.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the wild donkey, as is read, dwells in solitary and high places, where, thanks to the benefit of the winds, it lives free of drinking. Whence Jeremiah says: the wild donkeys stood on the rocks, they drew in the wind like dragons.

Pliny, book 8: Africa pours forth a multitude of wild donkeys. Male wild donkeys, individually, rule over herds of females and fear rivals in lust. And so they guard the pregnant ones and castrate the newborn males by biting. The pregnant females, on the contrary, seek hiding places and desire to give birth secretly, and rejoice in an abundance of lust. From a tamed wild donkey and a mare are bred mules swift in running, of outstanding hardness of hoof, as said above, of wrinkled body and untamed but noble spirit. From a wild donkey and a female donkey, however, the mule sired surpasses all.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: the wild donkey brays at the equinoctial season for twelve hours of the day, and likewise of the night, and wears and digs the earth with its feet, and is then provoked to thirst and flight.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the wild donkey, among all animals, hates the company and dwelling of men, nor can it be tamed. It is impatient of thirst, and drinks only the clearest water, and not easily any other. This creature, by natural cunning, when dogs pursue it, releases its dung, fragrant to dogs, and, while they are held back by it, mocks them and, escaping, flees to safer places. The female delights in an abundance of lust, and, not keeping any measure in this, is often made hateful to the male for this reason. Males lacking females, at mating time, climb into the mountains and, burning with the desire of lust, draw in the wind through their nostrils and bray vehemently, so much so that they shake other animals with dread. The wild donkey, among other animals, is said to have the fattest heart. And as much as it is patient once tamed, so much, when kept by the woods, does it grow savagely wild. It grieves when day is equal to night, for it would wish night to be longer than day.

Gloss: the wild donkey does not keep to domestic pastures, but wanders freely through the deserts and loves solitary habitation; to it are similar those who, withdrawing from God, fashion various idols, and for this reason are abandoned by God. Whence it is written: the wild donkey, solitary to itself, is Ephraim.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the wild donkey of India is a large and cruel animal, having the form of a donkey and a single horn on its forehead, exceedingly hard and sharp and long, for warring against opposing beasts, and this it has in the middle of its head. It also has strong and sharp hooves, as a natural benefit, so as to make up in these for what it lacks through having only one horn. These are of such strength that they tear huge rocks from cliffs, and this for no other reason than to test their strength against the mass of the rocks.
Pliny: wild donkeys in Phrygia and Lycaonia are outstanding. Africa boasts of their foals as excellent in flavor, which they call 'lalisiones.'

Isidore: Africa also has large and untamed wild donkeys, wandering in the desert. Individually, too, they preside over herds of females. They are jealous of newborn males. They cut off their testicles with bites, which the mothers, wary of this, hide in secret places.

Avicenna: the gall of the wild donkey, that is the wild ass, eradicates ringworm and benefits abscess marks when applied. It is also put in plasters for erysipelas and prevents it. The same is properly beneficial applied for elephantiasis and varicose veins. Flesh from the back of the wild donkey is plastered with oil over pains of the joints. Its fat, applied on cloth, is beneficial. The same fat with costus oil is good for pain of the kidneys and back from thick windiness; the urine, too, of the wild donkey, as Galen says, breaks a stone in the bladder.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the hoof of the wild donkey, if burnt and drunk, benefits epilepsy. Its ash, if mixed with olive oil, dissolves scrofula. And if applied as a poultice, it benefits baldness. The stag's member does the same.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'onocentaurus' is a monstrous animal of two-fold nature, having a donkey's head and a body like a human's. Its face is bristling with hairs. Its hands are formed suited to every action. When it produces a voice, it seems to begin to speak, but its untrained lips cannot form human speech. This creature also throws sticks or stones at those pursuing it, as the Experimenter says. The philosopher Adelinus says that this monster was not created such from the beginning among the other beasts, but sometimes and in some places is generated by chance, from an adulterous mixture. But very many contradict this opinion. The 'orasius' is an animal tall and exceedingly prominent in its front part, so that, with its head extended, it can reach a height of twenty cubits. In its rear part, however, it is low, like a stag's. It has an extended neck, a horse's head, though smaller, but feet and a tail like a stag's. Its hide, however, is so variously marked with every kind of color that a man would try in vain, by craft, to imitate its natural beauty. Nor does it seem unaware of its own beauty, for when it sees men standing around, it turns and twists itself in every direction, so as to turn the gaze of all to admiration of itself, for nature gave it beauty above all beasts in color: this animal, in our own times, was sent by the Sultan of Babylon to the emperor Frederick.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'oryx' is an unclean animal according to the law, following the book of Deuteronomy. Of which Isaiah too says: they lay down like an entangled 'oryx,' and so on. Some have thought this was the dormouse, but the dormouse seems rather to be counted among mice, and so its eating is forbidden in the law. Jerome, on Isaiah, says it is originally a kind of beast born in the wilderness, which is caught by the hunter's snare. It seems, however, to be of the kind of goats, by what has already been said above following Pliny, for goats take on many similar forms. For there are goats, there are chamois, there are also ibexes, and there are 'oryges.'
Pliny: Egypt calls the 'oryx' a wild beast that, they report, faces and gazes at the rising of the Dog Star, and, as it were, prays when it observes it.
Pliny, in the same: 'oryges,' called by some 'solitary,' clothed with fur turned the opposite way and toward the head.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: in Africa the greater part of wild beasts do not drink in summer, because of the scarcity of rain, for which reason Libyan mice, if they drink, die. Africa, by the nature of its region, provides the 'oryx,' perpetually thirsty and lacking drink, as a marvelous remedy for those suffering thirst. For Gaetulian bandits survive with this help, finding in their bodies bladders of most wholesome liquid.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'oryx' is a beast the size of a roe deer, similar in part to a he-goat, having a tuft of fur beneath its chin. It is born in that part of Africa that lacks water, and so it burns with perpetual thirst. The bandits of Gaetulia, a land lacking water, have reported, by most certain experience, a marvelous remedy for those suffering thirst, by which a man may endure thirst with the help of that most wholesome liquid poured from the bladders of these beasts, if used in a modest amount. This beast, as the Egyptians report, at the rising of the Dog Star naturally seems to dance, its bodily frame visibly sensing that the rain and cold have departed and that the fiery vapors of the sun are pressing near, so that the earth may be clothed with flowers and bring forth grasses and fruits. It is, however, impatient of cold. Whence it can bear neither cold nor snow easily.

Isidore: the panther is so named either because it is a friend to all animals except the dragon, or because it rejoices in the company of its own kind and returns in the same manner whatever it receives. For 'pan' in Greek means 'all.' It is, moreover, a beast marked with small circles, so that it is distinguished by black and white variety with tawny, eye-like rings.
Gloss: [it is] stronger than the lion, and nothing is swifter than the panther. So through the prophet the Lord says: I am like a panther to Ephraim, and like a lion to the house of Judah.

Physiologus: the panther is a precious and exceedingly gentle animal; only the dragon is not its friend. When it has been sated with various foods, it hides itself in its den and sleeps, and after three days, rising, it soon lets out a great roar with a most sweet scent, as of all spices, which, when the wild beasts hear it, all of them, both far and near, gather to that scent and follow the panther wherever it goes. Only the dragon, hearing it and unable to bear the strength of the scent, is drawn into itself in fear and, fleeing into underground caverns, grows numb and stays immobile.

Pliny: the panther and tiger are almost alone among wild beasts marked with a variety of spots. They report that the panther has, on its shoulder, a mark like the moon, waxing into circles and, in the same way, hollowing into a crescent. They now call various kinds 'panthers,' now the males, in every kind, 'leopards' - most common in Africa and Syria. Some distinguish panthers from these only by their whiteness. It is remarkable, however, that panthers and lions and similar creatures, as said above, walk with the tips of their claws hidden in sheaths of their body, lest they be broken or blunted, and run with their little claws turned back, extending them only when attacking.
Pliny: panthers have four teats in the middle of the belly. Males, in every kind, are stronger than females, except in panthers and bears.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: the hyena, as said above, strikes terror into the panther, so that it does not even attempt to resist it. And if anyone has something of its hide with him, he is not attacked by the panther. And, remarkable to say, if the skins of both hang facing each other, the panther's hairs fall out.

Solinus: panthers are numerous in Hyrcania. They report that herds are marvelously affected by their scent and sight, and, unless they sense them beforehand, gather in haste, and are frightened by nothing but the fierceness of the panther's face alone, for which reason panthers, hiding their heads, offer the rest of their body to be seen, so that they may plunder the herds, stupefied at the sight, with secure devastation. But the Hyrcanians, since nothing is safe from men, more often kill them with poison than with iron.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the panther is a varied and exceedingly beautiful animal. There are those who report that it has, on its shoulder, a mark like the moon, and that it sometimes grows round, and varies according to the moon's phases.
Avicenna: the panther and leopard, when they have eaten poison, seek out and eat human dung.

Isidore: the panther gives birth only once altogether, and the reason for this is clear. For when the cubs have grown together in their mother's womb, and, their strength mature enough for birth, hate the delays of time, they tear with their claws the womb burdened with offspring, as if it were an obstacle to birth, and she pours out, or rather releases, her offspring under the compulsion of pain. Thus afterward, the site having been damaged and scarred, the genital seed infused does not stick once received, but bounces off in vain. For Pliny too says that animals with sharp claws frequently cannot give birth. For they are damaged internally by the cubs moving within them.

Physiologus: the Hyrcanians, intent on hunting panthers, smear flesh with poison and scatter it at crossroads of paths, so that panthers may be lured by eating it. But these, while devouring human excrement, escape it.

Pliny: barbarians hunt panthers by means of flesh rubbed with aconite poison, scattering it, that is, at crossroads of paths. When panthers have eaten this, a choking sensation seizes their throat at once. But the beast counters this with human excrement as a remedy, and is otherwise so eager for it that shepherds deliberately hang it in a vessel higher than it can reach by leaping, so that, by leaping and reaching for it repeatedly, the beast is fixed in place and finally dies. Otherwise its vitality is so tenacious that, its innards spilled out, it fights on for a long time. Demetrius the physicist reports that a panther, lying in the middle of the road out of desire for a man, suddenly appeared to the father of a certain Philinus, a follower of wisdom. And he was seized with fear and began to retreat, but the wild beast rolled about, fawning gently and struggling with grief - for she was pregnant, and her cubs had fallen far off into a pit. And so the first marvel was that he was not frightened; the next, that he turned his attention to her. Confidently, then, understanding the cause of her grief from the gentle pulling of his garment with her claws, and at the same time as a reward for his own safety, he removed the cubs, and, she following with them, was led all the way out of the wilderness, joyful and exulting, so that it easily appeared she was returning gratitude, and holding nothing against him in turn - a thing rare even in man.

Solinus: Ethiopia nourishes the 'parandrus,' of an ox's size, with an ibex's tracks, branching horns, a stag's head, a bear's color, and equally deep fur. They affirm that this 'parandrus' changes its appearance out of fear, and, when it hides, becomes similar to whatever thing it approaches, whether it becomes white by a rock, or green by a shrub, or takes on whatever other appearance; octopuses do this same thing in the sea, chameleons on land. But both the octopus and chameleon are smooth-skinned, so that it is easier for the smoothness of the skin to mimic what is near it. In this creature, however, it is new and singular that the shagginess of its fur produces the changes of color. Hence it happens that they can be caught only with difficulty.

Isidore: the leopard [pardus] is second after the panther, a varied and most swift kind, and headlong toward blood. For it rushes to death in its leap. From the adultery of a leopard and a lioness, the leopard [leopardus] is born, and produces a third origin.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: as Basil the Great says, the leopard is a fierce beast, exceedingly sharp in its attack, and has a body suited to the movements of birds, and is varied in color. It pursues its prey by leaping rather than by running. Whence it often happens that, in a vehement leap, it rushes to its death. In Africa, because of the scarcity of water, various wild beasts gather at the rivers, and there lionesses mate with various beasts, whether by force or by will, and from this leopards are said to be produced.
Solinus: from the adulterous matings of leopards, the offspring of lionesses are degenerate, and from these indeed lions are produced, but ignoble ones.

Pliny: the lion detects, by scent, the mating of a leopard with an adulterous lioness, and rises up with all his force in punishment. And so either her guilt is washed away in a river, or she accompanies him at a greater distance. Now they call various kinds 'panthers,' and the males, in every kind, 'leopards' - most common, as in Africa and Syria; some distinguish panthers from these only by their whiteness.
[Pliny, on] leopards: hidden among the branches of these very trees, they leap down onto passing creatures and, by slaughtering birds, make their living.
Ambrose: the leopard, by the variety of its color, reveals the various movements of its spirit. Whence the prophet Jeremiah says: if the leopard can change its spots, and so on.
Aristotle: the leopard, as said, like the panther, when it has eaten poison, seeks out and eats human dung.

div.head: DE PILOSO ET PYROLO ET PUTORIO

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'pilosus,' as the Gloss on Isaiah says, is an animal that in its upper part begins with a human figure, but in its lower part ends as a beast, in its feet, such as the blessed Jerome describes in the Life of Paul the First Hermit, that it is human above, having a rough forehead with horns, and ending in goat's feet below - such monstrous creatures are called satyrs or fauns or incubi. He asserts, moreover, that there is no doubt this monster was caught in the East and sent to Alexandria; and from there, dead and preserved in salt lest it dissolve from heat, it was carried to Constantinople, to be seen by the emperor. In our own age a beast the size of a dog was brought to the king of France. Its head, indeed, did not differ much from a dog's head, but the rest of its bodily members were entirely like a man's. It had bare legs, like a man, and hands, arms, a neck white and bare; it fed on cooked meat. It took food with its hands and brought it to its mouth so fittingly and modestly that no one would doubt it had human manners in such things: it stood upright like a man, sat like a man, and was most gladly joined with girls and women. And it had the distinction of male and female in its sex. Its genital member, beyond what its bodily size would require, was large; when stirred by rage, then, this animal moved most cruelly and raged against men. But when calmed, it conducted itself most gently and fittingly, like a man, and was soothed by speech and applauded those who played with it. The 'pyrolus' is a small beast, larger indeed, but no longer than a weasel, of red color, but white on the belly. It thrives with marvelous agility, dwells in trees, and rears its young there. It behaves restlessly, and passes from tree to tree by leaping rather than by flying, although it sometimes uses its tail in place of wings. For it has a furry tail nearly the size of its own body, which it moves for this purpose when leaping. And if it ever wishes to cross water for the sake of feeding, it gathers a piece of wood light enough to float on the water. Sitting on this, it raises its tail like a ship's sail, and thus, sailing as the wind blows, is carried across on the wood. In summer it gathers food, on which to live in winter. It lives on nuts, and eats more readily food that is sweet. The polecat [putorius] is so named from its stench [putor], since it smells exceedingly, and this especially when it is angry: it, like the badger, has short legs on the left side and longer ones on the right. It inhabits the heights of houses and inner recesses, and is most eager for hens and chicks, for it lives on such things; and when it catches a hen or chick, it attacks the head first, so that, once this is overcome, it is not difficult to work on the rest of its members. The 'pathio' is an animal that nature seems to have created in the world for wonder and admiration. Its body is colored as if with red blood. And it gleams with a marvelous appearance when exposed to the sun's rays. And, remarkably, while this gleaming is seen in the living beast, once the beast dies, its beauty is soon taken away, as if it were unworthy for a carcass to possess such splendor of power - yet the innate beauty of the dead creature is not entirely removed, since a rather beautiful redness remains in the skin. This beast's bones are very strong and hard. Its sinews, however, are so vigorous and strong that, unless great force is applied to them, they do not easily break. Some believe this to be the same beast whose kind certain western pagans worship, as it were, as gods. For these pagans are said to raise beasts of this red color, and give them the most delicate dishes as food, and worship them, and keep them captive in chambers, and guard them most carefully, lest they be carried in any way outside their own land. And on this a capital law has been enacted. They are, moreover, the size of dogs. The Pegasus is a large and terrifying animal in Ethiopia, having the form of a horse, wings like an eagle's, but much larger. It has a head armed with horns, so monstrous that it terrifies nearly all living creatures by itself, though heavy of body, with a marvelous flight. Aided by the oarage of its wings, it runs rather than flies, and, beating the air with the power of its feathers, drives the winds like a whirlwind; it devours much food; it moves restlessly; it is hostile to animals, and this especially to man.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'ramiger' [branch-bearer] is an animal of the stag or fallow-deer kind, dwelling in Norway, large in body, of the greatest strength, of most swift flight. It has its name from the matter itself, since 'ramiger' means, as it were, 'branch-bearing.' For on its head it bears three rows of horns in the manner of small branches: of these it has two larger than the rest, in the place where the stag has its horns, but larger and longer, indeed of five cubits, increasing its branches sometimes to the number of fifteen. Two others, however, are set straight in the middle of the head, and these are nearly like a fallow deer's horns, broad, but only with short little branches surrounding them. Further, it has two other horns facing the forehead, made not of horn but of bone, quite similar to those usually found on the shoulder-blades. With these rows of horns, then, it is armed against adversaries, and its distinction increases the wonder among monstrous beasts. The 'rosurella' is an animal dwelling frequently around waters, smaller than a weasel and than the 'pyrolus,' reddish on the back, white on the belly. On land it makes dwellings, and excretes a very fragrant dung, similar to musk in scent, but unequal in power and violence of scent: it flees the sight of men, yet in one place it gathers this dung. And this is remarkable in a beast, that it places its good openly for all to take, so that it seems not to begrudge its good to others.
Physiologus: the 'rhinocephalus' has a horse's neck along with its whole body; men perish from the flames it breathes from its mouth.

Isidore: 'rhinoceros' in Greek is interpreted in Latin as 'horn on the nose.' The same is also called 'monoceros,' that is 'one-horned,' since it has one horn in the middle of its forehead, four feet long, so sharp and strong that it can pierce or shatter whatever it attacks. For it often has combat with elephants and, wounding them in the belly, brings them down: it is said, moreover, to be of such strength that it cannot be caught by any hunter's power. But, as those who have written on the natures of animals assert, a virgin girl is set before it, who opens her lap to it as it comes, in which, all its ferocity laid aside, it places its head, and thus, lulled to sleep, is caught as if unarmed.

Solinus: before the games of Gnaeus Pompey, Roman spectacles did not know the rhinoceros. This beast has a boxwood color; a single horn on its nose, curved back, which, worn down by repeated use, becomes a point, and with it fights against elephants. It is equal to elephants in length, shorter in legs, naturally aiming for the belly, which alone it understands to be penetrable by its blows.
Solinus: [on] the unicorn, a monster with a horrible bellow, a horse's body, an elephant's feet, a pig's tail, a stag's head. A horn extends from the middle of its forehead, of wondrous splendor.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the rhinoceros, also called the unicorn, is said to have, in the middle of its forehead, a most robust horn, four feet in length. And with it it fights against elephants, naturally aiming for the belly, which alone it understands to be penetrable by its blows. But when it is caught by hunters, this proud animal dies from sheer indignation alone.

Pliny: the rhinoceros has a single horn on its nose, such as has often been seen. This other one, born as an enemy to the elephant, sharpens its horn on rocks and prepares itself for battle. In fighting it aims especially for the belly, which it knows to be softer; its length is equal to the elephant's. Its legs are much shorter, its color boxwood.

div.head: DE SCIURO ET SCURULO ET STRYGE

cit.quote: Pliny: the squirrel thrives with this cunning, that it foresees a storm. And, having blocked the caverns from the direction the wind will blow, it opens the appointed doors on the other side; its rather furry tail serves it as a covering. In winter, food gathered beforehand serves some, but for others, sleep serves in place of food. The 'scurulus' is so named from running. This creature is accustomed to cross a river, using a plank or piece of bark as a boat and its tail as a sail. The screech-owl [stryx] is an animal in Africa similar to the hedgehog, named from the screeching of its spines, which, loosened, it releases from its back, so as to wound pursuing dogs.
Solinus: the screech-owl is born in Africa and India, a spiny animal indeed, having longer quills than the hedgehog; in the winter months, however, it hides itself.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: I judge this to be the same wild beast that Solinus and Pliny, with a letter added at the start, that is with an aspiration, call the porcupine, as we said above. For this is itself the spiny pig, or, as commonly called, the 'spiked' one. For Pliny says, book 8: India and Africa produce porcupines, covered with spines and of the hedgehog kind, but the porcupine's quills are longer, and when it tenses its skin, they are missile-like. It fixes them in the faces of pressing dogs and shoots them a little further away; in the winter months, however, it hides itself, which is the nature of many creatures, and above all of bears.

Isidore: the name of the ape [simia] is Greek, meaning 'flat-nosed.' Whence we call them apes, since they have flattened noses and an ugly face grotesquely wrinkled, although goats too have flat noses. Others think apes are so called in Latin because much likeness of human reason is perceived in them, but this is false: for these creatures, sensitive to the elements, exult at the new moon, and grieve at the half and waning moon.

Aristotle: who doubts that the ape is of mixed nature? For it agrees with the nature of men and the nature of four-footed creatures, and likewise uses its feet as hands, since they are composed of both hand and foot. The ape, then, is one of the animals that share in the natures of both, namely man and four-footed creature. Apes are not hairy in front, and their eyelashes are short and very fine. For they have front teeth, even molars, like man, and eyelashes on the eyelids. The other four-footed creatures, however, have hairs only on the upper eyelid. On the ape's chest are small teats, and on these two nipples. Its arms, too, are like a man's, but hairy. It bends its hands and feet, as a man does. But it has smaller hands, and also toes and claws, like man. It walks on four feet. And sometimes it stands upright for a short time. It does not have hips, as a two-footed animal does, nor a tail, as a four-footed one does. It does not have a protruding navel, but that place in it is hard. The female's vulva is like a woman's. The male's member is like a dog's. That species of ape, however, called 'kiboz,' has a tail. Its interior, however, is exactly like man's interior.

Pliny: the kinds of apes contain a perfect imitation of man in face, nostrils, ears, eyelids, which alone among four-footed creatures they have, and a lower lid too. For they differ only a little, having breasts too on the chest, and arms, and legs bent in the opposite direction likewise, likewise claws on the hands too, toes, and a longer middle one on the feet. For these are very long like hands, but make a footprint similar to a palm; these too have a thumb and joints like men's, except only the genital, and this in the males. All the internal organs, too, follow the same pattern.

Pliny, the same: those animals that produce a living offspring bend their knees forward; but for bears and the kind of apes it is the opposite, for this reason least swift, since they give birth to a quadruped.
Pliny, book 23, in the same: they deny that apes and four-footed creatures having toes grow when accustomed to drinking undiluted wine.
