Thomas Cantimpratensis: the ape is a beast thick with fur on its outer members, resembling above all animals the arrangement of the human body. In its interior, however, having no arrangement in common with man, or less than all other animals: for almost all beasts have their teats on the rear, facing the kidneys, so that, placed lower, their offspring can reach them and have them ready when they wish. Man, however, and the ape have them on the chest, since nature gave them hands suited to every action, with which they can lift their offspring from the ground and fit them to the breasts. This creature, however, lacks the human body's navel, since it lacks one, and the male's member is like a dog's member. It has a heel on its feet, and for this reason stands upright, as a man does, and sometimes runs, but this it can do only to a small degree, since nature created this beast to be prostrate in its face. For man alone naturally has an upright stature: this beast is restless in gesture, fierce in biting, lacks a tail, and, beyond other animals, thrives in taste. It gladly eats nuts and fruits, but when it finds a bitter rind in them, it throws away the whole thing, and thus, because of the bitter, rejects the sweet. Pliny says there are, in India, apes white over their whole body.
Alexander Neckam: a domestic ape recognizes its master, even returning after many years have passed.
Pliny: they report that apes, seen doing individual things with marvelous skill, imitate hunters. Mucianus reports that they have also played at draughts with imitation pieces.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the ape is teachable for every kind of play, and for forgetting its ferocity. It is never so tame, however, that it is not somewhat rabid. It gladly plays with children, and, if given the chance, sometimes strangles them. If someone harms it, it holds a grudge against him for a long time. They are strong in wit and imitate whatever they see, whence they more easily fall into hunters' hands; they dwell, moreover, in trees or on cliffs. But when hunters see them, they take men's shoes and go and sit in places where they can be seen by the apes. And they put those shoes on their own feet and tie them carefully, and after this, taking them off, they leave them under a tree and go far off: then the apes, coming down, imitate what they saw them doing, and thus, shod, are caught.

Solinus: [on] the kind of apes: nor are they without a cunning skill of imitation, by which they more easily come into men's hands. For while they eagerly copy the gestures of hunters, having deliberately left behind a birdlime-smeared snare, which they set up as a trick, they smear their own eyes, and, their sight thus blocked, it is easy for them to be seized. They love their offspring.

div.head: DE FETIBUS SIMIARUM AC SPECIEBUS EARUM

cit.quote: Physiologus: when the ape bears twins, it loves one and hates the other. If, however, it is sought by hunters, it carries the one it loves before itself, embracing it, and carries the one it hates on its neck. But when, going on two feet, it grows tired, it willingly drops the one it loved and unwillingly keeps the one it hated.

Isidore: apes carry before themselves the young they love; those neglected cling to their mother. There are five kinds of these, of which the 'circopitheci' have tails. The 'sphinges' are hairy in their coats, with prominent breasts, teachable so as to forget their ferocity. The 'cynocephali' too are similar to apes, but with a face in the manner of a dog, whence they are so named. Satyrs have a pleasing face and are restless with gesturing movements. The 'callitriches' differ from the rest in almost their whole appearance. For they have, in the face, a long beard and a broad tail.

Solinus: the 'cynocephali,' from the number of apes, are most common in parts of Ethiopia, violent in leaping, fierce in biting. Never so tame that they are not more rabid than not. The 'callitriches' are entirely different in appearance from the rest; these, indeed, are not hard to catch, but rare to bring forth alive. For they do not live anywhere but in Ethiopia, that is, under their own sky.

Pliny, book 8: the kinds of apes too, closest to man in form, are distinguished among themselves by their tails. Cornelius distinguishes that at the waning moon those of that kind having a tail are sad, but that the new moon rouses them to exultation. For the other four-footed creatures too dread the eclipse of the stars. In the kind of apes, affection toward offspring is especially strong. Those tamed within houses, once they have given birth, show their young to everyone and delight in having them handled, understanding this as a mark of congratulation; and so, in large part, they kill them by embracing them. The 'cynocephali' are of a fiercer nature, just as the satyrs are the gentlest. The 'callitriches' differ in appearance from the rest, having a beard on the face and a tail broadly spread at the front part. This animal is said to exist only under the sky of Ethiopia where it is born. The Indians hunt apes white over their whole body.

Pliny, in the same place: the 'tarandrus' is an animal of the size of an ox, its head more like a stag's and not unlike it. Branching horns, a cloven hoof, fur the size of bears'. And when it wishes, it takes on its own color and is like a donkey. Its hide is of such hardness that they make breastplates from it. It takes on the color of all trees, flowers, shrubs, and places among which, fearful, it hides. And so it is rarely caught. This animal, then, changes the colors of its bristles, and none other of those clothed with fur does, except among the Indians, and the 'lychaon,' to which a maned neck is attributed. For the 'thoes,' which is a kind of wolf, taller in length, unlike in the shortness of its legs, swift in leaping, living by hunting, harmless to man, changes its coat, not its color, shaggy through the winters, bare in summer.

Pliny, in the same place: the badger is a wild animal, having in body almost the size of a fox, but of lower stature, since it has short shins; it has fur of grey color, a hard and very strong hide, sharp teeth, and, when attacked by dogs or other animals, turns onto its back and fights back with teeth and feet. It is said, moreover, that the fox is in some way opposed to it, for the fox never prepares a burrow for itself, but takes over the badger's burrow by trickery. For when it knows the badger has left, it goes to the entrance and defecates there, and thus, the badger abandoning the place because of the filth, the fox occupies it. The same is said of the 'melo,' or 'melota,' of which mention was made above.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the badger is an animal the size of a fox; it has short legs, unequal on each side, but shorter on the left. Whence it happens that, placing the feet of its right side in the small ruts that a cart's wear makes, it runs powerfully, and thus escapes its pursuers. It has a furry hide, stiff with bristles, woven with white and black hairs.

Physiologus: [on] badgers: they prepare underground dwellings for themselves with labor, and choose one badger, who serves as the carrier of the earth dug out with their feet; lying on its back, then, with legs extended and raised above its belly, the dug-out earth is piled and loaded on it, and it is dragged out by the feet by the others. And they do this repeatedly until the width of the house can suffice for its inhabitants.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the badger's fat increases as the moon waxes, and diminishes as it wanes, so that, if killed at the last quarter of the moon, it is not found at all: ointments are made from this fat, by which pains of the kidneys and injuries of the members are calmed, and this is remarkable, that although the beast is medicinal in one respect, its bite is nevertheless usually most severe and deadly. But the reason for this is that it lives on hornets and animals that crawl in the earth and are venomous. And so its teeth are infected. Although even without venomous food, experience has proven that the teeth of wolves and foxes and many animals are venomous, whence bites of wolves inflicted on beasts are cauterized with hot iron, lest the harmful bite bring on corruption. But venomous food, through the mediation of a well-disposed internal nature, passes into the best matter. And what belongs to the venom, digestion expels, but the rest it purges and passes into the nourishment of cleansed flesh. And so, by this reasoning, it happens that the fat is medicinal and the bite deadly. This is better shown in the young serpent, which feeds on venomous things, and yet whose flesh, made into theriac, is set against all poisons.
Aesculapius: those with fever are healed, anointed with badger fat. Its brain, cooked with oil, cures all pains. And its testicles, cooked with honey, kindle desire.

Isidore: the tiger is named for its swift flight, for thus the Persians and Indians name the arrow. It is a beast marked with varied spots, marvelous in strength and speed, from whose name the river Tigris is called, since it is the swiftest of all rivers. Hyrcania especially produces these.
Physiologus: [on] the tiger, a most savage animal, raging with incomparable fury, especially when, its cubs stolen, it pursues hunters.

Aristotle: for nature formed narrower necks for tigers, as for bears and lions, since they live on flesh, and do not lower their neck and mouth to the ground for the sake of grazing, but either attack a stag or tear apart an ox or a sheep. And nothing is as fierce as lions or tigers, and yet these often serve man, and lay aside their nature through human training, as already said above of the training of the lion. The tiger, when it finds the den of its stolen offspring empty, at once follows the tracks of the thief. But he, though carried on a swift horse, seeing nevertheless that he cannot escape the beast's speed, when he sees it close to him, throws down a glass sphere. But the tiger is deceived by its own image, and, thinking it her offspring, checks her charge, wishing to gather up her young. Held again by vain hope, she then throws herself with all her strength to catch the rider, and thus, spurred by the goad of anger, presses hard upon him as he swiftly flees. He again, by throwing down another sphere, delays her pursuit, nor does the memory of the deception exclude the mother's diligence. She turns over the empty image and settles down as if to nurse her young, and thus, deceived by her own zealous devotion, loses both her vengeance and her offspring.

Solinus: tigers gleam with a tawny color, and this tawny is interwoven with blackish markings. They mate facing away from each other; they are so swift that nothing is so long a distance that they cannot cover it in a short time, nothing so far ahead that they do not overtake it at once. Their power, however, is best proven when they pursue the thieves of their cubs. Riders may take turns following each other, and, however much cunning they wish to use to save the stolen prey, unless they have the protection of the sea, every attempt is in vain. It is very often noted that, if they ever see their thieves sailing away, they waste away on the shore with futile rage, as if punishing their own slowness with willing self-destruction.

Pliny: the tiger and the panther are, of all wild beasts, almost alone marked with a variety of spots. For the rest, each kind has its own single color. The Hyrcanians and Indians report that the tiger is an animal of tremendous speed, especially, once known, when it is caught with its cubs. The whole litter of a tiger, which is always numerous, is stolen by an ambusher. But when the pregnant mother finds her den empty - for the males have no care for the offspring - she is said to track the scent headlong; as the thief senses her approaching with a roar, he throws down one of the cubs. She snatches it up in her mouth, and, though heavier, returns even faster than she came. And she pursues him again and again this way, until, once he has returned to his ship, her fury rages in vain upon the shore.

Isidore: 'tragelaphi' are named from Greek; although they are of the same kind as stags, they have shaggy shoulders like he-goats and long, shaggy beards on the chin; they are found nowhere but around the Phasis.
Pliny: the 'tragelaphus' is of the same species, differing only in beard and the shagginess of the shoulders, which they call the 'tragelaphon,' born nowhere but near the river Phasis.

Helinand of Froidmont: the 'tragelaphus,' as if 'goat-stag.' For 'tragos' means he-goat, 'elaphos' stag. It is, moreover, most similar to a stag in size and form, but has shaggy shoulders like a he-goat.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the same is also called 'platycerus,' that is, 'having broad horns.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'tragodita,' alone among beasts, grazes with lowered horns and a bent neck, so that it seems more to cut the grass thus touched by its mouth than to pluck it in the manner of other animals; for it has long horns hanging down along the slope of its head and jaws all the way to the ground, which prevent it from grazing on the ground in the usual manner.

div.head: DE VARIO ET UNICORNE ET UNCIA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'varius' is a small beast of the 'pyrolus' kind, a little larger than a weasel. It dwells in trees and rears its young there; it has its name from the matter itself. For on its belly it is white. On its back it has an ash-grey color, elegant and admirable. Men and women of both sexes glory in the pelts of these creatures for the adornment of their garments. Yet this little beast takes no pride at all in its own pelt, let alone another's. The unicorn is a small animal, but of bodily strength, having legs short in proportion to its size, and does not fear iron. It dwells in the highest mountains and vastest wildernesses. The 'uncia' [lynx-panther] is a most savage animal, no taller than a dog, but longer in body, very hostile to dogs. It does not eat its prey unless it carries it aloft, but when it reaches a tree, it brings the prey to the topmost branch and eats it hanging there. But when, in the heat of mating, it has wounded someone, mice gather upon him and urinate on him, and he dies. Whence a certain man, wounded by it, had himself carried by boat onto the sea, and the mice came to the sea to reach him, but because of the sea they could not; this animal's gall is deadly.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: [on] wild oxen, so strong that they lift trees and armed soldiers on their horns.

Isidore: the 'uri' are named from 'Orion,' that is, from the mountains. They are wild oxen, moreover, in Germany, having horns extended so far that vessels of remarkable capacity for royal tables are made from them.

Solinus: the 'uri' are in Germany, which the unskilled common folk call buffaloes, whereas buffaloes, with an almost stag-like face, are born in Africa. But these that we call 'uri' have bull-like horns extended so far that, removed for their remarkable capacity, they become drinking vessels among royal tables.

Helinand of Froidmont, book 26: in the Hercynian forest of Germany there are 'uri'; these are a little smaller than elephants in size, in appearance and color and shape like a bull. Their strength is great and their speed great. They spare neither man nor beast they notice. These, caught with much effort in pits, are killed, and, their horns brought back publicly as evidence, bring great praise. But they cannot become accustomed to men and grow tame, not even when caught young: the size of the horns, and their shape and appearance, differ greatly from the horns of our oxen. These, carefully sought after, they encircle with silver at the rims, and thus use them as drinking cups at the most sumptuous banquets.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the bear is so named as if 'orsus' [begun], namely in the womb, but completed outside, and this because it is born prematurely, whence it is shaped by licking. The bear is, moreover, a fierce animal, exceedingly misshapen in its members. It eats flesh and the fruits of the earth or trees indiscriminately, because of the moisture of its body. Ants, crabs, by natural instinct, for the medicine of a natural weakness. It climbs trees either from fear or for food, breaks beehives and eats their produce, gulps water rather than drinks it, in winter walks little, but comes forth in spring. And yet then especially the males are very fat. But in the winter season they sleep very little; its breath is so pestilential that no wild beast touched by its breath escapes, and, breathed upon, they putrefy more quickly. Its blood is very scant except around the heart. Its cooked flesh seems to increase in size, as Pliny says, which is contrary to the habit of all flesh. The bear, among almost all living creatures, always grows as long as it lives. Whence large and very strong bears are found. The world generally has black bears, but some regions have white ones, and these grow so large that they reach fifteen cubits in length. The female bear is stronger than the male, and bolder and more cunning, and is tamed more quickly; she has four teats.

Aristotle: the bear is an animal having teeth above, and a single lower belly, and, after the belly, intestine, like the wolf too. In some animals, however, the belly is larger, as in the pig and bear. It is clear, moreover, that the wild bear hides in winter, but whether it does this because of the cold or for another reason is a question. For males and females at that time are very fat, so that they cannot easily move; the female, indeed, at that time gives birth in caverns, until she wishes to bring out her young, which will be after the beginning of the third month and of spring. Her hiding, moreover, lasts at least forty days, and it is said that for fourteen days she does not move at all, nor is she hunted except rarely; in these days, too, she eats nothing. Whence if anyone hunts them at this time, they will find their intestines empty, and, as is said, because of the lack of food, they become as if congealed. Female animals in general are weaker than males, except the bear and leopard, in which they think the females are stronger and bolder; the bear, moreover, has four teats.
Isidore: bears have a weak head, but the greatest strength in their arms and loins, whence too they sometimes stand upright.
Ambrose: bears eat the flesh of animals, since they do not graze on plants on the ground; narrower necks were given to those that feed on flesh.

Pliny: the bear's head is the weakest thing, which for the lion is the strongest. And so, driven by force to throw themselves from some cliff, they leap with their heads covered by their paws, and often die on the ground with a broken blow. The Spanish believe there is a poison in the brain, and burn the heads of those killed in shows, having established that the drink drives one into bear-like madness. In Africa there are no bears. On the island of Crete, too, there are neither foxes nor bears.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: bears have no marrow, but their feet are fleshy in the footprint. Tails, however, are small in furry animals, like bears: males, in every kind, are stronger than females, except in panthers and bears. Female bears bear four teats.

Solinus: Numidian bears surpass the rest. Lucius Messala had a hundred Numidian bears and as many Ethiopian hunter-bears in the Roman circus. And he had this spectacle recorded among memorable achievements.
Aesculapius: if the 'sosach,' that is the horse, treads where there is the track of the 'dovin,' that is the bear, numbness befalls its foot.
Alexander Neckam: the bear, uttering a certain murmur, sucks its feet, as if drawing some nourishment from them. A skinned bear seems to clearly represent a naked man.

Solinus: bears lie in wait for beehives. And when they have tasted mandrake apples, they devour ants to recover their health. If ever they attack bulls, they know by which parts especially to weaken them. Nor do they aim at anything but the horns or nostrils. The horns, indeed, so as to wear them out with the weight; the nostrils, so that the pain is sharper in the more tender spot.

Aristotle: the bear, then, fights, as said, not only with stags, but also with wild pigs. And sometimes it throws itself upon bulls and falls on their backs. And when the bull wishes to strike it with its horns, it holds the horns and shoulder-blades with its hands. Then it throws the bull to the ground and walks upright on its hind feet, and eats its flesh.

Pliny, in the same place: bears walk on two feet. Turned backward, they strip a tree; they attack bulls, and, hanging with all their feet on the horns, wear them out with their weight, nor is there any craftier stupidity among animals for mischief.
Gloss: the bear is a wild and deceitful beast, weak indeed in the head, but very strong in the arms and limbs. Whence the prophet says: the bear, lying in wait, has become to me.
Gloss: [on] the bear. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Gloss: nothing, finally, is said to be more savage than the mother bear when she has lost her cubs, or when she lacks food. Whence the Lord too, through the prophet, threatening sinners, says: I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs.

Ambrose: the bear, a beast lying in wait, full of deceit, is said to bring forth shapeless offspring from the womb, but to shape them with its tongue and form them in its own likeness; wounded, too, it knows how to heal itself, and to cure its own wounds by the mere touch of the herb called 'phlomos' in Greek.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the bear, indeed, never attacks a man unless it has first received a blow from him. Struck heavily, however, and wounded, it knows how to heal itself by applying the herb 'phlomos' to its wounds. Besides wounds and lethal blows, it is said to draw out all injuries by licking them with its paws. They fight, however, not only with stags and wild pigs, but also with bulls. It does not easily overcome a bull without horns. It walks upright when it wishes, and wrestles with its arms. It also fights with the fox and the donkey. For it eats raw flesh. And this is said to be the cause of the fight. It devours ants and crabs, however, for medicine.
Solinus: Numidian bears surpass the rest, only in ferocity and in deeper fur. For their offspring are equal to their parents.

Solinus: bears mate not as other four-footed creatures do, but, suited to mutual embraces, are joined as if in human couplings; winter arouses the desire of mating. With secret respect, males revere their pregnant mates, and, although in the same dens, they are nevertheless divided by separate resting-places partitioned by trenches. The thirtieth day frees the womb. Whence it happens that such hastened fecundity creates shapeless offspring. It brings forth, then, tiny bits of flesh, having a white color and no eyes, and, from such hurried immaturity, only raw matter, except for the outlines of the claws; these they gradually shape by licking, and sometimes warm them held to their chest, so that, warmed by constant incubation, they may draw in the breath of life; meanwhile there is no food. Indeed, for the first fourteen days the mothers fall into such a sleep that they cannot even be roused by wounds. Once delivered, they hide for four months, and, soon emerging into the open day, suffer such unaccustomedness to the light that you would think them overcome with blindness.

Isidore, on the bear: rightly, then, the bear is named as if 'orsus' [begun], since it shapes its offspring with its mouth. Whence too it is said that the she-bear shapes the offspring with her tongue when she has brought it forth. But this is due to the immaturity of the birth.

Pliny, book 8: bears hide themselves in the winter months. Their mating is at the start of winter, and not in the common manner of four-footed creatures, but with both lying down and embracing; then a withdrawal into separate dens, in which they give birth on the thirtieth day, mostly five at a time. These are white and shapeless flesh, a little larger than mice, without eyes, without fur; only the claws project; this they gradually shape by licking. And nothing is rarer than for men to see a she-bear giving birth. And so the males hide for forty days, the females for four months. If they have no dens, they build them, impenetrable to rain, from a mass of branches and shrubs, and lined with soft foliage. For the first fourteen days they are weighed down by a heavy sleep, so that they cannot even be roused by wounds. Then, remarkably, they grow fat from lethargy. Those fats are suited to medicines, and are effective against hair loss. From these days they sit and live by sucking their front paws. They warm their stiffened offspring by pressing them to their chest, in no other incubation than birds do their eggs. Remarkable to say, Theophrastus believes that during this time even cooked bear's flesh, if roasted, increases in size. There is then no evidence of food, then the least moisture is found in the belly. There is blood, only a small drop around the heart, and nothing of blood is in the rest of the body. They come forth in spring, but the males very fat: the reason for this is not clear. For indeed they are not fattened even by sleep, except for fourteen days, as we said. Coming out, however, they devour an herb called 'aron' to loosen their intestines, otherwise congealed, and beforehand blunt the edges of their teeth on tree stumps. Their eyes become dull frequently, for which reason especially they seek out honeycombs, so as to relieve, with the blood of bee-stings on their mouth, that heaviness, namely of the eyes.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: animals whose division into toes of the feet is separate are more numerous in offspring; these also produce incomplete offspring, in which kind are the she-bear and the fox and the lioness. For they bring forth shapeless young, and it is rare to see them giving birth. Afterward, by licking, they warm their offspring and thus shape them, and mostly bring forth four at a time.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the she-bear is indeed very hot, which her continuous motion shows; her womb, then, is very hot and dry. Whence the cotyledons by which the offspring is attached to the womb are dried out, and for this reason it breaks; and so the offspring are born unformed. Others hold that the womb is very moist, whence they say the cotyledons break for this reason too. And for this reason too, form cannot be impressed on the offspring, since moisture does not hold an impression well.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the bear is caught in this way: hunters, having marked a hollow tree in which bees have stored honeycombs, hang there, by a certain rope, a mallet of great mass, so that it blocks the opening through which access to the combs is gained. And there, below the tree, they fix stakes, sharpened, into the ground all around. When, then, the bear, most eager for honey, finds the hanging mallet in its way, it grows angry and strives to push away the thing hanging there. But the mallet, returning to its place, strikes it back. And when this happens repeatedly, the bear, at last worn out and overcome by the mallet's blows, and, as said, greedy for honey, falls onto the sharp stakes fixed beneath the tree, and thus the watching hunters catch or kill it as it falls. Very often, however, hunters, having made a pit into which they want the bear to fall, so that it may be caught or killed there, sprinkle honey along the path leading toward the pit, so that the bear, licking and following the honeyed path, at last falls into the pit. But when it is caught, if it does not grow tame at man's command, its eyes are blinded with glowing bronze. For while it looks at the glowing bronze, it loses its sight, as it were, by sensation.
Isaac Judaeus: bear's flesh, most viscous and disobedient to digestion, gives the worst nourishment, whence it pertains more to medicine than to food.

Physiologus, on the bear: the gall is hot and dry, effective against epilepsy and paralysis. The gall, however, should be separated from the liver with its own little sac, and thus hung and dried; it keeps for two years.
Aesculapius: if you remove the eyes of the 'douin,' that is the bear, and bind them above a man's left arm, they will ease his quartan fever.

Pliny: bear's gall, mixed with honey, also calms hangnails of the fingers. Likewise, taken in water, it loosens the breathing passages. Bear's blood disperses vitiligo and abscesses in any part. Bear's fat heals gout, and so does bull's tallow, in equal weight with wax. The same fat, mixed with red ochre, heals ulcers on the shins and legs, and pains of the loins too, and, wherever softening is needed, it is fitting to be rubbed with bear's fat; finally, bear's testicles, eaten, benefit epileptics.
Avicenna, on the bear: [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Dioscorides: bear's fat is said to promote hair growth and correct baldness. Bear's gall, given as an electuary, heals epileptics. Likewise, applied on wool and placed on the navel, it loosens infants' bowels.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: as said above, following Pliny, bears for the first fourteen days are weighed down by a heavy sleep. And then, remarkably, they grow fat from lethargy. And those fats are suited to medicines, and are effective against loss of the pupil's tears.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the fox is a deceitful animal, which craftily seizes and devours domestic birds too, like hens. It has abundant, deep fur and a large tail. It is said, moreover, that the fox never makes a burrow for itself, but craftily occupies the badger's burrow. For when it knows the badger has left the burrow, it approaches the entrance and defecates there, and thus, because of the filth, the badger flees and the fox occupies its place; hunters pursue this creature for its pelt, not for its flesh, which is useless.

Pliny, book 8: in Thrace, in frigid regions, foxes, an animal otherwise of skilled hearing, cross frozen rivers and lakes only when going and returning to feed. And so it has been observed that a fox, placing its ear against the ice, judges the thickness of the frost.

Pliny, in the same: foxes, like she-bears and lionesses, produce incomplete offspring, for they bear shapeless young, and it is rare to see one giving birth. Afterward, however, by licking, they warm their offspring and shape them, and mostly bring forth four at a time.
Pliny, in the same: foxes have bony genitals, as do wolves and weasels too.
Pliny, book 24, in the same: foxes, if they eat almonds and do not have the chance to lap water nearby, die.

Pliny: they report, moreover, that cocks are not attacked by foxes if they have eaten a dried fox liver, or if a little skin from its neck is worn by the cock; similar things too are found in weasel's gall.

Aristotle: the fox is a cunning animal and one of evil deeds; it has a bony member, and mates with itself cast down to the ground. The bear and the 'cirocos' bird, that is, of hooked claws, fight with the fox, since they eat flesh. But the tortoise-serpent and the fox are friends, and both dwell in caverns of the earth. The vulture too catches the fox. Every four-footed animal having many clefts in its feet, like the dog and fox and lion and wolf, generates blind offspring. Afterward, however, their eyes separate and they see. Likewise animals whose nature is close to one another, especially if they do not differ in appearance and size, and are suited in the span of pregnancy, mate together. And this applies to dogs and wolves and foxes. Stags fear the voice of foxes. The 'ascelon' is a bird that fights with the fox, plucks its feathers, harms it, and kills its young. The crow, however, is a friend to the fox and helps it against the 'ascelon.' There is also a bird that does not brood its eggs, but wraps them in the hide of a fox or hare, until they hatch.

Ambrose, in the Hexaemeron: the fox is an animal worthy of hatred because of its plundering, but contemptible for its weakness. Careless of its own safety while lying in wait for others': the fox heals itself with a tear of the pine, and by such a remedy prolongs the span of imminent death.
Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the fox too, like certain other animals, becomes rabid.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the fox is a foul-smelling animal, especially in the mouth, and also in the rear part when death is imminent. It takes as food the sap that flows from the pine, and thus recovers its health and prolongs the span of its life. For the fox has burrows in the ground for protection, but is very often caught in them. For hunters, when they know the foxes are hiding in the burrows, send in small, skillfully trained cubs, which, reaching the top of the burrow, betray them by barking. And there, opposite, the hunters dig, and thus reach the lurking fox and catch it. If a fox eats almonds, it is said to die. It suffers a heating of the liver in the summer season, whence blood flowing to its extremities relieves it, and its skin ulcerates, and through this its fur falls from its body, as Constantine says in the Viaticum. The fox in hunger, from distress, is said to imitate the barking of dogs; that is, when it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it feigns itself dead and, lying on its back, draws in its breath with its tongue put out; then birds, incautiously coming down as if to a carcass, it seizes with its open mouth and devours. Foxes mate lying on their side, the female embracing the male. The cubs of foxes, carried in the mother's womb, pierce the little membrane of the mother's belly with their claws.

Isidore: the fox [vulpes] is rightly so named, as if 'volipes' [rolling-foot]. For it is nimble on its feet, and never runs in straight paths, but in twisting turns, a deceitful animal, deceiving by ambush. For when it has no food, it feigns death, and thus seizes and devours birds coming down as if to a carcass.

Physiologus: the fox, when it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, rolls itself in red earth, so as to appear as if bloodied, and throws itself on the ground and holds its breath. Birds, seeing it not breathing and, as it were, bloodied, and its tongue thrust out of its mouth, think it dead; then, coming down to sit on it, it seizes them and devours them.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the fox sometimes even escapes dogs, while it pretends to be a dog among dogs by a similar barking, and while it hangs itself from a branch, it forces the dogs, following uncertain tracks, to go astray. It is also accustomed to deceive dogs and the hunter, when, entering a herd of goats, it seizes one of them, leaping onto its back. For thus, through the running of the fleeing goat, it escapes, because of the terror of the unexpected and hateful rider. For the other goats too follow, and when the hunter fears they will be scattered, he calls back the scent-tracking dogs following the fox's scent. Caught in a snare, too, it sometimes bites off its own foot, so as to escape even this way. When no flight is open, however, it feigns itself dead, so that, drawn out of the snare, it may seize the chance to flee. When, as said, badgers have prepared their dwellings, in their absence the fox approaches and enters their labor. And it leaves a foul sign of its new lodging, so that the burrow, polluted by the stench of its excrement, becomes worthless. And indeed the badger, detesting the stench, abandons the place, and thus the deceitful beast occupies it. When a dog pursues the fox and, having caught up, strives to seize it, it drags its bushy tail across the pursuer's mouth and thus deceives the dog, until it can reach the thick woods; it especially lies in wait for domestic animals, and also hunts the hare, and at first indeed plays with it, then tries it with its teeth, and finally catches it, unless the hare escapes. But some hares, having experienced its malice, flee its play as an enemy's. The fox in flight moves in twisting courses, lest its tracks be perceived by hunters. They also say that a fox about to cross frozen lakes, with its ear placed against the ice, judges its thickness and does not dare to cross unless it finds it sufficiently strong.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: fox flesh, if burnt, is effective for asthmatics taken with wine; its blood and fat greatly benefit ear pains.

Haly Abbas: if fox is boiled with olive oil, this oil benefits arthritic knots and hardness that arise from it. Fox fat, melted with iris oil, heals pains of the ears and teeth. Its lung, pressed with squill vinegar, heals difficulty of breathing and asthma. Fox gall sharpens sight and benefits the onset of a cataract descending on the eye.

Pliny: fox boiled down until only the bones remain heals gout. They say those wearing a fox's tongue in a bracelet are not troubled by watering eyes; fox liver or lung in dark wine loosens the breathing passages. The same lung, dried to ash and drunk in water, benefits a diseased spleen. Its fat benefits ulcers of the head. Fox testicles, too, reduce parotid swellings.

Avicenna: fox boiled in water and applied as a fomentation greatly benefits a painful joint. Its fat, dripped into the ear, calms its pain. For this it is indeed very evacuative. Likewise its dry lung greatly benefits asthmatics. Its skin is hotter than others, and those who are moist benefit from it because of its dissolving power. The fox's testicle is hot in the first degree and moist in itself, and there is superfluous moisture in it. It benefits spasm and tetanus that occur in the hind parts from paralysis, stimulates appetite for mating and helps it, especially with wine, and stands in place of skink.
Dioscorides: dry fox lung, drunk with dark wine, helps asthmatics. Its gathered and melted fat marvelously cures ear pains.

Aesculapius: fox lung, roasted on embers and drunk, consumes the spleen, heals those with sighing breath. Its heart is effective for the flow and return of blood. Its gall cures ears and eyes. With honey it is effective for blemishes of the face, and for deafness of the ears with woman's milk. Its liver, eaten or drunk with wine, heals celiacs, and, its smoke applied to the eyes and washed with warm salted water, clarifies them. Its spleen, drunk, marvelously cures colic sufferers. Its fat benefits ears and gout-afflicted members. Its tallow is effective for those with tremors and for every pain. Its kidneys, cooked with honey, drive away throat pains. Its testicles too, often rubbed on, drive away gout and dissolve growths of the gums. The same, cooked in old oil with bitumen and applied beneath, heal a suffocated womb: they are also effective for ears and spleen and baldness. Likewise its skin, wrapped around a gouty foot, heals it. If its brain is often given to an infant, he will never be epileptic.

Isidore: the ichneumon is so called in Greek because by its scent wholesome and venomous foods are revealed, of which Dracontius says: it detects, by its bristly hairs, the power of any poison. It is named 'suillis,' moreover, from bristles [setae]; this creature also pursues serpents. When it fights against the asp, it raises its tail, which the asp especially begins to watch as if threatening, and, transferring its force against it, is deceived and seized.

Aristotle: the ichneumon, when it sees the serpent called the 'hoscos,' does not fight it until it calls for helpers. And because they fear the serpent's bite, they enter water and then sand, then fight with the serpent.

Pliny: the asp has a mortal war with the ichneumon. This animal is known for this glory, born especially in Egypt. It submerges itself repeatedly in mud and dries it in the sun. Soon, once it has armored itself with several such coats, it advances to fight against the asp, and, raising itself with its tail, receives the asp's futile strikes turned away from it, until, watching for its chance with its head turned aside, it attacks its throat. Not content with this, it wages war on another creature no less fierce, namely the crocodile. For, having observed this creature overcome by sleep, it gnaws through its belly, entering through its throat like a dart shot in.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: for this, see above, at the end of where the crocodile was discussed; it is clear that this beast, namely the ichneumon, is the same one Isidore calls the 'enydros,' of which we spoke above.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the hippopotamus is born on land, although it is as powerful in water as on land, and dwells there. It has a twisting tail, itchy teeth, and is similar to a horse in back and neigh, of which fuller mention was made above in the treatise on sea monsters and fish.

Pliny, book 8, on the hippopotamus: this creature is also a master in a certain part of the art of healing, for, made fat by constant excess, it comes out onto the shore, having observed a recent cutting of reeds, and, where it sees the sharpest stump, pressing its body onto it, wounds a certain vein in its skin. And thus, by the flow of blood, it relieves its otherwise diseased body, and covers the wound again with mud.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'zubro' is a beast of the wild bull kind, most strong and very large, indeed fifteen cubits in length. It is also of such speed that it catches, in its horns, thrown backward, the dung it discharges with force, and hurls it far behind its back. By this discharged dung, then, most abundantly, it blinds and weakens pursuing dogs and renders them entirely useless. It has blackish hair, very large horns of three cubits, ample beyond measure, so that they become drinking vessels at the tables of the wealthy. When, then, it encounters a man or dog in its path, it tosses him up on its horns, and, throwing him high into the air for a long time, catches him again on its horns, until it finally kills him, battered. Some, because of its speed, say this is the tiger, but wrongly, for the tiger is a rather modest beast and dwells in the East, whereas this tiger is found in Bohemia. It is deceived by hunters through this trick, nor is there another method of hunting by which it can easily be caught: once the 'zubro' is first tired out by dogs, the hunter positions himself against it around a tree of great mass; the 'zubro,' seeing him, runs to the tree and, encircling it with its horns and forehead, stupidly thinks it can overwhelm the hunter. Meanwhile the hunter, always protected by the tree, pierces the struggling creature's sides with his spear-point, and thus overcomes by wisdom what is unconquerable by human strength. There is, moreover, another kind of 'zubro,' which the Poles call 'turones.' Indeed smaller in form, but superior in speed.

div.head: DE MINUTIS BESTIOLIS ET PRIMO DE MURE

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: thus far we have spoken of beasts of burden and wild beasts. Besides these larger beasts, however, there are also certain small little creatures, which can partly be reckoned in the kind of beasts, partly in the kind of worms, such as mice, dormice, shrews, weasels, rats, shrew-mice, moles, and any similar creatures. Of these, then, it remains to speak, all of which seem generally to be of the mouse kind, and first of the mouse in general, whose name, however, is commonly applied to the shrew.

Isidore: the mouse [mus] is a tiny animal, which has this name. Whatever, moreover, is derived from it becomes Latin. Others say mice are so named because they are born from the moisture of the earth. For 'mus' means earth, whence too 'humus.' In these the liver grows at full moon, just as certain coastal creatures increase, which in turn diminish as the moon wanes.

Pliny: the mouse is a semi-wild animal, that is, neither gentle nor wild, but of a nature midway between the two. They placed mice as inhabitants of houses; these hide themselves in winter, and feed their parents, exhausted by old age, with remarkable devotion. Old age ends with winter rest. For, hidden away, they lie there, and again grow young in summer.

Pliny, in the same book: just as among winged creatures swallows are untrainable, so among land creatures are mice. On Aristotle's authority, and that of Alexander the Great's soldiers, the generation of mice is said to occur by licking, not by mating. From one female, they reported, a hundred twenty are born. Among the Persians, however, pregnant ones are found, some enduring mating and also with young in the womb, and it is thought they become pregnant from tasting salt. And so it ceases to be a marvel, whence such great force of wild mice devastates harvests. Among these, this too remains hidden, by what means so great a multitude suddenly dies. For they are found neither lifeless, nor is there anyone who has ever dug up a mouse in a field in winter. Very many, then, come to the Troad, and their numbers have already driven the inhabitants away from there; they attribute their occurrence to droughts.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: some mice have gall, and in most animals fat is without sensation, for which reason they report that pigs, breathing, are gnawed by mice.
Pliny, in the same: beechnuts are said to be most pleasing to mice, and so this is the reason for the occurrence of this animal.
Pliny: [on] the mouse. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: the mouse, like other great-hearted animals, is timid. Mice, too, have dwellings, like moles do. Animals in Libya are not accustomed to drink water in summer, because of the scarcity of water. And for this reason, if a mouse drinks water, it will die. Certain ruminant animals are found having teeth in both jaws, like mice. Likewise certain small animals produce many offspring, like the mouse kind. And in certain animals of the same kind, sometimes gall is found, sometimes not, as in the mouse and in man. For some men have visible gall on the liver, and some do not. A certain bird, the 'galy,' fights with serpents that eat mice, since it too eats mice. Likewise some animal that makes a saw with its teeth takes water with its tongue, like the mouse.
Ambrose: the elephant, formidable to the bull, fears the mouse.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the mouse is a small creature eager for bread and for things made from grain for human use. Most skilled in seeking out food, for which it avoids almost no danger, and out of desire for it gnaws through harder and solid materials. Further, if it drinks water, it dies, since it is of a very moist nature. Pliny says the Libyan mouse does not drink. But since it is certain the mouse urinates, it is probable its food turns into urine, just as certain men drink almost nothing and yet, their food changed into liquid substance, produce much urine. The mouse, finding many cheeses in one place, tries them all, and, eating the one it finds best, condemns the worse ones. The smell of mice troubles elephants. It is clear that a sudden multitude of these arises and suddenly dies, yet they are not found lifeless. It is also certain that white little stones are frequently found with their young. Whence common folk have concluded that they cannot give birth unless the little stone is present. In Egyptian Thebes, if the sky pours more abundant rains in the summer season, soon the whole region is filled with countless mice. In mice, at full moon the liver grows, and at full moon too they produce sounds, but at new moon are mute. Nor is there any doubt that in certain regions there are white mice, and some reddish ones too.
Gloss: the mouse moves on the ground and is reckoned among unclean things. In this Scripture forbids gluttony, since the mouse avoids no dangers for the gluttony of its belly.

Pliny, book 8: there are several kinds of mice in the Cyrenaic region. Some with a broad forehead, some with a sharp one, some of the hedgehog kind with stinging hairs; when white ones appear, they portend disaster, and mice too hide themselves in winter. Nigidius is the authority, as also do dormice, whom the censors' law lists among the leading delicacies. Quintus Scaurus and Marcus, in their consulship, admitted them at dinners in no other way than shellfish or birds brought from another region. Theophrastus is likewise the authority that on the island of Gyaros, when they had driven out the inhabitants, they even gnawed iron; it is established that this caused loss also in ironworking forges. In gold mines, indeed, their bellies are cut open for this reason, and this theft is always detected.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: they report, moreover, that a small worm is generated in the head of mice about to die. Egyptian mice have hard fur like hedgehogs. The same walk on two feet, as Alpine ones do.

Pliny, book 8, in the same: Alpine mice too hide themselves, of medium size, food having been gathered beforehand in their burrows. Some, however, relate that male and female take turns, one lying on its back with a bundle of straw clutched to itself, its tail seized in the other's mouth, and are dragged in turn to the burrow, and that for this reason their backs are worn at that time. There are also similar ones in Egypt. They likewise sit on their haunches and walk on two feet, using their front feet as hands.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: mice, as James says, in the manner of foxes, are large, and kill animals, and, although they do not kill men, trouble them with bites. In Arabia a large mouse is found, whose front feet are large, namely of one palm's size, but the hind feet of one finger's size.

div.head: DE HIS CUM QUIBUS MURES FUGANTUR

cit.quote: Pliny: mice are driven from crops by ash of weasel or cat dissolved in water, and the seed sprinkled with it, or by seed boiled in such water. But since this animal's stench also lingers in bread, they think it more useful to moisten the seed with bull's gall instead.

Pliny, book 20, in the same: wild or 'running' cucumbers, so called, are boiled down, and mice do not touch seed sprinkled with this decoction. Garlic is effective against a poisonous mouse bite; mallow too is effective against every stinging blow, especially the mouse's.
Pliny, in the same, book on the chameleon plant: the juice of this herb, with water and oil added, draws mice to itself and kills them, unless they immediately drink water.
Pliny, book 24, in the same: smoke of the yew tree too kills mice.
Hellebore too, mixed with barley meal, kills mice.
Pliny, book 26, in the same: further, if weasel's brain is added to rennet, they say cheeses are not touched by mice.
Pliny, book 27, in the same: likewise aconite kills mice from a distance by its smell.
Pliny, book 22, in the same: asphodel is among the most notable of herbs; mice are driven off by it, and, if their burrow is blocked, they die.
Rhazes, in the Almansor: mice flee a house fumigated with chalcanthum. They die from iron scale, or from copperas, or from hellebore, if they eat any of these, namely, mixed with flour.

Avicenna, in the second canon: squill is called 'mouse-onion,' so named because it kills the mouse. Likewise quicksilver kills the mouse. But wormwood oil, when poured into ink, keeps mice from gnawing the book.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: hellebore kills the mouse and causes lethargy, and the same hellebore, and seed of white henbane, and cabbage root. Of these too are mouse-onion and iron scale. To drive mice away, moreover, a male mouse is skinned and released in the house, or castrated, or its tail cut off; but skinning is more effective. And it is said that if one of them is tied by the foot with a thread to a stake in the house, the rest flee. Likewise when 'chiran,' that is pitch, is placed over their burrow, they flee it. Likewise they flee from bull's gall and from asafoetida and from ant smoke.

Palladius: if you pour thick olive-lees onto a plate and set it in the house at night, mice will stick to it. They will be killed, however, if you mix black hellebore with cheese or bread or fat or barley meal and offer it. Wild cucumber and colocynth juice too will harm this way. Against field mice Apuleius asserts that seed should be soaked in buffalo gall before sowing; some close their entrances with oleander leaves, which, gnawed as they strive to get out, kill them. If you stop up field mice's entrances with oak ash, mange will seize them from frequent contact and destroy them.

Avicenna, in the second canon: a mouse roasted and dried and given powdered to eat stops the flow of saliva from the mouth. All also agree that a mouse, if split open and placed on a scorpion's sting, heals it. Mouse blood eradicates warts. Its dung, moreover, benefits alopecia, especially when burnt and applied with onion. But drunk with frankincense and honeyed water, it breaks a stone. Likewise applied as a suppository, it loosens children's bowels. And when it is boiled with water and one suffering difficulty of urination sits in it, it benefits him.
Pliny: applied mouse dung restrains men's lust.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: cut-open mice applied are effective against serpent bites. And if a shrew has bitten draft animals, a fresh mouse with salt is applied. Mouse dung, according to Varro, fills in bald patches; for deep ulcers too, the heads of mice, mouse gall and dung with hellebore and pepper, are prescribed to be applied. For headaches the remedy is burnt mouse-skin ash applied with vinegar; ash of mouse head and tail anointed on is said to restore clarity of sight, much more so the ash of the wild mouse. Furthermore mouse ash dripped in with honey, or cooked with rose oil, calms ear pains. And if some creature has entered the ear, the chief remedy is mouse gall diluted with vinegar.

Ash from mouse dung is reported to heal toothache. African mice, especially with the skin removed, boiled in oil and salt and taken as food, cure lung ailments. Mouse dung too opens eye-films, mixed with powdered frankincense; mice applied benefit gout sufferers, and ash of the wild mouse with honey brings wounds to scarring. Fresh mouse blood applied, or the mouse itself split open, heals warts. Mouse brain given to drink in water benefits the delirious. The mouse, cut open and applied, draws out reeds and darts and other things lodged in the body; mouse dung diluted with rainwater restores women's breasts swollen after childbirth.

Haly Abbas: burnt and ground mouse heads, if their ash is mixed with honey, benefit alopecia and promote hair growth; their dung too, made into a poultice with olive oil, benefits alopecia; for children whose bowels are constipated, applied beneath, it softens them. And if the eyes are treated with a collyrium made from it, it removes the white [film].
Aesculapius: tiny mice with wine keep hairs from growing.
Pseudo-John of Foulsham: mouse dung greatly loosens [the bowels], whence physicians too sharpen medicine with it.
Isidore: we say dormice [glires] grow [crescere]; in winter they sleep the whole time and lie motionless as if dead, but in summer they revive.
Pliny: dormice hide themselves in winter; they are not found in the woods of Messenia in Italy except in one part.
Pliny: beechnuts fatten dormice, namely their own mast.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: eyes anointed with dormouse ash are said to have their clarity of sight restored. Further, a dormouse, its skin removed and its innards taken out, is boiled down with honey in a new vessel, and physicians prefer it boiled down with spikenard to a third part and thus kept, and, when needed, warmed with a scraper and poured in; for it is established that grievous ear ailments are healed by this remedy.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the dormouse is a modest-sized animal, varied in white, black, and reddish colors; it sleeps through the whole winter and, contracted like a ball, lies as one; and, remarkably, according to Isidore, it grows fat by this very sleep. Meanwhile, its vital spirit lulled, there is no movement in it. But this is remarkable, that if the sleeping animal is brought out into open air, its spirit gradually revives, being loosened between the hands of those holding it. And so, as spring's warmth comes on and the sun sends out its rays, it returns to strength in its natural way. It runs in trees as on the ground, and delights eagerly in the juice of fruits; its fat, boiled down, if the limbs are anointed with it, benefits, as Pliny says, those fearing paralysis.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the shrew is a beast said to be similar to the chameleon.
Radulfus of Flaix, on Leviticus: the shrew [mygale] is called as if 'mouse-glutton' [mus gulosus]. It is also deceitful, for it seizes by trickery what it afterward commits to its belly.

Avicenna, in the passage above: they have said the shrew is an animal smaller than the weasel. Its color inclines to ash-grey, with fineness and thinness; the length of its mouth extends to its very end, and its lip is at the very tip. And when it sees an animal, it leaps at it and hangs on by its testicles. Some, however, have said it has the shape and color of a mouse. But its snout is sharp and its eyes small, its teeth have three rows, of which one is twisted somewhat over the other, with a slight turning upward. From its bite come violent pains, a stinging in the body and the appearance of redness in the places along its teeth, and around the bite there arise blisters full of bloody moisture over dark-colored bases. Sometimes, moreover, the matter reaches a stinging in the intestines and difficulty of urination and cold, corrupted sweat. When, then, the corrupted flesh falls away, let the wound be treated with its proper treatment.

Isidore: the weasel [mustela] is so called as if 'long mouse' [mus longus], for 'telum' too is named from length; this creature, cunning by nature, moves its young from house to house where it is reared and changes its dwelling. It pursues serpents and mice. There are, moreover, two kinds of weasels: one is the wild kind, differing in size, which they call the 'ictis'; the other wanders about in houses. Those who say the weasel conceives through the mouth and gives birth through the ear are mistaken.
Physiologus: weasels are said to be skilled in medicine, so that, if by chance their young are killed and they can find them, they bring them back to life.

Ambrose, in the Hexaemeron: the weasel has a heavy odor on land, but a pleasant one in the sea. It knows how to avenge itself on land creatures by its stench; captured, it has no less grace than free.

Pliny, book 8: the weasel heals itself with rue when it has engaged in battle with serpents; the weasel's venom is death to the basilisk, for it kills it, easily finding its burrow, by decay alone, and both die together from the mutual stench, finishing each other off in nature's own battle.
Weasels have bony genitals.

Pliny, book 18, in the same: mice, as said above, are driven from crops by ash of weasel or cat dissolved and sprinkled with the seed, or by seed boiled in such water, but since this animal's stench lingers even in bread, they think it more useful for seed to be treated with buffalo gall instead.
Pliny, book 20, in the same: rue is proven effective against serpent bites, since weasels, by eating rue beforehand, arm themselves before doing battle with serpents.

They report that those anointed with ash of hyena's left temple boiled down with weasel's blood become hateful to everyone. Chameleon's gall thrown into water is said to draw weasels together. Goat's gall counteracts poisonings made from the wild weasel.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: the weasel that wanders about houses moves its young daily, as Cicero attests, changes its dwelling, and pursues serpents. The gall of the stellio lizard, ground in water, is said to gather weasels together. Moreover, dogs do not bark at one that has had a weasel's tail, cut off, hung on it. Likewise, against poisonings made from the wild weasel, a large draught of old rooster broth is the remedy; they say that if a weasel's eyes are pierced out, sight returns to it.
Weasel ash, if given to chickens and doves, is said to keep them safe from weasels. Further, if weasel's brain is added to rennet, they deny that cheeses are spoiled by age or touched by mice.
Avicenna, in the second canon: from unripe fig with an herb a plaster is made for a weasel bite.

Avicenna, in the same book: a weasel's bite causes swift pain, against which a plaster is made with onions and other things, and eating both together with pure wine and vetch flour. The smell of rue, moreover, drives the weasel away.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the weasel is a cunning little creature; it carefully nurses its young and moves them often from place to place, lest they be found. It dwells in crags and caverns and sleeps a very long time. When it wants to fight a serpent, it arms itself with wild rue; hence it is said to be skilled beyond all the physicians' art, so that, if it finds its own young dead, it revives them by means of some naturally known herb. Of this creature Pope Clement says that it conceives through the mouth and gives birth through the ear. In the island of Proselena weasels do not cross over, and if they are brought there they die. In Boeotia too, which is called Lebadia, brought-in ones flee at once. There are two kinds of these, of which the larger is called the 'ictis'; it is white on the belly, red on the back. The weasel, as said, pursues serpents, to the point that it kills the basilisk itself, but dies together with it once killed; entering the basilisk's burrow, indeed, the basilisk flees, but is killed as the weasel pursues. Thus, though small in body, by great cunning and spirit it conquers even large animals through the agility of its body. It is also a skilled hunter of mice, that is, of rats exceeding its own body in size, and is a most ready avenger of wrongs, both cleverly and harmfully.

Alexander Neckam: the weasel, when harmed by the venom of certain animals, hastens to help itself by the power of wholesome herbs. It has, moreover, such delight in wholesome herbs that it is thought to revive its young; furthermore it is a foolish thing that is said by the unskilled, that the weasel conceives through the mouth and gives birth through the ear.
Constantine the African: a weasel's bite brings very great pain to sufferers, and the color of that wound is livid.
Aesculapius: weasel ash and its blood heal elephantiasis sufferers.

Haly Abbas: the flesh of the 'ebenars,' that is the weasel, if pressed with strong vinegar, benefits epilepsy; its belly too, if drawn out, salted, and dried in the shade, and drunk boiled with wine, benefits epilepsy and venomous bites, and resists the worst poisons; but if it is burnt in a bronze pot, its ash heals gout sufferers. Its dry brain, if drunk, helps epilepsy. Its blood, made into a plaster over scrofulous swellings, dissolves them, and is also reported to benefit arthritic conditions.

Pliny: the gall of the wild weasel is said to be effective against asps, but otherwise a poison. The one, however, that wanders in houses, aged in salt, is given, a denarius's weight of it, to those struck, in three cups of wine. Against poisons too the common weasel, aged, is effective, drunk in two drachms. Likewise weasel ash heals cataracts of the eyes. Its brain, cooked, ground, and applied to the forehead, calms watering eyes, whether by itself or with pollen or with frankincense; thus it also benefits sun-damaged skin.

Pliny, book 30, in the same: weasel ash with wax heals pains of the shoulders. It also heals pains of the liver, the wild weasel taken as food, or its liver. Weasel blood benefits gout, applied with plantain. Likewise ash of a live one, burnt, if applied with vinegar and rose oil by a feather, or mixed with cider and rose oil with dog's gall, so that it is not touched by hand but applied by feather. Aged weasel brain, drunk, benefits epileptic seizures, and its liver too. Its testicles too, or its stomach, aged, with coriander. Further, weasel ash drunk in water benefits the delirious. It also heals elephantiasis, both weasel ash and its blood.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the rat and the shrew-mouse are [separate] species. And yet the name 'sorex' is commonly applied in vulgar speech to the ordinary mouse, and conversely, in the books of physicians, the rat is called by the proper name 'mus.' Whence physicians too use rat dung for alopecia, though this creature, namely the rat, is said to carry venom in its tail. There are, moreover, two kinds of rat, namely the land kind and the river kind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the rat is a kind of mouse, much larger than the rest. These are so harmful when inflamed with lust that, if their urine touches any bare part of a man, it makes his flesh rot down to the bone, nor does the wound ever close into a scar.
Isidore: 'sorex' is a Latin word, as has been said, because this kind of creature gnaws and cuts in the manner of a saw [serra].
Belbetus, in the passage above: if you fumigate a house with a mule's left hoof, no shrew-mouse will remain in it.
Pliny: on the shrew-mouse. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Dioscorides: shrew-mouse dung, ground with vinegar, cures alopecia; pounded with rosemary and drunk, it expels stones.

Isidore: the mole [talpa] is so named because it is condemned to perpetual blindness in darkness: for it is without eyes, always digs the earth and casts up soil, and eats roots beneath the crops; the Greeks call it 'aspalax.'
Radulfus of Flaix: the mole is a blind animal, which they say is created from earth together with rain.

Aristotle: certain animals have dwellings, like the mole and mice, the ant, and birds. All animals that generate their like have eyes except the mole, which is deprived of eyes, as it appears, for it does not see at all. But if one cuts the skin over the places of the eyes and examines it, one will find the places of the eyes and their blackness according to the arrangement of eyes. Wherefore this deprivation of light would not have occurred to it, except at the beginning of birth, because of the closing over of skin upon the eyes. And so the mole kind has no sight, because it has no visible eye. In a place of Boeotia called Orchomenus, moles are found, and in Leucadia they are not found at all, although the places are close to each other. And if one carries a mole to that region, it will not dig the earth nor live.

Pliny, book 8: moles brought into Leucadia of Boeotia flee that very soil, though nearby, in Orchomenus, they burrow through whole fields. Of whose skins we have seen bedroom coverlets made, so that not even religious scruple keeps delights away from portents.
The mole is an animal that, though buried in earth, so dense and, as it were, deaf an element by nature, nevertheless hears more clearly than man, although every sound tends upward.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: among four-footed creatures, moles have no sight, yet the likeness of eyes is present if one pulls away the stretched-over membrane.
Many kill moles, which harm trees, with olive-lees.

Palladius, in the passage above: the Greeks hunt moles in this way: they order a nut to be bored through, or some fruit of similar solidity, and chaff and cedar resin with sulfur to be sufficiently enclosed within it. Then all the small entrances and the rest of the moles' breathing-holes are carefully filled in, and one hole, the largest, is left open. At its entrance the nut, lit inside, is placed, so that it can draw breath from one side and spread smoke from that side. And so, the tunnels filled with smoke, the moles either flee at once or are killed.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: the mole is nourished by the roots of herbs and is sustained by them through the winter. And when it comes to the light of the sun and the open air, then it dies. When, moreover, it is dug out, if it is dug toward against the direction of the wind, it senses the one digging and hides itself in the earth.
Gloss: the mole, namely a blind animal born from the earth.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the mole is a small animal, black and blind, born of earth, soaked and muddy but corrupted; its pelt is of many hairs and very soft, but has a most foul color. It dwells in the earth, lives on a diet of worms, and in hunger even eats earth. Sometimes, indeed, it comes out because the earth is parched with drought, but because it is blind it cannot find its way back to the place it left, whence it often happens that it is caught unawares and killed. Though it is blind, however, it has, in the very place of the eyes, a certain blackness, and in the middle of it a pupil and the color of eyes arranged as they should be, but covered by skin. In which the providence of the Creator is to be considered, who gave to this little creature, dwelling in darkness and in the hiding-places of the earth, eyes fully formed yet deprived of light, so that it might both satisfy utility or necessity and yet not entirely deny it the beauty proper to its nature. Though buried in earth, so dense and, as it were, deaf an element, it nevertheless hears more clearly than any animal, which is indeed all the more remarkable in this, since every sound tends upward.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: mole, burnt to powder and sprinkled with egg-white on the face, is a remedy against leprosy. Its blood, if smeared on a head stripped of hair, forces the hair to return, as Avicenna says. Mole dung, too, is of great help for treating alopecia.
Haly Abbas: large shrews, that is, moles, if split open and applied to a scorpion's sting, heal it.

Pliny: moles, condemned to perpetual blindness and buried in darkness, resemble things already entombed. Yet they judge no animal more capable of a sense of duty, if indeed anything credible is found at all, except that they are hostile to shrew-mouse bites, since both are creatures buried in the earth.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is also said that the ash of a burnt mole is effective against fistula, namely to consume its putrefaction. Thus far we have spoken of beasts of burden and wild beasts. Now it remains to speak of the third kind of land animals, namely reptiles.

Petrus Comestor: reptiles, together with the beasts, as said above, serve man for exercise, just as beasts of burden serve for his help. There are, moreover, three kinds of reptiles, namely the crawling kind, like snakes, which move themselves by means of their ribs; the creeping kind, like the lizard or the toad, which creep on feet; and the trailing kind, like worms, which drag themselves by the mouth.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: among animals that lay eggs and generate worms, the female is larger, as in lizards and frogs, serpents and spiders. Worms that are generated from animals feed at first, then afterward take no food, but remain motionless, like those called 'apideni,' which are of golden color. Scaled animals, like small lizards and serpents, eat herbs and flesh indifferently. Creatures of this kind live and remain in the crevices of stones and walls and in narrow places. Further, the tails of serpents and lizards grow back after they have been cut off.

Andromachus of Crete, in the book on theriac: nature has contrived to enlarge the jaws and widen the mouth of rapacious, venom-bearing reptiles, so that seizing prey might be easier and more suited to them. Whence the enlargement of the jaws and their widening corresponds to the vehemence of their power and their boldness.

Al-Kindi, in the book on poisons: reptiles are drawn together by a preparation of plantain and 'zedim,' and are restored by it. Further, if a fasting man's spittle is mixed with powder of birthwort, the reptile that tastes of it dies.

Isidore: the serpent [serpens] is so called because it creeps [serpit] by hidden approaches, not with open steps, but crawls by the tiniest efforts of its scales. Those creatures, however, that use four feet, like lizards and the stellio, are named not serpents but reptiles. Serpents, however, are also reptiles, since they crawl on belly and breast. Of these there are as many venoms as kinds, as many destructions as species, as many pains as colors.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: serpents hide and lie concealed in the earth. They are, moreover, midway between land-dwelling blooded animals and water-dwelling ones, for more of them remain on land, and few in water. There are indeed various kinds of serpents in the sea, and they do not stay in the depths, but near the shore. What happens to swallow chicks happens to serpents too, namely that if one pierces their eye and blinds them, their sight will return again. The tails of serpents too, as has been said, grow back after being cut off.

Pliny: for certain animals in winter, food is provided in store; for others, sleep serves in place of food. Only the viper among serpents is said to hide itself in the earth; the rest, however, endure in the hollows of trees or rocks, or in caves, and elsewhere endure an annual fast, with only the cold removed. But all of them, at the time of their retreat, sleep drained of venom.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: the hiss of serpents is prolonged, but signs of feeling are found even in serpents, the most savage kind of animal.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: serpents lie hidden in winter in rocks or hollow trees and endure without food. They come forth in springtime. By nature they are hot; whence, once chilled, they harm little or not at all. And so they do less harm by night than by day, since they grow cold with the night dew. In winter's cold they coil into knots, but in summer they uncoil.
Ambrose: the lion's mane is shaken out along its curling neck, just as the serpent, its breast raised, lifts its head.

Aristotle: the intestines and inner parts of serpents are similar to those of the egg-laying four-footed animals, especially the small lizard. They do not, however, have testicles. They have two wombs, divided into two, each part proceeding upward on either side of the spine. Large serpents have hard scales, stronger than others, since their nature is like the nature of bone. This kind has no upper eyelid and does not close its eyes, because its skin is harder than the skin of birds. Nor does it need sharp sight, since its dwelling is among stones and in holes and crevices. This animal's head is divided into two, namely the upper part of the head and the lower jaw. The serpent has no neck, but something else corresponding to a neck, since that member is not marked off by known extremities. The teeth of serpents are sharp, various, joined together like a saw. Their tongues are fine, long, black, forked, that is, having two points. They do not have a distinct neck. Footless animals, like serpents, resemble lizards of long body. But some of these have lungs, since they breathe, while some do not, but have gills instead of lungs. None of these kinds has a bladder either, except the tortoise, since their moisture is small as in birds, and passes into scales. All such creatures have a single stomach, like animals having teeth in both jaws. They also have small inner organs, like those lacking a bladder. The inner organs of serpents are narrow and long, according to the formation of their body, and are not similar to the inner organs of other animals. No kind of serpent has feet, just as no kind of fish does. No kind of serpent has testicles, but has passages like the passages of fish. Their windpipe is very long, and likewise their gullet. The end of the windpipe is behind the mouth. The stomach is narrow, like a wide intestine. After the stomach they have a fine intestine reaching to the exit of waste matter; near the neck they have a small, long heart, similar in appearance to a kidney. After the heart is the lung, in which are fine, sinewy parts, coiled, hanging far from the heart. After the lung is the liver, long and extended. The spleen, however, is small and round, like the spleen of a small lizard; they have gall similar to the gall of fish, and it lies above the liver in large ones, above the intestine in small ones. They have many ribs, equal in number to the days of the month, namely thirty. They have a part corresponding to the breast, but have no teats, only passages near the mouth for breathing, and those passages are not clearly divided. They have very long tongues and extend them greatly, so that they draw them out of the mouth. In these they have two fine branches at their tips, like hairs, on account of the insatiability of their nature. And in them there is a twofold taste of moisture, since the sense of taste in them is twofold. They also have passages by which waste matter exits, like other animals, but they have no passage for the exit of urine, since they have no bladder.

Pliny, book 11: among serpents, dogs, and fish the teeth meet like a comb's teeth, so as not to be worn down by opposing contact; the serpent's tongue, however, is very fine and three-forked, of a dark, that is black, color.

Aristotle: all the remaining kinds of serpents lay eggs. The viper, however, generates live young. And in the wombs of serpents there is a difference both from the wombs of other animals and among themselves. The womb of serpents begins from the lower part and proceeds upward on either side of the spine; each part is like a passage proceeding toward the part that gives birth. And in it the eggs are placed in a row. And when a serpent lays eggs, it does not lay them all together continuously. The wombs of serpents, moreover, lie within, over the belly, and also outside; the wombs of live-bearing animals, however, are near the vertebrae. Further, animals of great lightness are, as it were, joined to one another when the time of mating comes round. And so serpents become entwined, coiled together, so that one watching would think it a single body having two heads. They lack testicles, however, because of the length of their body. And animals that lack testicles do so not for the better, but only from the necessity of swift mating, as is the nature of serpents. Serpents are wound around each other in mating, and have no member, since they have no legs, but have passages like the passages of fish; because of the length of their body, however, they are fitted to mating only with difficulty, and their separation is slower than the separation of fish. Several kinds of serpents lay complete eggs. Serpents indeed first form perfect eggs within, and afterward generate live young from the eggs outside. And that animal lays eggs outside not because of heat, but because of cold. Further, the serpent kind has many eggs, nor is monstrosity found among them except rarely, because of the shape of the womb, since their eggs are arranged in a row in the womb because of its length; nevertheless a serpent having two heads has already been observed.
