Pliny: serpents give birth, and also incubate covered eggs in the earth and hatch their brood the following year. They mate in an embrace, so entwined together that a single two-headed creature might be thought to exist. We have it from many that a snake is born from the marrow of a man's spine. Further, I judge fabulous what Democritus relates, naming certain birds from whose mingled blood a serpent is born, which, if one eats it, will understand the speech of birds.

Isidore, on the serpent: from the marrow of a dead man, which is in the spine, a serpent is created, according to Pythagoras and Ovid, so that just as death comes to man through the serpent, so too a serpent is born from man's death.

Aristotle: the serpent lives off the earth, and scaled animals, like small lizards and serpents, eat herbs and flesh indifferently, and serpents desire to eat indifferently, and drink little water. Serpents, however, greatly love wine, and are therefore hunted by means of it, when they are made drunk on it. They also suck the moisture of the animal to which they attach themselves, and the remainder exits by expulsion. And often they suck the moisture and leave the remainder. They can, however, live long without food. And this is known from those serpents that are sold by apothecaries.

Pliny, in the passage above: serpents eat dragons' eggs by a certain notable art: for they either swallow them whole, if their throat can already take them, which they then break inside themselves once coiled around them, and thus shake out the shell fragments; or, if the offspring is still too tender, having caught the egg in a coil, they compress it so gently and yet so forcefully that they cut off, as if with iron, the part that has been enclosed, and swallow the rest, held in their coil. In similar fashion, too, having swallowed birds whole, they force up feathers and bones again by contraction. And when the chance comes they especially seek out and drink wine, though otherwise they need little to drink. The same creatures, however, can be kept enclosed on the smallest amount of food, or none at all. Finally, no venomous creature dies of thirst or hunger, since it has no force of heat, blood, or sweat, which increase natural appetite through salt. Among this kind, those are the more deadly which have eaten their own kind before doing harm.
Ambrose: the serpent, by feeding on fennel, drives away blindness; it dies, however, if it tastes the spittle of a fasting man.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the serpent eats dogs and herbs indifferently, but drinks little and has no outlet for urine; instead the excess of what it drinks is consumed by its natural heat, which is very great in them.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the serpent moves its tongue with such speed that, though it is single, it seems to be triple. The bodies of serpents are very moist. Wherever they go, they mark the path with moisture. And although they lack feet, they crawl by their ribs and by efforts of their scales, which they have arranged evenly from the top of the throat down to the bottom of the belly. For they lean on their scales as if on claws, and on their ribs as if on legs; whence, in whatever part of the body, from belly to head, a blow strikes and bruises it, it is rendered weak and unable to move. For wherever that blow falls, it disables the spine through which the feet of the ribs and the body's motion were carried out. Serpents, however, live a long time, because, having shed their old coat, they lay aside old age and return to youth. And their coats are called 'sloughs,' since by them they strip themselves.

Aristotle: when the serpent moves, by the flexing it makes, it raises one part of its body from the ground and places another upon that ground. There is, moreover, a simple kind of serpent dwelling in caves, naturally having blood, and of scaled body, walking by crawling on its belly; serpents can move the head backward while the body remains still, and because their vertebrae are formed like rings and of cartilage, they are therefore good at bending. And this was given to serpents for the better, so that they might see their long, narrow body from behind, since they have no feet nor any instrument for taking food and for guarding what is behind them, nor would they be helped by raising the head, unless they could see behind them: this, then, was given to them for the guarding of their body, since it is feeble.
Pliny: [on] the young of serpents [and] the chicks of swallows. Serpents [and] lizards. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the serpent lives a long time, because in old age it consumes its own flesh by fasting. In Ireland no serpent can live, nor any other venomous creature. Indeed, wherever earth brought from Ireland is thrown upon a venomous animal, it dies at once.

Isidore: the serpent is cunning, for among the natural good qualities that we see to be common to us and to unreasoning animals, the serpent excels in a certain liveliness of sense. Whence it is also read that the serpent was wiser than all the animals of the earth. Pliny says it is believed that if a serpent's head escapes even with two fingers of it, it nonetheless lives, whence it exposes its whole body in place of its head.
Pliny, book 7, in the same: serpents also lay aside their annual old age by tasting fennel.
Avicenna, in the second canon: serpents, coming out of their dens after winter, rub their eyes on fennel, so that they may be given light.

Physiologus: when the serpent grows old, its eyes grow dim. And if it wishes to become new again, it abstains from food for forty days and nights, until its skin loosens on it. Then it seeks a narrow crevice in a rock and there squeezes itself violently and grinds its body, and thus lays aside old age and becomes new. When, however, it comes to a spring to drink, it does not bring its venom with it, but leaves it in its lair, and thus drinks the water without hindrance. If it sees a man naked, it fears him; if clothed, it attacks him.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the serpent, hiding its head, exposes its whole body to the striker. For if it saves its head, it lives nonetheless, though it loses its body. It lives, as has been said, a long time, because, when it grows old, it consumes its own flesh by fasting, until, its skin loosened by leanness, passing through a crevice in a rock, it lays aside its old skin and puts on youth. It sheds its skin, however, starting from the head.

Alexander Neckam: the serpent, as has been said, drives away threatened blindness by feeding on fennel. And so, when it senses its eyes clouding over, it seeks out the known remedy, and its purpose is not thwarted.

Isidore: of serpents there are as many venoms as there are kinds. As many destructions as species, as many pains as colors are found. All serpents, however, are cold by their nature, and do not strike except when they grow warm. For when they are cold they touch nothing, whence their venoms do more harm by day than by night. For they grow sluggish in the cold of night, and rightly so, since they are chilled by the night dew. For these cold pests, cold by nature, draw the body's vapor into themselves. Whence in winter they grow numb in knots, and in summer they uncoil. Hence it is that whoever is struck by a serpent's venom first goes numb, and afterward, once that poison has grown warm within him, it kills the man at once.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: Platearius, however, in his treatise on theriac, says that a certain venom is cold and a certain other is hot, though all is dry; Avicenna too holds the contrary view.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: some have judged that the venom of serpents, even of vipers, is cold, but this is an error. For what happens from cold to one bitten by them is due to the deadening of innate heat through the contrariety of the venom. For it is the innate heat that warms the body by its diffusion and inflammation. But when there is no innate heat, even if the heart is inflamed by a slight fire, the extremities need not, on that account, be warmed.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: although venom is death to man, it is nevertheless life to the serpent. Whence, about to enter water, the serpent lays its venom aside, and takes it up again on leaving. But if by some mischance it cannot find its venom again after losing it, it dies of grief, striking its head repeatedly on the ground. Pliny says that venom is nothing other than the gall of serpents. From there it reaches the veins beneath the spine, and afterward reaches the mouth, or the tail, as in scorpions.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the serpent's venom, as has been said, which is life to the serpent, is death to man.

Isidore: it is called 'serpent's venom' [virus serpentum] because it travels through the veins. For once its infection is poured in, it spreads through the veins, aided by the body's own vitality, and drives out the soul. Whence venom cannot harm unless it touches a man's blood. Lucan: the harm of serpents is a plague mixed with blood. All venom, moreover, is cold, and therefore the soul, which is fiery, flees venom. It is said, moreover, that a serpent does not dare touch a naked man.

Aristotle: the bite of serpents varies by region. For there is a dragon in the land of Ethiopia from which the viper is generated, whence the 'entycon' is obtained, and against it there is no remedy; and in a place called Cilicia there is a small serpent, from whose bite men are healed by a stone found in the tombs of ancient kings. For they dip the stone in wine and give that wine to drink: finally, among all venomous animals, the bite is especially bad when they have eaten one another, as the dragon eats the scorpion.
Pliny: [on] serpents. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny, book 13, in the same: Syria has trees peculiar to it, of the walnut kind, the well-known pistachio, and cotoneaster, said to benefit against serpent bites both taken as food and as drink. In Asia and Greece there are shrubs called 'epitactis,' which others call 'embolina,' with small leaves that, drunk, benefit against poisons, just as hedgehog-plants do against serpents.

Pliny, book 16, in the same: ash leaves too, their juice pressed out for drinking, and applied, are helpful against serpents. Oleander is poison to draft animals, goats, and sheep, but the same is a remedy for man against serpent venoms.

Constantine the African: the venom of serpents is hot, and those who are bitten suffer very great pain in that spot. Afterward, however, the pain spreads through the whole body. At the site of the bite two separate holes are seen, which are the marks of their teeth; after this, a moisture like that of vegetables flows from them, then a smoky moisture. And around the site there is a hot, painful swelling, which has redness and lividness and blisters, and the color of the body changes as if burnt by fire. They suffer disgust and vomiting of bile, and weakness and trembling and cold sweat. The flesh is consumed and eaten away from limb to limb, and blood too flows from the gums and is stanched with difficulty.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: one killed by venom first grows stiff, and afterward, once the venom has grown warm, kills the man through the dryness of thirst. The earth, as Pliny says, does not further receive a serpent that has struck a man, but, soon to die itself, pays the penalty a little while after. And so a serpent cannot kill more than one victim, except the salamander alone.

Priscian of Lydia, to Chosroes: reptiles are not harmful to all animals. For both pigs and stags eat serpents, and some are devoured harmlessly by others. Many other things too can be found, wholesome to some, harmful to others, having such a mutual relation of kinship or avoidance to one another. Scythian venom is a compound of viper and human matter, with which they dip arrows to speed the deadly wound. The bites of dogs and wolves, however, when rabid, are harmful from a different cause.

Avicenna, in the second canon: for a serpent's sting, bran applied like a plaster helps. Garlic drunk with wine also benefits. Finally, galbanum is a theriac against the venoms of serpents. Likewise the plant called chaste-tree: its seed, drunk, benefits serpent bites.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: in the bites of venomous creatures, the closing of the wound is forbidden until the hour the patient is cured of the venom's malice. Among the things applied to venomous stings are petroleum with cooked butter, or castoreum with oil. Also the juice of leek untouched by water, and river calamint, draw out venom excellently, and so does sulfur with urine. Likewise a live cock or hen, split open while still alive, applied as a plaster to the sting or bite, and changed and reapplied continually.

div.head: DE MULTIPLICI VARIETATE SERPENTIUM AC NOCUMENTIS IPSORUM

cit.quote: Aristotle: among serpents, as among fish, some have smooth skin, some scaled, some rough, and some spiny. Most remain on land and few in the water. In the sea too there are serpents similar to land serpents, except for their heads, since their head is very hard and rough in them.

Priscian of Lydia, in the passage above: some serpents inflict venom by biting, some by stinging, or even by a certain hidden power, or by breath, or by voice, or by their very gaze, just as happens with certain other animals and with men who cast spells. Some too are venomous by nature, some by contagion, and some indeed cause sudden death, some cause suffering, and some indeed danger. It should also be known that places, seasons, and food produce a differing variety of bites, for in winter, when they enter their burrows, or immediately after entering a burrow, they grow weak, and their bites are nearly harmless. In mountainous and rough places, however, dry and hotter as they are, all are more biting, since they are stronger there. In another region, however, they are moist and feeble. Through this too, around mating time, they are most fierce. But from whatever food it takes, one can judge a serpent's force and strength. Some reptiles, moreover, harm and kill not only by biting but even by their breath, through fields and wood or stones. Such too is the power of certain biting creatures, that if they bite the root of a tree, the whole tree sheds its leaves. They say a small serpent called the 'ieronos' appears rarely around Thessaly, and, using only its voice as it were, kills. While it appears, vipers and serpents and all other creatures flee.

Pliny, in the passage above: the kinds of serpents are innumerable; some have scales, others markings, but all have a deadly poison. Nor can one say for certain whether nature has more generously produced evils, or remedies.

Avicenna, in the passage above: some serpents are of vehement sharpness, not delaying, that is, to kill by their very disposition beyond three hours. Nor are their bites treated, that is, guarded against or anticipated, since they are 'mute,' that is, biting secretly in silence. Nor is anything effective against their bite except immediate excision of the limb, or cauterization, penetrating and burning away the outer parts of the limb, consuming the venom and constricting the passages, and sometimes in their treatment vomiting afterward, brought on by a surfeit of salted fish, is of benefit, and after this other treatments follow. Of this kind are the basilisk, the 'hyrundo,' the dry asp, the serpent called the 'spitter,' and the horned serpent. There is, however, no cure at all for the basilisk's bite. There is also another kind, that of vipers, whose species again are various. Among these are the 'alesilati' vipers, and among them are the oak-vipers and the thirst-causing vipers, and the rest that we shall speak of. There occurs, moreover, a diversity among serpents not of species but according to variation within one species, for example, on account of sex. For males have fewer teeth but more venom, and sharper; although some say that females are worse because of the closeness of their teeth. Likewise on account of age, since old ones are worse than young. Likewise on account of body, since large ones are worse than small or short ones, though their species is one; or on account of place, since those that dwell in mountains and waterless places are worse than those on the shore or in places of abundant water. Likewise on account of their condition of repletion and emptiness. For hungry ones have worse venom. Likewise on account of their passions of temper, since angry and bold ones are worse. Likewise on account of season, since their venom is worse in summer.

Physiologus: serpents are said to exist in Ethiopia that have wings. There are also certain serpents that eat white pepper, having precious stones in their heads, which, fighting each other every year, largely destroy one another. Certain serpents too have horns on their foreheads like rams, with which, by butting, they strike men.

Aristotle: in the land of Ethiopia, as has been said, there are serpents having wings. And indeed a serpent having two heads has already been observed. Nevertheless monstrosity is not found among serpents except rarely, because of the shape of the womb, since their eggs are arranged in a row in the womb because of its length.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: Aristotle, speaking of the serpents of the East that have two heads, says the cause of this monstrosity lies in the seed, so that if two seeds are contained in one womb with no partition dividing them, both heads of the serpent take food and pass it into one body. Both, too, crawl toward adversaries.

Solinus: Indian serpents are of such enormous size that they swallow whole stags and other animals of comparable bulk, and even penetrate the Indian Ocean, however vast it is, and seek out islands separated from the mainland by a great distance, for the sake of plundering them.

Pliny, in the passage above: Megasthenes too writes that in India serpents grow to such size that they swallow whole stags and bulls. Metrodorus, however, writes that around the river Rhyndacus in Pontus, they swallow, flying above and swiftly snatching, birds however high and fast they fly. It is a well-known fact that, in the Punic Wars, near the river Bagrada, a serpent of a hundred and twenty feet in length was overcome by Regulus, as if it were a town under siege, with ballistae and siege engines. Facing serpents are drawn out by song and forced into a stupor.

Orosius, book 4: Regulus, having drawn the lot of the Carthaginian war, marching with his army, pitched camp not far from the river Bagrada. There, when a serpent of astonishing size devoured many of the soldiers who came down to the river out of need for water, Regulus set out with his army to conquer the beast; but when he saw that javelins made no progress on its back, and every weapon's force was in vain, gliding off, as it were, along an oblique shield-wall through the terrifying lattice of its scales, and, remarkably, without wounding its body, were themselves repelled by that very body, and moreover that a great number of soldiers were crushed by its bite and its combined assault, and that a pestilential breath too was exhaled from it, he ordered ballistae to be brought up, by which a millstone-sized rock, hurled against its spine, broke the framework of its whole body. For the serpent, built of ribs and scales, wherever a blow fell on any part of its body, would have its spine disabled, through which the feet of the ribs and the motion of the body were carried out. Whence even this serpent, which for so long had resisted so many javelins unharmed, at the blow of a single stone yielded, weakened, and, soon surrounded by weapons, was easily overwhelmed. Its hide, however, was brought to Rome, and, said to have measured a hundred and twenty feet, was for some while a wonder to all.

div.head: DE HIS QUE CONTRARIA VEL NOXIA SUNT SERPENTIBUS

cit.quote: Aristotle: certain animals are hostile to serpents, as pigs, which eat serpents. There is also an animal called the 'galy,' which fights with the serpent and eats rue, since it is contrary to the serpent, even its scent. Further, the 'galy,' a certain bird, for the most part fights with serpents that eat mice. There is also a certain animal in Egypt which, when it sees a certain serpent, does not fight it until it calls for helpers. And because it fears the serpent's bite, it enters water and then sand. Then it fights the serpent. Moreover, human saliva is contrary to venomous animals.
Pliny, book 8: serpents are driven off by the odor of certain men called the Psylli.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: the scent of stag's horn too drives away serpents. Further, the spider suspends itself by a thread over the serpent's head, in the shade of a spreading tree, and seizes its brain in its bite with such force that the serpent, hissing repeatedly, whirling in dizziness, cannot break free even from the hanging thread, nor flee, and there is no end but death.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: locusts too kill serpents, whenever they wish, by seizing them one at a time by the throat with their jaws. Likewise the elephant's breath, that is its exhalation, draws serpents out, but burns stags. To pigs, serpents are food, which to others are poison. Wasps too feed eagerly on serpents, from which food they make their stings deadly.

Pliny, book 12, in the same: among the cedar-growing peoples there is a herb of remarkable scent, hostile to serpents, at whose bite death is immediate. If pure Syrian galbanum is burnt, serpents are driven off by its smoke.

Likewise, book 18: the ash tree has such power against serpents that a serpent will not touch even its morning or evening shadow, however long it stretches, but flees far from it. We report from experience that if one encloses a serpent within a ring of its leaves, along with fire, the serpent will flee into the fire sooner than into the ash. A remarkable kindness of nature: before the swallows appear, the ash flowers, and does not shed its leaves before they are gone. Finally, ash leaves, their juice pressed for drinking and applied to the womb, are effective against serpents.
Isidore: the serpent does not dare touch a naked man.
Isidore, book 16, in the same: burning jet stone drives away serpents.
Isidore, book 17, in the same: whoever soaks his hands in radish seed can handle serpents unharmed.

Ambrose: bramble leaves thrown over a serpent kill it. Likewise, if a serpent tastes the spittle of a fasting man, it dies; and so, if a fasting man kills an earthly serpent with his spittle, he rightly kills a spiritual one too by fasting.

Rhazes: serpents are driven away if a house is fumigated with stag's horn, or goat's hooves, or galbanum, or pitch, or bdellium, or the smoke of burnt pomegranates, or human hair, or if it is sprinkled with water in which ammoniac salt has been dissolved. If this same water is poured into their holes too, they flee.
Avicenna, second canon: fumigation made from the plant called chaste-tree, and its leaves too, drive away venomous creatures.

[on driving away] serpents by fumigations are stag's horns and lily root, pyrethrum, sulfur; mustard too kills serpents, and when placed on their paths, they flee from it. Likewise a fasting man's spittle, thrown into its mouth, kills a serpent, and especially when he holds ammoniac salt in his mouth.

Palladius, Agriculture, book 1: serpents are driven off by almost any pungency, and the smoke of a heavy-smelling fire disturbs harmful spirits: let us burn galbanum or stag's horns, lily roots, goat's hooves; by this means harmful monsters are kept away.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the serpent flees a naked man, and also a pleasant scent, by which it is often killed. In Ireland no serpent can live, nor anything venomous. Indeed, wherever earth brought from Ireland is thrown upon a venomous animal, it dies at once. In Syria snakes do no harm. On the mountain of Lacedaemon, visitors are not harmed by scorpions, but they kill the native inhabitants.

Avicenna, in the second canon: in the serpent's flesh there is strong drying, and in its skin too a vehement one, but the heating in its flesh is not vehement. The female's flesh is better, and her skin better than the male's skin: a property of its flesh is that it makes waste matter penetrate to the skin. And so eating it causes lice and corrupts. Whence it happened to a certain man, from eating it, that a great swelling arose on his neck. When it appeared and burst, his flesh had entirely turned to lice. Likewise its flesh, when used regularly, prolongs life, strengthens vigor, and preserves the senses and youth. It benefits leprosy greatly, and alopecia. Its flesh and broth, after the extremities are discarded, prevent the growth of scrofulous swellings, and likewise its skin; these also benefit pains of the nerves. Likewise its broth and flesh strengthen the sight. Its skin, cooked in wine and dripped into the ear, calms its pain. With vinegar too, in which the skin itself is boiled, the mouth is rinsed for toothache.
Dioscorides: a snake's [skin], boiled in wine and dripped into the mouth, calms its pain and heals toothache. It is also a help to the eyes, especially the sloughed skin of a viper.
Haly Abbas: serpent's [skin], if dried and ground, made into a collyrium, sharpens the sight. Likewise, if boiled with vinegar, it relieves toothache.

Isidore, book 12: 'anguis' is a name applied to every kind of serpent that can be coiled and twisted. Indeed it is so named because it is 'angulosus' [full of bends] and never straight. All snakes have dull sight, and rarely look straight ahead, nor without reason, since they have eyes not in the forehead but at the temples, so that they hear more quickly than they see.

Pliny: snakes shed their old age. In Syria, around the banks of the Euphrates, sleeping snakes do not, for the most part, touch the Syrians, or even if they bite one who is shod, that person feels no harm; but to men of any other people they are hostile, and kill them eagerly and with torment. For this reason the Syrians never kill them. The snake, in its wintry state, its body sheathed in a membrane, sheds that obstruction with the juice of fennel, and comes forth more brightly in spring; it sheds the skin first from the head, and no faster than in one day and night, turning it inside out, so that what was inside becomes outside. Likewise, its sight dimmed from its winter hiding-place, rubbing itself on the fennel plant, it anoints and restores its eyes; but if its scales have grown numb, it scrapes itself on juniper thorns.

Pliny: we have it from many that a snake is born from the marrow of a man's spine. For very many kinds, even of four-footed creatures, arise from a hidden and obscure origin: as the salamander, which never arises except from heavy rains, and fails in fair weather. This creature, born from what is not itself born, produces nothing in turn, nor is there in it a male or female kind, just as there is not in eels, none of which generate either an animal or an egg from themselves. Neither is there such a kind in oysters and other creatures that cling to shallows or rocks.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: behold, now that serpents in general have been discussed, it remains to speak of individual serpents and kinds of serpents, in our manner, according to alphabetical order.

Avicenna, in the passage above: the 'afferatus' and 'altariatus,' that is, the leaping and flying serpents, are small, short, tiny, which sometimes hide in trees lying in wait, so as to hurl themselves at passersby: I have seen this kind. They are very cunning and inclined to redness; from their bite, it is said, comes violent pain that passes through the whole body, from which death too may follow. Their treatment is the common treatment, that is, the treatment for vipers. The 'affudius' and the 'sabrin,' as the wise have said, are two serpents having sandy-colored bodies, and on their heads white and black spots, and sometimes they are black and red and white. On their heads are incised white scales, and there is a rustling in their movement because of the dryness of the scales of their bellies. And their bite is heavy in its effect, with even teeth; their bite tears open the pores and natural passages, making blood flow from them, so that it even flows from the corners of the eyes. And there follows blood in the spit and a flow of blood from the nostrils and vomiting and pain in the stomach. And it is said that the site becomes an abscess and turns black, and a small watery discharge runs from it, and the bowels loosen, and the breath is constricted, and difficulty of urination follows, and the voice is lost, and the limbs go slack, and a state of oblivion overcomes the body. And spasm follows, and the teeth fall out, and the patient dies. Their treatment, however, is very close to the treatment for vipers.

Isidore: the 'amphisbaena' is so called because it has two heads, one in its proper place, the other running at the tail, from both heads with the body's course circling round. This alone of serpents commits itself to cold; it comes forth before all others. Of which Lucan says: 'and the amphisbaena, heavy, bending toward its twin head'; its eyes shine like lamps.
Pliny: the amphisbaena has a double head, that is, both at the head and at the tail, as if it were too little for venom to be poured from a single mouth.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania, in the passage above: the amphisbaena serpent commits itself to cold; watchful and very anxious over its eggs, it broods with them, for while one part of it sleeps, the other then keeps watch. And when it moves along a path, it directs two heads, now the front one leading, now the rear one following in turn. There is another kind that moves on its heel, in its mating, and on its own tail.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of such monstrous serpents, namely those having two heads, mention has already been made above, following Aristotle, in the chapter on monstrous serpents.

Avicenna: the 'armena' is a serpent having properties close to those of the basilisk, for it kills not only by its bite but by its gaze and by the hearing of its hiss. Whatever animal it bites is dissolved, and whatever animal comes near it dies. In size, however, they say it differs from the basilisk: for they have judged it to be from one cubit up to a cubit and a half. And they say that nothing benefits one bitten by it; but if anything does benefit him, it is this, namely poppy seed and castoreum; for this some have already testified.

Isidore: the asp is so called because it kills by its venomous bite: for the Greeks call venom 'as.' Of this there are various kinds and differing effects of harm. It is said that when the asp begins to be tormented by the charmer, who calls it out with certain incantations to draw it from its cave, if it does not wish to come out, it presses one ear to the ground and blocks and covers the other with its tail, and, not hearing those magic words, does not come out to the charmer. Among the kinds of asp are the dipsas, the hypnalis, the haemorrhois, the prester, and the seps.
Physiologus: if the asp bites a man, it consumes him at once, so that he entirely dissolves in the manner of a serpent.

Gloss: the asp is a small serpent; the viper has a longer body, and the asp's venom kills swiftly, the viper's more slowly; whence it is written: it shall suck the head of asps, and the viper's tongue shall slay it.

Andromachus of Crete, in the passage above: the asp's habitation is in dry ground, in places where there is no water. And this is sometimes ash-colored, sometimes yellowish: the asp is a serpent of a sky-blue color, whose teeth are extremely long, so that they show outside the mouth as in a boar. By its bite it injects and spreads venom; whence too it took its name. It is charmed by the power of certain words, so that it does not kill with venom, or, as some say, so that it may be caught at rest, and the gem taken from its forehead, which is naturally born in it. The asp does no harm to Africans or Syrians. Whence they expose to it the children born to them. Those it harms they cast away as if born of adultery. But if it does not harm them, they raise them as their own.

Avicenna: the asp is among the deaf serpents; it is called the dry one because of the vehemence of the dryness of its skin, and in size it is between three and five cubits. Its color is ash-colored and inclined to yellow: its eyes are of vehement brightness, and it kills within two to three hours. Whomever it bites, his color changes and he is stupefied, and his hiccuping multiplies, and his limbs grow cold. His eyelids too close, and he sleeps deeply. For its bite, a plaster of lime with honey and oil is helpful.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the asp has, according to Pliny, a deadly war with the ichneumon, as has already been said above.

Pliny, book 8: it is asserted that the necks of asps swell with no remedy for the blow, except that the parts touched are amputated at once. This animal, so pestilential, has one remarkable feeling, or rather affection: they mate roughly in pairs, and an asp has no life except with its mate. And so, if one is killed, the other pursues the killer with incredible care for vengeance, and, by a certain recognition, attacks that one man alone in however great a crowd of people. It breaks through every obstacle, crosses every distance, and is stopped only by rivers or by his very swift flight; nor can one say whether nature has more generously produced evils or remedies, and so it first gave this creature dulled eyes, and made them see not in front nor face-on, but placed at the temples. And so it is roused more often by hearing than by sight.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: a marvel handed down by Philarchus about the asp is also recorded. For he is the authority that an asp, coming regularly to the table of a certain man in Egypt where it was fed, had repeatedly borne young, of which the host's son was killed by one of them. But the asp, returning to her usual feeding, understood the fault and brought death upon that offspring, and never afterward returned to that place.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: the asp's teeth bend inward toward the mouth, so that food does not fall out, having no other means of holding it; but there are two very long ones in the upper jaw, right and left, pierced with a thin channel, pouring in venom, like scorpions' stings.

Pliny, book 9, in the same: asps kill those they strike by numbness and sleep, the least curable of all serpents. Their venom, if it touches blood or a fresh wound, kills at once; if the wound is old, more slowly; but drunk in any quantity otherwise, it does no harm - its power is rabid only when in the wound. And so, the animals killed by its bite, their flesh is harmless as food. I would hesitate to offer remedies for these, had Varro not reported that asp bites are most effectively healed by drinking the urine of the one struck, taken from himself; the gall of the wild weasel too is effective against asps.

Solinus: of asps there are the dipsas, the hypnalis, the haemorrhois, the ammodytes, the cenchris, the elephantia, the chersydros, the chamaedracontes. There are many and varied kinds, such as the dipsas, the hypnalis, the haemorrhois, and besides these the ammodytes, and there is also the cenchris, the elephantia, the chersydros, the chamaedracontes. Finally, as many as the names, so many are the kinds of death. These monsters hiss and, as they say, have feelings, and do not wander far except in pairs; if one is caught or killed, the survivor grows savage. The females have finer heads and a more swollen belly, and a more harmful venom; the male is evenly rounded, taller, and gentler.

Physiologus: Lucan calls the asp 'sleep-bringing,' since one wounded by it passes into death through sleep. It is said, moreover, to be charmed thus: demons run to serpents with words, and by an inward infection cause the serpents to move at their bidding and show themselves docile without harm.

Isidore: the 'basiliscus' is Greek, interpreted in Latin as 'regulus' [little king], because it is the king of serpents, so much so that those who see it flee, since it kills them by its very smell. For it kills a man even by its gaze, since no bird flying past its gaze passes unharmed, but however far off it is, it is burnt by its mouth and devoured.

Solinus: near Egypt is an inaccessible wilderness that breeds the basilisk, a unique evil upon the earth. For it is given not only to the destruction of man and other living creatures, but also pollutes the very approach to the earth, burning wherever it takes a deadly lair. Finally it withers grasses, kills trees, and even corrupts the very air with its pestilential breath; it moves with the middle of its body, but is upright and tall in its midsection; even serpents dread its hiss, and, when they perceive it, flee wherever they can. Whatever is killed by its bite, no wild beast feeds on, no bird touches. Yet it is overcome by weasels; its power, moreover, is not lacking even in death. Finally, the people of Pergamum bought remnants of a basilisk, so that the famed temple of Apollo's precinct would neither be woven over by spiders nor flown into by birds.

Physiologus, on the basilisk: buildings in which any part of a basilisk's body is kept are indeed entered neither by serpents nor fouled by birds, nor woven over by spiders; it crawls on the middle of its body, but is upright and tall in its midsection.

Pliny: the basilisk has such power that all who see its eyes expire at once. The province of Cyrenaica produces it, of no more than twelve fingers' length. With a white mark on its head, as if a kind of distinguishing diadem, it puts all serpents to flight with its hiss, nor does it move its body in many coils as the rest do, but advances lofty and upright in the middle. It kills shrubs not only by touch but even by its breath. It scorches grasses, splits rocks; against this monster the venom of weasels is deadly - so true is it that nature has made nothing without its counterpart - for they kill it, easily finding its den, by decay alone. And they too die together at the same time from the mutual stench, both finishing off the battle that is nature's own.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: the basilisk's blood, which even by its smell kills other serpents and by sight kills a man, the magicians praise with wondrous acclaim, saying it becomes, when it congeals like pitch, brighter in color than diluted cinnabar. They attribute to it success in petitions to the powerful and even in prayers to the gods, and remedies in illness. Some call it the blood of Saturn.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania, in the passage above: the basilisk kills at once every animal upon which it breathes. And every animal, except the weasel, naturally flees it. For the weasel pursues and conquers it, and infects it with its bite, and thus kills it.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the basilisk is a serpent that kills by sight alone and by the hearing of its voice. Some say it is called 'regulus' because it has a crowned head. Its length is two palms, and its head is very sharp, its eyes red. Its color inclines to black and yellow: it scorches everything it passes over, and nothing grows around its den, and when a bird is placed near its dwelling, it falls dead; no animal fails to be terrified by it, and if one comes close, it is stupefied, so that it cannot move: by its hiss, when it exhales, it kills, and even one on whom its gaze falls from a distance dies. The body of the one it bites dissolves and swells, and venom courses through it, and it dies at once. Everyone dies, moreover, who comes near one killed by it, and rarely does anyone escape who is present near its vicinity. It is possible, however, in certain circumstances, for one to touch it with a rod, according to Pliny, and the one who touches it this way, by means of the rod, dies. Thus a certain soldier touched it with his lance, and both he and his horse died. This serpent multiplies in the land of Arorch and Nubia. A sign of its bite, then, is if one sees a person dead suddenly with no apparent cause, especially in a place where that animal is known to be, and there is absolutely no cure at all.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the basilisk, if it sees a man first, kills him by sight alone, since the rays of its eyes corrupt the man's visible spirit. Once that is corrupted, the other spirits too are corrupted, which descend from the brain and the life of the heart, and thus the man dies. But if it sees the serpent first, the serpent is destroyed instead, as James of Acqui says. Wherever its ash is smeared, spiders cannot weave, nor can any venomous creature come near; it is said that silver, smeared with its ash, is changed to a golden color. More will be said of this below, under the name 'regulus.'

div.head: DE GENERIBUS BASILISCORUM ET REMEDIIS CONTRA ILLOS

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the basilisk sometimes arises from a cock, since a cock, in decrepit old age, produces an egg from itself, from which a basilisk is bred. But for this generation to occur, many things must coincide. For it lays the egg in hot and abundant dung, and there it is incubated in place of a father, and after a long time a chick emerges and grows strong, as duck chicks are wont to do. It has a tail like a snake, but the rest of the body like a cock. Those who claim to have witnessed its creation say that there is no eggshell, but a very tough skin, so strong that it can withstand very heavy blows. Some also hold the opinion that a snake or a toad incubates that egg of the cock, but this is uncertain; we have this, however, in the writings of the ancients, that a certain kind of basilisk is bred from the egg of a decrepit cock.

Aristotle: of basilisks the first is the 'alochrysus,' called the golden one; whatever this sees, it breathes upon and burns. The second is the starred one, also called 'chrysocephalus,' that is, 'golden-headed'; whatever this sees grows faint and is killed. The third is the 'emathitis,' that is, 'blood-colored' like cinnabar, also golden-headed; whatever this sees or strikes wastes away, and only the bones remain. All of these are easily overcome by whoever carries the basil herb with him.

Isidore: the basilisk too is overcome by weasels, which men bring into the caves where it lurks; and so, on seeing it, it flees, and the weasel pursues and kills it. For that Parent of all things has set nothing in place without a remedy.

div.head: DE BEHEMOTH ET BERO ET BOA

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: the 'behemoth' serpent, whatever animal it encircles with its tail, binds it fast until it kills it with bites.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'berus' is, among all serpents, the most wicked and cunning; it calls the sea-eel to the shore with its hiss, and caresses it, and stirs it to mating. The eel, softened in spirit, submits to the coupling, but sometimes to its own destruction, for, caught by its enemies before it can return to the water, it is killed. The 'boa' is a snake in Calabria which, by sucking the milk of cows, grows to immense bulk, so much so that it swallows whole stags and oxen. Of this kind is believed to have been the one that Regulus, leader of the Romans, killed in Africa, a hundred and twenty feet in length, whose skin, stripped off, was brought to Rome as a spectacle. Pliny wrote of this, that when it was being captured, ballistae and various siege engines had to be used, as in the storming of a fortress.

Isidore: the 'boa' is a snake of Italy of immense bulk; it pursues herds of cattle and buffalo, and, with udders flowing with much milk, coils itself around them and, sucking, kills them. Hence, from its destruction of cattle [boves], it took the name 'boa.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: the 'boa,' in order to suck milk from the udders, follows the herd, and whatever it has sucked from, dies afterward.

Solinus: Calabria produces the 'boa,' a snake that, they say, grows to immense size. It first attacks a herd or herds of buffalo and coils itself around udders flowing with milk, and, gorged by continuous sucking, over a long life it is finally so swollen by this deadly satiety that no force can withstand its size. Finally, having laid waste the animals, it forces to devastation the regions it has beset. Indeed, under the divine emperor Claudius, in the Vatican field, a whole infant was found in the belly of a killed boa.

div.head: DE CECULA ET CHELIDRO AC CENCHRI

cit.quote: Isidore: the 'cecula' [little blind one] is so named because it is small and has no eyes. The 'chelydros,' also called 'chersydros,' is a serpent that dwells both on land and in water. For the Greeks call land 'cherson,' water 'hydros'; this creature makes the land smoke as it crawls over it, which Macer describes thus: 'whether foaming venom breathes from its back, or the earth smokes where the foul serpent glides.' And Lucan: 'the chelydrus, tracing a smoking path'; it always moves in a straight line, for if it twists itself while moving, it bursts at once.
Solinus: Calabria abounds greatly in chelydri, and also produces the boa.
Isidore: the 'cenchris' is a serpent without bends, which always makes a straight path, of which Lucan says: 'and the cenchris, always gliding in a straight line.'

Isidore, in the same: the 'cerastes' is so named because it has little horns like a ram's, for the Greeks call horns 'cerata.' It has four small horns, by whose display, as if by bait, it lures and destroys the animals it entices. For it buries its whole body in sand and gives no sign of itself except from the part by which it catches the birds or animals it lures. It is, moreover, more sinuous than other serpents, so much so that it seems not to have a spine at all.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'cerastes' is a serpent having eight horns on its head, from which handles for knives are usually made for the tables of emperors, since they betray by sweating any venom placed near them.

Avicenna: the horned serpent is a kind of deaf serpent, whose length is from one cubit up to two, and on its head are two projections, like two horns. Its body color is ash-grey, and its belly is like dry, hard scales, which rustle on the ground with a noise. Its teeth are even, not curved, and it is found mostly in sandy places. Its bite is felt in the affected places as if needles or nails were stuck in them. And it is said that a very great heaviness settles over the whole body. And its lips swell, and dizziness and darkening of the eyes follow, and reason is destroyed. Its proper treatment is to give radish seed in wine as a drink.

Isidore: the 'coluber' [snake] is so named because it inhabits shady places [colat umbras], or because it slides in slippery, winding coils. For whatever slides while being held is called 'slippery' [lubricum], like a fish or a serpent.
Ambrose: the snake, moreover, flees the stag but kills the lion.
Physiologus: the sloughed skin of the snake, boiled in oil, wonderfully soothes ear pain.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: what was said above of the serpent in general is true in particular of the snake too, namely, that having shed its skin, passing through a crevice in a rock, it lays aside its old age, but first, by fasting, thins its flesh, so as to be better suited to that passage. It is as long as an eel, moving with twisting motion and hissing. It lies in wait for passersby and, biting, pours in venom with its tongue. Whence it is written: 'let Dan be a snake in the way.' And elsewhere: 'whoever breaks down a hedge, a snake shall bite him.'

Pliny: against toad venoms, a snake living in water is helpful. Those who hunt crocodiles carry its fat or gall with them, and testify that they are wonderfully aided by these; the Greeks call the water-dwelling snake 'hydros,' of which more will be said below.
Dioscorides: a snake's [skin], boiled in wine, relieves toothache. It is also a help to the eyes.
Physiologus: the dragon is the greatest of all serpents and of all creatures on earth. It sometimes flies through the air, driving and propelling itself with great force.

Isidore: the dragon is the greatest of all living creatures on earth; the Greeks call it 'drakon,' whence the Latin 'draco' derives. It is often drawn out of caves and carried into the air, and the air is stirred because of it. It has a crest, a small mouth, and narrow passages through which it draws breath and puts forth its tongue. It is born in Ethiopia and in India, in the very furnace of continuous heat.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the dragon [draco], according to Isidore, is from the Greek 'derkein,' which means 'to see,' since it sees more sharply than other living creatures; true dragons, however, as Solinus says, have small mouths that do not gape widely when biting, and are without feet, and rest in caves. Leviathan, according to Gregory, is said to be a dragon that crawls on land, swims in water, and flies in air.

Avicenna: the smaller kind of dragon, they say, is five cubits; the large kind, thirty. Dragons have two large eyes, and beneath the lower jaw there is a protrusion like a chin, wherefore they have very many teeth; they multiply in the regions of Nubia and are found in the land of Asia. The Indian ones are very large, having yellowish and black faces, mouths of great width. Their brows cover their eyes, and on their necks are scales, and in each jaw three teeth. I myself have seen one of this kind, on whose neck, hanging down broadly, were thick hairs.

Pliny, book 8: dragons of Ethiopia and India are equal, of twenty cubits. This alone is remarkable, whence Juba believed them crested. The Ethiopians called the Asachaei report that on their coasts, four or five at a time, interlaced like a raft, with heads raised, they sail on the waves, borne to better pastures in Arabia. In springtime the dragon suffers nausea, but relieves this ailment with the juice of wild lettuce.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the dragon's dwelling is frequently in caves, because of the natural heat of its body and the added heat of the sun, which is greatest in the regions of the East. For this creature is rarely found except in hotter climates. And so it also readily settles its cave in a rocky cliff. Around the tower of Babel and in the deserts of that ancient Babylon and its ruins, the greatest dragons are said to dwell, whose voice and roar terrify men; growing to twenty-five cubits and more, it often gains still greater strength, and, coming to old age and its due size, lives a long time without food. But once it has eaten, it is not easily satisfied. In the depths of the earth, as Augustine says, a dragon sometimes dwells, and when it senses moisture in the air, it comes out and is borne through the air, stirring and driving the air with the great beating of its wings. Its wings indeed stand out with a leathery mobility, and, spread widely in proportion to the size of its body, they infect the air wherever it dwells. A certain kind of these crawls on its breast upon the ground, but another has feet, though this is rarer to find.
Aristotle: the dragon, when it is sick, eats the fruit of the 'therascon' with milk.

div.head: DE PUGNA DRACONIS CUM ELEPHANTE AC CETERIS

cit.quote: Ambrose: the dragon binds the elephant, whose fall is death to the victor too, and so the contest is fought fiercely on both sides: the one, that it may bind the leg, in which the fall of the vanquished cannot harm it; the other, that it may not be caught by its hind foot or heel in a narrow place, where it could not even free itself. And that it may crush the dragon underfoot with a heavy tread, or else lack the help of a following elephant.

Pliny, in the passage above: India has dragons and elephants locked in perpetual war, of such size that they easily encircle the elephants and bind them in a deadly knot. The fight ends in mutual death, and the loser, collapsing, crushes the coiled dragon with its weight. At first, indeed, dragons bind the elephants' legs with their tails, but the elephants loosen the knots with their trunks. But then the dragons thrust their heads into the elephants' nostrils, cutting off their breath at once and tearing the softest parts. When caught in the open, the elephants rear up against them, and aim especially for their eyes. Thus it happens that they are found blind, and wasted by hunger and the decay of grief. There is also another account of this struggle, namely that the elephant's blood is extremely cold, and for this reason is sought by dragons, especially in scorching heat. Wherefore, submerged in rivers, they lie in wait for the elephants as they drink, and, with their tails wound tight, fix a bite on the ear, since that alone is a place that cannot be defended with the trunk, and that the dragons themselves are so large that they can hold the elephant's whole blood supply. And so the elephants, drained by them and left dry, collapse, and the dragons, made drunk, are crushed beneath them and die together.
Pliny, in the same: the eagle too has a fight with the dragon that is dangerous enough, and much more uncertain still, even in the air.
Aristotle: the vulture and the dragon also fight, because they both eat animals.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: there is a tree called 'zilanim,' which the dragon habitually fears and flees, in whose fruit doves delight. And indeed, if the tree's shadow moves toward the east, the dragon flees to the west; but if toward the west, it flees to the east. And so it lies in wait for the doves this way, and kills and devours them when they are separated from the tree.

Isidore: the dragon has its power in its tail, not in its teeth, and harms more by a lashing blow than by a bite. It is, moreover, harmless in terms of venom, but venom is not necessary for it to bring death, since if it winds itself around anyone, it kills him, and against this not even the elephant is safe, for all its bodily size. For, lurking around the paths by which elephants usually walk, it binds their legs in solid knots and kills them by suffocation.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: there is in the land of Ethiopia a dragon from which the viper is bred, and from it the 'entychon' is obtained, against which there is no remedy. And among all venomous animals, the bite is especially bad when they eat one another, as the dragon eats the scorpion.

Aristotle, in the same, on the properties of the elements: in the days of King Philip, there was a road on a mountain of Armenia about which the king asked why no one crossed it without falling down dead. Socrates therefore set up a steel mirror facing it, in which he saw two great dragons. These opened their mouths, and a smoke came out from their jaws, corrupting the air. The king then ordered men to go up that mountain and kill them, and thus that place was made safe.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: dragons, as has been said, when they are lifted into the air, the air is stirred because of them and shines like fire. Of these Lucan says: 'You too, harmless gifts to every land, gleaming dragons, crawl in golden splendor; but blazing Africa makes you deadly, and you draw the high air on your wings, and, following whole herds, burst upon peoples with your coiling grip and lash; not even the elephant is safe for all his bulk, delivering all things to death, nor is any cloud's work needed to bring harmful doom by venom.' Peter Damian tells of a certain farmer who rose one day very early and, seeing a dragon of enormous size, thought it a log and, being tired, sat upon it to rest, whereupon the indignant beast at once swallowed him. The dragon, according to Jerome, is called in Hebrew 'Leviathan,' as will be said below, where Leviathan is treated.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis: the dragon, as has been said, has no venom; its mouth indeed gapes open, but it does no harm with its teeth. Its bite, however, is very bad, even if small, since it eats venomous things. The dragon's very gaze, too, is unbearable to men, so that sometimes they are frightened to death by the mere sight of it. Its tail too kills whatever it binds, and, breathing out, it even infects the air with its deadly breath, bringing pestilence.

Solinus: from dragons' brains is cut the stone 'dracontias,' but it is not a true stone unless it is taken from a living dragon. For if the dragon dies first, its hardness vanishes together with its life.

Physiologus, on dragons: they are made to sleep by drugged grasses, and thus the stone is obtained, in the use of which eastern kings especially glory. Venomous creatures flee the fat of dragons, nor does the dragon itself have venom; a dragon's head is said to bring prosperity and good fortune to a house. Its eyes, aged and ground with honey, when rubbed on, keep even the timid from being frightened by nighttime visions.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: from the brain of a dragon unexpectedly struck down, still throbbing in full vigor, the stone 'dracontias' is extracted; its tongue and gall, boiled in wine, are a remedy for those troubled by incubi, when their bodies are anointed with it. The dragon's flesh is of a glassy color, and refreshes those who eat it. Hence it is that the Ethiopians, dwelling in a scorching region, gladly eat dragon's flesh; indeed their thirst for gain grew so immense that traders, by certain charms, render the dragon tame for a time and, sitting on its back, guide it with a bridle until they reach Ethiopia.

Isidore, book 19: they say cinnabar is the blood of dragons when they entwine elephants. For the beasts collapse and the dragons are crushed beneath them, and their blood, poured out, stains the earth and becomes a pigment, coloring whatever it touches. It is, moreover, a powder of red color, which painters use along with other colors. Hence they say cinnabar is named from 'draco' and 'barrus,' that is, elephant.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: further, the 'dragon's blood' that physicians use in medicines is, they say, the resin of a certain tree, so called for its resemblance to blood, as has been said above.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: 'dracontopedes' are great and powerful serpents, having maidenly faces resembling human ones, ending in the body of a dragon. It is credible that one of this kind was the one through which the devil deceived Eve, since, as Bede says, it had a maidenly countenance. And the devil, joining or attaching himself to this creature so as to lure the woman by a similar shape, showed her only its face, and hid the rest of its body in the foliage of trees.

Augustine of Hippo: that serpent, moreover, is said to have been most cunning, or, according to others, most wise - not in the proper sense in which wisdom is understood of God, or of an angel, or of a rational soul, but by transference, as bees or ants are called wise because of works imitating wisdom, although the serpent, not having a rational soul but the diabolical spirit with which it was filled, could be called most wise in that sense. For evil angels, although cast down by pride, are nevertheless by nature more excellent than all beasts, because of the pre-eminence of reason. For the serpent did not understand words, nor was it made rational. For that serpents are drawn from their hiding-places by the words of magicians or enchanters is a diabolical power. This is permitted in memory of that first deed, so that it may be known that the devil once spoke familiarly with this kind. That serpent, moreover, is like Balaam's donkey, but the one was diabolical, the other angelic: for good and evil angels work in similar ways, as did Moses and Pharaoh's magicians.

Isidore: the 'dipsas' is a kind of asp, called in Latin 'situla' [water-drawer], because whoever it bites dies of thirst. It is said, moreover, to be so tiny that it is not seen when trodden on. Its venom extinguishes life before it is felt, so that the face of the dying man, overtaken by death, shows no sign of sorrow. Of which the poet says: 'the standard-bearing youth of Tyrrhenian blood, in his boldness, was bitten by the dipsas, trodden underfoot, its head twisted back; scarcely was there color or feeling, or the mark of its tooth.'

Andromachus of Crete: when the dipsas stings someone, an excessive heat is inflamed in him. And from this comes a violent thirst and a burning inflammation, nor does he stop drinking water, until his body bursts, and thus he dies.

Helinand of Froidmont: the dipsas is called 'situla' by way of opposite meaning. For the vessel called a 'situla' [bucket] takes away thirst, whereas this brings it on - just as a 'pharetra' [quiver] is so called because it 'brings' [fert] death, and a 'feretrum' [bier] because it 'carries' or 'takes away' the dead. Of these Lucan speaks, saying: 'asps stood dry on the bank, and dipsades thirsted in the midst of the waters.' And a little after, of the one 'whose head twisted back, the dipsas, trodden underfoot, bit.' Lucan relates: 'with iron he endured to open his swollen veins and fill his mouth with blood.' I have read in certain old glosses on Deuteronomy thus: the dipsas is a kind of serpent, a foot and a half long and of two palms' width.

Physiologus: the dipsas is also called 'scorching,' since one wounded by it is set ablaze with such a heat of fever that no abundance of water can quench his thirst. It is also called, for the same reason, 'situla,' of which more will be said below.

Avicenna: the thirst-causing serpent, according to some, is a palm's length, and on its body are many black markings. Its head is small and its neck thick, from which its body tapers to a fine tail, and it moves shaking its tail as it goes. It is found on shores, and the one bitten by it suffers a burning and inflammation of the belly so severe that no amount of water satisfies him, nor does he stop drinking without any relief by urine or sweat, so that his whole belly swells and water seems to run in his veins. Its treatment, beyond the general treatments, is to make the patient drink a great deal of oil continuously and vomit, then to give an enema with things that draw out waste matter and moisture.

div.head: DE HEMORRHOIDE ET ENHYDRO ET EXHYDRA

cit.quote: Isidore: the 'haemorrhois' is an asp so named because it makes the one it bites sweat blood, so that, its veins dissolved, it draws out through blood whatever life remains. For the Greek 'haima' means blood.
Alexander Neckam: the 'haemorrhois' is rightly named from blood, since one stung by it emits a great deal of blood; whence a menstruating woman is called 'haemorrhoissa.'

Isidore: the 'enhydros' is a snake living in water. For the Greeks call water 'hydor.' 'Exhydra' is the Greek 'hydra,' that is, the dragon of many heads, such as was in the marsh of Lerna, in the province of Arcadia. In Latin, however, it is called 'ex hydra,' because, once one head was cut off, three grew back, as was said.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of this, then, more will be said in its proper alphabetical place, where the hydra is treated. Of this, indeed, Jerome, speaking against his detractors in the preface to Ezra, quotes a line of poetry, saying: 'though the hydra hiss, though the victor cast no flames, my eloquence, with Christ's help, will never fall silent, and my severed tongue will still stammer.'

Constantine the African: the 'glandosa' is a serpent whose bite is putrid, and from which a most foul odor spreads from a distance. Some say that the feet of one walking over it are stripped of skin, and he suffers a swelling in the leg; even the hands of the one who treats it are stripped of skin. Whoever kills this serpent, his own smell becomes as putrid, and he loses every sense but that of this stench alone. A sign of its bite is that a swelling with redness follows at that spot, a blister surrounds those parts, sometimes blood runs freely as if it were water, and he also suffers pain in the mouth of the stomach.
Isidore: the 'natrix' is a serpent that poisons water with its venom. For in whatever spring it is found, it mixes venom into it. Of which Lucan says: 'the natrix, defiler of water.'

Isidore, in the same: the 'jaculus' is a flying serpent, of which Lucan says: 'and the winged jaculi.' For they leap out from trees, and, when some animal comes their way, they hurl themselves upon it and kill it, whence they are called 'jaculi' [javelins].

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: the 'jaculus' is a flying serpent; it kills any animal it meets while flying. And there is another kind by which an animal dies without any sensation of pain. Another kind, if it touches someone, wears him out with pain for a whole day, and afterward he dies.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'jaculus' is a serpent that, flying on wings, climbs into trees and lies hidden in them. From these, hurled with the greatest force, it strikes whatever animal it finds in its path. The 'hypnalis' is a serpent of the asp kind, which kills by sleep those it bites, for its venom brings on a sleep from which, once infected, nothing can rouse the victim. Cleopatra applied this to her left arm, lying down beside her Antony, so that, touched by it, she might fall asleep and end her life by a quiet death.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: Leviathan, according to Jerome, is called in Hebrew 'dragon.' It is said, moreover, that the dragon both crawls on land and swims in the waters and flies in the air, whence in Isaiah too it is called by three names, namely serpent, and whale, and Leviathan. For, speaking in the spirit of the devil under the figure of Leviathan, that same prophet says: 'In that day the Lord shall visit with his sword, hard and great and strong, upon Leviathan the bar-serpent, and upon Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he shall slay the whale that is in the sea.'

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: 'Levin' or Leviathan often lies in wait for the whale and fights with it, and all the fish of the sea that see the battle between them at once gather at the whale's tail; and indeed, if the whale is overcome by it, they too all die at once. For whatever its tail encircles, it swallows at once. But if the whale cannot be overcome, then 'Levin' emits from its jaws a most foul smell together with water. The whale, on the contrary, spits it back and repels the foul smell, and thus saves and defends itself and its companions.

Physiologus: some hold that the 'nepa' is a female serpent, which, in the hour of raging lust, bites off the head of its mate and kills him; whence it too is killed in turn in giving birth. And so this same creature, the 'nepa,' is the same as the viper, so called as if 'giving birth by force' [vi pariens]. For when it is near giving birth, its young, having gnawed through the mother's insides, burst out, bringing about the mother's own death.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of this kind of viper, then, more will be said fully below, where the viper is treated.

Isidore: the 'obites' is so named because it has the color of sand. Of which the poet says: 'the theophanus obites, spotted with scattered markings, of the same hue as the sun-scorched sands, and indistinguishable when approached,' and so on.

div.head: DE PADERA ET PARIA ET PRESTERE

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'padera' is a serpent in Germany, of the thickness of a human arm, golden-colored on the belly and green on the back. Its breath is said to be so harmful that, if you hold a freshly cut branch to its mouth, its breath makes the bark break out in gall-like blisters. And if you hold a shining sword to its mouth, its tongue infects it with venom, and, running up to the very tip of the blade, gives it a foul, dark-blue color, as if it had been seized by a violent flame. When it strikes a man on the foot, the venom in moments runs to the other limbs too, and this because of the excessive rising heat proper to its nature, as with wood-smoke, which always rises. When, rising, it touches the heart, then the man falls and dies. The remedy against it is for the man struck in the foot to be hung upside down by the feet, head lowered, so that the venom cannot rise; and the infected spot is then cut out and healed with medicines.

Isidore: the 'parias' is a serpent that always moves on its tail and seems to make a furrow. Of which Lucan says: 'content to furrow its path with its tail, the parias.' The 'prester' is an asp that always moves with mouth open and steaming. Whence the poet: 'and the greedy prester, its smoking jaws distended.' Whoever it strikes swells and dies of enormous bloating, for putrefaction follows the swelling.
Alexander Neckam: the 'prester' is a serpent breathing out smoke, and in its bite bringing such swelling upon the injured man that his human form is entirely destroyed.

Isidore: the 'regulus' is the basilisk itself, namely a serpent half a foot in length, marked with white spots. It is also called the 'hisser,' since it kills by hissing before it bites or burns. Basilisks, like scorpions, seek out dry places, and once they come to water, they cause hydrophobia and delirium.

Gloss, on Isaiah 14: the 'regulus' is himself the king of serpents, who, by sight or breath alone, consumes birds and kills men. Whence the prophet speaks thus of Ahab and his son Hezekiah: 'out of the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, and his seed shall swallow the bird.' The 'regulus,' moreover, is a winged serpent, whence where our translation reads 'swallowing the bird,' in the Hebrew, according to Jerome, it reads 'a flying serpent.'

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: hence also, elsewhere through the same prophet, it is said: 'in the land of trouble and distress, the lioness and the lion, and from them the viper and the flying basilisk.'

Andromachus of Crete, in the book on the compounding of theriac: the 'regulus,' also called the basilisk, is a whitish serpent, on which are three crests. Whoever sees it dies shortly after, and whoever hears its hiss when it hisses dies. Likewise every beast that eats of it once dead dies at once. It is the most malignant of serpents, and not suited for theriac.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania: an animal, if it becomes dropsical from a basilisk, dies.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of this serpent, that is, the 'regulus,' more has been said fully above, where the basilisk is treated.

div.head: DE SALPINGA ET SCYTALI AC SEPE

cit.quote: Isidore: the 'salpiga,' or 'salpinga,' is a serpent that cannot be seen. The 'scytalis' is so named because it gleams with such variety on its back that it delays onlookers by admiration of its markings, and, being rather sluggish in its crawling, catches those it cannot pursue by the wonder of its own appearance while they stand astonished. It is, moreover, of such heat that even in winter it sheds its hot skin. Of which Lucan says: 'and the scytalis, alone among Persian serpents even now to shed its skin amid the frosts.'
Solinus: the scytalis sheds its skin even in the frost of winter.

Isidore: the 'seps' is a tiny serpent, which consumes not only the flesh but even the bones with its venom. Of which the poet thus makes mention: 'the wasting seps, dissolving bones together with the body.' This same 'seps' is the wasting asp, which, when it has bitten a man, consumes him at once, so that he wholly dissolves in the manner of a serpent. Lucan: 'a small serpent, but one that carries no small share of bloody death... all others steal away the life, you alone the corpse.'

div.head: DE SITULA ET SPUENTE AC SYRENA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'situla' is a small and malicious serpent, which kills a man by thirst; it gleams with such variety that it delays onlookers by its beauty, and, though nature made it slower in crawling, it holds fast, by the wonder of its appearance, those it cannot pursue. It is, moreover, of such heat that it sheds its skin even in winter; whoever is touched by its bite, seized by a fiery burning, is set ablaze.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'situla' is a kind of asp, called in Greek the dipsas, of which more has been said fully above.

Avicenna: a certain serpent is called the 'spitter,' since it kills with its spit whatever it falls upon, spit which its teeth, pressed close together, cast out. The smell of its spit too kills; its length reaches up to two cubits, and its color is ash-grey inclining to yellow, and it kills the one it bites before he can return home. For the one it bites remains without sensation and lies motionless and quiet, sleeping deeply after continuous convulsions and the closing of the eyes, and a twisting of the neck and spasm and an irregular pulse, and he feels no pain in the intestines, and thrusts his fingers into his throat to vomit.
Isidore: winged serpents, which run faster than horses, are also said to fly; their power, however, is such that death from their bite follows before the pain is felt.
Physiologus: 'tarantae' are serpents of modest size, by whose sting one is violently afflicted. And unless treated with theriac, one sometimes dies of the affliction.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: some hold the tortoise to be of the serpent kind; it indeed lacks venom in life, but not at all after death. For its kidneys, as Ambrose says, if anyone treads on them barefoot after its death, at once infect him with venom. It has two feet, a head like an owl's, a tail like a scorpion's, and is covered with two very hard shields like shells, in which it is so encased that it can hardly be killed even by the strongest blows. It lays eggs like a hen, but its eggs are harmful to eat. The female tortoise, as Aristotle says, has only one passage for the exit of waste matter, though it has a bladder, contrary to the nature of all animals having feathers or scales or a shell. For all of these lack a bladder.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'tortuca' is also called 'testudo,' since it is covered with shell-like coverings in the manner of a cave. Most of these are aquatic, of which mention has already been made above in the treatise on fish. Some, however, are land-dwelling, also called wild, and are not venomous, but are eaten by men.

Aristotle: the tortoise is a four-footed animal, having a tongue and a lung and a weak voice; it has a small, dry lung and does not thirst, but abstains from drink for a long time; it has a very poor liver, since its body is of a poor complexion; it has a bladder and lays complete eggs. A four-footed egg-laying animal has organs of sense, such as a mouth, nose, and ears, which are not, as it were, open passages to it because of the hardness of its skin. This is evident in the tortoise, in large serpents, and in crocodiles. Likewise, animals that hide in caves do not shed their old age, except those that have thin skin, not shell-like, as the tortoise does, for it too stays in caves; an animal having feathers or scales or a shell has no bladder, because of the scarcity of its drinking and because the excess of water passes into feathers and the like, except the tortoise, since the tortoise's lung is very fleshy and full of blood, being similar to a cow's lung. When the tortoise has eaten a viper, it eats wild marjoram, whose location it marks beforehand and whose root it digs up. But when it comes back and does not find the root, it dies.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: note that the 'tortuca' is itself the land tortoise, of which more will be said below among the kinds of worms, because of the slug, which is a worm and a kind of tortoise.
Ambrose: the tortoise, fed on the innards of a serpent, when it perceives the venom, always resorts to marjoram as its medicine of health.

Avicenna, in the canon: the blood of the wild tortoise, with wine, heals epilepsy. Its gall, dripped into the nostrils of epileptics, and the drawing in of its smell through the nostrils, benefits the epileptic. Against suffocation too, the palate is smeared with it mixed with honey. Its egg is effective against children's coughs, and its gall too is effective smeared on scrofulous swellings.

Physicus: the 'tyrus' is a serpent found beyond the sea, in Jericho, whose flesh is hot and dry. It is indeed venomous, like other serpents, yet it has the power of expelling venom; its own venom is hot and dry. 'Tyri' are found in the morning nearly deadened by the coldness of the air, whence some judge them cold. But it is found in the Arabic antidotary that they are hot, and that this deadening comes from the opening of their pores as the air enters.

Aristotle: the serpent called the 'tyrus,' wherever it finds a nest, eats the young birds and swallows the eggs whole. And when it has taken something as food, it raises itself up and swallows, then contracts itself, until what has been swallowed reaches down, since its stomach is fine and small. Many blooded animals hide themselves, like the tyrus and the small lizard. And of those animals that hide in caves, some shed their old age, namely those that have thin skin, not shell-like. The tyrus, however, first sloughs off the skin that is between its eyes, so that one who does not know this happening thinks the tyrus is blind. Then it removes the skin of its head and the whole rest down to the tail in one day and one night, and its shedding is like the emergence of an embryo, when the membrane splits from it. There is in the land of Ethiopia a dragon from which the tyrus is bred, as has been said above, and from it the 'entychon' is obtained, against whose venom there is no remedy. There is also found a certain tyrus called by some 'caciem,' which great serpents flee. Its size is about a cubit, and it has hairs over its whole body. And when it bites something, it at once putrefies everything around the bite. There is also found a small tyrus in India, whose bite is so strong that no remedy is found against it. The tyrus and the fox are friends to one another, and both dwell in caves of the earth. Certain animals lack feet and generate a live animal, like the tyrus and the 'cheleti.' The tyrus indeed generates a live animal, but first lays an egg within itself. Then from that the animal is formed inside, before it comes out.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'tyrus' is a serpent in the parts of Jericho, around the wastes of the Jordan, harmful to birds and animals, especially to sheep, whose wool it eats along with the birds themselves. Its flesh, prepared with certain admixtures, expels every poisonous venom, and this preparation is called 'theriac.' Some, however, report that before the Passion of Christ this creature had no remedy at all and was especially harmful to men.
