But on the very day of the Passion, one of the most harmful of these was said by chance to have been caught in the region of Jerusalem and hung on the cross at Christ's side, and from that day the whole serpent kind gained power against every venom. Nevertheless, theriac is of no avail at all against the venom of the tyrus itself, which is called 'tyricum.' And this kind of venom, that is, the 'tyricum,' which is an incurable evil, the dragon acquires from the tyrus itself. The tyrus, worn out by old age, sheds its skin in this way: it first strips off the skin that is between its eyes, so that if you did not know it, you would think the beast blind. Then it removes the skin of the head, and once this is done, the rest of the body is more easily stripped, and once stripped it has the form and shape of an embryo. The tyrus lays eggs within itself and, before it comes forth, thus generates an animal like itself.
Al-Kindi: the venom of the tyrus serpent expels other venoms.

Constantine the African: the venom of the female tyrus is hot; whoever is bitten by it suffers excessive pain at the site of the bite, and the rest that has been said above generally about the venoms of serpents applies. There is, moreover, a kind of tyrus called 'esinus,' whose neck rises upward and stretches out, and blood is spat from its mouth; the wound its bite makes is extremely small, like the prick of a needle, and little blood flows from it, nor does it produce a swelling or lump. Those bitten by it, however, suffer a dimming of sight, and pain throughout the whole body, and lose feeling, nor do those it bites escape. There is also a tyrus called 'pychronis,' small indeed, but with a wider neck, which, if it bites someone, produces a softness in the flesh like dropsy, and his flesh wastes away from the moisture.

Haly Abbas: the flesh of tyri caught in favorable places and in the proper season, once you have cut off a length of four fingers from the head and tail, dries up venoms, purges the inner organs of all excess matter, and draws it out to the surface of the body and dissolves it sharply through sweat. They also benefit thick humors, from which leprosy and vitiligo and elephantiasis arise, and heal bites of venomous creatures and are effective in deadly potions.

Physiologus: because of its lightness, the venom of the tyrus readily seeks the extremities, namely the head and tail. Whence, once the head and tail are cut off to a length of four fingers, with the length carefully measured, the middle part is very well washed and thoroughly boiled down until the spine bones can be separated; once these are discarded, it is ground, and lozenges are formed from it.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the tyrus is reported to be the same as the viper. For authors writing in medicine on serpent flesh or the preparation of theriac rarely or never mention the tyrus under that name, but speak of the viper. From the tyrus, however, the name 'theriac' is derived.
Isidore, book 4: theriac is an antidote made from serpents, by which venoms are driven out, so that one plague is dissolved by another.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: theriac, 'affarath,' that is, 'freeing from death,' is the most exalted and best of compound medicines, because of the abundance of its benefit, especially in venoms from stings or bites, as of serpents and scorpions and rabid dogs, and even in venoms taken by drinking that would otherwise kill. It also benefits phlegmatic and melancholic illnesses and their fevers, and malignant flatulence, and paralysis, and apoplexy, and epilepsy, and cramping, and tremor, and madness, and especially leprosy. It also strengthens the heart and stomach, sharpens the senses and the appetite, eases the breath, calms the heartbeat, and checks the coughing up of blood. It benefits pains of the kidneys and bladder and ulcers of the intestines, breaks a stone in the bladder, and is especially effective too against internal hardnesses in the liver, spleen, and elsewhere.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: since theriac is prepared from the flesh of the tyrus mixed with certain other things, it extinguishes every other venom, but is of no benefit against the venom of the tyrus itself.
Ambrose: the viper is the most wicked kind of beast, and, beyond all that belongs to the serpent kind, the most cunning.
Pliny: among serpents, the viper alone is said to hide itself in the earth; the rest, however, in the hollows of trees or rocks.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: vipers have only cavities in place of ears, yet they hear with them; in them the teeth are set into the gums. The Scythians dip their arrows in viper's blood mixed with human blood - an irremediable crime, since it brings death at once from the lightest touch.
Ambrose: likewise, if anyone treads barefoot on a fresh viper's mouth, it is said to do worse harm than the venom itself, and to spread an incurable wound.

Physiologus: when the viper grows old, its eyes become clouded so that it cannot see, and it fasts for forty days and nights, until its skin loosens. Then, going, it seeks a crevice cut in a rock and passes through it, and is thus stripped, so as to grow young again.
Rhazes: [on] the viper, that if the eyes of a 'zamored' ox look upon it, they at once dissolve and flow from the head.

Avicenna, in the passage above: vipers are serpents having flat, broad heads and a very small and fine neck, whose short tails make a rustling noise as they move. They are caught by physicians at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, so that lozenges may be made from them, for which not all vipers are suited, but the yellow ones, and among the yellow, the females.
Vipers, coming out of their dens after winter, rub their eyes on fennel, so that they may be given light. A man's urine is usefully poured on a viper's bite, especially the bite of the rock-viper.

The males of vipers are worse, the females are safer. The female's bite, indeed, is recognized by finding the mark of more than two teeth fixed in the place bitten. At the start, blood comes out from the site of the teeth, then a burning venom, at first perhaps watery, then foamy, then like verdigris. And then indeed it turns to the substance and color of the venom proper, and the place aches. Then the pain spreads, and a hot swelling appears, having pustules and blisters like a burn from fire. And an inflammation follows in the internal organs, redness in the body with shivering, then cold sweat and a corruption of complexion inclining to greenish, and a disturbance of dizziness and rapid breathing and nausea and hiccuping and the rest. And most often death comes within three days, sometimes up to seven. Beyond the general remedies in treatment, the stronger treatment for this is to hasten to theriac made from vipers.
Aristotle: the tortoise eats the viper, and then eats the root of wild marjoram, whose location it marks beforehand. Otherwise it dies within three days, if it cannot find that root.
Gloss, on Job 20: the viper has a longer body than the asp, and kills more slowly with its venom.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: of the viper, Physiologus says that it has a human face down to the navel, but from the navel to the tail the shape of a crocodile. Its digestive passage is like the eye of a needle, and so, unlike other creatures, it cannot conceive in the usual way, but only through the mouth. It has cavities in place of ears, and only three teeth. Its bite causes swelling and inflammation and is said to be incurable. This serpent hides itself in the earth in winter. Ambrose and Basil, the sacred doctors, report that if anyone incautiously treads on the kidneys of a dead viper, it is said to do worse harm than the venom, and to spread an incurable wound.

Andromachus of Crete, in the book on the compounding of theriac: there are three kinds of vipers and serpents. Among these is the one called the asp, whose habitation is in dry ground and in watery places. This is sometimes ash-colored, sometimes yellowish. Another kind is called the swallow-colored, since it resembles the color of swallows. Among these too is the one called the spitter, so named because it spits its venom upon a man. There is yet another kind similar to the asp, whose habitation is sometimes in water, and this is called the hydra, sometimes in dry ground, and this is called the land kind, that is, not the watery one, and this kind is smaller than the asp, but with a wider head. Likewise among the kinds of vipers is the one called the 'astros,' which, when it sees someone, raises its neck and measures whether it can reach the man, then leaps upon him and spits venom on him and on his face, and kills him at once. There are, moreover, three kinds of this viper: one is called 'sersin,' another 'selidosa,' the third 'basilida.' And it is said that Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, killed herself with a viper of this kind. For when Augustus had defeated Antony, her lover, he wished to capture Cleopatra alive, so as to display her and disgrace her before the Romans; when she learned this, wishing to escape her enemy's hands, she took the aforementioned serpent and applied it to her left breast, since she knew the heart lay on the left side. The serpent then stung her, and she died at once. Some, however, have said that, wishing to kill herself, she bit her own arm until blood came out, and then took some of this viper's venom, which she had kept with her, and threw it onto the wound, and died at once. We too have seen this viper in Alexandria, and the speed of its killing. For when a judge condemns some nobleman to death, wishing to kill him swiftly, they bring such a viper and make it sting him near the chest, and he dies at once.

Isidore: the viper [vipera] is so named because it gives birth by force [vi pariat]. For when its belly swells for birth, the young, not waiting for the natural, mature release, burst forth by gnawing through its sides, killing the mother. Lucan: 'viper-born young come forth by tearing open the body.' It is said, moreover, that the male inserts his mouth and spits his seed into the viper. She, however, turned from the pleasure of lust into rage, bites off the male's head, taken into her mouth. Thus it happens that both parents perish: the male while mating, the female while giving birth. From the viper, moreover, are made the little cakes called 'trochisci' by the Greeks.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: although the male viper is, among nearly all kinds of serpents, the crueler, he is nevertheless gentle toward his own female, as Ambrose and Basil say. For the male seeks out the absent female and calls to her with a gentle hiss. And when he senses his mate approaching, he vomits out his venom, out of reverence for her, honoring the grace of their union.

Ambrose: the sea-eel seeks its known mate or prepares a new one. Coming forward to the shore, with its hiss announcing its presence, it calls the viper to their conjugal embrace. The viper, called forth, does not fail to come, and shares the sought union of coupling with the venomous serpent. But when it calls the eel with its hiss, it vomits out its venom, and after mating takes it up again.

Pliny: the male viper, as said above, inserts his head into the female's mouth while mating, which she, in the sweetness of pleasure, gnaws off. Among land serpents, the viper alone bears within herself eggs of a single color and soft, like a fish's, and on the third day within the womb hatches her young, then gives birth to about twenty, one by one, each on a different day. And so the rest, impatient of the delay, burst through her sides, killing the mother. Other serpents incubate laid eggs in the earth and hatch their brood the following year.

Pliny, book 21, in the same: further, the pregnant viper, once venom has been pressed by the recoil of the teeth, pours forth its poison into the bites it makes. The viper's womb, moreover, in those bearing young within themselves, is double.

div.head: DE QUIBUS VIPERIS CONFICIENDA SIT TYRIACA

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the fifth canon: not all vipers, as has been said, are suited for compounding medicinal lozenges, but the yellow ones, and among the yellow, the females. Their sign is that the males have one tooth on each side, but the females have several. One should avoid horned ones, mottled ones, and asps inclined to white. Nor should they be caught from fish-ponds and the banks of rivers and seas, nor rock-vipers, since among these are oak-vipers that cause thirst; rather they should be caught in a place far from moisture, and not the sluggish ones, but those of swift movement, having a raised head and a bold look.

Andromachus of Crete: among the kinds of serpents, only vipers are chosen for theriac, since serpent kinds are fundamentally of three sorts. Some have a strong venom that kills swiftly, like the basilisk and the asp and the oak-viper. Others are weak and sluggish and do not harm much nor kill at all, but produce pain and injury and a swelling at the site of the sting. Between these is the middle kind, the viper, since it is neither of great venom nor again very weak. Females, moreover, are chosen, since they have less venom in their given quantity. For in every kind of animal females are colder than males, and nature has contrived in them an abundance of cold, so that moisture may be multiplied in them and so that dissolution and loss from their bodies may be lessened, since they need the excess moisture, which is the food of their young. And so males come to have more heat and dryness than females, and greater anger and swifter vengeance and more venom and stronger. In females, however, the venom is weak and minimal, since there is not in them a predominant heat that generates venom, and again, since the predominant moisture extinguishes the sharpness of their venom and weakens it. And this is also why females have more teeth than males, since males, because of the abundance and power of their venom, do not need more than two teeth, whereas females need more, so that the number of their teeth may make up for what the males have in venom. Yellow ones, moreover, are chosen for the goodness of complexion of this color, since it is not of bad quality like black, nor of weak power like white, but balanced, for black signifies a vehemence of inflammation and burning. White, however, signifies weakness and a paucity of heat and an abundance of moisture. Yellow, however, is midway between these, balanced. It is also required that they be of swift movement, easy gait, and quick leaping, and that their heads be high and raised upward. For this is a sign of the vehemence of their heat and of great power in their bodies, and that they themselves are clean of excess matter. It is also required that their eyes incline to redness and that their gaze be intense and sharp, like one angered, for all this signifies the vehemence of their natural heat and the health of their body. Otherwise their eyes would be yellow or white, because of the scarcity of blood in their bodies. Likewise it is required that their heads be flatly rounded, with a broad forehead, which is a sign of vehement strength. Likewise that their bellies be wrinkled, which is a sign of vehement strength and paucity of excess matter, for softness comes from weakness and multiple excess.

Avicenna: when vipers are caught for this purpose, they should not be delayed if possible, and four fingers' length should be cut off from the head end, and likewise from the tail and the anus. And if much blood runs from it, and there is much movement in this state, and its death is slow, then it is a chosen one; if the contrary, it is a poor one. And when it is dead, its innards are removed, especially its gall, and it is washed with water and salt, the washing done very thoroughly, then it is boiled in water and salt, and if dill is added to it, there is no harm in that boiling, by which the flesh comes easily off the bone. Then the flesh is cleaned from the bone and ground in a mortar, and the one preparing it is instructed to smell balsam oil and rub it on his fingers. When it is ground, then, it is mixed with the little cakes according to the various formulas, and no formula should be chosen above that of Andromachus; then small lozenges are made from it and dried in the shade and stored away, and no ray of sun should fall on them at all, either before or after drying, since the sun strips away the power proper to viper's flesh that destroys the venoms coming from bites and from drinking.

Andromachus of Crete: vipers should be caught in spring, since they are then strong, from the warmth of the tempered air, and are nourished by foods suited to them. And this from places near the sea, since these are of a more vehement dryness, and there is not in them much excess moisture, which would weaken the power of their flesh, in which places, that is, are plants and trees, so that they may have suitable food from them. Nor, once caught, should they be left aside, but at once cut apart and cleaned, since the longer they linger, the more their venom sharpens and changes for the worse. For even a fasting man's spittle is a venom by which even scorpions are killed, and if a fasting man bites something, his bite is not healed. Their heads, moreover, are cut off, since in them the most venom is generated and gathered, especially in their orifices, and their venom is nothing other than their own spit. In the rest of the body, however, there is no venom at all, or very little. The tails too are cut off, since in them there is bad quality and many excess matters gather, for the tail draws filth from the whole body, through the abundance of its movement, for abundance of movement is the cause of attraction. This is why the parts of fish near the tail are more nourishing. The tails, then, are rejected because of the gathering of excess matter and the scarcity of flesh. They are also skinned for a similar reason, since it is a property of skin to receive all the body's excess matter, and nature prepared it for this purpose; whence, because nature wishes to cleanse the inner organs of harm, the skin itself, spread thin over the whole body, is made weak, so that when the body's excess matter gathers, which nature expels from the inner organs, it does not, by its own strength, drive them back to the organs deep within the body. Rather, when it receives what is expelled to it, what is fine and thin in it can gradually escape through the dissolving of its own substance, and what is thick from it necessarily remains in it. Thus only the skin itself becomes corrupted, so that it does not corrupt the inner organs. For, as Hippocrates himself says, the corruption of the outer skin is fitting for the inner organs. The skin, then, is not suited for theriac, both because of its weakness and because thick excess matters, which cannot dissolve, cling to it and corrupt it. The caul-fat too and the innards are removed from them, because of the gathering of all excess matters in the intestines and because the caul-fat is of a more vehement heat and burning. For in the intestines the excess matter of dung is retained, and in the gall is red bile, and in the spleen black bile, and in the liver unclean blood mixed with bile. Salt, mixed with it, is boiled down so as to penetrate deep into the flesh and thus, with the moisture of water, dissolve the venom from it. It is boiled over embers, so that its boiling may be prolonged with evenness - prolonged so that it does not burn, even so that it is cooked not on one side but throughout. For the heat of embers is even, with moderation. The sign of proper boiling is the separation of bone from flesh. Bread, moreover, is mixed with it, so that its moisture, lest the theriac putrefy, may be dried, and so that through this bread the remaining venom may be dissolved.

div.head: DE DIVERSIS MEDICINIS EX VIPERA ET CONTRA EIUS MORSURAM

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the second canon: viper's fat prevents, as some have said, the descent of a cataract into the eye. Viper's flesh benefits leprosy. Likewise it is melted and applied over the bite of the viper itself, and calms the pain. Burnt viper skin, applied to alopecia, benefits it. Likewise fresh viper's fat benefits eye-films and watering eyes, and prevents hairs plucked from the eyelids from growing back. Further, for a viper's bite, human teeth, ground or burnt and powdered, are beneficial, as is balsam oil, and likewise colocynth root or a plaster made from bitter vetch; costus too, drunk with wine or wormwood, likewise pitch applied, and human urine drunk. It is also said that fresh, warm goat-skin, when applied to a viper's bite, draws out the venom. Further, butter resists venoms, especially when applied to a viper's bite with it. Mountain-goat dung too, boiled with vinegar and drunk, is effective against viper bites.
Avicenna, in the same book: wine, into which viper is dropped, benefits the stinging of venomous creatures.

Pliny: a viper's head, applied to the one it struck, or even to another, is endlessly beneficial. If one holds it up on a stick over its own vapor, they say he will foretell the future. If one smears himself with the ash of a burnt viper, Nigidius is the authority, the serpent that struck him will return to him by natural necessity. The Scythians cut open a viper's head between the ears to extract a small stone, which they say, terrified, it swallows; others use the whole head. From the viper, moreover, are made the little cakes called by the Greeks 'theriac.' The innards and the discolored spine are removed, and the rest of the body, boiled in a pan with water and dill, with the spine-bones removed and fine flour added; and thus, the cakes dried in the shade, they are used for many medicines. Some also boil not only the body but even the fat with oil, reducing it to half, and, when needed, three drops of it added to oil, anoint themselves with it, so that all wild beasts flee them. Further, it is established that against the bites of all serpents, however incurable, the entrails of those same serpents applied are helpful, and that those who have once drunk a viper's cooked liver are never afterward struck by a serpent. Ash of viper-skin fills in bald patches most effectively. Also, burn a live viper in a new earthenware vessel with fennel juice added, and anoint the eyes - most useful for discharges and dimness - and a collyrium is made from a viper putrefied in a pot with little worms hatched, ground with saffron. It is also burnt in a pot with salt, and by licking this men achieve clarity of eyes and well-timed working of the stomach and whole body; this salt is also given to livestock for their health, as an antidote against serpents. Some use vipers as food. First of all, once killed, they order salt put in the mouth at once, until the moisture liquefies; with four fingers' measure cut off at each end and the innards removed, they boil them in water or oil with salt and dill, and either eat them at once or spread them on bread for repeated use. The broth, besides what has been said, drives lice from the whole body and itching of the skin's surface. Viper-head ash alone also shows this effect, and is also good rubbed on the eyes; likewise viper fat similarly. Further, concerning the gall, I do not confidently urge what some prescribe, since it is nothing other than the serpent's own venom.

Dioscorides: viper's fat heals cataracts and dullness and dimness of the eyes, mixed with cedar-resin of equal weight, Attic honey, and old oil. It also prevents hair from growing back in the armpits when rubbed on.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: viper's entrails are effective against the bites of all serpents, as Pliny says. Its sloughed skin, renewed, boiled in wine, heals teeth and eyes; its fat removes dimness of the eyes.

Isidore: the 'hydra' is called the dragon of many heads, such as was in the marsh of Lerna in the province of Arcadia; in Latin it is called 'excedra,' because, once one head was cut off, three grew back, but this is fabulous. For it is established that the 'hydra' was a place discharging waters that devastated the neighboring city, in which, when one channel was closed, many others burst forth. Seeing this, Hercules burned that place and thus closed the channels of water. For 'hydra' is named from water; 'hydros,' moreover, is an aquatic serpent, by whose bite one swells up. This ailment they call the 'boa,' since it is treated with cow dung [bos].
Pliny: [on] the snake. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Physiologus: the 'hydrus' lives in the Nile, and is smaller in size than the crocodile. And when it sees the crocodile sleeping on the bank with its mouth open, it rolls itself in mud, so that it may more easily slip into its jaws. The crocodile, then, suddenly swallows it whole and alive, whereupon it tears apart all its innards, and comes out of it alive and unharmed.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'hydros,' as Pliny writes, is the most beautiful of snakes in the whole world. This serpent's liver is kept as a remedy for those struck by it. The 'hydra' serpent, however, is spoken of fabulously: when Hercules wished to cut off its head, two immediately grew in its place, and thus, however many were cut off, others always grew back at once. This is what has been said of serpents; the second kind of reptiles follows, that is, lizards.

Isidore: the lizard [lacertus] is a kind of reptile, so called because it has 'arms' [brachia, i.e. lacertos] and rests on four feet. There are, moreover, several kinds of lizards, such as the frog, the salamander, the 'saura,' and the stellio.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: not without reason are the frog and toad reckoned in this same kind. For the 'batracha' is indeed similar to the frog, and the frog is called 'batracha' in Greek. Sometimes, moreover, 'lacertus' or 'lacerta' is taken for 'batracha,' that is, the genus for the species.

Aristotle: the lizard kind never closes its eyes at all. Small lizards, bees, and every ringed animal hide in caves in winter, but small lizards stay in the crevices of stones and walls, in narrow places. In these the female is larger, as in frogs and serpents and spiders. They have testicles attached to the vertebrae. In mating they are entwined just as serpents are coiled together, so that they seem to be a single body with two heads; they have a single stomach, and their tails grow back after being cut off. Scaled animals, like small lizards and serpents, eat herbs and flesh indifferently. In Arabia a small lizard larger than a cubit is found. The spider often hunts the lizard, and begins first to weave over it, until its opening is firmly bound; then it goes to it and bites it until it dies. This animal lays complete eggs, and its lung is small and dry, and swells when inflated.
Pliny, book 8: as often as lizards engage in battle with serpents, once wounded, they revive themselves especially with the herb dittany, against the bites of serpents.

Pliny, book 10, in the same: Aristotle denies, contrary to popular belief, that among four-footed egg-laying creatures, lizards give birth through the mouth. Nor do they brood, having forgotten where they laid, since this animal has no memory at all; and so the young burst forth by themselves.
Pliny, book 11, in the same: lizards have a forked and hairy tongue. Their eyelids, however, are on the upper lid only. They often have double tails.
Pliny, book 17, in the same: against caterpillars, and so that apples do not rot, they order the tips to be touched with the gall of a green lizard.
Pliny, in the same: a lizard, drunk in wine, heals its own bites.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: they call the lizard more a worm than a serpent, since it strikes more gently, though it hisses like a serpent and has a similar tail and a forked, hairy tongue. It moves, however, on feet. If one of two caught together is taken, the remaining one grows fierce. This animal has no memory, and so does not brood, having forgotten where it laid; the young burst forth by themselves, eleven in number. Some say the young are devoured by their mothers, except one left behind, which places itself on the mother's haunches, and this one, as an avenger of its siblings, kills its parents. There are lizards in India twenty-four feet in length, of a shining color. There is also, of the lizard kind, a certain small creature, unlike in color though not in shape, which has a black tail and feeds on wild spiders.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba II, king of Mauretania, in the passage above: when the lizard grows old, its eyes grow dim and it goes blind. Then it turns toward the sun, facing its rays, and directs its eyes for a while in the morning through a crevice, until its sight returns and it sees perfectly as before.
Gloss: the lizard, an unclean animal according to the Law, dwells in tombs and signifies the inconstancy of life.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the lizard's nature is close to that of the stellio, but better. Its blood strengthens the sight. Its dung benefits the white film of the eye and itching, and sharpens the sight and produces a good complexion.
Avicenna, in the canon: lizard's flesh is deadly, and one who drinks it suffers a swelling of the tongue and itching and headache and burning and darkening of the eyes.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'borax' is a kind of toad that carries in its head the gem of its own name; it is commonly called 'crapaudine.' But when it is extracted from the toad while alive and throbbing, the stone is said to have an eye in its middle. When, however, it is extracted from one dead for some time, the malice of the venom having extinguished the eye, the stone is spoiled.

Physiologus: the 'borax' is of the toad kind; because of the amount of its venom, it swells when touched. It fights with the spider and is defeated by it. For when the spider has repeatedly stung it, it, unable to take revenge, swells itself up so much by inflating that it bursts in the middle and dies. Its bite is very bad and becomes incurable. It nourishes a gem in its forehead, for which it is killed, and which is called 'borax' from the animal itself. When its eye has been extinguished, it uses a special herb, by which it recovers its sight, but is killed by rue. It gladly inhabits damp and rotting places, hates the brightness of the sun and does not easily let itself see it, walks by night, and especially along paths worn by men's footsteps; by day, however, it hides in secret places. It flees the scent of a flowering vineyard, and sometimes grows to nearly a cubit's size. In parts of Spain especially dwells that kind of 'borax' that carries a stone in its forehead.
Isidore: the 'batrac' is so named because it has the appearance of a frog. For the Greeks call the frog 'batracha.'

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the toad is a venomous animal known to all, which is said by authors to be called the 'rubeta' or 'crassancium,' of which more will be said below. The toad, moreover, is a most cold little beast and most foul in appearance, said to have its heart in its throat, whence it is not easily killed, unless pierced through the middle of the throat. It is thought to be born from the putrefaction or corruption of earth.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the toad too, a venomous reptile, has a pestilential gaze, a filthy touch. It feeds on earth, and this by weight and measure. For whatever it can enclose in its front foot is its daily food. For it fears that earth may fail it as food. In parts of Gaul there is a kind of toad called horned, since it seems to bellow like a horn, whence it is named from the sound of its voice. It has two colors, dark and saffron. These come forth and then make sounds like trumpets, and two and two answer each other with trumpet-like calls. Only in Gaul do the loud-voiced ones live; elsewhere, once removed, they lose their voice and are mute.

Physiologus: the toad is a horrifying animal, which fights sometimes with the spider, sometimes with the lizard, sometimes even with the snake or the serpent. Wounded, however, by the venom of another venomous animal, it receives healing from plantain. It gladly feeds on sage, whose root it sometimes infects with venom. Hence it is that a bed of sage ought to be encircled with rue, whose dew is deadly to the toad. The stone found in a toad's head, carried by a man, wards off the malice of venom. From a toad, moreover, reduced to powder by burning, when left to itself, a living toad is regenerated, and not only one, but even several.

Physiologus: the 'gamaleon,' or chameleon, is a four-footed animal, having a face like a lizard's, a long and twisting tail, a rough body, and skin like that of crocodiles; it puts forth from its skin something like wool, from which belts woven cannot be burned. It is, moreover, an animal sluggish in its movement, but, once killed, kills its conqueror. For when a bird eats of it, it dies at once. This same animal is also called the salamander in Greek, and even, as some hold, the stellio in Latin. But perhaps these are different species, though of the same genus, just as goats and roe-deer and chamois are. Whence Isidore places the chameleon among the kind of beasts, but the salamander and the stellio as different species among the kind of lizards. Pliny, however, says that stellios have in a certain way the nature of chameleons. Of these, then, more will be said fully below, where the salamander is treated, which is indeed sometimes called the salamander and sometimes the chameleon, as the salamander itself also seems to be called both 'gamaleon' and chameleon.
Isidore: the frog [rana] is named from its garrulity, since it makes noise around its native marshes and gives back the sound of its voice in troublesome cries.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: frogs mate more at night than by day, and their mating lasts a long time, and they emit much seed. The male frog carries those that have wings, and every fish nourishes its young, except the frog.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon, on the frog: its venom is recognized by an abominable taste, just as that of the sea-hare is by its smell. There are river frogs, green, and sea frogs, red, both venomous. From drinking them follows a darkening of complexion and a swelling of the body along the path of softness, and a burning in the throat and mouth, difficulty of breathing and darkening of the eyes and dizziness and foulness of the mouth. Sometimes too spasm or tetanus follows, and sometimes loosening of the bowels, dysentery and nausea and vomiting mixed with frog-matter and fainting. And sometimes it expels semen and urine and menses involuntarily; in one who survives these, the teeth are not merely loosened, but fall out. For the treatment of these, vomiting and much exercise and bathing and anointing with hot oils and much wine benefit, and reed roots, and likewise galingale and aromatic reed with wine, and everything that benefits dropsy. There are also yellow frogs, from which appetite for food is removed, and belching turns sour, and the complexion is spoiled. And fainting and nausea and vomiting and stomach pain follow, and the belly and legs swell. The treatment for these is close to the treatment described above.

Pliny: a small, green, and mute frog, which, if swallowed, is said to make an ox bloat. This one lives mostly among reeds and grasses. Its flesh is applied for eye pains; the humor of its body, thickened on splinters, is said to bring clarity when rubbed on the eyes. Frog flesh added to a fishhook attracts purple-fish; dogs, however, that are given a live frog in a morsel of food, are said not to bark.

Isidore: some frogs are called water-frogs, some marsh-frogs, some 'rubetae.' Because of this, those that live in brambles are the largest of all. Others are called tree-frogs, since they live among reeds and shrubs, the smallest of all, greenest, and mute and voiceless. 'Agredulae,' however, are small frogs dwelling on dry ground or in fields, whence they are also so named.

Walafrid Strabo, on Exodus: there are three kinds of frogs. One, the river kind, is vocal. The second, small, is called the 'calamitum,' which, if thrown into the mouth of a barking dog, makes it fall silent at once. The third, the largest, called the 'rubetum,' the worst and venomous, is commonly called the 'crassantium.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the frog is a worm, sometimes green in color, but the red kind is worse. It is talkative, troublesome with its voices, and has its own call, 'coax,' nor can it say anything else, except when it is squeezed or hurt, for then it changes its voice and gives out a thin sound like a mouse's. The reason for its voice, according to Aristotle, can be judged from this: with mouth closed and sides inflated, it sounds from the throat, but at the syllable 'ax' it opens its mouth and, like bellows, presses its sides together, so that a stronger breath brings out a louder cry; it multiplies its call when it lays its lower jaw evenly in the water and stretches out its upper. But when it stretches out both, its eyes shine like candles. It fears everything that breathes. And it suspects that it is held in hatred by all. In the month of August it can never open its mouth for any purpose of food or drink or voice. And even if you try with your hand or a stick, you will scarcely be able to open it. There is also a small green frog called the tree-frog, which climbs trees and rests among the leaves; sensing rain in the clouds by a natural foreknowledge, it cries out loudly, being indeed a messenger of coming flood, but at other times scarcely sings at all. Thrown into dogs' mouths, it is thought to take away their voice.

Pliny: they say the frog's liver is double, and that the part sought after by ants should be thrown away, and that the other part is effective against all poisons made from these creatures; and if they are burnt alive in a pot, their ash with honey fills bald patches, and even better with liquid pitch. Single frogs too are boiled in vinegar, so that aching teeth may be rinsed with it and the juice held in the mouth. Broth of frog boiled in a pan is said to cure a cough. Their heart, ground with honey, heals dysentery sufferers; for jaundice too their pickled flesh with pepper is effective, provided other meat is avoided. For gout and joint pains, the oil in which frog intestines have been boiled is useful. Likewise frogs boiled in myrtle oil, the flesh discarded, free those anointed with it from quartan fevers. Their heart, bound on, lessens the chills of fevers. If the ears swell, frog fat dripped in relieves the pain at once. Worms bred in a man are removed by frog gall; ash of frog gall also benefits fever. Live frogs' bellies applied put out erysipelas; bound facing downward by their hind feet, they are said to help by more frequent breathing; to stop nosebleeds too, frog ash is applied, or dried blood. A reversed frog bound on very effectively heals the 'syriasis,' or ulcers of infants' heads. A tree-frog's liver, bound in a crane's skin, arouses desire. Frogs boiled in water until they can be applied thin out horses' mange. Frogs boiled in oil and salt so that the juice is sipped benefit tetanus. If the flesh of river frogs is eaten, or the broth of ones boiled is drunk, they benefit against the sea-hare and against serpents and against scorpions, with wine.

Avicenna, in the second canon: frog ash placed over a bleeding spot stops it. The same benefits swellings of the tendons and joints when sprinkled on. Frog, boiled with salt and oil, is said to be a remedy against leprosy and venomous worms when eaten. From the decoction of a river frog the mouth is rinsed for toothache, and the pain is calmed. The body of the rock-frog, and especially its fat, makes teeth take root easily, and expels the teeth of animals that eat it.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: [on] this kind of frog. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny: the toad-frogs, whose life is spent partly on land, partly in moisture, are said to be full of many medicinal virtues, laying them aside repeatedly and taking them up again through feeding, keeping their venoms only for themselves.
Pliny: the frog is an ambusher by nature.
Pliny, book 25, in the same: venoms are especially strong in toad-frogs. Wormwood, moreover, is said to be beneficial against having drunk a frog.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: Marsyas of Smyrna reports that toads and other frogs are burst by spitting on them, and that if one splashes its saliva into an eye, the chief remedy is women's milk. The same is drunk and dripped in against its bite. Chameleon's liver, applied with a toad's lung, removes hair.

Pliny, book 32, in the same: the juice of sea frogs boiled in wine and vinegar is drunk against toad venom. They are called 'rubetae,' moreover, because they live only among brambles, the largest of all, full of double horn-like venom-glands. Authors report wondrous things about these, vying with one another: that a small bone found on the right side, thrown into boiling water, cools the vessel so it does not boil again afterward. That dogs' attacks are checked by it; that love and quarrels are stirred up when it is added to a drink. That desire is aroused when it is bound on. Again, that boiling things are cooled from the right side, and, this bound on in fresh lambskin, cures quartan and other fevers, and by it love is checked; toad ash with old fat benefits gout and joint diseases. Further, a toad's sinews bound to the right arm arouse desire, but a toad bound in fresh sheepskin ends love; the same water, boiled down and given as a drink, heals swine diseases, as does the ash of any frog.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'rubeta' is full of various medicinal properties, laying them aside and taking them up at will, and it is said to do this constantly in feeding; its venoms, however, it never lays aside, but keeps them by it as its own weapons; it has double horns full of venom-glands. Authors relate wondrous things about these, vying with one another: it is certain that its flesh placed on a fishhook especially attracts purple-fish. Against the venom of the sea-hare and the toad, its ash drunk in water is a remedy.

Isidore: the salamander is so named because it is effective against fires. Among all venomous creatures its power is the greatest. For the others strike individuals, but this one kills many at once. For if it creeps into a tree, it poisons all the fruit and kills those who eat it. Even if it falls into a well, the force of its venom kills those who drink from it. This creature, resisting fire, alone among animals extinguishes flames. For it lives in the midst of fire without pain or being consumed. And it not only is not burned, but extinguishes the fire.

Pliny, book 10: the salamander is an animal of lizard shape, starred, of hidden and obscure origin, arising only from heavy rains and disappearing with fair weather. It has such coldness that it extinguishes fire by its touch, in no other way than ice; from the same creature's discharge, which is vomited from its mouth like milk, whatever part of a human body it touches, all the hairs fall off. And the part touched changes color into vitiligo. In these there is no male or female kind.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: fed on venomous things, they themselves become harmful too. Those who eat wild boars in Pamphylia and in the mountains of Cilicia that have devoured a salamander die, and there is no perceptible difference in smell or taste.
Pliny, book 29, in the same: bread baked on wood touched by a salamander kills.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the salamander, which some call the chameleon, that is, the 'earth-lion,' is a four-footed animal, having a face like a lizard's, or, as Aristotle says, a face between that of a pig and an ape. It lives in fire and extinguishes flame; it also puts forth a certain pale wool, from which belts woven cannot be burned. It lacks a spleen, and, contrary to all other animals, has its liver on the left side; in the arrangement of its inner organs too there is great variety in it compared to other animals; it is very lean, since it has little blood. And so it is very fearful, since heat, which is the spur of boldness, is diminished in it. The cause of its fearfulness is also that its color is variable and changeable from moment to moment. It lays eggs in the manner of hens and produces young from them. In this kind, moreover, there is no male or female, but all lay eggs. Pope Alexander, it is said, had a garment made from this animal's wool, which, when it needed to be cleaned, was washed with no other water than being thrown into the fire, through which it grew white-hot.

Avicenna, in the passage above: the salamander is a kind of biting creature; from drinking it come violent pains in the anus, and a swelling like dropsy, and spasm in the belly, and retention of urine.

Avicenna, in the same: the salamander is thought to be a beast similar to a lizard, having four feet and a short tail, and that it is not itself burned, but, if thrown on a hearth, extinguishes the fire. From its bite come violent pain and swelling in the body, and heaviness of the tongue, and a stinging in it, and trembling and numbness. Often too a blackness of the limb follows, in a round shape, and a falling-off of it. Its treatment, as some have said, is the same as for cantharides. And the specific treatment is to give pine resin with honey as a drink. Lily decoction too is given with nettle leaves. Some, however, give boiled frogs and their broth as a drink.
Pliny, book 32: sea-turtle flesh mixed with frog flesh gives excellent help against salamanders.

Dioscorides: the salamander's power is astringent and hot, and is rightly mixed into astringent medicines, and removes unwanted hairs from the eyelids. It is kept in this way: it is disemboweled, its head and feet removed, and thus what remains is placed in honey and used when needed.

Isidore: as for the 'saura' [lizard]: when it grows old, its eyes go blind, and it enters a hole in a wall facing east, and, looking toward the rising sun, is given light. The stellio has its name from its color, for its back is marked with shining spots in the manner of stars, of which Ovid says: 'and, suited to its color, it has a name, its body starred with varied spots.' This creature is said to be so hostile to scorpions that, once seen, it brings them fear and numbness.

Pliny: stellios too, like snakes, shed their old age and immediately devour it, thereby forestalling remedies for epilepsy [that would otherwise be made from it]. They say these are deadly in Greece, but harmless in Sicily.

Chameleons and stellios have in a way the same nature, since they live on dew. Stellios are thought harmless only to those who themselves lack blood. They give birth to eleven at a time. Some think ten of these are devoured by the mother, and only one, the shrewdest, is left, which, placing itself on the mother's haunches, is safe from both her tail and her bite, and becomes the avenger of the rest, finally destroying its parents in old age.

A rather deceitful creature; they say it envies man, and hence the name 'stellio' came to be applied to a bad man. Thus they catch it: in summer they watch for its resting place, which is in doorways or window-hinges or in vaulted rooms or tombs. There, at the start of spring, they set woven traps of split reeds against it, in whose narrowness it delights, so as more easily to shed its stiffness; but once it enters, it cannot go back.
Gloss: the stellio has no wings, and so relies on its hands, and so on.
Radulfus of Flaix: the stellio and the lizard are feeble animals, yet malicious and venomous reptiles.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the stellio's venom is deadly; against it the remedy is made from ground scorpion flesh. Its gall, ground in water, is said to gather weasels by a certain hidden instinct: it is especially opposed to the scorpion, and they pursue each other with a natural hatred. But because the stellio is larger and stronger, the scorpion fears it remarkably, so much so that, on seeing it, it is drenched in cold sweat.

Pliny: the sight of the stellio brings fear to the scorpion and the numbness of cold sweat, whence they also putrefy it in oil and anoint wounds made by scorpions with it; but ground scorpion is also effective against the stellio's venom. A harmful medicine too is made from stellios, for, one having died in wine, whoever drinks it has his face covered with freckles - for which reason mistresses, plotting against a rival's beauty, kill it in an ointment. But the remedy against this is egg-yolk and honey and soda. The gall of stellios too, ground in water, is said to gather weasels.
Pliny, in the same: for epileptic seizures nothing from the stellio helps, even ash made from it drunk in vinegar, or its shed skin drunk.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the 'guaril,' that is the stellio, has a long tail and a small head, and is not the lizard. For the lizard is rarely or never found except in the country. Its head and body, too, differ from the lizard's, though perhaps it is closest to it in nature. Its flesh is very hot. In it is a power that draws out splinters and thorns. Its blood benefits the white film of the eyes. Its fat strongly fattens, and so does its flesh, especially for certain women. Its dung, like the lizard's, is good for the white film of the eye; it also benefits eye-films and freckles, and produces a good complexion. The same dung, ground, eradicates warts. Stellio liver, placed on decayed molars, calms their pain.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: stellio flesh is deadly; sometimes it falls into wine and dies in it and dissolves, and that wine becomes like a poison, and one who drinks it suffers vomiting and violent pain in the mouth of the stomach. When the stellio bites, it leaves in the site of its bite small, fine, black teeth. And the place does not stop aching and itching, until they are removed with a needle, or by a cupping-instrument passed over them that takes them up and gathers them. Sometimes, however, oil and ash extract them. Then the place is sucked and put in warm water, and if the pain from the bite grows greater, theriac of 'rutela' is given as a drink.

Haly Abbas: the 'papion,' that is the sword-stellio, if boiled with vinegar and chickpea, clearly benefits arthritic conditions. Stellio dung removes freckles from the face and clears the white film from the eyes.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: let this suffice concerning the kinds of lizards. There follows the third kind of reptiles, that is, worms.

Isidore: the worm is an animal that for the most part is born from flesh, or wood, or any earthly matter, or without any earthly coupling, although some are also born from eggs, like the scorpion. The worm, however, does not crawl like the serpent with open steps or efforts of scales, since it has no rigid spine as the snake does, but, extending forward the contracted parts of its little body in a line, and contracting the extended ones, it unfolds its movement, and thus, driven, glides along.

Aristotle: worms crawl on their belly. Certain animals generate worms, and of these some move at the very hour of their generation, some not until days later; flies, indeed, generate worms. And from the mating of bees come worms similar to eggs. Further, those things generated from worms are, when generated from animals, not complete, then grow outside. And what has the shape of a worm becomes large as it grows, and its shape becomes like an egg, since the outer covering, that is the enclosing skin, hardens. At that time, too, they are mobile, and this is shown in the worms generated from wasps and bees, and in those generated from vegetables. Worms generated from animals feed at first, then take no food, but remain motionless, like the little golden-colored ones. Some worms, however, have within themselves what feeds them and expel the excess of food, like the young of wasps or bees. Some feed from outside, like the worms of vegetables and other kinds. The beginning of a worm's growth is from the upper part, and its food from the lower.

Ambrose: the black Indian worm is said first to be changed into the appearance of a cabbage-stalk, afterward to become a silkworm, and afterward, with loose and broader leaves, seems to take on wings. From these leaves those soft things are made with which those in kings' houses are clothed.

Pliny, book 11: Statius Sebosus affirms that in the Ganges there are worms with paired arms sixty cubits long, sea-blue in color, named from their appearance, of which mention has already been made above among the sea monsters, and more will be said below.
Ground worms of the earth benefit, applied to a scorpion's sting, and many other remedies are found from them, for which they are kept in honey.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: those are properly called worms which are born from putrefaction, and so are born from flesh or from earth, without mating and desire. Their nature is to move at every moment; they creep in silence, bite and penetrate; they are vile and lowly, often trodden underfoot. Salt resists their origin, and so flesh and other foods are salted.
Al-Kindi, in the book on poisons: if a garden is sprinkled with the water in which worms have been boiled, then its fruits, the worms that eat them will quickly die.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: every propagation of worms is called 'insecta.' No insect, that is, worm, as Pliny says, has blood except in a modest quantity. Some worms are without feet, like serpents, and these crawl over the ground. Others have neither bones nor feet, and these draw themselves along rather by certain very fine wrinkles stretched in their skin. Others have two feet, others four, and these run and have a little blood. Others, however, have more than four feet, and these too run, but lack blood entirely, since the blood passes into nourishment for the many feet, or because the movement of those feet dissolves the blood. Every kind of worm has a moisture like discharge in place of blood. There is, moreover, another kind of worm that has feet and walks, and nevertheless, having wings or rather a membrane, is lifted flying into the air, and these live especially on the leaves of trees and gnaw them with their teeth; some worms of the flying kind, however, do not gnaw at all, but rather live on moist things. Worms in general, moreover, according to the nourishment of the elements, take on colors or powers, so that those that partake much of the element of fire seek the upper air; those that partake much of water or earth are naturally slower. For according to this the order of visible creatures is arranged. In the region of Chelidonia, as Augustine says, in certain naturally hot waters there are worms just as there are fish in cold water. And when they come out of the hot water into the cold, they die. Although the name 'worm,' however, applies to all worms, that one is specifically called the worm which is generated from pure and clean earth with no admixture of seed, by which too a hook is baited to deceive and catch fish; and to this the Lord, born of the Virgin, compares himself through the prophet, saying: 'But I am a worm, and no man.'

Isidore: worms are of the earth, or of water, or of air, or of flesh, or of leaves, or of wood, or of clothing; properly, however, the worm is born in rotting flesh. The moth is in clothing, the caterpillar in vegetables, the shipworm in wood, the 'tarmus' in bacon. Worms of the flesh are the migraine-worm, the roundworm, the pinworm, the 'costi,' lice, fleas, nits, the 'tarmus,' the tick, the 'usia,' the belly-bug. The migraine-worm is a worm of the head; the roundworm is of the belly or intestines, so called as if 'lumbicus,' since it slips [labitur], or because it is in the loins [lumbis]. The 'usia' is a worm of the pig, so called because it burns; for wherever it bites, the spot burns so much that blisters form. The tick is called the dog-worm, since it clings in dogs' ears; the louse is of the head, the 'tarmus' of bacon.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: there are many kinds of worms; when they begin with summer and end with summer, since they are born more from corruption than from seed. There is, however, another kind that begins with summer and, once it has laid its seed on trees or in dwellings, ends its life with summer, and the seeds remain once the parents are dead through the winter, and, in springtime, as the mildness of the air and the sun's warmth come forth, are quickened to life. There is also another kind that hides itself in winter and lies hidden as if dead, and when summer comes is renewed to life.

Petrus Comestor: it is asked, moreover, concerning certain such tiny creatures, which are wont to be born either from carcasses or from moisture, whether they were created on the sixth day. Of these there are six kinds. For some come into being from exhalations, like gnats from wine, moths from water. Some from the corruption of moisture, like worms in cisterns. Some from carcasses, like bees from oxen, beetles and hornets from horses. Some from the corruption of wood, like shipworms. Some from the corruption of fruits, like weevils from beans. Of these, then, it is said that those born without corruption, like those made from exhalations, were made then, at creation; but those born from corruptions arose from corrupted matter after sin.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of these, moreover, some are called 'ringed,' since their bodies seem to be formed and marked off, as it were, by rings; of these some fly, like bees; some walk, like ants and those properly called worms. These same kinds, according to Aristotle, are also called 'wrinkled,' according to Pliny, 'insects.'

Aristotle: an animal is called ringed and wrinkled because it has wrinklings in its body, front and back; this kind has no blood, and its ringed structure is either on the belly or on the back, or on both. Nor is there in bodies of this kind a bone separate by itself, nor flesh, but something else, whose composition is between flesh and bone, since bodies of this kind are, in the same way, hard both within and without. In those, however, that are of long body and many feet, the ringed structure is uniform. There are nine kinds of ringed animals, of which six gather in groups, like flocks, among which are wasps and bees, but three kinds are solitary. All ringed creatures, indeed, remain in their dens in winter, unless they are domestic, and some remain there long, some briefly. Bees remain in their hives during days of great cold, and remain after the setting of the Pleiades until springtime. Some ringed creatures shed old age, and among these are those that have covered wings. And those animals that give birth to live young cast off a web; those, however, that give birth to worms cast off what is called the 'fallator'; the same happens to wasps and locusts. In the body of a ringed animal there is no part that is by itself distinctly earthy, but, compared to bone, it is fleshy, compared to flesh, it is earthy. All these have three parts, namely the head and the belly and a third part between them, just as in others there is the chest and the back, and that middle part in most is single. Likewise ringed-bodied animals are creatures of much labor, like ants and bees and spiders.

Pliny: insects are creatures of immense fineness, and nowhere is nature's whole art more present than in the smallest things. And rightly they are called 'insecta' [cut into], from the cuttings which mark off, now the places of the neck, now of the chest and belly, separate parts joined by a thin, tube-like connection. Some, however, are not marked by a complete encircling notch, but only by overlapping, flexible ridges on the belly or above, nowhere else is nature's craftsmanship more remarkable.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: among ringed creatures, the male is smaller, the female larger. In bees and wasps, cuttings appear all around, since in these there is no respiration or lung, but they are nourished through their whole body by the whole surrounding air. And so, drenched in oil, they die, their pores blocked, and revive when vinegar is quickly applied, their passages opened.

Aristotle: the feet of a ringed-bodied animal bend to the sides, and its stings bend inward. In those, however, that are of long body and many feet, the ringed structure is uniform; and such animals are wont to live a while even after the head is cut off, as will be said below. Some ringed creatures mate while walking, and have hind feet larger than the front ones. Some mate and bend their feet backward, like four-footed animals, and the formation of their bodies is not like flesh within a shell, but between the two. And so they have no bone or spine, and are protected only by the hardness of their body, and this kind has a skin that is a thin membrane. Likewise, among ringed-skinned animals, some have many feet, because of their slowness and natural coldness, so that their movement may be lighter; and so a naturally cold animal came to have many feet: because of the length of its body and the abundance of its flesh, its body was ringed and had many feet. But that among them which is of small body and little flesh has fewer feet than others, and especially the solitary flying kind. In the bodies of certain such animals, the two front feet are larger, since their eyes are hard and they do not see with sharp sight, and they cannot fly except by the power of the front feet; but this is done by the fly kind and those forms resembling bees. The hind feet, however, are larger than the middle ones, for walking and so that they may be lifted quickly from the ground when they wish to fly, and what results from these mating is more evident in creatures like locusts and fleas, for these bend their feet by contracting them, then extend them, and are thus lifted from the ground; a bending inward in the feet is indeed necessary. The front feet, however, cannot be arranged this way, and all these kinds have six feet, with two additional feet by which they mate.

Pliny: the feet of insects move obliquely, and the outer ones of some curve outward, as in locusts. The front feet of insects are longer in those having hard eyes, so that they may wipe them repeatedly with their feet, as we notice in flies. Those among these that have long hind feet leap, like locusts. All of these, moreover, have half-feet; certain spiders have a pair of very long ones added, and three joints to each.

Aristotle: among ringed creatures, then, some have wings, like bees and wasps, but some do not, like ants. There is also a kind that flies by night and appears like fire. Likewise, of those having wings, some have only two, like flies. Others, however, four, like bees. There are also those that have a wing-covering resembling a shell. And none of these wings has a shaft, as the wings of birds do. And some of them have markings above the eyes, like little bees; none having membranous wings has a sting. Those, however, that have only two wings sting with a sting that is on the inside of their head, like gnats and the horse-flies and flies that trouble beasts. Solitary flying creatures of small body and little flesh have fewer feet than the rest. Those, however, that fly in company have four wings and are of light body, like bees and similar creatures, and have two feet on the right and two on the left, and have no more than four feet, so as not to hinder their flight. What among such animals is small has only two wings, like the fly kind. And what among these is small, having a fixed course of life, has many wings, like bees, and its wings are membranous, like the wasp's, so that its wings may be preserved. And since that creature is fixed and of little movement, opportunity comes to it more quickly than to animals of good movement. Its wing, moreover, is split in two, and has nothing resembling a shaft, and the wings are membranous, not feathered. And necessarily that web is separated from the body, since the fleshy part in them grows cold. And through this ringed structure the body gathers together and becomes short, having been long. And what in them is not enclosed becomes very hard, when it contracts and draws together in itself. This is evident in the wasp, since when it is afraid it does not move and becomes very hard. But an animal cannot exist having only two wings and also having a sting, since it is weak and lacks blood. And what has many wings has them because of the size of its body and for strength together with the parts that are behind, that is, what is in the place of the shoulders, because of its sharpness.

Pliny, in the passage above: insects are many and of many kinds, in the life of land creatures and of flying ones. Some indeed, like bees, are feathered. Others walk, like ants. Others do both, like locusts, some lack both wings and feet. Some, then, bear two wings, like flies; some four, like bees; some fly with membranes too, like cicadas. Those armed with stings in the belly have four wings. None that has a weapon in its mouth flies with more than two wings. For to the latter it was given for the sake of vengeance, to the former for the sake of appetite; in none of them do torn-off wings grow back, and none that has a sting in its belly has only two wings. In all insects the wings are without a slit, and none has a tail except the scorpion.

Aristotle: certain ringed-bodied animals have a sting for strength and benefit. What among such creatures lacks a sting has, in the front part of the body, certain teeth, some for taking food and some for feeling, like ants and the bee kind. But an animal cannot exist having only two wings and having a sting in the hind part of the body, since it is weak and lacks blood. And none having membranous wings has a sting. Those, however, that have only two wings sting with a sting that is in the front of their head, like the horse-flies and the flies that trouble beasts. And so some ringed creatures have their weapon within, like the wasp, some outside, like the scorpion, which has a long tail and two stings. No animal having a weapon behind has only two wings, but four. As has been said, the feet of ringed creatures bend to the sides. Their stings, however, bend inward. Likewise certain ringed creatures have an organ by which they perceive food from outside, like a sting, for through it they draw in and taste their food, which is evident in flies and bees and creatures like them, and the nature of this organ is soft and hollow. Through this organ, indeed, the flies that trouble beasts pierce the hide of an ox and other animals, for it has the power of lips and tongue, and in some it is a sting located within the teeth. And so in some the sting is near the place of the tongue, and in some near the place of the tail; and in some it is within the body, in some outside. For if the sting of bees and wasps were outside, it would easily be damaged because of its weakness and fineness. And if the sting were outside, as the scorpion's sting is, it would be a cause of heaviness. The sting that resembles a tongue is for drawing in food, just as the elephant's trunk is suited both for strength and for the use of food. What has the sting in the hind part of the body has it there because it uses it as a weapon. The bee, when it stings, dies as it casts out its sting, because the sting cannot come out unless its intestine comes out with it.
Pliny: [on] insects, of flies, of butterflies, of bees, of the horse-fly, of the gnat, of flies. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: ringed-bodied animals, especially those of many feet and long body, live a while even after the head is cut off, unless they are of a cold nature and quickly grow cold because of the smallness of their body. For we too often see that they are cut in two and live for some time. This indeed will happen if the head is cut off along with the chest, otherwise not at all. All ringed creatures, however, die when anointed with oil, and also when their head is anointed with oil and they are placed facing the sun.

Pliny, in the passage above: some have reported that insects lack blood. And many have denied that they breathe, persuading themselves of this too by reasoning, since through their inner organs there is no passage for breath; and so they said that they live as trees and crops do. But it matters a great deal whether something lives or breathes. For the same reason they also said these creatures have no blood, since it is present in no creature lacking a heart and liver; and so they deny breath to those lacking a lung too: and so they deny that these creatures even have a voice, despite the loud sound of cicadas and the humming of bees. Likewise insects do not seem to have sinews, nor bones, nor spine, nor cartilage, nor flesh, nor fat, nor even a fragile shell, as certain sea creatures have; nor can it rightly be called skin, but a body of a certain nature midway between all of these. Nor again is there anything else within, except, in very few, a coiled intestine. And so, when they are torn apart, there is a remarkable vitality, and each separate part throbs. For whatever principle of life there is, it is present not in fixed limbs, but in the whole body; least of all, however, in the head, and this alone does not move unless torn off together with the chest. In a certain kind, however, there are more feet, and among these, several live longer once torn apart, as we see in centipedes. With oil, indeed, not only bees but all insects are killed, especially if their head, anointed, is placed in the sun. Likewise, of insects, the feathered kind mostly die in autumn; horseflies even from blindness. But flies killed by moisture, if buried in ash, come back to life.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it has already been said above that bees and wasps, drenched in oil, die, their pores blocked, and revive when vinegar is quickly applied, their passages opened.

Aristotle: all kinds of such animals have eyes, and no other organ of sense is clearly evident at all. And some of them, as has been said, have an organ resembling a tongue. Each of them, moreover, has an organ by which it takes in food, sometimes soft, sometimes hard; this organ is, in the kind lacking a weapon, in the place of the shoulders, nor is it present in animals having teeth, except in a few kinds; with this organ flies and horse-flies sting and draw blood. Certain ringed-bodied animals have all the senses, for they perceive from a distance by a fine sense, like the bee kind. Some too die from the smell of sulphur; and if one sprinkles powdered sulphur and wild marjoram over ants' nests, they will be driven off by it. Certain ringed creatures have something akin to blood, and are of greater and finer intelligence than blooded animals, like bees, ants, and the like. Likewise a ringed animal breathes through a web at the wall and perceives kinds of smell. Some of these, however, have eyes and lack eyelids; and so nature made their eyes especially mobile; and such an animal has an organ between the mouth, by which it senses food, like the ant kind. An animal lacking a lung and drinking little water lacks a bladder and does not take in water as drink, but only for food, like ringed creatures and fish. Ringed creatures, moreover, have no veins nor do they breathe, nor do they have anything but the organ that necessarily corresponds to the heart. For the organ in which the sensation of the soul resides, and which is the cause of life, must necessarily be at the origin of the body's parts in every living creature. And indeed all such creatures have organs suited to food, but they differ in location, since the places that receive food vary. Finally, in a ringed animal, an organ has been found in which the sensitive power resides, between the head and the rest of the body, which contains the head: the noise of such an animal is within the body and is not produced by breath going out, since it does not breathe, as is evident in bees and the like. Among these, moreover, are creatures having a sweet voice, like the small animal resembling a locust that hisses by night. The noise and hiss of all of these, moreover, is produced through a web beneath the wall-like covering at the site of the body's division into two, as is evident in bees and the like. These indeed make noise only in flying, by extending and contracting their wings, and this through the air falling between the body and the wings. Locusts do likewise. Such animals, moreover, sleep, since they are still at night and do not cry out, since they do not see, although all animals having hard eyes have weak sight. And so, if one holds a candle to them at night, one will see them at rest. There is, moreover, a certain kind of such animal that gives voice by night and has no mouth, but a long organ that grows above the head, similar to a tongue, and that organ is not split, nor is there any excess matter in the animal's belly.

Pliny: insects, as has been said, are creatures of immense fineness, and nowhere is nature's art more entirely present than in the smallest things: such creatures have senses and eyes, touch, and taste, some also smell, few also hearing.

Aristotle: among ringed creatures, some are generated by mating, some by themselves, and some produce worms; and that which is generated having the shape of a worm, when it grows, becomes large, and its shape becomes like an egg, since the enclosing covering, that is the skin, hardens, and then it is motionless. The cause of this is that nature, as it were, prepares the formation of eggs before its proper time, because of the lack of completion. For worms grow after this growth and produce a soft egg; and this happens in other kinds too, which are not generated by mating, but from wool. All these kinds are at first motionless. And when the covering enclosing them dries and splits, then they come out, just as complete animals come out from animals, and their emergence is in the third generation. Flying creatures among them, indeed, are larger than walking ones; and this is remarkable to many people, namely that worms generated from animals feed at first, then take no food, but remain motionless, like the little golden-colored ones, and wasps from worms. The nature of eggs, when complete, does not grow, but they grow at their first formation and take in food until what is within is divided; and then the eggs are complete. Some worms, however, have within themselves what feeds them, and expel from themselves the excess of food, like the young of wasps and bees. Others, however, take food from outside, like the worms of all other kinds. Ringed creatures that mate while walking have hind feet larger than the front. Some, however, mate and bend their feet backward like four-footed creatures. Likewise a ringed animal mates in winter, if there is a favorable, southerly wind, especially those that build nests, like the ant and the fly. Ringed creatures, however, are separated only with difficulty, since mating lasts a long time in them, as is evident in flies and spiders. This kind mates from behind, the smaller upon the larger, that is, the male mounts the female. They grow fat at the time of their generation, especially if the season of spring is warm and moist. Some ringed creatures, then, come from mating and produce animals like themselves; some, however, mate and produce something unlike in kind, since they produce only worms and are not from animals; but some are from moist things and some from dry things, like the little bee and the fly and the beetle; some, however, are not from animals nor do they mate, like gnats and horse-flies and the like; in some of these the female places on the male an organ that receives the sperm, and this kind remains entwined together in mating for a long time. And when they separate, they give birth quickly, and only to something incomplete, since all such kinds produce worms. Likewise those kinds that do not always produce sperm remain bound together for a long time, until the sustaining of what has been received is complete, as ringed-bodied animals mate.
Pliny: most insects produce a little worm; for ants too generate something like eggs.

Isidore: bees [apes] are so named either because they bind themselves together by their feet [a pedibus], or because they are born without feet, for afterward they receive both feet and wings, and so on.

Aristotle: the bee is a ringed-bodied animal, having an organ or appendage coming out from its mouth, by which it tastes and draws in and receives food; it lacks blood, and has teeth similar to the teeth of other animals. It flies in company and is of light body, and has four wings, and has two feet on the right and two on the left, and has no more than four, lest they hinder its flight; this animal does not take in air, does not breathe: animals that eat many foods are of varied color over the greater part of their body. And so the color of bees is uniform, but the color of wasps varied. They eat honey especially in time of need. Whence, when they begin to fall ill, a lessening of the honey appears, since they eat from it and do not replenish it: they love pleasant smells and delight in running waters.

Pliny: nature gave bees a weapon joined to the belly. Some think that once this is fixed by a single sting, they die at once; some, that this happens only if it is driven in so deep that the intestine follows it out, but that afterward they are drones and do not make honey, but, as it were castrated of their powers, are equally able to harm and to benefit. There are examples of horses killed by them. They rejoice in clapping and the ringing of bronze, and are called together by it.
Pliny, in the same: bees dead in honey soften the hard edges of ulcers.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: bees love cleanliness, hate cold and stench and smoke. They fly in swarms, are diligent about their work and cast out the idle; they are rough outside, but have sweetness within; they are quickly hurt and quick to hurt, and, once their sting is lost, are useless.

Pliny: among all insects, the bee holds the first place. Born for man's sake alone among this kind, they gather honey, the sweetest, finest, and most wholesome juice, and fashion combs and wax. They endure labor similar to the tasks of human life, they complete works. They have a commonwealth, and always private councils and leaders in groups. And, most remarkable of all, they have morals, and know nothing that is not held in common.
Aristotle: the bee is cleaner than other animals. And so it casts out its dung while flying, since it has a strong stench. For a foul smell burdens bees, but a sweet one delights them.
