Ambrose: bees seem to tend a kind of commonwealth: these alone, among every kind of living creature, have offspring shared in common, and dwell in a single home. Their labor is shared by all, their food shared, their harvest shared, their flight shared, their generation shared.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: bees surpass other animals in dignity and usefulness, in splendid gifts and nobility; they flourish in agility, vigor, spirit, and subtlety of intelligence. All have virginal bodily integrity, and yet suddenly produce a very great swarm of offspring.

Virgil: they alone have offspring in common, share a common dwelling within their city, and pass their life under great laws, and know their own country and fixed household gods, and, mindful of the coming winter, undertake their labor in summer and store what they gather for the common good. For some watch over the food supply, and, by settled agreement, work in the fields; part, within the enclosure of their home, lay the first foundations of the combs from the tears of narcissus and sticky gum from bark, then hang up the clinging wax; others lead forth the grown young, the hope of the race; others pack in the purest honey and swell the cells with clear nectar. There are some to whom the guarding of the gate has fallen by lot, and in turn they watch the waters and the clouds of the sky, or receive the burdens of those arriving, or, forming ranks, drive the idle drones from the hive. All labor is one, the rest from work is one for all.

Ambrose: although the bee is feeble in body, it is strong in the vigor of wisdom and virtue: for what architect taught bees to arrange their swarms, distinguishing them by rank, and to hang fine wax between the roofs of their houses, and to store honey, and to swell their storehouses, woven through with flowers, with a certain nectar?

Aristotle: bees perceive from a distance what they do only by a fine sense. Some go out to work at the start of the day, and some remain still until others wake; then they fly out and go out together to work, but when they return, they buzz loudly at first, then their noise gradually quiets, until one of them remains flying and circling about, as if signaling that it is now time to sleep. Then they all rest together. They have, indeed, a greater fineness of intelligence than many blooded animals. They know winter, since then they do not go out or fly from the hives, but wander about within, and the guards thus know a coming rain. And when they hang inside the hives, it signals of itself that they wish to leave the hive. All of them, moreover, cast out their dung while flying, or in a small chamber of their own.

Pliny, on winter: for whence would they have the strength to endure frosts and snows and the blasts of the north wind? They shut themselves in on the third day before the Ides of October, that is, at the setting of the Pleiades in the evening, and remain hidden past their rising; before the beans flower they do not go out to their tasks and labors, and no day is lost in idleness when the sky permits. First they build the combs, fashion the wax, that is, make the houses and cells, then the brood, and afterward honey, wax from flowers, and bee-glue from the tears of trees, which produce a gluey substance. Those that carry loads seek a favorable wind, and if a storm arises, they steady themselves by grasping little pebbles with their tiny feet; but near the ground they fly against a headwind, sheltered by brambles. They observe wondrous discipline in their work; they note the idleness of those who slacken, and punish them, even with death, and there is remarkable cleanliness in their work. They remove everything from their midst, and no filth lies among their labors. Indeed, the excrement of those working within, lest it be carried too far off, is gathered in one place and carried out on stormy days when work is idle. And as evening comes on, there is less and less noise in the hive, until one flies around with the same buzzing or murmur with which it roused them, as if ordering rest to be taken, in the manner of a military camp. And then all fall suddenly silent. And, most remarkable of all, they have morals, and know nothing except what is common.

Ambrose: bees mingle in no coupling, nor are they undone by lust, nor shaken by the pains of childbirth, but, preserving the virginal integrity of their bodies, suddenly produce a very great swarm of offspring.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: to these words of Ambrose the statements of Aristotle seem to be opposed.

Pliny, in the passage above: how bees produce their young has been a great matter of dispute among the learned, for their mating has never been observed. Most have thought it must be accomplished from gathered flowers. And some think it comes from the mating of the one called king in any given swarm, and that he alone is male, chiefly so that his size may not fail. And so, they say, no brood is produced without him, and the rest of the bees accompany him as females do a male, not as followers do a leader. This otherwise probable opinion, however, is refuted by the origin of drones; for what reasoning would allow that the same mating produces some perfect, others imperfect offspring - a nearer or prior conjecture, were it not that yet another difficulty arises? For indeed there are sometimes born, at the edges of the combs, larger bees, which drive off the rest. What is certain is that they brood in the manner of hens; what hatches appears at first as a small white worm, lying crosswise and clinging, so that it seems to be feeding. The king, at once of honey color, as if made from the choicest flower of the whole gathering, is not a worm but immediately winged; the rest of the crowd, once they begin to take shape, are called nymphs, as are the drones, the 'sirenes,' and the 'cephenes.' If one removes the heads of either kind before they have wings, they are most welcome food for the mothers. As time goes on, they drip in food and brood, humming loudest at this time, for the sake, it is thought, of producing the heat necessary for hatching the young, until, the membranes broken that surround each one like eggs, the whole troop emerges together. This was observed at Rome, in the suburban estate of a certain consular man, in hives made with horn panes translucent like a lantern; the brood is completed within forty-five days. There occurs, moreover, in certain combs, what is called the 'clerus,' a bitter hardness of wax, when they have not brought forth brood from it because of disease, or laziness, or natural sterility - this is the miscarriage of bees.

Aristotle: we, however, say that bees are generated from bees, since they mate with one another. And kings are generated from kings. Other bees come from bees of this adulterated kind, either all from kings, or from the 'cicine,' those called the females of bees. Bees resemble kings in their sting and their vigor; the 'cicine,' however, resemble kings in size, and, if they had a sting, would be kings. It is necessary, however, that kings come from something. And since they are not from bees nor from the 'cicine,' they must necessarily be from kings. From the mating of the little bees a worm resembling an egg is produced, and no other animal will be generated from them if it remains so. And so the offspring of bees neither resemble their own kind nor differ entirely from it, since worms come out from them. At the first formation of bees and similar creatures, the lower part is small, the upper part large. And no monstrosity occurs in bee or wasp, since each of them has its own young in its own cell. Since, then, kings are created for the purpose of generation, they always remain within the hive and do nothing, and have a large body for the sake of generation; otherwise, unless the generation of bees came from them, they would not be left within the hive doing nothing. The 'cicine,' however, are the idle males of the bees, since they do not have an organ suited to fighting, because of the heaviness of their body. Bees, however, are of a size midway between these two kinds, and according to this are suited to the formation of young. Just as it happens with the lioness, that she gives birth to five cubs, then fewer, until she comes down to one, so it happens with the kings of bees, that at first they produce many, afterward few, since the excess matters in the body are lessened. That the generation of bees comes from mating, namely between kings and bees, is shown by the sign that they are found in the cells of the hive.

Isidore: bees, as has been said above, are so called in one way because they are born without feet, for after they are born, they receive both feet and wings. Very many, however, have observed that they are born from the carcasses of oxen, for, to produce them, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten, and from the putrefied gore worms are created, which afterward become bees.
Isidore: bees are born from bull-hide buried in the earth; from donkey-hide, however, wasps; from the dung of flies, the caterpillar; from orach plants, frogs; from air infected by breath, gnats.

Aristotle: bees gather their brood from leaves and grasses with their mouths, and suddenly produce a very great swarm of offspring, and while other birds scarcely produce a single brood a year, bees produce twins, and outweigh the rest by a double fertility.

Aristotle: in rainy years the young of bees multiply greatly, since, because of the moisture, excess matter multiplies in the bodies of the kings. In years of temperate complexion, however, a lessening occurs in the young. It is said, moreover, that when a young one is lost in some place, the leader at once seeks it out until it finds it, since it recognizes it by its smell; the 'cicin' and the drone do nothing, but corrupt the works of others, and so the good bees overcome them and kill their leaders, since they draw out the young of the bees. Bees, indeed, after they make wax, begin to produce young, and while they are producing young, nothing prevents the young and the honey and the 'cicines,' that is the male bees, from being gathered together in the same wax. The king of the bees does not leave the hive except with a great escort of bees, and he himself is in the middle. He goes out, however, three days before the young come out. Then a few bees go out and fly around the hive. And when the young gather together, they will fly and separate among themselves, and there a single company forms around each king.

Pliny, on bees, in the passage above: at the edges of the combs, moreover, larger bees are sometimes born, which drive off the rest. But once the membranes surrounding each of the young bees are broken, the whole troop emerges together in the manner of eggs. Further, the brood is completed within forty-five days. And once brought forth, by a certain discipline, they at once work alongside their mothers, and the young king is accompanied by a crowd of the same age. Several kings are begun, nor does offspring from these afterward cease, once it has grown up; by common agreement they kill the worst of them, lest they divide the swarms.

Aristotle: among the kind of bees, as among other ringed creatures, the male is smaller and the female larger. The female of the leader, moreover, is double the size of the better bee; males lack stings, and sometimes wish to sting as if with a sting, but cannot; male bees, however, are killed when the space they occupy grows too crowded. For a multitude of males in the hive does not make the bees more industrious. The bodies of young bees are soft, and those of old ones hard. The kind of bee that is strong makes hard honey, and it is said these are the young bees, since they are not yet practiced in the craft; moreover, young bees by no means sting as forcefully as old ones do.

Pliny, in the passage above: some think bees are produced by the mating of the one called king in any given swarm, and that he alone is male, chiefly so that his size may not fail, that is, be lacking. And so they say that without him no brood is produced, and that the rest of the bees accompany him as females do a male, not as followers do a leader.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: it is said that if the leader of the bees is alive, the males will be on one side; but if he has died, the males will be within, with the females. Finally, since males are solitary, they occupy several cells, and males often build cells for themselves. And it is better for the bees when there are few males with them, since a multitude of males does not make them more industrious. The bodies of young bees are soft, and those of old ones hard. Young bees, too, by no means sting as forcefully as old ones do. Old bees, however, make sweeter honey than young ones, since they have experience.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the leaders of bees are of two kinds; the better is reddish, the other black. The female of the leader is double the size of the female bees.

Ambrose: bees appoint their king not by chance, but by judgment, and, although placed under a king, are nevertheless free, since they hold the prerogative of judgment and the affection of loyal devotion, and love their king as if established by themselves. This king, moreover, is formed with clear marks of distinction by nature, so that he excels both in bodily size and in appearance, and, what is most important in a king, in gentleness of character: for even though he has a sting, he does not use it for vengeance. For these are laws of nature, not written in letters, but impressed in character, that those who hold the greatest power should be the more lenient in punishing. But bees that do not obey the laws of their king punish themselves with the condemnation of penance, so that they die of the wound of their own sting. Finally, they defend their king himself with the utmost protection, and think it a fine thing to perish for him. While the king is unharmed, they know neither how to change their judgment nor to alter their mind. But once he is lost, they abandon their loyalty to their duty, and themselves plunder their own honey, because the one who held the leadership of the task has been killed. Not the Indians, not the peoples of the Sarmatians, observe so great a reverence of devotion as bees do; so that none dares leave the hive or go to any pasture, unless the king has gone out and claimed for himself the leadership of the flight.

Aristotle: bees, like cranes, have watchful kings over them, whom they obey. The leaders of bees are of two kinds; the better is reddish, the other black; the female of the leader is double the size of the bee that is better. If the king falls from the hive, the bees at once raise him up and place a support beneath him. The cells in which the kings dwell are only at the end. And their number is great; bees come from kings, and kings are generated by themselves. Since, however, kings, as said above, are created for the purpose of generation, they always remain within the hive and do nothing, and have a large body for the sake of generation. These, as fathers, strike and expel the male bees. For it is good that fathers should punish idle sons. There are, however, few kings, and the bees generated by them, since at the first time they produce many, and at the second few, because the excess matters in the body are diminished. The kings of bees do not leave the hive except with all the bees. For if a little bee is lost, the leader of the bees seeks it by flying around it. Bees especially die, moreover, if there are many leaders; sometimes they abandon their own king and flee to the king who rules over more, and if the first king pursues them, they kill him.

Seneca, in the book on clemency: bees are most quick to anger and, for their size, most pugnacious, and leave their stings in the wound. The king himself is without a sting; nature took the weapon from him and left his anger unarmed. Great kings should take this as an example; it would be shameful not to draw a lesson in conduct from such small creatures, since men's minds ought to be the more restrained the more forcefully they can do harm.

Pliny, book 11: when the leader has been carried off by death, the common bees grieve with idle sorrow; they do not bring food, do not go forth, but gather about his body with a mournful murmur, and, unless helped, die of hunger. The brood of bees, once brought forth, by a certain discipline at once work alongside their mothers, and the young king is accompanied by a crowd of the same age. Several kings are begun, nor does offspring from these cease afterward, once it has grown up. There are two kinds of them, the black and the mottled, the better one always of outstanding form and twice as large as the rest, with shorter wings, straight legs, a darker mark on the forehead shining like a diadem, and differing much from the common bees in brightness. Nor is it agreed among authors whether the king alone has no sting, armed only with majesty, or whether nature indeed gave him one, but only denied him its use. What is agreed, however, is that the ruler does not use his sting, and there is a remarkable obedience of the common people toward him. When he goes forth, the whole swarm is one, and gathers around him, encircles him, protects him, does not allow him to be seen. At other times, when the people are at work, he himself goes about within, urging them on, as it were. He alone is exempt. Around him are certain attendants and constant guardian lictors. He goes forth outside with his authority only when the swarm is about to migrate. And this is understood several days beforehand by a murmur buzzing within, as preparations are made by those choosing a favorable day. If someone clips one of his wings, the swarm will not flee. When they set out, each one desires to be nearest to him and rejoices to be seen in attendance; they support the tired one on their shoulders, and, when he is more exhausted, carry him entirely. If any weary one falls behind or strays, they follow it by scent, and there, wherever he settles, is the camp of them all; as long as their leader is held, the whole troop is kept together, but once he is lost, the troop scatters to other masters. In any case they cannot exist without a king. Unwillingly, however, when there are several, they kill them, and rather break up the cells of those being born.

Pliny: there are, moreover, rustic and wild bees, of a rough appearance and much more prone to anger, but excelling in work and labor; there are also urban ones, of which there are two kinds. The best are short and mottled, compact into a round shape. Worse are the long ones, which resemble wasps. Worst of all among these are the hairy ones. In Pontus there are certain white bees, which make honey twice a month. Around the river Thermodon there are two kinds of these: some make honey in trees, others underground, in a triple layer of combs, which are the most abundant in yield.

Aristotle: there are several kinds of bees. The good bee is small and round, compact and tight in itself. There is a bee like a cube, long, and there is one of broad belly. The 'cicin' are all larger than the rest, heavy, and lack stings. Those bees are good that make fine honey. A strong kind of bee makes hard honey. Bees of small body are better and build more skillfully, are more patient of labor, and make more honey from mountain flowers and make it fine; they have fine wings, and their color is black, and they seem as if scorched. There are also certain solitary, idle bees, which, flying through the air as if exercising themselves with the working bees, enter the hives and eat the honey; but the working bees indeed fight the idle ones and kill them, and especially the kings of the bees do this, and drive them out of the hives. For it is better that fathers should punish idle sons. Ornamental bees, moreover, are of the number of those that do nothing with honey. Bees arising from those that feed on mountain flowers are smaller and stronger and more patient of labor. Bees, however, born from those that suck garden flowers, behave in the opposite way.

div.head: DE VITA EARUM ET VOCE VEL SONO

cit.quote: Aristotle, in the book on death and life: bees live longer than other larger animals.

From the book On Animals of Aristotle: the noise of bees within the body is not produced by breath going out, since they do not breathe; for their hiss is produced through a web beneath the wall-like covering at the site of the body's division, that is, the split into two, and they make noise only by flying, that is, by extending and contracting their wings through the air falling between them and the body. They do not cry out, however, by night.

Ambrose: bees betray, in the hoarse murmur of their voice, a sweetness, showing that they by no means have a lung or the use of breathing, but feed on an airy breath instead. Finally, if someone by chance pours oil over them, they nearly die, because, their pores blocked, they cannot draw in that airy breath. And continually, if one pours vinegar over them, they revive at once, since the force of vinegar, they say, quickly opens those pores, which are otherwise more continuously blocked by the moisture of oil.

Pliny: they think that infected creatures make not a voice, but a sound, produced by breath moving within and resounding when enclosed. Some, however, emit a murmur, like bees. For it is accepted that flies and bees, through two channels beneath the chest, with a mobile membrane meeting the moving breath, make a sound by the friction of it within. And so, after the daily labor, as evening comes on, as has been said, they buzz less and less in the hive, until one flies around, as if ordering rest to be taken, with the same buzz with which it roused them. They rejoice in clapping and the ringing of bronze, and are called together by it, by which it is clear that they too have the sense of hearing. Once the work is finished, the brood raised, and every duty performed, they nevertheless have a customary exercise, and range about in the open, and, given to flying in circles high up, only then return to food. Their life is very long, so that, if prosperous circumstances favor them against enemies and chance, it lasts seven years altogether. It is reported that hives have never lasted beyond ten years. There are those who think dead bees can be revived, if kept under a roof through the winter, and then warmed by the spring sun. Some think that a swarm entirely lost can be restored from fresh ox-carcasses buried with dung. Virgil, however, [describes this from] the lifeless body of beasts of burden, nature changing some things into others.

div.head: DE CIBO EARUM ET POTU AC SOMNO

cit.quote: Aristotle: the life and nourishment of bees is above the earth, and their proper taste is honey; they love sweet things, and do not settle on anything foul or of bad taste or smell. A foul smell burdens them, and a sweet smell delights them. And so they sting what smells bad, and cast out their own dung while flying, since it has a strong stench. And so they never fall onto anything foul. They also love clear, running waters. They do not, however, hunt at all, but work and store up food; they also have another food called 'cocizon,' which is as sweet as a fig. This they bring in on their legs, as they also carry wax. When honey is extracted from the hive, enough must be left for the bees' food in winter, otherwise the hive will suffer. For bees' food in winter and spring is from honey. They also prepare for themselves another food, sometimes bringing in a certain substance resembling wax. Further, the keepers of the hives, because of the scarcity of remaining honey, sometimes feed the bees with figs and other sweet things. They must, however, leave honey in proportion to the number of bees, since if they leave much, they will afterward work less; and if it is scanty, they will grow sluggish in working. They drink, however, from the nearest stream if they have one, and not from another; otherwise they will drink elsewhere, but do not drink until they have cast off the weight they carry.
Pliny, book 11: Aristomachus reports that bees never touch the flower of the tree-medick as pasture.
Pliny, book 14, in the same: bees gave their name to the 'apian' vines, being especially fond of them.

Pliny, book 21, in the same: for the sake of bees one ought to plant thyme, rose, violets, lily, bean, poppy, and the like, for they are most eager for these flowers, and even, remarkably, mustard, since they do not touch the flower of the olive. Further, if food is lacking for bees, it is useful to place dried raisins or crushed figs near their hives, or wool soaked in raisin-wine or in honeyed water, or even plain chicken flesh; the same foods should be provided in a dry summer that removes flowers.

Aristotle: it is clear that ringed animals sleep, from the fact that bees rest and do not cry out by night. For if one holds a candle to them at night, one will see them at rest. Some, then, go out to work at the start of the day, and some remain still until others wake; then they fly out and go out together to work, and, returning, cry out; then gradually their noise subsides, until one of them remains flying and circling about, as if signaling that it is now time to sleep, and then they all rest together.

Pliny: bees, from the rise of Arcturus, are sustained by sleep for sixty days without any food. And from Arcturus to the spring equinox, in the warmer season, they are already awake, but even then keep to the hive and take up the food kept for that time.

Aristotle: bees inhabit assigned dwellings, and construct their homes with an indescribable art: the bee is among those animals that have dwellings, like the ant and the mouse and the mole; bees remain in their cells on days of great cold, and eat nothing of their stored food. A sign of this is that when one of them comes out from its opening, it appears small and there is nothing within it. And it remains after the setting of the Pleiades until springtime; the cells of the males, however, are abandoned if honey is scarce. And what is found in the cells of bees is either brood, or honey, or 'cicines.' And so they first begin to make cells of wax for the bees, then, when there is much 'altemon,' cells for the kings, then cells for the 'cicines,' when there is much honey, and they begin to build beneath the walls of the hive above, and do not stop descending gradually until they reach the bottom of the hive, and each cell has two openings, one on the outside, the other on the inside, and they have a place for entering and for exiting. The cells of wax, which are covered with wax, are for the most part full of wax. The cells, however, in which the kings dwell, are only at the end.

Pliny: bees build their cells first for the common bees, then for the kings. In this way a more abundant yield is hoped for; chambers are also added for the drones - these are the smallest cells, but for larger bees themselves. Royal cells for future rulers they build in one part of the hive, ample, magnificent, separate, standing out by a swelling. If these are pressed flat, no offspring is produced. All the cells are six-sided, each made by the work of individual feet. At the solstice, when thyme begins to flower, grape-must is the chief material of the cells.

Palladius, book 5: bees should be sought in suitable places in the month of April. Honey-bearing places are shown by bees, if they graze most frequently around springs. For if they are seen more sparsely in such places, honey cannot usefully be made there. But if they drink there frequently, we can find, by this method, where their swarms are. And first let us find out how far off they are, and closer by. Let us carry liquid red dye poured into a small vessel, and watch the springs or nearby waters. Then let a thread dipped in that dye touch the backs of the drinking bees, and let us wait there. If those we have dyed return quickly, let us note that their dwelling is nearby; if slowly, after a longer interval, we judge it more distant by the length of time. You will easily come to nearby ones; to distant ones you will be led by this method. Cut one internode of a reed with its joints, and open it on one side; there put a little honey or boiled must, and place it near the spring. When bees gather to it and have first entered by the smell, close the hole with your thumb held opposite, and let only one out. Follow its flight, and it will show you the location of its home. When you lose sight of it, release another at once, and follow. Thus, released one after another, they will bring you, in turn, to the location of the swarm. Some place a very small vessel of honey near the water, and once a bee coming to drink has tasted it, going on to the common feeding-ground, it will show it to others. As their numbers steadily increase, follow the returning bees until you reach the swarm. But if the swarm is hidden in a cave, it is driven out by smoke, and, once frightened out by the noise in the air, will hang from a shrub or in some part of the wood, and thus, a vessel being brought near, it will be received. But if it is in the hollow branch of a tree, that same branch, cut off above and below with a very sharp saw and covered with a bare cloth, can be carried off and placed among the other hives. They are tracked, however, in the morning, so that the whole day suffices for following; for once evening comes and work is done, they mostly do not return to the water. The vessels in which they are received should be well rubbed with lemon balm or sweet-smelling herbs and sprinkled with a light shower of honey. If this is done in spring and near springs, hives thus scented, placed in locations where bees are frequent, will draw a multitude to themselves of their own accord, provided they can be kept safe from thieves.
Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: bees, as has been said, are better when small, round, compact and tight in themselves, making fine honey.

Palladius: if bees are to be bought, let us see to it that full hives are obtained. This can be shown either by inspection, or by the loudness of the buzzing, or by the frequency of the swarm's coming and going. From a nearby rather than a distant region, lest they be troubled by the novelty of the air. But if they must be carried from farther off, let them be carried by night, and let us not set down or open the hives except as evening approaches: let us then, after three days, watch that the whole swarm does not leave through its doorway, for this is a sign they are planning to take flight. For otherwise, each will return to its own place. They are, however, believed not to flee if we smear the mouths of the vessels with the dung of a firstborn calf. We ought to place the bee-station not far from the master's house, or in a secluded and sunny part of the garden, away from winds and in a warmer spot, laid out in a square measure, that keeps off thieves and the approach of men and livestock; it should be rich in flowers, which industry should provide, whether in grasses, shrubs, or trees, nourishing herbs like marjoram, thyme, wild violets, asphodel, sweet marjoram, hyacinth (which is called iris or gladiolus for the likeness of its leaves), narcissus, saffron, and other herbs of very sweet scent and bloom. Among the flowering plants let there be roses, lilies, yellow violets, rosemary, ivy; among trees, jujubes, almond, peach, pear and fruit-bearing trees, in which no bitterness matches the sweetness of the juice in flower. Among wild trees, mast-bearing oaks, terebinth, mastic, cedar, linden, holm-oak, and smaller thyme, but yews should be kept away as enemies. Let the trees be arranged on the northern side; shrubs and bushes should follow in their order beneath the taller growth, then grasses on the level ground, and after that we should plant the shrubs. Let a spring or a leisurely stream come this way, forming shallow pools as it passes, which scattered, crosswise bushes should cover, to provide safe resting-places for the bees when they are thirsty.

Aristotle: for bees, a warm place is suitable in winter, a cool one in summer. The hive's openings, too, are closed against a strong wind so it does not enter. It is also fitting to plant myrtle and mountain pear and peas and beans and poppy and almonds near the hive.

Pliny, book 21: bees do not touch the flower of the olive, and so it should be kept far from them. Some plants, however, should be sown nearby, which invite swarms of flying bees and do not let them go too far off. One should also beware of the cornel tree, since, once its flower is tasted, they die. The remedy for this is crushed sorb-apples with honey and human or ox urine, or pomegranate seeds sprinkled with Aminean wine. But planting broom near the hives is most harmful.

Palladius, book 2: new swarms of bees come out at the very end of the month of June. And so the keeper must be attentive, since young bees, being flighty in spirit, will easily escape unless watched. Those coming out, indeed, linger at their entrance for one or two days, and should be caught at once with new hives. The diligent keeper, however, will watch until the eighth or ninth hour, since after these times they are not accustomed to flee or migrate easily, though others do not hesitate to set out and depart at once: these are the signs of flight - for two or three days beforehand they grow more agitated and murmur sharply. When an attentive observer, ear held close, has often noticed this, he should be the more watchful against it: they are also accustomed to give this sign when they are about to fight, and their fighting is checked by dust thrown, or by a shower of sweet water sprinkled. There is in them, for restoring the harmony of their origin, a sweet authority, but when a peaceful swarm hangs suspended on a branch or in some place, if they hang from a single cluster, you may know that there is one king for all, or that harmony remains once all have been reconciled; but if the crowd, hanging, divides into two or more clusters, they are discordant, and there are as many kings as you see clusters, which they thus reveal. Where you see denser masses of bees, with a hand anointed with the juice of balm or celery, seek out the kings: they are a little larger, more oblong than the other bees, with straighter legs and not large wings, of beautiful, shining color, smooth and hairless, unless perhaps the fuller ones seem to carry something like hair on the belly, which, however, they do not use as a weapon. Others are dark and shaggy, and these should be killed, leaving the more beautiful one. If this one often wanders off with the swarms, let it be kept with its wings clipped, for while it remains, none departs; but if no new swarms are produced, we can combine the contents of two or three small hives into one. We will, however, sprinkle the bees with a sweet liquid and keep them enclosed for three days, with honey provided as food, and leave only a small breathing-hole in the cell.

Aristotle: bees delight in noise and are gathered by it. And they do this only out of delight or out of fear. When they hang within the hives clustered together, this signals that they wish to leave the hive; when the keepers notice this, they sprinkle sweet liquid within the hive.

Pliny: bees do not flee if the hives are anointed with balm, and in no flower do they delight more, and by sprigs of it swarms are very easily kept together. The same is also most excellent against their stings.

Palladius, in the passage above: further, if you wish, in a hive from which a multitude has been carried off by some plague, to restore the population by addition, you will look in other, fuller hives for the wax of combs and their edges that hold the brood, and where you find the sign of a king about to be born, you will cut it off with its offspring and place it in that hive. This is the sign of a future king: among the other cells that hold brood, one appears larger and longer, like a teat. But they must be transferred at the time when, the coverings gnawed through, ready to be born, their heads strain to emerge. For if you transfer them immature, they will die; but if the swarm suddenly rises, let it be frightened by a noise in the air or by clashing pottery, and then it will return to the hive or hang on a nearby branch, and from there be gathered by hand or scoop into a new vessel sprinkled with the usual herbs and honey, and once it has settled there in the evening, be placed among the others.

Aristotle: bees gather, as flocks do, and some go out to work at the start of the day, some remain still until others wake, then, flying together, go out to work, and drive out the idle ones, and work harder when hunger comes upon them, and at the start of spring. Their kings, created for the purpose of generation, always remain within the hive and do nothing; and the 'cicines' too, who are the male bees, are idle for the reason stated above.

Ambrose: no bees, however, dare leave their homes or go out to any pasture, unless the king has first gone out and claimed the leadership of the flight for himself; their advance, moreover, is through fragrant countryside, where there are gardens breathing with flowers, and a flowing stream through grasses and sweet herbs where they first lay the foundations of their camp.

Pliny: the laziness of bees is roused to work by more frequent smoke. For where they have brooded, they make the combs dark, and again they are affected by too much smoke. Their working schedule, however, is at the doors by day; by night there is a guard of the camp, rest until morning, until one rouses all the rest with a double or triple buzz like a trumpet call; then, if the day is going to be mild, they all fly forth, for they foresee winds and rain and then keep to their roofs. Bees do not go out to work and labor before the beans flower, and no day is lost in idleness when the sky permits. They come and go along two paths around each doorway, so that some enter by one, others exit by the other. And as evening comes on, they buzz less and less in the hive, until one flies around, as if ordering rest to be taken, with the same buzz with which it roused them, and this is in the manner of a military camp, and then they all fall suddenly silent. But once their work is entirely finished, the brood raised, and every duty performed, they have a customary exercise, and range about in the open, and, given to flying in circles high up, only then return to food.

Aristotle: bees are assigned to different tasks. For some bring in flowers, others soften wax, and others bring water. Their tasks, moreover, do not have a fixed time, but when they have suitable conditions, they prepare at once, and in fair weather they work continually.

Ambrose: you may see them all vying for their duty: some watchfully seeking food, others keeping anxious guard over the camp, others scouting coming rains and watching from a lookout for gathering clouds, others shaping the poured-out wax, others gathering with their mouths the dew infused in flowers, yet none lying in wait for the labors of others or seeking a living by plunder - and would that they need not fear the ambush of robbers, for they have their own stings, and pour venom amid the honey if provoked, and lay down their lives in the wound.

Pliny: and so, when the troop has gone out to work, some heap up flowers with their feet, others carry water in their mouth, and moisten the down of their whole body with it. The younger ones go out to work, carrying in supplies as said above, but the older ones work within. Those bringing in flowers are loaded on their front feet, and for this purpose nature made them rough; they return laden on their front feet, at their beak, and burdened with the whole weight of their load. Three or four others receive them and unload them, for there are divided duties within too. For some build, some polish, some carry supplies, some prepare food from what has been brought in - they do not eat separately, lest an unevenness of work and food and timing result.
Ambrose: bees, as has been said, have their own stings, by which they pour venom amid the honey if provoked, and lay down their lives in the wound out of the ardor of vengeance.
Isidore: bees have an army and kings, and wage battles.

Aristotle: bees do not flee any animal, but some of them flee others that fight among themselves, and if anything approaches, they kill it if they can. They die, however, when they sting, since the sting cannot come out unless the intestine comes out with it. And it often harms them to be stung by other bees, unless the spot is squeezed and the sting drawn out. For even large animals are killed by a bee's sting, as was once seen with a certain horse. Further, the leaders of bees never sting, but sometimes, when abandoned, if pursued, they are killed by the bees and driven from the hives; indeed the 'ciken' and the 'corch' do nothing among the bees, but spoil the work of the others. Thus the good bees overcome them and kill many of their leaders, since they draw out their young, and then all of them depart. Bees also fight against those wishing to take honey from them. Likewise the shorter bees fight fiercely with the longer ones and labor to drive them from the hives. Finally, if anything that does not belong to the hives enters, it will be killed by them. Some, indeed, sit apart individually, watching so that nothing foreign enters, and if it enters through their negligence, it will scarcely escape.

Pliny: bees too, if food fails in the hive, sometimes make an attack on the nearest ones with plunder in mind. But those direct their line against them in turn. If a keeper is present, whichever side he senses him favoring, he does not attack. They also fight often for other reasons, and two generals array these opposing lines. The greatest quarrel is in gathering flowers, each calling their own to them. This battle, indeed, is entirely dispersed by throwing dust or by smoke, but is reconciled by milk or water.

Pliny, book 20, in the same: they say that one anointed with crushed asparagus in oil is not stung by bees. Against their stings, the juice of rue drunk in wine is effective, and its crushed leaves applied or chewed. Those anointed with its juice, too, are said not to be struck by them.
Pliny, in the same: nature gave bees venomous points, against which it is healthful to anoint oneself with the juice of mallow or ivy leaves, or for those struck to drink it.
Pliny, in the same: wine is a remedy for bees. But a decoction of laurel leaves too, taken, resists venoms.
Pliny, book 24, in the same: a drop of propolis in water too is a remedy, however effective; for they say poplar trees produce a drop on their leaves, from which bees make propolis.
Pliny, book 29, in the same: those struck by a scorpion are never afterward stung by bees.
Avicenna, in the second canon: a decoction of marsh-mallow mixed with vinegar or with wine benefits a bee-sting when applied. Likewise laurel oil benefits it.
Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the bee has properties close to the wasp's, except that it leaves its sting in the sting-wound, and its treatment is close to the treatment for wasps.
Isidore: bees are skilled in the task of producing honey, and build their dwellings with indescribable art.

Aristotle: bees do not hunt, but work; they bring into their hives what they need for preparation, from kinds of flowers, namely of the oak and the willow and others, in which there is some stickiness, and with it they smear the surface of the hive against harmful creatures. And the entrances of the hives are narrowed, if they were wide. Then they gather honey and begin to make cells of wax for the bees. Then cells for the kings, then for the others, and they begin to build beneath the walls of the hive above, and do not stop descending gradually until they reach its bottom; each cell has two openings, one within, the other without. And when a bee flies, it does not aim for different flowers, but gathers what it needs from one and returns to the hive.

Pliny, book 11: bees first build the combs and shape the wax, that is, make cells from wax. Then the brood, afterward the honey. The wax is from flowers; the honey-generating substance from the tears of trees that produce a gluey substance, such as the sap of willow, elm, reed, gum, resin, and the like; with these they first coat the whole inside of the hive as with a kind of plaster, and, with other, more bitter juices, they do this against the greed of wild creatures, aware that it might be desired by them. Then they also build wider doorways with these substances.
Isidore: bees, then, build their shrine from various flowers and, with their woven wax, fill their camp with countless offspring.

Ambrose: bees arrange their combs in the fashion of a camp, in which small, round cells support one another by their connection. A sweet work, fashioned from flowers and sweet herbs. What architect taught them to build the hexagons of their cells with undistinguished equality of sides, and to hang fine wax between the partitions of their homes, to store honey, and to swell their storehouses, woven through with flowers, with a certain nectar?

Pliny, in the passage above: the combs, fixed at the top part, gradually cling together also along their sides and hang as one. They do not touch the hive, sometimes slanted, sometimes round, as the shape of the hive requires, sometimes even of two kinds, when two swarms of harmonious populations have had dissimilar customs. To support the collapsing wax like the pillars of a vault from within, from the base, so that there is access for repairs. The first three rows or so are built empty, so that there is nothing readily available to tempt a thief, but the last rows are filled most of all with honey, and so the combs are removed with the hive turned away. All the cells are six-sided, each made by the work of individual feet.

From the book On the Nature of Things, unknown author: 'favus' [honeycomb], according to Isidore, is so called because it is eaten [comeditur] more than drunk. For 'fagein' in Greek means 'to eat.' The honeycomb, moreover, is sweet and flavorful, since it holds honey within wax.

Aristotle: bees take wax from flowers and gather it with their front feet, then pass it to their middle feet, then to the thighs of their hind feet, then fly with it, and then its weight becomes apparent.

From the book On the Nature of Things, unknown author: wax, then, lies within the honeycomb; that which is pure and fragrant is fuel for light and material for writing; it is soft and sticky and brittle. Hardened, however, it softens at fire, and takes on whatever shape is impressed upon it.

Isidore: waxen tablets, material for letters, are the nurses of children; they give understanding to boys, the first beginnings of sense, whose use is proven to have been first handed down by the Greeks.

Pliny: bees fashion their wax from the flowers of all trees and crops, except dock and goosefoot; broom is wrongly excluded, since in Spain, in broom-fields, much honey tastes of that plant; I think olives are also wrongly excluded, since it is certain that very many swarms are produced from the olive harvest. They harm no fruits at all.

Book 21: let the wax be pressed from the combs, but first purified with water and dried for three days in darkness; on the fourth day, melted by fire in a new earthenware vessel with water covering the combs, then strained through a basket, the wax is cooked again in the same pot with the same water, and taken up in another cold vessel, its sides smeared with honey. The best wax is that called Punic; next is that which is very tawny and pure, of honey-like smell - by origin, the Pontic, which I am surprised is counted among poisonous honeys; then comes the Cretan. For it has the most propolis in it; after these, the Corsican, since it is made from box, and is thought to have some medicinal power. Punic wax is made this way: tawny wax is repeatedly exposed to the open sky, then struck in seawater drawn from the deep, with soda added. Then with small ladles they pick out the choicest part, that is, whatever is whitest, and pour it into a vessel that holds a little cold seawater, and again boil the seawater separately, then cool the vessel itself. And when they have done this three times, they dry it on a wicker tray of grape-skins in the open air, under sun and moon, for this produces whiteness, if dried this way. And, lest it melt, they cover it with a fine linen cloth. It becomes whitest, however, after exposure to sun even without recooking. Punic wax is most useful in medicines. Wax turns black with added ash of paper, just as it reddens with alkanet mixed in, and is drawn into various colors with pigments for producing likenesses, and for countless human uses, and even for the protection of walls and weapons.
Pliny, in the same: all bee's wax softens and warms, fills out bodies. Fresh wax is better in a broth, and is given to dysentery sufferers, as is the honeycomb itself.

Dioscorides: useful wax is reddish, fatty, and fragrant, having the smell of honey, and clean, as is the Pontic and Cretan. White, fatty wax has a secondary power; the power of all wax is warming and filling; it is mixed with juices and gruels prepared for dysentery sufferers, with a little honey added to it, so that the decoction is edible. Taken in the amount of a pea, it curdles milk in the breasts. All wax has the power to relax and soften hardnesses. For it is midway between hot and cold, dry and moist, whence it is the material for other medicines, since poultices and other things are bound together from it. Propolis wax is useful, reddish and fragrant, like storax, and not very soft, which you can shape with your hands, if you wish, like storax; its property is hot and drawing, that is, helpful and restorative and softening. It expels splinters lodged in the body; a fumigation of it with open mouth heals old coughs, and corrects rashes. This is found in the hive of bees, where they rub their bodies. It has powers similar to wax, but more effective. For it warms excessively, and has a projecting and thinning substance.
Avicenna: wax increases and provokes desire in mating.

Isidore, book 20: honey is shown to have its Greek name from bees, for the bee is called 'melissa' in Greek. Formerly, however, honey came from dew and was found on the leaves of reeds. Whence Virgil: 'thus far the celestial gifts of airy honey' - since indeed, even now in India and Arabia it is found collected, clinging to branches in the likeness of salt. All honey, moreover, is sweet, yet Sardinian honey is bitter, because of the wormwood on which the bees of that region are fed, in great abundance there.

Pliny: at first, honey is diluted like water, and in the first days it ferments, like new wine, and purifies itself; on the twentieth day it thickens, and is soon covered by a thin membrane, which forms from the foam of its own fermentation; bees gather this on clear days, and it comes from the air, especially at the rising of certain stars, and especially when Sirius itself shines forth, and not at all before the rising of the Pleiades, in the pre-dawn hours. And so at first light, the leaves of trees are found dewed with honey. And if anyone has been out under the open sky in the morning in August, they feel their clothes anointed with a liquid and their hair matted together. Whether it is the sweat of the sky, or a kind of spittle of the stars, or the juice of the air purifying itself, or whether it is of the water, and pure and liquid and of its own nature - now, however, falling from so great a height, and, growing soiled much in its descent, and infected by the earth's breath as it meets it; further, drunk in from foliage and pastures, and gathered into the tiny stomachs of bees - for they bring it up by mouth - and to this, too, spoiled by the juice of flowers, and steeped in the hives, and so often changed, it nevertheless brings a great pleasure of its heavenly nature. For bees are badly affected by too much smoke, an injury they feel very quickly, as does honey, which dries up even at the lightest touch of dew.
Pliny, book 12, in the same: honey flows, however, in the morning hours.

Pliny, book 21, on the beekeeper, in the same: they hope for an abundant yield of honey when thyme flowers abundantly, which they gather around the solstice, and bees too pick it clean. Attic honey has the highest praise in the whole world, whence too the name 'thyme' was transferred [as honey's epithet]. There is another marvel of honey in Crete. There is a mountain called Carina, twelve miles in circuit, within which flies are not found, and honey born there they never touch, and by this singular proof it is sought for medicines.

Ambrose: bees pour the moisture of dew into the middle valleys of their camp, which, with the passage of time, is gradually gathered into honey, and, through the union of wax and the fragrance of flowers, begins to breathe out the sweetness of honey. This fruit of the bees is distinguished by no difference of persons, but grows equally sweet for kings and common bees alike. Nor is it only for pleasure, but also for health, sweetening the throat, healing wounds, and pouring its medicine into the inner organs too.

Aristotle: honey is properly the taste-food of bees, and is their food in winter and spring. And when the keepers extract honey from the hives, the bees, out of the devotion they have for it, eat that honey beyond their usual measure; and when flowers appear, then they make honey, and so then the keeper ought to extract the finished honey, since in its place they will suddenly make more. The plants from which they take it are crown-daisy, myrtle, cinquefoil, and many others. The kind of bee called strong makes hard honey. And they say the young bees do this, since they are not yet practiced in the craft. There is, moreover, a small worm found in the depths of the hive, which, when it grows, makes a web like a spider's and dominates the whole hive, and so putrefies the honey.

Pliny: there are three kinds of bees' honey, in any given region or province. The spring kind, made from the comb of flowers, is therefore called 'anthinum'; some forbid touching this, so that a strong brood may emerge from abundant nourishment. Others leave nothing less for the bees, since a great abundance follows the rising of the great stars. Those who are more careful leave a twelfth part of this harvest for the bees; the harvest properly begins on the thirtieth day after the swarm is brought forth, and this gathering closes about the month of May. The second kind of honey is the summer kind, called 'orion' from its especially timely gathering, when Sirius itself shines forth, about thirty days after the solstice. Likewise from the rising of any star, or a rainbow, especially if it is very cloudy, and if rain does not follow, but the dew warms under the sun's rays. Medicines come from this, not honeys, gifts of heaven for the eyes, for ulcers, and for the inner organs; all summer honey is reddish, being made in the drier days. The most suitable, by reputation, is that from thyme, of golden color, most pleasant taste, being visibly thick in the little jars; for the summer harvest, Dionysius of Thasos thinks a tenth part should be left to the bees, if the hives are full, or proportionally less if not; but if the hives are empty, they should not be touched at all; for this harvest the Athenians assigned the day of the wild fig, sacred to Vulcan. The third kind of honey is the least esteemed, the wild kind, called 'hericeum,' gathered after the first autumn rains, when in Africa alone the tamarisk flowers in the woods, and because of this it is sandy in appearance; this harvest ends around the setting of the Pleiades, about the Ides of November; reason suggests leaving two parts of it to the bees.

Pliny, book 12, in the same: Arabia produces sugarcane honey, but it is more praised in India. It is, moreover, honey gathered in reeds. There are also trees called 'occhi,' resembling fig trees, in the valleys of Hyrcania, from which honey flows for two hours in the morning.
Gloss, on Matthew 3: wild honey in the desert was John's food, which he found on tree-trunks or among plants.

Avicenna, in the second canon: bees' honey is better when it is of true sweetness, of good smell, inclining to sharpness and redness, not too thin nor too sticky. And spring honey is better, then summer; winter honey, however, is bad. There is also a kind of honey that is sharp and poisonous.

Pliny, book 11: honey is best where it is stored in jars of the best flowers, namely of the Attic region. The best is sipped, and least tainted by leaf, from oak leaves and reeds. The height of quality by origin, indeed, consists of several kinds: for in some places notable honeycombs of wax are produced, as among the Peligni and in Sicily; elsewhere abundance of honey, as in Crete and Cyprus and Africa; elsewhere size, as in the northern regions - in Germany indeed a comb of eight feet in length was seen, black in its hollow part. Honey is gathered more abundantly at full moon, and more richly on a clear day. In all honey that has flowed of its own accord - like oil and must, and called 'silent honey' - it is most praiseworthy. All summer honey is reddish, being made in drier days. The most suitable, by reputation, is that from thyme, of golden color, most pleasant taste, being visibly thick in the little jars, thickened by dew from the sea. What congeals is least praised; thyme-honey does not congeal, and, when touched, sends out very fine threads, which is the first sign of its quality. To break off suddenly and have the drops spring back, however, is held to be a sign of poor quality. The following test is that it be fragrant, and, from its sweet nature, sticky, and translucent.

Aristotle: good honey is similar to gold; white is also better than black. It is effective against eye diseases and eruptions. In fruitful years honey multiplies, and the time for making honey is when flowers appear, as is the time for extracting it from the hives, for then new honey is suddenly made in abundance; spring honey is cleaner and sweeter and altogether better than autumn honey. Honey from new wax too is better, for that from old wax is reddish and spoils, just as wine does from old skins. Likewise honey from the lower part of the comb is cleaner.

div.head: DE OPERATIONE MELLIS IN CIBO ET MEDICINA

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the second canon: bees' honey is hot and dry in the first degree. Cane-sugar honey and reed honey, however, are hot in the first degree, but not dry, rather perhaps moist in the first degree. The power of honey is cleansing, opening the mouths of the veins, and dissolving of moistures. It expels moisture from the depths of the body and prevents putrefaction and corruption of the flesh; a liniment made from it prevents lice and nits, and kills both. Likewise it cleans deep, filthy ulcers, and clears dimness of sight, and strengthens hearing. Cooked, however, until thickened, it makes fresh wounds close. Cooked with dill, it heals impetigo. A gargle made from it heals suffocation; honey-water strengthens the stomach and produces appetite for food. Reed honey loosens the belly. Cane-sugar honey, however, does not loosen it, and honey whose foam has not been skimmed off inflates and loosens the belly, but sometimes binds the phlegmatic, and nourishes greatly. Boiled with water it strongly provokes urine. Warmed honey drunk with rose oil benefits the bite of venomous worms and one who has drunk opium. Swallowing it too is a treatment for the bite of a rabid dog.

Pliny: the very nature of honey, indeed, is such that it does not let bodies putrefy, with its pleasant, not harsh, flavor. Different from the nature of salt, it is most useful for the throat, tonsils, quinsy, and every desire of the mouth, and for a tongue parched in fevers; and indeed a decoction of it is given to those with pneumonia and pleurisy, and for wounds struck by a serpent, and against mushroom poisons. It inflates the stomach, increases bile, creates loathing; some think it useless by itself for the eyes.
Dead bees standing [in it] make honey effective against poison. Likewise it is most useful for the eyes. Drunk in wine it is a remedy for ailments arising from eating fish.
Pliny, in the same: honey in which bees have died especially heals vomiting, and also benefits dysentery sufferers, and colic is cured by the same.

Again, some advise touching ulcerated corners of the eyes with honey; dripped into the ears with rose oil it kills nits and foul creatures of the head; the use of skimmed honey is always more suitable, though it inflates the stomach and increases bile, creates loathing, and some think it useless by itself for the eyes.

Constantine the African: [honey] generates good blood for the phlegmatic and the old, and strengthens natural heat; it harms the choleric and the young, since it generates red bile and hot, acute illnesses, especially in summer.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: on honey too you have more above, in the treatise on the dew of heaven.

Avicenna: bees, indeed, gather honey, which is a hidden dew falling upon flowers and upon other such things. For vapor rises and is converted and matures in the air and thickens by night, and, once made into honey, falls. It differs, however, according to what it falls upon, namely tree or stone, and men gather what is visible of it, but bees the hidden kind, so as to be nourished by it and to store it up. I think, however, that the bees' labor has some effect upon it.

Isaac Judaeus: [honey's] nature has acquired [certain properties] from the bee. And so it cuts and cleanses bad humors, and casts out, through the pores of the skin, an abundance of bad humors from within the body. It cleanses the impurities of the veins excellently. And so it suits the cold and moist well, and the elderly especially. For it quickly generates blood in them, but is unsuited to the hot, especially if their complexion is dry, since it gives their bodies a burning sharpness and changes into choleric humors; but if it changes into blood, it does not, however, make it praiseworthy, but hotter. Nor does it give nourishment to any part of their bodies. Warmed, however, if mixed with rose oil, it eases a cough. It loosens difficulty of urination and moistens the belly; boiled, applied as a suppository, it cleanses impetigo. Tempered with bean flour it clears freckles. Bees' honey, however, or calamint and other such things eaten, is hot and dry. And so it suits epileptics and paralytics, and dissolves putrefied humors. It cleanses festering wounds. Further, those feeding on wormwood and similar things make honey especially cleansing and opening, most of all for constipation of the stomach, liver, and spleen. And so it benefits the dropsical, drunk with camel's milk or goat-hair-sifted milk. But if drunk skimmed, it is effective against a rabid dog's bite. Further, honey's action varies according to the different ways of taking it. For some take it raw, some cooked, and cook it in various ways; raw honey, eaten, generates bloating and flatulence, increases roughness of the chest because of its sharpness, and produces vomiting and looseness; honey boiled with mead is thinner and moister. Whence no sharpness at all is found in it, and accordingly it is diminished from the sweetness of its own pleasantness and moistens the belly, does not inflate or provoke vomiting, but quickly penetrates the bodies of those who eat it and nourishes swiftly, soothes roughness of the chest, and draws off urine. Boiled without water and skimmed, however, it has less sharpness than the rest. Its action, however, is close to the preceding, yet it does not relieve difficulty of urination.

div.head: DE AQUA MULSA CETERISQUE POCULIS MELLICIS

cit.quote: Pliny: there are two kinds of honeyed water, fresh and aged; this benefits, in the food of the sick, for restoring strength, soothing the mouth and stomach, and cooling fevers: it softens the belly, eases the passage of breath or spirit. And it soothes every impulse of the mind through food. It is useful to those coughing. Warmed, it induces vomiting; it is poured in against poison. With long age, it turns into wine, most useful for the stomach, contrary to the nerves. Mead made from old wine is most useful: it recalls appetite for food, softens the bowels with cold drinking for most, but checks them when warm. It increases the body, and for many prolongs old age, for the vigor of mind and body is preserved within by mead, on the outside by oil.
Pliny, in the same book: honeyed water, against the poison of white lead, is healthful with oil added; against henbane too, with donkey's milk.

Isidore, book 20: 'mulsum' is so named as if mixed with honey. For it is a drink of water and honey, which the Greeks call 'mellicratum'; further, 'vinomellum' is must mixed with honey and vigorously stirred and shaken. 'Oxymellum,' however, is so called because it is made from a mixture of vinegar and honey. Whence it retains both sweetness and sourness; 'rhodomellus' is so called because honey is mixed into rose juice; it is also called 'medus,' since it is made from honey as if 'better' [melius].
Rhazes, in the Almansor: a drink made from honey is vehemently hot and productive of red bile, yet benefits those suffering cold illnesses.

Pliny: there are also certain poisonous honeys among the bees' produce in Spain, and at Heraclea in Pontus, most harmful in certain years, made by the same bees. There is indeed a white herb, a torment to livestock but especially to goats, called 'aegolethron,' from whose flower they conceive a harmful power, withering in a wet spring. And so it happens that this evil is felt every year. The signs of poisonous honey are that it does not thicken at all, that its color is more reddish, its smell foreign, provoking sneezing at once. It is also heavier than harmless honey: those who eat it throw themselves to the ground seeking coolness. For they also break out in sweat. Against such things, however, the remedies are aged mead made from the best honey and rue, and salted foods too, if eaten repeatedly and then rejected. It is certain, moreover, that this evil reaches even dogs through the excrement, and torments them likewise, though it is established that mead aged from it is harmless, and that women's skin is bettered by nothing more than by being treated with costus and aloe. There is also another kind of honey in the same Pontus, from the honey-harvest, which they call 'menomenon' from the madness it produces. This is thought to come from the flower of oleander, with which the woods teem. And that people, though they sent wax as tribute to the Romans, never sent or sold honey, since it was deadly. In Persia too, and in Caesarean Mauretania, and Gaetulia bordering Massylia, poisonous combs are produced. To the bees themselves too, as has been said above, nature gave venomous stings, against which the remedy is to anoint oneself with mallow juice or ivy leaves, or, for those struck, to drink it.
Pliny, book 29, in the same: against poisonous honey, honey in which bees have died is effective.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the smell of sharp, poisonous honey causes thirst and takes away reason. Its eating too causes sudden loss of reason and cold sweat; its treatment, however, is eating salted fish and drinking honey-water and vomiting with it.

Avicenna, in the fourth: honey brought mostly from the region of Heraclea is bad and poisonous. It is sharp, causing one who smells it to sneeze, and causing fainting and cold sweat and bad symptoms. Its treatment, as for black henbane, is to eat rue and salted fish and drink syrup of gum ammoniac, and not stop eating or vomiting as much as possible.

div.head: DE ALVEARIBUS APUM FABRICANDIS ATQUE PURGANDIS

cit.quote: Pliny, book 21: [hives are made of] bark, or, second, of fennel-giant stalk, or, third, of wickerwork; many have also made them of transparent stone, so as to watch the workers within: it is most useful to coat hives all around with buffalo dung. Let the lid be at the back. There should also be a walkway, so that one can look inside to see if the hive's body is large, but the yield is poor; lest, in despair of working, they abandon their labor, this should be reduced gradually, the growth of their work concealing it from them. It is also useful to cover the hives with straw in winter, and to fumigate them often, especially with buffalo dung. Likewise it is fitting that hives face the equinoctial east, but should avoid the north wind, and no less the west wind.
Palladius, in the passage above: [on] lizards and other animals. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Palladius, book 4, in the same: in the month of March, around the calends of April, the hives should be tended and all refuse removed, and the filth that winter has gathered, and the little worms and moths and spiders by which the use of the combs is spoiled, and the butterflies that produce worms unknowingly with their own dung; then a smoke of dry, burnt buffalo dung should be applied, which is suited to the health of bees. This cleaning should be repeated often, up until autumn; for all this and the rest, you should make yourself chaste and sober, and abstain from others, and from sharp foods and foul smells, and from all salted things.

Palladius, book 5, in the same: also in the month of April the hives should be cleared of filth, and of butterflies, which are most abundant then, when mallow flowers, as will indeed be said below, where butterflies are treated.

Palladius: the hives of bees are gelded in the month of June, once shown by present signs to be ripe for the taking of honey. First, indeed, if they are full of bees, we hear a fine murmur. For empty comb-cells, like hollow buildings, magnify the sounds they receive. So, when the sound of the murmur is loud and hoarse, we know the honeycomb frames are not yet fit for harvesting. Likewise, when they drag drones - the larger bees - from their cells with great effort, this proves the honey ripe. The hives, however, should be gelded in the morning hours, when the bees are sluggish and not roused by the heat. Smoke is applied, of galbanum and dry buffalo dung, which it is fitting to kindle with coals made in a small pot, shaped so that, as if inverted, it can emit the smoke through the narrow opening of a clasp; and thus, as the bees give way, the honeycombs are cut out. At this time, a fifth part of the combs should be left as food for the swarm. Rotten and defective combs, indeed, should be removed from the hives. Then we prepare the honey, the combs gathered into a very clean cloth and carefully pressed. But before we press, we should cut away the corrupted parts of the combs, or those containing brood. For bad parts spoil good with their bad taste. Fresh honey should be kept for a few days in open vessels and cleaned at the top, until the cooling of the fermenting must has settled. The finer honey will be that which flowed out as if of its own accord before the second pressing. In this month too we prepare wax, which, in a bronze vessel full of boiling water, with the leftover fragments of comb finely cut, is softened, and then, dissolved in other small vessels without water, is shaped into forms.

Palladius, book 11, in the same: also in the month of October the hives are gelded in the manner already described. It is fitting, however, to inspect them, and, if abundant, to take some; if moderate, to leave the middle portion because of winter's scarcity; but if scarcity appears in the cells, to take nothing at all.

Aristotle: when flowers appear, then bees make honey, as has been said. And so the keeper should then extract honey from the hives, since they will suddenly make more in its place; but in extracting honey, enough should be left to suffice the bees for food in winter, otherwise the hive will suffer. The keeper, however, should leave honey according to the number of bees, since, if he leaves them too much honey, they will afterward work less, and if too little, they will grow sluggish in working. Further, sometimes, because of the scarcity of remaining honey, the keepers feed the bees with sweet things, like figs and the like.

Pliny, book 11: in removing the combs, careful management is needed, since bees despair and either die or flee from lack of food. Abundance, on the contrary, brings on laziness. When honey is removed, it is most useful to drive off the bees with smoke, lest they grow angry or greedily devour the honey themselves. It is prescribed, however, that those extracting the honey be washed and clean. Bees also hate a thief, and a menstruating woman.

Pliny, book 21, in the same: when honey is removed, the entrance should be encircled with broom or white vine, lest the bees scatter; the vessels for honey and the combs, moreover, they recommend washing with water, and, once this is boiled, they say the most healthful vinegar results.

div.head: DE UTILITATE IPSORUM ALVEARIUM IN MEDICINIS

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the canon on bees: the hives of bees are useful in medicine too. For their impurity is warming, at the end of the second degree. The green kind among them is better. It cleanses evenly and draws strongly. It cleanses impetigo and draws out splinters and thorns, and is also used in place of ammoniac gum.

Avicenna, in the same: pure 'mum' is the wall of the bees' cells, in which they lay eggs and young, and into which honey comes. Black 'mum,' however, is the grime of the outer window-openings. 'Mum,' moreover, is by nature evenly soothing. It fills foul ulcers and moistens accidentally, since it glues together and blocks pores, and is the material of all cooling and heating plasters. In it is a slight softening and some dissolving power, from the abundant dissolving power of honey. And in the black 'mum' there is a strong drawing power from deep within. For it draws out splinters and thorns lodged in the flesh. And in it are a certain fineness and a little cleansing, and a final smoothness; it soothes the sinews and the hardness of swellings. It also benefits, applied, roughness of the chest, and especially swallowed, and is effective for ulcers of the intestines. It is also said to draw out venoms, and is applied to wounds from poisoned arrows. Black 'mum,' by the strength of its smell, causes sneezing.

Aristotle: bees enclose, around the entrance at the edge of the hive, what is called 'micoz,' very black, like sediment, which comes from the wax and whose smell is very sharp, and is effective for cauterizing.
Pliny: [on] hives: propolis, which is the third layer in the crust, is of great use for medicines. It is heavy in smell, so that most use it in place of galbanum.

Propolis from hives draws out stings and everything lodged in the body, disperses swellings, softens hard growths. It soothes pains of the sinews. And it closes over, into a scar, ulcers already thought incurable.

div.head: DE HIS QUE CONTRARIA SUNT APIBUS VEL NOCIVA

cit.quote: Palladius, book 4: bees are often harmed by their own good fortune, for if the year is overflowing with too many flowers, while they devote all their care to producing honey, they think nothing of their offspring, and, this renewal neglected, the same population, worn out by labor, is extinguished, to the destruction of the whole race. And so, when you see an excess of honey flowing from a great and continuous harvest of flowers, close the entrance for three days at intervals and do not let them go out. Thus they will be turned toward generating offspring.
Isidore: bees are driven off by smoke, and exasperated by tumult.

Pliny, book 11: [bees] hate women's menses too, that is, menstrual blood, whence, when honey is removed, they are driven off with smoke. They also hate foul smells, and even perfumed ones. And so they are troubled by fragrant unguents. They themselves, moreover, are subject to the harm of many creatures: hostile to them are their own degenerate kind - wasps and hornets - and, from the gnat kind, those called 'muliones'; swallows and certain other birds plunder them; frogs lie in wait for them at watering-places, especially when breeding; toads too come uninvited and, creeping up, blow upon the flower-covered bees, which fly a short distance and are at once seized, and are said not to feel the bees' stings. Sheep too are hostile, entangling themselves with difficulty in their wool. If someone cooks crab nearby, bees too are killed by the smell. Echo, too, is their enemy, its resounding sound striking the fearful bees back and forth. Mist too is their enemy. Spiders too, most hostile of all, once they gain the upper hand in weaving, kill the hive; the lazy butterfly too flies about, a pest, at lit lamps. And not in one way only, for it feeds on the wax itself and leaves excrement, from which shipworms are bred. With its thread too, wherever it goes, it covers especially the down of the wings. Shipworms too are born in the wood itself, which especially seek out the wax. Their own greed for food troubles them too, an excessive glut of flowers, especially in spring, quickly filling the belly.
Pliny, in the same: it is certain that bees flee hives touched by menstrual blood.
Ambrose: if someone by chance pours oil over bees, they nearly die, since, their pores blocked, they cannot draw in that airy breath, as has indeed been said above.

Aristotle: bees are weakened in their work by what they suffer from small creatures. These indeed harm bees, but the bees kill them and drag them out. The creature that flies around a candle throws combs to the ground when it breathes in. And bees do not sting it, but it flees when the bees smoke it out. Wasps too, and swallows and frogs, harm bees, catching them when they drink. Bees, however, do not flee any animal, but some of them flee others, since they fight among themselves. The 'cacoynos' watches the entrance of the bees and attacks it strongly, so that they come out. And if one flies out, it catches and eats it. Nor is it harmed by the bees, but is perhaps killed by the hive's keeper. Further, it harms bees to have wasps and sheep nearby. A multitude of males, too, hinders the bees' business. Rainy seasons too harm bees. In hives a worm is found, which makes a web like a spider's and dominates the whole hive and putrefies the honey. There are also certain solitary, idle bees, which, flying through the air as if exercising themselves, enter the hives with the working bees and eat the honey, but the working bees fight the idle ones and kill them and drag them from the hives, and especially their kings do this.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: illnesses befall bees for the greater part in fertile hives, and sickness comes to them from their own idleness and from the hive's dung. And when they fall ill, they eat more than they used to before, because of the devotion they have toward the honey. They die, however, from many mischances, especially if there are many leaders and each rules one crowd. And if some part dies in the hive, the rest drag it out.
