Bees, indeed, have small, harmful little creatures, and if the bees are strong, they kill and drag them out. Other bees, however, are weakened in their work by what they suffer from those little creatures.

Palladius, book 4: in the month of March especially, illness is wont to fall upon bees. For after the winter fast, eagerly seeking the bitter flowers of spurge and elm, which appear first, they suffer a loosening of the bowels and perish, unless you come swiftly with a remedy. You will offer crushed pomegranate seeds with Aminean wine, or raisins with Syrian must and harsh wine, or all these ground together and boiled in rough wine, then set to cool in wooden troughs. Likewise rosemary boiled in mead congeals, and this juice is placed in a roof-tile. But if they seem shaggy and shrunken, sluggish in silence, and frequently carry out the bodies of the dead, you should pour in, through channels made of reed, honey boiled with gallnut powder or dried rose. Before all else, it will help to remove, with the sharpest saws, the rotten parts of the combs, or the empty wax that the reduced swarm cannot fill, and to do this promptly, lest, by disturbing another part of the comb, you force the bees to abandon their shaken dwelling.

Aristotle: bees fall ill especially when the 'arochezi' flowers swell, since that season is dry. They die, however, when their heads are anointed with oil and placed facing the sun. When a bee's wing is cut off, it does not grow back, and when it casts out its sting, it dies. Bees also die if they have many leaders. Illnesses too often occur from the fertility of the hive. Sometimes, however, from idleness or from the hive's stench.

Pliny: the health of bees is judged by cheerfulness and brightness. For they too sense their dead by their own instinct, of which a sluggish sadness is the sign, and they accompany the funeral in the manner of mourners. When their king has been consumed by disease, the common bees grieve with idle sorrow, not bringing food, not going forth. They gather about the body only with a sorrowful murmur, and, unless helped then, die of hunger. There are also illnesses of their work: when they fill the combs badly, they call it 'cleron,' and 'blasphigonia' if they fail to complete the brood. They are killed by oil especially, if their head, anointed, is placed in the sun. Sometimes they bring the causes of death upon themselves, greedily devouring the honey once they sense it is being taken.

Pliny, in the same, on the names of their work: the skilled call the first foundation of the work 'metin.' The second, 'pissoceros.' The third, propolis, of great use for medicines, between the outer covering and the wax. 'Metis' is the first crust, of bitter taste. 'Pissoceros' comes over it, in the manner of pitch-workers, sweeter, the beginning of wax and the gentler gum of poplars. Propolis, of thicker material now, with flowers added, not yet wax, but the stabilizing structure of the combs, by which every entry of cold or harm is blocked, its smell still heavy, so that many use it in place of galbanum; besides these, there is brought in 'hithace,' which some call sandarac, others 'cherinthum'; this is the bees' food while they work, often found stored in the empty spaces of the combs, itself of bitter taste, but a food full of moisture. It is produced from spring dew and from tree sap in the manner of gum. Smaller in Africa, darker from the south wind's blast, better from the north winds, and reddest chiefly in Greek walnut trees.

Isidore: the spider is a worm of the air, named from its nourishment from the air. With a tiny body it draws out long threads, and, always intent on its web, never ceases to labor, sustaining a perpetual suspension in its citadel.

Aristotle: the spider has its own proper taste and lives by hunting flies. For when it suffers hunger, it sucks the moisture of a captured fly, and its life is from that moisture alone. The spider, called in Greek 'phalidron,' is generated in the houses of bees and harms them, corrupting the honey, and makes its web around the walls of their houses.
Pliny: spiders live by sucking, and wasps and phalangium spiders and spiders are at odds with each other.

Pliny, in the same book: spiders are especially hostile to bees, and, once they gain the upper hand in weaving, kill the hive. In spiders there are omens, for at the future rising of rivers they raise their webs higher. Further, they do not weave in clear weather, but often weave when cloudy, and so a multitude of spiders is a sign of rain. They think the one that weaves is the female, the one that hunts the male, and thus that pairs are formed by merit. Spiders mate joined at the haunches: dust breeds moths in wool and clothing, especially if a spider is shut in with it, for it thirsts and absorbs all moisture and so increases dryness. In certain spiders a pair of very long legs precede the rest, with three joints in each.

Gloss, on Psalm 38: the spider has a thin body and does not stand on the ground, but weaves empty webs on high from the discharge of its own innards; the spider itself too is something hot and weak, failing at a light touch. Whence it is written: 'You have made his soul waste away like a spider.'

Gloss: the spider weaves empty webs, so as to catch flies by deceit; so too we, in our years, devote ourselves to deceitful and empty occupations, namely in corruptible things, whence it is said our years are meditated like a spider, not achieved.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the spider lives on juice, and so never dies of hunger. Suspended by a thread over the head of a serpent stretched out in the shade of a tree, such is the force of its bite that it seizes the serpent's brain until death; it sucks thick and dry moisture, but delights in the moderate and tempered kind.

Physiologus: the spider disembowels itself, so that material is not lacking for weaving its nets. The female indeed weaves and gives birth, the male hunts. The spider, sleeping, turns its back to the ground and its face toward the sky, and sleeps in the air, hanging from the threads it has woven. A plaster made from flies, applied over the site of the pain, calms the swelling arising from a spider's bite.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the spider, as is read, is so called because it is nourished by the infusion of air among the foliage. It has six feet, and disembowels itself, and weaves webs from its own innards, with which it catches flies; it wastes away from its own venom. It hangs itself in the air, and ensnares the flies it catches. It is swollen and, as it were, entirely belly. Many of its properties are noted in these two verses: 'Thick behind, girded, short, venomous, it fears fire; hanging for flies, it weaves its work from its own innards.'

Aristotle: spiders separate only with difficulty, since their mating lasts a long time. And when they wish to mate, the female draws the male by a thread of the web, and afterward the male draws the female. Nor will the drawing cease until they are joined, and the male is placed over the female's belly. This manner of mating is due to the roundness of the belly, and occurs especially at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, since they desire mating at that time. And when a spider gives birth, it is placed at once within the web. And its exit from within is not, as Democritus said, like the exit of waste matter, but it casts it out as if a covering from the body.

Pliny: spiders' offspring are of unequal age, as if illegitimate: one flies off, another is still an infant, another still a grub, and this happens in autumn, not spring; all of these grow especially at the full moon. Wasps called ichneumons, which are smaller than others, kill a certain kind of spider called the phalangium, and carry it to their nests; then they smear it, and, by brooding over these, breed their own kind. Spiders mate joined at the haunches, and bear little worms resembling eggs. All lay them spread out into webs, since they leap and thus release them. Phalangium spiders alone brood in their den, in great number. These, once hatched, sometimes devour their mother, and even their father. They bear thirty at a time; the rest, fewer, and brood for three days. Spiders are consumed within twenty-eight days.

Aristotle: the spider wraps its eggs and encloses them in a very thick web. And when the young reach completion, they open their web by biting through it. Spiders mate at the end of spring, though some in autumn and winter; at the time of desire, male and female, standing apart, bind their feet with thread and, in turn, draw each other close by pulling, until they reach an embrace.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the spider weaves very fine nets from its own innards, and disembowels itself for the catching of flies so often that, entirely emptied, it fails unto death. But when it is sated, it carefully ensnares in the net whatever is caught but not needed, so that it does not escape, but, when it is hungry again, finds food already caught and prepared.

Aristotle: the spider, like the ant and the other ringed animals, is of much labor, and is even more skillful than other ringed creatures. It weaves, and, standing in its web, waits until some small creature falls into it, and then leaps upon it and seizes it and carries it to the place where it stores it. But if something falls into the web so as to tear it, the spider does not hunt until it has repaired what was torn; at sunset and sunrise it hunts with a repaired web, since at that time small creatures are especially caught in its web. The spider hunts, then, but does not store food for a long time, as the ant does. A large spider, indeed, hangs beneath its web, so as not to be seen by small creatures. A smaller one, however, extends part of its web and, hiding in it, hunts the small creatures that fall into it. It also hunts the small lizard, for it first begins to weave over it until it binds its opening with a strong tie. Then it goes to it and bites it until it dies. It sucks, however, the moisture of the small creatures it catches and leaves the rest.

Physiologus: the spider, when it hunts, through a pattern arranged in the likeness of a net, places its seat in the middle of that same pattern, as if at the center of a circular surface, so that it may perceive from there the entangling of flies in every part of its net, toward which center, indeed, all the lines of the circumference of its net are gathered by threads binding them crosswise; the small creature that falls in, however, it wraps in the web until it is weakened. Then it carries it to the place where it puts what it catches, and, when it suffers hunger meanwhile, sucks its moisture, in which its life resides. When, however, it hungers, it returns to hunting, but first repairs what has been torn from the web.

Pliny: there are several kinds of spiders; phalangium spiders are named among these, whose harmful bite comes from a small, mottled, sharp body, given to leaping. Another species of these is black, with very long front legs, all having three joints in the legs, in the manner of wolves. The smallest do not weave. The larger ones open small entrances into burrows in the earth. A third kind of these, remarkable for its skilled work, spins webs, and the belly of the spider itself suffices for the material of so great a work, either because of a nature that discharges from its corrupted belly at a fixed time, as Democritus holds, or because there is within it a certain wool-bearing fertility; with such measured claw, such rounded thread, and such even spacing does it draw out its warp threads, using its own weight. It begins to weave from the middle, in a circling orbit, attaching the crossing threads, and the mesh-openings always at equal intervals, but gradually widening, expanding outward from the narrow center, and binding with an unbreakable knot. And when prey falls in, watchful and ready for the chase, though the outer edge is struck, it always runs to the center. From there it shakes the whole web most effectively, entangling its catch. It repairs at once what is torn, mending it to a fine finish.

Aristotle: there are many kinds of spiders. One is similar, which is called 'locos,' and is a certain small kind, of varied color, sharp, leaping. Another, however, is larger and of black color, having longer front legs, and is of slow movement and much leaping at mating time. The rest, the remaining ones, which apothecaries carry, either do not bite at all, or only weakly. The kinds of 'locos,' however, are many. One of them is small, another large. The small one, indeed, does not weave; the large one, however, is rough and bad, and weaves near the ground. It stays within holes and, remaining in its web, watches until some small creature falls in. Then it leaps upon it and cuts it apart. There is also found another, spotted kind, weaving a small and poor web in spring beneath trees. There is another kind, more discerning than this one, which first extends the threads of its web and places them at the boundaries. Then, between these extremities, it weaves in the middle and places a sufficient web there, and prepares a place suited to hunting. It comes to the middle, as it were a watcher, and if some small creature falls in, it moves at once and leaves its place and binds it and wraps it in the web until it grows weak, afterward carrying it to the place where it stores it, and sucks its moisture when it hungers.

Pliny, as has been said: the spider, suspended by its thread from a serpent stretched out in the shade of a tree. And with such force does its bite seize the serpent's brain that the serpent, hissing repeatedly and whirling in dizziness, cannot break free even from the thread hanging above it, or flee.

Avicenna, in the second canon: from a spider's bite much flatulence follows in the belly, with gooseflesh and coldness of the extremities, and the member is made erect. Among the medicines for this are black cumin and wine and dry rue.

Constantine the African, in the Pantegni: there are many kinds of spiders, which, where they bite, cause much pain, redness, cold sweat, and a yellowish color. Sometimes a kind of retention like strangury in the urine, and a hardness and stretching of the member down to the groin and knees, a resinous heaviness in the stomach, and a stretching of the tongue, so that speech cannot be understood. The patient vomits a moisture like a spider's web, and likewise a loosening of the bowels; if warm water is poured on, the pain is relieved, but if it evaporates, it returns. Another kind, where it bites, causes pain and redness, a tightness beneath the diaphragm, coldness in the urine, and also a stretching of the member.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the spider's web, as is clear from what has been said, comes from its own innards. For it disembowels itself so often in the weaving of it, that, entirely emptied, it fails unto death. Its web, moreover, is empty and weak, and is scattered and dissolved by a slight wind. Whence it is read of the hypocrite that his confidence is like a spider's web. Yet this same web is of use in many remedies, as is found among various authors.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the white web of a thick spider, dripped into the ear with rose oil, calms its pain. Likewise a spider's web placed on wounds checks the flow of blood. It also prevents ulcers and wounds from festering. Some have also said that spider's web, mixed with certain plasters and placed on the forehead and temples, heals tertian fever. For a broken head, spider's web with oil and vinegar applied does not come away until the wound is healed. Spider's web has binding powers; mixed with certain ointments and applied to the temples, it cures fevers. It stops flowing blood. Applied to a shallow wound, it prevents the formation of discharge. It keeps wounds free of swelling; cooked with rose oil it soothes ear pain. The white work of the spider, that is, the white web, bound in leather and hung around the neck, is said to remove quartan fevers.

Isidore: 'bibiones' are those born in wine, commonly called 'mustiones' from must [mustum], whence Afranius says: 'when you begin to tell tales in expectation of me, wine-gnats fly out of your mouth into your eyes.' 'Blattae' [cockroaches] are named from their color, since even when caught they stain the hand; whence too they speak of the color 'blatteus.' This creature cannot bear to see light, unlike the fly. For the fly seeks the light, but the cockroach flees it.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the cockroach is a worm that cannot bear to see light, whence it is accustomed to move about only at night.
Palladius: cockroaches are hostile to bees, as are lizards. Whence such creatures and their like should be kept far from the camps or hives of bees, by whoever wishes to keep bees well.

Pliny, book 11, on fireflies: they shine at night, glowing in the color of their sides and haunches, in the manner of fire, and not by the flashing of wings. Now indeed, when pressed together, they are darkened; not visible before their food is ripe, nor after it fails. The cockroach's nature, on the contrary, is a nursling of darkness, and it flees the light; weaker still, and bred or born especially in baths, in the moist vapor there.
Pliny, book 20, in the same: they report that if a bundle of the herb 'cunila' is thrown down, all the cockroaches of the whole house gather to it.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: they say a cockroach, its head torn off and ground together with rose oil, wondrously benefits the ears. Others, however, write that two or three of them, boiled in oil, most effectively heal the ears, and, ground and wrapped in linen, are applied. They have made several kinds of these: one, the soft kind, which they have found by experience, boiled in oil, most effectively applied to warts. Another kind they called 'mylochon,' born near millstones, and, its head removed and ground up, is left on record by Musa and Picton as healing leprosy. A third kind, hateful for the offensiveness of its smell, its wing sharpened with pitch-oil, is said to heal otherwise incurable ulcers and scrofulous swellings and skin blemishes applied for twenty-one days; crushed, they cure scabies and boils of malignant sores, their feet and wings removed. By Hercules, Diodorus reports they also cured jaundice and difficulty of breathing, with resin and honey. Their ash, from a most humane burning, is kept in a horn box for these uses, and it is said that, ground, it is infused in enemas for those with catarrh and difficulty breathing, and it is established that, applied, it draws out things lodged in the body.

Isidore: the silkworm [bombyx] is a worm of leaves, from whose weaving silk cloth is made. It is called by this name because it empties itself while it produces its threads, and only air remains within it.

Pliny, in the passage above: silkworms weave webs in the manner of spiders, for the luxurious clothing of women, called silk. There is a kind of silkworm arising in Assyria; they build nests of mud, applied to a rock in the manner of salt, of such hardness that they can scarcely be pierced by spear-points, and they make wax more abundant than bees do. Then, it is reported, a larger grub, and on the island of Cos, from the fallen flower of cypress, terebinth, ash, and oak, shaken down by rains, brought to life by the earth's breath, is said first to become small, bare butterflies; soon, unable to bear the cold, they bristle with fine hairs, and, against winter, prepare thick coverings for themselves, scraping with the roughness of their feet the down of leaves into fleece.

Physiologus: the silkworm is a worm that makes threaded silk from its own mouth, in which it buries itself, so that it may be reborn complete. And after it has cast out from its body all that is like dung, foul and black, then its body becomes translucent when looked at against the sun. It feeds on the leaves of the mulberry tree, commonly called the 'morus.' But once it begins to work, it refuses food, devoting diligent effort to its delightful labor. The industrious weaver goes around the walls of its basket-shaped cocoon, drawing out wool of a saffron color, which becomes snow-white through washing, before an artificial dye is applied over it. Once the noble weaver's work is complete, it enters, like a butterfly, the door of the covering it has wrapped around its own work. Afterward it casts out tiny seeds from the secret recesses of its nature, which are kept through the winter, so that, as milder air returns, brought close to human flesh, they receive warmth in a person's bosom, until nature confers animal motion upon the animated seeds. They then receive growth, both by the power of nature and by the benefit of food. This same worm is also called the wool-bearer, from the silken wool that it works from its own innards. Of this more will be said below. Silk, moreover, burnt, cleans and strengthens putrid wounds. And if it is burnt with salt, it cures the rusting of teeth.

Radulfus of Flaix: the locust-grub is modest in size and tawny in color. It is called 'bruchus' as the offspring of the locust before it has wings. Then, when it begins to fly a little, it is called 'athelabus.' When, however, it flies fully, it is called 'locust.' The 'bruchus,' moreover, is much more harmful than either the locust or the 'athelabus,' since, lying in one place, it gnaws crops down to the root.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the locust-grub feeds with a bitter bite on vegetables and herbs and the foliage of trees, and there is no remedy in a place where a multitude of these gather. It does more harm, then, than the locust, but is smaller in body than the 'adlacta,' and is less capable in leaping. The 'adlacta,' however, is different in color, but leaps nonetheless and has longer hind legs, like the locust. It lays eggs, from which offspring emerge in springtime.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the toad is reckoned among the other reptile worms, venomous and pestilential to the sight; we have, however, already placed the toad and the frog above among the kind of lizards, since they seem, by crawling, to rest on four legs or 'arms,' and there we have spoken more fully of both.

Isidore and Pliny, book 30: the 'buprestis' is a small animal in Italy, most similar to a beetle, long-legged, that leaps among the grasses, especially attacking cattle, whence too it has its name. Once swallowed, once its gall is touched, it inflames the animal so much that it bursts.
An oil made from hunting, washed by itself in water and taken as an emetic, is effective against the 'buprestis.'
Pliny, in the same: 'buprestis' applied with goat-suet removes freckles from the face by its corrosive power.
Pliny, in the same: milk resists the venom of the 'buprestis.'
Pliny, in the same: if the 'buprestis' is fed with soda, taken in water it induces vomiting.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: when an ox has devoured a 'buprestis' lying among the grasses and its gall has touched it, it becomes so inflamed and swollen that it bursts at once, its innards torn apart.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'cantharis' is an earthly worm, which, as soon as it is applied to a human body, produces, by its burning, blisters full of moisture.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: 'cantharides' are worms generated at the tips of the branches of ash or alder from moisture in the leaves; they are green in color, gleaming like gold in the sun's rays, and grow strong as caterpillars do, but also fully acquire wings. By day they fly; by night, however, they gather together into a single ball. Around the month of August they are collected at night for a remedy and, drowned in vinegar, are killed; dead, wine is poured over them, and, placed on any limb beneath a small wax vessel shaped like a cup, they raise a burning and a blister by their application, which blister, pierced in several places with a golden needle or a sharp reed-point, expels the harmful moisture. And its discharge is as effective for fifteen years as some cauterization would be within a year.

Avicenna, in the second canon: 'cantharides' are sharp and biting, causing a stinging and pain to occur in the limbs; they ulcerate the bladder with a painful ulceration and a swelling. They also cause a swelling of the member and of the pubic area, with vehement inflammation. With this too sometimes follow loosening of the bowels with excoriation, and fainting, and confusion of reason, and heaviness. Most of their harm is to the bladder.

Avicenna, in the second canon: cantharides are hot and very sharp, and, although they benefit scabies, they wound the bladder, if a large quantity of them is taken, or make one urinate blood, and kill. Taken, however, in a small quantity, they strongly provoke urine, and white vitiligo so intense it is thought leprosy, they bring relief for with a vinegar poultice.

Dioscorides: cantharides have a putrefying power, and are good for storing; they are gathered in a wheat-field and, put into an earthenware vessel, a cloth tied over it, are set over a pot in which vinegar boils, by whose vapor, enclosed, they are killed. Afterward they are threaded on linen and stored in an unpitched vessel. The better ones are mottled, thick, and longer. Those placed on a potsherd and burnt have an astringent and hot power, whence they are mixed into medicines that are effective for cancerous or leprous sores, or scabby scalp conditions, and control the menses. Those, however, gathered around roses are weaker and of a single color, though they are used in certain antidotes.
Haly Abbas: cantharides, hot and sharp, benefit itching, kill lice, and heal leprosy, if applied with vinegar.
Pliny, book 29: cantharides are opposed and resistant to all ants, and to salamanders too.

Palladius, in the passage above: finally, against the cantharis-beetles that harm vines, the cantharides that we are accustomed to find on roses, drowned in oil, should be left to dissolve into decay. And when the vines are to be pruned, the pruning-hooks should be anointed with this oil. Further, so that cantharides do not harm vines, they themselves should be ground into the whetstone on which the pruning-hooks are sharpened.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'cereleus,' as Solinus and Statius say, is a wondrous worm abounding in the river Ganges. For it has two arms of six cubits' length, with which it seizes even the elephant and drags it under the waves. But since this worm is huge and monstrous and aquatic, we have already placed it above among the sea or aquatic monsters, and spoken of it more fully there.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the stag-beetle is said to be a kind of cicada; the Experimenter, however, calls it a hornet. Beneath its wings, as he says, which are thicker, it has fine, thin wings like the locust-grub. They fly especially toward evening, and make a noise while flying. They have large, medicinal horns, very long, forked, toothed, and shining, meeting like pincers at the tip when they wish to bite. Their legs, however, are long and bent back; the sides and haunches shine at night in the manner of fire, the colors of their wings gleaming, and are sometimes darkened when pressed together; their severed head lives longer without the body, but even the body without the head, though not as long as the head.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: cicadas are worms, of which there are two kinds: some are similar to small locusts, and these inhabit houses and places that are warmer, where there is the heat of fires. The other kind, however, is dark in color, similar to butterflies; it is also said that the kind we call the stag-beetle belongs here, which the Experimenter above calls the hornet, as has already been said. Cicadas have on their chest a certain sting-like organ, resembling tongues, with which they lick the dew. Their chest, indeed, is like a pipe, and with this they sing sweetly. The males indeed sing, the females are silent. They mate lying on their backs. Their eggs are white but spoiled. They hollow out a place in the earth for their brood, and there produce their offspring.

Ambrose: in the throat of cicadas is a sweet song, by whose singing, in the midst of the heat, the groves resound, since they sing more in the noonday heat; and the more they draw in the surrounding air with their breath, the clearer they make their song.

Isidore: cicadas are born from the spittle of cuckoos; in Italy, among the people of Rhegium, they are mute, and nowhere else. For elsewhere they sing sweetly, and by their singing, in the midst of summer's heat, the groves resound.

Pliny, book 11: cicadas are not born where trees are sparse, nor in cold or shady groves; their wings are of the same nature as bees', but larger in proportion to their body. Cicadas live on dew alone, of which there are two kinds: the smaller, which appear first and are mute, and die last. There are, however, many that sing, and are called 'achetae,' and those smaller than these are 'tettigometrae,' but those are more resonant. In both kinds the males sing, the females are silent. Peoples toward the East eat these, even the Parthians, abundant in wealth. Before mating, the males come before the females; their mating is around the solstice. Their eggs, which are white, having spoiled, they mate lying on their backs. And they have a roughness, sharpened, on their back, with which they hollow out a place for their brood in the earth. And at first there is a small worm, then from it comes what is called the 'tettigometra,' whose shell, once broken, they always fly out at night, around the solstices, at first black and hard - this alone among living things is without a mouth, but in its place is a certain sting-like organ, resembling tongues, and this, on the chest, is what they use to lick the dew. Its chest itself is pipe-like, and this, as we have said, is what the 'achetae' sing with. For the rest, there is nothing in the belly. Roused as they fly up, they release moisture, which is the only proof that they are nourished by dew alone. In these alone there is no opening for excretion. Their eyes are so dull that if one brings a finger close to them, drawing it back and releasing it repeatedly, they let it pass as if it were a leaf. Some make two other kinds of these, namely the furrow-cicada, which grows larger, and the grain-cicada, which others call the oat-cicada, for it appears at the same time as the grain is ripening; cicadas, like bees, are thought to produce their shrill sound with their long tongues, by contraction. Some, however, deny that insects have a voice at all, despite the great sound of cicadas and the murmur of bees.
Solinus: nowhere else are cicadas mute except at Rhegium, which is such a wonder of that place, since those nearby, in the territory of the Locrians, sing louder than all others.

div.head: DE CICENDELA ET CIMICE AC COSTRO

cit.quote: Isidore: the firefly [cicendela] is a kind of beetle, so named because, walking or flying, it shines [lucet].

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the firefly is a worm in Italy that flies by night and, radiant amid the darkness of night, shines so brightly that if you see it in the dark you would think it a shower of sparks.
Isidore: the bedbug, moreover, is among the worms of flesh, as has been said above. It is called 'cimex,' moreover, from its resemblance to a certain herb, whose stench it shares.

Avicenna, in the second canon: from ash trees come swollen, pomegranate-like growths, in which there is a moisture from which bedbugs arise. For when such growths are opened, bedbugs come out of them. Bedbugs, moreover, are especially driven off by bull's dung, when a fumigation is made with it.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: bedbugs are also driven off if an ointment is made with radish oil, or if a fumigation is made from pine sawdust or with black cumin, or by the other means that will be spoken of below concerning the gnat together with the bedbug.
Rhazes, in the Almansor: bedbugs are driven off by the smoke of chaff, and by the smoke of cow dung, and especially by the smoke of reed and black cumin.

Palladius, in the passage above: bedbugs also harm gardens; they are destroyed, however, by anointing their beds or places with olive-lees and buffalo gall, or with ivy leaves ground in oil, or by burnt leeches.
Isidore: [on] the honeycomb. The Greeks call 'cosdri' those that are born larger at the outer edges. Some think these are called 'kings' because they lead the camp.

Isidore: the gnat [culex] is named from its sting [aculeus], since it sucks blood; for it has in its mouth a tube like a goad, with which it bores the flesh, so as to drink blood. Of which someone says: 'small gnat, guardian of the flocks, may you deserve more from me.'

Aristotle: a ringed-bodied animal has an organ by which it perceives food, and some have this organ outside, like a sting, whose nature is soft and hollow; through it they taste and perceive and draw in food; gnats and flies, however, the smallest of creatures, pierce the hide of man and of other animals through this organ.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: the gnat seeks out sour things and flees sweet ones, loves light, so much so that it sometimes burns itself at a flame. It has its name from the sting by which it sucks blood.
Pliny, book 10: gnats seek sour things, and do not fly toward sweet ones. Gnats are most welcome food for the bat.

Pliny, book 11, on the gnat: in such small and tiny creatures, what great reason, what force! What inextricable perfection! Where has nature placed so many senses in the gnat - though there are other things smaller still to mention. But where has it placed sight in it, where applied taste, where inserted smell, and where indeed engendered that harsh and, for its size, enormous voice? With what fineness has it fitted the wings together, lengthened the legs of its feet? It has fashioned an empty belly, as it were, hollow, and kindled a greedy thirst for blood, especially human blood. With what skill has it fashioned the weapon for piercing the hide, and, in a body so small that it cannot even be seen, produced such reciprocal artistry, that it might be equally sharp for piercing and tubular for sucking. And so the gnat has a sting in its mouth, as do certain flies. Bees, moreover, are attacked by a kind of gnat called the 'mulio.' The wild fig produces fig-gnats.

Pliny, book 17, in the same: there are also kinds of gnats troublesome to certain trees, like the oak and the fig, which seem to be born from moisture, together with a sudden sweetness in the bark. The ripening of the fig by caprification is when gnats are clearly born within it. For when they have flown out, no grains are found within, which had appeared turned into them. Their eagerness to get out is so great that most of them burst out, leaving behind either a foot or part of a wing. There is also another kind of gnat, which they call 'centrinae,' similar to the drones of bees in laziness and malice, to the ruin of the real and useful ones, for they kill them, and themselves die too.
Pliny, in the same: gnats are also born in turnips.

div.head: DE HIS QUIBUS EFFUGANTUR CULICES ET NECANTUR

cit.quote: Pliny, in the same: gnats infest well-watered gardens, especially if there are some small trees there. But they are driven off by burning galbanum, and killed by the smoke of burnt lupins.
Also with wormwood: gnats are driven off when it is applied with vinegar, and by its smoke, if it is burnt.
Pliny, book 33, in the same: the smoke of all metal-smelting furnaces is also felt to be harmful and pestilential to flies and gnats.
Ambrose: gnats do not touch a man, if he boils wormwood with oil and anoints himself with it.
Palladius: against gnats and slugs in gardens or crops, fresh olive-lees or soot from chimneys is scattered; they are also driven off with poured galbanum, or with sulfur.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: to drive away gnats and bedbugs, let there be a fumigation with pine sawdust or with black cumin, likewise with dry myrtle and with sulfur and bdellium and stinking spurge and cow dung and with cypress leaves and its nut. Likewise for the same purpose the house is sprinkled with a decoction of lupin root, or with a decoction of black cumin or wormwood or rue.
Isidore: 'cynomyia' in Greek means 'dog-fly.' For the dog is called 'cynos' in Greek.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'cynomyia' is the dog-fly, troublesome to the ears of puppies. Although the puppy shakes it off often, it always flies back troublesomely. When, however, it finds the puppy too sluggish to shake it off, it works its way in until it draws blood and causes wounds.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'cynomyia' is that most grievous fly with which the people of Egypt were struck in the fourth plague. Of this it is read in Exodus: 'there came a most grievous fly into the houses of Pharaoh and of his servants, and into all the land of Egypt, and the land was corrupted by such flies.' By this, according to the Gloss, canine habits are signified, by which the pleasure of the human mind, that is, lust, is condemned. So too the gnats by which the Egyptians were struck in the third plague signify worldly disturbances, which, provoking quarrels and lovers of slander, do not admit the rest of the spiritual sabbath. Whence the Psalmist: 'He spoke, and the dog-fly came.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'engula' is a worm taking its name from the fact itself. For it always has its head in blood, and, sucking continually, swells so much that it bursts in the middle. For it has no outlet for excess matter: this is called by some the wild louse. It is never bred in beasts of burden, but often in wolves and dogs. The caterpillar is a long worm set apart by many feet, varied in color. It feeds on vegetables and the leaves of trees. Around the month of September, drenched by heavenly dew or rain, it is said suddenly to change color and shape, so that what crawled on innumerable feet can fly with newly acquired wings. It consumes everything, and is itself in the end consumed. The caterpillar, once it has left behind, at the tips of trees, a woven covering like the silkworm's, joins together with worms the following summer. Some, however, entering the roofs of houses, having entirely changed their shape and color, hang on the walls in the open air, and there are reduced to nothing. The caterpillar, passing over a man's flesh, infects it and leaves pustules behind it. And this is a sign of venom, even if it is not strong enough to cause great harm.

Isidore: the caterpillar is a worm of leaves, wrapped in a vegetable or vine-leaf; named from gnawing [erodendo], of which Plautus makes mention: 'imitating that wicked, harmful beast wrapped in a vine-leaf.' It also wraps itself up, nor does it fly off like the locust, so as to run here and there leaving things half-eaten, but it stays where the crops are to ripen, and, with slow movement and sluggish bites, consumes everything.

Pliny: with much rain, dreadful creatures called caterpillars are born, and some gnaw the foliage, others the flower, and leave the eaten tree a shameful sight; this evil arises in a season that is moist and slow.

Palladius, book 2: against caterpillars, seeds that are to be sown are soaked in the juice of houseleek, or in the blood of caterpillars. Some, however, scatter ash of fig over the caterpillars; some sow squill in the garden; some even make a menstruating woman walk barefoot around the garden against caterpillars and other harmful things; some fix many river-crabs in several places within the garden.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the ant is a small animal, watchful, provident, and shrewd. It clears earth from its burrows, moves along a narrow path, and feeds on grain.
Isidore: the ant [formica] is so named because it bores [forat] crumbs of grain [micas farris].

Aristotle: the ant is a ringed animal, without wings and without blood, and is among those animals that live together with their own kind, and among those that have dwellings, like mice and moles. The ant, like the fly, mates in winter, if the air is favorable and a southerly wind blows; it has, within its mouth, an organ by which it perceives food; ringed animals that lack a sting-like appendage in the front of the body have another organ in the mouth, as ants do. And what lacks a sting in the front of the body has certain teeth for taking food and certain others for holding it, like the ant and the bee kind. The generation of ants comes from animals like themselves. Ants dig out earth to build their homes. They have no king; they are of much labor and industry, and work even at night when the moon is full, and store their food, and always walk along a single path.

Pliny, book 6: we have seen flints worn away by the passage of ants, and a path made by their work, lest anyone doubt what persistence can achieve in any matter, however small. Alone among living creatures, except man, they bury their dead. And among insects the ant alone has a tongue within.

Little pellets from the female cypress - for the male produces none - gathered and dried in the sun, and broken open, release seed sought after by ants for its myrrh-like scent, adding to the wonder that the birth of such great trees should be consumed as food for so tiny a creature.
Pliny, book 18, in the same: sluggishly, and against their own industry, ants, running about in hiding or carrying forth their eggs, signify coming storms.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, Thomas Cantimpratensis: the ant is an animal of remarkable foresight for itself; this alone among animals is strengthened and grows with age. Ants share their labors, as bees do, but bees make their food, whereas ants store it. They also carry out their dead and bury them, and this they do alone among all animals except man. The ant, for its kind, is the strongest, for it carries a weight equal to its own size. It gathers only the grain of wheat, not of barley.

Pliny: ants produce a little worm resembling an egg, and bees indeed make useful foods, but ants store them; and if one compares the loads to their bodies, one must admit that their strength is proportionally greater. They carry larger loads in their jaws, walking backward, and push others with their hind feet, straining with their shoulders.

Isidore: the ant has much skill, for it provides for the future and prepares in summer what it will eat in winter. In the harvest it chooses wheat, does not touch barley, and, while it rains on the grain, throws it all out. It is said that in Ethiopia there are ants shaped like dogs, which dig up golden sand with their feet, which they guard so that no one may take it, and, catching thieves, pursue them to their death.

Ambrose: the ant, though tiny, dares things greater than its strength, nor is it forced to work by servitude, but, by the design of its own spontaneous foresight, lays up in advance provisions of food for itself, storing up for itself a harvest from the labors of others. And while the farmer often is in need, the ant is not. No granaries are closed to it, no guard is impenetrable. It also knows how to detect fair weather. For when it notices that its crops, soaked by rain, are growing damp, having more carefully examined the air, as to when it can maintain a steady mildness, it carries its stores back and brings them out of its burrows on its shoulders, so that its own grain may dry in the steady sun. Finally, you will never see rain burst from the clouds on those days, unless the ant has already recalled its crops.

Physiologus: ants, coming out of their den, walk in order seeking grains. And when one of them finds an ear of grain, it discerns by smell whether it is of wheat or barley. If of barley, it passes on until it finds an ear of wheat; then, climbing up onto the ear, it deposits its grain, and so each carries a single grain in its mouth back to the den. Others, however, empty ones, meeting them, do not say to them, 'give us some of your harvest,' but go seeking along their tracks until they find it and likewise carry it back. Storing the grain in the den, they split it in half, so that it does not sprout.

Aristotle: the work of ants is plain to see; they labor, as has been said, even at night, at the full moon; they do not hunt, but store food, and always walk along a single path. For many blood-lacking animals are more refined than certain blooded ones, like bees and ants.
Pliny: [on] ants. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny, book 11, in the same: in these there is a kind of reasoning of a commonwealth, and memory, and care; they store gnawed seeds, so that they do not sprout again into crops from the earth. They divide larger ones at the entrance, and, once soaked by rain, bring them out and dry them. They also work at night at the full moon, but rest at the new moon. And since they gather from different directions, one unaware of another, fixed days are given for their mutual recognition, like a market-day. What a bustling then among them, how attentive a conversation and questioning with those they meet!
Gloss, on the ant: the ant, namely, lacking a leader, without reason, guided by nature, provides for itself for the future. Whence it is written: 'Go to the ant, O sluggard,' and so on.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the ant chooses a grain of wheat, and if it has been rained on in its pit, it takes it out to dry, and thus puts it back again until the time it is needed. To keep the grain from sprouting, however, it is said to divide it into three parts.

div.head: DE HIS QUE CONTRARIA SUNT FORMICIS

cit.quote: Palladius, in the passage above: since ants are harmful to gardens and crops, they are driven off if their form is sprinkled with crushed marjoram and sulfur. Again, if you burn empty snail shells and stuff their holes with the ash. Further, against ants, if they have a hole in the garden, an owl's heart is placed near it; but if they come from outside, the whole area of the garden should be marked with ash or white chalk.

Al-Kindi, in the book on poisons: when you introduce into an ants' nest an 'azath,' that is, a clinging bat, those ants will not leave the nest, nor gather food through it any longer. Likewise a place sprinkled with menstrual blood, ants will never approach, and plants wither from it.
Pliny, book 10: ants are killed by the smell of storax, marjoram, lime, or sulfur.
Pliny, in the same: the other lobe of the toad's liver is not touched by ants, because of its venom, as they suppose.

Pliny, book 17, in the same: ants are also pests of trees; they are driven off by anointing the trunks with red ochre and liquid pitch, and also by hanging a fish nearby, which gathers them into one place, or by anointing the roots with ground lupin and oil.

Pliny, book 19, in the same: if gardens are not well-watered, ants are their pest, against which the remedy is to block their holes with sea mud or ash, but they are killed most effectively by the herb heliotrope, or 'sunflower.' Some also think water diluted with unbaked brick is hostile to them.
There is a venomous kind of ant, which they do not know in Italy, which Cicero calls the 'solifuga' or 'salpyga.' The bat's heart is contrary to these, but cantharis-beetle too resists all ants.
Aristotle: if one takes sulfur and wild marjoram and powders it over the dwellings of ants, they will abandon them and flee. Likewise they also flee from the smoke of dry storax.

Rhazes: ants are driven off by tar, and by sulfur, and by asafoetida, and if any of these is put into their holes, they will die. Further, if a poultice of it is made around the hole, they will not come out.
Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: an ants' nest fumigated with sulfur and wild marjoram forces the ants to flee from it.
Solinus: ants, as has been said, are said to exist in Ethiopia the size of a large dog, which dig up golden sand with their lion-like feet, and guard it so that no one may take it.

Pliny: in the region of the northern Indians called the Dardae, ants dig gold from burrows in the earth, of the color of cats, of the size of Egyptian wolves. This gold, dug up by them, the Indians steal in wintertime, since in the summer's heat the ants hide in their tunnels because of the vapor. But roused by the scent, they fly forth and often tear apart the fleeing thieves, however swift their camels. Such is their speed and ferocity along with their love of gold.

Physiologus, on gold from the Ethiopian ants: those who wish to steal gold from the Ethiopian ants take mares with their foals and starve them for three days; finally they tie the foals at the bank of a stream that runs between them and the ants. And they drive the mares across that water, with pack-saddles placed on their backs, and these, when they see green grasses across the river, graze through the fields beyond the river. The ants, however, seeing the chests and pack-saddles on their backs, carry golden sand into them, wishing to store it there. And as evening comes, once the mares are sated and laden with gold, hearing their foals neighing from hunger, they return to them with much gold.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: in India, around the golden mountains, there are ants larger than foxes, strong and very fierce, having four feet, and hooked claws on their feet. They are, moreover, of such strength that they tear apart men they see. They do not easily harm beasts, however, being well aware that they should not take from them, against their will, the gold that they themselves guard. To punish the recklessness of greed, then, these beasts were placed there by God.

Isidore: the ant-lion is so called because it is the lion of ants, or because it is at once ant and lion. For it is a small animal, quite harmful to ants, which hides itself in dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is called ant and lion, moreover, because it is like an ant to other animals, but like a lion to ants.

Gloss, on Job: the ant-lion, that is, the lion of ants, is a small animal, which secretly lies in wait for ants and eats them, but to flying creatures and other animals that eat it, it exists as an ant. Whence 'the ant-lion perished,' and so on.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the lion of ants, called the ant-lion, is a worm of the ant kind, but much larger. While it is still small and weak in strength, it feigns peace and modesty, but once it has gained strength, it despises its former company and joins one large crowd. And so, growing bold with strength, it lies in ambush against the ants laboring to gather their needful stores, and, having prepared nothing for itself in summer, plunders and destroys their labors in winter.

Isidore: [the drone is] larger than a bee, smaller than a hornet. It is called 'fucus' because it eats the labors of others, as if 'fagus' or 'focus.' For it consumes what it has not worked for. Of this Virgil says: 'they drive the idle drones, a lazy herd, from the hives.' Drones, however, arise from dead mules.

Aristotle: the 'cephenes,' as has been said, are solitary among bees and do not work, but live off what the bees produce. They and the young of the bees are fed with honey, and, as if exercising themselves, fly in the air. Then they return to the hives and are fed.

Pliny, book 10, on drones: if a more abundant yield is hoped for, chambers are added for drones too. These cells, indeed, are the smallest, but the drones themselves are larger than the bees. Drones, moreover, are without a sting, like imperfect bees, begun last of all by the tired and already worn-out workers, a late brood, and, as it were, servants of the true bees; for this reason the bees command them and drive them first into the work, and punish the laggards without mercy. Nor do they help only with their mouths, but with the brood too, the crowd contributing much to warmth. Certainly, the greater their number, the greater the yield of the swarm will be. And when the honey begins to ripen, they drive them off. And many attack each one and slaughter them. And this kind is seen only in spring; a drone, its wings removed and thrown back into the hive, itself takes something away from the rest. Further, if the yield is disappointing, then they drive off the drones. Some have thought there is a distinct kind of these, like thieves among them, the very largest but black and broad-bellied, so called since they steal honey secretly. It is certain that drones are killed by bees, who indeed have no king of their own. And how they are born without a sting is a matter of question.

Isidore: the cricket [grillus] takes its name from the sound of its voice; it walks backward, burrows into the earth, and chirps at night. The ant hunts it by having a hair tied around it and thrown into its burrow, first blowing away the dust so it cannot hide, and thus the cricket is drawn out in the ant's coils.
Haly Abbas: long locusts, that is, crickets, if hung around the neck, benefit one suffering from quartan fever.

Pliny: the cricket, dug out with its own earth, benefits itching ears; Nigidius attributes great authority to this animal, and the magicians even greater. Crickets benefit an ear's parotid swelling, whether applied or bound on.

Pliny, in the same: they also advise applying a cricket, dug out with its own earth, to scrofulous swellings. Further, for stones and other difficulties of the bladder, it benefits to take a cricket dissolved in warm water; further, ash of burnt crickets in oil brings ulcers to scarring.
Petrus Comestor: the weevil is a worm born from the corruption of beans, just as the moth is from the corruption of vegetables, and the shipworm from the corruption of wood.
Isidore: it is called 'gurgulio' [weevil] because it is scarcely anything but a throat [guttur].

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the wool-bearer is a long worm, spotted, set apart by many feet, scattered white in color; this one produces silken wool from its own innards, and feeds on the leaves of the mulberry tree. This food, indeed, through the medium of its own innards, is turned into wool. And so it makes spindles of its own wool on small branches and works around itself, so that, once the spindles are complete, it is entirely enclosed within its own work; after this it makes an exit for itself at the top of the spindles, and, coming out, by a wondrous transformation of nature, appears entirely changed from its earlier form, so much so that the worms that crawled on innumerable feet now have wings and are fit to fly. Finally, entering upon mating, they mate for three days, after which the male dies, but the female, in a repeated cycle, lays innumerable eggs, on a small cloth laid beneath her, either white or red. Then she dies too; then the little cloth with its eggs is taken up and, where it cannot be reached by winter's cold, is put away; afterward, as spring's warmth grows strong, the eggs are exposed to the sun and warmed by its heat, until, quickened, they take shape as worms. The wool, however, naturally takes on two colors in the worm, namely white and saffron. The rest are produced by artifice. It is said that the eggs take on either a white or a saffron color from the cloth placed beneath them when they are laid.
Isidore: the slug [limax] is a worm of mud [limus], so named because it is born in mud, whence it is always held to be filthy and unclean.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of this more will be said below, where the tortoise is treated.
Isidore: the locust [locusta] is so named because it is like a spear [hasta] with its long legs, whence too the Greeks call both the sea and land kinds 'akris.'

Aristotle: locusts make no noise except by flying, in extending and contracting their wings, through the air falling between the wings and the body. Shedding old age happens to locusts as to wasps; in certain ringed-bodied animals the hind feet are larger than the middle ones, for walking, and so that they may be lifted quickly from the ground when they wish to fly. What results from these mating is more evident in creatures like locusts and fleas, for these bend their feet by contracting them, then extend them, and are thus lifted from the ground. For a bending in the feet, turning outward, is necessary. The front feet, however, cannot have such an arrangement. And all these have six feet, along with two additional feet by which they mate.

Pliny, book 11: the feet of insects move obliquely, and the outer ones of some curve outward, as in locusts. In India they are said to be three feet long, their shins and thighs serving as saws once they have dried. There is also another end for them: lifted together by the wind, they fall into seas or marshes and die. This perhaps happens by chance, and not, as the ancients thought, because their wings are wet with nighttime moisture. The same authors, indeed, reported that they do not fly at night because of the cold. The Parthians find them pleasant as food. Their voice seems to come from the back of the head. And in the place at the joint of their shoulders they are thought to have something like teeth, and, by rubbing these against each other, to produce a shrill sound, especially around the two equinoxes, just as cicadas do around the solstice. The locust, indeed, is thought not to make sound at all, but rather that it is the sound of its wings. Among insects, those that have long hind feet leap, like locusts.
Ambrose: locusts, by gnawing olive leaves, free themselves from sickness.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the locust is so called as if 'standing in place' [loco stans]; it is green in color, having a head shaped like a horse's, a mouth like a small square, a sting in place of a tail, longer legs bent back upon itself, and a single intestine filled with discharge and filth. Locusts are generated by the south wind, and die by the north and northeast wind. They fatten more quickly on the flowers of almond trees. They have a remedy for their own sickness, for gnawed laurel leaves free them from illness; they eat one another, and the larger devour the smaller. This animal is light and mobile, its flight brisk, but quickly spent.
Walafrid Strabo: the locust is so called as if 'long spear' [longa hasta], since it has longer legs at the back.

Gregory the Great: [on locusts:] other small creatures harm the crops, and so they represent the tongues of flatterers, which corrupt the minds of those who do good works and turn them toward a desire for praise.

Gloss: when locusts try to raise themselves into the air, they first lift themselves by pushing with their legs, and afterward call on their wings. In the morning hours, indeed, they scarcely lift themselves from the ground. But once the heat has grown, they fly higher. Whence it is written: 'Will you rouse it up like the locusts?'

Aristotle: a certain woman had a chirping locust and raised it while small. But when it grew, she found it pregnant of itself. And this is proof that any female naturally has seed. Certain ringed-bodied animals mate, and their generation will come from animals like themselves, as happens with blood-lacking animals, such as locusts, wasps, and ants.

Pliny, in the passage above: locusts lay, in the earth, with the tip of their spine lowered, densely packed eggs in autumn; these endure the winter underground, and the following year, at the coming of spring, release small, dark creatures, crawling without legs or wings. And so with spring rains the eggs perish, but in dry weather the yield is greater. Others report a double birth, twice occurring, namely at the rising of the Pleiades, then dying off at the rising of the Dog Star, and being reborn again. Some, however, report that they are reborn at the setting of Arcturus. It is certain that the mothers die once they have given birth, a small worm being born at once around their throat, which strangles them. At the same time the males die too, dying for so frivolous a reason as this; each one, when it wishes, kills a serpent, seizing its jaws with a bite. They are born, however, only in flat and cracked ground. Around the two equinoxes especially is the mating of locusts, just as of cicadas around the solstice. The mating of locusts is, among all mating insects, one in which the female carries the male, his tail bent back, in a slow parting. In this whole kind, the males are smaller than the females.
Pliny, in the same: the smallest locusts, that is, those called the lesser 'athelabi,' are hostile to bees and wasps and hornets and leeches.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: locusts, as has been said, are generated by the south wind, and die by the north and northeast wind. Their mating is around the solstice. They lay densely packed eggs in autumn, which endure the whole winter and burst forth at the coming of spring. The offspring, tiny in shape, crawl without legs or wings; it is certain that the mothers die once they have given birth.

Gloss: the 'bruchus' is the name for the offspring of the locust before it has wings. Then, when it begins to fly a little, it is called the 'athelabus.' When, however, it flies fully, it is called the locust. And the 'bruchus' is much more harmful than the locust or the 'athelabus,' since, lying in one place, it eats crops down to the root.
Gloss: the 'bruchus,' and the 'athelabus,' and the locust fly off as the sun grows warm, as the prophet attests.

Pliny, in the passage above: it is certain that locusts cross vast seas, in a fast lasting many days, and we marvel greatly that, for the sake of foreign pastures, they know how to seek out places so distant - a wondrous plague, for even larger ones are observed. And they fly with such a rustling of wings that they are thought to be birds, and darken the sun; peoples, when they see them coming from afar, are anxious lest they open onto their own lands. For everywhere, in a dreadful cloud, they cover the land meant for harvest, scorching much by their touch, and gnawing away everything, even the doors of houses and the crops. Sometimes, however, lifted by the wind, they fall into seas or marshes. In the region of Cyrenaica there is a law to fight against them three times a year: first by crushing the eggs, then the young brood, and finally the grown ones. And whoever ceases from this law is condemned to the penalty of a deserter. They often infest Italy from Africa in a huge host, the people often forced by fear of famine to take refuge in the remedies of the Sibylline books. On the island of Lemnos a fixed measure has been set, which each person must bring in of killed locusts to the magistrates. For this reason too they cultivate jackdaws, which meet the locusts in opposing flight, bringing them destruction and death. In so many parts of the world does this plague wander. In Syria too the inhabitants are compelled by military order to kill them and fight them off, but the Parthians eat them as food.

From the book On the Nature of Things, unknown author: the locust is an animal harmful with its teeth, and, though it has no appointed king, leads an army in order. This animal, as has been said, harms crops more than other enemies.

Ambrose: the locust, gathered in a host, occupying the breadth of a region, does not harm by merely dwelling there, nor does it consume the crops, unless it has received the sign of divine command, and then it carries out the vengeance of a heavenly offense; the bird called in Greek the 'seleuthis,' given as a remedy, devours it with an insatiable feeding and extinguishes the plague.
Gloss: when locusts come at the start of the rain, that is, in the springtime, when everything is green and every field is bringing forth, they consume almost everything.

Gloss, on Nahum 3: locusts grow numb in cold, and fly about in heat. Further, the 'athelabus,' with its small wings, crawling rather than flying, wherever it arises, consumes everything down to the dust, since it cannot leave until its wings grow; further, the 'bruchus' and the 'athelabus' and the locusts fly off to other regions as the sun grows warm, and do not remember the hedge in which they sat during the cold season, whence it is written: 'Your guardians are like the locusts, and your little ones like the locusts of locusts, which take refuge in the hedges in the day of cold; the sun rose, and they flew away, and the place where they had been was not known.'

Gloss, on Isaiah 33: locusts are buried in ditches so that they are not carried into the sea by the wind, and, cast down to earth from the eggs they had conceived while alive, even in death produce 'bruchi.' Whence it is said through the prophet: 'Your spoils shall be gathered as the 'bruchus' is gathered, as when ditches are filled with it.'
Pliny: the birds called 'seleutides' - whose coming the inhabitants of Mount Cassius obtain from Jupiter by prayers, when locusts are laying waste their crops.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: the people of Lemnos, each bound to a fixed measure set for themselves, bring in killed locusts to the magistrates. For this reason too they cultivate jackdaws, since these meet the locusts in opposing flight, about to bring them destruction.

Palladius, book 1: it is the opinion of the Greeks that, if a cloud of locusts suddenly rises while all men hide beneath their roofs, it can pass by. But if, watching, men are caught out in the open air, no harm at all will come to the crops if they all take refuge under roofs at once. They also say locusts are driven off if water in which bitter lupin or wild cucumber has been boiled is poured out mixed with brine. But some think locusts, or scorpions too, can be driven away if one uses any of these as a remedy.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: locusts, like many other animals, have within themselves medicinal properties useful for curing diseases of the human body.
Pliny: locusts' feet, ground with goat-suet, heal leprosy.

Avicenna, in the second canon of medicine: the better locusts are the thick ones that have no wings, and these are roasted and eaten as a remedy for a scorpion's sting. Locusts' feet eradicate warts, it is said. From the round ones, twelve grains are taken, their heads and extremities discarded, and a little dry myrtle is added, and they are drunk for dropsy, as they are. Likewise they benefit the dripping of urine and its difficulty. A fumigation is made with them, and it benefits difficulty of urination, especially in women. A vapor-treatment is also made with them for hemorrhoids. Locust dung benefits skin blemishes and vitiligo, and so on.

Isidore: the roundworm [lumbricus] is a worm of the intestines, so called as if 'lubricus' [slippery], since it slips, or because it is formed in the loins [lumbis]. There are three kinds of these: round, long, and flat.

Pliny: tapeworms of thirty feet, sometimes even more in length, are found already dead within flesh, and even in the hair of living men. By this foulness both Sulla the dictator and Alcman, one of the most famous of Greek poets, died. This affliction also troubles birds. Sometimes it kills pheasants, unless they dust themselves. They believe that the donkey, among haired animals, is immune to this affliction, and sheep alone as well.

Haly Abbas: roundworms are born from phlegmatic humors putrefying in the intestines, where an unusual heat arises; it is impossible for these to be born from blood or red bile. For red bile, with its bitterness and sharpness and dryness, kills such creatures. Blood, however, does not leave the veins or arteries, and if it does, it produces a swelling along with other ailments; whence children have this phlegmatic and thick-moisture affliction, together with their thick diet and neglect of purging. It arises especially in autumn, from eating fruit. There are three species of this: one of roundworms, which are like branches of purslane and are born in the fine intestine because of the excessive moisture of food gathered there; there are also flat ones, like squash seeds, mostly in the large intestine, causing the greatest illness; there are also other tiny little worms, like those found in vinegar, born mostly in the straight intestine. The symptoms of roundworms are twisting pain, disgust, and stinging, especially when the intestines are made thin by moistening. For roundworms draw from that moisture, and if they grow numerous in the intestines, strength fails, since the chyle that should nourish the body goes instead to nourish the worms, whence the body's moisture fails, the teeth grate, the lips itch, and there is disgust and vomiting. Sometimes, moreover, they rise as far as the stomach and come out with vomiting.
Isidore: the centipede [multipes] is an earthly worm, named from its multitude of feet, which curls itself contracted into a ball. It is born under rocks, from moisture and earth.

Aristotle: a ringed animal of long body and many feet has a uniform ringed structure, and lives a while after the head is cut off. Likewise, by the smoke of dry storax, the centipede is deceived and caught.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the centipede takes its name from the fact itself, and lacks blood. Augustine says this animal was once brought before him, and, as he watched, cut into many parts, and yet each part lived, separated from the others.

Avicenna: the red worm found under water-jars has very many feet, and curls into a ball when touched. If the palate is touched with it and honey, it is effective against suffocation, and likewise when eaten. It also benefits asthma and the shortening of breath, according to what is said. Likewise the many-footed worm, drunk with wine, benefits jaundice and difficulty of urination.

Isidore: the shrew [musaraneus] is a very tiny animal in Sardinia, shaped like a spider, also called the 'solifuga,' since it flees the daylight. It is very common in silver mines, crawling unseen, and, through the carelessness of those who sit upon it, causes death.
Pliny: the shrew's bite is venomous. The region of Italy beyond the Apennines has none. Wherever they are, they die if they cross their own track.
Pliny, book 20, in the same: a shrew's bite is healed with the powder of dried cabbage leaves. Caterpillar seed too is a remedy for the venoms of scorpions and shrews.
Ash of barley too counters shrew bites.
Pliny: [on] the shrew. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Wormwood too counters shrew bites.
Pliny, book 27, in the same: hare's rennet with vinegar is effective against the shrew.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: a shrew's bite is healed by drinking lamb's rennet, by ash of ram's hoof with honey. Likewise by a weasel's cub. Likewise, if it has bitten a draft animal, a fresh mouse with salt is applied, or bat's gall with vinegar. The shrew itself, too, split open and applied, is a remedy against its own bite. It will be best, indeed, if the very one that bit is applied. But for this use they keep others, coated with oil or mud. Further, a remedy against its bite is earth from its own track. For they say its track is not crossed, by a certain numbness of nature.
Pliny, in the same: moles counter shrew bites, and earth pressed down in their tracks, or caterpillar seed. Of the 'solifuga' too more will be said below.
Isidore: the fly [musca] comes from the Greek, as does 'mus'; flies, like bees, once killed in water, sometimes come back to life after the space of an hour.

Aristotle: animals having only two wings sting with a sting that is on the inside of their head, like flies and horse-flies. And since every ringed animal has an organ by which it perceives food, flies and horse-flies sting with this organ and draw out blood. The fly, like the bee, makes no noise or hiss except by flying, that is, by extending and contracting its wings through the air falling between them and the body. The fly and the ant do not build nests. In winter they mate if the air is favorable and a south wind blows. Certain ringed creatures, however, are separated only with difficulty in mating, since mating lasts a long time in them, as is evident in flies and spiders. The fly has a sting like the bee's, on the outside, whose nature is soft and hollow; through it it tastes and perceives and draws in food; and so the fly and bee kind have teeth that are not like the teeth of other creatures. Certain animals that are born neither resemble their own kind nor differ from their kind, like flies and little bees. For from these too are born creatures whose nature is unlike the kind from which they come; rather, worms come out from them.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: flies, it is said, are born from filth, cling to filthy things, and frequent unclean places. They are restless and troublesome and pestering, stinging and turbulent.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the fly flies impudently, and, circling about, makes a noise from the stirred air. Between its wings it has a beak like a hollow reed; with its hind feet it sharpens its wings, and with its front feet its beak and head; it loves light and does not know how to move about in darkness. It readily seeks out warmth, settles on moist things, craves blood, flees salty and rough things, and gladly soils white and cleaner things. Wherever it touches freshly slaughtered meat, worms follow at once, which corrupt the infected flesh, especially in the dog-days. It is a pest to every animal, and especially to man; flies are generated from the corruption of dung; drowned in water they revive when taken out; in winter they lie hidden, most like dead things. And in August they fly about troublesomely. They lay small black, hard eggs, from which flies come forth.

Pliny, book 10: the fly is especially food for the bird called the 'hematopodes.' Some creatures, indeed, produce something by mating, but it is imperfect and unlike themselves, and nothing further is generated from it, like the little worm of the fly.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: flies bear two wings. The wasp hunts larger flies, and, cutting off the head, carries away the rest of the body; in certain insects there are, in place of a tongue in the mouth, stings that in some are blunt, not for stinging but for sucking, as in the fly kind, in which the tongue is a clearly visible tube, and such creatures have no teeth. Flies killed by moisture, if buried in ash, come back to life: the front feet of insects are longer in those having two hard eyes, so that they may repeatedly wipe them with their feet, as we notice in flies.
Pliny, book 21, in the same: there is a mountain in Crete called Carina, nine miles in circuit, within which flies are not found, and where they never touch the honey.
Pliny, in the same: flies are indeed killed, if a place is sprinkled with a decoction of elder leaves.
Pliny, book 25, in the same: flies are also killed with white hellebore, ground and sprinkled with milk.
Pliny, book 27, in the same: further, book-ink tempered with a solution of wormwood protects writing from flies.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: fresh fly heads, first rubbed with a fig leaf, fill in bald patches; others use flies' blood, others, for ten days, apply their ash with ash of paper or even of nuts, so that a third part is of flies.
Pliny, book 34, in the same: the fumes of a lead-smelting furnace, when it is being boiled down, are felt to be harmful and pestilential to flies and gnats.
Avicenna, in the fourth canon: arsenic kills flies when some of it is put in milk and flies suck it; its smoke also kills them, and the smoke of frankincense, and a decoction of black hellebore.
Haly Abbas: flies benefit eye pains and drooping eyelids; if they are burnt and placed with honey on bald patches, they promote hair growth.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'ophimachus' is a worm quite small in body, but exceedingly bold in spirit and strong in cunning. It is said, moreover, to do battle with serpents, and to defend its life by skill in fighting. And though it is small in body and unequal in strength, yet by practiced combat it overcomes the serpent, stronger than itself, and lives secure more by boldness than by natural strength.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: since this creature, however, is numbered among the flying things in Leviticus, we have already placed it above among the birds, and included some remarks on it there. But since, as has been said, it is quite small in body, I think it more correct that it should be reckoned, like bees and flies, among the number of worms.
Isidore: butterflies are small winged creatures, most abundant when mallow flowers, and which cause little worms to be born from their dung.

Pliny: the butterfly, an idle and disreputable creature, flying about at lit lamps, is a pest, harmful to bees in more than one way, for it feeds on the wax itself and leaves excrement, from which are bred shipworms, which seek out wax. Certain insects have small, idle horns extended, like butterflies.

Pliny, book 20, in the same: a kind related to bees kills small creatures born within, like spiders and butterflies. Butterflies, however, are caught when the mallow ripens, at night at the new moon, in clear weather, with lamps lit before the hives, into whose flame they cast themselves.
The butterfly flying to the light of lamps is counted among harmful remedies. Goat's liver is its opposite.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: butterflies are flying worms, which rest especially on flowers and take their food from them. After August they mate, and, the male dying after mating, the female lays eggs, and dies once they are laid. Some, however, endure through the winter and in summer produce worms, which, growing strong from the sun's heat and the night dew, take on wings and fly off.

Palladius, book 5: since butterflies are harmful to bees, they should be killed in the month of April. For then they are most abundant, when mallow flowers: we will catch them by this method; let us place, in the evening, among the hives, a bronze vessel shaped like a milestone, that is, tall and narrow, and put a lit lamp at its bottom; there the butterflies will gather too, and fly around the light, and, trapped by the narrowness of the vessel, will be forced to perish by the nearby flame.
Isidore: lice [pediculi] are worms of the skin, named from feet [pedes]. Whence those in whose bodies lice swarm are called lousy.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: lice are so named from the multitude of their feet; this affliction is created, without doubt, from man's own flesh, though invisibly. Some say these are bred from man's sweat, others from the pores and vapors of the body. The chief remedy against these is said to be the frequent washing of the body in seawater or in still more vigorously salted water, or quicksilver boiled for a long time in olive oil, and to wear a belt dipped in it.

Haly Abbas: [on] lice in the body from sweat and dust and the scarcity of bathing.
