When this occurs, the body should be poulticed with quicksilver, killed with oil, with long birthwort and 'defalo' added; in the morning, too, one should enter the bath, and the body should be cleaned with vigorous rubbing, and the head washed with safflower, orach, and borax.

Rhazes, in the passage above: the use of the bath and washing prevents the generation of lice, as does frequent changing of clothes, and especially that the cloth touching the skin be of linen, for it is filled with lice more slowly. Lice already bred are killed by quicksilver, extinguished, if it is mixed with oil, and woolen threads anointed with this oil, which one wears on oneself or wraps around oneself.
Avicenna, in the second canon: stavesacre with arsenic kills lice, and likewise quicksilver extinguished.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the vulture's louse, as Galen says, is small, against which one takes no precaution, and its bite is perhaps not seen. It causes blood to burst out through the urine and through the nostrils and the anus and the stomach through vomiting, and from the chest and lung and the roots of the teeth, and sometimes accepts no medicine. For its bite, sweet, that is goat's, milk benefits, and raw butter and sealed earth and purslane, and other cooling remedies.
Isidore: fleas [pulices] are so called because they are nourished more in dust [pulvis]. Clearly the flea is a small, black worm, but a very biting one, especially in summer and rainy weather.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: fleas, dark in color, are said to be bred from heated dust and afterward spoiled moisture. They leap rather than fly, and trouble man more by night than by day, and, unless there is a heavy numbness or deep sleep in the limbs, one cannot defend oneself. When someone brings a hand near, they slip away swiftly in flight and cannot be found. But where rest is thought to be, they return more quickly to their pestering, sting a man with their bite, and by the force of their jaws draw blood, and feed on it so subtly that, the skin between remaining whole, they take the blood only through the pores and vapors, yet leave marks in the flesh where they settle. In humid air and moist earth they grow thicker with greater vigor. The best remedy against fleas is to rub the body every evening with wormwood, or to anoint the body with that same herb cooked in oil; further, if cold weather comes, that is, around the month of June, they quickly perish, and their abundance will not return for the rest of the summer season. A flea, divided into two parts, revives.

Rhazes: when the herb called 'canthar' is placed in a bed, fleas can neither leap nor move. But if the house is sprinkled with water in which caltrops have been boiled, the fleas will be entirely destroyed. Likewise water in which rue is boiled, or oleander, kills them.

Avicenna, in the passage above: against fleas the house is sprinkled with an infusion of colocynth, for then they leap and flee, and likewise with a decoction of bramble. Some, moreover, have said that when goat's blood is placed in a pit in the house, they gather at it and then die. Likewise they gather on wood smeared with hedgehog fat, and flee from the smell of oleander stalks and leaves. There is also a known herb called 'tecuntumen,' that is, the flea-herb, which, when placed in a bed, intoxicates and stupefies them, so that they are not roused to life.

Palladius, in the passage above: fleas are driven off by olive-lees frequently sprinkled over the floors, or by wild cumin ground with water, or by wild cucumber seed dissolved in water and often poured about.

div.head: DE PYRALI ET RANA ET RICINO

cit.quote: Pliny: the 'pyralis,' or 'pyrotes,' or 'pyrausta,' is a fly of larger size, found in the bronze-smelting furnaces of Cyprus, which flies out of the midst of the fire, a winged four-footed creature, and lives as long as it is in the fire. But once it has escaped and flown a little farther, it dies.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: in the region of Cyprus there is a four-footed kind of fly, which is winged and much larger than ours. And they are called 'pyrales,' since they fly unharmed out of the midst of the fires in the furnaces. And indeed it is remarkable that, as long as they are in the fire, they live. But once they fly out a little farther, they die.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the frog too is a worm, as has been said above, which, however, by the same reasoning as we placed the toad above among the kind of lizards, we have discussed more fully there.
Isidore: the tick [ricinus] is a dog's worm, so named because it clings to the throats of dogs; for 'cynos' in Greek is 'dog.'

Avicenna, in the passage above: the spider called 'rutela,' as one author says, is an animal similar to the spider, called 'Alphehed,' and is a hunter of flies. Its species, according to Galen, are many. For there is a certain red, round one; another white, having a round belly, small mouth, starred, and it has a sharp back with shining lines. Another is saffron-colored and hairy. And another is grape-colored, that is, inclining to black. There is also one whose head's middle and feet are short, sloping backward; when it wishes to sting, it throws itself onto its feet, and when it wishes to drink, it vomits out a small amount of moisture. Another is ant-like, that is, resembling an ant, having a red neck, a black head, a white back, and is spotted with various colors. Another too is wasp-like, red, that is, resembling a wasp; likewise another among them is called 'alkersenati' for its smallness, and is round, having a small mouth, a whitish belly, white feet with many hairs. Worse than the rest, however, is the Egyptian kind, malignant, having a large belly, and its head resembles the creature that flies around a candle; each of these, however, has its own particular symptoms. From the bite of the red kind comes a small pain, quick to subside. From the bite of the black or mottled kind, however, comes a strong pain with gooseflesh and coldness and trembling and heaviness in the hips, and itching or putrefaction of the belly with a flux. In the bite of the starred kind too comes a strong pain with itching and gooseflesh and numbness and heaviness of the head and softening of the body. From the grape-colored kind comes a violent pain at the site of the sting, and coldness of the whole body, and gooseflesh and trembling and spasm and cold running sweat, and loss of voice and numbness throughout the whole body, and a swelling in the belly, tension in the member and pubic area, vomiting, and cloudy urine. From the bite of the saffron-colored kind comes a very strong pain, trembling and cold sweat with swelling of the belly, and it often kills. The bite of the ant-like kind is violent, though only mildly painful, but from it come blistering of the body and heaviness of the tongue. From the wasp-like kind, a dominant deep sleep and spasm follow, and a swelling at the site, and weakness of the knees. Further, the 'alkersenati,' that is the 'berbina,' is malignant, whose symptoms are of the same kind as the grape-colored one's, but more difficult. The Egyptian kind too is malignant and causes a violent headache and a deep sleep, followed by death. In treating their bites, the universal method is applied, of drawing out and sucking, and washing with salt water, and giving the theriac described in the chapter on scorpions. A bath and a tub are the quickest things for calming their pains. For when one is soaked in the tub, the pain is calmed, and when one leaves it, it returns. Whence one must bathe continually, at every hour.

Isidore: the leech, an aquatic worm, so named because it sucks blood. It is nourished by mud, and lies in wait for those drinking. And when it slips into the throat, it clings there, draws blood, and, once soaked with too much gore, vomits up what it has drawn, so as to suck fresher blood again.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the leech is an aquatic worm, lacking bones and feet and wings; it attacks man and beasts, so as to suck their blood. By its excessive gorging it often brings death upon itself. It has a mouth shaped like a triangle, whence too it leaves a wound. And when it clings to flesh, the more it is pulled, the more firmly it settles, until it bursts. And so it draws out putrid blood, and, healing another by killing itself. Some, however, less wisely offer themselves to these worms to draw off excess blood from the body, without perceiving whether there is excessive corruption. For even in a healthy man they draw out the nobler, well-digested blood. The better and less harmful ones, however, are said to be those wrinkled and lined on the back; the worse are the black ones: the leech is stung with nettles and caltrops, so that it vomits out the venom, namely, that which it has drawn in from beasts or toads or water-serpents.

Avicenna, in the second canon: sometimes certain waters have small leeches, whose concealment makes it difficult to guard against them. And so they are swallowed, and sometimes hang visibly in the throat, sometimes in the inner part of the gullet, sometimes, however, they reach the stomach. And when it lingers there a long time, it sucks a great quantity of blood, and thus, as its body grows, its size becomes apparent, and so the one in whom it hangs suffers tightness and distress and coughing up of blood. And sometimes indeed it is treated with medicinal gargles, if they are near the throat. With those, however, that expel worms by vomiting and purging, if it is lodged deep, in the stomach.
Jerome: if a leech clings in the throat, once its smoke is inhaled it is vomited up at once, and difficulty of urination is relieved by its application.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the Indians have said that in the nature of certain leeches there is venomousness; one should beware, then, of those that have large heads, or down, and those of antimony-black or dark colors, or whose color is green or similar to the peacock, that is, a bird of various colors. In all of these too there is venomousness, and from them come swellings and fainting and flux of blood and looseness and bad ulcers, but they should not be taken from bad waters, in which the mud of the bed is black and slimy, and which, once stirred, at once cloud the water and stink; rather they should be gathered from clear waters, in which frogs dwell whose color is green, and over which two threads hang, colored like arsenic and reddish, round, of liver-color, and resembling small locusts, and mouse-like ones, tiny, with small heads. All of these are chosen for reducing excess blood from the body; none, however, is more to be chosen than those having red bellies and a green back, especially if they come from running water: extraction of blood by leeches is deeper than that done by cupping, and their application benefits diseases beneath the skin, but before they are applied, they must be gathered a day beforehand, and, if possible, made to constrict, so that they vomit what is in their bellies, and in the meantime, until they are applied, they should be fed a small amount of lamb's or another animal's blood; after this their stickiness and filth should be cleaned off with some spongy material, and the very place where they are to be applied should be washed with borax, that is soda, and reddened by rubbing. Then, thrown into fresh water, they are cleaned and thus applied. What makes them willingly attach themselves is that the place be smeared with blood. And when they are full and you wish to remove them, sprinkle over them a little salt or ash or borax or burnt bristle, or burnt linen, or burnt sponge, or burnt wool, and they will fall off.

Isidore: hornets [scabrones] are named from 'cabo,' that is, 'horse,' since they are believed to be created from them. Just as hornets are born from the putrid flesh of horses, so too from them, in turn, beetles are often born, from which they take their name.

Pliny: hornets are a degenerate kind of the same family as bees. Some think that a swarm entirely lost can be wholly restored from fresh ox-carcasses buried with dung. Virgil, [describes]: from the lifeless body of bullocks, as of horses, wasps and hornets, as of donkeys, beetles, nature changing some things into others. Hornets build their nests in caves and underground, and the cells of all these are six-sided. Wild hornets live in the hollows of trees, and hide in winter like other insects. Their life does not exceed two years. Their sting is never without danger of fever. Authorities say that a man is killed by twenty-seven stings. Of the other, gentler kind, there are two sorts. The workers, indeed, smaller in body, which die, and the mothers, which endure two years - these and the gentle ones. In spring they build nests with about four openings, in which the workers are generated; once these are raised, they then build other, larger nests, in which they produce the future mothers. And so the workers, once produced, discharge their duty and feed them. The mothers' form is broader, and it is doubtful whether they have stings, since they do not go out, and these have their own drones. Some think that all of these lose their stings before winter. Further, neither the hornet nor the wasp kind has kings or swarms, but their number is continually renewed by new offspring.
Pliny, in the same: wild rocket grows in well-watered places, similar to cress. And both are effective against stinging creatures, like hornets.
Pliny, book 24, in the same: wine too is a remedy against hornets, and the nature of fig-tree sap resists their venom.
Those once struck by a scorpion are never afterward stung by hornets.

Pliny, in the same: the owl is opposed to hornets. Those who carry with them the beak of the green woodpecker are not stung by hornets. Wingless small locusts, which they call 'athelabi,' are also hostile to them.
Pliny, book 31, in the same: the nature of salt with vinegar is effective against hornets.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things, and Pliny: wasps build nests high up from mud, and wax within them; hornets build in caves and underground. And of all of these the cells are six-sided; the rest, however, are of bark. The brood of spiders too is uneven and irregular; one hatches quickly, another is still in its infancy, another still a little worm. And in autumn, not spring, all these feed on flesh, grow at the full moon, and hide themselves in winter. Authorities say that a two-year-old child is killed by twenty-seven hornet stings. Hornets and wasps by no means have kings as bees do, and so are subject to many more dangers; they utter harsh sounds and murmurs, and this more in hollow places. Their honey is useless for human purposes, and whoever wishes to steal it exposes himself to foolish danger, for he is pierced by their stings.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: among the kind of hornets, moreover, the Experimenter places those we have called stag-beetles, of which mention has already been made above.

Isidore: they are called beetles [scarabei] because they are often born from the putrid flesh of horses. Ground-beetles are called 'bulls,' resembling the tick. The firefly, too, is a kind of beetle, as has been said above.

Pliny: [on] beetles: their wing is thinner and more fragile; their sting is denied them, but in a certain large kind of them there are very long horns, forked, toothed like pincers, meeting at the tip when they wish to bite. These are hung from infants' necks as a remedy; Nigidius calls them 'Lucani.' There is another kind again, which roll huge balls of dung backward with their feet and nest their small offspring-worms within, against the harshness of winter; others fly about with a loud murmur or bellowing; others hollow out hearths and meadows with frequent holes, vocal with a nocturnal chirring. Of the same kind gleam very large beetles, which dig dry earth and fashion small, tube-like combs like a sponge, filled with medicinal honey. Some think beetles are restored from the lifeless body of donkeys, nature changing some things into others: beetles are drawn to the rose.
Pliny, in the same: the small beetle gnaws the cantharis-beetle's grain.
Pliny, book 28, in the same: if a menstruating woman walks naked around a cornfield, beetles fall off, and harmful creatures too.

Pliny, book 30, in the same: the nature of the green beetle sharpens the sight of those who gaze at it. And so gem-engravers rest their eyes by gazing at it. 'Bulls,' as has been said, is the name for ground-beetles resembling the tick; their little horns gave them this name; others call them 'earth-lice,' which, applied to scrofulous swellings, benefit them.
Avicenna, in the passage above: the oil in which a beetle is ground is effective, poured into the ear, for ear pain, and likewise its body, very well ground.
Isidore: 'cynips' are very tiny flies, most troublesome with their stings, with which the proud people of Egypt were struck in the third plague.

Origen, on Exodus: this creature is borne on wings, flying through the air, but so fine and tiny that it escapes the sight of eyes unless very sharp. It bores with a most bitter sting into the body it has settled on, so that one who cannot see it flying feels it stinging.

Gloss, on the same: 'cynips' were born in the land of Egypt from mud, that is, very tiny and most restless flies, flying disorderly and rushing into men's eyes, taking away their rest, and, once driven off, returning.
Belbetus, in the book on the senses: stretch a hair of a black horse over the doorway of a house; 'cynips' will not enter that house as long as the hair remains there.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: 'cynips' are tiny flying worms, which follow the breath of livestock, and men most of all. They sting sleepers with their stings, with quite sharp pain as far as they are able. Whence, in places where their impudence abounds, delicate people weave nets around their beds so finely woven that 'cynips' cannot pass through them to do harm.

Isidore: the scorpion is an earthly worm, which is reckoned rather among worms than among serpents, an animal armed with a sting, and named from this, that it fixes its tail and, with a curved wound, spreads its venom: it is a property of scorpions, moreover, that they do not strike the palm of the hand.
Pliny: horses [produce] beetles, mules locusts, crabs scorpions, whence Ovid: 'the hollow claws of the shore-crab, if you remove them, will come out as a scorpion, and threaten with a curved tail.'

Aristotle: the scorpion kind is long-tailed, and has a weapon on the outside, and the scorpion has two stings. In Persia scorpions are not large and evil, but such they are in many other places, so that if they bite a man or another animal, they kill it. And when they bite black pigs, they kill them. An animal that has a sting has it in the hind part of the body, since it uses it as a weapon. Scorpions, since they crawl and have a sting, necessarily have it outside, and this suits their vigor.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the scorpion is said to have a gentle, almost maidenly face, but has in its knotted tail a venomous sting, with which it stings and infects whatever comes near. It strikes, however, with a slanting, bent blow, and never for a moment stops planning and finding opportunities to strike: for a man struck by it, its ash drunk with wine is thought to be a remedy. The scorpion alone among insects has a tail and arms, and a point in its tail. It has two stings, as he says.

Aristotle: it lives on land and lays eggs in spring, and likewise in autumn. They bear little worms resembling eggs, which, when the parent wishes to devour them, are safe, since they place themselves on the mother's haunches. A black pig, if stung by a scorpion, doubtless dies. A pig of another color, however, sometimes escapes, though not always.
Pliny: scorpions live off the earth.

Pliny: land scorpions bear little worms resembling eggs: a troublesome plague, with a venom worse than that of serpents, except that they bring death by a slower torment, over three days. To virgins the sting is always fatal, and to women too almost entirely, but to men it is less so, especially when they come out of their dens in the morning before they have discharged their venom on any chance blow; their tail is always poised to strike, and never for a moment stops planning, so that opportunity is never lacking; it strikes with a slanting, bent blow.
Pliny, book 12, in the same: when the sun is in Cancer, serpents are tormented by the stings of scorpions.
Gloss, on Ezekiel 2: scorpions strike with a curved wound and a hollow sting, so that with the same blow they open the skin and pour out their venom.

Gloss, on Luke: 'Behold,' says the Lord, 'I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions'; for scorpions are those who lie secretly in wait with their tail, serpents those who harm openly with their tooth; the venomous sting of the former is to be feared from behind.
Gloss: the scorpion, gentle in face, stings secretly with its tail; one does not feel it when it stings, but afterward it pours out its venom.

div.head: DE DIVERSIS SPECIEBUS SCORPIONUM ET MORSIBUS VEL ICTIBUS EORUM

cit.quote: Pliny: Apollodorus is the authority that some scorpions have double stings, and that the males are the most savage. For he attributes mating to them; he distinguishes them, however, by slenderness and length. Their venom is at its worst for all of them at midday, when they have grown hot with the sun's blaze. Likewise when they are thirsty, insatiable for drink. Apollodorus is the authority that their venom, poured out, is white, in nine kinds described mostly by superfluous colors: always, however, as has been said, the tail is poised to strike, and never for a moment stops planning, so that opportunity is never lacking, and it strikes with a slanting, bent blow. It is also established that those with seven joints in the tail are more savage, for most have six. This plague is also produced, winged, by the south wind of Africa, spreading their arms as if raising oars for flight. The same Apollodorus reports that some fully have wings; they are seen, nevertheless, sometimes in Italy, but harmless, and in many other places, as around Pharos in Egypt. In Scythia, however, they kill even pigs, which are otherwise more resistant to such venoms.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: of scorpions, as some have said, the female is larger than the male. The male is thin and small, the female fat and large, but the female's sting is fine, while the male's is thick. Certain scorpions, moreover, as some think, have two stings, since they leave two holes in their sting-wound, and the sting-site grows cold while the rest of the body grows hot, and then the sweat grows cold again. For there is a scorpion with large wings, which the wind often prevents from flying, so that it falls. For this reason it travels overland to another region. In the joints of scorpions' tails there is variation. For some have six joints, whose malice grows strong at the rising of 'alssehara,' and their bite kills. Some, however, have fewer. And some have thought there are scorpions of nine colors: white, saffron, red, ash-gray, iron-gray, green; and some are golden with black tails, and some of a wine-color, from whose sting one feels a needle-prick and a harmful pain. Some, however, are smoky, from whose bites confusion of reason results.

Constantine the African: the scorpion called the 'small Latin rake-tail' is small and does not have a raked tail behind. This one is nourished mostly where sugar is produced. Whoever it bites suffers no pain at first, but on the second and third day suffers the worst symptoms, such as swelling of the tongue, urinating blood, trembling, failure of the heart, and distress, and many die from bites of this kind.

div.head: DE ACCIDENTIBUS PUNCTURE VEL MORSUS SCORPIONIS

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the passage above: from the scorpion's sting, from that hour, comes a red swelling and a spreading pain. And sometimes it is inflamed, sometimes chilled, and the patient imagines that his body is being pressed with grains of salt, and the sting feels like a needle. There follow sweat and trembling of the lip and its coldness, and from time to time vomiting of a viscous matter, which congeals upon it, and gooseflesh and the breaking of hairs, and trembling and coldness of the extremities, a softening too of the whole body, and a swelling of both groins, and tension of the member, and bloating of the belly, swellings of the armpits, and much belching. For if the scorpion is of vehement malice, the symptoms will be very bad. For the sting occurs like a cauterization in its burning, and the whole body suffers rigors with cold. A viscous moisture rises on the lip and congeals there; likewise moisture runs from the eyes, then congeals in the corners as rheum. The tongue thickens, the teeth grate and sometimes clench together on one another and cannot be opened. The anus too protrudes and the penis swells.
Pliny: scorpions have stings that pour in venom, with which, as has been said, they harm men, and kill certain serpents.
Ambrose: the lion, king of beasts, is troubled by the scorpion's tiny sting and killed by its venom.

Constantine the African, in the passage above: the scorpion's venom is cold. Whence those bitten suffer a blow as if of cold snow; the place quickly swells and has redness and hardness and stretching, sometimes burning and sometimes coldness; sometimes the pain increases, sometimes it lessens, and it is like a needle-prick; sometimes it causes fainting, if it has struck near an artery, sometimes epilepsy, if it has struck a nerve.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: when the sun is in Cancer, as has been said, according to Pliny, serpents are tormented by the stings of scorpions. And when they bite black pigs, they kill them, and the sooner if the pig quickly enters water.

div.head: DE REMEDIIS CONTRA SCORPIONES AC MEDICINIS EORUM

cit.quote: Palladius, in the passage above: some think scorpions can be driven off, if some of them are burnt in the middle of the house.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the spittle of a fasting man kills scorpions. Likewise radish is hostile to the scorpion, so that if a piece of radish is placed over it, it dies. Its juice too has been tested for this, and is stronger still. Finally, if a scorpion bites someone who has eaten radish, it will not harm him.

Avicenna, in the same book: scorpions are indeed driven off by fumigation with arsenic and cut radish. If this fumigation is made at their hole, one need not fear that they will come out with it. Scorpions, moreover, are killed by the spittle of a fasting man of hot complexion thrown upon them, and by chewed radish and its juice when it touches them, and its leaves.
Isidore, on scorpions, book 2: the 'genicularis' herb is spread beneath to repel their force.

Rhazes, in the Almansor: scorpions are driven off if the house is fumigated with donkey's hoof and sulfur and galbanum. Oil too, if poured into their holes, keeps them from coming out further. Likewise, if asafoetida is dissolved in water and the house is sprinkled with it, they do not come near it; further, if many of them are caught and the house is fumigated with them, all the others will flee.
Those once struck by a scorpion are never afterward stung by hornets or wasps or bees.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: the stellio is so opposed to scorpions that, once seen, it brings them fear and numbness; it is a property of scorpions that they do not strike the palm of the hand, but only touch the hairs.

div.head: DE HIS QUIBUS PUNCTURE MORSUS SANANTUR

cit.quote: Pliny: scorpion stings are healed by ear-wax. Men struck by these, it is reported, are also relieved by intercourse, but women are harmed by it.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: any small stone, from the side that was in the earth, applied to a scorpion's sting, eases the pain. Ash of hen droppings also relieves it; a dragon's liver too, or a lizard split open, or a mouse split open, helps. Likewise ground earthworms applied. The scorpion itself, applied to its own sting, or roasted and taken as food, or drunk in two cups of wine.
Pliny, book 32, in the same: the flesh of river snails, raw or cooked, resists scorpion stings. Some also keep them salted for this purpose and apply them to the stings themselves.

Avicenna, in the second canon: for a scorpion's bite, the juice of wormwood benefits, and myrtle fruit drunk with wine benefits its sting. Likewise, if the root of white thorn is chewed and placed on the scorpion's bite or sting, it draws out the venom. Balsam oil too drunk with milk benefits. And again hazelnut with figs and rue helps, likewise pine nuts with figs and dates. Likewise the herb gentian is the ultimate medicine for this sting. Pennyroyal too benefits. And colocynth root is most effective of all. Likewise a plaster made from ammoniacum with the herb 'rog'; for this too thick locusts that have no wings are roasted and eaten, for which a plaster is made from marjoram with vinegar, or myrrh is given to drink with wine; a plaster is also made from salt with linseed; scammony too, drunk or applied, benefits the same. Wheat too benefits this sting. Likewise wild calamint; a mouse too, if split open and placed on such a sting, heals it; fig juice is also effective for this, and the juice of wild lettuce given as a drink, and laurel oil with wine and 'arob,' and likewise lily. River crab benefits scorpion bites, applied like a plaster or eaten. Finally, galbanum is a theriac against the venoms of scorpions.
Avicenna, in the fourth canon: a scorpion's sting is treated by the common methods, and by a vapor-treatment with salt and millet and similar things.
Pliny, book 11: if a scorpion bites a man, its own ash, drunk in wine, is thought to be a remedy.

Pliny, book 29, in the same: ground scorpion is opposed to the venom of stellios. For indeed the stellio itself, as has been said above, is so opposed to scorpions that its very sight brings them fear and numbness. The scorpion itself, too, helps its own sting, applied, or roasted and taken as food or drink.
Avicenna, in the second canon: scorpion oil greatly benefits ear pain.
Avicenna: the scorpion itself is also a good plaster against the scorpion, and likewise its tail, and also the plant called scorpion-plant, because of its resemblance to it.

Avicenna, in the fifth: scorpions too, in their natures, are opposed to stones formed in the kidneys and bladder, just as viper's flesh is opposed to the venoms of serpents and other venomous reptiles. And so scorpion ash breaks stones and makes them descend at once in the urine.
Dioscorides: a raw scorpion too, ground and applied, is opposed to the sting of its own kind and their like.

div.head: DE SETA ET SIMULTATE AC SOLIFUGA

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'seta' is a worm, or, as some hold, a serpent, taking its name from the thing itself. For it is very thin, like a bristle, of nearly a cubit's length, hard and white, with no difference at either end, having, indeed, no head, but crawling from either end. It is born in stagnant but not foul-smelling waters, and is so hard that it can scarcely be crushed underfoot. Its venom has such power that, drunk by a man, it makes him grow faint and waste away, until he loses his life in dire torment.
Papias: the 'simultas' is properly a worm in a ram's head, which, when it moves, makes the ram shy away.
From the same: the 'simultas' is a worm in the head of a horned animal, stirring it to strike with its horns.
Isidore: the shrew is that same creature already spoken of above.

Solinus: Sardinia is indeed without serpents. But what is a serpent elsewhere is, in the fields of Sardinia, the 'solifuga,' which crawls unseen and, through the carelessness of those who sit upon it, causes death. To this misfortune is added the herb 'sardonia,' which grows too abundantly along the banks of springs; this, if eaten, contracts the sinews of those who eat it and draws back the mouth in a grimace, so that those who meet death perish with a face like one laughing. On the other hand, whatever waters there are, serve various useful purposes; indeed hot and healthful springs bubble up in several places, bringing remedies, either setting broken bones, or dissolving venom instilled by the 'solifuga,' or even dispelling hidden illnesses. And those that heal the eyes are also effective in exposing thieves.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'phalangium,' according to Pliny, is a certain kind of spider, as has been said above, whose bite is harmful, small in body, mottled, sharp; this, among the kinds of spiders, alone broods in its den in great numbers, and, once hatched, sometimes devours its mother, sometimes even its father. Against the bites of 'phalangia' there are many particular remedies, of which mention has been made above in various places.
Pliny: wasps and 'phalangia' and spiders. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Pliny, book 18, in the same: there arises, as a kind of disease in bitter vetch, the 'phalangium,' a small creature of the spider kind, if the winter is rainy.

'Phalangium,' unknown in Italy, is of several kinds: one resembles an ant, but is much larger, red-headed, black in the rest of its body, sprinkled with scattered white spots, and its bite is more bitter than a wasp's, and it lives mostly around ovens and mills. And it is a remedy if another of the same kind is shown to the one struck, and for this purpose they are kept when found dead, but even their crushed shells, drunk, heal. The Greeks likewise call the 'phalangium' among the kinds of spiders, but distinguish it by the name 'wolf.' A third kind bears the same name 'phalangium,' a woolly spider with a very large head, which, when cut open, is found to contain two little worms inside, which, bound to women in deerskin before sunrise, prevent them from conceiving, as Caecilius left recorded in his commentaries. Worse than all of these, however, is the sea-blue one, with black down, causing dizziness and spider-like vomiting. Worse still is one differing from the hornet only in its wings, and this too brings on wasting; the 'myrmecion,' resembling an ant, with a white head marked by black spots with white dots, causes pain like that of wasps. There are two kinds of the 'tetragnathus,' the worse marked with a white line dividing its head in the middle and another crosswise; this causes swelling of the mouth. But the ash-colored one, whitish at the rear, is more sluggish and least harmful in its bite, and spreads its webs for flies most widely on walls. Against the bites of all of these, however, the remedy is chicken brain drunk with a little pepper. Likewise five ants drunk; also ash of livestock dung applied with vinegar, and any spiders whatsoever putrefied in oil.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'phalangium' is a kind of spider, venomous in its bite, small and sharp in body. It readily enters the nostrils of men and livestock. And when it has struck stags in the woods, unless they eat crabs as food, their lives are in danger. These brood in their dens and lay eggs in great number. And as soon as the young hatch, they devour father and mother, for the father too helps to brood the young.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'spoiler of the snake' is a worm of golden color, which also has a greenish tint in shadow; though small and weak, it deceives the snake by cunning, whence it took its name. For when it sees the snake lying in the heat, climbing up its tail to its head, it runs along it, and, first as if soothing it by rubbing, at last attacks its flesh with bites; the wounded snake flees, its pursuer follows and presses on with a deadly bite, until it penetrates the inner brain and is sated on the flesh of the slain creature: this is called by some the golden worm. Aristotle, moreover, says of worms of golden color that, when they are born, they are at first fed by their parents, then remain without food for many days, and lie so motionless that they seem dead. After a time set by nature, however, they revive and rise to seek their own food. The 'star,' as Pliny says, is a worm shaped like a star, which shines at night like a star; it arises only from heavy rains, and signals coming fair weather. It has such great coldness that, touching fire, it extinguishes it in no other way than ice does; if a man's flesh is touched by its discharge, all the hair falls out. And what is touched changes color to a greenish hue. These worms produce nothing, nor is there in them a male or a female.
Isidore: the horsefly, commonly [called that], also called in Latin 'asylus' and in Greek 'oestrus,' is a flying creature very troublesome to herds with its stings.

Pliny, book 11, on bees: sometimes larger bees are born at the edges of the combs, which drive off the others. This affliction is called 'oestrus,' and they brood in the manner of hens. What hatches at first appears as a white little worm, lying crosswise and clinging, so that it seems to be feeding, for indeed many insects are born differently than locusts are; and first the 'asylus' settles from its mouth, like a radish leaf, and in early spring, thickened by the sun, is compressed to the size of a millet seed; from this a small worm arises, and, over three days, a caterpillar, then soon a chrysalis, which, with added days, grows motionless within a hard shell, and is stirred only by the touch of a spider; this caterpillar, which they call the chrysalis, then, its shell broken, flies out as a butterfly. Horseflies are also born from wood, and die of blindness.

From the book On the Nature of Things, unknown author: the horsefly itself is the 'assilus,' of which the prophet Hosea speaks, according to the Seventy interpreters. For where our edition reads: 'Israel has turned aside like a wanton heifer,' the translation of the Seventy has: 'like a heifer struck by the gadfly.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis: it is called Solomon's worm. For when Solomon had ordered marble of Paros to be brought from distant parts for the building of the Temple, aware of the Law's prohibition forbidding the stones of the altar to be cut with iron, he sought a method in worms that human skill did not know. For he shut an ostrich chick in a glass vessel, and when the ostrich saw it and could not reach it, attempting an art known to it by nature, it ran to the desert and, returning, brought back a small worm, with whose blood it smeared the glass; and the glass broke, and thus it freed its young. Seeing this, Solomon used this same kind of worm for cutting the hardest marble. The 'tabula' is also a four-footed worm, living equally on land and in water. On land, indeed, it runs very swiftly, but even more so upon the water, so that it crosses long stretches of water at speed. Sometimes, however, it stops and, wearied, catches its breath. This is remarkable in it, that, running upon the water, it keeps its body and feet dry. And if it is even held violently underwater for a long time, it is nevertheless not made wet, nor does it die.
Isidore: [on] termites. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the shipworm is a wood-worm having a red head and a white body. By successive boring it perforates wood, and, reducing it to dust, builds itself a home, purifying itself by consuming the wood and casting it out as dust. In the eastern regions, few kinds of wood breed worms. In the regions of Italy, Germany, Gaul, and Spain, however, almost all trees do, except oak and linden and a few others. And this is remarkable, that box and hawthorn, which are among the hardest of trees, breed worms. Linden, however, though it is the softest of trees, wherever its wood is kept dry, worms never grow from it, but it remains forever free of worms.

Gloss, on 2 Kings: David is compared to the tenderest little worm of wood, since the wood-worm, though it appears fragile and small, nevertheless most powerfully wears away and consumes the wood. And so it takes the name 'teredo' from wearing away [terendo].

Pliny, book 11: nature has fixed teeth in the shipworm for boring through oak timbers with a sound, and it makes its hollow chiefly in wood. The butterfly, flying about at lit lamps, feeds on bees' wax and leaves excrement, from which shipworms are bred.

Pliny, in the same, on the shipworm: the soft and worst part of wood, easily rotting even in oak, is subject to the shipworm. And so it should always be cut away. They say larch, in seagoing ships, is subject to the shipworm, and everything except wild olive and cultivated olive. There are four kinds of these infesting worms, of which one kind gnaws with teeth, its head disproportionately heavy; these alone are found properly to be called 'shipworms' at sea. Land ones, however, they call moths, and those resembling gnats they call 'triphae.' There is also a fourth, of the little-worm kind. Of these, some are born from the putrefying sap of the material itself, others are born as in trees. Among these, the one called the 'cerastes,' once it has gnawed enough to turn itself around, produces another; its birth is prevented in some woods by bitterness, as in cypress, in others by hardness, as in box.

Isidore: the tortoise [testudo] is so called because it is covered with the covering of a shell in the manner of a vault; the 'morphnos,' which is a third kind of eagle, breaks captured tortoises by dropping them from on high.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: there are, indeed, several kinds of tortoise, but the one born in mud is properly called the mud-tortoise, or slug, and this is reckoned among the kind of worms.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the tortoise is a worm born from the corruption of grasses through an excess of moist and hot weather. It is a slow animal, thick with abundant blood; some of these are red, some white, some black, some saffron-colored, according to changes in the air and in the corruption. This creature, in a remarkable way, forms for itself, from spittle that is slippery and thick, a dwelling of bony, or rather marble-like, substance, wondrously vaulted, since it gradually hardens into stone in the sun's heat. And though it wallows in marshy pools, it knows how to cure itself with its own proper antidote, and shows that it knows the powers of herbs. For, as Ambrose reports, fed on the innards of a serpent, when it perceives the venom creeping upon it, it treats itself with marjoram; but if someone throws salt upon it, it almost entirely dissolves into nothing, and you will find little of it left except a fat that is useful as a remedy.

Physiologus: the slug is a tortoise born in mud, and eats earth. It has four horns, but two are longer. As it crawls, it extends its horns, but as soon as it is touched, it draws them back and folds itself inward; it hides in winter, and is revealed in spring. Its blood closes pores and effectively prevents hairs from growing. Broken and ground into certain wounds, it heals swellings.

Isidore: there are four kinds of tortoises, namely land, sea, mud - that is, living in mire and marshes - and river tortoises, that is, those that live in fresh water. Some report, incredibly, that ships carrying a tortoise's right foot go more slowly. The tortoise, fed on the innards of a serpent, when it perceives venom creeping upon it, treats itself with the medicine of marjoram for its health.

Pliny, book 2: there are kinds of tortoises: land, sea, mud, and those living in fresh water. The flesh of land tortoises, used as fumigations and in magical arts to be condemned, is said to be salutary against venoms. Most are found in Africa: there, with head and feet removed, they are said to be given as an antidote. And their broth, taken as food, is said to disperse scrofulous swellings and remove spleen ailments and epilepsy. Their blood restores clarity of sight, and removes cataracts of the eyes, and helps against the venoms of all serpents and spiders and similar creatures and frogs. Their blood, kept and made into pills with flour, is given, when needed, to be rubbed on. Tortoise gall with Attic honey benefits glaucoma when drunk with wine, and, dripped in, benefits scorpion stings. Ash of the shell, worked with wine and oil, heals cracks and ulcers of the feet. Scales scraped from the top, given as a drink, restrain lust. This is the more remarkable, since flour of the whole shell is said to kindle desire. The flesh of sea tortoises is sipped for stomach pains; mixed with frog flesh it gives excellent help against salamanders. Their blood cures baldness and itching and every ulcer of the head. It is also dripped in for ear pain, with women's milk. Against epilepsy it is eaten with wheat flour. Tortoise gall gives clarity to the eyes, reduces scars, calms tonsils and quinsy and every ailment of the mouth. It is also effective against salamanders. The mud-tortoise is broad and curved, unpleasant to look at. Some remedies come from it too, however. Its flesh is used against paralysis and joint diseases. Its gall, however, draws out phlegm and spoiled blood. The bowels are stopped by this remedy taken with cold water. The fat of the fourth kind of tortoise, that is, those in rivers, torn apart, is said to be effective for quartan fevers. Its blood, dripped on the head, calms headaches, and likewise scrofulous swellings.

Palladius, in the passage above: so that vegetables do not breed harmful creatures, sow all the seeds you intend to scatter, dried, in a tortoise's shell, or sow mint in many places, especially among cabbages. Further, against slugs, scatter fresh olive-lees or soot from chimneys.

Isidore: the moth [tinea] is the worm of clothing, so called because it holds [teneat] and lies in wait until it can gnaw through. Hence too it is called persistent [pertinax], since it presses at the same thing again and again.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the moth is a worm bred from corrupted air, in clothing, from a rotting moisture that is bred in their wool. And it settles there so persistently that it gnaws through them.

Pliny, book 11: dust breeds moths in wool and clothing, especially if a spider is shut in with it. For it thirsts, and, absorbing all moisture, increases the dryness. This also arises in paper. There is, moreover, a kind of these that drag their own coverings, like snails, but when their feet are seen stripped bare, they die.
Pliny, book 17, in the same: moths trouble fig seeds, against which the remedy is to bury a mastic-tree cutting in the same trench, its top end reversed.
Ash of stag's horn drives off kinds of moths.

Gloss, on Hosea 5: moths slowly gnaw away clothing, and rot slowly gnaws away wood. But the moth consumes faster than rot, whence, concerning the captivity of the ten and two tribes, the Lord says through the prophet: 'I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like rot to the house of Judah.'

Gregory the Great, in the Morals, book 4: the moth is born from cloth, and, by being born, corrupts the very cloth from which it arises. Whence Scripture says that those who have an earthly foundation shall be consumed like a moth. For man is consumed like a moth, when from himself, that is from the flesh which is the soul's garment, carnal temptation arises, by which he is worn away. The moth also does damage without making a sound; so too the minds of the wicked, since they neglect to consider their own losses, lose their integrity as if unaware, and so are consumed as if by a moth, since they do not feel the bite of their fault by any sound, while they remain ignorant of how great a loss of life's innocence they suffer. Whence, rightly, it is added there too: 'from morning to evening they shall be cut down' - the sinner is cut down from morning to evening, since, from the beginning of his life to its end, he is wounded by the commission of wickedness.
Avicenna, in the fourth canon: wormwood protects cloth from the moth, and likewise calamint, and also citron rinds.
Isidore: the wasp is a small, flying, venomous, stinging creature, said to be born from the putrid flesh of donkeys, just as drones are from mules, hornets from horses, and bees from calves.

Aristotle: the wasp is a flying, ringed animal, which does not take in air, that is, does not breathe, and its life and food center on dung and flesh. And it is among those animals that live with their own kind, like the ant and the bee; it has, however, a weapon within, as the scorpion has outside. It lacks blood, and has wings covered with membranes. It happens that wasps shed old age. Bees, moreover, are properly harmed by wasps, and so it harms bees for them to come near. And so the keepers of hives catch wasps by this method: taking a pot, they put meat in it, and when many wasps have fallen into it, they cover it and set it over a fire: the wasp, however, has its sting within its body, like the bee, since if it were outside it would easily be damaged because of its weakness. If one takes a wasp's legs and lets it wander about with its wings, then wingless wasps fly around it, but those having stings do not fly over them; for this reason they are often found in winter in burial-places.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: wasps are sometimes bred from horse-flesh. They are said to grow larger at the full moon; their life centers on dung. They do indeed make wax, but not from gathered flowers, and so it is useless.

Aristotle: wasps are of two kinds: one is the wild kind, which is not found in the mountains nor breeds young in the ground, but in trees, and is larger than the domestic wasp, longer and darker and stronger, and stings with a strong sting; its sting too is larger than the sting of the other kind in proportion to its body. Their lifespan is two years, and often, when trees are cut down in winter, wasps come flying out of them, since they hide in trees at that time, and that is always their dwelling: domestic wasps, however, are of two kinds; one kind of them are the leaders, called 'mutira,' the other called 'argilta,' which does not live two years, but all die at the coming of winter, which is shown by this, that when winter begins, an illness befalls the 'argilta,' namely a wasting of the head, and if the winter is severe, they do not appear at all. The leaders, however, called 'mutira,' appear the whole winter and build nests in the ground, whence many have seen them hollowing out the earth, and the 'argilta' are never seen doing this. The kind of wasp called 'mutira' is broad and heavy, thicker in body than drones, and, because of their heaviness, are not of good strength and cannot leap much. It appears to us, however, that the leaders have a sting like that in the leaders of bees, but they do not draw it out or sting anything with it. Likewise some wasps have no sting, but others do: those lacking a sting are smaller and weaker and do not sting, but those having a sting are large and strong, and so are called by some the males, and those lacking a sting, the females. Wasps have sometimes been seen mating with another kind of wasp, as the wild with the domestic. And it appeared that one indeed had a sting, but whether the other had one likewise was uncertain.

Aristotle: wasps' food is from flowers and fruits. Often too they live off the food of animals. The 'mutira' hunts at the end of winter, and most of them hunt around 'calez,' and the 'mutira' hunts near great embankments and very high places, and all are seen with stings. Wasps, however, do not gather flowers or feed on them as bees do. But their food, for the greater part, is flesh. And so they stay around dung-heaps and catch large flies and cut off their heads, and, carrying the body with them, fly off with it; they also eat sweet fruits. They build nests underground and, like ants, dig out earth; some build small nests, some large. And when the hives are prosperous, they take out two or three combs and do not store them, as has been said, as bees do, but remain in the hives through the winter. And so many more of them die, nor is there more than one leader in a single nest, as bees have in a single hive. And when one of the 'iribeon' is lost from its nest, they all gather near some place where there is pasture and build a nest there, and the wax that appears is for the greater part on the outside, and in a single nest they place a single leader. And when that leader has grown and comes out, it will take the 'iribeom' with it and place it in one of the chambers of that nest.

Pliny: wasps build nests on high, from mud, and wax within them. Hornets build in caves or underground, and their cells are six-sided. Bees touch no body and do not feed on flesh. But wasps hunt larger flies and, cutting off the head, carry away the rest of the body. Wasps called ichneumons, which are smaller than the others, kill a certain kind of spider called the phalangium and carry it to their nests; then they smear it, and, by brooding over these, breed their own kind. All of these, however, feed on flesh, and eagerly eat the serpent too, from which food, indeed, they produce deadly stings.

Pliny, book 11: the generation of wasps happens in this way: the leaders in summer seek a suitable place, and there build small houses of wax having four doors, or something similar, and in these wasps are bred, not those called 'mutira.' But when these have grown, others larger than these are generated afterward. And when those have grown, still others are generated, because of this there are many and large 'kephenes' at the end of autumn, and they have leaders, namely those called 'mutira,' and that one does not generate 'kephenes,' but 'mutirae.' There will be large worms in four continuous holes, and there are often more than four holes, in which are the young of the leaders. And when the young have grown, they will bring, serving them, whatever they are to be fed with, which is clear to us from this, that the leaders of the servants do not fly but remain in the houses. And when the leaders of these that ruled the previous year die, they place a new leader over them. Wasps multiply in their own places and in rough regions. They are underground, and prepare nests from earth and mud, and all trace back to one origin, just as things are generated from some root. Worms, moreover, are generated from wasps, as from bees; red and yellow wasps are generated only from wasps called males. And they themselves first prepare the houses in which they will dwell, and repair them. And when they mate with one another, the young of wasps are generated, for their mating has often been observed. Monstrosity, however, does not occur in bees and wasps, since each of their young exists by itself in its own cell.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is also said, as noted above following Isidore, that wasps are born from the putrid flesh of donkeys, just as drones are from mules. Further, according to Pliny, certain wasps kill a kind of spider, the phalangium, and carry it to their nests, then smear it, and, by brooding over these, breed their own kind.

Constantine the African, in the passage above: wasps and bees produce a hot swelling and redness in those they sting, and their sting-mark remains where they touch; and sometimes the stung suffer sweat and disgust, twitching of the lip, swelling of the groin, and erection of the member.

Avicenna, in the second canon: for a wasp's sting, germander is good, applied like a plaster. Likewise leaves of wild mallow calm it, applied as a poultice. Likewise goat's dung draws out a wasp's venom. A plaster is also made from salt with vinegar and honey for a wasp's sting, and laurel oil too benefits its biting.

Avicenna, in the fourth book: wasps flee, moreover, from a fumigation of sulfur and other things, and do not approach one anointed with marsh-mallow or mallow juice and oil. Further, from a wasp's bite come pain and redness and a swelling; among large wasps there is a kind having a black head and very many stings, and thereby killing; indeed, the large ones require the greatest caution and are more dangerous. And so they lead to spasm and weakness of the knees, but even in the bite of small ones the swelling sometimes grows large. For they mostly cause blisters to appear and make the tongue heavy. Its treatment, however, is in cooling juices and cooling drinks; further, among poultices for it is mallow water, marsh-mallow too benefits, and fig and vinegar and mud. Cow dung too benefits, especially with vinegar. Likewise leaves of savory and leaves of fresh laurel, and the greenish scum that gathers on flowing water; further, if the sting is left in warm water for an hour, then suddenly changed to salt water mixed with vinegar, it will be calmed at once. Among rubbing remedies for it are flies, since they calm the pain.

Aristotle: the wild wasp stings with a strong sting, for its sting is indeed larger than that of the other kind in proportion to its body; some, however, lacking stings, are smaller and weaker, and these do not sting.
Pliny, book 11: wasps eagerly eat the serpent, from which food they produce deadly stings.

Rue leaves, ground and taken with wine, are effective against wasp stings. Cultivated and wild mallows too are effective against all stinging blows, especially wasps'. Anointed beforehand with any of these ground with oil, or carrying them, one is not stung by wasps.
Pliny, in the same: balm is most excellent against wasp stings.
Pliny, book 33, in the same: wine is a remedy against wasps, and the nature of fig-tree sap, and a decoction of laurel leaves, resists their venom.
Pliny, book 28, in the same: those once struck by a scorpion are never afterward stung by wasps.
Pliny, in the same: the owl is not stung by wasps. Wingless small locusts too, which they call 'athelabi,' are hostile to wasps. The nature of salt with vinegar is also effective against wasps.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: having discussed, one by one, the nature of animals, briefly setting out their special properties, it remains that we also fulfill what we promised at the start of the previous book, namely to describe their nature in general, going through their individual parts and members, their whole anatomy.

Aristotle: an animal is defined as that which has sense, and first of all the primary sense, that is, touch. Animals, indeed, are generated in earth and water, since in earth there is a part of water, and in water a part of air, and in these is the heat of the soul. For in some way we say that all these things are full of the power of the soul. And so the creation of the body is for the sake of the soul, and the members are created for the sake of their functions. When, then, an animal or a member lacks a soul, it will remain neither truly an animal nor truly a member, but only in shape and form. That which is naturally more perfect among animals is that of greater heat and moisture, and since heat is the cause of growth and shapes the bodies of animals rightly, man, for this reason, has a more upright body, and is more capable of generating offspring than the other four-footed animals. Naturally cold animals, however, are of great fearfulness, and it happens to animals, from fear, that the bowels or bladder empty. Animals of subtle, clean, hot blood are more inclined toward wisdom and boldness and the like. Strong anger, however, will not occur except in a body of much dryness. In certain animals there is blood, and in certain others another moisture corresponding to blood, that is, an incomplete moisture, like venom, and indeed everything having blood and generating a live animal has all the instruments of sense except the mole kind. Likewise every breathing animal has a lung and a windpipe and a stomach. Finally, it happens to all animals that they emit a voice. Another thing common to them, too, is the desire for mating and its pleasure, and even loud chattering and much noise at mating time, except in man. Likewise all animals move the lower jaw except shellfish, which move the upper. Likewise every animal that generates an animal like itself has teeth, and males have more teeth than females. Horned animals do not have upper teeth, nor does any animal have both sharp teeth or rows of teeth and horns at once. Every animal having a saw-like row of teeth eats flesh, and those that eat raw flesh fight among all animals.

Aristotle: the kinds of animals differ according to their manner of life, their functions, and their nourishment; some of these move about, some crawl, some are solitary, some joined with their own kind, some always remain in their own places, some sometimes withdraw. Likewise some are hunters, and some gather their food. Likewise some dwell in crevices of stones and walls, some in pits, some above ground. Again, some are silent, some make noise, some roar, some even sing beautifully. Likewise some are warlike, some of great restraint, some strong in boldness, like the lion, some in cunning, like the serpent, some are gentle, like the cow, some ill-tempered, like the boar, some quickly become tame, like the elephant, and some even please men, like the dog. All animals, however, have one thing in common, namely sense; some have all their members, some do not. Some give birth to complete animals, some to worms, and some to eggs.

Aristotle, in the same, on plants: there are also animals that lack the female sex. And there are those that do not reproduce; there are also those that have no motion. And there are some of various colors. And there are those that grow. And there are those that produce offspring unlike themselves.

Pliny: [on] field mice and salamanders, and whatever summer or spring or a fixed season of the year generates. Of these, moreover, some produce nothing, like salamanders, nor is there in them a male or female kind, just as there is not in all eels, which produce neither an animal nor an egg.

Aristotle: an animal's body is divided into two, upper and lower, right and left, front and back. The inclination of brute animals' bodies was necessarily toward the earth, for the sake of protection. And nature placed for them front feet in the place of hands. And there necessarily were two feet in front and two behind, that is, four feet together, in all these kinds, so that they might be able to bear weight. In all of these too the front of the body is larger than the rear, except in man, since the upper part of his body is proportionate to the lower, and indeed it is smaller in the old, who are bent by age, but the opposite in children, namely that the upper part is heavier than the lower, and for this reason they walk bent over and cannot lift their bodies upright. But as a man grows up, the lower part increases. The arrangement of four-footed animals, however, is the reverse, namely that the lower part is at first very large, but as they grow up the upper part grows; for this reason the raised height of many horses is greater in front than behind, and a foal touches its head with its hind foot, but when it comes of age it cannot do this. And so the growth of the upper part is according to the diminishing of the lower. The bird and fish kind, too, has more flesh in the upper, that is, front, part of the body. For this reason all animals are of lesser intelligence than man, and children too compared to their elders, since, when weight is in the upper part, it lessens intelligence. Likewise, when heat is less in animals and the earthy part greater, the body of that animal must necessarily be smaller, that is, more inclined toward the earth, and it will have many feet, and when this is complete it will be without feet and will crawl on the ground, and the member in which the primary power resides will be turned toward the earth, namely the head, nor will it have sense, but its power will be in the lower part, as it is in trees, since their lower part is greater than the upper. And, at the extremities, man's chest is broad, and this makes it upright, since the shoulders are placed at the sides. In four-footed animals this cannot happen, namely a broad chest, because of the extension of the front feet and because of walking. For this reason too a four-footed animal does not have two breasts on the chest, since it is narrow. Likewise man is upright in body, and so has very fleshy hips and legs. For nature took flesh away from the upper part of his body and added it to the lower, for the sake of the body's weight and so that the body might be upright. In other animals, however, the hips and legs are deprived of flesh, and are made of bones and sinews for carrying the body, and their four feet are four supports; for this reason a four-footed animal is born able to stand without effort, but man cannot remain upright for a long time, but needs rest for the body. Animals of large body produce one offspring; those of small body, many. For in large animals food goes toward the growth of the body, and only a little remains from it.

Aristotle: in an animal's body there are three modes of composition. The first is the mixture of the elements in like-membered parts. The second is the mixture of these like parts into organic parts. The third is of organs from unlike parts, as the hand is composed of sinews and bones and the like. Sense, indeed, is first present in all like-membered parts, but functions are in organic members, through the power of sense and motion and the appetites of animals. It is necessary, then, that there be a member in the body receiving these principles, and since the receiver of all that is sensed, namely the heart, must be composed of simple substance, and since it is also the mover and the source of appetite, it must be organic; this member, in blood-lacking animals, is that which corresponds to the heart. The heart, moreover, is divided into like parts, as is each of the other inner members, and the nature of all of these is bloody, since their location is along the paths of the veins, and there is empty space between them. All the members of the body, then, are composed of veins through which blood runs; in the heart, however, is the source of the veins and the primary power that creates blood; the members, indeed, were created for the sake of their functions, as the body was for the sake of the soul. And a member is called healthy when it performs its work without diminishment and is not weakened by its work. Just as an animal's body is divided into two, namely right and left, and so on, so too most of the members are double, either in number, like the two kidneys and the instruments of each of the senses, or, if not double in number, yet divided into two, as the single heart has two chambers, and the lung two lobes, and the liver likewise, though there is an opinion among some that the spleen is an impure liver; the tongue too is one, but divided, and thus a single animal is, as it were, two. In certain animals all the inner members are present. In others, not. And members that agree in number differ in existence among different animals. For the heart is of one kind in all animals. The liver is divided by many fissures in some, and not at all in others, especially the liver of fish and of egg-laying four-footed creatures and of birds, since these creatures' bodies exist by reason of respiration and dissolution, and there is not in them much excess bile. And so many lack gall entirely. All the inner members are enclosed within a membrane containing them, since they need a covering, and the nature of this membrane is such that it be smooth and thick enough to withstand injury. And let it be fleshy, so that it does not draw excess matter to itself. All animals have two members in common, namely the member by which they take in nourishment and the member by which they expel it. There is also another shared member to which nourishment goes after its entry into the mouth, which is the stomach. Every animal, then, having a bladder also has a stomach, but not the reverse. The liver and spleen can cook food, since they are made of blood and have much heat. The liver's location, indeed, is on the right, the spleen's on the left. The kidneys, however, exist to filter the excess of moisture that runs to the bladder, and since natural heat governs the body as princes govern a region, every blood-having animal has a heart and a liver. The heart to preserve heat as in a furnace, and the liver to digest; a breathing animal also has a third member, namely the lung. The members of a large body are the head, the neck, the trunk, that is, everything between the neck and the end of the belly, and also the two arms and the larger legs, that is, from the hip to the joints.

Constantine the African, in the Pantegni, part 2: each animal, moreover, has bodily instruments suited to the power of its soul. For the lion, since it is of bold and irascible spirit, has a strong and heavy body, claws on its feet, and very sharp teeth in its mouth. The hare, however, since it is most timid, has members of exceeding lightness, most suited to flight. For man too nature made hands, so that he might work with them, in which there are many fingers, divided, so that through them large and small things might be grasped. It made the liver red, as suited its role in creating blood. It made the breasts and testicles white, for creating milk and seed: in this way it made all the members suited to their own proper actions.
Pliny: now let the history of animals' bodies be treated part by part, member by member. All creatures having blood have a head, but some also have crested heads.

Aristotle: the part of the head where the origin of the hair is, is called the crown; its front part is the forehead-region, the back the occiput, and the middle the top. Beneath the front part indeed is the brain, but in the occiput is a hollow. The skull is created from hard bone, which contains the skin and flesh; in this there is a natural suture, which in women is a single one, circling around. Men's heads, however, contain many sutures. Man alone has an upright and raised head above other animals. And the head was created without flesh, so that it might have better, more perfect, and quicker sense. For if it were of much flesh, the brain's function would be contrary to the natural function for which it was created, namely to cool the heart, nor could the senses exist in it, if the brain were like some kind of excess matter. The origin of sense, however, is in the heart, and indeed two of the senses are continuous with the heart, namely taste and touch. The remaining three, however, are in the head: sight in front, around the brain; hearing in back, which is hollow; smell, however, in front, in the middle of the three instruments. Likewise, if the head were fleshy, it would also be heavy, whereas in all animals it ought, on the contrary, to be raised and upright. For these three reasons, then, there is no flesh in the head, namely for the fineness of sense, and the function of the brain, and the lightness of the head itself. What is below the suture of the head, moreover, is called the face, though properly only in man; the upper part of the face, however, is the forehead. Every animal has a hairy tail, has a small head and large jaws, but man has a larger head in proportion to his body. Children are of lesser intelligence, since they have a thick and heavy head; it is proper to the serpent to move its head backward while the rest of its body is still, and this was given to it for the protection of its body, since it is feeble.

Pliny, in the passage above: double crowns occur in men alone; some heads have flat and thin bones without marrow. In others the joints are structured like a saw, comb-fashion; once broken, they cannot be mended, but when a piece is removed, in moderate amount, it is not fatal, a fleshy scar taking its place. The weakest skulls are those of bears, the hardest those of parrots. All animals having blood have a brain, but man has proportionally the largest and moistest, the coldest of all the inner organs, veiled by two membranes above and below, either of which, if torn, is fatal; in all creatures, moreover, small bones are present within the middle of the brain: in man alone it throbs in infancy, and is not strengthened before the first beginning of speech; this is the most excellent of the inner organs, closest to the covering of the head, without flesh, without blood, without impurity; this holds the citadel of the senses, here all the force of the veins from the heart tends, here it ends, here is the highest summit, here is the seat of the mind, from it comes sleep, hence changes of the head. Creatures that have no brain do not sleep.

Aristotle: every animal having a brain has it in the front part of the head, since the senses are in front, and also because the brain must be directly opposite the heart. The brain and heart, moreover, need much protection, since in them is the chief power of life. The brain is exceedingly cold, more so than the other members, and is more deprived of blood than of any other moisture, since no blood appears in it, nor is there in it a vein, large or small. It is, moreover, a divine member, whose function is intellect and sense, nor could it bear upon itself the weight of another member, since weight burdens the motion of the intellect. And so the brain is the instrument of sense, and its nature is eternal, and it is not continuous with any member. Man, indeed, in proportion to his body, has a larger brain than other animals. A man's brain, too, is larger than a woman's.

The same: since the spinal marrow, however, is continuous with the brain, many think that the brain is the source of the marrow and of the vertebrae, but the truth contradicts this, since the nature of the brain is divided from the nature of the marrow, which is hot. And for this reason the marrow of the vertebrae, that is, the spine, is continuous with the brain, since nature always works to give a power that aids and expels the disorder of any member through its opposite, and places that opposite near it. And so nature was also contrived to place the brain opposite the heart, since a member cannot exist in any complexion by itself, without the contrariety of another. And so the brain is composed of earth and water, and its touch is exceedingly cold; for this reason every blood-having animal has a brain, and it is had by no other kind. And so the many-footed animal and such kinds are hot because of the lack of a brain. The brain, then, improves the complexion of the heart's heat and boiling, so that the heart may be temperate, [drawing] heat in the greater vein, whose passage is into the membrane containing the brain, that is, the pia mater. And so that no harm may come to the brain from heat, the veins containing it are thick, fine, and the blood clean and subtle. And so, if the brain, of temperate complexion, becomes colder, catarrhs occur, since the vapor of smoke rises upward and is cooled, just as the generation of rain happens from vapors, since vapor rises by heat and, when it reaches cold air, is held back and altered, and becomes water because of the cold, and then falls below. When, however, the brain dries out, or becomes moister than it should, it does not perform its function, but the body grows cold, and there follows a loss of intellect and illness and death, since the heat of the heart and of the primary member is great and is easily harmed by other things, and sense is very quick and is altered, or something from the blood flows together into what contains the brain. Sleep, too, occurs in an animal having a brain, since it cools the food coming to it from the flow of blood. Heat, then, together with blood, flees and gathers below, and then sleep occurs.

Isaac Judaeus, in the Diets, book 1: Aristotle says, in the book On Animals, that the brain is hot by nature and cold accidentally; accordingly it is moist and thick, viscous, and corrupts an already loathsome appetite in the stomach, and quickly turns to putrefaction.

Avicenna: the brain is cold and moist, generates phlegm and thick humors, and loosens the bowels; it causes nausea during its digestion and destroys appetite, and should be eaten with seeds; whoever wishes to vomit after a meal should take it on top of his food. It is, moreover, of slow digestion, making the stomach heavy. The better brains, indeed, are those of birds, and especially mountain birds. Among the brains of four-footed animals, the ram's brain is best, then the calf's.

Aristotle: horns naturally occur in animals that generate live animals, in others only in a transferred sense; they were created, however, for strength and benefit. Some, however, have weak horns, suited neither for strength nor for combat. And so no animal with many divisions in its cloven foot has horns, since it has another kind of strength, and most animals having cloven hooves have horns, though some solid-hoofed animals have them too. There are animals to which nature gave no other means of benefit, as it gave speed to horses and stags, size of body to the elephant and camel, and projecting tusks to pigs. Rightly, then, solid-hoofed animals do not have horns, since nature placed strength in their hooves and deprived their heads of horns, except perhaps that some have a single horn, like the Indian donkey. Horns ought to be on the head and not on another member, since a great weight would hinder their functions and there would be no benefit from them elsewhere. Stags, however, have horns that are very hard and solid out of necessity, and they cast them off because of their weight. They cast them off, moreover, where it is hard to find them, and once cast off, stags do not appear, since they lack weapons. In other animals, however, they are hollow near the root. The rest, however, is solid, since that is suited for thrusting. The branching of horns, as in the stag, however, is closer to harm than to benefit. And so female stags have the teeth of males, and yet do not have horns, since they are of no benefit to them, just as they are not in the males either. Likewise the stag alone changes its horns every year. Every horned animal naturally has a cloven hoof. The milk of horned animals curdles, but not that of others. Likewise horned animals do not have upper teeth, and so they chew the cud and cannot chew properly. Nor does any animal have both sharp teeth or rows of teeth and horns at once, except the hare. Only horned animals have rennet. The colors of horns and claws and hooves follow the colors of the hide and hair. The colors of teeth, however, follow the colors of bones, and so the teeth of Ethiopians are like their bones. Likewise horns are more attached to the hide and fixed upon it than upon the bone, and for this reason perhaps certain animals move their horns as they move their ears.

Pliny, in the passage above: horns, indeed, have been given in various ways to many water and sea creatures and to serpents, but what may rightly be understood as horns is given only to the four-footed kind, and nowhere has great nature played more with its abundant invention, scattering weapons among animals; some it scattered into branches, as in stags, but to others it gave simple ones.
