On others it fashioned them into palm-shapes and put forth fingers, whence they are called broad-horned. It gave branching but small ones to roe-deer, and did not make them shed. It gave coiled, spiraling ones to the ram kind. Those of bulls threaten forward. In this kind indeed it gave them to the females too, but in many kinds only to the males. To chamois, curved backward; to fallow deer, forward. Erect, however, and twisted in a circle of ridges, and sharpened into a smooth point - as suits the dormouse - to the 'strepsiceros,' which Africa calls the 'addax.' Mobile, however, like ears, to the flocks of Phrygia. Those of the Troglodytes, however, are pointed straight into the ground, for which reason they graze with head turned aside. To others too, single horns, and this in the middle of the head or in the nostrils. To others, robust for charging; to others, for striking, joined to the spine in several ways, all tapering to a point. In one kind, in place of hands, for scratching the body. To snails, for feeling out the way ahead. On the body these horns are as in the horned viper, sometimes single, but in snails always paired, so as to be extended and drawn back. Northern barbarians drink from the horns of the aurochs, and the horns of a single head fill two vessels. Others fix spear-points to these and use them as javelins. Among us they are cut into thin sheets and become translucent, and even spread a wider light when a flame is enclosed within, and are put to many other decorative uses, sometimes dyed, sometimes coated, sometimes worked in the kind of pattern they call horn-inlay. In all animals, however, they are hollow, solidifying only at the tip; only in stags are they entirely solid, and shed every year. Farmers heal oxen's worn hooves by anointing the horns with fat. The Indian donkey is armed with a single horn. Cloven-hoofed animals have two; in others they are attached to the bones, but in stags alone they grow from the skin.

Haly Abbas: [horn of] goat and stag, burnt, firms loosened teeth and hardens the gums. If a collyrium is made from them, carefully ground, it clears the sight and benefits the eye, toward which it draws the flow of matter, but they should be washed after burning. If, however, they are ground with wine and placed on the teeth, they strengthen them and promote their growth. Their ash, if carefully washed and drunk, benefits dysentery and chafing; further, if unburnt, boiled in vinegar, it benefits molar pain. If, however, ground and drunk, it benefits a scorpion's sting, and if drunk with gum tragacanth, it eases bladder pain.

Aristotle: the composition of the ears is from cartilage and flesh. The inner part of the ear is called the sebaceous part, and the outer, round part is called the shell-like part. Within, indeed, is a winding passage similar to a spiral bracelet. The end of the ear, however, is in the bone, and similar in the creation of the ear's shape. And every sound and ringing reaches it and returns from it to the brain. For one vein goes out from the brain and reaches the right ear, and another the left, and the movement of the ears depends on these. Every animal having ears has them mobile, except man. But every scaled and winged creature lacks ears, having only an opening and a passage for hearing; large sea animals have visible ears and good hearing. For when the formation of the ears is visible, and the membrane containing them, that is, the eardrum of hearing, is thin, hearing will be sharp. Ears of medium size signify goodness; but prominent and large ears signify stupidity and garrulousness.

Albertus Magnus: four-footed creatures do not have ears in the middle of the head, as man does, but on the surface, above the head, toward the back, and this for two reasons. Avicenna gives one, namely that such creatures have a hanging head, and so the stirred air would not freely reach the ears unless they were in a high position, nor could they hear well. For near the ground there is much disturbance hindering sounds. Whence bells hung higher, where they reach open air, sound better and are heard from farther away. The other reason is that in these creatures the lower jaw is very long and large, extending beyond the middle of the head, preventing a fitting placement of the ears in the middle. And so nature, ordering everything most excellently, found for them a high place. Furthermore, the prominent ears of animals are raised and bent back a great deal from the rear of the head toward the front, since the auditory nerves are directed to the front of the head. And so nature, so that the reflection of sound might occur toward the same part, raised the ears backward, so that the sound, striking from behind, might come from behind to the front. A sign of this is that animals, as soon as they hear a sound, raise their heads and turn their faces toward it, since they hear what comes from in front better than from behind. For from the front the sound's entry is direct, but from behind it is hindered by the projection of flesh. Further, birds, for two reasons, do not have prominent ears: one is that birds would be hindered in their flight, since they would catch much wind. The other is that in flight there would be much reverberation of air against the ears, and because of this the sound would be continuous, and from this two unsuitable things would follow, namely that hearing would be confused by the continuous sound, and that, from the continuous jarring of the brain, the bird would be killed.

Pliny, in the passage above: only the ears of men are immobile. In some animals they are larger, in others smaller. In stags, however, they are split and, as it were, divided; in shrews they are hairy; in the sea-calf and in vipers there are only hollows in place of ears. Among winged creatures, only the owl and the eared-owl have plumes like ears. In others, however, there are hollows for hearing, similarly in scaled creatures and serpents. In horses and the whole kind of beasts of burden, they show signs of mood: drooping in the weary, twitching in the fearful, upright in the enraged, relaxed in the sick.

The same, in the same: a face, indeed, belongs to man alone; other creatures have a mouth or a beak. A forehead is present in others too, but in man alone is it an index, by its expression, of sadness, cheerfulness, mercy, severity.

Aristotle: the forehead is the upper part of the face, lying between the top of the head and the eyes. The face, however, is not properly named except in man alone. A large forehead signifies one who is heavy, inclined to foolishness, but a small one signifies goodness in the movement of one's works, that is, of the soul, and when it is broad it signifies a perverseness of discernment. When, however, it is round, it signifies irascibility. On the forehead are the eyebrows, which, when lowered, signify an envious person, and when they are straight like a line, softness and feminine changeability are signified. When, however, they are arched, to the point of meeting at the tip of the nose, it signifies one who is light, subtle, and diligent in all his works. When, however, that arch slopes toward the temples or the fullness of the cheeks, it signifies one negligent and disorderly. The eyebrows, indeed, were created to keep off moisture that descends to the forehead from the head. The eyelids, however, to keep off what falls upon the eye from outside, just as a hedge keeps entry from a garden. The eyebrows are set upon bones, and for this reason hairs increase upon them in old age.

Pliny, in the passage above: eyebrows in man move both together and separately, and in them is a part of the mind. We deny, we assent: these especially indicate arrogance; pride has its dwelling elsewhere, but its seat is here. It is angered in the heart, but rises here, and hangs here.

Aristotle: below the eyebrows are the eyes, and their parts are the upper and lower eyelids, created, indeed, to keep off what falls on the eye from outside. Within the eye, however, the moisture through which one sees is the pupil, and what follows it is called the black of the eye, and what is outside that blackness, the white; the location of the eyes, moreover, corresponds to the emission of the seed. Likewise the parts of the eye are the corners too, namely near the tip of the nose and the fullness of the cheeks, and the tear-duct, upper and lower. And when the tear-duct and what follows the corner of the eye are small and fine, it signifies a poor disposition, habit, and shape, that is, of the eye. When, however, that place is fleshy, as happens with a kite's eyes, cunning and evil timidity are signified, that is, a desire to deceive another out of fear of being deceived by him. Likewise eyes of medium size signify goodness of judgment and intellect; if they are deep-set, sharpness is signified in all animals. If, however, protruding, disturbance of judgment and evil disposition are signified; if medium, it is a sign of goodness. Likewise if they are much open and little closed, foolishness and shamelessness are signified; if much closed, it signifies great fickleness, shallow judgment, unsteadiness in action. When, however, medium between the two, goodness of disposition and judgment in every work and time is signified. The passage of the eyes, indeed, reaches the veins that are around the brain, and passages also go out from the ears and are continuous with the back of the head. A deep-set eye sees well even from a distance, since its motion is not divided or dispersed, but the visible power going out from it goes straight to the thing seen. A protruding eye, however, does not. And when there is no covering outside the eye, sight is necessarily weakened. The formation of the eyes, indeed, is from water, and from an abundance of moisture comes a black color. When, however, the moisture is scanty, a grey-blue color results, as is evident in the sea. And so grey-blue eyes are not sharp in sight either by day or by night, since their grey-blue color, because of the scarcity of moisture, is more scattered by sunlight. Black eyes, however, see less by night, because of the abundance of moisture, since night's light is weaker, and also because moisture in general moves sluggishly at night, and the eye's movement comes from brightness, not from moisture.

Aristotle: the eyelids, as has been said, are the upper and lower parts of the eyes. Every animal that generates its like has eyes, except the mole, and it likewise has eyelids and a covering for the sense of sight. For since the nature of the eye is created from moisture, it needs this protection, and, so that sight may be very sharp, man closes his eye more than all other animals, since his skin is thin. For over the eyelid is skin containing it, and for this reason neither the eyelid nor the foreskin heals over with scarring, since they are skin without flesh. A bird does not close its eye except by the lower eyelid, and its closing must be very quick, since birds necessarily need sharp sight, since they see from a distance, especially the hook-clawed birds; walking creatures, however, close the eye with the upper lid; the lizard kind does not close it at all. A four-footed egg-laying animal has a scaled hide, and what surrounds its head is very hard; for this reason it does not have an upper eyelid, but only a lower one, having flesh and hardness and the extension suited for closing the eye. Fish and other ringed and hard-skinned animals lack eyelids most of all, because of the hardness of their skin, since the work of eyelids must be quick, but in place of this covering and protection they have hard eyes, and because of this hardness they see poorly. All animals, finally, having hair have eyelids. Birds, however, and scaled creatures by no means have hairs in their eyelids, except only on the upper one, except man, who has them in both, since nature always prepares an advantage for the nobler animal. Every animal closes its eye so that nothing may fall upon it, and this not by will, but by nature.
Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: every animal having eyelids closes them in sleep, except the hare and the lion.

div.head: DE DIVERSITATE OCULORUM IN DIVERSIS GENERIBUS ANIMALIUM

cit.quote: Pliny: [on the eyes] of animals: of oysters, of scallop-shells, of moles among four-footed creatures, of the white-eyed heron among birds, of snails, of little horns, of earthworms among worms, of man, of horses among animals, of men, of hares among animals, of man, of periwinkles, of night creatures, of cats, of the goat and the wolf, of the calf, of the hyena, of fish, of the chameleon, of the crab, of locusts and shrimps, of serpents, of swallow chicks, of insects. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: the eyes of children at birth are green, and afterward change to the nature that predominates in them. The eyes of other animals have only one color, like the eyes of cows, which are black, and the eyes of sheep, which are more watery than those of other animals. The eyes of horses, however, are of varied color among animals, and by chance one eye will be grey-blue, the other its opposite, which does not happen in other animals besides man. The cause of grey-blue eyes in children is that these members are weaker in them than others, and grey-blue eyes in man and horse, namely that one eye of a man or horse should be grey-blue and the other not, has the same cause as that by which man alone, and the horse, turn grey in old age. For greyness is a kind of weakness of the moisture in the brain and a scarcity of digestion, and grey-blue eyes likewise. When, then, nature is weak in cooking what is in each eye, and cooks one thing but not another, then it happens that one eye is grey-blue, and the other not. The goat too, sometimes, like the horse, has eyes of different color.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: man's eyes are set closer together, in proportion to his body's size, than in other animals. All sea animals have bony eyes and a hard skin, since salt water would penetrate fine and delicate things, and they could not survive unless nature gave them skins stronger than others. Certain animals see better by night than by day, since their eyes abound in a very white moisture. Whence, by day, the visual spirit is more dispersed, and thus the discernment of things seen is lost, but at night it is gathered together.

Pliny, book 11: cheeks are present in four-footed creatures only on the upper part. In birds, on the lower, and in those with a soft hide, and in serpents and four-footed creatures that lay eggs, like lizards. The ostrich alone among birds, like man, has eyelids on both sides.

Aristotle: the nose is the instrument of the sense of smell and of breathing, and the passage for sneezing, when wind multiplies in the brain and comes out unexpectedly; breath, however, that comes from the mouth beyond necessity is foul and unfitting, since by nature it should come out only through the nostrils. The nose, moreover, belongs to good sense and motion, and the wall in its middle is of cartilage. The passage of breath and mucus, however, is empty, and this instrument, that is, of smell, is called the nose in animals having two long voice-passages. In others, however, it is divided near the jaws. The elephant's nose is a long and strong member, soft and flexible, by which it brings food to its mouth, and it uses it in place of hands for everything it needs, even for uprooting trees. And when it swims, it raises that appendage upward to draw in air. Long-nosed hounds have a good sense of smell. Birds, however, and serpents and other egg-laying blood-having animals have nasal passages that are not divided, clearly near the mouth, for breathing. And it can be said that they do not have a nose, but only a beak, formed, as it were, from the nature of the bones in which the passages of smell lie; in place of a nose, mouth, and teeth, then, they have a beak, both for food and for smell or breath. The other breathing animals, however, breathe through gills or windpipes. A ringed-bodied animal, however, breathes through the membrane at the wall and perceives smells.
Isaac Judaeus: the nostrils are cold and dry, for they are cartilaginous, and so are difficult to digest and produce little nourishment.

Aristotle: the mouth and the parts and instruments in it are suited to the use of food; since indeed an animal that feeds needs its food cut into small parts, and this cutting is not the cause of the food's digestion entirely, but of its quicker digestion. The function of the mouth, indeed, is to send food to the stomach, which digests it by natural heat. A mouth that is needed for strength is of much cleft, as in wolves and other hunting and rapacious fish; man, however, in proportion to his body, has a small mouth. Sharp-toothed animals, however, have a mouth of much cleft. The lips, beneath the nostrils, were created from flesh of good movement, for the health and protection of the teeth, and so that they might be suited to the production of speech and to the tasting of moisture.
Pliny: [on] the crocodile. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Isaac Judaeus: [on] animals. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: fish, however, have a tongue, but not divided, since the sense of moisture is present only briefly in a small water-dwelling animal. For food passes quickly to the stomach, since it cannot remain long in the mouth, since its moisture is drawn out by the water. If one does not turn the mouth to one side, the tongue will not be visible. Likewise in the heads of all animals, beneath the tongue, deep within it, is a worm-like vessel. And so the tongue is a restless member.

Pliny, in the passage above: tongues are not the same in all creatures. Very thin in serpents, and three-forked, quivering, of a dark color; if you draw it out, it is very long; in lizards, forked and hairy. In the sea-calf too it is double, but with the fineness of hair, unlike the ones already mentioned. In others, for licking round the mouth. In fish, only slightly less than entirely attached. In crocodiles, entirely attached. But in taste, water-dwellers have, in place of a tongue, a fleshy palate. In bees too it is very long and prominent, and in cicadas. Those that have a hollow sting in the mouth have neither tongue nor teeth; in certain insects the tongue is inside, as in ants. Otherwise, broad in the elephant, in the rest of its kind always free. In man alone it is so often bound by veins that it becomes necessary to cut them. The perception of taste is in the tongue for other creatures, in man also in the palate. The sea-turtle has no tongue and no teeth, but crushes everything with the edge of its beak. In lions and leopards and all of that kind, even cats, it has a scaled roughness like a file, and, by licking, wears away human skin - which is also the reason that, when tamed, once it reaches nearby blood, the saliva invites it to rage. In frogs it is attached at the front. The inner part is free from the throat, by which they emit their voice. The males are then called 'Ololygones,' and this happens at a fixed season, when they excite the females to mating. Then indeed, with the lower lip lowered to receive a little water in the throat, and the tongue quivering, a howling cry is drawn out. Then the pouches of the cheeks, stretched, become translucent. The eyes blaze, driven by the effort. Those that have stings at the rear have both teeth and a tongue.
Isaac Judaeus: the tongue, among tender flesh and lizards, is of medium quality, and so alone, eaten, gives soft and moderate nourishment.

Aristotle: all animals, indeed, have an appetite for food. A ringed-bodied animal has such an organ, by which it perceives food, within the mouth, like the ant kind and many others of hard shell. Some of these, however, have that organ outside, like a sting, and its nature is soft and hollow; through it it tastes and perceives and draws in food, as is evident in flies and bees and the like.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the jaws [maxillae], as Isidore says, are named by diminution from the cheeks [malae], just as 'paxillus' [peg] is from 'palus' [stake], 'taxillus' [die] from 'talus' [ankle-bone]. The jawbones [mandibulae], however, are parts of the jaws, so named from chewing [mandendo], for they contain the teeth.

Aristotle: every animal having a hairy tail has a small head and large jaws. Man, indeed, and four-footed creatures move their jaws up and down and sideways, since they bite, chew, and ruminate. Birds, however, and fish move them up and down, but not sideways, since they do not chew, but only bite. Every animal moves the lower jaw, except shellfish, which move the upper.
Pliny, book 11: the crocodile alone moves the upper jaw.

Aristotle: every animal that generates an animal like itself has teeth. The quality and quantity of man's teeth, indeed, are suited to speech, especially the front ones. In certain animals, however, the nature of the teeth is for the use of food. In certain others, for strength against harm. And some have sharp, strong teeth, fitting into one another like a saw, so that they do not grow blunt. Others, however, have two projecting tusks, like pigs; and of these arrangements, one is for strength, the other for fighting. No animal has both at once, since nature does nothing superfluous; for this reason pigs do not have projecting tusks and bite only by the sharpness of their teeth. Nature indeed does not give members suited to strength except to animals that need them, like a sting, claws, horns, projecting tusks, and the like. And so there is no animal that has both sharp teeth or rows of teeth and horns at once. Horned animals, moreover, do not have upper teeth. Sharp-toothed animals have a mouth of much cleft, since they need it for strength. And every animal having a saw-like row of teeth eats flesh. And since the males of animals are stronger than the females, the aforementioned members, that is, those suited to strength, will perhaps be present in males only, or stronger in males than in females. For this reason male stags have horns, females do not. There is also a difference between the horns of bulls and cows, and in the horns of sheep; likewise the teeth of fish are sharp, except the parrotfish, since, because of the moisture, they cannot hold food long in the mouth. They are also curved, since their strength lies in them. Birds, however, do not have teeth, but a beak in place of lips and teeth. The teeth of serpents are sharp, various, joined together. An old stag has no teeth, or has small ones. It is read that in India there is a kind of wolf having three rows of teeth, upper and lower. There is also a certain animal that opens its mouth, and small birds entering clean its teeth, feeding themselves on the filth from them. Male animals have more teeth than females, as is evident in men, pigs, and goats. In others, however, this is not apparent, and those having many teeth are, for the most part, long-lived. Those, however, having few and separated teeth are short-lived. In animals lacking upper teeth, milk curdles, but the milk of an animal having teeth in both jaws by no means does.

Pliny, in the passage above: there are three kinds of teeth: saw-like, continuous, or projecting. Saw-like ones fit together like a comb's teeth, so as not to be worn down by opposing contact, as in serpents, fish, dogs. Continuous, as in man, horse. Projecting, in the boar, the hippopotamus, the elephant. Of the continuous kind, those that grind food are broad and sharp, and those that break it are double. Those that separate them are called canine, and these are the longest of the saw-like ones. Continuous teeth are either on both sides of the mouth, as in the horse, or the upper front ones are absent, as in oxen and sheep, which ruminate. Goats have no upper teeth except a pair of front ones. None of the projecting-tusked animals have saw-like teeth. Tusks are rare in females, and even then without use. And so, when boars strike, the females bite. None of the horned animals has projecting tusks, but all of them are hollow at the base. In the rest, however, they are solid. All fish have saw-like teeth, except the parrotfish, the only water-creature with flat ones. And in many of them, moreover, there are teeth on the tongue and throughout the whole mouth, so that, like a crowd of wounds, they soften what they cannot subdue by grinding. In many, too, on the palate and even on the tail. Further, the teeth of the asp and serpents bend inward toward the mouth, so that food does not fall out, having no means of holding it otherwise; but two on the upper side, right and left, very long, pierced with a fine channel, pour in venom like scorpions' stings. This is said to be nothing other than serpent venom, and the most careful authors write that it reaches the mouth from veins beneath the spine, and travels through the belly. Some say there is only one such tooth, and, since it is hooked, it is turned back when the creature bites. Some say it falls out at that time and easily grows back, and that in most creatures there are three. A viper's teeth are set into the gums; the same creature, pregnant, pours venom into its bites when the teeth are pressed by the recoil. No winged creature has teeth, except the bat. The camel, one of those without horns, has no upper front teeth. None of the horned animals has saw-like teeth. And snails have teeth, as is shown by vine-shoots gnawed by the smallest of them. But that crustaceans and cartilaginous sea-creatures have front teeth, and likewise that sea-urchins have five, I marvel how this could be known. Insects have stings in place of teeth. Apes have teeth like man's. The elephant has four inside for chewing, besides those that project, curved back in males, straight and forward in females. The male sea-creature that precedes the whale has none, but in their place a rough mouth inside, and a tongue too, and a palate. Among land four-footed creatures, small ones have a pair of front teeth, very long on each side. In the rest they are born together with the animal, but in man not until the seventh month after birth.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: every animal having saw-like teeth draws water with its tongue. Animals having even teeth draw water into the belly by sucking. Animals with many teeth are, for the most part, long-lived, but those with few, short-lived. Likewise ruminant animals have teeth only on one side, since it was not necessary; for when they ruminate, they chew deliberately and pass on the food. All animals, however, that live in water and have teeth, have crowded, sharp teeth, so as to cut through food more quickly and pass it to the stomach, lest their food be washed away from their teeth by the water.

Pliny, book 11: in the rest of the animals the teeth remain permanent; they are replaced in man, the lion, the beast of burden, the dog, and ruminants. But in the lion and dog, only those called canine. A wolf's right canine tooth is held in great value among rich people. No animal changes the molars that come after the canines; in man the last, called wisdom teeth, appear around the twentieth year, in many even the eightieth, in women too, but it is established that in those in whom they were not born in youth, they fall out in old age and soon grow back again. Mucianus reports that he himself saw a citizen of Zancle in Samothrace whose teeth grew back after a hundred and four years. In man, sheep, or goats, males have more than females. Timarchus, son of Nicodes of Paphos, had two rows of molars. His brother did not change his front teeth, and so passed them by. There is an example of teeth being born on the palate: canines lost by some accident never grow back. In other creatures they redden with age, but in the horse alone they become whiter. The age of veteran animals is shown by their teeth. A horse has forty teeth. It loses two front teeth on each side at thirty months. The following year, as many of the next teeth, called the pillar-teeth, come in. In the beginning of the fifth year it loses a pair, which grow back in the sixth year. And in the seventh it has all its teeth, both regrown and unchangeable. In a gelded horse the teeth do not fall out as early. The donkey kind loses them similarly at thirty months, then again at six-month intervals. But if they have not foaled before the last teeth fall, sterility is certain. Cattle lose these teeth too. Pigs never lose them. With this reservation understood, old age in horses and other veteran animals is judged by the protrusion of teeth, the greying of the eyebrows, and hollows around them, when they are thought to be nearly sixteen years old. In human teeth there is a certain harmful power, for they dull the shine of a mirror when facing it, uncovered, and kill unfledged doves' chicks. The rest of the animals having saw-like teeth are the fiercest in their bite.

Aristotle: man loses his teeth, but only the front ones, not the molars. The horse too, and the mule and the donkey lose their teeth, but the pig does not lose them at all. The dog, however, does not lose any until a similar one comes up in its place. Wild animals too shed their tusks. For it is doubted concerning the front ones. Young dogs are not distinguished from old ones except by their teeth, since the young have white and sharp teeth, the old black and blunt ones. Every animal's teeth blacken as it advances in age, except the horse, whose teeth, on the contrary, whiten. When the elephant is born, teeth appear suddenly generated with it, but the large tusks do not appear until it grows up. The teeth that are born within the gum do not arise in men and women except after twenty years, and perhaps in certain women after seventy years. And their coming is with great pain, especially when they come at an untimely age.

Aristotle: the location of the windpipe, moreover, was necessarily in front of the gullet, since the nobler and better member deserves to be more worthily placed, that is, in the front part and not the rear, and likewise on the right, not the left, and above, not below, unless some other, nobler thing prevents it from being there. The heart, however, is placed in the front of the chest, and in the front of the heart is all sense and motion. The origin of life and breath, indeed, goes through the windpipe and lung to the front of the heart, but what enters the gullet goes to the stomach. The neck-bone of lions is continuous, and there is no ringed structure in it. Serpents do not have a distinct neck for the most part. The length of birds' necks follows the length of their legs. Swimming birds, however, having skin between their toes, are an exception. In fishing birds the neck is like a reed, and the beak like a hook.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: [on the length of the neck] in horses, camels, and elephants, so that they may stretch to feed. For since these animals are taller, they could not otherwise graze on the shortest grasses. Almost all ruminant animals too have a long neck. To some, however, it gave shorter and narrower necks, like the lion and the tigers, since they do not bend their neck and mouth to the ground for the sake of grazing, but either attack a stag or tear apart an ox or a sheep.

Pliny, in the passage above: the tonsils in man are in their own gland. What hangs between them, called by the name 'uvula,' from the palate, belongs to man alone. Beneath it is a smaller tongue. None of the egg-laying creatures have these. Its functions are twofold, with two passages interposed. The inner of these is called the epiglottis, the windpipe reaching to the lung and heart. This it covers while eating, and while the voice passes through it, lest, if food or drink strays into the wrong path, it cause choking. The other, outer passage, is properly called the gullet, through which food and drink are swallowed. This leads to the esophagus, which leads to the stomach. This it covers in turn only when breath or voice passes, lest an ill-timed backflow from the belly disturb it. A neck is present only in those that have both of these. In others there is only a throat with the gullet. But those that have a neck have it made flexible, from many jointed and vertebrated bones, articulated for looking around by knotted joints. Only in the lion and wolf and hyena is it rigid, of single, straight bones. In others it is attached to the spine. The spine is bony in the loins, but of round structure, with the marrow descending from the brain through the middle openings. They gather that it has the same nature as the brain, since, its very thin membrane cut, death follows at once. Those that have long legs have long necks. Likewise water creatures, although they have short legs, similarly have hooked claws. The throat swells in man alone, and in pigs, mostly from a defect in the water they drink. The top of the gullet is called the jaws, the bottom the stomach. Under this name, beneath the already fleshy windpipe, is an emptiness attached to the spine, spread out in breadth and length like a flask. Those that have no voice have neither stomach nor neck nor throat, as fish, and their mouths join directly to their bellies.

div.head: DE ARMIS ET PECTORIBUS ET COSTIS

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the shoulders [armi], according to Isidore, are properly of four-footed creatures, as the shoulders [humeri] are of men. There are, moreover, two shoulders in an animal, of which the right was called, in the Law, the 'shoulder of separation,' since, in the division of the parts of the sacrificial victim, it was first separated from it, and, as more worthy than the other parts, was assigned to the portion of the priests. Some also report that the formation of an animal's body in the mother's womb begins from the right shoulder. The animal's front feet, with their legs, are joined to these, just as men's hands with their arms are joined to the shoulders.

Aristotle: since man has more intellect than the other animals, nature gave him hands, as pipes are given to a piper, so that he might use them in various ways, since, being highly intelligent, he needs many instruments. And so the hand is not one instrument, but many; the other animals, indeed, have only one mode of strength, and cannot have another or change their weapons. For man, however, the hand is like a claw and a hoof and a spear, a sword and other instruments, since it can do all of these things. In animals, however, nature placed front feet in the place of hands. And so an animal having many toes on its feet uses its front feet as man uses his hands, since it fights with them and drives harm from itself. An animal having hooves, however, does this with its hind feet, since the front ones are not suited for this. The ape uses its hands as feet, and its hands and feet as hands, since they are composed of both hand and foot. The elephant uses its trunk in place of a hand for taking food and drink, and for everything it needs, even for uprooting trees. The left hand in men is not of quick movement, nor is the left foot in animals, except in the elephant.
Pliny, in the passage above: nature surrounded the chest with the vital organs around the heart: broad in man alone, keel-shaped in the rest.

Aristotle: the chest is broad in man; in four-footed creatures, this cannot be, because of the extension of the front feet and because of walking. And so they do not have breasts on the chest; man alone, then, will have a broad chest. For the other animals have a narrow one: man's chest has little flesh. Birds, however, have a fleshy and sharp chest, for the reason stated above.
Pliny, in the passage above: ribs number eight pairs in man alone, ten in pigs, thirteen in horned animals, thirty in serpents.

Aristotle: some animals have breasts on the chest, some on the belly, some near the hips. Women indeed have them on the chest, where the ribs meet, because of the breadth of the space, and separated from one another, since they are fleshy and that place is fleshy. And in males this is for walking, but in females it is for the food of their young. And they begin to grow full at marriageable age. The other animals, however, could not have them on the chest in front of the front feet, because of the weight, since it would hinder movement. Animals having few offspring, hooves, and horns have only two breasts, near the hips. An animal, however, of many offspring and much cleft in the feet has many breasts, like the dog and the sow. A certain one has only two, on the belly, like the lioness. The reason for this is not that it has many young, but that its milk is scanty. Its food passes into its body, since it eats rarely, and eats flesh. The female elephant, however, has only two, since it bears only a single offspring, and has them under the armpit, which is the primary location of breasts. Not near the hips, since it has a cloven foot. For no cloven-footed animal can have breasts near the hips. Likewise certain animals have many breasts and much milk, like the sow, which has this property, that it gives the first breast to the first-born. The primary breasts, indeed, are near the armpits, and for this reason the female elephant has two breasts there, as has been said. The breasts of animals with many young, however, are on the belly, since they are many, for they need many, and since in breadth there can be no more than two, namely on the right and left side. Their location is along the length of the belly. An animal, however, lacking much cleft in its feet and hands, having few young, has its breasts distinguished near the armpits, like the she-camel and the mare and the she-donkey, since such animals bear only one at a time. A similar arrangement is also found in hoofed animals, like the doe, the cow, the goat, and the like. The reason for this is that the body's growth is in the upper part, and so it needs more food. The other part, on the contrary, needs less, and for this reason nature placed the breasts in that part.

Aristotle: breasts are present in an animal that generates an animal, and in a haired animal, like man or the horse, and in four-footed animals. And in large sea creatures, like the dolphin. And all of an animal's milk is in the breasts. Egg-laying animals, however, do not have breasts, like fish and birds. Likewise, of the aforementioned animals, all the females have breasts, but the males of some do not. Horses, when they resemble their mothers, have breasts. When, however, they resemble their fathers, they do not, and in certain males the breasts are more visible, especially in those having moist and smooth bodies. In the breasts of certain males, moreover, there is milk, but little: the sagging of the udder downward before birth is a sign of an abundance of milk. The milk of animals having many breasts is not suited for cheese.

Pliny, in the passage above: man alone among males has breasts; the other animals have only marks of breasts, but not even the females, unless they can lift up their offspring. None of the egg-laying kind has them, nor milk, except an animal that bears live young; among winged creatures, the bat alone. For I think it fabulous that owls suckle infants' lips with their udders. It is agreed, indeed, that the owl is among the ancient omens of evil, but I do not think it certain which bird it is. Those having a solid hoof and no more than twin offspring have two breasts, and nowhere else than on the thighs, in the same place as cloven-hoofed and horned animals. Cattle have four, goats two. Those fertile with numerous offspring, and those having toes on their feet, have more, spread over the whole belly in a double row, as pedigreed sows have twelve, common ones two fewer, likewise dogs; others have four in the middle of the belly, like panthers, others two, like lionesses. The elephant alone has two, under the forelegs, not on the chest, but nearby, hidden in the others. None of those having toes on the thighs has them there. The first-born, in each part, press first upon the first breasts of the sow, and, even if food is nearest at hand, each nevertheless knows its own place in the order of its birth, and is nourished by it and no other. Bears bear four breasts. Dolphins, two, at the bottom of the belly, mere nipples, not prominent, but stretched slightly aslant, and no other animal is nursed while swimming. Whales too and the sea-calf nourish their young with breasts.

Aristotle: the heart is present in all blood-having creatures. For the vessels of blood are the veins, and their origin is the heart, whence the veins seem to come out from the heart, not to pass through it. The nature of the heart's formation, moreover, is from the veins, and it is of the vein kind. Its location, moreover, is suited to its primary being, since it is placed in the upper and front region, which is nobler, naturally arranged in the nobler place, namely the middle of the body, where it must necessarily be, for it is between the member that receives food and the member through which excess matter exits, since every animal needs these two members, and a third, in which is the source of life. Those, however, who imagined that the source of the veins is in the head, erred, since they place many distinct sources in a cold location. But where it is possible to have a single root, it is better than to make many sources. The heart, then, since it is the source of the veins, is hollow to receive blood, and dense to guard the source of motion. And in no member is there blood without veins, except in the heart alone. Nor does it come to the heart from another place, since the heart is the fount and source of blood and the member that receives blood, while the veins are channels or beds; and this is clear because the heart's formation is the first to appear as blood-colored, and it is the source of motion for pleasurable and sensible things, and universally the motions of any sense begin from it and return to it. It must, then, be one, and in the middle, as the source, since that location is more fitting, being both central and single. And its power spreads to all members in a uniform way, and this is also evident to the senses, since the heart appears in the body of the embryo at the beginning of its formation, and seems to move among the other members like an animal, since it is the source of the nature of a blood-having animal. The heart, moreover, is placed in the front of the chest, so that it is not quickly chilled; for this reason the front of the chest was formed with little flesh, but the back with more flesh, for it has much covering on the side of the spine. In other animals, indeed, the heart is placed in the middle of the chest. In man, however, it inclines to the left, so that the cooling of the left side equals the cooling of the right, since the left side in man is colder than in other animals. Again, the pointed part of the heart is opposite the head, and motion is in it. The heart is divided into like parts, as each of the other inner members is, and all of these are present in blood-having creatures and not in others. And the nature of all of these is bloody, since their location is along the paths of the veins, and there is empty space between them. And so all the members of the body are composed of veins, in which blood runs. In the heart is the source of the veins and the primary power creating blood. In the heart of a large animal there are three chambers, and in a small one, two, since it is the place of receiving pure blood. For the sources of the veins in the heart are two, namely the great vein and the aorta, since the nature of blood is divided into two. It is better, however, that there be three chambers, so that there be one common source, and there is a single middle one. In the chambers on the right side, indeed, the blood is very hot, and so the right side is hotter than the left, and the blood on the left is less and colder. The ventricles, however, have blood tempered in quantity and quality, and it is very moist, and so it must be in the member in which the primary power resides. In hearts, moreover, there must be a division resembling a suture. In the hearts of the horse and the cow there are bones, and there is one in the heart of the stag too.

Aristotle: hearts differ in largeness and smallness, softness and hardness. For the hearts of animals having sense are soft, but of those lacking sense, hard. Likewise an animal of large heart is timid, like the donkey, stag, hare, mule, for just as a small fire heats a large house less than a small one, so a small heat in a large heart cannot fill it, since it is spread thin, and for this reason the blood becomes colder. For this reason too an animal of large ventricles will not be fat, nor an animal of large veins, but rather the opposite. An animal having a heart of medium size, however, is more courageous. Likewise, among all the inner members, the heart alone cannot suffer pain or severe illness. For when the source is corrupted, none of the remaining members are helped: and a sign of this is that in a dead heart, illness never naturally appears, as it appears in other inner members, like stones in the kidneys, or wounds or swellings, similarly in the liver or lung. All the mischances, then, that happen to animals do not appear in it. The heart and brain need protection, since in them especially is the power of life. The source of life and of all sense, moreover, is from the heart. The hawk eats the hearts of the birds it catches.

Pliny, in the passage above: in other animals the heart is in the middle of the chest; in man alone, below the left breast, its pointed tip projecting forward at an angle. In fish alone it points toward the mouth. It is reported that this is the first thing formed in the womb of those being born, then the brain, as the eyes are formed last, but that this is the first to die, the heart last. In this is the chief heat. It certainly throbs and moves as if it were a separate creature. Among animals it alone is covered by a soft yet firm membrane wrapping, protected by the wall of the ribs and chest, so that it may be evident it is the chief cause and origin of life. It provides, within itself, the first dwelling for the spirit and blood, in a winding cavity, and in large animals, triple. In none is it not double. There the mind dwells; from this fount two great veins run forward and backward, and, spread in a series of branches through smaller ones, water the vital blood to all the other members. Alone among the organs it is not worn down by ailments, nor does it draw out the sufferings of life. Once wounded, it brings death at once, while, once the other organs are corrupted, vitality still lingers in the heart. Animals whose heart is hard and rigid are thought dull. Those in which it is small are bold; those in which it is very large, timid. It is largest, proportionally, in mice and the hare and stag, the panther, weasels, hyenas, and all timid or, from fear, harmful creatures. In Paphlagonia, partridges have two hearts. Bones are sometimes found in the heart of horses and cattle. The Egyptians think a man cannot live beyond a hundred years for want of heart, they whose custom it is to preserve embalmed corpses; they report that certain men are born with a shaggy heart, and that none are braver in daring, like Aristomenes of Messene, who killed three hundred Spartans. He himself, wounded and captured, once escaped through a narrow opening in the rock, following the paths of foxes. Captured again, while his guards slept, he freed himself, rolling near the fire, burning through his bonds along with his body. Captured a third time, the Spartans cut open his chest to see, and a shaggy heart was found. It is denied that the heart can be burned in those who die of heart disease, and denied too in those killed by poison.
Isaac Judaeus, in the passage above: the heart is of hard and slow substance; it is expelled from the stomach, but yet, when well digested, gives much good nourishment to the body.

Aristotle: the lung is the instrument of breathing, and the source of its motion is in the heart. It is itself prepared for breadth in the intake of air, because of its softness and hollowness and cavity and the size of its body. And when it inflates, air enters, and when it contracts, air exits. Since, indeed, the lung is suited to the heart's pulse, it is not inflated but is raised a great deal. The heart's pulse, moreover, does not occur especially except in man, since man hopes and fears. A walking animal has a lung, since it needs cooling. And a blood-having animal needs it more, since it has greater heat. A blood-lacking animal, however, is satisfied by the cooling of the natural spirit that is in it. The blood in the lung is not fixed, but that in the heart is fixed. All breathing animals have a lung. All walking animals breathe, and also certain water creatures, like dolphins and all large sea creatures, since they draw in air. Many animals, too, are of shared nature, that is, both water and land, and breath is the completion of their life. An animal that generates live young has a large, blood-filled lung, because of the heat of its nature. The lung of an egg-laying animal, however, is small and dry; birds have a modest, hollow lung, resembling foam. Such animals, then, do not thirst much and abstain from drink for a long time, because of the scarcity of heat. For they cool through the lung's motion, since its motion brings in much air. In animals that generate live young, the lung is divided into two, for which reason many think they have two lungs.

Pliny, in the passage above: beneath the heart is the lung, whose function is breathing, drawing in and giving back the breath of life; for this reason it is spongy and hollow with empty tubes. Few water creatures have it, and the rest that lay eggs have a small one, foamy and bloodless, and so they do not thirst. This is also the reason why frogs and seals can stay long underwater. The tortoise too, although it has a very large one under its shell, has it bloodless. The smaller this is in body, the greater the creature's speed. In the chameleon it is proportionally the largest, and nothing else is within.

Avicenna: the lung's nourishment is small, inclining toward the phlegmatic. In it is a constriction of the belly, and its digestion is easy. There are, however, medicinal lungs, like the ram's, the fox's, and the hare's.

Isaac Judaeus: the lung is easy of digestion and quickly expelled from the stomach because of the lightness and looseness of its substance; accordingly it produces less nourishment than other members, and belongs to the phlegmatic humor.

Aristotle: the liver is the principal member in all blood-having animals, and is for cooking and digesting. For the liver and spleen can cook food, since they are of blood and have much heat. There is, moreover, an opinion that the spleen is an impure liver. In an animal lacking a spleen, or having one very small, like a mere point, the liver is found divided into two, the larger part on the right, the smaller on the left. And since the liver's location is on the right, the spleen's location will be on the left. Those whose liver's nature is healthy have little gall. Man's liver is similar to a bull's liver.
Avicenna: the liver is of slow passage in the veins, except the liver of a fat duck; the moisture generated from livers is thick, and the healthiest of these is the liver of the duck and of fat hens.
Avicenna, in the same: besides this, there are also certain other medicinal livers, like the liver of the goat and of the dog, even the rabid dog.

Isaac Judaeus: the liver is thicker than all the members and harder to digest, yet it generates praiseworthy blood. It is also more nourishing than fatty flesh, but the liver of a suckling animal is better than the rest, and that of a hen better than that of suckling animals.

Aristotle: the spleen exists in the bodies of animals accidentally and not necessarily, since it is not a vessel of nourishment, but of excess, and resembles the excess of the belly and bladder. For this reason too it is small in certain animals, especially in birds of hot belly, like the dove, the hawk, the kite, and in egg-laying four-footed animals, and in many having shells, that is, lacking feet, since the body's excess inclines toward the fleshy part, and from the fleshy part proceeds to the part of the feathers. The spleen indeed draws excess moisture from the belly and cooks it, since its formation is of blood, and if it ever draws too much, this will be the cause of the belly's drying out. And the cause of the spleen's hardness is the gathering of moisture in it. Something similar also happens to those who urinate much, from the drawing out of moisture from its proper place. Man's spleen is like the spleen of the pig. The spleen of horned, cloven-hoofed animals is round; that of animals with many divisions in the foot is long, and of hoofed animals, medium.

Pliny: the spleen is attached to the belly on the left side, opposite the liver, with which it sometimes exchanges place, but this is a portent. Some think it is present in egg-laying creatures. Likewise very small in serpents. Thus indeed it appears in the tortoise and crocodile and lizards and frogs. It is agreed there is none in the cynocephalus bird, nor in creatures lacking blood, and it is a peculiar hindrance sometimes to running. For this reason it is cauterized in runners troubled by it. And animals are reported to live even after it is removed through a wound. Some think that laughter and intemperance of that region in man is taken away at the same time as the size of the spleen is settled.
Avicenna: the pig's is better. The spleen of the pig is nonetheless of bad chyme. In it is a certain astringency, and it generates melancholic blood, slow to digest because of its astringency.

Pliny, in the passage above: the liver is on the right side, and in what is called the twisted head there is great variety. And in Brylessus and around Tharne, and in the Chersonese near the Propontis, hares have two livers. And, remarkably, if one is transplanted elsewhere, the other dies. In the same is the gall, not given to all animals; in Euboean Chalcis, none in livestock. In Naxos it is very large and doubled, so that, as a kind of portent, visitors go there from both directions. Horses, mules, donkeys, stags, goats, boars, camels, dolphins do not have it; some mice have it; a few men lack it, whose health is firmer and life longer. Some think it is present in the horse not in the liver but in the belly. And in the stag, in the tail, or the intestines. And so it has so much bitterness that dogs will not touch it. It is, moreover, nothing other than the purging of the worst blood. Certainly the liver exists only in blood-having creatures. It receives this from the heart, to which it is joined, pouring it into the veins, but in man black gall is the cause of madness and, when entirely discharged, of death. Hence in behavior, the fault named for bile - so great is the venom in this part when it pours itself into the mind. Indeed, wandering through the whole body, it even takes color from the eyes. This same discharge, even at Athens - and things touched by it turn black, lest anyone marvel that this is the venom of serpents. Those who feed on wormwood in Pontus lack it, but in some it is joined to the intestine only on one side, as in ravens, quails, pheasants. In some, only to the intestine, as in doves, the hawk, moray eels. In few birds, in the chest. In serpents it is proportionally most abundant, and in fish. In most, however, it is throughout the intestine, as in the hawk, the kite; besides this, in the chest, in other birds. In sea-calves too, useful for many things. Bulls' gall is said to be golden in color. They say the little livers of mice, and the beaver, correspond in number to the days of the moon's month, and that as many are found as it has days of light. Further, it increases in midwinter. Rabbits' livers, in Baetica, are often found doubled outside the body. The other lobe of the toad and 'rubeta' frog is not touched by ants, because of its venom, as they suppose. The liver is most tolerant of age, and examples from sieges have shown it can last a hundred years. Providential nature has enclosed all the principal inner organs in their own membranes, like sheaths.

Aristotle: certain blood-having animals have gall; in some it is found over the liver, in some it hangs from the intestine. Since the nature of gall comes from the nature of the lower belly, it is clearly something excess. Nearly all fish have gall. Certain animals, however, have no gall at all, like the horse, mule, and donkey. The camel too has no distinct gall, but small veins in which gall is present. The cuckoo, moreover, has no gall, nor the dolphin. In the same kind, too, in some it is found and in some not, as in man and in the mouse, for some have visible gall over the liver and some do not; the same happens in goats and sheep. It seems to us, however, that gall is like a residue of the body, and like the sediment that gathers in the belly and intestines. And perhaps nature makes some use of excess matter for some benefit. In those, then, whose liver's nature is healthy and whose blood's nature is sweet, either no gall is found, or it is found in very fine veins, or in the belly. In some, for this reason, their liver, lacking gall, is of good color and sweeter than others. When, however, some animal has gall over the liver, the part of the liver beneath the gall is found to be very sweet. If, then, the substance of gall were from excess, it would be contrary to food, since the complexion of excess matter must be contrary to food. And so bitter is contrary to sweet, and blood is sweet, but gall bitter. The cause of gall, then, is not for some purpose, but is an excess, like raw phlegm and the sediment of the belly. And it is impossible for such moistures to come near the heart without killing it at once, since it cannot at all endure such strong disorders. The liver, however, has such excess out of necessity. All kinds of fish and birds, and every egg-laying and four-footed creature, has gall, more or less, and it will perhaps be in fine passages extending from the liver to the intestine, and then those passages are foul-smelling; or it will perhaps be in the upper intestine, or perhaps in the middle, or perhaps in the lower, as happens in the bird kind. For some of these have gall in the belly, some in the intestine, like the dove and the quail, the swallow and the swift, and some in the liver and intestine only, like the hawk and the kite. The stag, however, according to the opinion of many, has gall in the ear. Anaxagoras says that gall is the cause of acute illnesses, but the lack of gall and good color, and the absence of gall, is thought to be the cause of long life.

Avicenna: all gall is hot and dry in the fourth degree, and the strongest galls of four-footed creatures are cow's gall, then the gall of the 'adhubna,' that is the wolf, bear's gall, then goat's, after that sheep's, and the healthiest of bird galls is the cock's. The rest of birds' galls, however, are stronger than the galls of four-footed creatures, when their raptors are compared with grazing birds and their hunters with wild beasts; and indeed gall is strongly viscous, the gall of raptors especially, and of large ones. And of these the one chosen is that whose color is naturally yellow. What is purely red, however, is bad, and weaker than the rest is the pig's. Further, the gall of the fish called the scorpion-fish, and of the tortoise, is stronger than the galls of four-footed creatures. All gall, moreover, is cleansing, and differs according to male and female and according to the condition of thirst and hunger and the condition of satiety and the condition of rest and exercise. Gall mixed with soda and pine gum and Cimolian earth benefits ulcerated scabies. And cow's gall is put into plasters that benefit wounds from erysipelas and violent pains, and goat's gall eradicates bad flesh, and indeed the necessity of ulcers is such that a strong or a weak gall should be applied to them, differing according to their stage and according to their cleanliness or foulness. All gall benefits dimness of sight, and the gall of raptors, especially the dry kind, benefits at the onset of a watery discharge and dilation of the pupil. Nor is it permitted to be administered except after the cleansing of the body and head. Likewise all gall benefits constriction of the nostrils, greatly opening blockages that are in the filtering passages. All gall, too, is loosening, whether applied or used as a suppository; specifically, however, the galls of certain animals are medicinal, like the ox's, the donkey's, the bull's, the cow's, the he-goat's, the goat's, the tortoise's, and the sea-scorpion's.
Dioscorides: [gall] of the scorpion-fish, of the partridge, of the peacock, of the capon, of the roe-deer. Sheep's, goat's, pig's, and bear's, bull's. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny, in the passage above: beneath [the gullet] lies the stomach, for those having a gullet; in others it is simple, in ruminants double, in blood-lacking creatures absent. For in some the intestine, beginning from the mouth, bends back along the same path, as in the cuttlefish and octopus. In man it is attached to the lowest part of the gullet, resembling a dog's stomach; these alone of animals are narrower in their lower part. And so they alone vomit, since, once filled, food is held back because of the narrowness, which cannot happen in those whose spacious width sends it below. Finally, those creatures are more eager for food that have a longer distance from the belly. The same creatures are less clever whose belly is most bulging. In birds, the belly is fleshy and calloused; the stomach and intestines are covered with a fatty membrane, except in egg-laying creatures. Birds too have two pouches: some have one into which fresh food is plunged, and a throat, and another into which they release it from there once it has been digested, as in hens, wood-pigeons, doves, partridges. Nearly all others lack this, but use a wider gullet, like jackdaws, crows, ravens. Some have neither, but have a stomach close by, in those with very long, narrow necks, like the purple gallinule. The stomach of solid-hoofed animals is rough and hard. Among land creatures, in some it has a tooth-like roughness, in others a lattice-like bite. Those that have neither teeth on both sides nor rumination process their food in this way, and it slides down into the belly. This is attached, in all, at the midpoint by the navel. In man that part in its lowest section is similar to a pig's, called by the Greeks the colon, where there is a great cause of pains. It is narrowest in dogs, for which reason they relieve it only with violent strain and not without agony. Insatiable are those animals in which food passes straight from the belly into the straight intestine, like wolves, lynxes, and, among birds, gulls. The elephant too has four stomachs. The rest are similar to pigs'. In the bellies of swallows, the chicks have small white or reddish stones, called swallow-stones, reported by magical arts to be found there. And in the belly of young cows, a ball of blackish stone-like matter, of no weight, is thought, uniquely, a remedy for women having difficult labor, provided it has not touched the ground.

Aristotle: beneath the chest is the belly, reaching to the place of exit of excess matter. For it is the intermediate connector between the member that receives nourishment and that through which it is expelled. And in any animal these three are present. It was not possible, however, for nature to place the belly above the heart, in which is the primary power, nor above the second member, that is, the brain, in which is the operation of intellect. Beside the gullet, then, is the belly in animals having an esophagus. In those lacking one, however, it is placed directly after the mouth, joined to it, and after the belly is the intestine. An animal that generates an animal, having teeth in both jaws, whether it has hooves, like the horse and mule, or a cloven hoof, like the pig, or many toes, like man, the lion, and the dog, has a single stomach. An animal, however, lacking teeth in the upper jaw and having horns, and whose food is of woody, thorny material, has many stomachs. For this reason the camel's stomach too has such an arrangement, although it lacks horns, for it has teeth formed like those of horned animals. And for this reason it ruminates like them, and its stomachs are like theirs, and, since its food is thorny, its tongue was necessarily fleshy, because of the hardness of the palate, for nature indeed uses the palate as the earthy part of the teeth. The first stomach in these animals receives raw food, the second, digested food, the third receives it in better digestion, the fourth, well-digested food, and this animal is called a ruminant, since the mouth of the stomach receives from the mouth's side and proceeds to the side of the lung and passes through the wall, until it reaches the larger stomach, and what is inside that stomach is rough. Then there is another attached to the same, and after the third a fourth, long, shaggy, smooth, and after that the intestine.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: every blood-having, four-footed animal, then, has four stomachs. Properly, however, that part of the body is called the belly which encircles all the inner organs generally in its expanse; this, by its bulk, sometimes exceeds such enormity that it brings death to the one nourishing it. And so all the parts near the belly are small, so as not to hinder the belly's swelling because of the animal's food. Every belly, indeed, receiving moist excess matter also receives dry, but not the reverse. For everything that has a bladder also has a belly, but not conversely, as is evident in birds. In these, however, the belly receives the excess of moist and dry in temperate measure, and expels it through a single exit. Insatiable are the animals in which food passes straight from the belly to the straight intestine, like gulls, wolves, the pelican. The cause of the belly, then, is for the sake of food, that it may be digested. And so the nature of the belly is to animals what earth is to earth-born things: and every ruminant animal has four stomachs. Birds too have, in addition to the stomach, an appendage called the crop, that is, the pouch of the throat. For since birds lack teeth, food, by lingering in the crop, receives the preparation that it would receive by chewing in other animals. For this reason too birds have several flattened, strong stomachs, so that what cannot be chewed may more easily be digested. Fish too, since they do not chew, have appendages to their stomachs, and ruminant animals lack teeth in the upper jaw. Since, then, they cannot chew, they ruminate, and have many stomachs. Man's belly, that is his stomach, resembles a dog's belly, though it is larger. Likewise man's belly, that is his intestine, resembles a pig's belly. Diarrhea in a pig, however, has no remedy.

Avicenna: [the stomach] of a small animal is of poor nourishment and bad chyme and slow digestion. The stomachs of birds, however, when digested, are of better and more abundant nourishment, especially those of hens and geese. It is thought, moreover, that the dried inner lining of animals' stomachs benefits the mouth of the stomach and its pain, especially the stomach-lining of a cock.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: [on] the fetus. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: every animal that generates a live animal, and every egg-laying one, has a navel at the time of birth, and, as the animal grows, the navel becomes hidden. The formation of the navel is nothing but a covering containing veins. For nature draws two large veins from the heart, from which fine veins go out, reaching the womb, and around them is a covering of skin, since they need protection because of their weakness; these veins, indeed, are numerous in large animals, two in medium ones, and one in small ones; from this the embryo receives its blood nourishment. While the embryo is small and unable to take much food, the veins will be wide. But when it has grown, they will diminish and draw together. The growth of any member, then, is by way of the navel, since in animals there is a nourishing power of the soul by which the navel sends food to the womb's attachment points, like the roots of trees, and when the growing embryo can no longer be sufficiently fed this way through the navel, because of its size, then milk is prepared, as has been said above.
Physicus: rennet is the stomach of an animal, so called because it makes milk curdle. It is extracted from the animal before it begins to eat grass, and is salted and preserved.

Aristotle: rennet is found only in the stomach of a ruminant animal still suckling, and of the hare. All animals having a single stomach, then, lack rennet, since they have thin milk, and so it does not curdle. The milk of those having many stomachs, however, curdles, and rennet is found not in the first two stomachs, but in the third, which is before the last. An animal of hairy foot, however, lacks rennet, since it feeds on herbs of much moisture.

Dioscorides: hare's rennet, if fumigated... Taken with wine, three obols' weight, it counters venomous bites, wonderfully benefits celiac and dysentery sufferers. Lamb's, calf's, and goat's rennet all have one power: drunk with wine, they expel poison from the stomach, and dissolve curdled milk. Rennet of the sea-calf has a power similar to castoreum. It benefits epileptics and suffocation of the womb; gather rennet from these animals, then, while they are still too young by nature's brevity to graze.

Avicenna: all rennet is hot and dry and fiery, thinning and drying. It dissolves every congealing of blood and of curdled milk and of thick humor. And it curdles every liquid and cutting thing, and prevents every course and flux of women's blood. Galen says that what is sharp among rennets should not be administered where constriction is needed. All rennet, drunk, benefits epilepsy, especially camel's rennet, which dissolves congealed blood in the lung and stomach. It also dissolves curdled milk in the stomach when drunk with wine, though it is itself harmful to the stomach. After the purging of the menses, if drunk or applied as a suppository, it helps toward conception, and benefits suffocation of the womb, especially camel's. It also benefits ulcers of the intestines, especially the rennet of a foal. All of them, however, benefit against black henbane, especially the rennet of a kid, a fawn of a stag, a calf, and a lamb, and heal against all venoms and bites. Among rennets, however, the best in kind is hare's rennet.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the intestines, according to Isidore, are so called because they are held [cohibentur] within the body's interior part [interiore], and are arranged in long coils in the manner of rings, so that they may gradually digest the food received and not be hindered by further additions of food; these are also called the entrails [viscera].

Aristotle: intestines differ according to the difference in the stomach. For in some animals the intestine is simple, that is, uniform, and, when dissolved, resembles itself throughout its parts. And perhaps the part of the intestine nearest the stomach comes out wider, but that near the end, that is, the anus, narrower, for which reason a dog's excrement comes out with pain. In some animals, however, it is the reverse, and they have much convolution, as in horned animals; and the size of their stomachs is greater, and likewise of the intestine, because of the size of their bodies. For all the bodies of large-horned animals are, because of the moisture required for their food, provided with a colon and a part of the intestine called the caecum. Then the intestine becomes narrower and coiled, and then straight, until it reaches the place of the exit of excess matter. A gluttonous animal, however, does not have much width in the intestine near the lower belly, since excess matter stays there so as not to come out suddenly. Every animal, however, whose intestines are wide vessels and whose intestine is straight, is very gluttonous, since the exit of food happens quickly, and so it desires food quickly again.

Aristotle: the kidneys were created so that the function of the bladder might be better and more complete. Nor does nature use the kidneys except for the exit of excess moisture through the veins. In all kidneys, then, there is depth, and especially in certain animals, because of the abundance of food, and in them there is sediment, from the filtering of moisture within them. For this reason too they are more foul-smelling than other inner members. From the middle of them, indeed, something like excess matter goes out and travels along two strong passages, until it reaches the bladder. In the kidneys are powers befitting their essence, and in them much fat, especially more than in other inner organs, because of the filtering of excess matter, since the blood that remains there after filtering is of good digestion. And the completion of the goodness of the blood's digestion is fat, which, however, is not in the substance of the kidneys, but surrounds them from outside; for the sake of health, however, the kidneys' formation was hot, since, being among the last of the inner members, they need great heat and also much fat for the digestion of moisture, since fat is more suited to digestion, and heat digests. In all animals, moreover, the right kidney has less fat than the left, and is higher than it, so that it reaches the liver, since the nature of members on the right side is lighter and of greater motion. Motion, however, is contrary to the coagulating power of fat, since it dissolves fat. When fat multiplies in sheep's kidneys, they die quickly, for their fat is greater than that of other animals, and their kidneys grow fat quickly. For fat in fat animals is moist. The moisture, then, that is in the kidneys is burned and produces flatulence, from whose pain they quickly die, since the pain, passing through the great vein and the aorta, quickly reaches the heart. For the passages proceeding from these to the kidneys are continuous with each other in succession. And so, when the kidneys' pains increase, they quickly lead to death. Man's kidneys are very hard, more than other members, and resemble a cow's kidneys, as if made of many small kidneys, not of smooth, uniform flesh like the kidneys of sheep and other four-footed animals; for this reason pain in man's kidneys is difficult to cure when they are ill, since the illness is, as it were, in many kidneys.
Pliny: [kidneys] of stags, of men, of the sea-calf. Animals. Of sheep, kidneys, four-footed creatures, animal. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Avicenna: the kidneys of a suckling kid are of equal nature, inclining toward dryness, of little nourishment, difficult digestion, and unpleasant taste; their moisture is bad; the more praiseworthy of them are the kidneys of a suckling kid.

Isaac Judaeus, in the passage above: kidneys are unpraiseworthy in two ways: one, because of the corruption of their substance, hardness and thickness; the other, because their nourishment was the fat of urine, whence they generate thick and very bad blood.

Aristotle: since, moreover, the function of the kidneys and bladder is one, we must also know its nature, and it seems, indeed, that nature gave it only to animals having a blood-filled lung. For any animal having a lung thirsts much, and so needs food that is not only dry, but moist rather than dry: it is necessary, then, that it have a member to receive this excess, and this is the bladder. An animal, however, lacking a lung and drinking little water lacks a bladder; for it does not take in water as drink, but as food, like a ringed-bodied animal and a fish. An animal having feathers or scales or a shell also has no bladder, because of the scarcity of drinking and since the excess of water passes into feathers and the like, except the tortoise, since the tortoise's lung is very fleshy and blood-filled, similar to a cow's lung. In those lacking a bladder, however, the flesh extending to the kidneys is separated into parts, whose formation is similar to the formation of the kidneys in certain birds. Serpents and lizards, then, do not have a bladder, since their moisture is small, as in birds, and passes into scales.

Pliny: [on] the tortoise, wolves, of men, the belly, bladder, lung, of the feet, arteries, flanks, the stone called syrtites, calculi, the fineness of bristles, membrane. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the hips [coxae], according to Isidore, are so called as if 'joined axles' [coniuncti axes], for by them the thighs move. Their hollow parts are called the sockets [vertebra], since the heads of the thighs turn [vertuntur] in them.

Aristotle: slenderness and weakness of the legs suits mating, since food passing there turns into seminal excess. Men too who have much hair at the hips and on the lower parts of the feet mate much. Man's hips and legs are very fleshy, since man's body is upright; so that there may be an inclination of the body and a path toward the upper part, nature removed flesh from that part and added it to the lower, for the weight of the body and so that the body might be upright. In animals, however, the hips and legs are deprived of flesh and are made of bones and sinews for carrying the body. The four feet, moreover, are four supports, for which reason a four-footed animal is born able to stand without effort. Man, however, cannot remain upright for a long time, but the body needs rest. The other animals have breasts near the hips, but man on the chest. The feet of animals, that is, the larger ones from the hip to the joints, have little flesh, except in man, who has two feet. In the others, however, nature placed front feet in place of hands, for these needed four feet, so as to be able to bear the weight of so great a body. And a certain animal having many toes on its feet uses the front ones as man uses his hands, since it fights with them and drives harm from itself. An animal having hooves, however, does this with the hind ones, since the front ones are not suited for this; for this reason many-toed animals like the lion, lynx, dog, wolf, have five toes in front and four behind. Some animals, however, have five behind, since they move as if crawling, and for this reason are supported on many claws, and their movement becomes swifter and lighter, so that their sides are raised from the ground and thus the head too is raised. The feet of animals, moreover, are paired. In all footless animals, and those having two or four feet, there is blood. Those, however, having more, lack blood. In the feet of four-footed creatures, indeed, there is variety, since some have only hooves. And some have paws. Some, however, have cloven feet. Hooves are in animals of large body.
