For the earthy part that passes into them becomes hooves in place of horns and teeth, and hooves are like a single claw in place of many claws; for this reason such animals do not, for the most part, have a hock in their feet, and so the movement of bending in their hind feet is difficult. Those having paws, however, have a hock in their feet, and so their feet are of lighter movement, nor do they have hooves. An animal having many toes, however, does not have a hock. For if it had one, it would not have many toes. Paws, then, occur in the majority of hock-having feet.

Aristotle: the camel has much fleshiness, and in the cleft of its foot is a skin like that in the feet of geese. And so, when they must travel much, they develop paws. The lion and camel, when they walk, move the right foot first. The left foot in animals is not of quick movement, except in the elephant. The elephant's front feet are much larger than the hind. For it sits by bending two feet, and sleeps propped on one side. For it cannot bend all four. Four-footed creatures, once born, at once raise themselves on their feet and walk. A foal touches its head with its hind foot, but a full-grown horse cannot. A bird, properly, has only two feet, since it has two wings in place of front feet. The ostrich has two feet, like a bird, but a cloven hoof, like four-footed creatures. The ape's hand is composed of both hand and foot. Man, properly, has very large feet in proportion to his body, since the feet that carry the body must have size and breadth and toes. The size of the toes of the feet, moreover, is the reverse of the size of the fingers of the hands. For the function of the hands is to grasp and hold, and so the fingers of the hands are longer. The function of the feet, however, is for fleeing and for carrying weight, and so they are of strong formation. Further, the division at the end of the feet is better, for if there were no division of the toes, the loss of the whole member would often result; for this reason too there are claws at the ends of the fingers of the hands and feet, for protection.

Aristotle: among land creatures, man alone is two-footed. His hands are fleshy inside, but made of sinews and skin outside; the fingers have three joints, the thumb two, and it bends opposite all the fingers, but is by itself extended obliquely and is thicker than the rest; the little finger is equal in length to it, and the other two to each other, between which the middle one extends the longest. Four-footed creatures that live by hunting have five toes on their front feet, four on the rest. Lions, wolves, dogs, and a few others also have five claws on the hind feet, one hanging near the leg-joint. The rest, which are smaller, have five toes. Not all have equal forelegs. Certain animals, as if using their front feet as hands, sit and bring food to their mouths with them, like squirrels. All of these have claws where they have toes. But the ape's are scaled. In men, however, the nails are flat; in birds of prey, hooked; in others, straight. All that have feet have toes, except the elephant, for in it they are shapeless, five in number indeed, but undivided and slightly distinct, resembling hooves rather than claws, and the front feet are larger. In the hind feet the joints are short. It bends its hocks inward, in the manner of man; the other animals do the reverse, and the hind feet have more joints than the front. For those that generate a live animal bend their knees forward, and their hock-joints backward; man's knees and elbows are opposite. Likewise for bears and the ape kind, for this reason least swift. Among egg-laying four-footed creatures, the crocodile: lizards bend their front knees backward, their hind ones forward, and their legs are angled like a human thumb; so too are many-footed creatures, except the last-jointed leapers. Birds and four-footed creatures bend their wings forward, their hocks backward. Man's knees have a certain religious quality observed among peoples: at these, suppliants touch, to these they stretch their hands, these they worship as altars, perhaps because vitality resides there. For in the very knee, at the joint on either side, right and left, from the front, there is a certain double hollow of the cheek-like parts, through which, once pierced, the spirit escapes as if through bonds. Varicose veins occur in the legs of men alone, rarely in women. All animals set out walking from the right side and lie down on the left; the rest walk as they please. The lion and camel, however, walk foot by foot, that is, so that the left foot does not cross the right, but follows it. Man's feet are largest; women's, more slender. In every kind, only man has fleshy calves and legs. Four-footed creatures have solid hooves, which are not horned. In place of these, then, the hoof is their weapon.

Avicenna: feet generate a viscous humor, not thick, but praiseworthy and of few excesses. A sign of their good digestion is the speed of their swelling and their dissolving in cooking. But their nourishment is not abundant. They benefit hot coughs, especially with barley gruel; they dissolve with their own viscosity.

Isaac Judaeus: feet are medicinally useful, for they soothe roughness of the chest and lung and are effective against a dry cough. They also help those suffering discoloration in the bladder, and, if eaten by those suffering dysentery, the wounds of the intestines are closed and looseness is accidentally checked. For their nature is lubricating, because of the viscosity they have. The front feet, however, are better than the hind, because of the proximity of their base to natural heat. But among all the extremities of animals, the feet are best.

Aristotle: every animal having toes has claws. Claws, as has been said, are at the ends of the toes of the hands and feet for protection, that is, so that the loss of the whole member does not occur; men's claws, however, are not hooked as others' are, but cover the tips. Every animal having curved claws feeds on flesh; birds of poor flight have a straight claw, for curved ones would hinder their gait.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of the hook-clawed birds, mention has already been made above.

div.head: DE MEMBRIS GENITALIBUS ET PRIMO DE TESTICULIS

cit.quote: Aristotle: the arrangement of the testicles differs among blood-having animals; for some males lack testicles entirely, like the fish kind and serpents. Nor do they have anything but two passages in which only seed is present, while others have testicles inside the body near the kidneys, and from these two passages go out to the exit of the seed, which unite in one place. Such passages, indeed, are found in all egg-laying, air-breathing, lung-having animals, like the tortoise and lizards, and in all kinds of scaled hide, but certain animals have hanging testicles, like man, and some near the anus, like the pig. And just as any animal with a straight intestine is gluttonous in food, so any animal having seminal passages and lacking testicles mates quickly, and what is contrary to this arrangement is more chaste, just as an animal of coiled intestine is less gluttonous. The nature of the testicles is of the nature of bone, so that they are vessels of this excess. And when they are cut off, the passages contract upward. And so a castrated animal cannot produce offspring, since the passages are not fixed along their proper path. Animals, however, that lack testicles, not for the better but only from necessity, are of swift mating, like the fish kind and serpents. For fish mate when one touches another and eject seed swiftly; and just as it happens to men and other kinds that they hold their breath before emitting seed, so it happens to fish that they do not then take in seawater, and when they do, they quickly perish. Fish, however, have passages like men's, since the seed is in the last part of the female. Serpents are entwined in mating, since they lack testicles and even a member, since they have no legs. They lack testicles, moreover, because of the length of their body, since the seed would grow cold because of the slowness of its exit.

Aristotle: the member of males suited to mating, that is, the organ, grows and shrinks, among all other members, without any injury to the subject. For its substance is such that growth and diminishment can suit it; for its formation, indeed, is from sinew and cartilage, and it stretches by the wind that comes to it, and its growth, indeed, suits mating, but its diminishment, other functions. Certain females of four-footed creatures urinate backward, like the elephant, the lion, the camel, and hairy animals. But an animal having hooves and urinating backward cannot exist. Wombs in all animals have two parts, just as the males' testicles are divided into two. Wombs, moreover, differ greatly, since animals that generate a live animal have wombs within, above the belly, like the cow, goat, dog, and the like, since there ought to be no weight at all upon the womb, for health's sake and for growth. In animals producing incomplete eggs, however, as in all egg-laying fish, the womb is below the belly and below the location of the kidneys, since the growth of the eggs does not hinder any function of nature, because they are completed outside. Fish, indeed, lay incomplete eggs outside, and they grow there. The reason for this is that they have many eggs, and nature cannot complete them inside because of their number. In woman the womb is below.

Aristotle: an animal's tail is for the protection of the member from which excess matter exits. And so nature placed it over that member. Man, indeed, has no tail, but hips, nor does any four-footed animal have hips, but a tail, since man's hips and legs are very fleshy. In the other animals, however, they are deprived of flesh and are of bones and sinews, and the cause of nearly all of these is one and the same, namely that man is of upright body, as said above in the chapter on the hips; for this reason man has no tail, since his food passes into the flesh of the hips and legs; he has hips, then, and lacks a tail. A four-footed animal, however, is the reverse, since the abundance of flesh is in the upper part, for which reason it has no hips and has a tail. A four-footed animal, however, is the reverse, and so also has very thick legs, unlike man. For the food that would pass into the hips passes into the tail. The ape too, since its form is common between the form of man and of a four-footed creature, has no hips. In tails there is much difference, nor does nature use them only for protecting the anus, but for benefit. Every animal having a hairy tail has a small head and large jaws: sheep in Paeonia have a large tail, so wide it measures a cubit. The scorpion has two stings in its tail. There is, moreover, a fish of the oyster kind, which swims and crawls by its tail.

Pliny: [tails] of goats and boars, small and shaggy, as in bears, drooping and very long, as in horses; cut off, they grow back in lizards and serpents. In fish, they steer their course like a rudder. And, moved right and left, they propel them as if by a kind of oar.
Aristotle: some think the stag has gall in its tail or intestines. For this reason it has such bitterness that dogs will not touch it.
Avicenna: [on the stag]: the tip of a stag's tail is poison, and one who drinks of it suffers violent distress and fainting and death.
Isidore: it is certain that the moray eel has life in its tail. For, struck on the head, it is scarcely killed, but on the tail, it dies at once.

div.head: DE TEGUMENTIS ANIMALIUM ET PRIMO DE PILIS

cit.quote: Pliny, in the passage above: animals that give birth to live young have hair. Those that lay eggs have feathers, or scales, or a shell, like tortoises, or bare skin, like serpents. The feather-shafts of all birds do not grow once cut, but grow back if plucked. Insects fly with fragile membranes, swallows with moist ones over the sea. The bat with dry ones among rooftops; the wings of these too have joints. Hairs come out from thick skin, shaggy; in females, finer. Abundant in the mane of horses. On the shoulders of the lion. On the cheeks inside and on the feet of the hare, as both Trogus and history report also of the hare; the hare is the most hairy of animals. Man alone reaches puberty with hair, and unless this happens, he is sterile in generating, whether male or female. Hairs in man are born partly at once, partly later. Those born together with him do not cease, nor do women's hairs greatly. Some, however, are found weakened by loss of head-hair, as if more languid when the flow of the menses has stopped. In some, hairs are born afterward. In men they are not born by choice. In four-footed creatures, hair shedding and regrowth are annual. In men they grow especially on the head, then on the beard. Cut, they do not increase as grass and other cut things do, but grow out from the root, and grow with certain illnesses especially, coughing, and in old age, even on the bodies of the dead; hair in the lustful sheds more quickly once matured, but, once fallen, grows back faster. Four-footed creatures thicken with age and their wool grows sparser. The backs of four-footed creatures are hairy, and the bellies smooth.

Aristotle: man alone is smooth-bodied; yet no animal has as much hair on the head as man, since his brain, in proportion to his body, is more moist than that of other animals. His head, too, has little flesh and many sutures, and so needs the protection of hair. Likewise man has hair at the pubic area, while in other animals those parts are bare. Men with much hair at the hips and on part of the feet mate much. The prepubescent, if castrated, do not grow a beard. The bearded, however, if castrated, become beardless. In other places too hairs grow sparse, except at the pubic area. For women too have hair there. Women's bodies, however, are softer and smoother and have less hair than men's bodies. Nakedness of hair, especially on the chest, is a sign of natural coldness. Hairs do not return to the bald. The cause of the lack of baldness in other animals, less than in man, is that their brain is little moist, and so heat is not weakened in its cooking there. For in man baldness occurs because of the diminishing of hot, fatty moisture.

Haly Abbas, in the passage above: hairs, indeed, are medicinal; burnt wool is drying, sharp, and fine, and dissolves flesh that is diseased in ulcers. So too burnt hair, if applied, benefits the site of a fire's burn. Burnt sackcloth too, powdered over the anus, restores it to its place. All burnt hairs, ground with vinegar, if applied to a rabid dog's bite, benefit it excellently. Wool or hair should be burnt this way: an earthenware vessel is filled with it and covered with a pierced lid, and thus set on the fire.

Aristotle: hairs differ according to hardness and softness, length and shortness, smoothness and roughness, abundance and scarcity, and according to colors and ages, especially in men. The cause of the difference in hairs is from the side of the skin, for hairs are not generated from the body, but from the skin, when the moisture that is in it is dissolved and becomes vapor. For this reason thick hairs are generated from thick skin, and fine ones from fine. And when the skin is porous and dense, the hairs will also be thick, because of the abundance of the earthy part and the breadth of the passages. When, however, it is very continuous, they will be fine and thin, because of the narrowness of the passages. Likewise, when the moisture that is in the skin is watery and of swift dryness, the hairs will not be large or long. When, however, the moisture is thick and fatty, the opposite will happen. For what is fatty does not dry quickly. For this reason, then, an animal of thick skin will have thick hairs, just as pigs' bristles are thicker than cows' hairs. And so the length of the hair of man's head is because his skin is very fatty and has much moisture in it. Curliness and smoothness, however, occur because of vapor. When the vapor is smoky, hot, and dry, hairs become curly, since they travel along two contrary paths. For the earthy part goes to the lower part, but heat to the upper, and thus the hairs curl and become curly because of their own weakness. We can also say that this happens because of the scarcity of the hair's moisture and the abundance of the earthy part, which dries out from the surrounding air and shrivels and thus becomes curly, for this happens to smooth hair too, when the moisture that is in it is dissolved, as happens to hair from fire, when it shrivels and curls. And a sign of this is that curly hairs are moister than smooth ones. For what is dry is hard. Smooth hairs, however, do not occur in animals except from an abundance of moisture. For moisture flows down smoothly until it reaches the hairs, for which reason the hair of those dwelling in Thrace is smooth, since their complexion is moist. And the surrounding air is moist. Ethiopians, however, are curly-haired because of the dryness of the brain and of the surrounding air.

Aristotle: certain animals are of thick skin but fine hair because of the narrowness of the passages. Such is the arrangement of sheep's wool, and certain animals have soft hair, not very fine, like the hair of hares. For it is in the surface of the skin and so does not have length. And what happens to it is like what happens to something made of flax, since it is soft and has no length. Sheep, however, that dwell in a highland region have hard hair, since cold hardens by congealing and dries, and when heat is pressed out, moisture dissolves with it and the hairs of the skin become earthy and dry. Whence too hedgehogs, whose dwelling is by the Phrygian sea, have many hard spines, though they are of small body. And the size of the spines comes from this, that the growth of the body passes into them because of the scarcity of natural heat. For since food is not digested, much excess matter is generated in their bodies. Hair and the like, however, are generated only from excess. The hardness of the spines, and their being like stone, is because of the abundance of congealed cold. For this reason it happens that growing hairs become very hard and stony, especially in the northern region, since there such hedgehogs are more numerous than in the southern, and in windy regions more than in flat ones, since they grow colder in such places and moisture goes out from them, which dissolves with heat, since moisture cannot be nourishing without heat. Cold, however, does not only harden, but also thickens and condenses the body; heat, however, rarefies. For this reason too, when haired animals grow old, their hairs harden more than before. But the plumage of birds and the shell or skin of animals also become thicker and harder in old age, because of the diminishing of heat and the passing of moisture along with animal heat. Men properly become bald, though not all, and the rest, as will be said below in the treatise on man.

div.head: DE COLORIBUS PILORUM ET MUTATIONE EORUM

cit.quote: Aristotle: the color of hair and fur in animals follows the color of the skin, but not in man. For some have very white skin and very black hair: the cause of this is that man's skin is much finer, in proportion to his body, than that of other animals, and so cannot change its hair, but the color of the skin can be altered to blackness by sun and winds. In other animals, however, the skin has a power like that of earth, because of its thickness, and so the hairs change with the change of the skin. The color of hair, however, does not vary in man, except for the whiteness that comes to it, not only in old age, which happens naturally without whitening of the skin, but sometimes from illness, and then it whitens together with the whiteness of the skin, since that illness is in the skin, and so, when the skin whitens, the hair necessarily whitens too. Natural greying, however, is because of the weakness of the heat that leaves the body and the abundance of cold. For old age chills and dries the body, and the vapor or earthy food that is in the hairs, when it is not well digested, putrefies from the heat of the surrounding air, and from that greying is generated. For all putrefaction is from heat that is not natural but accidental, and this happens to water and earth, to all bodies and the like. The cause of whiteness in the bald, however, is that in every earthy vapor there is a power of thick air, and if the vapor congeals, ice or greyness results from it; but if it putrefies, wrinkling results, for which reason both these effects, namely wrinkling and greying, will be visible on the body. In illnesses, however, greying occurs, since color is weakened in the digestion of food. For food reaches any member of the body and is digested by the natural heat that is in it. When, then, that heat is weakened, the food is corrupted, and then the member suffers loss or illness, and hence the hair greys. When, then, health returns, the power returns, and the hairs blacken. Whence such illness may rightly be called accidental old age, but old age itself is natural illness. The hairs at the temples grey first, since the back of the head is empty of moisture, since the brain is not there. In the front part of the head, however, there is much moisture, and it does not putrefy quickly. The temples, however, are between these two states, since there is not so little moisture there that it digests, nor so much that it does not putrefy, and so their hairs whiten before others. The cause of the absence of greying in other animals is according to the cause of baldness that we have mentioned, since their brain is only slightly moist, and so heat is not weakened in its cooking. Among other animals, horses grey, because of the thinness of the bones of the head. Whence a blow that falls on those bones is fatal, and especially one that falls on the temples. Red hairs whiten sooner than black, since redness and whiteness are, as it were, illnesses accidental to hairs, and everything among animals that is weakened greys quickly. Some, moreover, imagine that cranes, when they grow old, turn black; the cause of this change is that the nature of their plumage is indeed white, and when they grow old, moisture multiplies in their plumage and quickly putrefies. A sign, indeed, that greying is a kind of putrefaction, and not dryness, as some say, is that covered hairs grey quickly. For the covering prevents wind or exposure, but exposure to air expels putrefaction; and perhaps the hairs will come out white at the root and black at the tip. Or perhaps their tips whiten, since there is little heat there. White hairs in the bodies of other animals besides man occur naturally, and not from illness.

div.head: DE CAUSIS DIVERSITATIS COLORUM IN PILIS

cit.quote: Aristotle: [on] the peacock and the lion, since the color of all lions is one. Sometimes, however, not throughout the whole kind, but some are of different colors, as happens with goats, cows, and doves. And animals of many colors indeed change according to colors, having more than one color, since the mixed color comes from both, and this is throughout the whole kind, since, indeed, it is in their nature not to receive only one color, but various ones, since nature is quick in motion in transferring them, that is, into others. The kind of animals of a single color, however, is the opposite, since they do not change color except because of illness, and this rarely. For a white partridge has already appeared, and a white hawk and sparrows and a white raven, but this does not happen from the time of birth. The change, indeed, of animals that are naturally of many colors often happens because of the difference of waters, for hot waters make hairs white and cold ones black, as also happens with kinds of trees. And the cause of this is that in hot waters there is more spirit than water, and when the water is clarified, whiteness results from it, as happens with foam. In the Atander region there are two rivers, one of which makes lambs' colors black, the other white. The river called Aschamida, however, makes them red. The colors of hairs, then, differ because of illnesses and according to ages and according to nature. And whiteness, indeed, sometimes comes from natural heat, sometimes from accidental heat. For it comes from vaporous heat retained in all the members. And so the heat of that part which is under an animal's belly, not attributed to a single color, is whiter than another's, because of the abundance of heat in that place. Its flesh, too, is more flavorful, for the same reason. For digestion, which comes only from heat, makes flesh flavorful. And this too is the cause of an animal attributed to a single color, namely white or black. For heat and cold are the cause of the nature of skin and hairs. For in any member heat is proper to it. Likewise certain kinds of wild birds and four-footed creatures change colors according to the changes of the seasons, just as change according to ages happens to men. For the difference of the seasons is stronger than the difference of ages. Likewise animals eating many kinds of food are, for the most part, of varied color, for this reason the color of bees is one. But the color of red and yellow wasps is varied. For rightly, different excesses are generated from different food, and from these excesses skin and hairs, shell and plumage are generated.

Aristotle: the skin is fine in certain animals, and thick in certain others; hard in some, and dense in others. The cause of this difference is the difference of humors, for the humor is sometimes watery, sometimes thick. And the humor that is on the surface of the body, when it is dissolved into vapor, becomes hard and membranous as residue. From the skin, moreover, hairs are generated, when the moisture that is in it is dissolved and becomes vapor; for this reason thick hairs are generated from thick skin, fine ones from fine, as has already been said above. Yet certain animals are of thick skin but fine hair, because of the narrowness of the passages, or their fineness, which is necessarily followed by fineness of hair. And so sheep's hairs are of this arrangement. Cold, however, as has been said, not only hardens the body, but also thickens it, while heat rarefies it. For this reason the skin of animals is thicker and harder in old age, because of the diminishing of color and the passing of moisture with heat. Likewise in animals the color of hairs follows the color of the skin. In man, however, not for the reason stated above; man alone receives the sensation of heat's tickling, since his skin is very fine. In the bodies of the old, however, the skin is wrinkled. Boars harden their hides by constant rubbing against trees, when they wish to fight. Some fish and serpents have smooth skin, some scaled, some rough, some spiny. The serpent, however, casts off old age by shedding its skin. There is a bird that does not brood its eggs, but wraps them in the skin of a hare or fox, until they hatch. Birds' eyelids are membranous, and so are the wings of bats. In swimming birds nature placed skin between the toes, but not in the rest. The camel too has similar skin in the cleft of its feet.

Pliny, book 11: glue is boiled from ox-hides, and from bulls' foreskins. Some think that fineness of mind depends not on thinness of blood, but on the skin. And that the coverings of bodies make creatures more or less dull, as oysters, tortoises, the hides of oxen, the bristles of pigs, obstruct the fineness of innate spirit, and that a pure and clear spirit is not transmitted. So too in man, when the skin is thicker or more calloused, it shuts it out. What reasoning, then, could explain crocodiles, if this is attributed not to blood but to the hardness of the hide, and their cunning? The thickness of the hippopotamus's hide is such that spear-shafts are turned from it. Elephants' hides too have impenetrable shoulders, although the fineness of all four-footed creatures is said to be especially attributed to them. The skin itself, then, lacks sensation, especially on the head; wherever it is wounded by itself, without flesh, it does not heal together, as on the cheek and eyelid.

Avicenna: the skins or hides of suckling animals are better, because of their moisture. Their nourishment is pure and viscous, close to the nourishment of feet. There are, moreover, medicinal skins of animals - sheep's, goat's, serpent's, mule's, and the like, and bird's skin: the inner skin of the neck is hot and dry in the first degree. In it is a gluing and drying power; it is applied to a scab and benefits burning of the bladder. Burnt and washed, however, it is effective for treating nits.
Rhazes, in the Almansor: glue from old hides benefits facial pustules, which occur with hardness and redness of the skin. It also helps beginning hemorrhoids and those coughing blood.
Dioscorides: old hide, burnt, ground, and applied as a poultice, is effective for burns and cramps. Likewise soles of old footwear, burnt, heal open wounds. For their ash is drying.

Aristotle: flesh is the instrument of touch and the primary organ of this sense, just as the pupil is of the sense of sight. It is necessary, however, that this sense be in the body and in a bodily instrument, more than the instruments of the other senses. For it is evident that all animals are created only for the sake of this sense. Likewise flesh is the first member and is, by itself, the animal's body. And all the other members, I mean the bones, sinews, skin, claws, hairs, and the rest, exist for the health of the soft body, that is, the flesh. Man's flesh, more than other animals', has fleshy hips, since his body is upright, and so the hips that support it must have size and breadth. In other animals, however, they are deprived of flesh.

Isidore, book 20: flesh [carnes] is so named because it is dear [cara], or from creating [creando], whence it is called 'creas' by the Greeks; this was granted to men for use after the Flood, whereas before that only fruit-bearing wood and seed-producing plants had been given for food.

Avicenna: flesh is a food that strengthens the body, and its conversion into blood is closer than other foods. Roasted or cooked in a pan, it is of drier nourishment. Boiled, however, of moister nourishment. Fat and grease, however, are of poor and scanty nourishment, and lighten food, nor is anything suitable in them except a small quantity, according to the measure that pleases. Fatty flesh, indeed, loosens the belly, with the scarcity of its nourishment and the speed of its conversion into smokiness and bile, and is quickly digested. Salted flesh, however, although moist at first, has a more vehement drying than all other flesh, and its nourishment is scanty. Better and more nourishing, however, is the flesh that is around the bone, and the right side is better and lighter than the left, and that in the middle of the muscles is cleaner than the flesh of the sinews. Loose flesh, over which there is no sinew, is perhaps pleasant, and especially that which exists for the generation of milk, like the flesh of the breasts, or of saliva, like the flesh of the root of the tongue. Less good, however, is that which was created to be a support, like that which is woven within the veins of the liver, and the flesh of the heart and its root. The breast, indeed, is good nourishment, but if it contains milk, it is thick. The testicles' flesh is better than others. The flesh of the flanks and buttocks is bad in digestion and nourishment, hotter and thicker than fat. But of every animal of dry complexion, the flesh of a small one, that is a young one, is better, like the kid; for this is good, but goat's flesh is not very good. He-goat's flesh, however, is absolutely bad. The flesh of a suckling animal is good if from praiseworthy milk, bad if not. One should also consider the conditions of animals, both in age and in the place of their pasture, their exercise, and other such matters.

div.head: DE DIFFERENTIA CARNIUM IN CIBO ET MEDICINA

cit.quote: Isaac Judaeus, in the Diets, book 1: certain animals' flesh nourishes human nature, being close to its complexion, like pig's, lamb's, kid's. Others, however, are deadly and repellent, either from excessive heat, like snake's and serpents' and the like, or great cold, like scorpions' and spiders'. Others, however, are intermediate, that is, neither similar nor contrary, but nevertheless repugnant and so harmful, like hedgehog, fox, hares and the like, whose nourishment is either foul-smelling - those far from human complexions are the worst, though not deadly. This is shown by the heaviness of the smell of their flesh and the nearness of its stench. Whence Galen: of animals whose flesh is heavy, some differ, and some, not similarly, are closer to human natures. Nourishing animals, however, are divided into two: wild and domestic.

The same, in book 3: wild animals are hotter and drier, or more indigestible, and generate unpraiseworthy nourishment because of the abundance of their movement and labor and because of the heat and dryness of the air they inhabit. They are, then, not of good nourishment, except wild goats alone. For, by the excess of their swift movement and the labor they are accustomed to, their natural coldness is tempered. And by their excessive exercise, the heaviness of their flesh's taste and smell is lessened. Help is also given to the digestive power, so that the flesh is digested most easily and excellently. The other domestic animals, however, compared to wild ones, have more tempered heat and dryness, because of their stillness and the temperateness of the air, and accordingly are more nourishing and praiseworthy, though thicker and harder to digest. Again, animals are divided into male, female, and castrated. Males are hotter than females and of less moisture; they are also more praiseworthy and easier to digest. Females, however, have less heat and greater moisture, and so are slower to digest. Castrated animals, however, though close to females because of moisture, differ in heat, since their heat is midway between the two sexes, namely greater than the females' and less than the males'; and so they are more digestible than females.

Isaac Judaeus: [on] male and female animals, whether suckling, decrepit, or in the perfection of youth. The suckling animal is naturally hot and moist, having more tender flesh than all the rest because of the blood naturally predominating in its complexion. But certain animals are, in their own kind, moist, like pigs and sheep; their suckling young, then, necessarily have moisture from two sources, namely age and complexion. Whence what is generated from them is viscous, difficult to digest, though it descends easily from the stomach, but is not easily dissolved by the members, generating viscous phlegm, especially if they are not from male animals. But if the animals are, in their own kind, dry, like cattle and goats, the dryness of their complexion is tempered by the moisture of their age. Whence they are lighter and suited to digestion, especially if male. And so the suckling young of goats and cattle are more praiseworthy than those of pigs and sheep, though all of these need some praise. Animals remaining in youth, however, are hotter than suckling ones. Their flesh, too, is drier, given the distance from their birth. Whence, if they are also naturally dry, like oxen and goats, they have dryness from two sources, namely age and complexion. They are, then, hard and more indigestible, slow to dissolve, and give unpraiseworthy nourishment: but if they are, in their kind, moist, like sheep and pigs, their natural moisture is balanced against the dryness of their age. And so young pigs and sheep are better than young oxen and goats. Yearling animals, however, are midway between the moisture of sucklings and the dryness of the young, and so are more praiseworthy, since tempered. Better still, however, are those animals that are naturally hot, since their heat aids their digestion, whence they give more praiseworthy nourishment; for this reason pig and cattle flesh become better than the rest, since their natural heat is more vehement and predominant. Decrepit animals, moreover, are drier and harder, since their natural heat is most deficient, and their moisture is coming to its end, and since their digestive power is deficient, they have an accidentally acquired moisture, raw and unnatural. And so they are difficult to digest and slow to dissolve. For they generate unpraiseworthy chyme, being viscous phlegm. Yet if they are naturally hot, they are less harmful. And, conversely, if they are, they cause the worst injury. Sheep are hotter than oxen, goats, and pigs, and moister too than oxen and goats, though less moist than pigs. For pig's flesh is colder and moister than that of other animals, especially domestic pig.

Isaac Judaeus, in the same, book 3: the extremities of animals, since they lack all fat, are slow to digest, for they are of the substance of skin and sinews. But since they are in motion and labor, they are more digestible than sinewy, immobile members. Their nourishment, however, is small: feet are medicinally useful, for they soothe the roughness of the chest and lung, and are effective against a dry cough. They also help those suffering discoloration in the bladder. For those suffering dysentery, if they eat them, the wounds of the intestines are closed and looseness is accidentally checked. For their nature is lubricating, because of the viscosity they have. The front feet, however, are better than the hind, because of the proximity of their base to natural heat. Lips are more praiseworthy than ears, since ears are composed of skin and cartilage. Cartilage, however, if from young animals and well cooked, will be indigestible. But if from a suckling animal and well cooked, it will be digestible; but among all the extremities of animals, the feet are best. Nostrils are cold and dry. For they are cartilaginous. And so they are difficult to digest and produce little nourishment. The tongue, between the muscles and tender flesh, is of medium quality. And so, eaten alone, it gives soft and moderate nourishment. Aristotle says, in the book On Animals, that the brain is naturally hot and accidentally cold. Accordingly it is moist and thick and viscous, loathsome; it corrupts appetite in the stomach and quickly turns to putrefaction. The heart is of hard substance, slowly expelled from the stomach. But yet, when well digested, it gives much good nourishment to the body. The lung is easily digested and quickly expelled from the stomach, because of the lightness and looseness of its substance. Accordingly it generates less nourishment than other members, and belongs to the phlegmatic humor. The liver is thicker than all others and harder to digest, yet generates praiseworthy blood. It is also more nourishing than fatty flesh. But the liver of a suckling animal is better than the rest. That of a hen, however, is better than that of suckling animals. Kidneys are unpraiseworthy in two ways. In one way, because of the corruption of their substance, hardness and thickness. In another way, because their nourishment was the fat of urine, whence they generate thick and very bad blood.

Pliny: [sinews], arising from the heart and wrapped around the whole body, have a similar nature and function everywhere, joined to slippery bones and to the joints of bodies called articulations. In some places by intervention, in others by encircling, in others by passing through, binding, here rounded, there flat, as the shape of each part requires; nor do these heal once cut, and, remarkably, when wounded the pain is greatest, but once fully severed, none at all. Some animals are without sinews, like fish. For they consist of arteries. But not even these are present in the soft kind of fish: where sinews are, the inner ones draw the limbs together, the outer ones pull them back.

Aristotle: the strength of all animals lies only in the sinew, for this reason young animals are stronger than children, since children's sinews and joints are not yet strong, likewise nor are the old's, because of the weakness of the sinews too. The voices of castrated animals, likewise, are similar to the voices of females. Veins, indeed, rejoin after being cut, but not sinews. Cartilage and flesh are of the same nature, and differ only in degree, more or less, and when a bone or cartilage is cut, it does not grow back. In a walking animal there is cartilage without marrow, for if there were distinct marrow, it would become soft, like mucilage. For indeed the vertebra of a certain fish called the 'celetus' is cartilaginous, and in it is marrow, since, because of its moisture, its support must be soft, not dry. The earthy part of that animal, however, passed into hide. In an animal that generates a live animal, there are many bones similar to cartilage in certain places, like the ears and nose.
Isaac Judaeus: cartilage, if from young animals and well cooked, will be indigestible. But if from a suckling animal and well cooked, it will be digestible.

Pliny: sea-calves have cartilage, not bones. Likewise the joints and nostrils of all animals, wherever they slightly protrude, are of flexible softness, by nature's providence, lest they break. Broken cartilage does not heal, nor do cut bones grow back, except in beasts of burden, from the hoof to the pastern.
Isidore: bones are the body's solid foundations. In these consists all its stability and strength, and everywhere they are hidden, covered by skin and inner organs.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: bones are the hardest and most solid part of the body, white on the outside, filled with marrow within, and, once broken, cannot be reunited.

Aristotle: the creation of bones was for the sake of flesh. For those who wish to fashion an animal out of mud place something else, hard, beneath it, then build the mud around it; nature did the same with bones. Bones, then, were placed beneath the fleshy parts. In members that move, for the sake of firmness. In members that do not move, for protection, like the rib containing the chest. For the rib was created only for the safety of what encloses the heart. Bones near the belly, however, are small, so as not to hinder the belly's swelling because of the animal's food and because of the pregnancy that occurs in females. The bones, indeed, of an animal that generates a live animal are of the same arrangement, inside and out, in hardness and strength. And they are much larger than the bones of an animal that does not generate a live animal, in proportion to its body. A large animal needs a large, strong, and hard support, especially if it is a strong animal living by hunting. The bones of males, too, are stronger than the bones of females, and especially when the animal is of the flesh-eating kind, like the lion, whose bones are very hard. Whence, if struck together, fire will come out of them, as from stones, nor is there marrow in them, except in the hip-bone and its socket, that is, from the shoulder to the elbow. In blood-having animals that do not generate another live animal, however, nature gradually changed the formation of bones. For in birds it made the bones weaker than others. In egg-laying fish, however, it created a spine. The bones of serpents too are of the nature of fish-spine, unless the serpents are very large.

Aristotle: in an animal lacking bones, then, there is some member suited to the nature of bones, like the spine in fish and cartilage in certain animals. This benefit, in certain blood-lacking creatures, is inside the body, and in certain others outside, as in animals of soft shell, like crabs, and hard shell, like oysters. For that protecting part is outside. In ringed and 'malacian' creatures, that is, animals composed only of flesh, like the cuttlefish, there is no bone or any earthy part distinct by itself. But so that the body would not be of such quick decay, nature placed its formation between flesh and sinew, so that it might be soft like flesh yet have extension like sinew. The nature of bones resembles the nature of veins, since both are continuous, coming from a single source. The source of the veins, indeed, is the heart; of bones, the vertebrae, for the vertebrae guard the uprightness of animal bodies. And since bodies necessarily bend, other bones too are bound and continuous with the vertebrae. In an animal having hands and feet, too, there are, at the ends of the hands and feet, places suited for the entry of certain parts into others. For this reason the ends of some are hollow, of others prominent, and are bound with sinew. By the sense of touch, however, bones are like the touch of similar things, like the hoof, the paw, the horn, and the beaks of birds. Bone neither bends nor curves nor is eaten nor takes on a variety of colors naturally. After being cut, too, it neither grows nor heals. The neck-bone of lions is continuous and has no ringed structure. There are bones in the hearts of the horse and cow, but not in the hearts of other animals, except in the heart of the stag.
Avicenna: [on the bones] of pig and he-goat likewise, and the legs of the cow, and the bones of man. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: marrow is of blood-nature, for it is the excess of the blood-food from which the fresh bones and spines of animals are nourished; for this reason it is retained between bones, and is generated only from blood of good digestion. Many, indeed, think the brain is the source of the marrow and vertebrae, since the marrow is continuous with the brain, but the truth contradicts this, since the brain's nature is different from the marrow's, which is hot, as has been said above. The marrow of an animal, indeed, is of much fat, very fatty. And the marrow of an animal having teeth only in the lower jaw is similar to caul-fat. That of an animal having teeth in both jaws, however, is similar to fat. In strong, dense bones, like the bones of the lion, there is no marrow, or, if there is, it is small, since the food passes into the bones. For marrow is the excess of food, as has been said, from which bones are generated. In the bones of the lion and pig, then, there is no marrow, or very little. A gloss on this: in the lion, I think, because of excessive dryness and consuming heat. In the pig, however, because of excessive moisture and non-congealing cold.

Pliny: marrow seems to be red from youth, whitening in old age: it is present only in hollow bones, and not in the legs of beasts of burden or dogs. For this reason, when broken, they do not knit. It is, moreover, fatty in those creatures that have fat, tallowy in horned animals, sinewy, and present only in the back-spine of those lacking bones, like the fish kind. The bear has none. The lion has very little, scant even, in the bones of the thighs and arms. For the rest of its bones are so hard that fire can be struck from them, hard like flint in those parts that do not grow fat. Donkeys' bones are resonant for trumpets. Dolphins' bones are not of the spine kind, for they bear live young. Serpents have spines. Soft-bodied water creatures have none, but a body joined by rings of flesh, like the cuttlefish and squid.

Isaac Judaeus, in the passage above: the marrow of the vertebrae, compared to the marrow of the bones, is coldest and moistest, which, if well digested, will give thicker and more nourishment than the brain. Bone marrow, however, is more flavorful, but causes disgust. Yet, well digested, it generates much nourishment.

Avicenna: marrow is warming and cleansing, and of much nourishment if digested. Among these, the marrow of the calf and stag is more suitable, then the bull's, after that the goat's, then the sheep's. The marrow of he-goats and bulls, specifically uncastrated ones, is drier. The marrow of the extremities, however, is fattier. Marrow is good for hardnesses and stone-like growths, namely that of the calf and stag, but not that of wild he-goats: for theirs is dry and not good. Marrow disturbs the stomach and destroys appetite. A suppository from praiseworthy marrow benefits hardness of the womb. It is also said that a liniment from it, especially from stag's bone marrow, drives away venomous worms.
Haly Abbas: stag's marrow, after that calf's, then that of bulls and goats. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: fat and caul-fat differ according to the excess of blood, since both are blood cooked for the betterment of food. And a sign of this is that they are found only in a fertile, well-conditioned animal. For part of the fat shares in the nature of fire and air, and this is not found in a blood-lacking animal. As much as fat increases, so much blood decreases, and when there is little of it in an animal's members, it helps, since it does not hinder good sense and brings health and strength. But when it multiplies, it harms and corrupts the animal, so that, if the whole body becomes fat, it must necessarily die. For fat and caul-fat, indeed, are in the member in which the sense of touch resides, that is, in flesh. Blood, however, has no sense, and so neither do fat and caul-fat, since they are nothing but blood of good digestion. If, then, the whole body becomes such, it will have no sense: for this reason a very fat animal ages, since its blood is scanty, because it has passed into fat. For corruption in old age is nothing but scarcity of blood and many mischances, since it is more quickly affected by cold and heat.

div.head: ADHUC DE PINGUEDINE AC SEBO ET ADIPE

cit.quote: Aristotle: again, an animal of much fat is of little offspring, or none at all, for the same reason, since the blood that would become seed passes into fat. What is near the pupil of the eye in all animals is of much tallow. In the kidneys too there is much tallow and fat, more than in other inner members, because of the filtering of excess matter, since the blood that remains there after filtering is of good digestion, and the completion of the goodness of digestion is fat and caul-fat. Fat, however, is not in the substance of the kidneys, but outside, surrounding them, in all animals. The right kidney has less fat than the left, for the reason stated above. But sheep, when fat multiplies in their kidneys, die. Sheep, however, grow fat from drinking; and so shepherds often give them salt, and they remain healthy. The pig, however, grows fat quickly from roots, and when the pig is fat it can mate at any time, in winter and summer, night and day. An animal of wide veins does not grow fat, but one of slender veins does. Fish, however, grow fat in rainy seasons. What is fat does not dry out quickly; movement, however, dissolves fat. Every animal of much tallow is of little seed. Men and women too who are very fat rarely reproduce, drawing hindrance from kidneys bound up with great fat.
Haly Abbas: [on the fats] of animals, from which they come, and according to food and age and sex, and castrated ones, and those having testicles. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Dioscorides: pig's fat, indeed, is hot; bull's fat, however, is hotter and diaphoretic and softening. It is also astringent, like buffalo's fat too, but goat's more so, because of its pasture.

Avicenna: duck's fat is much finer and hotter than hen's fat. Cock's and stag's fat, however, are of more vehement heating. Cow's fat is midway between lion's and goat's. In all of these, however, the male's fat is stronger. He-goat's fat, however, is of more vehement dissolving power.
Helinand of Froidmont, book 10: 'adeps' [fat] is the name for an animal's inner fat, like tallow in cattle and sheep and other ruminants, and lard in pigs.

Petrus Comestor: outer fat, namely that which is over the flesh, is properly called suet or lard. That mixed with flesh is properly called fat. That in the intestines is called 'adeps.' There are, moreover, three kinds of 'adeps': the fat of the vital organs, that is, of the heart and belly. The fat of the liver, called the caul, since it is wrapped like a net. And the fat of the kidneys. These three fats, in the sacrifices of livestock, were once burnt by the levitical priest on the altar.

Pliny: horned animals with teeth on one side only, and those having ankle-bones in their feet, grow fat with tallow. Cloven-hoofed or toed animals lacking horns, however, with fat. Certain ones do not grow fat, like the hare and partridge. All fatty creatures are more sterile, both males and females: very fat ones age faster. In all animals there is something fatty in the eyes. Fat is universally without sensation; those lacking arteries or veins have, in most animals, fat without sensation. For this reason they say pigs breathing are gnawed by mice unnoticed. These same mice, it is said, gnawed the fat from the son of the consular L. Apronius, relieving his body of the motionless burden.

Isaac Judaeus, in the passage above: 'pinguedo' is mixed with flesh and bones, as is found in the ribs and tail and such places. 'Adeps,' however, is separate from flesh and bones, like lard and that which is in the kidneys. 'Adeps,' moreover, is thicker than 'pinguedo,' and, mixed with flesh, more nauseating and more easily dissolved; both, moreover, cause disgust and soften food in the stomach, and have the property of floating above all other foods, and of making food viscous, thick, and disobedient to digestion, and of generating false satiety, especially if eaten with sweet things. Whence Rufus says: whatever members have an abundance of fat provide little nourishment to the body. For the fatty part, because of its slipperiness, passes out of the stomach and intestines once cooked.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: on tallow, too, mention has already been made above, in the chapter on ruminant animals; on fat and 'pinguedo' too, in the chapter on flesh.
Pliny: [on] birds having neither veins nor arteries, likewise serpents, tortoises, lizards. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]
Aristotle, in the book on sleep and waking: the veins are the location of blood, and their source is the heart.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: since the soul is one in act, it is fitting that there be one member in which resides the power, that is, the vital heat. The heat of blood, then, is from one source, namely the heart, since in it is the source of sense and the primary heat. And so the veins are from one source. And a certain great vein is nobler than the pulsating artery, since it is placed in front. The arteries, however, are in back. And it is right that the course of blood in the veins, and in the whole body, follow nature, since the sustenance of any member comes from blood, and this resembles channels of water prepared in gardens, which come from one fountain or one source and are first divided through channels, and those again through others, so that one reaches any given place. From the excess of small veins comes sweat, when the body grows warm and their openings open. A certain greater vein proceeds from the larger, upper right chamber, in which there is always blood, and passes deep through the middle of the neck. The artery, however, comes from the middle chamber, and does not share in the heart as the aforesaid vein does, and its interior is narrow. The formation of the greater vein is from membrane and hide. That of the other, however, from sinew. The brain, however, lacks blood entirely in every animal, and so there is no vein in it, large or small. In no member is there blood outside a vein, except in the heart. An animal of wide vein does not grow fat, but an animal of slender vein does. Veins, indeed, rejoin after being cut, but sinews do not. The nature of the great veins does not appear in the bodies of the dead, since they contract suddenly at the exit of the blood.

Aristotle, in the same: blood is present in all footless animals, or those having only two or four feet. Those, however, having more, lack blood. In certain animals, then, there is blood. In certain others, however, another moisture corresponding to blood, namely an incomplete moisture, like venom. And a moisture inclining toward paleness, resembling water within. In blood-having animals, all the body's members are composed of veins in which blood runs. In the heart, however, is the source of the veins, and the primary power creating blood. And it must be from the food that it receives. Nor is there blood in any other member outside a vein, except in the heart. Earthy blood coagulates, watery blood does not. In certain blood, then, there is something fine, like a hair, and it is of earthy nature. Such an animal is irascible and bold, because of the irascibility that stirs heat and becomes, at the time of anger, like a burning coal, for this reason the pig and bull are very irascible, since in their blood there are many such hairs. Bull's blood, too, congeals or coagulates fastest of all blood. In certain blood, however, there are no such hairs, as in the blood of stags, and so such blood does not coagulate. Animals of much water, that is, of watery blood, which naturally grow cold, are of much fear, since fear chills an animal. A blood-lacking animal too is of greater fear, and so moves only slightly. The wateriness of blood, however, is that which is fine in it, since it was not yet digested, or because it was corrupted. Blood is always in the body while the animal lives. And every blood-filled body putrefies quickly, especially around the bones. Every animal of much blood is of much seed. The menses, moreover, is the flux of an animal's blood. Woman, then, since she has more blood within than the females of other animals, therefore has the menses. For this reason too she suffers less illness than man. The taste of blood is naturally sweet, when it is healthy, and its color red, not very thick. As much as fat increases, so much blood decreases. If a sleeping person is pricked, as much blood will not come out as if he were awake, since then it is scanty on the surface, but abundant within. Likewise all blood-lacking animals are of smaller body than blood-having ones. And every blood-having animal that generates an animal has all the instruments of sense, except the mole kind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: what Aristotle says, that animals having more than four feet do not have blood, is understood of blood arranged through veins; hence worms and lice or fleas do not have it, and lack veins. The soul of brute animals is blood. Congealed blood, however, is wont to turn into flesh, and corrupted flesh returns to earth. Rightly, then, is the soul of beasts of burden perishable. Blood, then, is a natural moisture always remaining in blood-having creatures. And there is no vital blood except in the veins and in the heart. Its taste is sweet and its color red, unless it is corrupted. Every animal having blood has a brain, sleeps and wakes, and walks.

Avicenna, in the second canon: the blood of certain animals is medicinal, like the blood of the horse, bull, camel, he-goat, goat, lamb, stag, dog, hare, lizard, tortoise, frog. Also of birds, like the dove, turtledove, eared-owl, bat. There is also a woman's menstrual blood. It is fitting, however, that blood administered in medicines be taken from healthy animals, in whose color neither excess moisture nor putrefaction predominates.

Aristotle, in the passage above: there are, indeed, differences in blood. For some is finer, some thicker; some cleaner, some more turbid; some colder, some hotter. Thick blood is of more nourishment to the body and less sense. Clean blood, however, is of greater sense and more suited to intellect, and colder. Likewise the blood that is in the upper members differs from that in the lower according to these differences; for this reason bees and such animals are of greater intelligence than blood-having animals. Better, too, are animals having fine, clean, hot blood, since they are more suited to wisdom and boldness and the like: the upper members too differ from the lower according to this distinction. And the male's members from the female's. And the members of the right side from those of the left. It is necessary, however, that everything that grows be nourished. And so the veins take food from the belly and are, as it were, vessels of blood. And when an animal is not fed on blood or on what suits blood, it will be lean and of poor condition. When, however, it is well fed, it grows well and is of good condition: and if that food is clear and good, the body will be healthy; if bad, sick.

Pliny: those with much and rich blood are irascible. Blood is darker in males than in females. And more so in youth than in old age, and richer in the lower part; and there is a great portion of usefulness in it. Emitted, it draws breath with it, but does not feel it drawn. The stronger of animals are those whose blood is thicker. The wiser are those with finer blood. The more timid, those with least; but those with none are dull. Bulls' blood coagulates and hardens most quickly, and so is deadly, especially as a drink. That of boars, stags, goats, and all buffalo does not thicken. It is fattest in donkeys, thinnest in man, and none at all in those having more than four feet. In the obese it is less abundant, since it is consumed by fat; its discharge, in the fat, occurs in a single place, the nostrils, in man. In others, one nostril. In others, both. In some, from below. In many, from the mouth, at a fixed time. Sacrificial victims, indeed, pour it out more abundantly if they have drunk beforehand. Those animals that hide during other seasons then have no blood, except very small drops around the heart, by a remarkable work of nature, just as in man its force changes in the smallest moments, not only in the material suffused in the face, but in each disposition of mind - shame, anger, fear, pallors, and many kinds of blushing, for the blush of anger is one thing, of modesty another. For in fear it is certain that it retreats and is nowhere to be found. And in many, when pierced through, it does not flow, which happens to man alone; every illness too, and death, consumes blood.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: this we have briefly said concerning the individual parts or members of animals, alike and unlike. Now let us add what follows concerning animals in other respects, that is, their nourishment and senses and motions and generations and excesses.

Aristotle, in the passage above: every animal, then, has an appetite for the taste-flavor of food, and appetite is only for what is sweet, delightful, and well digested. For what is digested is, in all things, sweeter and more delightful. And what is small is quickly digested. It is necessary, indeed, that everything that grows be fed, and this by dry and moist things, whose digestion is by the strength of heat. The upper and lower belly, then, digest food by natural heat. A ruminant animal, however, has four stomachs, as has been said above. The function of the mouth, indeed, is to cut food and send it to the stomach, so that its digestion may be better and quicker. The veins, however, take food from the belly and are, as it were, vessels of blood. A ringed-bodied animal has such an organ, by which it perceives food within the mouth, like the ant kind and many others of hard shell. Some of these have that organ outside, like a sting, since its nature is soft and hollow, and through it it tastes and perceives and draws in food, as is evident in bees and flies and the like. The elephant uses its trunk in place of a hand for taking food and drink. Every animal of straight intestine is very gluttonous, since food exits very quickly and so is desired again quickly. Likewise an animal having much width in the intestine. A gluttonous animal, however, because of excessive appetite, swallows food before chewing. All fish, because of the limited use of their food, expel raw and undigested excess of food, and so are very gluttonous. Animals eating many kinds of food differ in color. For the kinds of food are the cause of the diversity of colors, since from different food different excesses arise: because of an abundance of food, however, fruit on trees and offspring in animals is spoiled. Any kind of animal loves what is proper to it and hates another. Every animal having a saw-like row of teeth eats flesh. The donkey eats thorns when they are soft. The pig, however, eats serpents. Likewise the pig eats more roots than any other animal. In this it grows fat quickly. Wolves eat only flesh, except for a certain medicine, which they take when sick and vomit up, and are healed. The wolf, however, eats without chewing, and in one day what suffices for three. The 'cabonetia' wolf is maned like a lion, and drags carcasses out of tombs and eats them. The sparrow and many small birds similarly feed on worms. The ant stores food. Bees too eat honey in time of need, and delight in clear, running waters. Fish feed their young at the time of breeding. Cows love to drink clear water, horses, however, muddy water. Sheep grow fat from drinking. Hook-clawed birds drink rarely and little.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: every animal having saw-like teeth draws water with its tongue. Animals having even teeth draw water into the belly by sucking. The reason hook-clawed birds do not drink water is this, that they eat flesh, which is moister than the food of other birds. Every animal devouring food, like the lion or wolf, is of lean body, since where there is no chewing of food, it passes badly into nature. All heavier beasts feed on grain, but the more agile ones on flesh.
Pliny: [on] wolves, stags and, among birds, gulls. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny, book 10: goats and quails grow fat on venoms, most peaceful animals; serpents, however, on eggs - the dragon's skill indeed is worth watching, for they either swallow them whole, if their throat can already take them, which they then break inside themselves once coiled around them, and shake out the shell fragments; or, if the offspring is still too tender, having caught the egg in a coil, they compress it so gently and yet so forcefully that they cut off, as if with iron, the part enclosed, and swallow the rest, held in their coil. In similar fashion, too, having swallowed birds whole, they force up feathers and bones again by great contraction. Scorpions live off the earth. Serpents, when the chance comes, especially seek out wine, though otherwise they need little to drink. The same creatures use very little, and almost no, food, as spiders too, living by sucking. No venomous creature dies of hunger or thirst. For it has neither the force of heat, nor of blood, nor of sweat, which increase natural appetite through salt. Among this kind, all are more deadly if they have eaten their own kind before doing harm. The kind of spider called satyrs and sponges store food in their jaws' treasuries, then gradually squeeze it out to chew with their hands. And what is an annual practice for ants is, for these, a matter of days or hours. One animal among the toed kind, the hare, is nourished by grass, but also by grain. Solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed pigs eat all kinds of food, including roots. Wallowing is peculiar to solid-hoofed animals. All saw-toothed creatures are carnivorous; bears live on grain too, foliage, grape-harvest, fruit, and bees, even crabs and ants. Wolves, in hunger, eat earth too; livestock grow fat from drinking. So salt is most suitable for them. Besides the aforementioned, wild stags too ruminate when raised by us. All creatures, however, ruminate lying down rather than standing, and more in winter than summer, for about seven months. As for drinking, those with saw-like teeth lap. And common mice too, though of another kind. Those with continuous teeth suck, like horses, oxen. Bears do neither, but even bite at water. In Africa, most wild beasts do not drink in summer, from lack of rain. For this reason captured Libyan mice, if they drink, die. Of animals, too, some seek different tastes, some prey with their teeth, others with claws, others crush from a height, others hollow out with sharpness, others catch with a hooked beak: others suck, others lick, sip, chew, devour, nor is there less variety in the use of their feet, to seize, tear away, hold, press, grasp, and to never stop scraping the ground.

Pliny, book 11, in the same: boars are found in Pamphylia and the mountains of Cilicia. Those who eat a salamander devoured by these die, with no perceptible difference in smell or taste. Wasps eagerly eat serpents, from which food they make deadly stings. Theophrastus reports that oxen too feed on fish, but only living ones. The most useful food for man is simple. A pile of flavors is deadly, and seasonings more dangerous still. All foods too sharp, and greedily gulped, are digested with difficulty, and more so in summer than winter, and in old age than youth. Vomiting, devised for man as a remedy for this, cools the body. It is especially harmful to the eyes and teeth. To digest through sleep is more useful for corpulence than for firmness. So athletes prefer to digest food by walking. Food is indeed overcome especially by staying awake.

Aristotle: ruminant animals lack teeth in the upper jaw; since, then, they cannot chew, they ruminate, having four stomachs, as said above. Horned animals ruminate. The camel too ruminates, although it lacks horns, since it has saw-like teeth like horned animals, and so ruminates like them, and its stomachs are like theirs.
Isidore: rumination is named from the 'rumen,' namely the projecting part of the throat, through which food, once swallowed, is called back by certain animals.

Helinand of Froidmont, in the Chronicles, book 10: Adelard of Bath, in his Natural Questions, asks why some animals ruminate and others not. He resolves it thus: some animals are of hot nature, some cold. Those that are hot digest their intake better and convert it more easily into blood. Those that are cold, worse. For everything that is changed is converted more gently by heat than by cold. For fire has, as its proper power, to dissolve all things. Those animals, then, that have a hot stomach cook their food easily. Those that have a cold one, however, unable to convert food because of lack of heat, call it back to their teeth, so that, ground a second time there, it may more easily be dissolved, like cattle, goats, stags, and the like. Their cold nature is shown by their fat, which is harder and more solid than what the common people call tallow. Hotter animals, however, have softer fat, being more cooked, which common people generally call grease. To this, however, an objection is raised: if coldness is the cause of rumination, then the horse and donkey, which according to the physicians are melancholic, ought to ruminate. To this he himself replies that they are not so cold, and have a somewhat hotter stomach and teeth more effective for grinding. But it is objected in turn that sheep are hot, yet ruminate and have tallow. To this he replies that, although they are of hot nature, the scarcity of their teeth causes them the labor of rumination, for they have only two, whence they are also called 'bidentes' [two-toothed], and are of such little heat that they have tallow like the melancholic animals. What, he says, if one asks why certain cold men do not ruminate? They have teeth effective for grinding, and men in general, compared to animals, are called hot. Yet certain of them have such cold stomachs that they do not digest the food they take, but retain it badly, and not long after the meal reject it undigested. There are, moreover, three things that go together: to ruminate, to have tallow, and to lie down rear-first, arising from the same cause, that is, coldness. Coldness, however, is not equally present in all members. For it is greater in the rear parts, distant from the heart. Greater heaviness, then, must necessarily be present in them too, and so they lie down rear-first and rise rear-first too. For whatever rests does so in order to regain the strength that labor had diminished; these animals, then, once their strength is restored through rest, while that fresh strength is more effective, undertake to lift first that part of their bulk which is heavier. Just as any fresh and vigorous laborer, unless I am mistaken, undertakes the heavy work first to set in order, and then, once tired, the lighter.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: Isidore gave another reason concerning the 'bidentes' above, where sheep were discussed.

Aristotle: voice is produced through the lungs and windpipe. The distinctness of the voice, however, is through the tongue. Certain animals are of deep voice, some of medium, some even small, and some pleasant, some the opposite. The cause of sharpness and depth of voice follows the change of ages, since the voice of young animals is sharper than that of old, but the calf's voice is the reverse. The voices of females of all other animals, too, are sharper or finer than the males', but the voices of cows are the reverse. A deep voice comes from slow motion. A sharp one from swift. The depth of the voice, then, comes from the size of what is moved and from the stronger power of the mover, since, if the power of what is moved exceeds the power of the mover, that is, of the windpipe, the motion of what is moved will necessarily be deep. If, however, the reverse, then it will be swift, but strong because of its strength. And perhaps the voices of the weak and of women and children are sharp, since, because of weakness, they move a small amount of air, and what is small moves quickly. A swift voice, however, is sharp. Cows and calves, however, which move much matter, make a deep voice. The voices of males and females change at the onset of the emission of seed. And since the strength of animals lies only in the sinews, the voices of castrated animals, because of the weakness of their sinews, resemble the voices of females. The voices of males, then, change when they mate, or when they are castrated or gelded. And so the change of voice is a sign of the impulse to mate. There is also something common to all animals except man, namely much chattering and noise at mating time, especially in birds, as said above. Every animal, at mating time, calls its mate by its own voice, and especially the frog. Small birds are of much chattering, so that some recognize the intentions of certain others by their calls. The noise of bees and cicadas, however, is not a voice, since it does not breathe, but occurs because of the friction of certain parts; speech, however, is proper to man alone.

Pliny, book 11: only those creatures have a voice that have a lung and windpipe, that is, those that breathe, Aristotle thinks. And so insects too have sound, not voice, produced by breath moving within and resounding when enclosed. Some emit a murmur, like bees. Others, with a drawn-out sound, a shrill noise, like cicadas, for, breath taken in beneath two hollows in the chest, with a mobile membrane meeting it, it is well known that the innards resound by its friction within. And the rest begin and stop being heard together with their flight, like flies and bees. For sound is produced by friction and the inner breath, not by the soul. Water-creatures' scallop-shells make a shrill sound when they fly; soft, shell-covered creatures have no voice and no sound at all. But the rest of the fish, though lacking lung and windpipe, are not entirely without any sound; they claim a grinding sound is made with the teeth. And the one called the goat-fish, in the river Achelous, has a grunt. Among egg-laying creatures, it is prolonged, in the tortoise abrupt, and frogs have a sound of their own kind, unless doubt must be raised even about these, since it is conceived at once in the mouth, not the chest; for much depends, in these creatures, on the nature of the place too. They are said to be mute in Macedonia. Boars too are mute. Among birds, the smaller are more talkative, and especially around mating; some have a voice in fighting, like quails. Others before fighting, like partridges. Others when they have won, like domestic fowl. The same have their own to the males. Others the same to the females, like the nightingale kind. Some sing all year, some at fixed times. The elephant, around its nostrils, with its very mouth, produces a sound like a sneeze. Through the nostrils, however, it is like the hoarseness of trumpets. Only in cattle is the female's voice deeper. In every other kind it is thinner than the males', even in man among castrated men. No voice is heard from an infant being born before it has fully emerged from the womb. First speech comes at a year old. Croesus's son spoke at six months, an omen by which that whole kingdom fell. Those who begin to speak sooner begin to walk later. The voice grows strong from thirteen years. The same grows thinner in old age. Nor in any other animal does it change so often. A remarkable thing about voice, worth mentioning: the same words spoken, even in a light tone, along a straight or curved space of a wall, carry to the other end, if no unevenness impedes them.

div.head: DE VARIETATE VOCUM IN DIVERSIS GENERIBUS ANIMALIUM

cit.quote: From the book of Papias: it should be known that articulate voice belongs to men alone, which can be written; confused voice, however, cannot be written, like man's groaning, an ox's bellowing, and the like. For, declaring the voice of dumb animals as well as of men, they say eagles scream, hawks pipe, vultures cry, ravens croak. Kites wail, orioles drone, cranes trumpet, storks clatter or croak. Peacocks screech, geese cackle, cocks crow or sing, ducks quack, turtledoves and doves moan, wood-pigeons coo, cuckoos call, partridges cackle, jackdaws chatter, owls hoot, blackbirds warble. Starlings chirp, swallows twitter or chirp, sparrows chirp, bees hum or buzz, cicadas chirr. Wild beasts too have their own voices: lions roar, tigers snarl, others growl. Leopards yowl, panthers roar. Bears growl, or grumble. Boars gnash, lynxes screech, wolves howl, serpents hiss, elephants trumpet, wild asses bray, stags bell, bulls bellow, horses neigh, donkeys bray, pigs grunt. Boars squeal or grunt, rams bleat gruffly. Sheep bleat. Goats bleat shrilly, kids bleat, dogs whimper or bark, foxes yelp, puppies whine or yip, hares squeal, weasels chirp, mice squeak or peep. Shrew-mice chirp, frogs croak or croak.

Aristotle: the source of sense is in the heart. And the motion of all the senses begins from the heart and returns to it. Two senses are continuous with the heart, namely taste and touch. The remaining three, however, are in the head; the sense of sight, in all animals, is above the sense of hearing, and below these, smell. Especially, too, in the kinds of fish, which hear and smell. And rightly the sense of sight is around the brain, since the nature of this sense is cold and moist. For it is water, of very clear moisture, and its clarity is fixed and remaining. Nor should we think sight is from fire and water, as Empedocles imagines, namely from water and not from fire. It is also necessary that this sense be the finest, near the member whose blood is best and purest, that is, the heart.
