The brain, then, is the instrument of sense, by which sensation in front occurs, and for this reason it is in the front of the head, and since this sense must be located near the heart - but the heart is at the front of the body - sense, indeed, occurs through blood-filled members. The instrument of hearing, however, is airy, and nature placed it in the middle of the round head, in the rear, which is hollow, since it does not hear only straight ahead, but all around. Sight, however, is in front, since an animal must see toward the front. Smell, however, occurs only through the drawing in of air, in an animal having a nose, and this instrument is in the front of the head, in the middle of the three instruments, like a balance placed there, because of the motion of breath. All animals, too, have taste for the flavor of food, and this kind of sense is near the swallowing passage, that is, the opening of the esophagus. What is digested, indeed, is sweeter and more delightful. The hearts of animals having sense are soft; of those lacking it, hard.

Pliny: among the senses, indeed, man has, before the rest, touch, then taste. In the others, however, he is surpassed by many: eagles see more clearly, vultures smell more keenly, moles, though buried in earth, so dense and deaf an element by nature, hear more clearly; further, they hear the speech of all voices tending upward, and, if you speak of these things, they are even said to understand and flee. Whoever is denied hearing from birth is also deprived of the use of speech. Nor are creatures naturally deaf without also being mute. In sea oysters it is not likely that hearing exists, but they are accustomed to submerge at a sound. And so there is silence for those fishing at sea. Fish, indeed, have neither organs of hearing nor openings, yet it is evident that they hear; as is shown, when it is observed, in certain fish-ponds, that wild fish gather to accustomed food at a clapping sound. And in Caesar's fishponds, certain individual kinds of fish come when called by name. And so it is reported that the mullet, the sea-bass, the salpa, and the chromis hear most clearly, and so live in shallow water. That smell exists in these is clearly evident. Indeed not all are caught with the same bait, and they smell before they desire it. Some too, hiding in caves, a fisherman drives out with a lure smeared with salted bait tied to a rod, as if fleeing recognition of their own kind's carcass. And they gather from the deep even to certain scents, like burnt cuttlefish and octopus, which for this reason are caught in traps. They flee far from the smell of ships' bilges. Especially, however, from the blood of fish. The octopus cannot be pulled from the rocks. The same creature, however, recoils at once from the smell of a burning ember applied. Purple-fish too are caught by foul-smelling bait. For who would doubt this of the rest of the animal kingdom? Serpents are driven off by the scent of stag's horn. But especially killed by the scent of storax, marjoram, lime, or sulfur. Gnats seek sour things, and do not fly toward sweet ones. The sense of touch belongs to all, even those lacking every other sense. For it exists in oysters and earthworms too, from which I would judge that all have the sense of taste as well. For why do different creatures seek different flavors?

Aristotle, in the passage above: touch is the first sense. An animal, then, is that which has sense, and first of all the primary sense, that is, touch. Flesh, however, is the instrument of touch and the first organ of this sense, just as the pupil is of sight. It is necessary that this sense be present in the body more than the other sense-instruments, since it is evident that all the other members were created only for the sake of this sense. Man, however, has the better sense, that is, touch, of all other animals, and so his flesh is soft. Man too, and four-footed creatures desiring mating, emit seed suddenly, some through simple, light touch, some through sight alone. Animals of much motion necessarily need much sight. Grey-blue eyes are not sharp of sight by day, nor black eyes by night, for the reason stated above. And generally, when sight is weak, it cannot look at bright things, since it suffers from them and the moisture is disturbed by much motion. Sight, however, will be sharp from moisture that is temperate in quantity, for thus it will not hinder the motion of colors because of scarcity, nor burden it because of abundance; nor is moisture alone the cause of sharpness of sight, but also the skin over the pupil, since it must be very clear. And so it should be thin, for lightness of the motion of sight, and also smooth, so that there is no wrinkle in it and it becomes, as it were, a shadow over the eye - for this reason the sight of the old is not sharp, since their skin is wrinkled. It should also be white, since black cannot be clear. Certain animals are of sharp sight, some not. Sharpness, moreover, in sight and hearing and smell, is said in two ways: either because one sees from a distance, or because one well discerns the differences of things seen; whenever, then, the moisture that is in the pupil is clean, tempered, and its motion tempered, and its own covering thin, and the eye deep-set, it sees well from a distance, since its motion is not divided or dispersed, but the visible power going out from it goes straight to the thing seen. A protruding eye, however, does not see well from a distance. For since there is no covering outside the eye, it is necessarily weakened. Sight cannot see from a distance except weakly; hook-clawed birds are of sharp sight, since they see their food from a great distance. Birds, however, that stay on the ground, like the hen, do not need sharp sight. When man engages much in mating, his sight is weakened.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: certain animals see better at night than by day, since in the eye there are several moistures, one white and clear, through which the visible spirit is diffused, another black, through which care is taken lest the white, shining moisture be too much dispersed. Those animals, then, that see less by day abound in the very white moisture. Whence it happens that the spirit is more dispersed, and, by reason of this dispersal, the discernment of things seen is lost by day. At night, however, because of darkness, the spirit is gathered, and so discernment becomes greater. For we too, when we wish to see something distinctly, narrow our brows, so that the gathered visual spirit does not wander.

Aristotle, in the passage above: if the formation of the ears is clear, and the membrane containing them, that is, the eardrum of hearing, is thin, hearing will be sharp. And likewise for smell. For the passages of all the senses extend to the heart, or to members corresponding to the heart. And the instrument of hearing is full of natural spirit, since natural spirit produces a pulsating motion in the veins, and so produces the motion of breathing in the nose, and likewise the motion of hearing in the ear; for this reason things are learned through the sense of hearing, and man says he 'hears,' since, just as speech enters through the ear, so too the motion of the voice exits, produced through the tongue. When, however, a man groans and yawns, his hearing is weakened, since the origin of this sense's instrument, that is, the jaw, is set upon the member in which the spirit resides, and moves with it, that is, with the motion of the jaw, when the spirit moves in the instrument where it is. And this occurrence, that is, heaviness of hearing, occurs in the temples in those of moist complexion. The cause of good hearing and smell, then, will be the cleanliness of those instruments and the membranes containing them. For if these instruments have an outer covering, they will perceive from a distance, since this sense, that is, its powers, goes out from the instruments as water from channels; for this reason long-nosed hounds have a good sense of smell. Likewise the hearing of those having well-formed and well-coiled ears will be sharp. Man's sense of things and voices and smells at a distance, however, is weaker, in proportion to his body, than in other animals. But close up he discerns the differences of colors and smells and voices better, since the instruments of these senses in man are very clean, and there is only a little of the earthy part in them. Hearing and smell too, like sight, are weakened if too exposed. A female partridge, hearing the male's voice and smelling him, becomes filled with eggs. Women and mares, however, miscarry from the smell of a candle.

From the book On the Soul: concerning motion too, one might say it is related to sense in an animal: it is well known, however, that a certain animal has the power of the sense of touch, yet not of motion, like the shellfish kind. We say, however, that motion is of two kinds: voluntary, that is, local motion, which is from place to place, and the motion of contracting and drawing back the animal's members, from which no motion of the whole from its place results. And so it is impossible for an animal to have the sense of touch without having some kind of motion in itself. For how would one know it has the sense of touch, unless some motion were seen in it, fleeing one contact and seeking another? The example of shellfish, then, is useful here. For we see motions of contraction and expansion and bending and stretching in their parts, although they do not leave their place, and from this we know that they perceive by touch: it appears, then, that whatever has this act has voluntary motion in itself, either in itself or in its parts.

Aristotle: [on] the motive power in animals, which is located in an organ, and this in two ways. For it is located in an inner organ, namely the imagination, and in an outer one, namely that motive power which is in the sinews and muscles of the moving members. But this too has two ways: for some is ordered, according to its object, toward the animal powers, which are intellect and imagination and sense, like that which is in the feet and hands, the muscles of the eyes and eyelids, and the like, and this is immobilized during sleep, since it is founded upon the sensitive power that is in those members, whence sense is first immobilized, and motion follows accordingly. Some, however, is ordered toward the natural powers, like that which is in the genital members, and this is not always bound in sleep.

Aristotle: sleep occurs in animals having a brain, since it cools the food coming to it from the flow of blood. Heat, however, flees downward with the blood, and, when it gathers in the lower place, sleep results. And so the heads of four-footed animals too grow heavy before the time of sleep. Sleep seems to be midway between living and not living. And so, if the body of a sleeping person is pricked, as much blood will not come out as if he were awake, since then it is scanty on the surface, but abundant within. The fish too rests in sleep, and nothing moves from it but the tail, and that only slightly.

The same, in the book on plants: waking is the effect of sense, sleeping the weakness of the same. And when an animal is fed, vapor rises to the head, and it sleeps. When, however, that same vapor is consumed, it wakes. In certain animals this vapor is abundant, yet they sleep little, and sleep is a compression of motion, and the compression of motion is the rest of a moving thing.

The same, in the book on sleep and waking: waking and sleep are proper to animals. If, however, waking is nothing other than that in which one perceives, it is clear that in that by which they perceive, in this they also wake. We say, then, that sleep is a certain affection of the sensitive part, as it were a binding of sense and a certain weakness, but waking is its loosening and release. And so sleep is an interception of the primary organ of perceiving, so that it cannot act. It is not present in plants for this reason, that without sense there is neither sleep nor waking. In those, however, that have sense, there is also sadness and joy; and in those that have these, desire too. In plants, however, none of these are present. But touch's affection is sleep and waking, and so it is present in all animals. For touch alone is present in all animals. And when the organ of touch is powerless, the organ of all the senses must necessarily have a defect. Rest and sleep, however, exist as it were for the health of animals. For rest is necessary and useful for everything that is born to move, since it cannot always and continuously move by will. For the nourishing part too does its work more in sleeping than in waking, as if needing nothing of the senses for this; nor is it possible for anything to move and do something without strength. Vigor, however, is produced by the persistence of spirit in breathing creatures.
Pliny: [on the sleep of] tunnies, dolphins, and whales. Insects. Man, horses, cattle, livestock, goats. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle, in the passage above: sleep, however, is not just any powerlessness of the sensitive part, but this affection arises from the evaporation around nourishment. For it is necessary that what has evaporated be driven up to that point. Then it is converted and transformed. Animal heat, however, is naturally borne upward, and when it is in the upper places, it suddenly returns and is carried down again, and, descending, drives the heats down, weighs them down, and induces sleep. And so dreams occur especially after meals. For then much moist and thick matter is suddenly carried upward. When, then, it stands there, it weighs down and induces drowsiness. When, then, by falling back downward and returning, it drives the heat down, then sleep occurs and the animal sleeps. A sign of this is that all who take opium, mandrake, wine, darnel, and things carried downward, and who grow drowsy, are seen to suffer this, that they cannot raise their head and eyelids. And sleep occurs especially after food, since much evaporation comes from food. Sleep also occurs from labors, and from certain illnesses, namely those arising from hot and moist excess, like fever and lethargy. Further, the first age too produces sleep, for children sleep vehemently, since all their nourishment is carried upward. Whence growth occurs in them, a sign of which is that the size of the upper parts exceeds the lower in the first age. For this reason too epileptics arise. For sleep is similar to epilepsy, and the onset of this affliction happens to many while sleeping, since, when much spirit is carried upward, descending again it swells the veins, by which it constricts the passage where breathing occurs. And so wine does not benefit children, nor nursing mothers, but they should drink watery and moderate drink. For wine is windy. Generally, however, lovers of sleep are those who have hidden veins, like the empty-headed and those with large heads. For their veins are narrow, so that the descending moisture does not flow out easily. Those having visible veins, however, are not sleepy, because of the easy flow through the pores. Nor are the melancholic, since the place within is chilled, and so no abundance of its evaporation occurs. For black bile, being naturally cold, also makes the nourishing place cold. It is clear, then, that sleep is a gathering, that is, a certain congregation of heat within, and a natural reciprocation. And so a sleeper's motion is abundant. After food, however, sleep is strongest, since wine and other such hot things are sleep-inducing. The cause of sleeping, then, is heat.

Gloss on the same book: Aristotle here touches on the fourfold cause of sleep: one, which is the cause by itself, namely the evaporation of food; three, however, which are accidental causes, namely labor, a certain illness, and the first age. Then he shows how the cooling and weighing-down of the senses is the cause of sleep.

Aristotle, in the passage above: the belly, however, when empty, is hot. Repletion, however, cools, because of motion, that is, the filling food cools because of its falling into the belly, and thus in the head the passages and hot places are cooled, the evaporation being lifted, that is, carried upward. Further, much, that is, the food falling in, is what raises the heat, just as fire, wood being placed under it, is cooled and grows faint, until it is digested. For sleep occurs, as has been said, while thick matter is carried upward from heat through the veins to the head. But when it can no longer do so, but the multitude exceeds what has been raised, it is driven back again and flows downward. There is, moreover, a place around the brain that is the coldest of all that are in the body. Whence, in the rising of heat to the brain, the excess evaporation, indeed, is turned into phlegm. The nourishing matter, however, is carried gathered downward, and what is hot is cooled. They wake, however, once digestion has occurred. And thick and purest blood are also distinguished. The thinnest and purest blood, moreover, is in the head, but the densest and most turbid is in the lower parts.

Gloss on the same book: just as, then, sleep is created in the cooling and immobility of the senses, so, from the dissolving of that cooling after the completion of nourishment and after the separation of pure from impure blood, waking occurs. And indeed the upper parts are nourished from purer blood. The lower, however, from thicker and less pure. Whence, especially after the taking of nourishment, the blood becomes undifferentiated, for which reason sleep occurs, and then blood is gathered together, the purest upward, the most turbid downward. When this happens, they wake, the heaviness of the food resolved.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: and so, besides the four aforementioned causes of sleep, others too are cited, namely a withdrawal of heat, as in attentive study of something, of which more will be said fully in the treatise on the soul. Avicenna too says that anxiety or fear sometimes induces sleep. Some also add exhaustion, but this cause is reduced to illness and labor.

div.head: UTRUM IN OMNIBUS ANIMALIBUS SIT CAUSA SOMNI EVAPORATIO NUTRIMENTI

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: since, however, the primary cause of sleep, according to Aristotle, is the evaporation of nourishment, and sleep is common to all animals, it is clear that this same cause is shared by all living creatures. For certain other causes of sleep too, like labor and the first age and illness, do not cause sleep except through the action of nourishment. For the philosopher says that labor is a straining of nourishment through the multiplying of heat, namely that the nourishment, liquefied, rises to the brain and induces sleep. The first age too, since in it the nourishment rises to the upper parts and weighs down the head. Likewise exhaustion too, from weariness, comes from this, that the heat withdrawn from the outer members multiplies around the place of digestion and dissolves the nourishment found there, and it rises to the head and thus induces sleep. So too with the other causes. Whence it is clear that all act through the action of nourishment, and this, as has been said, in all animals. But someone might perhaps object that the origin of sleep is from the heart and liver and brain, or similar members, from which the evaporation of nourishment proceeds. And no evaporation is the cause of sleep, except that which is first hot from digestive heat and afterward cooled by the brain's coldness. But in certain animals there is no head or brain, as in those that have only the sense of touch. Whence in them there is no upward evaporation cooled, and so the aforesaid cause is not universal for all sleepers. We can answer that in every animal there is a brain, or a member similar to the brain, as is expressly held in the book On Animals. Nor is it necessary that this member have all the functions of the brain. Otherwise such animals would have common sense and memory and imagination, which is false: for, as is read at the beginning of the Metaphysics, by nature things having sense are animals, and from sense some of them have memory, some not. Whence it is clear that certain animals lack memory. And since, according to the philosopher, memory is an affection of the common sense, it is also proved from this that they lack the common sense. And this some concede, adducing also the reasoning that the common sense serves two purposes, namely for discerning things sensed in common, which are least perceived by touch, and for comparing the objects proper to the senses. Whence, since in such animals there is only touch, the common sense would be present in them in vain, as regards both its functions. We, however, say that just as such animals are deficient in the number of outer senses, so too in the number of inner ones. Whence they have only a weak common sense and a scant imagination. We also say that the common sense not only compares the objects of different senses, but also the objects of the same sense, like hot and cold, smooth and rough. Nor is it true that the common sense does not perceive magnitude through touch. Otherwise it would not even perceive heat existing in any magnitude. In such animals, then, it perceives the proper object, which is magnitude, even if undetermined, and it composes the objects of touch among themselves and with magnitude. There is also in them an imagination discerning the harmful and the suitable, though weakly. Whence, if the philosopher says that things having only touch do not have imagination, it should be understood that they do not have a complete one, since they are not moved except to the avoidance of a thing. For which movement, however, three things are required, namely imagination, something determining the harmful or suitable, and the common sense composing the object with magnitude, and the proper sense apprehending. But if it is objected that such animals are immobile as to place, it should be said that, although they do not proceed from place to place, they nevertheless move with the motion of expansion and contraction. For they contract at the touch of something harmful and expand at the touch of something suitable. For without this motion, as Avicenna says, there is no animal, nor can it be recognized except through that motion.

div.head: QUOD ANIMALIA QUEDAM IMPINGUANTUR SOMNO ETIAM CESSANTE ALIMENTO

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: since, according to Aristotle, there is no animal that is always awake or always asleep, the nourishing power indeed always acts in the waking, and even more in the sleeping. For thus the same Aristotle says, in the book on sleep and waking, that the nourishing power does its work in sleeping more than in waking. For the animal is nourished and grows more then, as if the sense were doing nothing. Whence certain animals too, like dormice, sleep through the whole winter, as has been said above, and, remarkably, according to Isidore, grow fat by this very sleep. But as spring's season comes on, when the sun sends out its warm rays, they return to strength in their natural way. Aristotle says, in the book On Animals, that certain animals and certain serpents can live a long time without food, and so sometimes lie hidden in caves. Avicenna too says, in the book On Animals, that there are certain scaled creatures, like serpents and shellfish, which stay in their places for four months in winter and eat nothing. Likewise the bear and hedgehog sometimes hide themselves. The she-bear too sometimes hides herself for forty days, and sometimes for many months. Whence she also gives birth then, of which the proof is that her giving birth is not well perceived, and that her young are very lean when small; such animals, however, when they hide themselves or sleep, their nourishing power does not rest, except according to the taking in of nourishment from outside. For there are certain cold animals of weak heat, not having much hunger. For the cause of hunger is the vehement dissolving of nourishment. The cause of dissolving, however, is the scarcity of matter and its fineness, and the thinness of the skin and strong natural heat, the heat of the surrounding air also helping, and likewise motion. And so, when any of these is lacking, or several, certain gluttonous animals, from appetite, gather much excess matter that their weak natural heat cannot dissolve, especially when they are not helped by outer heat or motion. Such animals, then, because of the much cold excess matter gathered and their weak natural heat, in cold weather become very sluggish and desirous of rest and immobility of their body, and so hide themselves; and indeed, if in some of them the heat is strong enough to consume those excesses and dissolve them throughout the whole time of their hiding, then those animals will become thin and weak. But if it is too weak for nature to cook it, then the uncooked excess is congealed by the coldness of the intestines into fat, and thus the animals become fatter during the time of their hiding. Further, according to whether heat can do this more quickly or slowly, accordingly the time of their hiding is shorter or longer. This also often happens in certain men, and especially women, if they are immobile as to place, as in the city of Padua a certain woman abstained for forty days. It should also be known that certain powers of the soul move their organs by the soul's own proper motion, and not by nature, like the power of motion as to place, and the sensitive power. And since such motion is not of the nature of the organs according to their composition from the elements, it therefore induces pain and labor in the organs. From this, then, arises the desire for rest and immobility, just as in waking there is a desire for sleep. Certain powers move their organs according to the nature of those organs themselves, and that motion is always pleasant to the organs; thus all the powers of the vegetative faculty move, especially the nourishing power. And so the philosopher says that the motion of generating what is nourishing is following its own nature in moving, and so, if the sensitive, motive power rests in sleep because of the desire for rest for the reason stated, the nourishing power, however, as has been said above, never ceases from its action. Whence the philosopher says, in On Generation and Corruption, that the body is indeed nourished until it is dissolved and corrupted, but it is not always growing.
Aristotle, in the book On Animals: not man alone dreams, but the horse and dog and bull and goat and every animal that generates its like, which is clear from a dog's barking in sleep.
Aristotle: [on] the inner images of things sensed. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny: for it wakes in fear too, and imitates suckling. Sleep, moreover, is nothing other than the mind's withdrawal into itself; it is clear that, after man, horses, dogs, oxen, sheep, and goats dream. For this reason it is believed to be so in all animals that bear live young. Concerning those that lay eggs, however, it is uncertain, but it is certain that they sleep.

Aristotle, in the passage above: the sense of animals follows their intelligence. Some, however, have stronger thought and a great share of memory. One should understand, moreover, character more in small animals than in large ones, and more in birds. Animals of fine, clean, hot blood are more inclined toward wisdom and boldness and the like. Naturally cold animals, however, are of great fearfulness. And strong anger occurs only in bodies of great dryness. Animals of great heart are timid, like the stag, the donkey, the mule, and the hare. What among animals is more intelligent has greater concern for its young. In treating their own illnesses or injuries, too, many animals have a certain natural skill. For wolves and dogs, when they fall ill, eat the root of some herb or another medicine, so as to vomit, and are healed. The roe-deer, shot with an arrow, seeks out dittany of Crete, so that the arrow may be drawn out. The leopard and panther, when they have eaten poison, seek out human dung and eat it. The tortoise, when it has eaten a viper, eats wild marjoram; otherwise it dies. Birds too, when they fight one another, place wild marjoram on their wounds. The 'galy' is an animal that fights the serpent and eats rue, since it is contrary to the serpent, even its scent. The dragon, when it is sick, eats the fruit of the 'cherastos' with milk.

Pliny, in the passage above: let credit be given to the raven too for its own worth. Some have thought it worth recording that one, seen dropping stones from thirst into a funerary urn where rain had left water, but which it could not reach, so, fearing to sink too low, expressed as much as it needed by that method of piling stones. Nor should it be omitted, while we discuss intelligence, that among birds swallows are untrainable, and among land creatures, mice, while elephants obey commands and lions submit to the yoke. In the sea too, seals and many kinds of fish grow tame.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: there is also, among ants, a certain skill in providing for their own needs; the fox is cunning, the dog more eager for food, the horse more ardent for mating, the sheep gentler, the lion more irascible, and so on for the rest, of which mention has been made above.

Augustine, on Genesis, book 9: every soul, whether rational or irrational, is moved by what it perceives, but the rational soul either consents or does not consent to what it perceives, by the judgment of the will. The irrational soul, however, does not have this judgment, but, for its own kind and nature, touched by something perceived, is driven onward, nor is it in the power of any soul that such perceptions come to it, whether into the bodily senses or into the spirit itself within, by which perceptions the appetite of any living creature is moved; and thus, when these perceptions are ministered from above through the ministry of angels, God's command reaches not only men, or birds and livestock, but even those hidden in the waters, as to the whale that swallowed Jonah. And not only to those larger creatures, but even to the little worm. For we read that this too was divinely commanded to gnaw the root of the gourd, under whose shade the prophet had rested.

Aristotle, in the fourth book on the soul: concerning the local motion by which an animal moves, it is clear that it does not come from the vegetative power or from the nourishing power. For the motion of this always occurs for the sake of something, and is either accompanied by imagination or appetite. For nothing is moved except by desire for something or by flight from it, unless its motion is forced. Likewise neither is that which can perceive, that is, the sensitive power, the mover of an animal from place to place. For there are many animals that have sense and yet do not move at all, but remain still in the same place. But neither is the rational or cognitive part, called the speculative intellect, the mover. For the speculative intellect understands nothing actual, nor does it speak of what is to be avoided or imitated, that is, what should be fled or followed. Further, though the practical intellect extends itself and says that something should be avoided or followed, the bad man, according to intellect, is not moved by this, but does what suits his pleasure, since he cannot restrain himself. But neither is appetite the mover, that is, motion does not dominate in it entirely or always. For the abstinent desire and crave, yet do not do the things they have appetite for, but follow the intellect. But it should be known that there are two movers as to place, namely appetite and intellect. I mean the intellect that reasons for the sake of something, namely an actual good, and is practical. And perhaps someone might posit imagination as a kind of intelligence. For in other animals, that is, brutes, there is neither intelligence nor reason, but imagination, namely in place of cognition or intelligence. Every intellect, indeed, is correct, but appetite and imagination are both correct and incorrect. And so the appetitive faculty always moves, but the intellect not always, since it moves only toward the correct. And that toward which the appetitive part is moved is either good or seems good. Further, when imagination moves, it does not move without appetite, but neither does intellect without appetite seem to move. There is, then, one mover, which is the appetitive faculty, or appetite.

div.head: DE NATURALI PIETATE ANIMALIUM ET CONCORDIA AD INVICEM

cit.quote: The same, in the book On Animals: animals gather together not only of one kind, but also those having similar pasture, when that pasture is very abundant. The raven is a friend to the fox and helps it against its enemy. The horse kind naturally loves its own species, so that, when a mare dies, another takes up the nursing of her orphaned foal. Wood-pigeons too naturally love one another. There is also an animal such that, if another approaches to harm it, many of its own kind, especially the large ones, gather to defend it. When a dolphin dies, other dolphins surround it, so that fish do not eat the dead one, and carry it into the deep and bury it. The 'cocas' is a bird at whose death birds of the same kind cry out with a mournful yet sweet cry. The turtledove, once its mate has died, never admits another. The young of the swallow feed their parents in old age. The 'macoka,' however, feed their parents not only in old age, but at all times from when they first become able. What among animals is more intelligent has greater concern for its young, the females more than the males. When the dove has hatched young, however, the male at once rules the chicks, and if the female is slow to return to them, he strikes her and forces her to return. All fish nourish their young except the frog. The dolphin especially loves its young, and so nourishes them for a long time. Birds of heavy flight, on the contrary, cast out their young, since it is hard for them to bring food. Hook-clawed birds too, as soon as they see their young fly behind them, strike them and drive them from the nest, except the hawk, which cares for its young even after they fly. There is also a bird that nourishes a cast-out eaglet, and one that nourishes a raven's chick.

Pliny: [on friendships among] peacocks and doves, turtledoves and parrots, blackbirds and thrushes, the crow and herons, against the fox kind by common enmity, the osprey and kite, against the buzzard. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny, book 9, in the same: there are also examples of friendship, like the whale and the little fish [pilot-fish], which, when its eyes are overwhelmed by the heavy weight of its brows, swims ahead and shows it the shallows that threaten its bulk, serving in place of its eyes.

div.head: DE NATURALI DISCORDIA QUORUNDAM ANIMALIUM ET PUGNA AD INVICEM

cit.quote: Pliny, book 10, in the same: there are certain wars among animals, and friendships with one another: swans and eagles are at odds, the crow and the owl, who seek each other's eggs by night. Similarly the crow and the kite, the latter perceiving food from the former. Crows and screech-owls. Eagles and the wren, if we believe it, since it is called the king of birds. Owls and other smaller birds. Again, with land creatures: the weasel and the crow. The turtledove and the pyralis moth, the ichneumons and wasps, the phalangium spiders and spiders. The wagtail, the smallest bird, is at war with the donkey, for, rubbing itself against thorns to scratch itself, it scatters its nests, which it so dreads that, hearing the donkey's braying at all, it throws out its eggs. The chicks themselves fall from fear; the donkey, flying at it, then hollows out its sores with its beak. Foxes and kites, snakes and weasels and pigs. The merlin is a small bird that breaks the raven's eggs; its chicks are attacked by foxes. In turn it tears out their cubs and them themselves. When the ravens see this, they help against it, as against a common enemy, and the finch lives among thorns. And so it too hates donkeys, which devour the thorn's flowers: at odds too are the wild goat and the lion, the smallest creatures as much as the greatest. Shrews avoid an anthill-covered tree. The spider suspends itself by a thread over the head of a serpent stretched out in the shade of a tree, and with such force does its bite seize the brain that the serpent, hissing repeatedly and whirling in dizziness, cannot break free even from the hanging thread, so far is it from fleeing, and there is no end but death.

Pliny: there are also wondrous enmities among water creatures. The mullet and the sea-bass burn with mutual hatred. The conger eel and the moray gnaw each other's tails. The lobster dreads the octopus so much that, if it sees one nearby, it dies outright. The lobster is preyed on by the conger. In turn, congers tear apart the octopus. Nigidius is the authority that the sea-bass gnaws off the mullet's tail, and that the same creatures are at peace in certain fixed months. All, moreover, live on though their tails are thus cut off.

Aristotle: friendship and enmity among animals occur for the sake of food and life. Nor is there any fight among beasts except for food and for a dwelling and for a female. And so all animals are warlike at mating time. Likewise, if food is scarce, they fight and drive each other off. Bulls fight over a cow, and the victor mounts the female. Those that eat raw flesh fight among all animals, and are called diviners, since it is said that when animals divide among themselves, they signify coming battle. But when they follow one another, there will be peace. The black crow fights with the donkey and the bull, and, flying over them, pecks their eyes with its beak. The 'ibex' is a bird that hates the horse and, imitating its voice, stuns it, and forces it to flee, and sometimes kills it. The 'aschelon' bird fights with the fox, plucks its feathers, and harms it, and kills its young. The crow, however, is a friend to the fox and an enemy to the owl. The owl too is hated by a great part of birds.

div.head: DE ARMIS QUIBUS UTUNTUR AD PUGNANDUM VEL AD TUITIONEM

cit.quote: The same: in certain animals, as has been said above, horns were created for strength and benefit, but certain animals have weak horns, suited neither for strength nor for fighting. Some, however, have none at all, since nature gave them another means of strength and benefit, like speed to horses and stags, size of body to elephants and camels, projecting tusks to pigs. To some too it gave strength in their hooves, and so deprived their heads of horns, unless perhaps they have a single horn, like the Indian donkey. The multitude of branching in stags' horns, however, is closer to harm than to benefit for them. And so another benefit was given to them, namely speed of running, as has been said. The wild ox too has horns inclining toward each other. And for this reason nature gave it another benefit, namely the ejection of dung from a distance, that is, far off, so that the hunter is thereby kept at bay. The elephant too has a long and strong trunk, which it uses in place of a hand for taking food and drink, and for everything it needs, even for uprooting trees. An animal too having many toes on its feet uses the front ones as man uses his hands, since it fights with them and drives harm from itself. An animal having hooves, however, does this with the hind ones, since the front ones are not suited for this; the other animals indeed have only one mode of strength and cannot have another or change their weapons. For man, however, the hand is not one instrument, but many, since he can use it in many ways, according to many purposes, as will be said in its place. It is, then, like a claw and a hoof, a sword and a spear and other instruments, since it can do all of these. In flesh-eating birds, the beaks are curved, so that they can hold what they grasp. Their strength, indeed, is in the beak; hook-clawed birds also have abundant feathers and large, strong wings, but to others nature gave excellence of flight for their safety. Certain ones too have, in place of wings, a benefit of claws on their legs, suited to fighting, going fixed upon the ground, like the cock. No bird, however, has claws on both feet and legs, since nature does nothing superfluous.

Gregory of Nyssa, in the book On the Image: the lion, indeed, and the boar, and anything similar, possesses naturally sufficient strength for its own safety. In the bull are horns, swiftness in the hare, and leaping and keen sight in the stag. And in other animals, size; in others still, a prominent function of the mouth. In winged creatures too, the function of feathers, and in bees, a sting, and to absolutely all, one natural defense is seen to have been granted. Man alone, however, naked of natural coverings, unarmed, even poor, and most destitute of all necessary things, is brought into this life. From what is observed, then, he seems worthy of pity rather than good fortune. For he is not armed with the growth of horns, nor protected by the sharpness of claws or teeth, nor does he pour in a deadly wound with any sting. Nor is his body covered with hair. But compared to those who excel in speed of running, he is heavier; and compared to those who excel in bodily bulk, he is slighter; and compared also to those who excel in natural weapons, he is known to be more contemptible. Yet through this very thing which is believed to be lacking in his nature, a sure opportunity is given him, by which he attains dominion over all subject creatures. For if he had such natural aids attributed to his body, he would first indeed be similar to beasts, and then he would neglect to exercise dominion over other creatures, of whose help he would have absolutely no need. And so the slowness of our body made us apply the foresight of horses, and, to restrain beasts by vengeance, what we lacked, the nature of dogs supplied; and in place of horns or claws, a stronger and more piercing thing, iron, was invented by nature.

div.head: DE MOTIBUS MEMBRORUM ET EXTREMITATIBUS ANIMALIUM

cit.quote: Aristotle: animals of much motion necessarily need much sight. Motion, however, dissolves fat and is contrary to the coagulating power of fat. Every blood-having animal, if it has limbs arranged for motion, has only four, as in man there are two feet and two hands. In birds, two feet and two wings. In four-footed creatures, four feet. In fish, four fins. In serpents, however, and certain fish, since they are of long body, four would not suffice, and so they lack such limbs. Whence serpents crawl over the ground. Long fish, however, creep through the water and do not swim. It is proper to the serpent to move its head backward while the rest of the body remains still. Eyes of much opening signify foolishness and shamelessness. Nearly every animal closes its eye, not by will, but by nature, so that nothing falls upon it. But birds close the eye with the lower eyelid, walking creatures with the upper. The lizard kind, however, does not close it at all. Man closes his eye more than all other animals, since his skin is fine. Every animal having ears has them mobile, except man. The elephant moves its trunk, using it in place of a hand, as said above. Every animal moves the lower jaw except the seal and the crocodile, which move the upper. Man, indeed, and four-footed creatures move their jaws down and up and sideways, since they bite and chew or ruminate. Birds and fish, however, down and up but not sideways, since they do not chew, but only bite. The left hand in men, and the left foot in animals, is not of quick movement, except in the elephant. The elephant bends two feet and sits, and, propping itself on one side, sleeps. For it cannot bend all four. The lion and camel, when they walk, move the right foot first. Likewise four-footed creatures, once born, at once raise themselves on their feet and walk. A foal touches its head with its hind foot, but a horse cannot.

Augustine: I pass over that it is naturally implanted in certain animals that, if they sense something in any part of their body that must be driven off, they move that part alone, where they feel it, and shake off not only landing flies, but even lodged spears, by a tremor of the skin. Is it, then, because man cannot do this, that the Creator of all things could not give it to whatever living creatures he wished? But we know too the natures of certain men, remarkable for their very rarity, doing with their bodies what others cannot at all, and can scarcely believe even when they hear of it. For there are those who move their ears, singly or both together. There are those who, without moving their head, bring down their whole head of hair to the forehead and call it back when they wish. There are those who, of the incredibly varied and numerous things they have swallowed, bring forth, with a slight touch to the chest, whatever pleases them whole, as if from a bag. Some too imitate and reproduce the voices of birds and livestock and any other animals so well that, unless seen, they cannot be distinguished at all. Some too, from below, without any shame, produce so many varied sounds at will that they seem to sing even from that part. I have known a man accustomed to sweat whenever he wished. It is known that certain people, when they wish, shed tears abundantly.

Aristotle: male and female are the principles of animal generation. By definition, the male is that which can generate; the female, however, is that which can generate within itself, or rather that which generates from another. For the female does not generate by herself, since she needs the principle of motion, which is from the male. The female, however, is like matter. And in mating, indeed, nature makes one from male and female, and so one animal results. Empedocles says, moreover, that the cause of generating a male is a hot womb, but a cold one for a female, and so on, as will be said below. The young too generate more females, and likewise the old, and those who have moist bodies.
Gloss: because all such digest badly, which indigestion is the immediate and necessary cause; the causes assigned above, however, are neither proximate nor necessary.

Aristotle: all the inner members are the same in males and females, except the womb. Among all animals, the females have a finer, or thinner, voice than the males, except the cow. The voices of males, however, change when they are castrated. Males, too, are stronger than females, except in the bear and leopard, in which the opposite is true. And so the members suited to strength are not present, or less present, in females. Those, however, that are necessary are present in them too. A man's brain is larger than a woman's. Males too have more teeth than females, as is evident in men and goats and pigs. Woman and the mare, above all female animals, love mating, and so on, as will be said below. Generally, however, I say that wild males do not graze with the females before the mating season. In all, males are formed in the womb sooner than females. After birth, however, females grow and age sooner than males. It is not customary for males, however, to be concerned about their young, but for females. Internally, woman has more blood than the females of other animals, for which reason she has the menses; for this reason too she suffers less illness than man. Every female animal, however, urinates backward, and the female is naturally contrary to the male. Female stags have neither horns nor teeth. The hyena is an animal whose female has both member and vulva together. If a man has both the male and female organ, one will be principal, the other not.

Rhazes, in the Almansor: in all kinds of animals, females have a more base spirit and are less able to endure force, and are more timid and of worse character, and can be changed more quickly and are more quickly calmed; they are also of greater heat, hasty and shameless, have a small head, a fine face and neck, a narrow chest and shoulder-blades, and slender ribs, but thick hips and belly, and likewise nostrils. Their legs, however, are slender, their hands and feet fine.
Pliny: [on] the salamander, nor is there in these a male or female kind, just as there is not in all eels, which produce neither an animal nor an egg from themselves.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: in the Metaphysics, indeed, Aristotle says that male and female sex occurs in all animals, but in the book On Animals he makes an exception of a certain kind of fish in which a male has never been seen. This necessarily occurs because of the similarity of the parts of this fish. For when an animate body is entirely similar in its parts, or has minimal diversity, then the excess of food, from the final digestion, proceeds to produce such a body, nor is it necessary that it receive, beyond this, any further influence from the power of a specific organ. And so, since the organs of generation, by influencing a specific power into the excess of the fourth digestion, produce the distinction of male and female, there cannot be a distinction of sex in such an animal. And certain experimenters and natural philosophers say that this kind of fish is the eel, in which neither male nor female has ever appeared.

Aristotle: all castrated animals change into the nature of females. Not only their body, but their spirit too becomes effeminate, so that they differ little from females. And so, because of their weakness, the voices of castrated animals are similar to the voices of females, and indeed if a boy, that is, one not yet at puberty, is castrated, hairs will not grow in him where they should grow. But if he is castrated after the emission of seed in sleep, hairs of the pubic area alone will grow, but few, fine, and slender. Finally, when a man is castrated, either the hairs that grow last do not grow in him, or he sheds them, if he was castrated after their appearance, except the pubic hairs, since women too have hair there. Baldness, too, befalls no castrated man, because of the change of his body's complexion toward the complexion of a woman. When four-footed animals are castrated, the shape of their bodies changes, except in wild pigs. For all animals, if castrated in youth, become larger. If, however, after maturity, they will not grow further. Stags, if castrated before the growth of their horns, will not grow horns. But if after, they grow no further, nor do they shed them. Calves are castrated after one year. But if not castrated by that time, they will be small. If, however, in the castration of a calf a swelling occurs at the site of the incision, they will cauterize the testicle and place ash upon it. Often too the womb is cut out of sows, so that they need no mating, but quickly grow fat; they are, however, kept from food for two days, and then suspended by the hind feet, and what is called the 'antaron,' the place where the males' testicles are, is cut from them. Camels too, which men use for fighting, are castrated, since then they do not grow fat. Since, moreover, male and female are the principles of animal generation, when the member suited to mating is destroyed, the rest of the body will be altered along with it. For it must necessarily be altered along with the alteration of its own source. A castrated animal cannot produce offspring, since, when the testicles are cut off, the passages of the seed contract upward. It happens, nevertheless, that a certain bull mated suddenly right after being castrated, since the passages had not yet contracted.

Petrus Comestor: what Scripture, in Genesis, records the Lord as having said to the birds and fish, 'Increase and multiply,' should be understood also of these animals that were created on the sixth day, although it is not written; this is the common cause of the creation of all.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: the act most suited to the nature of every living thing is to generate its like in species. Animal too produces animal, and plant, plant, so that they may always share in the divine, that is, imitate the very perpetuity of divinity, insofar as they can. For all things desire that, namely the divine, and act for its sake, whatever they do according to nature, since, since they cannot always share in it, and in continuous divine union, because it does not happen to corruptible things to remain one and the same in number, according to what each can participate in, each thus shares - this one more, that one less - and so it remains, not the same thing, but its like, one not in number, but one in species.

The same, in the book On Animals: animals, indeed, are generated in earth and water, since in earth there is a part of water, and in water a part of air, and in these is the heat of the soul. The generation of animals, however, differs according to the species of their own nature. For some indeed generate and produce a complete animal, not in size but in form, like animals having hooves and paws, and, among fish, the dolphin. And every animal that generates its like has teeth and blood. Blood-lacking animals, indeed, do not generate simply; some, however, generate an incomplete animal, that is, undistinguished and unformed, like animals with much cleft in the foot. And what among these has blood makes eggs. What, however, lacks it, makes worms, which gradually complete themselves in their own species, like bees. Worms, indeed, and eggs differ, since in eggs an animal is generated from one part, and the remainder will be food for the newborn. Worms, however, pass entirely into the substance of what is generated, and some produce complete eggs, like birds and four-footed creatures, like the tortoise, the small lizard, and many kinds of serpent. Others, however, incomplete ones, like the soft-shelled fish and cuttlefish kind.

Aristotle: the sustaining, that is, the generation, of hard-shelled animals occurs in some by itself, in some through another power going out from them, that is, from those generating, as in trees. Some are generated from seeds, some from the tree's trunk, some from branches. Everything generated by itself, however, is generated from putrefied matter mixed with its own watery element, since what remains from the excess of the first sustenance gathers and takes on form. In these, the putrefied matter is, as it were, the mother, and the heavenly heat, as it were, the mover or father. There is, moreover, much of the earthy part in the sea, from which hard-shelled creatures are generated, since the part containing what is conceived is congealed and hardened all around, just as horns and bones congeal. And these things do not melt in fire, no more than bones do. Nor has any of these kinds ever been seen to mate, except the kind called 'cailion.' Nor has it yet been observed whether such creatures are generated from mating, or not. Of these, that is, of hard-shelled animals, whose shell is softened neither by water nor fire, the food will come from a member, like that of what is generated from eggs, and their growth is like that of worms. For the beginning of a worm's growth is from the upper part, but its food from the lower. This is evident in the first formation of bees and creatures like them, since the lower part is small, but the upper large. So too a hard-shelled animal grows first in its upper part, and the front of that part, the member called the head, becomes larger than the rest of the body.

Pliny, book 10: we have it from many that a snake is born from the marrow of a man's spine. For very many kinds, even of four-footed creatures, arise from a hidden and obscure origin, like the salamander, an animal of lizard shape, starred, arising only from heavy rains and failing in fair weather; this creature, born from what is not itself born, produces nothing in turn, nor is there in it a male or female kind, just as there is not in all eels, which generate neither an animal nor an egg from themselves. Neither is there such a kind in oysters and other creatures that cling to shallows or rocks. Those, however, that are generated by themselves, as males and females, have been described; they generate something by mating, but imperfect and unlike themselves, from which nothing further is produced, like the little worms of the fly. Further, the generation of birds seems to be simple, although it too has its own wonders, as has been said above in the treatise on birds.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: further, there are many kinds of worms, as has also been said above. They are born more from corruption than from seed. Whence they begin with summer and end with summer. There is, however, another kind that begins with summer and, once it has laid its seed on trees or in dwellings, ends its life with summer. And the seeds remain once the parents are dead through the winter, and, as spring's season comes on, with the mildness of the air and the sun's warmth, are quickened to life. There is also another kind that hides itself in winter and lies hidden as if dead, and when summer comes is renewed to life.

Constantine the African: [on] animals: the Creator, then, wishing the animal kind to remain firm and stable and not perish, arranged for it to be renewed through mating and generation. There are, moreover, three things in mating: appetite, arising from imaginative thought, and spirit, and moisture. Appetite from the liver, spirit from the heart, moisture from the brain. For since there is a pleasurable motion in mating, while all the body's members grow warm through motion, through that heat the moisture that is in the brain is liquefied, and, liquefied, is drawn through the veins that lead through the ears to the testicles, and from there, through the member, is cast into the womb. Whence Hippocrates says that those whose veins, which lead behind the ears, have been cut, once their seed is discharged, cannot generate. If, however, they emit something, it is not seed but a watery moisture. Whence no conception can occur.

Aristotle, in the passage above: slenderness and weakness of the legs suits mating, since the food passing there turns into seminal excess; hence a small-bodied bird mates much and lays many eggs, since its growth turns into seed. Men too who have much hair at the hips and on the lower part of the feet mate much. But when a man mates much, his eyes are weakened; there is also an animal that mates with difficulty, whence the female cries out in mating, and blood comes from her eyes, and she gives birth with difficulty. Every animal, at mating time, calls its mate by its own voice, and especially the frog. In those mating, moreover, their voices change, whence the change of voice is a sign of the impulse to mate.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: on the various ways animals mate, too, mention has been made above, through various chapters.

Aristotle: man, and living creatures that live with man, mate at any time. But every four-footed creature desires mating more in spring. Man naturally begins to mate after two periods of seven years, but does not yet generate, except rarely and weakly. The menses, however, cease in a woman after forty years, but in some remain until fifty. Nor has a woman ever been seen who gave birth after fifty years. Men, too, generate up to sixty years, and perhaps up to seventy. The ram and he-goat mate at one year, and especially the boar, but produce something weak. The dog and pig mate at eight months, but produce something weak. The ewe mates after one year, and gives birth up to nine years, or up to eleven, that is, her whole life, if well kept. In Ethiopia a sheep lives fourteen years, a goat eleven, and mates its whole life and bears twins, if the food is suitable and the ram or he-goat is vigorous. The horse mates at two or three years, but produces something weak. It is strong, however, from four years to twenty, and what it generates is strong. It mates and lives, however, up to thirty or thirty-five years. The mare, however, lives up to forty years, and mates, and desires mating to the point of frenzy. The donkey mates after twenty months, but after two years or two and a half, produces offspring. The camel mates after one year, and its female is pregnant for a year. The male elephant mates after five years, the female after twenty, and is pregnant for two years. Once pregnant, however, she is not touched at all by the male; after giving birth, she rests for three years. The pig mates at any time, that is, both winter and summer, day and night. The sow, however, is pregnant for four months. The ox mates after one year, and perhaps after eight months; after two years, however, it can impregnate.

Aristotle: in all animals, indeed, there is appetite and pleasure in mating. Woman, however, and the mare love mating above all females greatly. For the mare desires mating to the point of frenzy. Generally, however, I say that wild males do not graze with females before the mating season. It happens, moreover, in men and in four-footed creatures desiring mating, that they suddenly emit seed at a touch or even a sight. Animals are warlike at mating time, the males among themselves, though before this they were peaceful. Bulls fight over a cow, and the victor mounts the female. Boars too fight each other to the death at mating time. The cow, however, cannot be tamed at mating time. She flees mating, however, because of the hardness of the male's member. The camel, at mating time, is wild and fierce, and stays alone with the female, riding her the whole day beyond mere mating. But hook-clawed birds do not mate much. The turtledove is joined to only one mate for life, and the wood-pigeon does not mate again if it loses its partner. The 'cubech,' too, though a lustful bird, still each male takes only one female. The elephant, as has been said, does not touch a pregnant female. The female herself rests for three years after giving birth. But the she-camel too rests from mating itself for a year after giving birth. The camel, though lustful, does not recognize its own mother: once, indeed, with its mother's head covered, it mounted her, and, the covering removed, recognizing its mother, broke off the shameful act it had begun, came down, and killed the one who had contrived it. The same happened with a horse which, recognizing its substituted mother, fled and threw itself down a cliff.

Pliny: serpents mate in an embrace, so entwined together that a single two-headed creature might be thought to exist. The male viper inserts his head into the female's mouth, which she, in the sweetness of pleasure, gnaws off. Crocodiles, male and female, take turns brooding: only among men is there repentance for the first act of mating - an omen, as it were, of life from a regretted origin. For other animals, mating is fixed to certain seasons of the year. For man, as has been said, at every hour of day and night. For other animals there is satiety in mating; for man, almost none. Among men, diversions of lust have been devised - every crime against nature - and for women, abortion, so much more harmful are we in this regard than wild beasts. Hesiod reported that men are more eager for love in winter, women in summer. They say that sows, in mating, pour foam from the mouth on hearing the boar's grunt as it goes into heat, and, unless allowed to mate, refuse food to the point of wasting away. Females become so frenzied that they tear at a man, especially one dressed in white. This rage, however, is calmed by sprinkling vinegar on the animal's private parts. Eagerness for mating is thought to come from food, as arugula does for a man, onion for livestock. Pregnant four-footed creatures refuse mating, except the mare and the sow.

Aristotle, in the passage above: if one may wonder how small animals conceive many young from one mating, and not rather one large one, the reason for this is that they emit more seed than suffices for a single formation. Any kind of animal has a determined size to which it grows and does not exceed. For this reason too, from that excess of seed and matter, many are created, not one. For the male's power can create and sustain the female's excess in many parts, even if there is moderation in both. But even in large animals generating one offspring, if the male has produced much seed and the female's excess has been abundant, even two offspring will be created from them. Man, however, is between these two kinds. For he naturally generates one, but because of the heat and moisture of the body, may perhaps generate many, since the nature of seed is hot and moist. From one mating, then, if he produces much seed, and it divides, many children will be generated. A hairy-footed animal, like the hare, conceives a second time and bears complete offspring, because of the abundance of seed. For this reason too men of much hair mate much.

Aristotle: the pig, then, generates twenty young, and often in one year. The dog too generates twelve at once. And often the lioness likewise; for she first bears six or five, then four, then three, then two, and after this one, and finally none. In Ethiopia sheep and goats bear twins. Likewise among birds too there is a diversity in generation, as has been said above. In sheep too twins occur, of which two are yellowish. Large animals are almost never impregnated again after the first pregnancy; the reason for this is that the excess passes into the growth of the first conceived, which must be large, since the conception is large, as the offspring of an elephant is as large as a bull. Animals of many offspring, however, are impregnated again after the first, the reason for which is the smallness of the body, namely of the fetus, and the wideness of the womb and the abundance of seed and menses; this also happens to woman, since she has an affinity with animals of many offspring, because of the abundance of excess matter. Nor is there any large animal that receives a second mating after the first, except woman and the mare: and this because of the size of the womb and the hardness of its material. But the second conception will not be completed because of scarcity of food. And so these two kinds love mating because of the sensitivity of the womb and its sinewy nature.

Pliny: [on the number of offspring of] elephants, camels, horses, the linnet, twelve at a time, the smallest bird. Above all, however, the offspring of mice, although, on the authority of Aristotle and Alexander the Great's soldiers, their generation is said to occur by licking, not by mating. From one female, they reported, a hundred twenty are born, and they think they become pregnant from tasting salt.

Aristotle: in animals there is no milk before pregnancy. Every kind, moreover, has a time suited to its fertility and to the goodness of its condition. And so, when the north wind blows, males are generated; when the south wind, females: this happens in sheep and goats. For if they are impregnated against the blast of the north wind, they bear males; if against the south, females. No female, however, receives mating after pregnancy, except woman and the mare. And the periods of pregnancy of other animals are fixed, but those of men are many and various. The spans of pregnancy of other animals are fixed not according to their lifespans, but according to the size of the animal conceived, since a large-bodied animal cannot be formed in a short time; for this reason the elephant's pregnancy is extended over two years. Rightly, indeed, the spans of pregnancy and life of all kinds of animals are distinguished according to the revolutions of the stars, and their durations counted accordingly. For even the winds do not move or rest except according to the revolutions of sun and moon. We see, moreover, the sea and all watery things stand still or move according to the motion and rest of the winds, and it is necessary that the motion of lesser things follow the motion of nobler ones. Finally, tempered heats and colds suit the modes of generation, and after this suit corruption. Naturally, then, the number of periods of generation and their completion will be according to the revolutions of the stars. And so the she-camel is pregnant for a year, the female elephant for two years, the cow, however, for nine months. The sow for four months. The female dog, however, for sixty days, or seventy, or a hundred and ten. The female dolphin for ten months. Woman is pregnant for nine months, or seven, or eight.

div.head: DE DISTANTIA MULIERIS PREGNANTIS A FEMINIS CETERORUM ANIMALIUM

cit.quote: The same: in most women, indeed, the condition worsens at the time of pregnancy, but not in other females. Woman and the mare miscarry at the smell of an extinguished candle; further, because of an abundance of food, fruit on trees and offspring in animals is spoiled too. Pregnant women too suffer miscarriage sooner from rest, since a bad condition befalls them because of this, while much excess matter gathers in them. In those who labor, however, it is not so, since labor makes much of the excess evaporate, so that the woman, at the time of birth, will be able to hold her breath. When she does this, birth will be easy, and when not, the opposite. The females of other animals, however, remain of much bodily fertility for a long time after pregnancy. And so miscarriage does not happen to them. Further, women menstruate much. Other animals, little or not at all. Certain women, however, at the beginning of pregnancy, grow very tired and sick because of the retention of the menses, since, because of the smallness of the conceived, the excess is not consumed in them, which is consumed more at the end, in the food of the fetus, and then their bodies improve. In other animals, however, the excess is small, tempered according to the need for growth of the conceived. The illness called 'mola,' too, befalls pregnant women and not other animals, since a woman's womb, compared to other animals, is continuous, and the blood gathered in it is abundant, and cannot be digested. When, then, the sustenance of the conceived comes from vapor and moisture of poor digestion, then a mass is generated in the womb, called 'mola.' A sick and pained woman cannot be impregnated, and if she is, she loses the fetus. A female, properly, is not impregnated except when the place, that is, the womb, is suited for motion.

div.head: DE TRANSFUSIONE SEMINIS IN PREPARATIONE EMBRYONIS

cit.quote: Aristotle: seed, indeed, comes out from the animal thick and white, and after it is cooled becomes moist and watery; the cause of its whiteness is nothing but foam. For foam is of white color, since it is sustained by small parts and hidden bubbles, and when the bubbles are finer and more hidden, the foam becomes whiter. So too oil, when mixed with air, thickens, and silver dross mixed with oil and water becomes clear and grows because of the mixed air, just as happens with foam and snow, since snow too is a kind of foam. Water too, when mixed with oil, thickens and whitens, since air enters it from motion, and much air enters from the oil itself too. For in the fatness of oil there is nothing of water and earth, but of air, for which reason it floats on water, since the air in it carries it as if it were in a wineskin. In cold weather, indeed, it thickens, but does not coagulate, because of the air. Finally, the ancients, knowing that the nature of seed is foamy, also named the goddess of seed the 'foamy one,' namely Venus. Seed, however, does not come from the whole body, nor as a part of what is generated, but is like a mover and a form. Nor does a man's seed correspond to the size of the animal, but to its quality. With the seed, indeed, goes out a spirit, which is the power of the soul's principle, and the seed has in conception a soul potentially, but not actually. The womb, however, draws the male's seed because of the heat that is in it, and sustains it. When, however, it has been sustained, it goes out from the female through the male's power, just as happens in milk through the power of rennet, since the nature of milk and rennet is the same; moisture will go out around the body, whose earthy parts, once dried, become the containers of the conceived, so that the animal is not in the moisture, but distinct from it. They are dried, however, necessarily when heated, and afterward cooled. Some of these are called the afterbirth, which indeed directly holds the fetus. Others, however, are membranes, which prevent moisture from entering the afterbirth. Such is the case in animals that generate a live animal and in egg-laying ones. When, moreover, the conceived has been sustained this way, what happens to seeds happens to it, namely of herbs and trees. For in these, when the primary power, that is, the vegetative, moving power, which was first in potential, appears in act, then branches arise and roots go out, through which it draws food, since trees too need formation and growth. According to this manner, then, the growth of all the members of the conceived will occur, after the primary power that is in it. For it already lives, as it were with a life similar to the life of a tree.

div.head: DE IMPRESSIONE FORMARUM VISARUM IN CONCEPTU

cit.quote: Jerome, on Genesis: Jacob, as is read, placed varied rods before the eyes of the sheep, so that, from the twofold desire or fervor, namely of drinking and of mating, they might conceive offspring such as the shadows of the rams and he-goats mounting them, which they gazed upon in the mirror of the waters. Nor is it strange that this is the nature of conception in females, namely that they conceive offspring resembling the image they beheld, in the heat of extreme pleasure, since this too is said to happen among the herds of mares among the Spaniards. Quintilian too, defending a matron accused of having borne an Ethiopian child, argued that this happened to her from a beheld image. It is read in the books of Hippocrates that a certain woman was about to be punished on suspicion of adultery, because she had borne a most beautiful child unlike either parent, had not the aforementioned physician resolved the question, advising them to look for whether such a picture might be in the bedroom. Once found, the woman was freed from suspicion.

Augustine, in the book on the Trinity, book 11: if an outward thing is regarded with great eagerness, as happens in the lustful gazes of women, it affects not only the sight itself, but even the rest of the living body more vehemently, and, where a harder or thicker material does not resist, it changes it into a similar appearance and color. Whence one may see the little body of the chameleon change with the greatest ease into the colors it beholds. In the case of other animals, however, whose flesh is not easily changed, the offspring often betray the lust of the mothers as being such as what they beheld with great delight, for the tenderer and more formable the beginnings of the seed are, the more effectively and readily they follow the intention or appetite of the mother's soul and the image formed in it through the body which she beheld with eagerness.

Aristotle, in the passage above: in Thrace there are two rivers, from one of which, drunk, sheep bear black lambs, but from the other, drunk, they bear white ones; there is also another from which they bear red ones.

Aristotle, in the passage above: and since, before its formation is completed in the womb, the embryo is distinguished into male and female, it is doubtful whether that difference comes from the male or the female, or from the locations in the womb - since the male will be on the right side, the female on the left? Empedocles says, however, that seed falling into a hot womb becomes male, but into a cold one becomes female. Democritus holds that this difference comes about according to the greater or lesser abundance of seed coming from the male. Further, certain men imagine that if the right part of the testicles is bound, a female will be generated, if the left, a male, which Lucan too said, but this is not correct, since many animals are generated without testicles, like the footless kind, such as the fish kind and serpents. The account of those, however, who imagine that heat and cold are the cause of generating male and female, and also of those who imagine that the cause of this is the exit of seed from the right or left side, has some element of truth in a certain way. For the right part is hotter than the left, and what is hotter is more digestible, but this is to assign a remote cause. According to the proximate cause, however, male and female are distinguished by a certain strength and weakness, or by the female's digestion and indigestion. For seed can digest something, and if this is the moving principle in it, it will necessarily be male. For seed is, as it were, the active agent, and the female's matter is, as it were, the passive one. And since everything digested is distinguished only by heat, the males of animals must necessarily be hotter than the females. When, then, the seed's heat cannot at first overcome, but is weak for digesting because of scarcity of heat, nor can it cause the embryo to resemble its own form, that is, the male sex, an alteration to the opposite necessarily occurs. The female, however, is contrary to the male, and since these two differ in power, they must necessarily differ in instrument too, since nature gives every member power together with instrument, and the male has his own instrument, namely the member suited to mating, the female her own, namely the womb. When, however, some principal member is altered, the sustenance of the whole animal is necessarily altered too, as is evident in castrated creatures, and one is called male only because he can; but weakness is attributed to the female. Strength and weakness, however, are attributed to food, since these are nothing but the digestion and indigestion of the final food. The cause of this, then, that is, of male and female, is the primary power existing in the member in which is the principle of natural heat; for this reason the heart's sustenance comes before that of other members, whether it is a male or a female that is being created.

Aristotle, in the passage above: seed, moreover, is the excess of the final food, that is, of the food passing into any member. Nor is there any difference between the statement that seed comes from any member, and the statement that seed passes into any member. And when the male's seed prevails, the son will be like the father, since it will bring him to its own form. But when it is overcome, then to the contrary form, that is, the female. And accidents attest to this. For the young and the old generate more females than others, since heat in the former, namely the young, is not yet complete. In the latter, however, namely the old, it is diminished. Moist, that is phlegmatic, bodies too, whose formation is similar to women's bodies, generate females. Likewise, when the north wind blows, a male is generated. But when the south or southerly wind, a female, since then bodies are moist, for which reason the seed multiplies and remains undigested.
