Shepherds say, moreover, that males and females are generated not only because of the north and south winds, but also because of facing toward those directions: the alteration, then, will perhaps be a small cause of the cold and heat that are the cause of the difference in generation. In men, however, more males are conceived by chance than females, since, because of the heat of their nature, they are of greater motion, and so injuries and fractures befall them; in other animals it is not so. For this reason too, that is, because of the strength of heat, there is a difference in the completion of the formation of males and females in the human kind, which does not appear in other animals, since there is no diminishment of the females of brutes compared to the males. And so males are distinguished in women's wombs in less time than females, since females are colder and so weaker. Femaleness, however, is a natural occasion; because of cold, then, they are distinguished slowly, since distinction is a certain mode of digestion, and heat digests. After birth, however, females grow and age sooner than males, likewise because of the weakness of their nature. For all smaller and weaker things reach completion sooner. When, however, a woman is impregnated with twins, and one is male, the other female, their distinction will not be equal, but the male's distinction will occur first. For this reason too they are less often saved, that is, they more quickly suffer miscarriage. It does not happen this way, however, in other animals: for the reasons stated, however, some children resemble the father and mother in their whole body, and some do not; some too resemble their fathers and not their grandparents, and perhaps the reverse. Perhaps too males will resemble females and females males. Some, however, resemble neither parent, but have a nature foreign to their own kind. But when the motion of the first generator prevails and works well in the excess of the menses, so that the embryo's form is completed by the male's motion, then the child born will be male, resembling his father.

Aristotle, in the passage above: all animals, indeed, have their principle within, for which reason the heart appears first distinguished in all blood-having animals, since it is the source of the members alike to one another, for what has generation grows by food, so that the final food is nothing but blood or what corresponds to it. The vessels of blood, however, are the veins, and their source is the heart. Since, then, an imperfect animal necessarily receives food from another place, namely from the womb, nature therefore draws two large veins from the heart, from which fine veins go out, reaching the womb, and from these the navel is formed. For the navel is a vein, in some one, in some many. Around them is a covering of skin, since it needs protection because of their weakness. The heart, then, is the first member in blood-having animals; in others, however, there is a member corresponding to it. This too is clear from the fact that the spiritual power remains last in the heart, as if nature proceeds by a circular path, and the inner members exist before the outer, and their size appears first. The upper part, too, is distinguished, which is from the wall upward, and is larger compared to the lower, which appears undistinguished. For the lower exists only through the upper, and for this reason, in the formation of the embryo, the head and eyes appear first, very large, but what is below the navel very small. Further, the animal that breathes, while it is within the womb, receives its distinction there, but does not breathe before the formation of the lung. The generation of like members in their parts, however, is sustained by heat and cold. For some coagulate from heat, some from cold. From the veins, then, and the passages that are in any given member, namely proceeding from the heart, food reaches its proper places. And the first thing that comes from that food will be flesh, or the member corresponding to it. The sustenance of flesh, however, is from cold, for which reason it is dissolved by fire. Earthy members, however, in which there is little moisture and heat, when heated, that moisture goes out from them and is dissolved by the abundance of earthy matter, like claws, horns, hooves, and paws: for this reason they soften in fire, and some do from moisture. From inner heat, however, veins and bones are dried; and so bones are not dissolved by fire, no more than an earthenware vessel is, since they are like things baked in a furnace. Bones, then, are formed from the heat of generation. Cold, then, is the food of heat, since nature uses both. Thus nature, then, works the individual members in various ways, and flesh will be soft, sinew dry and drawing, and bones dry and quick to fracture. Skin, however, is formed from the heat of the flesh, making moisture exhale while cold restrains it, just as happens with cooked things, when something inclining to dry rises above them. Nor is there any difference between skin and shell, except that in shell there is more of the earthy.

Aristotle, in the passage above: from very clean matter, then, the bodily instruments of sense are created. From excess matter, however, hairs, horns, hooves, claws and the like are sustained, for which reason their formation is last, namely when there is sustaining excess matter in the body. The nature of teeth, however, is like the nature of bones. Nevertheless, among all the bones, teeth alone continue to grow as long as the animal lives, for otherwise they would quickly be worn away. For indeed the teeth of animals that eat much and lack large teeth are quickly worn down. These also differ from bones, since the other bones are created from the primary sustenance of the body, that is, from seed. The formation of teeth, however, is from the final, that is, from food. The growth of any member, however, comes from the navel, as has been said above. In men, males are formed in the womb sooner than females. If the conceived is male, it takes shape in forty days, but a female in about seventy.

Aristotle: sometimes, indeed, when the motions of the active power are weak and do not overcome the matter, the universal shape indeed remains and there will be an animal, but it will perhaps have the head of a ram or a bull or something similar, and perhaps a calf will be generated having a man's head, or a lamb a bull's head. Such monstrosity occurs sometimes according to this manner, that is, through the mating of different species, or also through the manner of impregnation, that is, of coupling, namely an unnatural one. Something, moreover, is called a monster because of the multitude of its members and the diversity of its shape, since it will perhaps have many feet or many heads. Democritus imagines that a child is monstrous because of two seeds contained together in the womb, and this is true in birds, especially hens, whence sometimes two yolks are found in eggs, because of the gathering of seeds. And so, when no wall has divided between them, then a monstrous chick will be generated from them, having one head and one body, but four feet and four wings, since the upper part is formed first from the white and fed from the yolk, then the lower part is formed afterward, and there is one food, not divided by walls. But if there is a membrane dividing between the seed of the first mating and the second, there will be two chicks. Thus, then, from mating upon mating, twin or monstrous offspring are generated. A serpent having two heads has already appeared for this same reason, since the serpent too lays eggs and has many eggs, yet monstrosity is not found among them except rarely, because of the shape of the womb, since their eggs are arranged in a row in the womb because of its length. Further, this does not happen to bees and wasps, since each of their young is in a cell by itself.

Aristotle: and so we should think that monstrosity arises from matter, and for this reason is found in creatures generating many offspring, and especially in sheep and goats. In women, however, and in others, only rarely. In animals too of much-cleft feet, it occurs more than in others, because of the multitude of offspring, and because they do not bear a complete offspring, as the dog, which most often bears blind young. For multitude hinders the completion of formation, and that diminishment sometimes proceeds to a monstrous formation, which arises from an error in the working of nature. And perhaps a child will be born having many toes, or only one, and likewise in other members. Perhaps, too, it will have both a male member and a female one, which happens to women and to goats. A he-goat has already appeared having horns on its legs. Such alteration and diminishment is also found in the front members, since the formation of some is sometimes diminished, and sometimes an animal has been found lacking a heart or liver, or perhaps it will lack a spleen, or perhaps it will have a single kidney or two galls, or perhaps it will have the spleen on the right and the liver on the left. All this, as we have said, has been seen in complete, living animals. But what departs from nature lives a short time, and what departs much from nature does not live at all, especially if the alteration of nature is in the principal members. The cause of the generation of twins, however, is the same as the cause of superfluous members. For in the first conception, when much matter, that is more than is needed, is sustained in some member, it will happen that that member is larger than another, like a finger, hand, or foot; and perhaps, if the matter divides, the formation of twins will result from it, just as happens with the roots of trees struck by lightning, since they are divided in two, and from one root the sustenance of two trees results. That which happens to certain creatures too, that they have the nature of both male and female, comes also from the deviation of excess seed toward that part whose matter is, as it were, overcome in one part but not the other, and one member will be principal and the other not. Finally, it should be known that portentous occurrences among animals are signs of future events.

Isidore: among animals, moreover, those born from different kinds are called hybrids, as the mule from a mare and a donkey, the hinny from a horse and a she-donkey. The 'hibrida' from wild boars and pigs, the 'tityrus' from a sheep and a he-goat. The mouflon from a wild sow and a ram. It is, moreover, the leader of the flock. The Jews assert that Anah, grandson of Esau, was the first to have herds of mares mounted by donkeys in the desert, so that from this new animals, mules, might be born against nature. Wild asses too were admitted to she-donkeys for this purpose, and this coupling was found to produce, from them, the swiftest donkeys. So too Jacob, against nature, procured resemblances of coloring. For his sheep conceived offspring such as the shadows of the rams mounting from above, which they gazed upon in the mirror of the waters. Finally, this same thing is said to happen among herds of mares, that they expose noble-bred horses to the sight of females in heat, so that they may conceive and produce offspring resembling them. For lovers of doves too place painted, most beautiful doves in the places these birds frequent, so that, their sight captivated, they may breed like ones. Hence it is that some order pregnant women to look at no most ugly countenances of animals, like baboons and apes, lest, encountering such sights, they bear similar offspring. For it is the nature of women, that whatever they have looked upon, or conceived in mind, in the extreme heat of pleasure while conceiving, such offspring too they produce. For indeed the animal, in the act of love, transmits forms from outside within, and, sated with their impressions, carries their likeness into its own quality. And so human ingenuity has also forced different animals to mate, and thus, by adulterous mixture, has found another kind. For the Indians are accustomed to tie female dogs at night in the woods, exposed to tiger beasts, by which they are mounted, and dogs so bred, they say, are so fierce and strong that in a single grapple they can bring down lions. Wolf-dogs too, as Pliny says, are said to be born from wolves and dogs, when they happen to mate together. The leopard too is born from the adulterous union of a lioness and a pard.
Pliny, book 10: they order the manes of mares to be shorn, so that they will submit to mating with donkeys.
Aristotle, in the passage above: every animal differing in species from its parents is naturally sterile.

Gloss: like the mule and the hinny, for it is not necessary that they generate their like, since the mixture of species suffices for that purpose. For nature does nothing superfluous, but neither can it generate dissimilar things indefinitely, for otherwise the course through dissimilar things would go on to infinity, which nature rejects.

Aristotle: every animal generating few offspring can easily produce them, but such animals bear complete young, like those having hooves or paws. Animals of cloven feet, however, generate incomplete young and have many, and can produce them at the start, but when they have grown, do not feed them, but bear them as animals do that bear worms; perhaps, then, they will bear undistinguished, defective offspring, like the fox, the lion, and certain of these offspring will be blind. The sow, however, generates many complete offspring, since her nature is midway between the two aforementioned modes. For this animal is not large, like an animal having hooves. But the food that should pass into the body passes into the excess of seed and completes what she conceives, because of the goodness and fertility of her body. For she is like a tree planted in fat earth, having abundant food. Some animals, then, generate incomplete offspring because of a deficiency of food, as is evident in the children women bear in the seventh month. In this too, the time of pregnancy differs between man and other animals. For a woman gives birth in the seventh month, and in the ninth, and perhaps in the eighth, but dies more often in a larger birth. Strong pain befalls women properly at the time of birth. Other animals, however, not so. All the young of animals, when born, sleep, because of their habit of sleeping in the womb. And within the belly, indeed, up to the time of birth, they have their head turned upward; but when they move toward birth, they turn their head downward. Naturally, then, the exit of all animals is head-first, since the upper part is heavier than the lower, as happens with a scale, since the heavier part inclines toward the ground.

Pliny, in the passage above: among land creatures, the viper alone bears within herself eggs of a single color and soft, like a fish's. On the third day within the womb she hatches her young, then bears them one by one, each on a different day, about twenty in number. And so the rest, impatient of the delay, burst through her sides, killing the mother. Other serpents incubate laid eggs in the earth and hatch their brood the following year. Those that produce the most offspring give birth fastest. The larger the animal, the longer it is formed in the womb; those with longer lifespans are carried longer. Nor is the maturity for breeding proportional to growth. Those having solid hooves bear single young; those with cloven hooves bear twins - the more numerous the division of the toes of the feet, the more numerous the offspring. But all the aforementioned bear complete young; these bear them at an early stage. In this kind too are lionesses, foxes, and bears: shapeless indeed compared to the aforementioned; afterward they warm and shape their offspring by licking, and bear at most four at a time. Dogs, wolves, panthers, and jackals bear blind young. Dogs that conceived before the proper time keep their pups blind longer. Hares breed every month and superfetate, as do rabbits. For only the rabbit and hare superfetate, being filled and conceiving again immediately after giving birth, and, though their udders are drying from the litter already born, bear young not blind. Whatever animals bear young headfirst, do so with the offspring curled and braced; others bear them stretched out in the womb: four-footed creatures are carried with legs extended to their length and pressed against the belly. Man, however, curled in on himself between his two knees, with his nostrils pressed to them. Aristotle denies, contrary to popular belief, that among four-footed egg-laying creatures, lizards give birth through the mouth. Nor do they brood, having forgotten where they laid, since this animal has no memory at all; and so the young burst forth by themselves.

Aristotle: an animal's growth comes only from that in which it naturally delights, and that from which it is generated is the same as that from which it grows, that is, food. Fish grow fat in rainy seasons, and generally nothing grows well unless soaked by rain. Females grow and age sooner than males. In men, however, as has been said, males are formed sooner than females. A man's body grows for five years, as it were according to half of its full growth. The elephant grows for forty years and is the largest of all animals. The hind part is smaller than the front, except in man, in whom the upper part is proportional to the lower, though smaller in the decrepit, but the reverse in children, for which reason infants cannot lift themselves, since their upper part is larger and heavier than their lower. But when they grow up, the lower part grows more. In four-footed creatures it is the reverse. For when born, the lower part is larger than the upper, then the upper part grows more. And so four-footed creatures, once born, raise themselves at once and walk. For this reason too a foal touches its head with its hind foot, but a grown horse cannot. Likewise birds and fish have more flesh in front than behind; for this reason, then, every animal is of lesser intelligence than man, since the weight of the upper part diminishes intelligence, and for the same reason children are of lesser intelligence, since they have a thick and heavy head. Large-bodied animals generate one offspring, and small-bodied ones many, since much food passes into the growth of the body, and so only a little remains from it, namely that from which seed is generated. What nature diminishes in number, it adds in size, and conversely, for it does nothing superfluously. Children have no seminal cause. Whence they do not go bald, no more than women do. Man, however, and the horse go bald in old age, for the cause stated above. Other animals, however, by no means. The young among animals are stronger than children, since children's joints are not strong, nor their sinews; likewise nor are the old's. The voice of young animals too is sharper than the voice of old ones, except the calf, in which the opposite occurs. Likewise in the young the blood is thin, watery, and abundant. In the old, however, thick, dark, and scanty. Haired animals, when they grow old, their hairs harden. Likewise the plumage of birds. The shells or skins of animals, however, thicken and harden then, because of the diminishing of heat and the passing of moisture with heat, hardening more. For cold does not only harden, but also thickens and condenses the body. A very fat animal ages quickly and generates little and has many mischances; in the first age and in old age, and in the sick, there is no seed.
Gloss: in the first age, indeed, since food passes into the growth of the body. In old age, however, and in the sick, because of the weakness or scarcity of heat.

Aristotle, in the book on plants: in every animal and plant and mineral, when the matter of moisture is finite, dryness comes in place of moisture because of the predominance of indigestion. For digestion occurs where moisture and heat sometimes reach an end. And there will be indigestion in stones and minerals, but in animal and plant not so, since their parts are compact, whence flux comes from them; in minerals there is no flux or sweat, since their parts are not porous, and so nothing goes out from them, as certain excesses do from animal and plant, since heat draws moisture to the extremities, and the matter is dispersed through all its parts, and what is in excess flows out; just as in a bath, heat draws moisture, which, turned into vapor, rises, and when in excess turns into drops, so in animal and plant, excesses rise and again descend in their workings.

The same, in the book On Animals: in large-bodied animals, indeed, it is necessary that the excess be small, and so they are of little generation, since the excess passes into the size of a body needing much food. All excesses have places in the body, known; the place of dry excess is the lower intestine, and of moist excess, the bladder. The place of seed, however, is the womb, and the places suited to mating are the testicles and the member. The place of milk, however, is the breasts. There is also something else leaving the body not by the path of a needed excess, but by the path of dissolution, nor does it have a natural place in the body, but wanders by chance, namely like sweat and the like.

The same, in the book On Animals: from the moist excess of small veins, indeed, comes sweat, nor does it occur except when the body grows warm and the openings of the veins open. Now indeed, in certain men, bloody sweat occurs because of a defect of complexion, since their body was very porous and prone to flux, and the blood very moist and watery because of the weakness of heat in the small veins. For blood, when digested, thickens. Heat, however, cannot digest because of the abundance of that food.

Avicenna, in the second canon: sweat is the wateriness of blood, more choleric, and more digested than urine. For it is the excess of oiliness and moisture after the final digestion. Urine is the excess of the second digestion. Heat, however, differs according to animals, and in it is no small dissolving power. The sweat of athletes benefits swellings of the groin and dissolves them. The dry sweat of wrestlers, with henna oil, dissolves swellings of the breast; with rose oil, however, it is applied for the congealing of milk in the breast. Further, the grime of wrestlers, which gathers on their bodies when they are anointed with oil and mixed with dust, or that which gathers on the walls from their vapors and sweats, is effective for sciatica. It also benefits hardness of the womb.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: the sweat of venomous beasts is poisonous, and from drinking it the face turns green and swells, and a foul-smelling sweat runs from the body and from the armpits. Its treatment is vomiting with warm water and theriac of sealed earth.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: some think that the tear [lachryma], as Isidore says, is named from the laceration [laceratione] of the mind, since it is wont to proceed from mental grief, and to show, in a certain way, the mind lacerated by the affection of sorrow. But this is only in man, endowed with a rational mind; yet some other animals too are found to have wept from a similar feeling. A tear, moreover, is a drop or droplet, liquid, clear or salty, flowing from the eyes, sometimes indeed from anger and indignation, sometimes from anguish or pain of heart or body, sometimes from pity or compassion, sometimes proceeding from desire or joy or love.
Isidore, in the book of Etymologies: only the horse, besides man, is said to weep and to feel the affection of grief. And so, when their masters are killed or dying, many horses shed tears.
Gregory the Great, in the Morals: saliva slides into the mouth from the head, and from the mouth is led to the stomach when it is swallowed.

Avicenna, in the fourth canon: saliva differs according to the species and complexions of individuals. Its power is entirely maturing and dissolving; it cleanses eye-films and freckles and dead blood, and resists venoms too, and the spittle of a fasting man kills scorpions. Likewise impetigo is rubbed with a fasting man's spittle and camphor. The same, dripped into an ear afflicted by worms, kills them and expels them at once.

Aristotle, in the passage above: every female animal urinates backward. Among males of four-footed creatures, those that urinate backward are the elephant, lion, camel, and hairy animals. But an animal having hooves and urinating backward cannot exist. Birds do not urinate, since they drink little, and what remains of moisture passes into plumage. Likewise neither do fish, nor generally any egg-laying creature.

Avicenna, in the passage above: urine is hot and dry. All of it, moreover, is cleansing. And so it cleanses vitiligo, benefits nerve pains, and especially the urine of domestic and mountain goats, specifically for spasm and stretching or tetanus. Likewise, congealed in a bronze vessel, it benefits the white film of the eye and scabies, especially children's urine. Likewise boiled with leeks. Urine sediment benefits erysipelas as a suppository. Applied, it also benefits scabies and scab and venomous ulcers, ulcers of the feet. Among urines, indeed, the most beneficial is the urine of the Arabian camel. Human urine, however, is weaker than the rest; yet weaker than that are the urines of castrated domestic pigs, and stronger than these are those of old ones. Further, the urine of a castrated man is weaker than the urine of every other kind. Among urines, however, the most cleansing is human urine. There are, moreover, medicinal urines - human, donkey's, camel's, goat's, bull's, pig's, dog's, hare's, lynx's - of which more will be said below, each in its place.

bibl.author: Etymologiarum sive Originum Isidori libri XX

cit.quote: From the Etymologies, book 11: dung is the filth that flows out from an animal's purging.
Haly Abbas: [on] the animal. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Avicenna: duck's [dung] is not used because of the excess of its heat. That of the hawk and kestrel and other raptors is rarely used, since they are of too much excess matter. Used in medicine, however, are the dung of man, horse, mule, donkey, ox, goat, pig, dog, locust, mole, mouse, lizard, crocodile. Among birds, that of the hen, dove, stork, thrush, wood-pigeon, vulture, and swallow.

Augustine: what is more contemptible than dung? Yet it brings such benefit to fields that the Romans thought divine honors should be paid to its discoverer, Stercutius, from whom too dung took its name.
Palladius: [on the dung] of geese, donkeys, sheep, goats, beasts of burden. Pig's, dove's, of marsh birds. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Aristotle: the ancients said seed was that which comes out from the whole body, proving this too by the fact that the greatest pleasure is in it, and that from the perfect the perfect is generated, and likewise the reverse. And since offspring resemble their parents, not only in natural formation, but even in accidental features, and many offspring have marks resembling their parents, in the same places. We, however, say that seed is that which has the nature of being suited to the whole, and not coming from the whole. They said that seed is a dissolution of the body. We, however, say it is the needed excess, and it is better that it be the final one too. For that it follows the path of excess and not the path of dissolution is shown by the sign that large-bodied animals are of little generation, since much must necessarily be dissolved in them and little left as excess, for the reason stated above. Everything, moreover, that is dissolved from the body is corrupted, changes its nature; further, what is dissolved has no natural place in the body, but wanders by chance. Likewise dissolution always weakens, but the emission of seed relieves. And seed does not come from the male alone, but seed together with an excess, which is bad and weak; for this reason many men do not generate. Seed, however, is not present in the young because of growth, for seed passes into the growth of the body. Nor is it present in the old, because of indigestion, since their nature cannot digest well; nor in the sick, because of weakness. Some, however, are of much seed, some of little, some of none at all - not because of illness, but for the opposite reason, for when they are healthy and of much flesh, they produce little seed and desire mating rarely; the same happens to women too, for the excess in fat bodies is digested and passes into fat. Such an occasion also happens in fertile vines because of the abundance of food, since their fruit diminishes and spoils. And so goats, when they grow very fat, mate only rarely; wise shepherds thin them before mating, likewise growers do for fertile vines. It is clear, then, that seed is the needed excess of food, and of the final food, namely of blood-food, which is spread through the members and gives them great vigor. And so seed weakens the body, and, once digested and cooked, comes out changed and altered, namely white, not in the color of blood, unless it comes out undigested. When, however, a man engages eagerly in much mating, blood-colored seed comes out. Children, rightly, are like their fathers and parents, since what came out from the members is like what remained. And so seed, although in it no distinction of members appears, is nevertheless potentially similar to any member. Seed multiplies in a body whose complexion is hot and moist. Every animal of much tallow is of little seed. Man, however, among other animals, in proportion to his body, is of much seed; natural and accidental moisture, indeed, is suited to the generation of seed. The heat of the sun and animal heat, then, are in seed, and so on.

The same: the menses in females is similar to seed in males. Nor is it anything other than undigested seed; but it is not suited to generation, since if it is seed, it will not be menses, and conversely. A sign of this is that the nature of females is weak and of less heat, and their bodies are softer and lighter and of less hair than the bodies of males. They are also smaller in every kind of animal that generates a live animal. Nor is there an outflow of menses except in these kinds alone. But the generation of seed and of menses does not occur by the same path. Nor is offspring from the mixture of two seeds, since a woman is often impregnated without pleasure at mating time, and sometimes both man and woman produce seed, and yet nothing is generated from them unless there is, in the womb, moisture tempered from the residue of the menses; for this reason a woman does not conceive at all while menstruating, nor when she menstruates heavily. Egg-laying animals do not menstruate, because of the dryness of their bodies. Animals that generate a live animal, however, expel moisture, except in those that occur by chance in generation, like the mule kind. The flux of blood, however, is not manifest in the females of other animals, as it is in women. For internally a woman has more blood than the females of other creatures, and so has the menses; for this reason too she suffers less illness than man. Nursing mothers do not menstruate at all, or only slightly. Those, however, who lack the menses are, for the most part, sterile.

Isidore, book 11: milk [lac] is derived from the Greek, for whiteness. For the Greeks call white 'leucon.' Milk, indeed, and blood are that which nourishes and that which is nourished. For we are fed by milk, we live by blood. Cheese [caseum], moreover, is so called as if 'careum,' since it lacks [careat] whey. For all the whey is drawn off from it, as is shown by its weight.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: milk is a moisture separated in animals after pregnancy. Sometimes, however, as Aristotle says, it also breaks out in males, but does not appear because of the thickness of its formation. The milk of dark-skinned women is better than that of fair ones. In goats, however, the opposite is true.

Aristotle: sheep, above all animals, give milk for a long time, namely eight months; certain pastures, however, lessen milk, and certain increase it, like those that are inflating, such as bean, which suits goat and cow. The sign of an abundance of milk before birth, moreover, is the sagging of the udder downward. Among fish, the dolphin has milk in its breasts and suckles its young.

Isaac Judaeus, in the Diets: milk has a tempered complexion in heat and moisture, which are in the first degree. Whence it is less moist than fish and phlegm-generating; and it is close to blood, being nothing but blood cooked a second time in the breasts. It has, however, from the breasts, whiteness, flavor, and suitability. This same milk is divided into three kinds: for it is either sweet, coming out close to the breast, or sour, or midway between these. The sweet kind is less hot than the middle of the first degree and the beginning of the second. Its flavor shows this, and its closeness to the flavor of blood and its easy changeability into blood. Whence it is less moist than fish, and far removed from phlegm. And so its nourishment is more praiseworthy and easily assimilated to flesh and other members. Milk should not be taken, however, unless the body is tempered and the stomach emptied of choleric and phlegmatic humors. For if the body is cleansed of these, and the milk well digested, it gives much nourishment, generates praiseworthy blood, increases flesh, and moistens the whole body praiseworthily, softens the outer parts and makes them beautiful. Whence Rufus says: those drinking milk should be fasting, and it should be drunk warm as it comes from the udder; nor should anything be eaten until it is digested, and excessive labor and motion should be avoided. For if it finds the stomach weakened by too much motion, the milk is expelled before it is digested; but if it finds it strong, it is changed into corruption.

Aristotle: an animal's milk is entirely in the breasts. The breasts, however, are present in an animal that is generated either within or without. Nursing and pregnant women do not menstruate, since the nature of milk and menstrual blood is the same. Nor can nature provide matter sufficient for two things at once, namely the outflow of the menses and of milk. But when that excess passes into one part, it will be cut off from the other, unless something contrary to nature occurs. And since food for the conceived can no longer pass through the navel, because of its size, then milk is prepared, and again, when the passage of food is no longer through the navel, the veins over which the membrane called the navel is placed contract at once, for which reason nature comes out elsewhere. And so it is not said that there is milk before the time of birth, nor much after, unless it happens contrary to nature. Since, then, the time of birth of other animals does not vary, the digestion and completion of milk will occur at that time. The time of women's birth, however, varies, and so milk must necessarily be good after the seventh month. For now the part of good digestion, which was previously taken, will no longer be taken from her, and is no longer needed. For the food of all animals is nothing but sweet and very digested, and what remains from it is salty and of poor digestion. And so milk before that time is of that kind, but then good milk gathers in women's breasts and in the upper places, because of the order of sustenance, since in the place that is above the wall is the principal member, in which is life, and the upper place is proper to food and excess. From these places, then, for the reasons stated, the excess of seed too will occur, which is of blood-nature. In that kind of animal, indeed, there will be milk before pregnancy, and there is no benefit in the first or the last. Females that are not pregnant, however, sometimes have milk in their breasts from the herbs they eat, and this occurs rarely. In certain regions too, the goat's pregnancy is not awaited, but her udder is rubbed with nettle, and first blood comes out, then something like discharge, afterward good milk, no worse than milk from pregnancy. In the breasts of males too, milk is sometimes found, but little when pressed out, and if by chance much is pressed out, this happens to few, and rarely.

Isaac Judaeus: milk differs in four ways: either according to the animal's nature, or its pasture, or the seasons of the year, or its freshness and age. From the animal's nature, since it is either from a temperate, well-fleshed animal, and this is better, especially if newly milked from the breasts. Or from a sick, poorly complexioned, and lean animal, and such milk is worse and generates unpraiseworthy blood, especially if milked long ago. From pastures, however, it differs, since some animals feed on tender, fresh herbs, and these have watery, fine milk, harmful to the stomach. Others feed on dry things and the tips of branches, and these have less watery milk, not loosening but astringent and strengthening to the stomach, like goats. According to the seasons of the year, milk differs, since at the start of spring it is finer and resembles water, for then the animals are near giving birth and watery humors gather in the womb, with which it must be mixed. And so at this time watery milk is harmful to the stomach, causing disgust and vomiting, softening and loosening the stomach's roughness, whence it also loosens the bowels. But after forty days, until the end of spring and the beginning of that age, that thick moisture is consumed and, obeying its function, is tempered. For it is now perfectly digested in the breasts and becomes praiseworthy and nourishing. At the end of summer, however, and the beginning of autumn, the heat of the air increases, and so the moisture lessens and the milk becomes thick, hard to digest, and astringent. Whence this kind of milk especially coagulates in the stomach, and the worst illnesses are generated, since, smoke rising to the head, suffocations occur, and difficulty of breathing, and the whole head aches. But if it reaches the end of autumn, its own substantial moisture is now properly consumed and thickened. It differs according to freshness and age, since it is either newly milked, or already old, or in between. Newly milked, it is hotter and more tempered, yet close to the animal's own nature. Whence it will be more praiseworthy and nourishing food, especially taken as it should be. Milk already long milked, however, has departed from the nature of sweet milk toward coldness and natural dryness, like vinegar from wine, to which, when milk arrives, it is hard to digest for a tempered stomach. The harder it is, then, for the cold stomach, yet for the hot stomach it is medicinally somewhat, or a little, beneficial; taken in quantity, it gives thick and bad nourishment. It generates stone and gravel in the kidneys and bladder. Yet it does not coagulate in the stomach as the sweet does, since two qualities have already been taken from it, moisture and heat. Whence coagulation too is removed. Milk in between these, however, is slower than the sweet to digest, and quicker than the sour. Its butteriness removed, it will be more nourishing than other milk, especially cow's.

Avicenna: the better milk is that drunk sucking from the udder, and, of that, the better is of vehement whiteness, of even substance, which, dripped on a fingernail, stays fixed and does not run, and when the animal's own pasture is good and there is no foreign taste in the milk itself, like bitter or sharp, nor a horrible smell. And it should be administered as soon as it is milked, before it changes.
Haly Abbas, in the second part of the Royal Book: better milk is of clean whiteness, tempered liquidity, from a healthy animal's body, not too far from giving birth.

Dioscorides: plain milk is good, loosening to the belly and generating good humors, but it causes bloating of the stomach and softness of the inner organs. Snow-white and rich milk is good. And spring milk is better than summer. All boiled milk binds the belly, especially if stones have been boiled in it. Boiled milk benefits wounds of the intestines. Milk tempered with honey and part water, however, is effective for ailments of the intestines, kidneys, and bladder, and for itching too and bad chyme; salt too should be added to this, since salt does not let the stomach bloat. Milk, indeed, is of great value for nourishment, especially when natural heat is present in it, and first of all the milk of well-nourished women. After this, however, sheep's milk is contrary to those with spleen and liver ailments, to all nerve troubles and fevers and headaches and vertigo sufferers and epileptics. If, however, it is given as a purgative, it does no harm, like milk artfully boiled. All milk, moreover, has a scum, which is separated by boiling; this, if taken, loosens the belly more, and especially benefits the melancholic and leprous. Fresh milk is contrary to poisons taken and to those with fever. And it benefits those who have drunk cantharides or henbane. All milk, however, helps better if sucked directly, since it nourishes more and does not spoil easily. Milk just milked, drunk, soothes all bloating. Likewise all milk benefits the sharp discharge of the eyes, and if applied externally with egg-yolk and rose oil in inflammation of the eyes, it induces sleep and calms pain.

Avicenna, in the passage above: sour milk is cold and dry, of raw humor and very slow digestion; it constricts choleric flux and blood, and often expels hectic fevers when its butter is removed and it is so prepared that it is well digested.

Avicenna, in the canon: corrupted milk, which turns, on the path of sourness, toward another kind of putrefaction, is poison, and from it come vertigo and fainting and a stinging in the mouth of the stomach; sometimes too a fatal choleric affliction results from it. Its treatment, however, is to vomit with honey-water, then drink pure wine with 'diapiperon,' and steam the stomach with spikenard oil. Further, milk sometimes congeals in the stomach because of some harmful, congealing cause, either because of a strong preparation in the milk itself, or because of drunk rennet. And from it come cold sweat and fainting and rigor fevers. And such congealing is a poison, like the congealing of blood, being of the same kind. From it, in turn, comes coldness of the body and smallness of the pulse and suffocation constricting the breath, and sometimes inflammation of the belly. For its treatment, dry calamint is given as a drink, and it dissolves it at once by its own power, since it also prevents milked milk from coagulating and preserves it. Something from rennet too is given as a drink. For these dissolve it, or expel it either through vomiting or purging.

Aristotle: certain animals have much more milk than their young need. And it is suitable material for cheese, especially sheep's and cow's milk. Other milk, however, is not suited for cheese, especially that of an animal having many breasts. Milk is coagulated, however, both by rennet and by fig's milk. For fig's milk is gathered on wool, then that wool is washed with a small amount of milk. Afterward that milk left there is discarded, and when it is mixed in, it coagulates. Milk of much cheese-content, however, is of most food, and the denser it is, the more suited to cheese. The milk of horned animals coagulates, but other milk does not. Milk does not coagulate through cold, but its wateriness is separated from it. What remains, however, becomes thick and dense, but through fire it is thickened. Likewise the milk of an animal lacking upper teeth coagulates. The milk of an animal having teeth in both jaws, however, by no means does, just as neither does its tallow, and its milk is thin and sweet. Camel's milk is the thinnest compared to others. And mare's milk follows it, and then donkey's; cow's milk is very thick. And it is suitable material for cheese; sheep's and cow's milk, and goat's milk too, is good.

Palladius, in the passage above: milk should be coagulated with the rennet of a lamb or kid, or even with the membrane that usually clings to the stomachs of young birds, or with the flowers of the wild thistle, or with fig's milk.

Pliny, book 28: it is most useful for anyone to take his mother's milk; a wet-nurse's is harmful. For these are the infants called 'beestings-fed,' the milk thickened into a cheese-like substance. Colostrum, moreover, is the first spongy thickness of milk after birth. Human milk, of whatever kind, nourishes most; goat's milk next. Whence perhaps the fable says Jupiter was so nourished; the sweetest is from a human, camel's the most effective. It is more easily given back from large animals and bodies. Goat's milk is most suited to the stomach, since goats feed more on foliage than grass. Cow's milk is more medicinal, sheep's sweeter and more nourishing, less useful for the stomach, since it is fattier. All spring milk is more watery than summer's: most approved is that which sticks on the fingernail and does not run off, most harmless when boiled, especially with sea-pebbles. The bowels are most loosened by cow's milk. Whatever is boiled inflates less. It heals grape-like swellings and lichen sores. Useful for all bruises or dislocations, especially of the kidneys, bladder, intestines, throat, lungs. There are examples among those freed from gout or hand-gout by drinking donkey's milk. Physicians have added one more kind of milk to the kinds, which they called 'schiston.' It is made this way: in a new earthen vessel, goat's milk especially is boiled and mixed with fresh fig branches, with as many cups of honey-wine added as there are half-pints of milk. While it boils, so that it may be poured around, a silver cup lowered with cold water is best, so that nothing is poured in. Then, taken off the fire, it separates on cooling and the whey parts from the milk. Some boil down this whey itself, already very potent, to a third part and cool it in the open air. It is drunk most effectively in half-pint doses at intervals, on five healthy days set aside from the usual drinking of it; it is given to epileptics, the melancholic, paralytics with leprosy, elephantiasis, joint diseases. Milk is also poured in against corrosive effects of medicines. And if dysentery burns, boiled with sea-pebbles or with barley gruel. Likewise, against corrosion of the intestines, cow's or sheep's milk is more useful, and fresh is also poured in for dysentery sufferers. Raw, however, on the neck. Likewise for the womb and against serpent bites, for consumptives, against the venoms of cantharides or salamander or 'buprestis' or caterpillars. Specifically cow's milk for those who have drunk hemlock or cicuta or 'dorycnium' or sea-hare; likewise donkey's, against gypsum and white lead and sulfur and quicksilver. Likewise for a hard belly in fever. It is also gargled most usefully for ulcerated throats and is drunk by those regaining strength from weakness, whom they call 'atrophic.' In fever too that lacks headache, it is fitting to give children a half-pint of donkey's milk before food, or if at the end of a meal they feel corrosion. The ancients kept this among their secrets, but if this were not available, they used goat's instead.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: rennet, moreover, as has been said above, is the stomach of an animal, so called because it makes milk coagulate. It is extracted from the animal before it begins to eat grass, and is salted and preserved for the aforesaid use.

Isaac Judaeus: donkey's and mare's milk does not generate thick blood. What, however, is more abundant for cheese, like cow's and sheep's, makes thick blood, though naturally more so cow's. Whatever, however, is tempered in its three substances, like woman's and goat's, generates perfect nourishment and temperament. Whence the ancients chose goat's whey. Milk, with its buttery substance, changes into smokiness and choleric kinds, since butter is naturally the nourishment of heat. The thickness of cheese, however, changes into sourness and putrefaction.

Avicenna, in the second canon: milk is composed of a dissolving element, which is its wateriness, and a binding one, which is its cheese-content. Colostrum, indeed, is of slow digestion and thick humor and slow descent. Honey, however, corrects it, and the body gains from it very much nourishment.
Dioscorides: whey has a purgative power, drawing out the humors of the belly.

Isaac Judaeus: the watery, sharp substance of milk, as has already been said above, cuts and thins thick humors, also washes the inner organs, bites the intestines, and, applied, moves them, expelling swiftly. And so it is loosening to the belly, and the wateriness of milk is praiseworthy in cases where you wish to cleanse gently. Especially if there are putrid and corrupted humors in the inner or outer skin of the body, or sharp melancholic ones from the inflammation of red or blood-related bile. Whichever milk, then, has greater wateriness is more healthful than another and of less harm, as has already been said.

Avicenna, in the passage above: the wateriness of milk is hot, thinning, washing, loosening, and in it there is no biting. Likewise whey fattens those of hot and dry complexion, since with drinking it they are loosened for that reason. It does not fatten them, however, except because it moistens and because it draws out bad humor, and for this reason it corrects nourishment. Likewise it removes eye-films and scars, applied, and sometimes benefits them drunk too. It stimulates mating in bodies of hot complexion. Likewise in whey there is a certain heat, since in it there is a slime acquired first from blood, and part bile; it greatly fattens dogs and nourishes them. Its drink, with cleansing medicines, benefits melancholy and eye-film. The same, fresh, boiled with as much wine as there is of it, in pomegranate rind until consumed, prevents facial spasm. Likewise, by loosening, it expels burnt bile, and its cleansing helps, because of its alkalinity; mixed with honey, however, it becomes more beneficial. It is also drunk against scabies.
Isidore: they call cheese [caseum] as if 'careum,' from the fact that it lacks [careat] whey. For all the whey is drawn off from it, as is shown by weight.

Palladius, in the passage above: cheese should be coagulated in the month of May with pure milk, from which all the whey should be drawn off, so that it is also shown by weight; but when it begins to solidify, it should be placed in a shady or cool spot, and then pressed, weights applied in proportion to the solidity gained, and, once dry and roasted salt sprinkled on, and, once already harder, pressed more vigorously. After several days, once already solid, the little forms should be arranged on wicker frames, so that they do not touch each other. Let it be, moreover, in a closed place, away from winds, so that it keeps its tenderness and richness. The faults of cheese are if it is either dry or full of holes, which happens if it is either pressed too little, or receives too much salt, or is burnt by the heat of the salt. In preparing it fresh, some grind green pine kernels and thus curdle it mixed with milk. Some curdle it with ground and often strained thyme. Whatever flavor you wish, too, you can achieve, by adding whatever seasoning you choose, whether pepper or any other spice.

Isaac Judaeus, book 1: cheese is composed of three substances, one from the milk, another from the rennet, a third from salt. Milk too, as we have said, is composed, namely, of cheese-content, butter-content, and water-content, and, beyond this division, cheese too falls into a threefold division, for it is either fresh and watery, or old and less watery, or in between the moisture of the fresh and the dryness of the old. For rennet, by the power of its sharpness and heat and dryness, dominates in it, by which its moisture is limited. In the fresh, however, it is not so limited. And even if rennet is inseparably present in any cheese, in the fresh it is imperceptible because of the abundance of its moisture.

Isaac Judaeus, in book 3: cheese in general is the worst, burdensome to the stomach, difficult to digest. And so those who use it very often incur colic disease. And stones are generated in their kidneys, but in various ways. Fresh cheese is less hot than the rest and sharp. Whence it is close to cold and moisture, as it were in the first degree, which is because of the moistening effect, containing the wateriness of milk within it, wherefore it is more nourishing than the rest and moistens the belly without any harm to the stomach, especially if it lacks salt. Old and very dry cheese, however, has sharpness and heat evidently because of the salt and the dryness of the rennet. Accordingly it quickly changes into smokiness and choleric humors, which happens in two ways: one is that its oiliness is exposed, because of the lack of its wateriness. The other, because of the sharpness it acquired from rennet and salt. And so it is astringent and to be avoided, since it is not good for nourishment, nor for generating good blood, nor for moistening the belly. Cheese, then, between new and old, midway, becomes praiseworthy according to its closeness to either extreme.

Avicenna, in the passage above: the better cheese is midway between that which stretches like glue and the brittle kind - both indeed are bad - and that deprived of flavor, and inclining to sweetness. That made from sour milk, however, is better than these. The harm of cheese is increased by thinning agents, since they make it penetrate, driving it forward. And the cheese of goats that feed on thinning plants is better than that of goats that eat nothing, and of those on rough terrain. In it there is a cleansing power, and from it a plaster is made for ophthalmia and for the injured edge of the eyelid. It generates stone in the kidneys and bladder, especially moist cheese. But it benefits ulcers of the intestines, especially roasted, and prevents looseness. Boiled in water and given as a drink to nursing mothers, however, it multiplies their milk. It is also said that cheese with mountain thyme is applied as a poultice against venoms. Fresh cheese is cold and moist in the third degree, nourishing and fattening, and is eaten with honey afterward. Fresh, unsalted cheese indeed prevents wounds from swelling, softens the bowels, and its water, by loosening, expels bile. Salted but not old cheese is quicker in digestion and descent. But both salted and unsalted are bad for the stomach. Dioscorides said, however, that fresh is good for the stomach, but this is among the points on which there is disagreement. Old cheese, however, is hot, cleansing, purifying, and, eaten, produces a colic humor. It is good, however, for bad ulcers and recent light wounds. Fresh cheese is stronger in this and prevents their swelling. Likewise old cheese with oil is effective as a plaster on hardness of the joints. It is also effective, according to Galen, for gout and contraction of the limbs, and is also effective for other pains. Old, salted cheese is hot and dry, and reduces swelling and pustules. Salted but not old cheese is between the two.

Dioscorides: [on the cheese of] buffalo, dogs. Green cheese without salt is good for the stomach: it makes rich humors, fills out flesh, softens the belly. Boiled and roasted, however, it binds the belly, heals swellings of the eyes, removes bruises. Salted, however, it makes fat creatures lean. It is bad for the stomach, since it causes burning, especially buffalo cheese, which, however, coagulated, heals all swellings when applied, especially to the eyes. Goat cheese binds, and buffalo too, but causes more burning, since it is drier. Sheep cheese nourishes more and binds the belly less, since it is fatty. Likewise salted cheese softens the belly, but old binds it, while cheese-water fattens dogs.
Pliny: cheese is not made from double-toothed animals, since their milk does not curdle.

Pliny, book 28, in the same: Sestius reports the same effects for mare's cheese as for cow's. Useful for the stomach are those that are not salted, that is, fresh. Old ones stop the bowels and reduce the body, more useful for the stomach. In general, salted ones reduce the body; soft ones nourish. Fresh cheese with honey corrects bruises. The soft kind stops the bowels. It calms colic when boiled in harsh wine as small cakes. And again roasted in a pan with honey - what they call 'saprum' - which, ground with salt and dried sorb-apples in wine, drunk, heals celiac sufferers. For genital carbuncles, goat cheese ground and applied. Likewise sour, with oxymel.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: Galen's statement that cheese in general is bad should be understood of the pure cheese substance. For of the threefold substance of milk, whey indeed is good, and butter better. Cheese, however, is most perfect. And so cheese close to milk, thick and buttery, is good, and healthful for the healthy; whence Pliny says Zoroaster lived on cheese alone in the desert for twenty years, so temperately that he felt the pain of no illness.
Isaac Judaeus: butter, as has been said, is naturally the nourishment of heat, and is a soft, oily, buttery substance.

Isaac Judaeus, in book 3: the nature of butter, however, is like that of fat, which is mixed with flesh and bones, and so it is suited to wounds of the lung, chest, and diaphragm. For it cleanses and strains and brings wounds to maturity. It also gives relief to infants' gums aching from teething. If mixed with honey and given as a drink, it works against poison. And habitually taken, it harms the stomach, since it soothes or softens its villi and roughness.

Avicenna, in the passage above: butter is hot and moist in the first degree, maturing, dissolving, softening, and its dissolving power works in tender or medium, not hard, bodies. Its smoke is drying and easily astringent, and it is calming for pains from matter effused into the members. The body and belly are anointed with it, and it nourishes and fattens. It benefits ulcers of the sinews and fills and purges ulcers. It also benefits a cold, dry cough, especially with almonds and sugar. Likewise for pleurisy and pneumonia. And it makes coughing up easy and matures it, but prevents coughing up blood. And it benefits vomiting of blood and discharge, when licked with honey. Likewise medicines for the swellings of the brain's coverings, and abscesses of the roots of the ears and nostrils and mouth and gums, and for the throat, are drunk with it. The gums of infants' flesh, too, are anointed with it, and the coming of teeth is made easier. Likewise it is loosening; much use of it relieves. From it too an enema is made for hot, hard swellings in the intestines and womb, and it is put into medicines for wounds of the bladder's opening. It resists venoms, and especially a viper's bite is anointed with it.
Dioscorides: [on] serpents' eggs, in oil. [Fragmentary heading in the source.]

Pliny: from milk too is made butter, the most praised food of barbarous peoples, and one that distinguishes the rich from the common people, mostly from cow's milk, whence its name. The richest is made from sheep's and from goat's, but in winter from warmed milk, in summer only pressed out, by frequent shaking in long vessels with a narrow opening, which take in air beneath the mouth itself, otherwise tied shut. A little water is added so that it sours. What congeals most floats on top, and this, taken out with salt added, they call 'oxygala.' The rest they boil down in pots. There, what floats on top is butter, oily by nature, which rejects rankness the more, and this is judged superior: it is mixed into many compounds when aged. Its nature is to bind, soften, fill, and purge. Oxygala is also made another way, sour milk added to fresh, which, while it sours, is most useful for the stomach.

div.head: DE UNIVERSALI PROPRIETATE LACTIS SECUNDUM MEDICINAM

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the passage above: milk, indeed, is nourishment, and equalizes the humors, strengthens the body, and cleanses. Likewise milk is close to digestion, since it is generated in blood, which is at the summit of digestion, upon which a certain further digestion comes, although it is from a member that inclines toward cold. For the breast is not nourished by it unless it occurs in the disposition of food that needs much digestion. But when good heat dominates in it, it returns quickly to the nature of equal blood; because of its own inclination, however, toward cold, it harms the phlegmatic, since their heat converts it to blood as it should. It suits the mature, however, more than the young of hot complexion, since in them it turns to bile. For the old, however, it benefits, since it moistens and removes the itching that is proper to them. But it should be helped toward digestion with honey. Milk drunk with honey cleanses inner ulcers of thick humors, and matures and washes them. And it is of good chyme, and also makes blood abundant. All milk, however, causes blockages, especially in the liver, except the milk of nursing camels and the like, because of the scarcity of its cheese-content and the cleansing of its wateriness. It harms those having a flux of blood, however, and is not good for the inner organs. In its substance, indeed, it is of quick conversion, and especially toward heat, nor is anything more harmful to the body than bad milk. Much use of it generates lice. But it cleanses foul scars on the skin, applied, and produces good color, drunk. Often, however, it causes filth to occur. It also harms the teeth, and hollows and consumes them, especially when they are of cold complexion; it loosens the gum, and also causes dimness of sight. Nevertheless, when milked into the eye, it benefits ophthalmia and roughness. It is also more suited to the chest than the head and stomach. It heals ulcers of the lung and wasting. And, gargled, it benefits suffocation and quinsy and swellings of the uvula and tonsils. It harms, however, those with a moist heart tremor. It also harms those with spleen and liver ailments and those needing a thinning regimen, except the milk of nursing camels, for this does not harm, but helps. Likewise milk causes stone to occur. And boiled until its wateriness is consumed, it binds the belly and retains the flux of blood within. All thick milk, moreover, stimulates colic and generates stone, especially colostrum. Likewise milk stimulates mating, so much so that even sour milk, and the water of milk, in bodies of hot complexion, does this by moistening and inflating, and often softens the belly. Boiled, however, with quenched coals in it and heated with fired stones and iron plates, it doubtless binds the belly. Likewise milk benefits the scraping of the intestines and the drinking of deadly medicines. It is, moreover, a treatment for dry forgetfulness and sadness and alienation. Often too those who suffer bad swellings and carbuncles and scabies and itching are healed by drinking milk, when there is nothing in their complexions that would corrupt it and turn it to bile. It harms, however, those with inner swellings. Freshly milked, thick milk often causes fevers to occur.

div.head: DE DIVERSITATE LACTIS SECUNDUM DIFFERENTIAM ANIMALIUM

cit.quote: Avicenna, in the passage above: milk differs, moreover, according to the species of animals and according to age, as whether it is small, large, or medium. And according to form, as whether it is of smooth or hard flesh, thin or fat, of white color or another. For all milk of a white animal is called weaker, and is of quicker descent. And cow's milk indeed has much butter-content. But the milk of camels near giving birth has less cheese-content and is very thin. Likewise the milk of donkeys and mares is thin. Goat's milk, however, is tempered. Sheep's, however, thick and fatty. And so cheese-content in camel's milk is scanty, then in mare's, then in donkey's, and for this reason it rarely curdles in the stomach and upper parts of the belly more than other milk. And indeed the milk of any animal whose pregnancy is longer, when compared with a woman's pregnancy, is bad. Wherefore that which is closest is proportional, like cow's. And just as spring milk is watery compared to summer's, so too the milk of an animal whose pasture is riverbank or muddy land. For spring plants are watery, compared to summer plants, and the more summer approaches autumn, the thicker milk becomes. And that which is in the middle of summer is best. In it, however, there is fear that heat may convert it after it is drunk; this, however, is not feared in spring. Loosening to the belly, properly, are mare's, camel's, and donkey's milk, then cow's, after that goat's, and the more its wateriness diminishes, the less loosening it becomes.

Isaac Judaeus: of all milk, the most praised is the thinnest, like woman's, second donkey's, then goat's. Donkey's, however, is so close to it in thinness. The thickest, and most nourishing, is cow's, then pig's. Pig's milk, however, has more cheese-content than cow's, and more watery than pig's is camel's, then horse's and donkey's. More tempered, and more moderate in its three substances, is woman's, second goat's. For all milk imitates the nature and complexion of the animal to which it belongs. If, then, it is from a thick animal, it will be thick. If from a thin one, thin. As Galen says, however, pig's milk is heavier in smell than cow's, and so more phlegmatic.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the kinds of medicinal milk, according to Avicenna, are cow's, sheep's, goat's, camel's, mare's, donkey's, dog's, and woman's. Of nearly all of these, mention has already been made above, each in its fitting place.

Pliny: for a woman, milk before the seventh month is useless. From that month, in which birth is viable, it is healthful, and in most it flows from the whole breast and even into the hollow of the armpits. Camel's milk is milked so that it does not thicken again; it is thought most pleasant mixed with three parts water. The cow before calving has none. From the first milking after birth, colostrum is always made, unless water is mixed in, in the manner of pumice-stones it congeals hard. Pregnant donkeys lactate continuously. When their foal has rich pasture, tasting the mother's milk two days after birth is fatal. This kind of illness is called 'colostration.' The thinnest milk is camel's, then mare's, thickest donkey's, so that it is used in place of rennet. It is also thought to contribute something to whiteness in women's skin. All milk, boiled by fire, thickens with moisture. Cow's milk is more productive of cheese than goat's, from the same measure, by almost half again as much. Those with more than four teats are useless for cheese, and those with two are better.

Aristotle, in the book on life and death: some animals are of longer life, some of shorter. Fire and water, and things close to these, are the cause of generation and corruption. For whatever things are composed share the nature of that from which they are; animals, then, are corrupted since they are subject to contraries. For it happens that a thing is corrupted only by its contrary. It is impossible, however, for that which has matter not to have a contrary present in it. For as soon as potentiality is present, a contrary is possible for matter. For this reason man and the elephant are of longer life among animals. And likewise, larger creatures, as is more often said, are of longer life than smaller ones. It should be understood, however, that an animal is naturally hot and moist, and this is youth. Old age, however, is cold and also dry, and moribund. Whence the moisture must not be easily, that is, readily, dryable, but rich. Nor again should it be a small amount of moisture, since a small amount of moisture is easily dried out. And so large animals and plants live longer. For it is reasonable that larger creatures have more moisture. There are, moreover, two causes of longer life, namely quality and quantity, that is, heat and moisture, and their amount. In certain creatures, indeed, there is heat and richness, which together produces both not drying quickly and not cooling quickly. Such a creature is destroyed, however, either by illness or by nature or even by diet or even by age. It is fitting, then, that heat and moisture not be excessive, for excess is contrary to nature and destructive. Whence too those with excessive and abundant seed age quickly. Further, whatever tires the males quickly ages them quickly. For labor dries, and old age is naturally dry. But in man, males live longer than females, since the male is hotter than the female, for the same reason too that creatures in hot places are of longer life than those in cold ones. And since seed is an excess, the mule is of longer life than the horse and donkey, from which it comes, just as females live longer than males; so it happens with males, while sparrows are of shorter life than females. Those, however, that receive nourishment, like plants and animals, are corrupted, for they consume themselves. For just as a great flame burns and consumes a small one when taking it in as fuel, so too physical, that is natural, heat is first digestive, and its digestion consumes the matter in which it is. Water creatures are of shorter life than those walking on feet, since they are moist and watery, and such a thing is quickly corrupted, since it is cold and easily condensed; and also a blood-lacking animal, for the same reason, is quickly corrupted. Bees, however, are of longer life than other larger animals.

Aristotle: the elephant lives two hundred years, and perhaps three hundred. The horse, however, lives up to thirty or thirty-five years, but the mare only up to eleven. The male ox lives fifteen years, but castrated, twenty. The camel lives thirty years and more. The dog up to fourteen. The pig up to fifteen. The sheep in Ethiopia lives nearly fourteen years. The goat, however, eleven. The dolphin lives a hundred twenty years or more, which is proven when one, caught, has its tail cut off and is released, and is thus found again after a long time. The peacock lives twenty-five years. The dove and turtledove fifteen. Man, however, lives longer than all animals except the elephant. Man's longevity, moreover, is only because his complexion resembles the surrounding air. An infant born before seven months does not live at all; born in the eighth, it perhaps lives, but for the most part dies. In the bodies of the dead, the nature of the great veins does not appear, since they contract suddenly at the exit of blood. Hair, indeed, is harder after death, and the same happens with claws.

div.head: QUA ANIMALIA IN QUIBUS REGIONIBUS NON SUNT

cit.quote: Pliny: this too is remarkable, that nature has not only given animals to some lands and not others, but in the very same region has denied certain creatures to certain places. In the Messenian forest of Italy, dormice are found only in one part. In Lycia, gazelles do not cross the mountains bordering Syria, nor do wild asses cross the mountain that divides Cappadocia from Lycia. At the Hellespont, stags do not travel into foreign territory, and around Arginusa they do not go beyond Mount Elaphus, even with their ears split on that mountain. On the island of Pordoselene, weasels do not cross into the neighboring territory; in Boeotia, those brought to Leucadia flee that very soil. Nearby, in Orchomenus, moles undermine whole fields, whose skins we have seen made into bedroom coverlets. So true is it that not even religious scruple keeps delights away from portents. On Ithaca, hares brought there die, right at the shore itself. On Ebusus, rabbits swarm on the shores; near Spain and the Balearic Islands, frogs on Cyrene were mute. Once brought in from the mainland, their vocal kind persists there. In Italy, shrew-mice have a venomous bite. The region of Italy beyond the Apennines has none of these. On Mount Olympus in Macedonia there are no wolves, nor on the island of Crete. There indeed neither foxes nor bears, nor any harmful animal at all, except the phalangium spider. In Africa there are neither boars nor stags nor roe-deer nor bears. Now indeed, certain animals harmless to natives kill newcomers. As serpents spare people at Myrinthus, whom the earth is reported to have produced. For in Syria, snakes around the banks of the Euphrates especially, while sleeping, do not touch the Syrians. Or even if trodden on, they bite without ill effect being felt. But others, hostile to people of any other nation, kill them eagerly and with torment. For which reason the Syrians do not kill them. On the contrary, however, on Mount Aletenius in Caria, Aristotle reports that visitors are not harmed by scorpions, but natives are killed.
Solinus: the Scenite Arabs, who dwell in tents of goat-hair, entirely abstain from pork. Indeed, if this kind of animal is brought there, it dies at once. India alone raises the parrot.

Isidore: this too, among fish, is not thought to exist without a certain gift of nature, that each kind of them has dwellings prescribed to it, which none of its kind exceeds, none intrudes upon another's. For this kind of fish is nourished and born in this bay of the sea, and that one in another. Finally, you will not find mixed kinds of fish, but what abounds here is lacking elsewhere. And that bay of the sea nourishes gray mullet, that one sea-bass, and that one rock-lobsters.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: animals also differ according to the places they inhabit, as pigs that stay in hot places have black hair, hard and curling. Those in cold places, however, have flat and soft hair, hanging down; so too with wool in sheep.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: let this suffice concerning the nature of animals, in general and in particular.
